Editors’ note: We decided to copy and issue afresh the memoir written by WWD because of its intrinsic interest as a family memoir for his grandchildren and their children. There was also a practical reason because there were only four or perhaps five original copies, and much of it had been reproduced by photocopier. As a result, the print had begun to fade and in due course would become unreadable. We have left the text mostly exactly as written, including the slightly idiosyncratic capitalisation of certain words, correcting only the occasional spelling and punctuation where it is not clear and italicising the names of ships, as is normal practice these days. We have however broken up some of the long paragraphs and added photographs as these both enliven the text and help to record the context. We are grateful to Mary Rawstorne for lending us her father’s photographs. Where photos do not belong to the family, this is noted in each case. We thank Paul Hitching for rephotographing some of the photos. We have also added the occasional footnote and editorial note. The memoir records a naval career of some significance, and it is worth referencing a minimum of key works particularly on events of wider historic interest. The two major authorities used are: N.A.M. Rodger, The Price of Victory: A Naval History of Britain 1815-1945, Allen Lane, 2024 ODNB Oxford Dictionary of National Biography Rodger’s recent completion of his three-volume history of the Royal Navy is an essential companion and reference work on naval history, and worth reading before exploring works on particular topics. The ODNB is an excellent biographical source on people of note, in which WWD himself appears, and where those mentioned in the text are in the ODNB, this is noted. It is available online through any major public library or university library. Where names of places have changed, we have added the current designation. No index has been made, but WWD made a brief list of contents at the beginning of each of the eight original ‘volumes’ which is helpful guiding the reader to a particular year or ship in which WWD served. There is also a useful chronology of WWD’s naval appointments. WWD’s naval papers were donated to Churchill College, Cambridge, and may be examined there. Finally our most grateful thanks to Keith Hodgson for his generosity and time in laying out the text for print. Sophie Forgan and Johnnie Davis 2026 iii

1. Introduction March 1968 My Children It may well be that I am leaving it rather late to write a story of my life. Nevertheless, odd bits here and there may be of interest to my family, and anyway it is pleasant to try to recapture incidents of interest in one’s life. So, you who read this may feel that it was probably due to a measure of selfish egoism which prompted me to take pen to paper. Therefore, there can be no possible duty for you in having to read this! I hope, and believe, what I say and such comments as are made are reasonably near the truth. However, one knows only too well memory does play one tricks, and however carefully one tries to recapture the course of events which are long past, every now and again one finds oneself believing what one wanted to believe, rather than what actually happened! Much of this is very trivial and quite probably of little or no interest even to those who read it. Nevertheless, it may help to build up the background of conditions in which I saw, lived and judged events. Events described will be mainly from my own papers and from my own memory and no attempt has been made to document carefully all evidence on the subject. So from the historian’s point view, these jottings must be regarded more as transient impressions of events rather than a carefully analysed essay, fully documented, on a particular event or series of events. One way and another I have, I suppose read a good number of books, official and otherwise, some accurate and some misleading, about the events described. It has been my good fortune to take a very small and insignificant part in some of the crucial events of this century, and it has also been my added good fortune to know, meet, listen to and see some of the men, great and small, whom destiny called on to play important parts. As far as memory serves, I will try to record my impressions at the time and maybe add further comment in the light of after knowledge, but again it is not easy to differentiate between one’s thoughts at the time and the judgement one formed later, in the light of the later events. My remarks about personalities are, I hope, reasonable and certainly seem to me to be fair comment, but again, they relate to certain events and must never be regarded in the context of an overall judgement. For instance, I saw a fair amount of Winston Churchill, both during and after the last War, but it is early days yet for his place in history to be assessed, and it would be the grossest of impertinence for me to attempt any overall assessment. Should any of what is said be considered of interest for publication, I hope the foregoing disclaimer will be taken into account. Critical remarks which are merited, and indeed, sometimes desirable, should, I believe, as a very general rule, not be published until after the person’s death. I have been, as you will read, exceedingly fortunate – far more so than my deserts and far more so than many good friends. A tolerably retentive memory, coupled with good health, has helped to give me much joy and appreciation of what life has to offer. This book starts with a brief essay on my father and mother, to whom I owe much. William Davis 20 March 1968 v

Walter Stewart Davis My father was born on 23rd August 1865 at Boulogne, where his family were living. His parents were fond of France, and spent some time there, and at Ross in Herefordshire, before moving into the family home at Wellclose, Brockworth in 1870. Father was married to Georgina Ross on 5th August 1897 at Slough by the Rev. Elliott, who later became the Bishop of Buckingham. He died at his home in Longhope on 6th January 1946 in his 81st year and was buried at Huntley with my mother who had died in 1925. These three events cover in the briefest outline the span of his life. It is never easy to write about a father, especially when, because of circumstances, there were considerable periods when I did not see him, particularly in my boyhood days. I only saw him for one holiday between the ages of 10 and 17. He was serving in India, and I was at school in England and later in the Navy towards the end of World War I. Although my father was a most regular and imaginative letter writer one’s actual recollections and impressions, whilst still a boy, were inevitably rather fragmentary. Furthermore, this little note about him is being written in his old home, no less than 22 years to the day on, and after, which he died. Nevertheless, after his return to England in 1919 one did see as much of him as service in the Navy permits, and due to having a proportion of home service appointments this amounted to quite a lot. He often talked of his life in India and Persia and his experiences in these and other countries and I believe one got to know and really appreciate him. You have only to read the account of his life started in 1916, and written for his children, to see the man he was. Written in his fine and well-formed handwriting in a pleasant and lively style, the whole story drawn vividly, a picture of his life – what he thought and did at the time, and on reflection how he judged his actions. He had a singleness of purpose combined with an honesty of thought not alas sufficiently often met nowadays. His standards were high, and in his actions and thoughts he never tolerated humbug, insincerity or dishonesty and not infrequently made this plain. He could be most outspoken when he encountered in folk a priggishness or dishonest and selfish outlook. But what fun he was! Gifted with a sense of humour he loved practical jokes and was good company. Hot tempered at times, especially if he sensed an injustice, he never harboured any malice and storms soon passed and were forgotten. A modest and clever man. If his father had not been forced to take him away from his private school, “Tuck’s” in Hertfordshire, because of gross bullying by the Headmaster of the time, who lived in the traditions of Dotheboys Hall, he would in all probability have got a scholarship at Eton. Fond of the classics, with a real love and appreciation of Greek and Latin, he was considered up to scholarship standard for New College, Oxford, to which he was going if family finances had not made it necessary for him to take up his uncle’s (Sir John Warson) offer of giving him a start in India. A good Oriental linguist and well versed in the literature of languages with which he was acquainted, he could speak, read and write Hindi, Persian and Arabic, though he regarded himself as very halting in the last named. In addition he spoke Pushtoo [Pashto] fluently and effectively and other dialects used in the North West Frontier Province of India. Winston Churchill, who shared a tent with him in the Malakand Campaign, refers to father in his 1

book and recounts how father gave the General in Command warning of the big attack on us at Nawagai, in which we decisively defeated the enemy. He read quite widely, though his tastes in reading were perhaps more to the traditional and orthodox rather than the avant garde. A good memory and quite an adequate public speaker, though apart from the time when he was Conservative Candidate for the Forest of Dean in 1928 and 1929, he never really practised, or liked, public speaking. A training in the legal aspects of administration in India helped him to become a sound and respected Justice of the Peace for 15 years in Gloucestershire. A fine-looking man; thin, lean, wiry and very tough, and about 5ft.10ins. in height. He held himself splendidly and, right up to his death, had a distinctive and purposeful way of walking, which was typical of him. Though fair haired and fair skinned he had unusually bright brown eyes which would flash with enjoyment and animation when in company. His eyes were one of the most distinctive features about him, for when sad and lonely, they would, by their dullness, betray his feelings. As a boy he rowed for Westminster, and later became a very good shot with a gun, being counted at one time as one of the best shots in India. A steady rifle shot and practised and fearless horseman.1 He came near to winning the Kadir Cup for pigsticking in India. Very fond of hunting, which he did whenever his leaves coincided with the hunting season, and also a more than average skilful fisherman. Most forms of sport appealed to him and he enjoyed such games as tennis and golf as a second choice when sport was not available. Also, a keen gardener, who was seldom happier than when working in the garden; possibly budding and grafting, at which he had some skill. He shared this love with my mother, who helped him to do much for the gardens of the many houses and bungalows which they occupied in India. He cherished his garden at home and loved to work in it in company with his Labrador dogs who always accompanied him and gave him companionship. Blessed with splendid health, he survived two attacks of Typhoid Fever in India and showed little of the infirmities of old age until a few months before his death. He conformed to the best traditions of the English gentleman and sportsman. There were not many contradictions in father’s character. He was an impulsive man; not always very perceptive and sometimes untactful, but those who came to know and respect him realised soon that no harm was meant. On the other hand, some clever and able men whose minds and methods were, at times, tortuous, did Kurram Valley 1896; ‘Jurgas [assembly of not like him and clearly were frightened he might blurt out the truth too forcibly! in which father was absolutely right in refusing to condemn or water down an untruth, but which resulted in his career being greatly harmed. His great services among the wild, fanatical and, at times, bloodthirsty tribesmen of the North West frontier province of India, where, with a company of Sepoys, he successfully administered a province half the size of Wales, were never recognised. With a turn of the wheel of luck father might well have become one of the great frontier administrators, whose names are still a legend, and whose judgements often still hold in that part of Pakistan, as it now is. Father’s understanding and leadership of Oriental people was confirmed only recently when my son Hugh visited Kurwai State in central India, which father rescued from intrigues and put on its feet over 50 years ago. Hugh met a number of men who remembered, greatly loved and respected his grandfather, and told him many anecdotes redounding to his wisdom and understanding of Indians. Father’s name will long be loved and revered in that part of India. The full story of his life is told in his diaries. He went to India just after his 18th birthday in 1883 and finally left it in 1919. In these 36 years he served in many parts of India, but the bulk of his service was spent with the turbulent people of the North West Frontier Province. He served in the Persian Gulf at the beginning of the century and visited many of the Sheikhs, with whom we had, or were negotiating, treaties of friendship. He played a part in concluding our first treaty with the Sheikh of Kuwait which has stood us, and him, in good stead more than once up to the present day. The last 8 years of his service were spent at Bhopal, where his influence and knowledge of the Mohammedan rulers and Hindu people of that, and other, adjacent states, proved to be of much value to the Government of India. The following anecdote illustrates his robust and practical method of dealing with day-to-day One of Father’s Bears problems which made such an appeal to the ordinary Indian. The residency of Bhopal State was at Sehore, and the Court House was adjacent to the Residency. One very hot afternoon, just before the Monsoon broke, Father was trying one of those interminable cases in regard to the ownership of some minute piece of land. Both sides were represented by Vakils (lawyers) who not only were very long-winded – as are some barristers of all nations – but also kept wandering completely off the point and raising utterly irrelevant issues. One of the Vakils was particularly to blame in this respect and had frequently been warned to stick to the point. On his raising yet another irrelevant issue Father told his orderly to release the two tame bears who lived in a big cage on the verandah of the Residency. These bears were devoted to Father, as indeed he was to them, and whenever loose they would seek his company. Suddenly there was a slight commotion in the back of the Court as the two bears entered. The Vakil, who was still addressing the Court, looked round in some alarm and immediately said “I have nothing more to submit your Worship” and sat down. This allowed Father time to sum up, give judgement and take the bears for their evening walk. 3

Retiring from India in 1919, he bought our present home in Longhope in 1921 where he lived, with some short breaks, until his death in 1946. He threw himself, as I shall later relate, into the many country activities which look for support and inspiration from those who, for want of a better phrase, endeavour to live up to the traditions of a Country Gentleman. My father was a hardworking man with an abundance of energy and physical toughness to be envied in our age. We all used to think he kept his home cold and draughty, yet he seemed to thrive on this. Very modest in his tastes for food and drink, he was far from being an ascetic, and thoroughly enjoyed a good dinner. Generous and unselfish to a degree, he never seemed really interested in his own personal needs and comforts. Not given to self-pity, and though absolutely devoted to my mother, he lived on alone for 21 years after her death purposefully, energetically and usefully. In this he was greatly helped by my sister Jane, whose home was only 3 miles distant at Huntley, and who, from her abundant warmth of heart and spirit, gave him that comfort and encouragement which made the last two decades of his life a time of joy and service to his fellow men. My brother Buddie, who also for times lived at Coglan, provided him with that company for which he so longed. Father liked his fellow men and always had a cheerful greeting for any acquaintance he met, but he did not like those he would class as “slackers” and not infrequently made them aware of his feelings. The many people who came to see him in his home, to talk over their problems and difficulties, never went away empty handed, and found in him there was a person who, without prejudice, would give sound and fair advice. He played a useful, and at times, a leading part in many local activities – British Legion, S.S.A.F.A., Sports Club and activities, Junior Imperial League, Boy Scouts etc., etc., and not least the many local church activities, for Father was very much a practising Christian, who was regular in his devotions and believed in practising what you preached. In the second World War he immediately volunteered at the age of 74 and became the Head Village Air Raid Warden. He also became general counsellor and adviser to all and sundry on how to live and follow the innumerable War time restrictions. In fact, his home, at one time, almost became the Village Information Bureau. In spite of his age, he made light of his work, which might well have tested a man 20 years younger than him. A devout Christian all his life he never had any doubts and would be regarded as a middle of the road Christian. He disliked equally extreme Low church and very High church usage and practice. He found much comfort and support throughout his life in his unquestioning belief in God and I do not doubt that the comfort he got from his belief and indeed his companionship with God helped him much in the years following my Mother’s death. Indeed, during their 28 years of married life they both had that unquestioning bond of union in their belief in God and his teaching. How difficult to sum up, even from the viewpoint of 22 years after his death. An upright, clever and selfless man, who was very loveable. By reason of his forthrightness, he may not always have been wise in his personal relationships, but he commanded the abiding regard of those who served him. It is true he could be rather blind and perhaps not in all cases very 4

perceptive, but with some people he showed deep and profound understanding. When one thinks of the changes from his youth and his old age, it is not surprising he found it difficult to adapt himself to the customs ruling in his old age. He was, for instance, quite one the worst motor drivers I have ever known, and yet he was completely oblivious of this fact! He was liberal and farseeing in his political views and always foresaw the time when India would be given back to the Indians to rule and administer. He never forgot Warren Hastings’ promise to this effect, and often said that the British duty was to lay a framework of justice, straight dealing and honourable relationships upon which the Indians must build their future. He hoped for a United India but feared partition. A letter he wrote to Winston Churchill in 1931, and quoted in his diaries, shows how right he was and how wrong Winston was! The latter would, I know, be the first to admit this. Perhaps they are continuing their discussions above the stars. I suppose one would say Father was an emotional and impulsive man, and often found his emotions and reason battling with each other. This would perhaps account for the fact that some of his judgements of men and events were uncertain, but then whose judgements are not! We were lucky to have a father like him, and I am in no doubt when he went to see his Maker he could say, from the fullness of his heart, that in so far as he was able he left this world, if only by example of uprightness and honesty, a better place than when he entered it. But again, if you want to meet him, read his account of his life. William Davis, 6th January 1968 5

Georgina Jessie Chisholm Davis My mother was born on 2nd November 1870 at Lahore, where her father and mother were living. Her father was closely concerned with the building and running of railways in and around the North West Frontier Province of India and lived at Lahore, where his headquarters were located. There is a good extract in Debrett’s Companionage on page 755 for 1887 of David Ross, C.I.E., which gives the outline of his career and which is also enclosed in the foresheet of one of his books “The Land of the Five Rivers and Sindh”.2 My mother married father at Slough on 5th August 1897 and died in a London Nursing Home on 28th September 1925, being buried in the Parish churchyard at Huntley, Gloucestershire, which is a few miles from our home at Longhope, and a few hundred yards from where her daughter, and my sister, Jane Ackers then lived. My Grandfather was a fine Scottish railway engineer, who, having learnt the elements of his profession in Scotland, went out to India in 1862 at the age of 25 and did some splendid work building not only parts of the North West Frontier Province railway, but also in developing other railways in India. He was awarded the C.I.E. in 1881, a rare honour to be given to one who was not in the Government Administrative or Military Services. He retired, probably about 1887, and lived first at Worlingworth in Suffolk, where he came to know well my father’s ‘French’ relations and whose elder daughter, my aunt, Wilna, married Edward French, later Sir Edward French, C.I.E., etc., the Chief Commissioner of Police in Punjaub [Punjab]. Grandfather later moved to Perth and lived at 10, Athole Street, and was buried there in 1891. David Ross was one of the Ross of Balnagowan Chieftains of the Ross Clan, who trace their ancestry back for many centuries! His crest and coat-of-arms is that of the Ross of Balnagowan. My grandfather married Isabella Calder Bremner of Inverness in 1863, who later died at Lahore in 1885, when my mother was only 14 years old. I have always understood she died from one of the many illnesses which people who lived in India, in those days, contracted. There are two photos taken I believe in about 1882 of my grandfather and grandmother. They show him to be a fine looking full bearded man with an obvious twinkle in his eye, and my grandmother perhaps a little sad and thoughtful, as well she might be, at the problems of bringing up children in India. Grandfather was a clever man, a witty conversationalist and an author of a number of books. Mother had, in a way, rather a sad upbringing. Her parents, I have always heard, lost the boys who were born to them and in fact the only surviving ones were my Aunt Wilna (later Lady French) and my mother who was the youngest. As a result of these losses my mother was sent home to England to live at about the age of 7 and saw little of her mother before she died when at the age of 46 in 1885 at Lahore. India was an unhealthy place for children – Typhoid, Cholera, Plague and many other epidemics cut short the lives of many children and indeed grown-ups as well. Mother, though sensitive and reserved and never given to self-pity, did talk with affection of 2 Debrett's Peerage, Baronetage, Knightage, and Companionage, London, 1887; David Ross, The Land of the Five Rivers and Sindh, London, 1883. CIE stands for Companion of the Indian Empire, an Order founded by Queen Victoria in 1878. 6

her father and mother and said she hoped we would see more of our parents than she did. She was a companion to her father at various times in the short time between his retirement from India and his death in Scotland. It was old Miss Taylor, or “Grandmudge” as we used to call her, who looked after my mother in England, and in a sense acted almost as her guardian until she married. Miss Taylor was a great character. She was, my mother always said, an excellent teacher and most cultured woman. She taught my mother and, at one time, ran a girls school in Dartmouth Row at Blackheath. Miss Taylor was one of those Victorian women who set great store by education and worked ceaselessly all her life. She died within a year of my mother when well past 90. It was a great pleasure to mother that she was able to make provision for Grandmudge’s old age, for these were the years before women could even earn pensions! My last recollection of Miss Taylor must have been in 1921 when I went to see her at Swindon, where she was living with some people who worked at the old G.W.R [Great Western Railway] works. We had an animated discussion about Charles Dickens and I remember her so well saying, with reference to some character in one of his books, “Yes I told Mr. Dickens he had drawn this character wrong. No person would have acted quite as described!” She was a great character and influence on my mother’s life. Mother, like her own mother, was far from strong as a girl, and though she enjoyed the country and open air, it was never thought she would be strong enough to marry. Though she was only taught a little Latin, my mother had a considerable love and appreciation for classical art and literature. She could, of course, speak French well, and some Italian. She had no difficulty in mastering Hindustani and the various Indian dialects with which she met in India. She was well read, a thoroughly competent pianist, which she much enjoyed, and a watercolour painter of more than average standard. She spent the early part of her life with Miss Taylor, travelled a bit in France and visited her married sister, Wilna French, in India, where I think she may first have met my father. Or, alternatively, when she was staying with her father at Worlingworth she may have met him staying at the Rectory with his French cousins, who were numerous and of about his own age. Mother was very modest about her accomplishments and was far, far more interested in the well-being of my father and us children than anything else. It was a great achievement bringing her three children up without losing one or two in India – in fact this achievement in those days was unusual. At the time I was the only baby to survive the hot weather in the Persian Gulf and the only mark I have are some scars on my forehead which were the legacy of what was known as Persian Gulf Sores! The secret of her success was unremitting care in all matters of hygiene. She always boiled our milk and personally supervised the cooking of what we were given to eat the whole time her children were in the tropics. But I have not yet described her! Small, she must have been about 5ft. 2 ins., and slight in build, a lovely complexion with dark brown eyes and brown hair. But there was something very charming, if perhaps distant and reserved, in her expression; but her face would light up when she saw us after a longish absence! Attractive looking, yet behind it all there was a reserved dignity which quite automatically commanded the respect and regard of all with whom she came into contact. 7

Have a look at some of her sketches and you will see the delicacy and fastidiousness, which was so much part of her nature. But she could be forthright, and, like my father, abhorred humbug, cant and hypocrisy. A thoroughly practical and even approach to the problems of life, she provided some of the balance emotionally, which at times my father, with his warm temper, lacked. Her religion meant a great deal to her - she was devout and unobtrusively practised the simple Christian virtues which never lose their value. She read fairly extensively on religious subjects and once, when under great stress, due to pain, said there was much to be said for the Roman Catholic doctrine. She had tremendous determination, but not great physical strength – for one reason and another – possibly stone and other causes – she was very nearly constantly in pain, and acute Arthritis for the last 8 years of her life added to this. She took latterly, when in pain, a rather serious and sombre view of life and obviously envied the tremendous vitality and good health of my father, yet she never entirely lost her sense of humour. Never robust she found the long rides on horseback in India very tiring and her tastes for food had to be regulated by an uncertain digestion. But she liked travelling and seeing where pictures and beautiful scenery and buildings were evident. Her judgement was always to the point and not swayed by emotion, and she had, I found later, an uncanny instinct for summing up people. Unlike my father, she was not gregarious, and preferred the company of a few chosen friends rather than a host of acquaintances. Always at hand to give good counsel in her quiet, perhaps shy, and friendly way, she had a gift for friendship, as many of the women in India and especially Bhopal, came to know. How pleased she would be to see how emancipated many of them have become! Much to her surprise she was awarded the M.B.E. for her War work in India, which was concerned with Red Cross and other activities as well as looking after the dependents of WWD’s parents in their Simla garden Indians serving overseas. My mother had a thoroughly good and orderly brain, with a reliable memory, which she used to good effect in ordering her affairs. But yet right up to the last few years of her life she was always ready for adventure, and cheerfully – at least so I thought – rode on the pillion of a racing motor bicycle I had! Like my father she was very fond of animals and was seldom without a pet. Her sudden death – though not entirely unexpected – nevertheless made a tremendous gap in our lives. For it was then we realised fully what a warm hearted, unselfish, and above all, wise friend and companion we had lost, and we forgot what at times young people regardeed as her rather pessimistic outlook on life in her last few years. What little success one has ever been able to achieve is, in no small measure, due to my mother’s influence, who set us a high standard for courage and honourable conduct, and, above all, never accepted the second rate. 8

The photo above was captioned: It may perhaps be worthwhile to try to capture the atmosphere and condition in the first ‘This is where he was born – decade of this century when I was a very little chap and starting to get impressions of life Simla Oct 11th 1901’ around me. I suppose the dominant features were late Victorian habits, customs, values and such like about which many books have been written, some good and some bad. But, perhaps such ones as the Forsyte Saga, Eminent Victorians by Strachey, Kitchener by Philip Magnus, though I don’t think his judgement of Kitchener was entirely without malice, Wheeler Bennett’s Edward VII, Kipling’s books, Trevelyan’s and Fisher’s books and many others, give quite a vivid picture of the differing aspects and ways of life in and around the first decade of the century. As children we were very fortunate in our mother and father. Mother took an immense interest in us and somehow was never out of sorts in spite of the many vexatious things rumbustious little boys can do! She had a telling and simple way of explaining the whys and wherefores of the numerous events and things children encounter as they grow up. Father 9

loved children and was never happier than when playing with us before bedtime. There was nothing of the austere and forbidding parents, sometimes caricatured in Victorian times, about our father and mother. There was a confidence and purposefulness about life in those days which seems singularly absent now. The British Empire, the greatest since the Roman Empire, was a dominant feature in world affairs. Rather over one quarter of the world’s surface was red, the Empire’s colour. As Kipling observed, the sun never set on our Empire. The Englishman held himself erect in the face of the world – he may have been arrogant here and there, but this was not common and there is little doubt the peoples of the world held an abiding and healthy respect for the Englishman of those days. We were rich in the material sense, though relative to other nations our heyday of economic strength was probably in the latter part of the 19th Century, rather than the earlier part of the 20th century. Christian observance was fairly universal and the saying that an English ‘With his attendant at Khandala, April 1902’ man’s word was his bond was no idle cliché. In the latter part of the nineteenth and early part of the 20th Century we produced probably as fine and outstanding a number of administrators, governors, and rulers, as can be found at any time in the history of mankind. The lasting and beneficial effect of these men in India on her body politic is apparent to this day and will last far into the future. Indeed, the same with truth can be said of other parts of the world governed by Englishmen. Nor was this an entirely Philistine age – far from it - in all spheres of the Arts, in writing, in painting and drawing, in Mathematics and scientific achievements, in philosophy and the realms of thought, many English men and women made signal contributions to this age. In his heart of hearts many Englishmen regarded himself as worth two or three foreigners and maybe twenty or thirty of any of the non-European races! After all, he had, in not inconsiderable measure, the testimony of history to support him in these ideas. Socially there were the ‘classes’ and the divisions between them were a deal more sharply defined than they are nowadays, when there has been a very general and, on the whole, beneficial ‘William in his verandah, with his blurring of what were once called class distinctions. Though most of them would have friend Skipper’ Quetta, May 1903 abhorred this idea, many Englishmen felt inside they had a mission in this world to provide justice and straight dealing to folk less fortunate than themselves. They were proud of the achievements of their Empire; they knew where they were going! They, on the whole, worked hard from top to bottom of the social scale, though there were, of course, a number 10

of ‘flashy no goods’ who received perhaps undue amounts of publicity at that time. But most people were pretty sure of themselves. The education at Public Schools was, on the whole, good and did much to produce what one might dare to call ‘an elite’ who gave such tremendous service to the whole Empire. Those educational reformers in the present day who have some sort of chip on their shoulders should remember that the training and production of an “elite” is a necessity for any country like ours which must now perforce rely on quality rather than quantity more than ever before if we are to retain any position of influence in the world. Above all, Public Schools left boys with a sense of responsibility to their fellow men and to the establishment, which is not nearly so apparent with many other nations. This sense of responsibility is perhaps one of the most enduring legacies of the schools of those days, and probably more than any other single factor made the Englishman and Englishwoman so respected. Politically, feelings between Conservatives and Liberals ran high - much higher than they do now. My parents were, what one would call, liberal Tories. They abhorred Gladstone and Lloyd George, but were none the less by no means on the right of the Conservative party. The conversation at table often turned to political events and one learnt quite a lot from hearing opinions expressed. The Christian religion meant a lot in those days. Christian observance was a deal more general than it is now, and many folk were guided throughout their lives by the immutable precepts of Christianity. Folk did go to Church on Sundays at 11.a.m. and the Churches in the countryside were as crowded as one finds say in Jamaica nowadays. “Fear God, Honour the King” was not just an idle slogan. In every household I stayed in up to the end of First World War, family prayers attended by all the household, were said in the dining room before breakfast. The Army and Navy held pride of place in the affections of many Englishmen, for we contrived our affairs in such a way that order and justice was maintained throughout the Empire by a small highly professional regular Army and a big Navy which was the strongest in the world, and which played no small part in giving the world the Pax Britannica for nearly a 100 years. Our Navy was out of sight but did have a most profound effect in policing the world and preventing conditions from arising which might have triggered off big conflicts. Looking back, it is amazing how little this wonderful service cost the country and how immeasurable a debt the whole world owes to the Royal Navy. It was in the early part of the century that the building up of a big German Navy presented a threat which, with other causes, led to the First World War, which alas, like the Second World War, need not have taken place. But those are for the Historians, of which there are many, to describe. One might also think from what has been said that the first few years of this century was a golden age. Perhaps it was for some but like many periods in our history there was a darker side. Industrial conditions were not always humane. Some folk, it could fairly be said, were underprivileged, social injustices were not by any means unusual. On the other hand it was not a case of all work and no play. Sport and games were giving a wider and wider enjoyment to our countrymen. We were accustomed to doing things well! We produced the best racehorses and steeplechasers in the world and many of the best cricketers, tennis players golfers and athletes. We introduced Association football to the world and led the way for a 11

long time. Life moved at what we now realise was a much slower tempo. There were no motor cars, and one relied on horse and carriage to go from place to place at an average speed of say 7 to 8 m.p.h. The railway train was the only way of getting from and to places at a distance. Aircraft had not been invented. The horse was, in the main, the principal method of local transport. Even to his dying day my father would, I suspect, have preferred to go from his house to Gloucester in a pony trap, which took an hour and a quarter, than in a motor car which took a quarter of an hour. Life was a deal less comfortable in many ways than it is now; houses were often cold and draughty. Lighting by lamps, though pleasant, was nothing like as effective as modern lighting. Men, women and children wore much more formal dress than now. Shorts or an open neck shirt for grownups were unheard of. The first tar macadam road I ever saw must have been in 1910 and consequently travel by road was dusty, dirty and often uncomfortable. The surfaces of many roads were not a great deal better than in Roman times some 1900 years ago, when some of our road systems were laid out and planned. Health was not nearly as good as nowadays. Many diseases, such as T.B. and other ailments, were a scourge, whereas now they are easily and successfully treated. When overseas, typhoid, cholera, dysentery and plague carried off many Englishmen, women and children, whereas inoculations and injections have now reduced the casualties from these causes to a negligible figure. Money was real in those days! I remember well being given a half sovereign tip by an uncle and a penny packet of sweets would last a little boy quite a time. It would be easy to fill many pages drawing comparison between the present day and life any 60 years back, but if what has been said will serve to give the outlines of a picture of what The Residency Bushire, people saw, felt, thought and acted when I was very young and impressionable, these few Persian Gulf 1900-01 preliminary and random jottings have achieved their purpose. 12

Early Life My father was stationed in the Persian Gulf when I was born and was in fact on his way back to India from there, to have some leave. He was the Political Assistant to the British Resident of the Persian Gulf (Colonel Kemble) with headquarters at Bushire [Bushehr]. The great Arabic administrator and scholar, Sir Percy Cox,3 as he later became, was a contemporary of father’s and tried hard to persuade father to make his career in the Gulf. Though he would have found the life challenging enough, Father knew well my mother had no chance in surviving overlong in the Gulf, which was the hottest and one of the most unhealthy places on earth. Soon after I was born father and mother came home for a short time and stayed at Eversley, near Finchampstead in Berkshire. However, we were soon on our travels again and returned to Bushire in the Persian Gulf where I had my first birthday. Father was acting as Resident for quite a time and helped to conclude, among other things, our Treaty with the Sheikh of Kuwait, which only recently has been abrogated alas by our Government. Father, in due course, applied for service on the North West frontier of India, which he knew well, and was appointed as Political Assistant to Colonel Yate (later Colonel Sir Charles Yate, C.S.I., C.I.E., M.P), who was the High Commissioner of Baluchistan [Balochistan] with headquarters at Quetta. Quetta was a healthy place, with a good climate, and it was here my sister Jane was born – a little prematurely. Lady Yate and my mother were great friends, and her family were contemporaries of ours and have remained our closest friends ever since. Father had a great admiration for Colonel Yate who was a shrewd and forthright administrator. Later on father was transferred to other parts of the North West frontier and, in August 1904, my brother Howell was born at Ziarat, a hill station not far from the Indus Valley. My Loralai, Balochistan, 1904. first recollections start soon after he was born. I remember attending my cousin Nancy Sailor costumes were very popular French’s wedding to Vivian Short at, I think, Peshawar, and I remember well our fierce and for children, though the choice was tempestuous old Nanny known as Denyer. Mother and Father said she was a very good perhaps prescient in this case! Nanny and looked after my brother and sister, who were both delicate, exceedingly well, but she had a completely ungovernable temper and I still have memories of some of these displays, usually at the expense of my unfortunate parents.4 We also had a nice Indian amah, who taught me Hindustani, a language I could speak as much as a three or four year old can speak, before I learnt English. 3 Sir Percy Cox (1864-1937), diplomat and colonial administrator, ODNB 4 WWD never lost his temper, a self-control perhaps learnt early. 13

I remember a little of our journey home when I was just four. Father took a house on the outskirts of Wokingham, called Hagville Farm, which we thought was heaven as we could run about without the fear of snakes and did not have to put on our big heavy solar topees whenever we went out in the sun. Hagville Farm stood in its grounds and had a drive up to it of about 100 yards leading off the Wokingham Finchampstead road. I remember being taken to tea with my old Great Uncle John Watson (General Sir John Watson,V.C., G.C.B., etc), who lived in a nice house called Northcourt and with whom I stayed later during school holidays. This might be an appropriate moment to talk a little bit about our close relations and family. My father had four brothers and one sister. The eldest of the Davis family was Colonel Cecil Davis, O.B.E., who, after leaving Eton, went into the Army and shortly afterwards transferred to the Indian Army in which he spent his Service life. He commanded the 1st Bengal Lancers (Skinners Horse) before retiring in 1912 to live at the family ‘Minding Budh Budh’.The youngest of the family, home Wellclose, near Brockworth. Short, thickset, a good Howell, was nicknamed Buddy because he apparently horseman and shot, he was rather a shy man and was much the looked like a little Buddha. WWD was always immensely most reserved of my uncles. We liked him very much and with loyal to his siblings and kept in touch with Buddy, writing small boys and girls he unbent completely and had a most letters almost every week until the end of his life. sympathetic way with us all and genuinely took much interest in our play and work. We always had a very warm welcome Hagville Farm, Berks 1906. from him when my brother, sister and I stayed at Wellclose, where he and his wife, my Aunt Kitty, who died in the 1970’s, were bringing up their young family of four boys, who were all quite a bit younger than us. My uncle had a good sound career in the Indian Army without in any way being distinguished. He was, I have heard, a first rate Commanding Officer of his Regiment and was well liked and respected. He saw little active service though he did take his regiment to Peking [Beijing] at the time of the Boxer Rebellion and formed part of the force under General Gaselee who commanded the British contingent on that occasion, under General Count Waldersee who was the overall Commander-in-Chief. My Aunt Adeliza came next and was older than my father. She married David Thomson who became a Colonel in the Indian Army, and after serving in the 1st Bengal Lancers (Skinners Horse) spent much of his time in the Judge Advocate’s Department of the Indian Army at Simla and elsewhere. My Uncle David was a splendid and very wise old character. Widely read, he took the somewhat unsettled life with my Aunt with 14

philosophic calm. He was a great favourite with us and helped me quite a lot in my various attempts at winning prize essays on military subjects. But more about my Aunt Addie as she was known. She was a character if ever there was one. A strong character who would run any one if they so allowed it! But she was one of the most generous of people and never forgot any of her numerous nephews and nieces either at their birthdays or Christmas. Tall, she must have been nearly 6ft., with somewhat wild and untidy hair, she loved company and people. She dressed, usually in black, in rather a Victorian way, and I remember her well once with one of those big floppy hats which made her resemble a three masted sailing ship under full sail. Restless by nature, she seldom spent more than a few months at any one place. They had a nice little cottage called Longview at Cooper’s Hill and a little house near Olympia in London when we were young, and what fun we all had staying there. Perhaps we were allowed greater freedom than elsewhere, for visits were one long adventure! My cousins David Thomson, Angela Thomson, Loveday Cameron (Lady Cameron, since died) were great friends of ours and we got up to any number of pranks with them. My Aunt Addie had one very fixed article in her creed and that was, “No Davis could really do wrong and must be supported to the last whatever other folk might say.” A great correspondent she kept in close touch with all her brothers who she regarded as more or less the salt of the earth. My father came next and you can read all about him in his own diary. Then came his favourite brother, my Uncle Somerville Davis, who studied medicine and became a doctor. He emigrated to Australia and from scratch built up a big practice at Perth and bought quite a big farm there. Alas, through gross overwork in the First World War he died from a tumour on the brain just at a time when he was becoming established and moderately prosper ous. He married the daughter of Canon Groser in Perth and left children, my cousins Merville, Adelaide (Mrs. Hind, since died), Dorothy (died in early 20’s), Cecil, Jesser (Mrs. Hind), and Georgie. I only saw a little of Uncle Somerville, but I remember when he came home in, I think, 1912 he took me for a motor tour in an old “T” type Ford which was a great adventure and enormous fun. I liked him a lot, for though short and stocky he reminded me of father, and I wished I had seen more of him. Then came Uncle Jim, who had a fairly adventurous career. He spent some time in Uncle Somerville and girls in car – Australia, living pretty rough, and eventually set up with others a thoroughly prosperous and not I think a T type Ford! successful trading company in leather know as Fleming and Co. in Bermondsey. He married late in life my Aunt Dora, and had one son Wilfred. Uncle Jim was a very generous Uncle indeed; he never failed to slip a gold sovereign in one’s pocket when we saw him, and gave most generous Christmas presents. Up to the great slump in 1930 he was a prosperous and generous man, but alas this hit leather trading very hard, and Fleming and Co., in which my father and others of the family had invested money, went into liquidation. Hindsight is easy enough now and if he had greater financial backing and supranormal foresight, he could 15

possibly have saved the firm, but many others of greater strength and resources went to the wall in this slump. Uncle Jim did a certain amount of business to earn a precarious living after this, but he never had much to spare and died soon after my father. He was good company, a fine and very good-looking man, who, with better luck, might well have made a mark in some walk of life. Finally, one comes to my Uncle George – not really the black sheep of the family! A great extrovert who really ought to have gone onto the stage, but he could never hold down a job for really long as a youngish man and sometimes forgot that only twelve pennies went into a shilling. This sometimes resulted in “a whip round” with his brothers and sisters. But he never got into deep water, was very popular and a bit of a bon viveur, that is as far as circumstance allowed. However, he settled down later and became a clerk in the Bank of England office at Liverpool. They all liked him so much that it is said the Bank would never allow his creditors to prosecute him! A figure in the Formby Golf Club he was, at one time, a fine golfer. His marriage alas broke up after having one son, Stringer Davis, who became an actor and was the husband of Margaret Rutherford, the great character actress. The Davis’s were impetuous and not infrequently hot tempered. My father was by a good deal the cleverest and most able of his brothers, and like all of them had a very clear idea what was right and what was wrong. Then on my mother’s side we had only one Aunt, my Aunt Wilna, and undoubtedly my favourite aunt. Very small and “petite” she was my mother’s elder sister and cannot have stood much more than 5ft. She married Edward French (my father’s first cousin) who became Sir Edward French, K.C.I.E., and head of police in the Punjaub in India and elsewhere. I remember a wonderful visit to their home near Henley-on-Thames in 1912 or 1913, after he had returned, and what fun it was. Uncle Edward was a very fine administrator, a good athlete and good company. They had two children, my cousin Noel, who died of typhoid in Palestine in the First War, where he was serving as a soldier, and my cousin Nancy Short, who died in 1968, the widow of Vivien Short, who had died soon after the last War. My Uncle Edward alas got pneumonia in 1913 and died from it to the great grief of all of us. My Aunt was very shrewd and amusing and, in spite of being widowed so soon after their retirement from India, never lost her interest. She was absolutely devoted to my mother and felt her death very much. In spite of her small stature she had considerable presence and yet, with a twinkle in her eye, soon would get the shyest child to confide in her. She refused to allow herself to get lonely in her widowhood and built up many friendships and interests which gave her great comfort. She died in Scotland not far from the Ross home of her forebears by Dingwall just after the end of the last War. She gave us that lovely Dresden china coffee set for a wedding present and took a lot of interest in us – a most loveable and amusing person. Well, that finishes my Uncles and Aunts. We were a very united family. We might, indeed and did, quarrel among ourselves, but were absolutely united against what we might call an outside aggressor! In those days family homes were, in a sense, common to the family. For 16

instance, as a young man, I never had any hesitation at staying at any of their houses if I so wanted. In fact they would have been hurt if I had not done so! Uncle Jim, in his prosperous days, had a house in Regents Park Terrace in London, in which I doubt if he slept more than once a fortnight. But I often used it as a base for my youthful forays in London especially if my motor bicycle had no lights or was unreliable. So did my uncle’s other relations and one often met one’s cousins there. In fact, we were brought up perhaps in the atmosphere that members of our family had certain obligations to each other which must be met however much we might disagree with each other at that moment. This is much less generally the case now, partly because very few people have servants, and maybe the family, as a unit in society, is regarded as of less significance than in our parents’ days. This, I believe, is a retrogressive step as the family, as a unit, from earliest days, has formed the basis of civilised society. There is still, I believe, quite a lot to be said for family spirit and I hope, in the Brave New World of tomorrow, with its test tubes and computers, there will still be found room for the “togetherness” which is to be found among families and close relations. Now let us return to the narrative. Whilst we were at Hagville Farm in 1906 our first governess Miss Malden joined us. The daughter of a clergyman, she was powerfully built; in many senses a muscular Christian. She could walk for miles, was seldom tired and played a good game of tennis, and so could cope with rather energetic and sometimes naughty children which we were. A fair Their ‘Turi friends and protectors’- teacher, she taught me arithmetic well, but had difficulty in making me pay attention to other lessons, with the result I was an indifferent reader when I went to my private school later. She gave however my sister and brother a good grounding, and, though not an imaginative teacher, was a good sound one who never forgot the validity of Christian precepts. She was good fun and we all became very fond of her. She left us in 1914 when my mother brought my sister and brother home to England to finish their education with our Slessor cousins and at school. We thought Hagville Farm was great fun and first got to know some of our cousins who stayed with us from time to time. The time soon came for us to return to India and I have intermittent memories of rather a rough passage in the P. & O liner S.S. Persia to India. I think one of the first things that impressed me about India was that apparently all our servants had come down to Bombay to greet us, and decorate father and mother with the Cherat, 1907: ‘Their Steeds’! traditional garlands of welcome. We were, of course, overjoyed to 17

see our old friends again.Father first was sent to Peshawar where he became the Deputy Commissioner and worked very hard indeed. It was a time when there was a good deal of trouble on the boil, and many of the plots to overthrow any form of orderly government were hatched in the bazaars of Peshawar. Father had a pretty shrewd idea what was being said in the bazaars at that time. We had a bungalow next to the General commanding the district and his wife kindly gave me a little Dachshund puppy, who was named Toby and who became a tremendous character. Toby lived his whole life in India and died during the latter part of the War at Sehore at the ripe old age of 11 or 12. No party was complete without Toby, whose photograph you will see in some of my father’s photograph albums. We spent some time at Peshawar and then moved onto such places as Lorelai, Derah Ismail Khan, and eventually Parachinar at the foot of the Piwa [Peiwar] Kotal Pass into Afghanistan. I saw my first motor car at Derah Ismail Khan – it was an old The garden, Parachinar Renault and was owned by an eccentric colleague of father’s, by name Rennie. He drove us round Derah Ismail Khan to the astonishment of the inhabitants; everybody bowed down and worshipped this “strange machine” which the “Sahibs” had bought to their country. Derah Ismail Khan had a fine residency, but being on the banks of the Indus, was a very hot, unhealthy and stuffy place. The visits to the hill station at Sheikh Badeen were great fun and we acquired a tame mountain goat who loved to prance about on the edge of precipices of which there were many in this mountainous district. The Indian Army had a base up there and it was a wonderful sight to see once, as I did, the Black Watch and Gordon Highlanders on parade. Magnificent looking fighting men, almost all with beards, of whom the old Indian warrior Sir Pertab [Pratab] Singh once said “If I had soldiers like that I would have them all carried into battle in a “doolie” by four coolies each and then nobody would stop me”. Eventually, father, who was not at all well at Derah Ismail Khan, got moved to Parachinar right on the borders of Afghanistan. This had a splendid climate, was over 5,000 feet up and had the A family picnic in the Safed Koh mountains, towering Hindu Kush mountains of 15,000 feet and over, July 1909.The orderlies were Zafar Ali and always snow covered, towering over the Kurram Valley with Safdar Ali. Parachinar at its head. We had deep snow in Winter and my sister and I each had a pony, whilst the Governess and my brother used to ride a magnificent old donkey who rejoiced in the name of Polly. As it was a pretty wild place two or three of father’s Khurram militia always used to come out with us, and 18

what fun they were, with their songs and yarns which they loved to tell with gusto. We soon learnt to chatter in the local dialect of Pushtoo [Pashto], which now, I believe, is a written language with a complicated syntax and grammar! Mother painted some of her best sketches at Parachinar. Father loved the life there and proved himself to be much liked and respected by the inhabitants of that wild valley. I learnt to shoot with a rifle and father always pitted me against the son of the local chief; great fun it was too; and it called for an accurate aim to hit a silver rupee at 25 yards, which not infrequently was the challenge. Here I also saw my first motor bicycle, a Triumph of, I suppose, 1908 or 1909 vintage, owned by the sapper officer who had his H.Q. at Parachinar. After about two years father alas fell out with the agent of the Governor General, Sir Henry Roos-Keppel, for the Punjaub, for very good reasons indeed of which you have already heard. Anyway, the upshot of it was he was offered the post at Derah Ismail Khan again, where he had been so ill and nearly lost the sight of one eye, so decided to come home to England and take leave. We all were sad to leave Parachinar where we lived in a nice two storey house with a fine garden in which we had many games. The chief and headmen of surrounding villages gave us all a tremendous send-off as we left in the traditional tonga for the rail head about 50 miles distant. So ends my time in India, which I left as a little boy of 8½ and about which I had many pleasant memories to be revived 18 years later when I served in a cruiser in the East Indies squadron. We had a pleasant voyage home in P.O. liner S.S. India and made many friends with the children on board. The summer of 1910 was a splendid one to arrive in England and we went to Greyhounds in Burford, a nice old home which had once been a Coaching Inn in Sheep Street, Burford, and which is now the Headquarters of “The Countryman”. Father took it from Mrs. Percival, who was the sister of the vicar, old Willie Emeris, who is the sporting parson in Masefield’s “Reynard the Fox”. A great character with a nose like Mr. Punch’s he did his job splendidly in Burford and there can have been few people in the Parish who did not know the Vicar well. Burford was a splendid place in which to spend my parents’ leave. It was not so “arty” then as it has become and we knew the Priory well, where two Edwardian characters, Colonel and Mrs. La Terriere, lived after restoring it. We alas never saw the ghosts there which however had been seen by Mrs. La Terriere. Again, the motor car, even in 1910, was a rarity and if on a walk on what is the main Oxford/ Chelteham Road one met more than two cars it was a rarity.5 We had a good tennis court and I started to play with much keenness and soon became tolerably proficient. Mother did a number of very nice sketches here which are hung in Coglan. Father decided to send me to Summer Fields School at Oxford, whose headmaster was Dr. Williams. It had a fine classical reputation and used, in my days, to get a considerable number of scholarships at Eton. I remember being taken there one September day in 1910 by my parents and feeling a bit sad and lonely when they left. But I soon settled down. We had to work hard and my educational deficiencies were soon laid bare. However, by starting in the bottom form I got a magnificent classical grounding. It was a thoroughly 5 This is now the A40 main road 19

good school - strict, but no bullying whatever by masters or boys. We were a happy crowd of somewhat over a hundred youngsters. I suppose a bit spartan as one judges things now – the heating was a bit primitive and the food far from appetising. The routine was strictly enforced and, looking back, this I think taught us to plan out and use our time to the best advantage. A happy balance was kept between games and work, though I am afraid I paid more attention to the former than the latter. The masters, Drs. Williams and Alington, as joint heads, were a first-rate pair; then we had Mrs. Crofts, Evans, Case, Penney, Gmelin, Smith and many others on the staff, never forgetting the redoubtable Miss Hills who took the two bottom forms with exemplary patience and success. When discussing my future with my father, Dr. Williams said one of the reasons for their exceptional and then continuous successes in the scholastic field, particularly at Eton, was that the boys were often the sons of clever professional men. I think Dr. Williams rather wanted me to go for a scholarship at Eton, but I and my father were determined on the Navy without any second thoughts whatever. I am doubtful if, in fact, I would have got a scholarship at Eton as, though I like classics, I have no great aptitude for them, and would not have been in the genuine classical scholarship class. On the other hand, I think I could perhaps have got a mathematical scholarship at some school if I had not been minded on the Navy, as I had a modest talent for figures and mathematical symbols. But I am racing ahead. Oxford was very different in those days – one usually got a hansom cab from the station to take one to school, but if unlucky one caught a horse tram which took the passengers at a leisurely trot up the Banbury Road to about 100 yards from the school entrance. Everything was run efficiently at Summer Fields; work, games and recreation, and even though it may have been rather a restricted life we acquired the habits of orderliness and, I think, respect for efficiency. My progress up the school was steady if not spectacular. Fortunately, I had a sure aptitude for games and, ’ere long, found myself in the first X1 for all games and became the school golf expert with “gutty” [gutta-percha] balls and some borrowed hickory club. Some sentimental nonsense is talked by people about their school days being the best of their lives. This was certainly, in my case, untrue. Of course, I much preferred holidays where one was free to follow one’s own bent and had satisfying and good food and so on. On the other hand I quite enjoyed school, made a number of friends whom I have kept to this day and, being only human, one thoroughly enjoyed the successes especially in the sphere of games which came one’s way. Greyhounds, Burford Our time at Greyhounds, Burford was filled with adventures and much fun. As children – being out of India - we were allowed much greater freedom to roam about as we liked. In those days the roads were safe; the sight of a motor car was an event certainly to be discussed fully at Nursery Tea. Burford had no train service and was just over 5 miles from the nearest station, Shipton, to which a horse bus ran to connect with the trains to and from Oxford and London. There was another station at Bampton, the site of the present big Air Force Station Brize Norton, on the Oxford/Fairford line – long since closed – which we used from time 20

to time, and I remember some very cold drives there in father’s pony trap usually to catch the train which took me back to school at Oxford. One of the events in early 1911 I remember best was when Professor Dickson, the father of one of my particular friends at Summer Fields, bought a very old car, a Wolseley I think, and took us all for a round tour to Warwick, Kenilworth, Stratford-on-Avon and Stow-on-the-Wold. Apart from a few punctures we completed the trip inside twenty-four hours. My mother and father much enjoyed it and you can imagine the party dressed as you see people dressed for the annual London to Brighton old crocks race. Dickson, my friend at Summer Fields, was about eighteen months older than I and went to Osborne College in 1913. He never lived up to his early promise as a boy, and retired as an over zone [large regional] Naval Lieutenant Commander, having specialised in submarines. He did, however, get some award for saving life in the China Seas. He died in his early 40’s and I have lost touch with his family. Another great friend to this day I made at Summer Fields was Robin Durnford Slater. He followed me into the Navy and retired a few months after I did, having had a distinguished career, reaching the rank of Admiral. Robin and I were supposed to be the two most mischievous boys at Summer Fields for a longish time, but I think, for all that, old Dr. Williams and Mr. Alington, the joint headmasters, rather liked us. To my great joy I missed half of the Summer term of 1911, having contracted Whooping Cough. We went down to Sandown in the Isle of Wight to recuperate, and had enormous fun there, having our first experience of sea bathing. 1911 was the year of the Coronation Naval Review at Spithead and we spent a day in a steamer inspecting all the ships. I was particularly thrilled at the impressive number of ships there. I think the four funnel cruisers attracted me most as they looked so graceful. The Good Hope, later to be sunk off Coronel in the First War, was there and especially took my fancy. I think, if I ever had any doubts about going into the Navy, they were resolved by this spectacle. I wonder what I would have thought if somebody had whispered in my ear then that in 47 years’ time, I should be the Commander-in-Chief of this fleet! An event which we all remembered at school was Edward VII’s death. The headmaster gave us a good talk on him and the responsibilities of monarchy in the democratic age in which we then were living. I once saw the King and recollect rather a nice dignified old man with a big beard and a generous happy looking smile. This was at some procession in London and I was lifted onto father’s shoulder to see the king. The time soon came for my parents to return to India for my father had had a little over 18 months furlough leave and anyway money was getting short as he only got half pay and no allowances when on long leave. These were the days before it became the custom to give generous leave allowances to Government Servants. One September, or maybe October, day in 1911 I went down with my parents to Dover to see them off to India. I was sad and must have seemed rather a forlorn little boy as I knew I should not see them again for 3 or 4 years which, at my age, seemed very long time. Uncle Jim and my Aunt Addie took me back to school and I soon got immersed in the life there. My parents were splendid letter writers and I used every week to get a letter from them. I don’t think they ever failed though maybe in the First War mails may have been a bit irregular and a few were lost by enemy action at sea. 21

Now came a bit of a change in life for me. My parents had arranged for two splendid middle aged ladies, Miss Sarah and Miss Louisa Newton-King, soon known to us as “Aunt Bessie” and “Aunt Judy”, to look after me and later my brother and sister when they came home, whilst my parents were in India. They lived at No.5, Upton Park on the outskirts of Slough and next door to the Eton College playing fields. The house was admirably adapted for children. My mother’s great friend Sybil Ffolkes (Lady Ffolkes) with her husband (Everard Ffolkes), then a bank clerk in the Bank of England, with their son Rupert Ffolkes, lived nearly next door at No.8 Upton Park. Upton Park covered about 25 acres and was reserved for use of the inhabitants of the 25 odd houses in Upton Park. Some of these were large ones and a few were owned by what we would call tycoons nowadays. Everard Ffolkes came in for the family baronetcy and a lot of money before the War and moved to a nice property at Congham Lodge, near King’s Lynn. Their only son, Rupert Ffolkes, was an especial friend of mine – small for his age, about 2 years older than I, he was a first rate games player and shot and was in every first eleven for which he qualified. He was at Radley where I saw him from time to time. Alas, with so many others he volunteered at the first opportunity and was killed with hundreds of the best of our country in the trenches in France in the First War. He had a tremendous sense of humour and nobody could be dull for long in his company. He was very fond of my sister Jane, then about 11 or 12, when she came home, and I have no doubt whatever it would have been the dearest wish William, Biking of Sybil Ffolkes and my mother if they had married when they grew up. Upton Park was a heaven-sent place for children to play. We had bicycle tracks and there was everything a child could want, including a muddy pond into which we fell from time to time. Bicycle polo was a favourite sport of ours. But, let us get back to the two fine ladies, Aunt Bessie and Aunt Judy, who looked after us. They were the daughters of an Irish landowner, Colonel Newton-King, who lived at a place called Macmine, near Wexford and who had fallen on hard times and sold up the family place towards the end of last century. They had two brothers, Colonel Francis and Colonel Coote Newton- King, who we met from time to time. But it was Coote’s two sons, Rex and Richard, who we knew best. They were looked after by Aunt Bessie and Aunt Judy as Coote married again after losing his first wife, their mother, in India where he was serving. Rex was a wholly splendid young man, good looking, absolutely charming and as fine a character as one could want to find. He followed his father into the Army in 1912 and, alas, was killed in the first few months of the War in France in 1914. This was a great blow to Aunt Bessie as he was very much the leader of what she always called “The boys”. Richard, his younger brother and about 2 years older than I, was also a good friend of mine. He went to Marlborough and I think got a scholarship there, after 22

which, in the latter part of the War, he went to Sandhurst and later transferred to the Indian Army. Richard was a tough and robust character, good at games and fond of sports, who never married. After retiring from the Army at the end of World War II, he became Secretary of the Hill Club at Nuwara Eliya in Ceylon [Sri Lanka], eventually returning to England where he died rather suddenly of Leukaemia a few years ago. Always reputed to be a first-rate regimental officer, not much active service came his way and he reached the rank of Colonel, like his father, before retiring. A great favourite of ours was however Aunt Bessie’s brother, Colonel Francis Newton-King, who might really be “Colonel Newcombe” come to life,6 enormous charm, very good looking and well dressed in an Edwardian manner, he was quite one of the most courteous and kindest men I knew and was always prepared to spend endless time with young people. He carried with him a dignity and courtliness of a bygone age, seldom seen now. He had two sons and two daughters. Pierce, the eldest, who we knew quite well, had a brilliant career, as far as it went, in the Army. He passed out top of Sandhurst and was awarded the King’s Sword, alas to be killed soon after in France. Eileen, again with much charm, married Sir George Hammick and died in childbirth. Dennis, my contemporary and friend, had an interesting life in his father’s old regiment, the Oxford and Bucks, and retired in 1933 to farm in South Africa at Kings Kloof, Somerset West, Cape Province, which he did with success. We stayed with them in 1961, but alas he died after a hip operation for arthritis some years later. Nora, the other daughter, was a somewhat reserved and restricted person of whom we saw little. The “Aunts” believed very much in our old Summer Fields motto “Mens Sana in Corpore Sano”. Good Christians, they practised what they preached. We went regularly to church in the old church at Upton nearby. But seldom was there not a twinkle in their eye and the many Eton boys they knew used regularly to come out on Sunday to tea and joke with them. Straightforward characters, neither of my aunts knew what it was to dissemble, and one could always he certain of a straight from the shoulder answer even if one did not like what one heard. Aunt Judy, who was always the delicate one of the pair and who left everything to Aunt Bessie, eventually outlived her and died when over 80! A more wholesome and straightforward upbringing which these ladies provided would be hard to imagine and our family owe a great deal to them. My mother bought my sister and brother home in March of 1914 to settle them in England and accustom them to school and their new life, before she returned to India at the end of the year. My sister went to share a governess with my “Aunt” Tiny near Oxford. Aunt Tiny (Mrs. Slessor – wife of Captain Slessor, Bursar and Steward of Christ Church, Oxford) was, in fact, my father’s cousin. Their daughter Betty (now Mrs. Fellowes) was the same age as my sister Jane and had a fine time sharing governesses, one of which, Miss Jolly, stayed with them a long time and to whom my sister was devoted. My brother “Buddie” was a bit ill on return from India and did not join Summer Fields straight away, but joined up about half way through the Summer Term of 1914. Though a bit old when he joined, he soon caught up and had no difficulty in passing the common entrance exam into Marlborough just before 6 This is probably a reference to the 1920 silent film ‘Colonel Newcombe, the Perfect Gentleman’, based on the novel by W.P. Thackeray, The Newcomes: Memoirs of a Most Respectable Family, 1854-55 23

the end of the First War. He. I think, enjoyed himself at Summer Fields and certainly prospered at the games. Being of a quieter and more reserved nature than his elder brother, he got into considerably less trouble than I did. The Summer Term of 1914 was great fun and though we were interested in playing soldiers then nobody dreamt, or had any idea, what a War could be. The Summer holiday in 1914 was a memorable one for me – the first time we three children had been together with my mother. We spent it at Stoke Fleming, near Dartmouth, with Miss Parry Okeden who had a splendid large and very affectionate bulldog. The weather was perfect, and we bathed most days at a private cove about half a mile from the house. What with picnics and bathing the effect of the battles which were taking place in France had little impact on us. On our return to school in September 1914 the War became very important to us. We played war games and examined the relative strengths of the Armies and Navies of the world as given in the Daily Mail and as also provided by Hilaire Belloc.7 Like horrid little boys we wanted to know why any master who did not have a grey beard had not immediately enlisted and so on. Again old Dr. Williams gave the boys one or two very good talks on what this War was about and why it was being fought. Then, towards the end of that term and beginning of next term, the War was suddenly brought home to me. Some boys, one or two of which were Eton scholars who were at Summer Fields when I joined in 1910, had been killed in action. One boy I remember particularly well as being the sort of hero a small eight-year-old has on going to his first school. Nevertheless, apart from the departure of a few of the younger masters for the War everything seemed to go on much the same as before, and we were shown our first cinema in New Room when Isaac Pitman’s father gave a special and exciting demonstration to the school. That holiday we spent with Lady Yate at Asfordby and had a splendid Christmas there. Their children, who matched us for age, were always good friends and we almost regarded Asfordby House as a second home. Sir Charles Yate was the M.P. for the Melton Mowbray division of Leicestershire and was much liked and respected by many people. My sister and brother soon settled down and we much enjoyed meeting up again in the holidays. We were based on the Newton-Kings at 5, Upton Park and did a round of visits to the Yates and various Uncles and Aunts. At Summer Fields there was a special modern class which did German as well as French, but was excused Greek, to my joy! They were the boys destined for the Navy – besides myself included Burrows (killed in a motor smash in Newfoundland), Durnford Slater (retired Admiral), Tupper Carey (retired Captain); Furse and Jones, both of whom left the Navy at Osborne as they were not particularly well suited to the rather rigorous discipline and routine to which we were subjected. 7 Hilaire Belloc (1870-1953), ODNB. Best known for his Cautionary Tales for Children, Belloc had recently resigned as a Liberal MP and was an important journalist and writer. 24

The day soon came round in February 1915 when I had to appear before the interview Board at the Admiralty. Once this hurdle was surmounted one sat for a competitive written examination which however presented little difficulty to an average intelligent little boy. Taking all in all Summer Fields was a thoroughly good school with a high standard of work and a first-rate tone. Quite a number of boys who were there in my time have made some mark in the world. Lord Runciman, Stephen Runciman, Harold Caccia (Lord Caccia), Isaac Pitman (Sir Isaac), Roger Mynors (Sir Roger), Ralph Assheton (Lord Clitheroe), Hendy (Sir Philip), Christopher Hollis, G.O. Allen, Anthony Asquith, who died only last year, reminds me of the time I poured some ink over his face on the day the Prime Minister, his father, and the redoubtable Margot paid the school a visit!8 Dr. Williams was splendid and, apart from being told I was not tactful, I received no other reprimand and Anthony’s parents were entertained with the dignity due to the First Minister of the Crown and his wife. Old Dr. Williams gave all the boys, on leaving, a splendid and intimate talk.
