I remember to this day that talk where he set out so well, in homely language, the simple Christian precepts to which we must adhere if we wanted to live a worthwhile life. Straight dealing, decency and service to one’s Fellows, could epitomise that talk. What gave one the greatest thrill at school is difficult to name, but perhaps the award of one’s 1st IX colours at cricket after a memorable match with Horris Hill quoted in the S.F. book; the award of 1st XI colours at football, and, when only just 10 or 11 years old, being top of the school in Mathematics in the yearly school test paper, though I was only half way up the school in forms. Whilst I was at Summer Fields no wartime restrictions had been imposed, and, as I have already related, routine continued as usual. I went up for my interview for the Navy in the Admiralty in February 1915 and was confronted by a nice crowd of men with the president, a bearded Admiral, sitting at the centre of the table with a most benevolent expression on his face. They could not have been more friendly and, in a minute, put one at one’s ease and I soon forgot the awful “trick” questions I had been told to expect! They soon found out father’s first cousin (Colonel Mansell Jones and his uncle, General Sir John Watson) had won the V.C. in the Boer War and Indian Mutiny, and though I could not answer all the school master’s questions which included the translation of “oeuf à la coque”, they soon, I suspect, made up their mind to pass me subject to getting through the medical, which presented no obstacle, and of course later passing the written examination which we took in some place in Bedford Square in London in March. 8 Walter Leslie Runciman, 2nd Baron Runciman, shipowner (1900-1989) ODNB; Stephen Runciman (1903-2000), historian; Harold Caccia, diplomat (1905-1990) ODNB; Isaac Pitman, educationist and publisher (1901-1985) ODNB; Roger Mynors, classical scholar (1903-1989) ODNB; Harald Peake, Director of Public Relations RAF and company director (1899-1978); John Rowlett, lawyer (1898-1956); George Binney, explorer and blockade runner (1900-1972) ODNB; Ralph Assheton, politician and business (1901-1984) ODNB; Philip Hendy, art administrator (1900-1980) ODNB; Christopher Hollis, author and politician (1902-1977) ODNB; G.O. Allen (Gubby Allen), cricketer (1902-1989); Anthony Asquith, film director and aesthete (1902-1968) ODNB; Robin Durnford Slater, Admiral (1902-1984). 25

The papers set did not present any difficulties though I did not do as well as old Dr. Williams would have wished. Some 109 out of about the 300 who sat the exam passed. I passed in 18th, but it was hoped I would be in the first three, who were specially named and commended by Their Lords of the Admiralty in the passing out list. However, as I passed out from Dartmouth 3rd or 4th, honour was satisfied! The top boy of my term, R.M. Ellis, was an exceptional boy and would have, without doubt, been a first class honours man at any University in a wide range of subjects. So, we were set a hot pace at both Osborne and Dartmouth. Our holidays with the Miss Newton-Kings and relations went much as in the past. My mother being home for the summer holiday in 1914 was an enormous joy and then meeting my sister Jane and brother Buddie at subsequent holidays added to my enjoyment, for we were a very close-knit family in spite of some quarrels and occasional fights! My sister, who had a quick and imaginative brain, shared governesses with her cousin (Betty Slessor) at their home not far from Nuneham Courtenay outside Oxford. The Slessor’s children were of an age with us and we could always be certain of a boisterous welcome from them when we stayed there. My Aunt Tiny (she was in fact father’s first cousin) ruled the house with great determination. A most forceful woman, who when she ran over the point duty policeman’s foot at Carfax in Oxford, told him he should not have such big feet! Old “Uncle Arthur”, her husband, who was the steward at Christ Church, was also a character, but seldom got a word in edgeways. Jack, the eldest boy, was very tempestuous and also partially crippled. He ran away from home, got himself into the Royal Flying Corps by borrowing an aeroplane and flying it to the interview Board to prove he was fit and capable. A clever man, he eventually became Chief of the Air Staff after a most distinguished record in both Wars. A controversial figure.9 I believe many of his ideas are not in accord with sound strategy, and I have always felt he tried to bend his facts to show that the Air Force was the all-important arm of our defence with inadequate regard to the maritime and land aspects of modern warfare. But perhaps more of this anon. Rodney Slessor, a few months older than me, was a great favourite and had a delightful sense of humour. His descriptions of the scenes in his home were entrancing. Then Betty Slessor, now Mrs. Fellowes, who lives in Rhodesia, was my sister’s contemporary. A nice girl, but, I thought, apt to be bulldozed by her mother. The youngest, Tony, went into the Army and died between the Wars in Burma. Of our visits and jaunts as children to relations and friends, the ones that stood out were those to the Yates at Asfordby House, to my Aunt Addie at Cooper’s Hill, expeditions to London with my Uncle Jim, and later to my Uncle Cecil at Wellclose. My brother I think enjoyed his time at Summer Fields and went to Marlborough College in 1918 after having shown his aptitude at cricket and football. Our time at Slough with the Newton-Kings was always full. One of our favourite hobbies was to take the names and types of the Great Western Railway engines as they raced through Slough Railway Station hauling the expresses to the West Country. We went everywhere on bicycles and the roads were safe in those days. Rides to Beaconsfield, Maidenhead, Marlow and Henley were especial treats. An old, retired bachelor planter (Mr. Ward) from Ceylon was another favourite of ours. I shall never forget the day he took us to watch the Test Match at the Oval against the Australians when C.B. Fry made a big score. 26 9 Sir John Cotesworth Slessor, air force officer (1897-1979) ODNB

1915 It must have been on about 1st May 1915 that as a rather self-conscious little cadet in our naval uniform for the first time, I with some hundred other little boys, caught the train at Waterloo for, I think, Portsmouth where we took the steamer over to Cowes and joined Osborne House. Looking at the other cadets some seemed rather strange, I thought, and one or two very large! We were welcomed kindly by the two masters of our term [i.e. entry group], Mr. Bunting and Mr. Bates, who had taken the place of term Lieutenants, who were all required at sea. I think the idea of having wise and experienced masters in charge of herds of little boys is much to be preferred to term Lieutenants, however dedicated and good they were. For young Lieutenants who had sole responsibility for the boys at that age just did not have the knowledge or experience to know what little boys’ minds were thinking! We had a Chief Petty Officer of the term, who was a wholly admirable figure. I think I can remember his name sixty years later – C.P.O. Moxon – who was an absolute fund of information about the College and who was prepared to spend endless time listening to little boys’ prattle and answering their unending store of questions. We soon settled down to a syllabus of education which had been designed by the great educationalist, Professor Ewing, under Lord Fisher’s directions.10 The standard of teaching was high, some say very high, and it was clear that it was the custom to work as hard as one could. For even then the term “the good of the Service” meant something very real to all of us. Classics were not taught at all, and one third of one’s time was spent on practical engineering which probably accounts for the fact that so many naval officers are good with their hands. Mathematics and Science teaching especially were first rate, and history with a William in uniform joining the Navy naval basis was taught by Professor Callender of ‘Sea Kings of Great Britain’ fame.11 I soon reached the top form in Mathematics, and was either first or second in it for most of my time at Osborne and Dartmouth. I remember rather a laconic report by the Headmaster, the famous mathematician Mr. Godfrey, on coming out second in the term.12 All he said was “could do better”, which I thought a trifle unfair at the time. Osborne was organised into sharply defined Terms, which bore the name of famous Admirals.13 I was in the ‘Exmouth’ term, other terms were Grenville, Hawkins, Blake, St. Vincent, Duke. Terms did not mix at all, in fact segregation was encouraged so one had to find one’s friends in one’s own term, not a hard task with something like 109 boys, as there were in my term. 10 J. A. Ewing, Professor of Applied Mechanics, Cambridge. See Rodger, pp.201-202, for comments on the educational scheme. 11 Sir Geoffrey Callender )1875-1946), naval historian and first director of the National Maritime Museum, Greenwich (ODNB). WWD was fortunate to have Callender as a teacher, ‘a born conversationalist and brilliant lecturer’, as the emphasis tended to be on higher mathematics, which however also suited WWD. 12 Professor Charles Godfrey (1873-1924), headmaster of Osborne Royal Naval College and campaigner for mathematics education (ODNB). 13 There were six ‘Terms’, with the course of study spread over 2 years. 27

The boys were rather a mixed lot, perhaps because of the greatly increased numbers who were accepted, which was nearly three times the normal pre-war figure. Some a bit rough but, again some with the traditional naval officers’ background and upbringing. Recreation was also carefully organised, as every cadet had to account daily for his activities, and these were entered into a ‘log’. There was in a way less freedom, certainly less freedom of thought than at Summer Fields, and it was clear we were intended to conform to a strictly moulded pattern with high ideals of service. Probably a good thing, for disciplined service on which the whole security of the empire depended. At every turn loyalty to one’s dormitory, class and term was drummed into one. The feeding was excellent, much better than Summerfields, and by and large one was happy there with the excellent games facilities and first rate teaching, which certainly kindled one’s interest. I think I liked science best, and this with mathematics were my two favourite subjects. Our term masters, Bunting and Bates, were good especially the former, who was a most sympathetic character and understood little boys. Instead of prefects each term had ‘cadet captains’ selected from the terms senior to the one. These were with very few exceptions good and performed the duties which in most public schools are carried out by prefects. One rebelled a little, I suppose, at what seemed to be the over-regimentation of the College, but I think that shows a healthy enquiring if sometimes rebellious spirit. The tone of the College was very good, and the staff from the Captain downwards set an admirable example. 1916 Time passed very quickly whilst we were there. The Battle of Jutland - May 1916 - caused a bit of a stir but we were convinced that the German losses were in fact much greater than claimed, and our confidence in the invincibility of the Royal Navy was in no wise shaken! My father and mother, who took some leave in the summer of 1916, visited me there to my great joy, for I had not seen my father for five years and my mother for two years. They were just as I imagined, and I was as happy a little boy as one could meet anywhere at seeing them again. They both seemed to be able to enter into a child’s mind, and I soon realised how splendid it was to be in their company. We spent the summer holidays of 1916 at Lullingworth in Painswick, a nice house on the hill leading to Painswick from Stroud. Robin Dunford Slater, Summer Fields friend, came to stay and we had any amount of fun with plenty of mischief. But father and mother could not have been more tolerant. Father thought of buying Lullingworth, as it was a very nice house with a lovely walled garden but mother, having heard an old motor bike trying to climb the main road hill adjacent to the house, warned father that when the motor age came the house would be very noisy, as abundantly proved to be the case. The house also wanted a lot of repairs and alterations carried out to it, so we did not pursue the project of acquiring it. This is written actually sixty years later, and the bypass for Painswick has not been built and probably will not be in the author’s lifetime, and the house is dreadfully noisy. The truly memorable summer holidays will always stay in my memory, for it was the first time in five years that we had been united together as one family, and my mother was in good health and in spite of her frail constitution ready to tackle anything. 28

At the end of the holidays my father sold the pony he had bought for us for the holidays for £14, which he gave to me to help buy a motor bike upon which I had set my heart. A most generous present, for money then was worth I suppose at least five or six times what it is now worth sixty years later. That autumn father and mother, both looking much less tired, returned to India by the usual route via Calais, Paris and Marseilles, where they caught the P.O. mail steamer for Bombay [Mumbai]. The Western front was stabilised, but the submarine campaign which was just starting in earnest gave cause for anxiety. I was allowed off for a day to say goodbye to my parents, but I felt this time it would not be long and, anyway, I now had my brother and sister in England with me. The autumn term at Osborne was to be my last there. I think I performed just adequately, having taken up rugger and getting into the First XV. Rationing was now starting to come in, but we only noticed this on holidays as Osborne was regarded as a special case and not subjected to rationing. In the Christmas holidays, having passed my fifteenth birthday, I bought a 250 cc New Imperial J.A.P. motorcycle. A. splendid machine with a top speed of about 45 m.p.h., of which I was inordinately proud. The Newton-Kings were pleased, and as traffic other than bicycles and horse drawn traffic on the roads was then pretty well nonexistent, they did not worry. In spite of petrol rationing, I managed to do as much riding as I wanted, and what fun it all was. My brother and sister soon settled at Summer Fields, and with a shared Governess with the Slessors near Nuneham, about five miles from Oxford. My brother, who was late going to Summer Fields, was behindhand to start with, but he soon caught up to the average standard in classics, though maths was not his strong suit. Janie, my sister, was always great fun and was turning into a very pretty and lively girl who seemed to be universally popular. She was Rupert Ffoulkes. K.I.A. 1917 quick and clever, and inherited my mother’s love of beautiful things. Rupert Ffolkes, our great friend, joined the Army as soon as he could after leaving Radley and, alas, to our great grief was killed in the trenches later on in 1917, soon after getting to the front. A most delightful man, heir to the baronetcy and greatly loved by his father and mother who never got over his death. In addition to Rex Newton-King, who was killed early in the war, another nephew, Pierce Newton-King, elder son of old Uncle Francis, was also killed – an absolutely outstanding and delightful young man who got the sword of honour at Sandhurst and was invariably top of all his classes. So many of one’s close friends were killed in France, and it always seemed that the best were taken. My time at Osborne ended with the Christmas term in 1916. On the whole a reasonably enjoyable time, though I had in no way distinguished myself above the ordinary at work or games. But one had perhaps absorbed some of the dedication to service which every naval officer must have. Boys were treated fairly, and there was no bullying whatever as sometimes occurred in the gunrooms of the Grand Fleet. 29

Our arrival at Dartmouth in January 1917 in bitterly cold weather was heralded by an epidemic of measles, to which I succumbed, so the term was a bit broken up. We were well looked after in the sanatorium. Dartmouth seemed a much more enjoyable place than Osborne – cadets were allowed a deal more freedom and we were encouraged to regard ourselves as young officers and no longer schoolboys. I went for some walks over to Stoke Fleming to see where we had spent our holidays in 1914. The work was much the same, admirably organised, and it was here I first took a real interest in history and I think when we left I was top of the term in history. Boat sailing in the ‘Blue Boat’ on the Dart was much encouraged, and it was not long before one got the hang of how to sail a boat. The summer term of 1917 was enormous fun, and one could take long walks all over the lovely countryside where one not infrequently had a tea with Devonshire cream. We had a term lieutenant to look after us, a nice fellow called Howard who had, it was reported, a bit of a breakdown in submarines and had been sent to Dartmouth to recuperate. Another colourful character was Lieut. Lord Burghersh, who rather scandalised the Captain by having one of the leading actresses of the day, Julia James, a charming girl, down to visit him there. We all hoped he might elope with her! To get back to the teaching, the Head of History, Mr. Hodges, was a great inspiration to me. A pleasant summer holiday, a part of which was spent at Wellclose, when to my great surprise we were told by Admiralty that all our term would go to sea as Midshipmen in September, and would not go back to Dartmouth to complete our three or four more terms. This was rather a surprise! My first feeling was I fear one of regret having to put my beloved motorcycle into storage for the rest of the war, but soon the excitement of “going to sea” and serving in the war overshadowed everything else. I was only fifteen at the time but remember that in our past history midshipmen of only fourteen years of age were sent to sea! A busy time getting all one’s uniform from the redoubtable Mr Gieves [in Savile Row, London] and nobody could have helped more than old Aunt Bessie (Miss Newton-King), who by now regarded us as one of her family and we were known as “honorary nephews”. 1917 So one September evening when London was having one of its few air raids, I went up with Auntie Bessie to King’s Cross to catch the Naval Special train to Inverness. The train was delayed, so I went into the street to see if I could see anything of the air raid. I was not lucky, beyond seeing any number of searchlight beams in the sky and hearing an occasional bang from an anti-aircraft gun. Lots of other midshipmen in my term were on the train, and we soon started comparing notes. The men who were destined for the Battle Cruisers left the train at Edinburgh, and we were taken charge of by an old Lieutenant. The others went on to Inverness, where we arrived in the evening to report to the Resident Naval Officer there. He said there were no more trains to Thurso, the terminus for which we were bound, so went to the emergency accommodation which seemed to be always available at the Inverness Station Hotel. On arrival in Thurso, after a lovely journey on a single line railway through the north of Scotland, going through Invergordon, Tain, Bonar Bridge, Golspie and many other small places, we were told to embark in the ferry which would sail to Scapa Flow some time during the night. I had time to stretch my legs around Thurso, and what a bleak and poor little 30

place it was, all the children were barefooted because I am told shoes were expensive luxuries which their parents could not afford. Even then, late September, Thurso was windswept and cold. The Resident Naval Officer who met the train was a jovial old Captain with a wooden leg, and who did not let this impede him. A twinkle in his eye for the many little midshipmen who he addressed as “young gentlemen”. A bus took us down to the harbour where Thurso/Scapa ferry was lying. It was blowing quite hard, so we delayed our departure until the tide turned and the notorious Pentland Firth would not be so rough. This Firth, with one of the fastest currents met anywhere, can in certain conditions of sea be a most dangerous place to cross, for very short yet big seas are generated which on one occasion nearly swamped a battleship. We set off after midnight and got quite a gruelling going across the Firth which made quite a lot of us pretty squeamish. Nevertheless, soon after seven we passed the Gutter Sound entrance to Scapa Flow, and moored alongside the old Imperieuse which was the depot ship whose duty it was to handle all personnel, and also all fleet mail for the Grand Fleet. Gutter Sound is hidden from the flow proper and all one could see was rows upon rows of destroyers with their depot ships, and the Rear Admiral D’s cruiser flagship. The islands (Flotta, Garve, Faros etc. etc.) which surround the flow are all low lying except for the westernmost one, the island of Hoy, which on its western side falls sharply into the Atlantic Ocean. This can be seen in Claude Muncaster’s picture of the Hood steaming through the Pentland Firth in our drawing room, and in fact the place where Lord Kitchener was lost when in 1916 HMS Hampshire was mined on her way to Russia. It was I remember a fine but blustery day at the end of September, and we were soon mustered in groups who would soon embark in various drifters to deliver passengers and mail to ships of the Grand Fleet. HMS Neptune was a battleship of the 4th Battle Squadron, whose flagship was HMS Hercules in which Admiral Sturdee of Falkland Island fame flew his flag.14 Our turn soon came, and about a dozen midshipmen, of which two others were for the Neptune, Alexander and Scott, of my term boarded the drifter which in peacetime was a sturdily built fishing drifter. What a sight met the eye as we steamed through the channel between Flotta and Fara! Rows after rows of battleships. There was the fleet flagship, HMS Queen Elizabeth, with Admiral Beatty flying his flag.15 Then the First Battle Squadron with Revenge, Admiral Madden’s flagship, and four other R’s class battleships and four Iron Duke class battleships.16 Then the 2nd Battle Squadron with Admiral de Robeck in the King George V Battleship, and four others of her class and four Orion class battleships with Erin and Agincourt, the ships we were building for Turkey when the war broke out, to make up numbers.17 Next came our own squadron, the fourth Battle Squadron of eight ships, all armed with 12-inch guns, and away anchored a little further out in the Flow were the four battleships of the 5th Battle Squadron with Barham as the flagship. They were our latest ships, armed with 15-inch guns 14 Admiral Sir Frederick Sturdee (1859-1925), ODNB. The Battle of the Falklands was against Admiral Von Spee’s German cruiser squadron in December 1914. 15 Admiral Lord Beatty (1871-1936), ODNB. He was at this time Commander-in-chief of the Grand Fleet. 16 Admiral Sir Charles Madden (1862-1935), ODNB. 17 Admiral Sir John de Robeck (1862-1928), Commander of the 3rd Battle Squadron of the Grand Fleet. 31

and probably the most formidable battle squadron in the world. Then a number of cruiser squadrons, mostly of the Southampton class, were anchored on the flanks of the battleships. What an absolutely breathtaking sight, all anchored in this inland flow about fifteen miles long and nine or ten miles wide. Little things one notices, and one of these was the amazing clearness of the water. One could see under the surface down to nearly thirty feet, and the outlines of the underwater features of the ships we visited. This was I suppose the largest and certainly most formidable fleet the world has ever seen, and gave one an impression of silent power never to be forgotten. It never occurred to me that forty years later I should command the British Fleet but, alas, a much smaller one than I now saw. As we steamed round the 4th Battle Squadron, disembarking mail for the ships’ officers, I looked for Neptune which was third in the line headed by the Squadron flagship Hercules. On deck I saw the Commander, Hamilton, carrying a telescope, who gave us a gruff but quite a warm welcome. Perhaps he remembered when he joined his first ship, probably twenty years earlier. I think he said, “Welcome aboard the Neptune”, and then sent for the Sub-Lieutenant of the Gunroom, Derek Stevens, to take charge of us, show us our quarters and what were our duties. Perhaps a little bewildering for a little boy not quite sixteen years of age, but we were given forty-eight hours to “sling our hammock” as the old service saying is. We had one of the Bandsmen who actually slung our hammocks for us, and in a desultory sort of way looked after our clothes. The Gunroom contained about eighteen or nineteen midshipmen, Assistant Clerks as they were then called, and Sub-Lieutenants. Rather cramped quarters, but we all just could sit down at meals together. Though in some gunrooms of the fleet there was some bullying of the junior midshipmen, there was none of this in the Neptune. We had an officer who was known as Snottie’s Nurse to look after us and ensure we learnt all we should as young officers. Ridler, the Gunnery Officer, started off with us but was relieved by Clayton, the Navigating Officer, shortly after we joined. Later in the morning the Sub. took us off to see the Captain, Capt.V.N.G Bernard, a little man in stature. He did not impress us much, though in a rather cold way he gave us some encouragement. I think he then knew he was shortly to be relieved and go on promotion to Rear Admiral as the Admiral Superintendent of Chatham Dockyard. Quite a pleasant if not very exciting set of companions in the Gunroom, who soon reminded us we must remember that junior midshipmen are the lowest of God’s creatures! The routine was as follows. We started the day at 6 a.m. with P.T on the Quarter Deck with the ship’s pretty tough Physical Training Instructor, or if a gig or whaler was available, we rowed around the Squadron. Later in the year and in January we found these P.T exercises in a freezing Atlantic gale far from pleasant, but I expect it helped to toughen us up! Then the usual harbour routine, Divisions at 9 o’clock sharp, at which the Padre took prayers, then usually throughout the day some form of instruction, navigation, gunnery, torpedo and engineering were the main subjects to be as it were book taught, but seamanship was practically taught. The old first Lieutenant, “Gaffer” Dolphin as he was known, gave us a very thorough grounding in anchor and cable work. In those days officers had little money to spare. My pay 32

Mountaineous seas! was 4/3d per day [approx. 21p.], out of which my mess bill took a good half. Officers were HMS St Vincent from HMS Neptune very frugal – I remember one evening finding the Gunnery Officer sitting down in his cabin darning his socks and being told by him the sooner I learnt how to use a darning needle the better. Some officers were married, but in the rather austere atmosphere in which we lived wives were never mentioned. The officers were bye and large a steady average lot, but none reached any height in the Navy beyond the Commander, who I think became a Rear Admiral, and Derek Stevens, the sub who became a Captain and who I relieved in 1943 in Mauritius. One of the very good young Lieutenants (Chamberlain) volunteered for the attack on Zeebrugge and was killed there, I don’t think any of the Gunroom reached Commander’s rank other than Stevens and self, but after the war the wastage of officers was high. Out of working hours, we took time in watchkeeping, and by that means one soon found as a good “midshipman of the watch” one could learn quite a lot of seamanship. Then for recreation we went for walks on the islands surrounding the Flow, and sometimes played golf, usually with some borrowed clubs, on the island of Flotta. The walks were great fun, and not infrequently we persuaded some of the local farms to give us tea with wonderful baps, scones and eggs. These generous farm folk not infrequently absolutely refused to take any payment for teas from midshipmen. There were few if any games facilities at Scapa, so we had to make our own recreation. We got ashore whenever we could, as at our age plenty of exercise was necessary. Ships exercised under way with what are known as subcalibre practices in the Flow most weeks. This consists of fitting in the main armament guns small “rifles” with a range of about 5,000 yards, firing a small solid shell weighing some 6 lbs. In this way all the controls can be 33

exercised without properly firing the guns with their heavy shells weighing some 850lbs [approx..385 kilos]. Then about every four to five weeks we would steam out in the Pentland Firth and carry out full calibre firing against a battle practice target. The firing of our 12-inch guns, sometimes all together, in broadsides with their muzzle velocities of 2800 ft a second made a tremendous and quite frightening noise - anyway that was my first impression on hearing a broadside discharged. I thought the end of the world had come, and from then onwards always wore ear drum protection with scrupulous care, which probably accounts for the fact that my hearing was as good in retirement as when I joined, even after in the last war my ship bombarded the enemy more times than any other cruiser afloat! About every six weeks the Commander-in-Chief took the Grand Fleet to sea for what are known as P.Z. exercises. They were in fact tactical exercises on the grand scale, where parts of the Fleet were pitted against another, and they were intended and succeeded in getting ships to work together cohesively and, in a sense, know each other. For when action is joined the minimum of signals are used and these don’t always get through, so it was essential to know what one’s divisional, squadron and Fleet Commander wants. Then of course there were the occasional scares when it was reported the [German] High Sea Fleet had put to sea. As far as I remember they only put to sea as a whole Fleet twice or perhaps three times when I was serving in Neptune. Once they were missed by ill chance and last minute change of plan on their part, and another time the sortie was very half hearted and they turned back long before they could be brought to action. In addition, units of the Grand Fleet used to go to sea to cover the convoys from Bergen, whose escorts the destroyers Mary Rose and Strongbow had been sunk fairly recently by a fast German raiding force. We did this on one occasion in company with the battleship St. Vincent, and the framed photograph taken of St Vincent from Neptune shows what mountainous seas one met in the winter of 1917/1918. I remember the trip vividly, for we shipped quite a lot of water. Battleships tend to go through the seas rather than over them, hence a lot of water comes onboard some of which finds its way below, and I think not a member of the Gunroom avoided being seasick! Climbing up the struts of the foremast to my action station in the foretop situated at the top of the foremast was a rather hazardous job, for if one fell off or was blown off one would probably fall into the sea where the chances of rescue in those sea conditions were negligible. It was also very cold, for in those days we were not provided with proper arctic clothing. We relied on the generous supplies of scarves and woollies provided by our families and voluntary workers in England. On these occasions we remained “closed up” at action stations from dawn to dusk, a pretty long stretch for a young midshipman just after his sixteenth birthday. I think I must have been too young to get bored, but there is no doubt these long periods based at Scapa Flow proved boring to older men. Life was enlivened by coaling ship, an evolution [i.e. action] which was conducted on return to harbour and at other intervals, when we seldom fell below [loading at the] 300 to 400 tons per hour rate. Everybody took part in this evolution, and nobody was excused and there used to be keen competition between ships to get the best input average per hour. Anything over 300 tons an hour was good and over 400 tons was exceptional. We used not to do too badly in Neptune, and thanks on one occasion to the gallant action of one of the Petty Officers in charge of distributing the sacks of coal to the bunkers I was not crowned by a hoist from the collier, which broke and came onboard faster than I had expected! Perhaps if he had not 34

dragged me out of the way in time I might not be writing this account. A very nice oldfashioned Petty Officer, who was I suspect a little embarrassed when I gave him a Christmas present later of a nice leather wallet! Coaling was not popular, everybody and the whole ship got absolutely filthy with coal dust and the meals for at least twenty-four hours after finishing tasted of coal dust. Everybody looked like the coal miners who had just come up from working in the coal face. There were no “bright lights” of any sort at Scapa, though a big canteen had been built in Flotta which was deservedly very popular. Towards the end of 1917 volunteers were called for to take part in a very dangerous operation which, though we did not know it at the time, was for the storming of Zeebrugge. I and one or two volunteered, only to be told some months later that we were too young to be accepted! Although quite right, as we felt at the Dardanelles young midshipmen performed with effect, so why should not mature sixteenyear-olds such as us not be accepted! One of the Wardroom Lieutenants was accepted and was killed in the attack on the mole at Zeebrugge. A very good officer indeed, who stood out head and shoulders above the other Lieutenants. Sometimes one got ashore for a few hours, and much enjoyed walking through the heather and scrub on the various islands. The “north shore” island on which the towns of Kirkwall and Stromness were situated was the most popular. The former was the capital of the Orkneys, a rather dour little town which relied for its livelihood on fishing trawlers whose crews were tough and magnificent seamen. Stromness was much the most picturesque little town with narrow streets and overhanging houses, all built as it were to give shelter from the Atlantic and Arctic gales which mercilessly hit the town. There was nothing much to buy except the few odd curios, and it certainly did not seem as if any new houses had been built in the little town for the last two or three hundred years. The Orkneys are completely windswept, and I located I think the only trees there in a sheltered part of the manse garden in the village of Longhope [South Walls Island]. By way of recreation, we had a cinema which was turned by hand by the Chief Yeoman of Signals, a very formidable black bearded C.P.O. who was held in awe and fear by all the signal boys on the flag deck! Apart from occasional concerts got up by the ships company and boxing tournaments, the ship’s company had little recreation at Scapa. So as to be nearer the German bases and enable the personnel of the Fleet to get some much needed recreation, it was decided to move the main Fleet base from Scapa Flow to Rosyth, a move which eventually took place in the early summer of 1918. The progress of the war did not seem to be of great interest in the Gunroom though every now and again we heard of a brother or great friend being killed on the Western front. This was when I heard of Rupert Ffolkes death, which hit one hard at the time for I suppose he was my closest friend. His parents never really got over it, for I remember when we all stayed at Cougham Lodge, near King’s Lynn, before the war how they adored him but never to the extent of spoiling. Sybil Fflokes, his mother, was one of my mother’s greatest friends. Of the “boys”, as old Miss Newton-King used to call us all, Rex and Pierce Newton-King and Rupert Fflokes were killed, and only Richard Newton-King and I survived. A heavy toll of outstandingly promising and able young men to fall. 35

I used to hear regularly from my parents, who both wrote regularly each week. Their letters were of great interest, not too long and not too short, which enabled one to picture their life in India. The mail was eagerly awaited. In the Gunroom we learnt customs of the mess life not too painfully, and learnt that as a Naval Officer you must never admit anything was impossible! On the whole the midshipmen in the Gunroom were a nice lot. Tidd, Hobbs, Lucy, Manders, Rose, Bisgood, de Moleyns, Bodoano, Philpotts, Burroughs, Alexander, Scott and self and a couple of Assistant Clerks which one would now call Paymaster Midshipmen! Not very brilliant but sociable. Quite a number left the Navy after the war, some lost their lives early on after the war and in fact I think I was the only midshipmen who reached Commander’s rank! Though the Neptune was regarded as one of the older and out of date battleships she was only six years old when I joined her, and in very good shape. Our Captain was soon relieved by Captain Slayter, a typical grey bearded old seaman who was an uncle of a great friend of mine, Admiral Sir William Slayter, since deceased. An impressive character whom we held in holy awe. Then the Admiral of the Squadron, “Hooky” Browning because he had only one hand having lost the other in the breech block of a gun which closed too quickly for him. A very formidable character, and a fighting Admiral in all senses of the word. His flagship Hercules, whilst admiring him, were also pretty frightened of him. But I am discoursing too widely. We soon learnt the meaning of all signals, and were looking for the signal ‘Q0’ which meant ‘raise steam with all despatch’, and as a corollary ‘be prepared for battle after leaving harbour’. We never saw this, but read some of the lesser urgency such as ‘raise steam for full speed with moderate despatch’. I interested myself much in Gunnery, and soon invented and designed a deflection calculating machine which gave one the amount necessary to offset one’s aim due to wind, range, gyroscopic effect of ships and miscellaneous other causes to hit the target. This was rather scornfully received by the Gunnery officer of that time, ‘Victor Danckwerts’ a very clever man indeed who eventually quarrelled with Winston Churchill in the Second World War when he was Director of Plans. A bit arrogant – I still remember his remarks to me when I said in support of an argument ‘I thought’, he said ‘Young man you are not paid to think’. But a very clever man, who I believe in spite of his propensity to speak his mind and support it with ruthless logic should have made more use of in the Second World War. Baldwin Walker was the torpedo officer, and succeeded by Howse. The former, also a clever man, I believe after the first war inherited a title and left the Navy. But I knew his kinsman, Admiral Wake Walker, one time Controller of the Navy in the Second World War. Ships refitted once a year, usually in a floating dock in Invergordon, when to our intense joy we were given just over a fortnight’s leave. Our time for this did not come until the summer of 1918. The joy of going to Rosyth in the spring of 1918 and seeing our splendid battlecruiser fleet, Lion, Tiger, Princess Royal, Repulse and Renown was marked. Then the Americans joined us and formed the 6th Battle Squadron, with the Texas, Wyoming and three or four other battleships to form a most effective Squadron. They enthusiastically joined in all our activities, and became very much a part of the Grand Fleet. 36

We were host ship to Wyoming and made many friends among her officers, who rank for rank were a bit older than we were. A splendid set of men. Their discipline was stricter than ours, for quite a minor leave breaking offence the culprit would find himself in for a good stretch of penal servitude! Rosyth enabled one to go up to Edinburgh for a short spell. Shore leave was from 1:30pm till 7pm, and arrangements were made for early recall if one’s ship was ordered to sea. What a joy it was to see civilisation again. Some kind people had put up a Junior Officers’ club at the head of Hawes Pier in South Queensferry in which we could get tea. A very popular rendezvous for hungry midshipmen. I remember going to some rambles through Lord Dalmeny’s woods near Dalmeny, and Lord Linlithgow’s woods at Hopetown quite without knowing to whom they belonged. We put up a few wild cock pheasants who were much too wily to fall to a midshipman’s wiles! Time passed quite quickly, and we kept wondering and hoping the German High Seas Fleet would give us a chance to put into practice the work we had put in to get our respective ships into a battle worthy condition. It must have been in July or early August that our time for refitting in the dry dock at Invergordon arrived, and how we looked forward to that fortnight’s leave, in our case sixteen days as the completion date was delayed due to some extra defects having been found which had to be corrected. As soon as the ship was safely docked we raced up to Invergordon station and crammed into the special which took us to London, where we all dispersed to our homes. I went straight to Slough to the Newton-Kings, picked up by my motor bicycle and rode off straight away up to Asfordby where my sister and brother were staying with the Yates, whose family always gave us an enormous welcome. Lois was a little older than I and Adelaide about the same age as my brother. What a wonderful holiday, the first we had for nearly a year. Many strenuous games of tennis, and I soon found I had got back into form. Colonel Charles and Mrs Yate, as they then were, were the most hospitable people and treated us as one of their family. He was the M.P. for the Melton Mowbray Division, and I could see how popular they both were, as they wholeheartedly did to the best of their ability look after their constituents’ interests. As August wore on it was clear we were winning great battles in France on the Western front, and we believed in the Gunroom the war would be brought to a finish in 1919. Suddenly we heard in October that the Germans were putting out feelers for peace, so more than ever we expected the German Fleet to come out and attack us. As it now appears they attempted to do this, but some ships mutinied rather than take part in a forlorn hope, so the German High Command called off the attempt. Then on the 11th November 1918, just one month after my seventeenth birthday, we heard the Germans had signed the Armistice. I think every ship’s siren in the Grand Fleet hooted its joy, and not a few sailors obtained something to drink! Our first feeling I think was of sadness that now we would never be able to put to the test this wonderful fighting Fleet. 37

The British Grand Fleet The Grand Fleet of Great Britain – probably the biggest and most powerful Fleet in the world’s history. Looking across rows upon rows of battleships and multitudinous cruisers and destroyers one wondered “what happens next”. Soon it would be our task to receive the surrender of the German Fleet, which was one of the terms of the Armistice. There was a general air of relaxation onboard, though we were still a bit shaken from the world wide flu epidemic which had struck the Fleet about a month before. I got it but not badly, and I think onboard Neptune we lost only a very few of the lower deck and none of the officers. One stayed “turned in” in one’s hammock for a few days and soon perked up. But we had many discussions in the Gunroom – would the Germans really surrender their Fleet or would they come out for a last fight? We unanimously hoped for the latter, so we were more determined we should give of our best if the crunch came! At this stage all our thoughts were on the war, and I never remember anybody speculating on what sort of a world we were entering! The morning of Thursday, 21st November, was a dull and rather misty morning but without much wind. The Grand Fleet unmoored during the night and went to sea. The 4th Battle Squadron, being the furthest up the Firth, just opposite Grangemouth and Lord Elgin’s property on the north side, were the last to pass under the Forth Bridge. The plan of the surrender was to be – the Grand Fleet split into two lines and the German Fleet, led by one of our cruisers, HMS Cardiff, to steam down between the lines before they anchored in berths allotted to them in Leith Roads opposite the suburb of Edinburgh. I was midshipman of the watch on the bridge in the forenoon watch when we were expected to make contact with the German Fleet to the east of Moy Island. There was an air of suppressed excitement, everybody was at ‘action stations’, until we intercepted the signal from Cardiff to the Commander-in-Chief that they had met the German Fleet deployed in single line ahead at the arranged rendezvous. We still kept at action stations, but as far as one could in those days 38

all men at action stations were kept informed of what was happening. Then as the Grand Fleet drew abreast of the German battleships each column turned 180 degrees in succession and steamed back towards the Firth in parallel courses at a range from the centre column comprising the German ships of about three miles. HMS Neptune We were all straining our eyes to catch a first sight of the German ships, and sure enough there they were, looming up out of the mist just like we had learned to recognise them from the recognition cards issued to all control positions. I remember clearly recognising the Baden, their latest 15 inch gun battleship, then the battlecruisers Derflnger, Molke, Von derTann and, sure enough, also their battleships keeping quite good stations. I think perhaps one’s first feeling was of relief that here on this cold and misty November morning was the Fleet who had challenged our country for our age long control of the seas. As we saw the German ships in the mist anchoring in Leith Roads the whole Grand Fleet formed up in single line and steamed past the Fleet Flagship, the Queen Elizabeth, and cheered our Commander-in-Chief, Sir David Beatty, to the echo, and what cheers we gave him! I think folk in both north and south Queensferry could have heard our cheers. One could see the C-in-C clearly as he stood out in a prominent position on the Q.E.’s bridge, and acknowledged our cheers with a generous smile. What a fine figure he was, courage and determination were writ large on every feature of his fine face. I like to think the Neptune’s cheer was as good if not better than anybody else’s.18 Then back to our berth just as it was getting dark, in time to read Admiral Beatty’s signal to the German Fleet before sunset that “At sunset today the German Flag is to be hauled down and not hoisted again without permission”. There was a pretty gay night onboard, and I am certain the “port” was passed round the Mess more than once. 18 David Beatty, 1st Earl Beatty (1871-1936), ODNB; see also Rodgers for an assessment of Beatty and his influence. 39

The next morning I think there was a slight feeling of anti-climax, not that midshipmen just passed their seventeenth birthday had much time to appreciate it. The first thing I remember was the chance of some leave, and getting back to my beloved motorcycle. Then I should see my father and mother, at any rate in the not too far distant future, as in one of his letters he told me his time in India would be up in a few years’ time and he was longing to come home and settle in England. In fact he took a year’s leave in May 1919, and then retired directly afterwards on reaching retiring age which was then fifty-five. My mother had not been very well in India, and had some acute abdominal pains which the doctor said was probably due to passing stones. She was never strong, so perhaps we did not realise this illness foreshadowed her death a few years later. Having won the Great War, as it was then called, we imagined the British Empire would be greater and more important than ever before. We believed with the collapse of Russia there would only be two great powers left, the British Empire and the United States of America whose immense strength and potential we had hardly begun to appreciate. France was regarded perhaps as a bit of a lame duck, to be rescued by the British Empire. We did not perhaps realise the immense sacrifices France had made on the Western Front. The Germans we regarded as beaten anyway for our lifetime and not likely to be a trouble again to us. Africa could we believed now be almost wholly British, and the dreams of some imperialists would come true. How little did we realise events in the generation to follow would wholly falsify our hopes! It was soon made clear that with demobilisation all the old 12 inch gun battleships of which Neptune was one would be paid off and put into reserve. As a special concession all who had served in the war would be entitled in due course to six weeks leave when that could be arranged. It never I think seriously occurred to us that the British Navy would be reduced to a fraction the size it was now, and that maybe the all-pervading Pax Brittanica was on the way out, but this did not happen until the second world war, about twenty one years later. In December the old Neptune moved into Rosyth dockyard, and from there we embarked in special leave trains shunted into the yard. 1919 The time soon came for us to leave the old Neptune for the last time. Not that she was really old – only eight years since her first commission! But at the rate which we built ships before the war she soon became dated. The Senior midshipmen, about two years older than my lot who were the most junior of all, soon took their exams for acting sub-lieutenants, and the way things were being put back, it was clear none of us would be sub-lieutenants by our eighteenth birthday as we had hoped! We were perhaps a little sad to leave the old Neptune, though our time in her had not left any lasting impression. Unlike some Gunrooms in the Fleet we were quite moderately happy, but I don’t think at that time I had any ambitions to build a successful Naval career. 40

Victory Parade, 1919, with Admiral Arrangements had to be made for some force of battleships to look after the German Ships, Beatty leading the naval contingnets. which after a spell in Leith roads were sailed for Scapa Flow where they were to be interned until the peace treaty had decided what was to be done to these formidable warships, which had in some ways proved to be more than a match ship for ship with ours. I remember one day landing at Hawes Pier at South Queensferry on my way up to Edinburgh, just catching sight of the German Warships, dull and already a bit bedraggled. I wondered what the officers were thinking and whether they had any midshipmen onboard. 1919 was a hectic year for us, and with the newfound freedom conferred by a motorbike I took the fullest advantage of it, though there was still some form of petrol rationing as, indeed, there was also some food rationing, but the old Miss Newton-Kings made light of any difficulties. News that my father and mother hoped to be home in early summer cheered us up no end. My sister Janie had turned into an outstandingly pretty girl, and with my younger brother who was at Marlborough College enjoyed life to the full. What a six weeks’ leave we had, visiting all our friends. Already many of one’s friends who were about to be demobilised wondered what they were going to do. But perhaps the euphoria of winning the war and Lloyd George’s slogan at the Khaki election to make ‘the country fit for heroes to live in’ dominated one’s thoughts. Contrary to what some people say now they made quite tremendous efforts, but I don’t think it was apparent that our country had suffered an economic decline really ever since the turn of the century. Some of my friends were all for emigrating to the colonies – alas only a few made good for none of us realised to be successful in the colonies you needed a lot more financial support than any of us had. 41

We had inevitably some industrial trouble, including a railway strike, but with the sweeping majority in the Coalition Government headed by Lloyd George most of our disputes were resolved by good sense. In April the Grand Fleet ceased to exist, and ships were distributed to the main fleets, mostly to form the new Atlantic Fleet. Then after leaving Neptune I was when on leave appointed to HMS Barham, the flagship of the famous Fifth Battle Squadron. This pleased me much, for these were the finest battleships we had, armed with 8 fifteen inch guns and capable of speed of 25 knots. We had a cheerful if rather undisciplined Gunroom in Barham, but we certainly enjoyed ourselves. Cawdor, whose father had once been First Lord of Admiralty, was our Senior midshipman. Admiral Leveson, called “Levi” rather uncharitably, was the Admiral in charge of the Squadron and Madden was the C-in-C of the Atlantic Fleet with his flag in Queen Elizabeth. Horne was the Captain and Wellwood Maxwell, a great character, the Commander. A good if rather wild set of Lieutenants in the Wardroom, who were very good to the midshipmen! In fact Barham was a happy if slightly easy-going ship and the midshipmen Page from midhshipman’s log, kept in certainly never overworked themselves. I am sorry to record that for over six months I never Barham by WWD with many attended any form of set instruction in the ship! I suppose it was a little bit the general post technical drawings and charts. war reaction, but nothing to be proud about! One kept wondering throughout 1919 whether it would be a good plan to leave the Navy, for some of the yarns we heard of life in the peace time Navy were not encouraging. Some of my contemporaries went, some prospered and quite a lot did not. This was a constant theme of discussion in the Gunroom. Then in the summer, in I think June, the Barham and her Squadron went to Southend, and we landed big contingents for the Victory march through London. It was steamingly hot, and it was a question whether some of the Admirals could last the course for marching was not always their strong suit! We as midshipmen thoroughly enjoyed the prospect of a good march. The sailors’ remarks were to the point, and there were any number of cockneys among them who kept up a running fire of banter with the crowd. But what a sight it was! The march past culminated outside Buckingham Palace where the King, Queen and their principal Ministers were assembled to take the salute. The Navy was led by Admiral Beatty, who looked more debonair than ever wearing his three button monkey jacket, which was in marked contrast to the King who wore the standard uniform four button monkey jacket.19 We started in I think Hyde Park, and then went up Victoria Street, up Whitehall, along the Mall, past Buckingham Palace. The crowd went absolutely mad, 19 WWD was mistaken here. In the photograph the King is wearing military rather than naval uniform. 42

and we were cheered and cheered. I remember one old lady saying to me ‘Come on laddie, smile better than that’. But as to be expected the whole day was truly a memorable one, and how wonderful the King looked as he took my Company’s salute. I thought he looked everybody through and through, and how proud I thought he looked as his old Service the Navy marched past, at the head of the Fighting Services. But I am jumping ahead. My parents arrived home in I think June and, as to be expected, stayed for a few days in Regents Park Terrace with my Uncle Jim whilst they were looking round for somewhere to stay. What a welcome they gave us, and I thought both of them looked well and younger then I had expected. It was fun feeling now they were home for good, and we would have our own house to go to when on leave. This was to us something special, as though our various guardians could not have been kinder and more thoughtful, a young person or child has only one home and that is with its parents! My father looked young and fit for his years and it was difficult to realise he was just over fifty four. Looking close to mother one could see the lines in her face showing here and there, and one sensed she had some recent agonising pains. We learnt by chance that mother had been awarded the M.B.E for her splendid work with the women in Central India, who did under her inspiration much useful war work. These were the days before the Army, and for that matter the Navy, provided all the clothing required and a lot was left to voluntary work. Mother played it down very much as she was very sad, and I know so was my father, that he never received any order or form of recognition for his outstanding services to the people of India from the Government. He never, never mentioned this to me though the Indian Government should have recognised in his thirty five years pretty hazardous service in India, how he finally steered Bhopal, which was the second biggest Muslim state in India, through our declaration of war on Turkey, which was then the spiritual head of the Mohammedans, at what was a difficult time for the Empire. But father was philosophical about it all, especially as he had proved himself an outstanding Frontier Officer, and always maintained that the true reward was in the satisfaction one gets from work well done. Maybe father, who could be very outspoken and forthright as his own diary shows, had ruffled some feathers in influential places! But, anyway, you will see father’s campaign medals in the family medal case, which records where he served. We spent summer holidays at Poultry Court in the Hyett’s park at Painswick, and very pleasant it was with lots of tennis and motorbiking. I had thought of leaving the Navy, but already then the supply of young men far exceeded the jobs available. My father warned me against going in for some of the plausible fruit growing schemes in South Africa, Canada and Australia as he wisely observed that a lot more financial backing is required than the advertisements would have one believe. I thought with my record at Dartmouth, where I was top in most engineering subjects, I would have no difficulty in finding a post, but all I could get was the promise that one might be considered after one had fully qualified in a two or three year course at either a University or Technical College at one’s own expense! The Atlantic Fleet did some cruises to Spanish ports like Arosa Bay and Vigo Bay, which was a pleasant change from the North Sea. These places were pretty rugged, especially Arosa Bay where most of the farming folk seem to be living at or near subsistence level. 43

We changed our Captain and Admiral towards the end of 1919. Old Nicholson, known as “Thumby” Nick, replaced Leveson who went as C-in-C China, and a terrific character, Bob Dalgleish, became Captain. Bob Dalgleish had been a great athlete in his day, and was still a fencer of international class when he took over Barham. He was an inspiring character, and the midshipmen would have done anything for him. In the Autumn the Admiralty very wisely decided to give all midshipmen training in destroyers, to which we were appointed singly for a period of about six months. This was a quite admirable break in our training, and suddenly one realised one was a “grown up” officer in the Wardroom. I was appointed to HMS Thanet, one of the new ‘S’ class destroyers, with a great character and a bit of a wild Irishman as the Captain. He was Commander J.V. Creagh, who had a distinguished career with a D.S.O. in the Harwich force during the war. What a man he was, and he took endless trouble telling me all about the Navy and the reasons for its rather quaint customs! The First Lieutenant was Lt. Faulkner, a senior Lieutenant who had commanded during the war and was the first officer to win the Distinguished Service Cross at, I think, the Heligoland Bight action. Also very encouraging and, by a strange coincidence, his father, who had a living in Devon, was acting at Lythe and, with the Bishop of Whitby, married us fourteen years later! A very good Wardroom in Thanet, who made one most welcome and treated one as a grown up officer. December 1919 We were due for service in the Baltic, where we were supporting the White Russians – General Yudenitch and others, against the Bolsheviks.20 Our C.M.B.s earlier in the year had successfully attacked units of the Russian Fleet in Kronstadt Bay in the approaches to Petrograd [St. Petersburg]. Lt. Cmd. Aga won the V.C. and a number of C.M.B.s were sunk in the attack. In the Baltic States there were a lot of warring factions. General von der Goltz, a German General, was leading a considerable force of near freebooters who recognised no armistice between his country, Germany, and either the Allies or the Russians.21 We soon set sail for Copenhagen, which we reached in mid-December to find the harbour frozen over solid and great floes of ice in the Belts, the approaches to the Baltic. It was very cold indeed, and one of our destroyers, the Seawolf I think, had got into trouble with freezing onboard and became pretty top heavy! We lay alongside the wharf, which is well in the centre of Copenhagen, and a few curious onlookers visited the ship. There was not much in the shops other than furs. Soon after arrival we left for Libau [modern Liepāja], which was one of the main ports of Latvia, where we had a military mission under a very young Col. Alexander, later Lord Alexander of Tunis. He and his staff had a determined and robust outlook, and managed in keeping Von der Goltz and his Germans out of Libau and Riga, the two main ports of Latvia. We had a charming young White Russian liaison officer living on board. He was utterly carefree and never missed an opportunity for a party at which he always let himself go and sang Russian songs, whilst he danced wild Russian dances. The only form of 20 Nikolay Yudenich (1860-1933), leader of White Russian attacks on the Bolshevik government 1919-1920. He quarrelled with the Estonians and his British advisers and died in exile in France. 21 General Rüdiger von der Goltz (1865-1946) tried to build a German Baltic government based in Latvia in the turbulent years after the Russian revolution. He was defeated by an Estonian-Latvian force and forced to retreat to East Prussia. 44

exercise was skating and playing ice hockey, at which we became quite adept. Skating by myself on the lake near Libau one day I fell in, because I had not noticed the ice had been cut an hour or so before to draw fresh water and only lightly frozen over. I swam to the nearest firm ice, climbed on it and soon skated off to the ship. By the time I reached the ship my clothes were completely frozen stiff. A lesson not to be too adventurous! Many meetings at Libau with the local White Russians, who seemed much encouraged by the presence of a British warship. Our next mission was to Hango, a port in Finland which can only be reached through the Aaland Islands at the entrance to the Gulf of Bothnia. A fascinating trip, following the ice breaker through these Islands which looked just like fairy tale islands, very pretty and mostly uninhabited. Occasionally a man would skate out to the ship and welcome us in Finnish, and we usually gave him a loaf of bread and a packet of tea, a drink much liked by the Finns. Hango, which is not far from Helsinki, is a dull and cold looking little port, so for that matter would most places seem in that cold January in the Baltic We collected Lieutenant Napier, one of the officers who had been sunk and captured by the Bolsheviks from the C.M.B.s which attacked Kronstadt and, I think, two ratings, a mechanic and a Stoker Petty Officer. They were all in pretty poor shape, having endured the rigours of Russian prisons for some seven or eight months. Their descriptions of what they had to eat would have been considered tough even in the Middle Ages. It must, however, be remembered that large parts of Russia were at that time in the grip of a famine. They were also pretty shaken, for the treatment they received in prison was brutal in the extreme. 1920 After talking to our Consul in Finland, who had brought the ‘prisoners’ to the ship, we delayed little and were soon on our way to Danzig [Gdansk] where we went as Guard Ship. Danzig was not sure, nor were we, whether they would end up in Germany or Poland and was being administered by a wise old British General whose name I think was Haining. Our Captain was just the chap for a tricky international situation, and his handling of some bombastic Germans who thought they were going to run things was quite admirable. I found my own German soon came back, and I could make myself understood in Danzig. There was virtually nothing in the shops, though as ever the night clubs were still going. We went to one or two, and found life there was pretty stimulating. James Creagh was a great man for leading a party. He always ensured it was the maximum of fun without ever getting out of hand! Then some cruising in the Baltic, which still was dreadfully cold, before returning to Copenhagen. A visit to Flensburg in Jutland, and we set sail for Rosyth. The Captain had his doubts about the accuracy of our standard magnetic compass by which we steered, for these were the days before Gyro compasses, so he told me for I had the morning watch as officer of the watch to look out for anything strange. As dawn broke and we approached the Scottish coast I looked out especially hard, and found we were steaming up the Firth of Tay and not the Firth of Forth. This was soon corrected, and it was not long before we were berthed in the Penns at Port Edgar, which was the main destroyer base during and, indeed, after the war. Life in Thanet was great fun, for destroyers and wardrooms were as friendly a crowd as one 45

would meet anywhere, and one made any number of friends. About this time the new Naval Engineering Scheme came out, in which the Admiralty said that officers specialising in ‘E’ would not be precluded from posts in the executive branch. As I had won many prizes in Marine Engineering, and had perhaps a little aptitude for the subject, I applied to become an ‘E’ specialist. But James Creagh had other ideas, without saying so he thought the Admiralty would go back on their promise as in fact they did, and one’s whole career would be narrowed by becoming an ‘E’ specialist, so he tore up my application and said he would not forward it! How eternally grateful I am to him for his far-sighted action. Even if I had stayed in Engineering specialisation and had reached the top of that tree, which was by no means certain, I might have become the Engineer-in-Chief of the Navy. But that does not compare with being Vice Chief of the Naval Staff, and C-in-C of the British Home Fleet, which posts I eventually reached! About this time, partly I guess because of my experience in HMS Thanet which widened one’s whole outlook, I gave up the idea of leaving the Navy, at any rate of one’s own free will, and determined to make a career in it and do one’s very best. For I had been much impressed with the old saying that “whatever one puts one’s hand to, do it with all thy might”. The post war boom was already dying down, and jobs and posts were becoming increasingly difficult to come by. A good honours degree in Oxford or Cambridge were not by any means an open sesame to worthwhile employment. Some people had retired straight away from the service without waiting for any axeing scheme, and one heard some of them had fallen on very hard times with little or no money to keep the wolf from the door. Whilst many events, political and otherwise, were taking place in 1919, such as the evacuation from Arkangel in September, of great importance, we as midshipmen kept our eyes perhaps closer to the ground than our elders and those in positions of responsibility. 1919/1920 Admiral Beatty was appointed First Sea Lord in the first half of 1919, in place of Admiral Wemyss who had been a very good First Sea Lord. Admiral Beatty’s appointment gave much confidence to the Navy, as he was known to be a strong and clever man of completely independent views, and one unlikely to be bullied by politicians! The family had taken a house in Headington, a suburb of Oxford, to be near Janey who was at a day school there, and spent Christmas and some months there. A pleasant house with a big garden, they moved to our old home in Burford, ‘Greyhounds’, in the first part of 1920 and stayed there, using it as a base for house hunting until they brought Coglan House in the spring of 1921, to which they moved with little delay. In 1919 my old Great-Uncle, General Sir John Watson V.C., G.C.B., died at the age of well past ninety. He was a splendid old man, who had been very good to my father as a young man, and had in fact launched him on his career in India. My chief memory of him was as a very dignified white haired old man who still stood bolt upright, and had an excellent seat on a horse. He hunted to well past eighty. 46

1920 In the late spring the time came to return to Barham and start working up for the exams for sub-lieutenants, which would start in December of this year.Very sad to leave Thanet, and got a wonderful sendoff from the Wardroom who could not have made my life happier and, in a sense, more useful. In after life Creagh retired as a Captain after an adventurous career, which included a noteworthy spell as Senior Naval Officer Persian Gulf. I think he ought to have been made an Admiral, but I suspect he was a trifle too unconventional for the rather uniform and strict postwar Navy. The First Lieutenant, Faulkner, ended his career as the Commodore-in-Charge of the New Zealand Navy, a job which, by reason among other things of his transparent integrity and dedication, he did with great success. The Barham’s Gunroom was in good heart, and it fell to my lot to be the Senior Midshipman upon whom fell the task of organising all the midshipmen’s duties. Rather fun, especially as we had a splendid set of young men which included some of the liveliest members of my term, such as Roundell, Bertie Scott etc., who could be relied upon to be in the thick of every activity. Then it must have been later in the year that we had the great ceremonial of the ‘Burial of the Unknown Warrior’ in Westminster Abbey. Representatives of all ranks and rates in the Navy took part, and there was a most impressive Naval Guard of Honour. I was chosen to represent the midshipmen of the Navy. As we processed round the burial place in the aisle of the Abbey, with the King standing there in full Naval uniform, all were tremendously impressed with the solemnity of the occasion. I could not guess that fifty-five years later I should process round the same route bowing to his grand-daughter, the Queen, on the occasion of my installation in the Henry VII Chapel in my stall as a Knight Grand Cross of the Order of the Bath. The autumn passed all too quickly, with a quickening tempo in our work for the exams for sub-lieutenants, which would be done in two stages, the first half, i.e. seamanship, at the end of the year and the other subjects, i.e. gunnery, torpedo and navigation, in March. The seamanship exam was final, and we would be awarded First, Second and Third class certificates on our performance. But with the others the marks awarded would go halfway towards the final results, which would be declared after our examinations following short courses at the Gunnery, Torpedo or Navigation Schools. The day soon arrived when we would take our seamanship exams, with the midshipmen of the Queen Elizabeth, with old Jaggers Troup,22 the Master of the Fleet, as President of the Board. It was a fairly formidable experience, as the syllabus embraced the whole science and art of seamanship! But the Board was very friendly. I was lucky as I was the only midshipman from Barham to get a First Class Certificate, having achieved this by the skin of my teeth having obtained only a little over the 85% required for a First Class. The others got either Second or Third Class Certificates. 22 Vice Admiral Sir James Troup (1883-1975) 47

The amount of seniority awarded to a sub-lieutenant depended on how he did in the exams. The maximum one could obtain with five First Class Certificates was twenty months over somebody who had only obtained five Third Class Certificates or ten months over a person with five Second Class Certificates. Having achieved a First in seamanship I set myself to obtain all Firsts in other subjects, which included one’s work at Cambridge University. We were rated Acting Sub-Lieutenants in January 1921, with the prospect of doing eight months acting time before being confirmed in the rank. 1921 During 1920 old Lord Fisher, in many senses the maker of the modern Navy, died. 23 A highly controversial character, who was at times unscrupulous but who did an intense amount for the Navy. The pre-war controversies between Lord Fisher and Lord Charles Beresford were by this time quite forgotten, but there was in the opinion of most of us more right on the side of Lord Fisher, in spite of his eccentricities, than wrong! Lord Jellicoe was appointed Governor General of New Zealand, a task he performed with great charm and success. In 1920 also the unfortunate Admiral Koltchak was shot, this signalling the coming success of the Bolsheviks in taking over Russia.24 The spring of 1921 was spent in a spring cruise to Gibraltar and the coasts of Spain. In March we took our Gunnery, Torpedo and Navigation examinations. I did well in all of them, especially Navigation, getting well over 80% required for First in these subjects. Spring 1921 Our Sub-Lieutenants’ courses were planned for six months in Cambridge, followed by four months at Portsmouth doing courses at Whale Island in Gunnery, Vernon in Torpedo and at Navigation School in Portsmouth Dockyard in Navigation, with a short Signals and Physical Training course sandwiched in during our time at Portsmouth. I found I was to go to Pembroke College, Cambridge, for my Cambridge time. But before this happened we were all mobilised to deal with a national coal strike and I found myself with a Naval battalion mostly of stokers drafted to Tidworth for training in maintenance of the peace duties. Great fun. We borrowed some of the horses there and had great fun galloping over the Tidworth downs. But it was not long before the Sub-Lieutenants were released to start their course at Cambridge. I must digress for a moment at this most enlightened action by the Admiralty in arranging with the authorities at Cambridge for the young officers who, like myself, had their education cut by the war to go to Cambridge to help broaden their minds. After all, from the time we went to sea until now we had lived a very restricted and highly disciplined life. It was I have always heard arranged by the Second Sea Lord, Admiral Culme Seymour, and a great character Sir Arthur Shipley, who was Master of Christ’s College, Cambridge, and Vice 23 Admiral Sir Jack Fisher, 1st Baron Fisher (1841-1920), ODNB 24 Admiral Alexander Kolchak (1874-1920), leader of the White Russians opposed to Bolshevism. 48

Chancellor of the University. A liberal course of education was planned, with any number of ‘optimes’, a thing unheard of in our highly organised training.25 What enormous fun it was. We did two terms, the summer and long vac term, and soon found ourselves mixed up with many University activities. Our Master at Pembroke was a man by the name of Hadley, very friendly, perhaps a bit shy, and we had living in the College a Commander known as Bill Wynter – an old destroyer hand – who was one of the two “unit” Commanders whose job it was in a sense to see the young and perhaps rather wild Naval Officers conformed to the spirit of the University. We did not wear uniform, and donned a cap and gown when University rules prescribed, and in fact we were encouraged most wholeheartedly to enter into the life of the University. I was accommodated in New Court, and shared rooms with a Sub-Lieutenant called Cox, a pleasant and quiet companion. On the first day of term we all mustered at the Senate House and were formally entered in statu pupilare to the University. Our routine was very relaxed, with perhaps one lecture in the morning and a couple a week in the subject of one’s choice. I chose ethnology, and listened in fascination to a lecturer called Fay. In addition, I took maths with one of our instructor Commanders, who had I believed been a wrangler. Most fascinating, he introduced us to the attractions of the differential and integral calculus. I was almost tempted at one time to leave the Navy and sit for a Mathematical degree, but I came to the conclusion my talents at mathematics were a bit too patchy to be sure of becoming one of the Wranglers, even after three to four years pretty intensive study!26 It was a lovely summer, very hot with any amount of sport. I went in for the University open tennis tournament but did not get very far, though I later won the Naval officers open tennis tournament.27 Commander Blagrove was the other Naval ‘Unit Commander’, who understood fully the purpose of our stay at Cambridge and encouraged us to take part in every activity. There was rather a difference between the undergraduates like ourselves who had served in the war and those straight from school. We seemed to be so much older than the latter, though in age there was not much difference. We had much fun boating on the Cam and enjoying our walks in the Backs from which the view of Colleges, St. Johns, Trinity, King’s, Queen’s, etc., were quite unsurpassed. Then the season of the May week Balls got well into its stride in May and June. I went with my sister Jane, Christopher Brockhurst and, I think, Charles Ackers, to the Pembroke Ball, finishing up on the Cam where we had an eggs and bacon breakfast. But our time passed all too quickly. We had immensely enjoyed the freedom, and made many friends, some of which we kept, and above all, the Dons at Pembroke like old Coomber, Fennel and young Hadley, son of the Master, made us particularly welcome. 25 ‘Optime’ generally referred to students taking second or third-class honours in the Mathematical Tripos, but the sense here is probably closer to ‘options’. 26 A wrangler was one who achieved first-class honours in the Mathematics Tripos at Cambridge. 27 WWD could still play a mean game of tennis in his sixties; however we never saw him ride, play rugby, cricket or other sports, activities to which age and the Second World War put an end. Sport played a large part in the lives of young men at this time. 49

A quick summer holiday at the end of August before we went to Portsmouth to do our courses for Gunnery, Torpedo, Navigation and other miscellaneous subjects. These courses were rather a cram as they represented work for about twice the length of the allotted time. Six weeks at Whale Island, three weeks at Vernon and Navigation School passed quickly enough. Fortunately, we in most cases had spent the money we had at Cambridge, and so had to economise at Portsmouth, and therefore had no distractions from work.
