As I had already done pretty well in the sea part of my examinations, I had no difficulty in getting First Class Certificates in all subjects and took life fairly easily. I missed the special Annual Beaufort Wharton Testimonial Prize for Navigation by a couple of marks by, I have to confess, taking my navigation course far too easily, for I knew I was pretty well bound to get a First as in the sea written examinations I had obtained nearly 100% marks, so did no more work than was absolutely necessary! I think three or four other midshipmen in my term and those other on course at the same time obtained all First Class Certificates, which meant in addition to extra seniority that one could be certain of being selected for the specialisation of one’s choice, which in my case would be Torpedo. 1921/22 At the end of the year I found myself appointed to the Fleet Flagship HMS Queen Elizabeth as the Sub-Lieutenant in charge of the Gunroom. A splendid Gunroom, which included Prince George, for whom the Captain said I was to be especially responsible. What a wonderful ship. Charles Madden as C.in C., Fuller and Fullerton, the Chief of Staff and Captain of the Fleet respectively, Geoffrey Blake as Captain – a great leader in every sense of the word. Then in the wardroom we had an outstanding set of officers, Troup as Master of the Fleet, Douglas Fisher as Gunnery Lieutenant, “Turtle” Hamilton and Tom Troubridge as Lieutenant Commanders, Alan Scott Moncrieff, with whom I shared a cabin, as one of the watchkeepers and a host of other very good officers, many of whom like the ones mentioned became Admirals. In such a ship of exceptional talents among the officers it was perhaps surprising things always went so well, but they did and in every activity from the Gunnery competition to all forms of sports, regattas, the Q.E. was always top or a very good second. The ships company were first rate, and the whole spirit of the ship was exceptional. The good name of the ship meant a lot to every officer and man serving. The best ship as regards spirits in which I had so far served. 1922 Early in January we set sail for our spring cruise, which included a trip to the Mediterranean where we visited the South of France before calling at Naples where we met the Mediterranean Fleet.Villefranche was especial fun, and a few visits to Monte Carlo soon depleted most of our funds, though one evening I had a lucky spin on the tables, on which the whole party I was with had an outstanding dinner at one of the best restaurants in Monte Carlo! March 1922 It must have been around this time that I heard my sister Jane was engaged to Charles Ackers, a splendid man who owned a neighbouring estate, i.e. Huntley Manor, but who was quite a 50

bit older than Jane by some nineteen years. He was, however, young for his years and had fallen absolutely head over heels in love with Janie. My mother was a bit anxious about the disparity in age, especially as Janie with her outstanding beauty and vivaciousness could have married almost anybody of her choice. But Charles Ackers was tremendously stable and reliable, so my mother albeit with some reservations gave her consent. About this time I was awarded the special Admiralty Prize of £10, which had to be spent on books, for getting all First Class Certificates in my Sub-Lieutenant’s courses. The Q.E. was proving a splendid ship, and I soon learnt much of what there was to be learnt about harbour and, indeed, sea watchkeeping. By this time the great depression was in full swing. The Geddes axe had been applied to the Navy when nearly half the officers of my seniority were axed. Sub-Lieutenants were given I think three months’ notice and a gratuity of £300 to £400, and told to fend for themselves. Many did not find it all easy and, after all, we had no professional qualification other than that intangible and undefinable one of “common sense”. The axe cut at the very roots of the officer structure of the navy, and those axed were permanent list officers and not those who had entered for “hostilities only”, as so many in the other services had done. The axe went right down to Dartmouth, where a percentage of each term was axed. The reasons were twofold, firstly the great contraction of the Navy to well below pre-war size and, secondly, during the war we had recruited far too many officers on to the permanent lists. For instance my own term in Osborne started at over one hundred strong, whereas it should in fact have been about thirty-five strong! The summer cruise of 1922 was great fun, we visited many Scottish ports and ended up with the whole of the Atlantic Fleet in Torbay where the King paid us a visit and inspected the Fleet. The King stayed onboard and visited the Gunroom, where his son Prince George was one of the midshipmen. As nice a young chap as one could expect to find anywhere, and very popular in the Gunroom. He had none of the shyness of any of the Royal Family. A trifle idle perhaps, as indeed are many young men with lots of spirits! I was sent for to have a talk with the King, and as far as I remember the conversation went something like this. The King, gruffly, “How is George doing?” Self, “Very popular, lots of spirits, enjoys himself to the full. Should sometimes like to see just a bit more energy, but very capable when he had the mind to!” The King, “Damn lazy, you mean! Keep him up to the mark and don’t let him get away with anything”. Self, “Yes, Sir, we will certainly see to that!” Then the King visited the Gunroom, and how he enjoyed it. He sat in one of our few serviceable armchairs and started yarning, and suddenly became quite at home, talking to the young midshipmen of far-off Gunroom life when he had been a midshipman. Time had no significance. I caught sight of the C-in-C Flag Lieutenant on more than one occasion coming in to tell me that the C-in- C’s lunch party for the King was mustered and ready! But I took no action, as people said to me afterwards, they had never seen the King so completely relaxed and enjoying himself as when he visited the Queen Elizabeth’s Gunroom. 51

This was the day when Janie was married in Brompton Parish Church in London. Though our Captain, Geoffrey Blake, said I could certainly get away, that was the day the King would visit the Gunroom, and it would be nice if I was there. So there was no question of rushing up to London for her wedding. In September I with some others in my term were promoted to Lieutenant and joined the Wardroom. John Dillon Robinson, who became one of my closest friends, relieved me as Sub-Lieutenant of the Q.E.’s Gunroom, and what a perfectly splendid job he made of it, for John was not only of commanding presence but of great professional ability, allied to a lively sense of humour. September saw the fall of the Coalition Government, but Lloyd George remained Prime Minister. Sir Henry Wilson, the late C.I.G.S., who had become a Member of Parliament, was murdered by Irish Gunmen in Eaton Square, but passers-by gallantly attacked the gunmen and handed them over to the Police. Kemal Ataturk raised what was known as the Kemalist Army in Turkey, and inflicted some extensive defeats on the Greek Army of Occupation. Bonar Law soon became Prime Minister in place of Lloyd George, as he was the leader of the Conservative Party. Towards the autumn of 1922 Admiral Sir Charles Madden, the C-in-C, was relieved by Admiral Sir John de Roebeck, who had been the C-in-C Mediterranean, and who had showed great diplomatic ability out there. 1923 1923 was a very pleasant in Queen Elizabeth. Sir John de Roebeck, the C-in-C, with the redoubtable W.W. Fisher as his Chief of Staff, proved a first-rate combination. I sometimes thought W.W. Fisher took too much on himself as C.o.S, for John de Roebeck was a great character in his own right and still to this day I remember when he entertained all the younger officers in his relatively spacious Admiral’s quarters. He impressed on us all that one must be prepared to play hard as well as work hard. He was very fond of cricket, and greatly encouraged the first-class cricketers we had in the ship, like Cornwallis, Cunliffe and some in the Gunroom. A new character replaced old “Jaggers” Troup as Master of the Fleet – one John Cunningham who after the second world war became First Sea Lord – also a remarkable character with a mordant wit.Various changes in the ship, Geoffrey Blake, our muchloved Captain, was replaced by Charles Forbes, a very efficient but rather dour Scot, who became C-in-C of the Home Fleet at the beginning of the second world war. Rupert Drummond was the Commander, a truly delightful if easy-going chap. The ship was certainly one of the happiest and best in which I ever served. I went in for boxing mildly, and became the welter weight champion of the Fleet, but for recreation concentrated on tennis and golf, with much enjoyment. The slump was still pretty fierce in 1923. Bonar Law resigned due to illness, and was succeeded by the almost unknown Stanley Baldwin who, however, in contrast to Lloyd George was completely trusted. Having settled our war debt to America on what seemed rather onerous terms, Baldwin went to electorate at the end of the year, asking for a mandate to abandon our free trade policy and adopt a mild form of protection. He was defeated on, I suspect, the dearer food issue when the results were declared early in the New Year, or to be more accurate, he did not win sufficient seats to have a majority over the combined strength of the Liberal and Labour Parties, who combined together to bring down the Conservative Government. To many of us this seemed sad, as the Conservatives still had the greatest support as a single party, and had one believed much the most constructive policy. 52

1924 A good spring cruise to start the year, with a visit to the Western Mediterranean which we all enjoyed. A new Labour Government with Ramsay Macdonald as Prime Minister set some of us wondering if the Navy would be still further cut. But it was clear soon that they would not act irresponsibly. The year saw in its early part the death of two famous, or perhaps infamous, men! Lenin, the architect of the Soviet Communist State, and Woodrow Wilson, the in some respects discredited President of the United States. Lenin had been ill from the effects of a stroke from quite a long time ago, and the affairs of state were run by Trotsky and a formidable and as yet hardly known Russian by the name of Stalin. Woodrow Wilson never got over the refusal of the United States to join the League of Nations, and was for the last few years of his life incapacitated from the effects of a stroke.Yet another railway strike in the early part of the year, which to my mind confirmed the opinion that nationalisation, far from being the panacea for industrial troubles, sometimes is exactly the opposite. A great summer cruise when at the Fleet Regatta after intense excitement the old Q.E. came in a close second. The Olympic Games took place this year, and the best athlete of my term, “Morty Neame”28, represented England and, I think, won a silver or bronze medal in the hurdles. An event which was most impressive, and was very well done, was the British Empire Exhibition at Wembley. I had some very stimulating evenings with John Dillon Robinson there. He had just been invalided from the Navy, and had apprenticed himself to his old Uncle’s firm of Aldous & Co. It was a magnificent Exhibition, and brought home to people who saw it the magnificence and, indeed, variety of the British Empire on which Royal Naval College Greenwich Kipling reminded us the sun never set. I left the Q.E. in the summer, having been appointed to a ‘long specialist torpedo course’, which started with three terms at the Royal Naval College, Greenwich, followed by a year in Vernon doing the practical side of the course. But before spent a wonderful leave with Charles and Janie, who had taken a Scottish place called Belmaduthy in the Black Isle about halfway between Inverness and Invergordon. Good rough shooting with a nice stretch of salmon fishing in the Beauly. My sister Janie was much better, and my mother and father stayed there. This was the last time I saw my mother fairly well. She looked cheerful and much enjoyed perhaps being in her native Scotland. We went over to Dingwall, where some of her Ross ancestors had lived, but did not visit Balnagowan Castle, as I think the then owner, Sir Charles Ross, was out of England due to a dispute with the Tax Authorities over tax due on the extensive woodlands he had felled during the war! Anyway, from a complicated Ross family tree there seems to have been some dispute about the lawful succession, for the present Rosses were originally Lockharts. But that is another story! The Rosses who dated from the tenth or eleventh century were even for Scottish families 28 Douglas Neame (1901-1988). WWD has mixed up the years here. Neame was eliminated in the 1928 Amsterdam Olympics, but won bronze medals in the British Empire Games in 1930. He later became a Commodore. 53

accounted pretty wild. Anyway, my grandfather Ross always was shown in books of reference with the traditional Ross coat of arms. But what fun this holiday was. My Father and Charles both shot and fished very well, and my mother and Janie much enjoyed life and especially the Inverness Ball, at which we all danced reels, perhaps a little unskilfully but with no lack of vigour. Then in September I joined the R.N.C [Royal Naval College] Greenwich with seven others for the long ‘T’ course – the academic side. We were given a course in Science, Engineering and Mathematics which in some respects was rather similar to the first half of the B.Sc. degree at Cambridge or London. The course found it took varying times to get everybody completely into ‘school’ running condition. I found little difficulty, but some on the course who had been longer away from school than I found the going pretty hard. A very wellplanned syllabus, which succeeded in unrushing[?] everybody and giving us all a glimpse of how Science increasingly affects the Navy. A very clever Australian called Morgan and I usually shared top place in most subjects. He had left school later than I, and I had to steam to keep up with him. Then the others in the course, Dimsdale, Bingemen,Voelcker, Bury, Brown and somebody else were in their various ways good value. A very happy team. Perhaps I and Morgan took most interest in this side of the course. Of the five mentioned above Bury was the cleverest, but also by quite a long chalk the laziest! Regular rugger twice a week kept us all fit, and the whole atmosphere of Greenwich with the Observatory on top of the hill in Greenwich Park we found conductive to enjoying ourselves, and at the same time doing a little work. The instructors, who were half civilian and half uniformed instructor officers, were good teachers and prepared to take quite a lot of trouble with us. We sometimes saw the Admiral President and Captain of the College, but they concerned themselves mostly with staff courses, war courses and Sub-Lieutenants courses which were the modern counterpart of our course a few years back at Cambridge. We usually had the weekend free, when as often as not I used my motorbike to go and stay with my parents at Coglan. My mother had recurring attacks of illness. She seemed to start off with influenza, but this turned into gastric trouble which left her in very poor health. She had attacks of depression at times, and I believe found it difficult to match up to my father’s robust health. She was moreover very sensitive to noise, and sometimes said Coglan was getting too noisy for her. But whenever me and the other children were home she always put on a very good showing, and was a great companion to my sister at Huntley who herself was very delicate but imbued with tremendous vitality. In the autumn my brother was offered a post in the Leather Merchants, Scriven & Co. in Bermondsey, as for a variety of reasons my Uncle Jim could not fulfil his intention of giving him a start in Fleming & Co., Leather Merchants, which was his own firm. My brother always described Scriven as ‘Scrooge’ & Co., and he started off with princely salary of £104 per annum. It was a pretty old-fashioned firm, which indeed might have come out of one of Dickens’ novels, and in fact did little or nothing to encourage and train youngsters. We found digs for my brother in Greenwich, and it was nice to see a little of him and be able to join together in laughing at the experiences he underwent. Jobs were difficult to come by, and these were the days you had to grin and bear it. 54

Towards the end of the year Parliament was dissolved, and an election held. The notorious Zinovieff [Zinoviev] letters, which encouraged British Labour Party supporters to become Communists and overthrow their own constitution, played a big part in the results. Mr. Baldwin was returned in a landslide victory with a majority of over two hundred.29 1925 A pleasant Christmas (1924) at home with all the family. Janie’s little son David seemed to be flourishing, and they had a big party at Huntley with many of Charles’s friends and relations. My parents decided to go to Pau in France for the months of February and March. The climate there was a lot milder than England, and a Doctor seemed to do Mother quite a lot of good, especially in respect to her lameness. I went out and spent my Easter leave there, and much enjoyed playing golf on the local golf course which is always alleged to have been started by Wellington’s officers in 1814 when they occupied that region. I think this must be quite apocryphal! Mother certainly seemed a bit better, and I noticed when I met her on her return she had, what was unknown for her, quite a good appetite. Baldwin had made the rather surprising appointment of Winston Churchill as Chancellor of the Exchequer, which in fact turned out to be a disastrous failure! The summer of 1925 was great fun, but I was sorry to hear my mother had a very bad attack of influenza and could not get rid of it. The Greenwich course for Torpedo ended at the end of July, and we were given a whole month’s leave before starting the practical long Torpedo course at HMS Vernon at Portsmouth. This was now a shore establishment, established on the old Gunwharf next door to the dockyard and Portsmouth harbour station.Very well set up and organised, and the instructional facilities were first rate. But unfortunately in the summer mother got no better and was still very ill, so Father decided she must consult a Harley Street specialist which she did, and who said she must go straight away into his Putney Nursing Home. My sister Jane was also not at all well and was convalescing in this Nursing Home. My mother had disease of the liver, possibly started by the stone she passed into her liver about ten years previously in India.Various treatment was tried but without success, though I think she was relieved of some pain. We visited her at Putney fairly frequently from home and from Portsmouth. But when in September it was apparent she was dying I obtained a week’s leave from my course at Vernon and stayed with my father at Putney, so as to see as much of her as I could and comfort father. Though very weak she was wonderfully composed, and most interested in what I was doing. She told me she had great confidence in me, and I said I would always do my best and hoped to get somewhere in life! She said I must always be prepared to face life truthfully and without fear, and live by the Christian virtues which had supported her throughout her life. She also deprecated people who were always complaining. 29 The Zinoviev letter was almost certainly a forgery, though it has not been agreed precisely who was the forger. 55

I still remember the last time I saw her, she was very weak and after a little talk she would sleep. There was not a wrinkle on her face. All the lines seemed suddenly to have disappeared, and she looked quite a young woman. That was the last time I saw her, and she died peacefully two days later, to the great grief of my father and all her children. September 1925 We had a very moving funeral service a few days later at Longhope, and the burial took place in Huntley so as to be near her daughter Janie’s home, to whom she was wholly devoted. Father, Buddy and I were at the service, to which many folk came, for though we had only been a few years at Longhope many people loved and admired her. In my father’s diary you will read about my mother’s death, and an experience he had a few days after her funeral. My mother was a most loveable and exceedingly gallant person. She had ill health for most of her life, and had a rather lonely upbringing having lost her mother when quite a little girl, and her father when she was only just twenty. A very shrewd observer on life, she was not easily humbugged. A devout Christian all her life, she conducted herself selflessly on Christian principles. Quite a sense of humour, she could laugh at all of us and especially at Father when he was trailing wild ideas. I certainly never realised until her death how much she meant to us, and how much one relied on her advice. My great regret was that I did not learn more about her early life and her parents, who are still rather shadowy figures to me. A great influence in her early life was old Miss Taylor, who in a sense acted as her guardian and at whose school in Blackheath she learnt much. Mother had considerable artistic tastes. She was a good watercolour painter, and you will see many of her pictures hanging at Coglan and elsewhere. Her post card reproductions of Indian scenes brought in appreciable sums for war charities. A first-rate pianist, she played with much sensitivity and feeling. Small and always well dressed, I never saw her look untidy. She was a very good hostess, and always contrived to make the less grand people feel at home and welcome. Father wisely shut up the house and did a round of visits, after staying with Janie, who was convalescing at Brighton. We went and spent Christmas with old Sir Charles and Lady Yate at Madeley, and had a very gay time with their two daughters who WWD about this time. His contemporaries remarked how good-looking were old friends of ours. he was as a young man. Good looks, an easy sociability, athleticism, ability at maths and a competitive drive which helped him head the list 1926 of exam results, were useful in a career in uncertain times and doubtless Much solid work in Vernon, where we learnt all about torpedoes, helped to make sure that he was noticed. mines, electric equipment and the special low power electrical fire 56

control equipment for which we were responsible. All enjoyable, and as much of this work was practical, we never had time to lose interest. But politically the year was very disturbed. After a great deal of threatening the Trades Union Congress called a General Strike in May, primarily to force the Government to pay what were considered uneconomic wage demands. Stanley Baldwin, having had the wisdom over the previous year of perfecting the contingency plans to maintain the life of the country, dealt with this challenge to established authority with great firmness and humanity. After a few days the strike collapsed, but the miners decided to stay out. The Forces took a considerable part in maintaining essential services, though to our great disappointment the long course specialists, as we were at that time, were not allowed to go and drive trains. My brother volunteered to work, and drove motors in London to help in the distribution of food. Above all the spirit of the country was truly inspiring, and many young people whether they were Trade Unionists or not rallied to the call the Government made for volunteers to maintain essential services. I think very nearly nine people out of ten were wholly behind Mr. Stanley Baldwin, who resoundingly defeated the Unions without leaving a trace of bitterness. As we were nearing the end of our strenuous long ‘T’ course in the Vernon, we were as it were held in reserve for strike duties, and meanwhile carried on with our course. The work was hard and entailed acquainting oneself with many quite unrelated facts, and also each member of the course had to give a ‘lecture’ on some technical subject – an excellent idea. Of all the major specialists of those days, i.e. Gunnery, Navigation, Torpedo, Signals and perhaps Anti-Submarine, it is probable Torpedo that embraced the largest number of unrelated subjects. Some of the members of the course were by now evidently feeling the pace. The exams lasted over a fortnight, and were thorough in the extreme, half written papers and half practical tests. I did well in all subjects, and excepting Morgan, the Australian, who in the aggregate just topped my marks, I came out well ahead of the others and was awarded the Ogilvy Gold Medal, which is given annually to the top man in the Torpedo specialist long course. The question of an advanced theoretical specialist course at Greenwich arose. The course was designed to acquaint one with most modern scientific advances, and fit one for service in the experimental departments of any specialists. I was selected for this, as were two of my Gunnery long course opposite numbers, Tom Pakenham and Ronnie Mackay. In September of that year I joined Greenwich again for a two-term course, what was known as a ‘T’ dagger course. The economic state of the country was not good, and the continuing coal strike which did not end until November, when the miners had to go back on the owners’ terms, did nothing to help. Greenwich was enormous fun. I was allowed to work out my own syllabus and, encouraged by Professors Haigh, Bryan and others, I lived almost a university style of life. In mathematics one of the Instructor Commanders was a one-time wrangler, and he enthused me in many aspects of modern Mathematics. 57

I also took to rugger keenly, and captained the college XV which in those days was a match for most London clubs. As a wing three quarter I found I could outstrip most people, and in this season, due to ‘good service’ from the forwards, scored many tries. In a way the time at Greenwich proved invaluable, as it enabled one to take stock and teach oneself many things that would matter in after life. Quite a gay social life, and I went to many London dances which, by and large, were great fun. The custom was that the maximum number of dances you had with anybody should not be more than three! If you went above that number it was assumed you were engaged, or about to be engaged! I returned to Vernon, having also been awarded a £10 prize for passing a good dagger course at Greenwich, and did a fill-in job in the Instructional Department in April. As I was due to go to sea in the autumn there was no point in giving me a job which in the ordinary run of events would last for two years. The summer of 1927 was a good one, and I played a lot of cricket making one or two big scores. I also took part in athletics, and was in the Navy’s relay running team doing the 220 yards. Portsmouth was a very pleasant place to be stationed. Lots of games and any amount of good and diverse company. The young officers of the Navy were a splendid lot, and by and large as dedicated a team of young men as one would find in any walk of life. The axe of the early twenties had, however, left its mark and the young officers, i.e. Sub-Lieutenants and midshipmen, were perhaps less carefree and more ‘safety first’ than their predecessors, and one’s own contemporaries. We lived perhaps a rather philistine life. One’s memories of events in 1927 were apt to fade. Father was keeping splendidly cheerful, though he missed my mother a lot, and I heard they wanted him to become the Conservative candidate for the Forest of Dean. In the late summer I heard I was to be appointed to HMS Enterprise, then serving on the East Indies Station, which covered on the west side Persian Gulf, Aden and East Africa down to Dar-es-Salaam, and the east side Burma and the entrance to the Malacca Straits and down to a latitude of about 20° south. A pretty extensive station, on which three cruisers and four sloops served. I immensely looked forward to it, as this was the first foreign station I had served on and it covered India, where my father and mother had spent much of their lives. So in September I embarked in the Rawalpindi at Tilbury and set sail for Bombay. The Rawalpindi was one of the P&O passenger line mail streamers, which did a weekly service to India. A lot of interesting people onboard, including Lord Linlithgow, a future Viceroy of India. We soon arrived at Bombay, where I transferred to a B.I. steamer which took one with little delay to Karachi, where the Enterprise was lying alongside the harbour wall which then was about three to four miles from the town of Karachi. My first sight of Enterprise was impressive. I saw her in the early morning as the B.I. steamer berthed, and was immediately struck by her beautiful lines. Not long after I arrived onboard and was given a tremendously warm welcome by all the officers and little Haines, who I was to relieve. The Captain, Stephen St. Leger Moore, rather a distant and at times remote character, was just a little bit inclined to 58

have his favourites. Faultlessly dressed, a tall and impressive character who once one realised his initial shyness was really quite easy and not half so ‘difficult’ as many Captains were in those days. Then what a Wardroom we had! Guy Russell a great character, Schofield the Navigator, Grindle the Gunnery officer, Whitfield, Thomson, Everard the Watchkeeper, my old friend Webb Bowen the Marine and a host of other characters. For sheer talent and ability it would be hard to beat the Wardroom, and how well everybody worked together in the not too comfortable climatic conditions. Karachi was still very hot, but we could expect cooler weather in the Persian Gulf where we were destined to go about ten days after I joined Enterprise. October 1927 The Persian Gulf was interesting – we called at Kuwait, Bandar Abbas, Dofar [Dhofar, Oman], Bahrain, Abadan and Basra, where we made very close relations with the R.A.F. stationed at Shaibah and who flew Vickers Victoria transport, and an American designed recce aircraft left over from the war, and called I think a DH91.30 A good aircraft, except when it crashed, it always caught fire. A particularly pleasant time at Abadan, which was entirely and most efficiently run by the Anglo-Persian Oil Company (APOC) of D’Arcy exploration fame.31 The Shatt-al-Arab, the river that is the combination of the Tigris and Euphrates, is carefully dredged up to Basra, which must be about eighty miles from the sea and has numerous plantations of date palms on either side of the river. Not far from Basra is the alleged site of the Garden of Eden, where we went early one cold morning to catch the morning flight of duck! A short visit this time was enough to whet our appetite, for father at the end of last century and the beginning of the present one was the acting British resident at Bushire [Bushehr] with responsibilities in the Persian Gulf. In those days British responsibilities in the Gulf were carried by the Government of India. Then back to Colombo and Trincomalee, which were the main bases of the East Indies Squadron. Colombo, a fine town and big artificial harbour from which all the seaborne trade from Ceylon [Sri Lanka], mostly tea, rubber and coffee, were despatched. Colombo, a splendid town run pretty well entirely by the British with the help of some historic Portuguese and Burgher (Dutch) families. It was the period when Ceylon was one of the main sources of supply of tea to the world, and the big and highly respected British firms such as George Stewarts and Colombo Commercial and many others had an appreciable hand in this trade. 30 Shaibah was a desert airbase near Basra established in 1920. The Vickers Victoria was a biplane freighter and troop transport aircraft. The DH91 was a de Havilland Albatross 91 aircraft, but de Havilland was a British company and designed this model in the mid-1930s, so it not clear precisely what WWD saw. 31 William Knox D’Arcy (1849-1917) signed an agreement with the then Shah of Persia in 1901 giving him exploration rights over a vast area. D’Arcy himself never went to Persia, and work was carried out by his engineer, George Barnard Reynolds. After initial difficulties, oil was found in 1908 and APOC established in which the majority shareholder was the British government. Oil was strategically important as the Royal Navy switched from coal to oil over the course of World War I. 59

Trincomalee, by far the finest natural harbour in the Indian Ocean, was a heavenly place to visit. A great place for picnics on the enchanting ‘Sober Island’ in the middle of the harbour, plenty of big game, fishing and shooting in the surrounding forests and ‘paddy fields’. This had been the base for the British Navy in those waters ever since the latter part of the eighteenth century. Later I spent some weeks there on my own laying experimental mines for HMS Vernon. Christmas 1927 But we were due to spend Christmas at Calcutta [Kolkata], where we would see the Viceroy’s Cup Race which was certainly then the most important horse race in India. A very warm welcome indeed from everybody. We were made honorary members of all the famous Clubs in Calcutta – a great honour and much appreciated. The Hooghli [Hooghly] is a fascinating river, and it was necessary to be piloted up it by one of the most famous Hooghli pilots to our billet, which was near the Maidan (the Park) and not far from the racecourse. I had an introduction to the Governor, Sir Stanley Jackson, and called on him in the very impressive Government House, rather like Buckingham Palace but in a much more impressive setting. Politically India still seemed fairly quiet, and there was an air of permanence in those days about the British Raj. Calcutta seemed rather prosperous, as indeed it has usually been since the days of the great Clive. Our stay at Calcutta was followed by visits to the Burmese [Myanmar] coasts, Akyab [now Sittwe, capital of Rahkine province] and other places where we met an entirely different culture. The Burmese seemed more akin to Chinese culture than the India ones. People very cheerful and friendly. I was unwise enough to go to one of classical Burmese Concerts, which lasted for nearly five hours with music which seemed to have only two notes! New year spent on the Burma coasts. 1928 A pleasant visit to Madras [modern Chennai] and some of the surrounding Ports, such as Pondicherry, where I made a century against the local cricket team. Then back to Trincomalee for a little gunnery and torpedo practice. The facilities for full scale armament practice were not very profuse in the East Indies station and Trinas, as we called it, was about the only place where it could be undertaken. A visit to Colombo where we entered a ‘four’ in the sliding seat four races of the Colombo Rowing Club. Having two outstandingly good and powerful oars in Guy Russell and John Whitfield, it was not surprising we won. I rowed bow in this race, for which we practised assiduously. It was about this time I met who was to become one of my greatest friends, Frank Webster, an architect working in the Colombo Commercial Company. He was, among other things, a very keen oar, and taught me a lot about rowing as well as about the life in Ceylon, and the effects of various cultures on the country. I brought an old car, a Crossley, from Ronnie, a colonial office man who I think was in the Governor’s office. An admirable machine which I kept in Ceylon, and which was of great use to all onboard! 60

Spring/Summer 1928 A change of plan became necessary as the sloops the Admiralty ‘contracted’ with the Government of India to keep in the Persian Gulf for, I think, £50,000 per annum, all broke down and it was decided to send one cruiser with three funnels up there for the summer instead of three sloops with one funnel each! So Enterprise and Emerald were to share this doubtful pleasure throughout the summer. We went up there in early spring, but it soon got very hot indeed and in fact my cabin temperature seldom dropped below 100°F. There was trouble at Kuwait, and the Sheikh invoked his treaty with us to come to his aid as he was being threatened by the fanatical sect of Arabs known as the Wahabis, who said they would carve him up and nail the bits onto his Palace wall.32 So we landed a force there and encouraged the local Kuwaitis to show some martial ardour. The Sheikh was a most dignified looking old man, who was advised by rather an odd looking but for all that very able British resident – Colonel Reilly. The ship lay off the town, and our headquarters were in one of the Sheikh’s summer palaces – a modest two storey building about the size of a big country house in England. It got hotter and hotter, and the temperature of sea water rose to over 95°F. The Sheikh lent us some of his rather frisky Arab ponies, which we much enjoyed riding. Troubles and threats to Kuwait blew over, and we left in the late summer in time to reach Colombo for August week, which was the gay week of the year there. A very pleasant and relaxing time there, and quite a lot of dances were given, including one that we gave onboard. The traditional rugger matches were played ‘up country’ against ‘low country’, the Services and Colombo R.F.C. were all included in a pretty light hearted triangular tournament which I think ‘up country’ won. Also cricket matches and races where the standard of straight dealing was certainly not up to English jockey club standards. But the races were great fun, and it was interesting to note that on the last race of the meeting always the most unsuccessful owner’s horse won! We got to know quite a lot of the ‘Taipans’ [powerful foreign-born businessmen] as they would be called in China, old Tom Villiers, Sudlow and a host of others who always seemed to keep open house for the Navy. The Ship’s company spent the best part of a fortnight in camp at Diyatalava, situated in the high country just below 5000 ft, not too far from the hill station Nuwara Eliya which at times closely resembled the Highlands of Scotland. A visit from the C.in C. Admiral Thesiger to the ship, which went off well. Our new Commander, Renouf, was doing splendidly and held the peace in the Wardroom and knew how to handle the Captain, St. Leger Moore, when he was in one of his temperamental moods! The Captain was up to a point very good. He expected a very high standard, especially of cleanliness and outward appearance of the ship, but he was inclined to be moody and had his favourites, a fact which everybody in the Wardroom was fully aware. But Enterprise by and large was a very happy ship. I ran various boxing tournaments in which the ship eventually emerged victorious. The ships company was a first rate one, and very 32 The Wahhabi sect came to dominate the Arabian peninsula after the creation of the state of Saudi Arabia by Ibn Saud in 1932. 61

happy especially as they realised the officers stretched themselves to the limit to ensure the sailors on the station got good value for their time. Not always easy, as there were in some places not a lot of people of what one might say the same social class as the lower deck. Again, we knew quite a number of prominent Ceylonese, the de Saram family, old Solomon Bandaranaiyka whose son, alas, went to Cambridge, got a chip on his shoulder and became a deplorable Prime Minister in later years. His old father, a quite splendid old man, asked us to be kind to his son which we in the Wardroom endeavoured to do. But nobody took to the young man very much, as he always boasted he knew ‘all the answers’. Autumn Then as the autumn started we went for a cruise in the western half of the station. A fascinating visit to Mauritius, and well entertained at ‘La Reduit’, the Governors’ residence. Most of the sugar planters there are French – pre-Revolution French – and still held to the customs of that period. I met a family called Adam, none of whom had a word of English, and when I asked Madame Adam if she would be sending her daughters to Paris to finish their education she indignantly said ‘non’, for the Paris they learnt about was the Paris of Louis XIV and they had no use for the present day French Society made up of parvenus. She went on to say, of course they would go to London for their season. Mauritius is a lovely island where the classic [novel] ‘Paul and Virginia’ was written by Pierre Loti.33 The harbour was a good one, and the town of Port Louis is inhabited by a mixture of Creoles, Indians, Chinese, a few Arabs and fewer Europeans. At that time they all seemed to live amicably together. A visit to Seychelles, quite one of the most beautiful area of islands in the world, was a never forgotten experience. A certain number of beachcombers had pitched up there, running true to the Somerset Maugham type.34 One who had come from South Africa asked me to go shares with him buying the now defunct Admiralty wireless station for a virtual “song”, and he would ship it onboard Enterprise for delivery to Durban or Cape Town! I declined politely but firmly, as I could see raised eyebrows in the Contract department of the Admiralty when they discovered a serving naval officer was mixed up in a deal of doubtful propriety. I went fishing one day and hooked what must have been a giant Barraconda [barracuda], but after an hour’s hard work playing it, just as I was pulling it alongside our boat a shark came up and bit off the main part of the Barraconda, leaving me with only the head that was about 5 feet long! Seychelles was utterly unspoilt, rejoiced in a mail boat once every two months and provided one with a lotus eating existence if one was inclined to an easy life. Unlike Mauritius, the Seychelles were outside the typhoon area of the Southern India Ocean. But the greatest fun was to follow, when we set course for Mombasa. John Whitfield had arranged an eight to nine day rugger tour for the ship’s side, which included visits to Nairobi, 33 The novel was in fact written by Jacques-Henri Bernardin de Saint-Pierre (1737-1814), first published 1788, and set in Mauritius which at the time belonged to France. Pierre Loti lived a century later and was popular for his novels set in exotic places, so the confusion is perhaps understandable. 34 W. Somerset Maugham wrote the short story The Vessel of Wrath in 1931 about a drunken dissolute man of the tropics. The 1954 film The Beachcomber was based on it. 62

Nakuru, Eldoret, Kitale and Kampala in Uganda. All enormous fun, we won most of the matches played but found the height, sometimes about 5000ft. to 6000 ft., a bit testing on our lungs. But perhaps the hospitality of our hosts was the most testing of all. With John Whitfield, a near English International leading the side, and one or two representative Navy players, we had a good side. By this time we had changed Captains. The new Captain, Pridham-Wippel, was an outstanding man. A great sea commander, with lots of small ship experience, he had one of the sharpest and most incisive intellects I have ever met. A most awfully nice man in every way, who was simply adored by officers and men alike. Nairobi in those days was still partly built out of four-gallon petrol tins used in the first war, and there were only a few stone buildings like the New Stanley Hotel to be seen in the town. Lions used to come into the gardens of people living in the suburbs, so it was best not to go strolling about in the open at night. The famous Muthaigha Club was a great meeting place for all who were passing through Nairobi. These were the days of the big European owned farms, especially at Rift Valley. Most were very well run by hardworking people who threw themselves into farming with both skill and energy. Of course there were some wild people who behaved pretty irresponsibly, and who got the headlines in the English newspapers. But the great majority were most efficient hard-working farmers, who both worked hard and played hard. One met a few ex-Naval officers who had been axed by the Geddes axe. The more resourceful of them seemed to be doing well. Lovely country – in some parts rather like the downs of Dorsetshire and Wiltshire. A fairly light handed Colonial Service administrator ran the colony well, which was mainly devoted to farming of all sorts, including coffee, tea, sisal as well as crop and stock farming, which presented some problems from the numerous predators in Kenya. The colonial or expatriate Englishman is proverbially hospitable, and those living in Kenya were no exception to the rule. The warmth of the welcome one got in their homes was never to be forgotten. But there was no doubt in most cases England was ‘home’, and some hoped eventually to retire there keeping perhaps a foot in both countries. Later a visit to Zanzibar, where the Sultan paid us a visit. A warm-hearted anglophile like many Arab chiefs, he made us exceedingly welcome to the islands of Zanzibar and Pemba, famous for their cloves whose smell permeated the whole island. A lovely trip in a motorboat round parts of the island. Then into Dar-es-Salaam, the capital of Tanganyika [modern Tanzania], which was governed by a formidable old Scot of the Colonial Service, Sir Donald Cameron.35 He had everybody under control, including the ivory poachers who seldom got away with it. Dar-es-Salaam is a fine town, having been laid out without regard to expense by the Germans when it was the Capital of German East Africa. Then from there, with a short visit to Tanga, on to Aden [in present day Yemen] which in those days was a busy port. A short visit to the island, Socotra, which was completely uninhabited. From a strategic point of view we ought, I think, to have taken it and fortified as the guardian of the western approaches of the Indian Ocean. The Captain managed in getting one of the itinerant Arab fishermen to lend him a camel, which took him some way up the mountains of Socotra. Then it must have been whilst we were at Aden we learnt that King George V had become seriously ill, and we were to go to Dar-es-Salaam again with all despatch to pick up the Prince of Wales, who at this time was on a shooting expedition in Tanganyika. We were soon 35 Sir Donald Charles Cameron (1871-1948), ODNB. 63

there, and embarked the Prince of Wales and his equerry, Lascelles, who boarded the ship in his working shorts which he always wore when on safari. As soon as he was onboard with his very scanty luggage, and with his shooting companions, we set off to Aden at the best speed we could make, about 25 knots – a novel experience in these fuel economy days. The Prince of Wales soon settled down and spent most of his time in the Wardroom, and also visited various parts of the ship. He was a very pleasant and attractive companion, though even then we thought some of his ideas about ‘to hell with custom, habits and tradition’ when in fact it suited him, a bit wild! Basically he seemed very sincere, was very fond of his younger brother, Prince George, who I had in my charge in the old Queen Elizabeth about six to seven years back. He talked freely and seemed to enjoy the relaxed atmosphere on the ship. In conversation with me he frequently expressed anxiety about his father, the King’s, health. He said again and again he did not wish to become King yet. He evidently chafed much at the customary restraints on royalty. A most likeable and charming man, who seemed young for his years, but he never minded if one refused to agree with some ‘avant garde’ ideas which he espoused, perhaps just to tease us. I sensed even at that time his relations with his father were not close, and though he did not always agree with his mother, the Queen, he was at heart very fond of her. But as I have said, the favourite was Prince George and he also had a great liking for his sister, Princess Mary. He had great vitality and was very restless. His ideas seem to be mostly pretty liberal, and he abhorred the pompous and more than once said he could not stand Lord Curzon! I reminded him that my father had said in his opinion Curzon was one of the greatest Viceroys we had ever had. He was at times strangely unsure of himself. I remember when taking him to visit some of the Petty Officers Messes he kept asking me how he went down! He in fact had a very easy and pleasant way with him, and surely must have appreciated the Messes he visited much liked him. The ship was slightly delayed in the Suez Canal when he visited Lord Lloyd, who was Governor of Egypt in those days, but who he found a bit didactic and protocol minded! A slightly unfair assessment of what was in many ways a great British Proconsul! As soon as we reached Port Said we re-embarked the Prince and took him in rather rough weather with all speed to Brindisi, where he was met by the Naval attaché and put into a special train which took him across Italy and France to Calais. The King was round the corner by the time he reached London, and had quite a few more years to live. What were one’s impressions of somebody I got in some measure to know fairly well? First of all a most awfully nice fellow without a trace of side, at times a bit unsure of himself, but determined to do his best by the lights of what he considered just and right. Did not like what one now calls a ‘stuffed shirt’. Not a strong character, though a very humane one. It was evident even then he had a streak of obstinacy and on some subjects he had a pretty closed mind. Christmas 1928 We arrived in Chatham for a short refit and recommission in very cold weather, before returning to the East Indies for further service. 64

1929 The ship was in splendid heart, not a lot wanted doing as the ship had been running not much more than three years since first commissioning. We got a good new ships company, which marched down to join the ship to the strain of our new volunteer band which I had organised complete with instruments. A lot of new faces in the Wardroom. Clement Moody, the new Commander, a forceful character, Chads and a number of others who though good were not quite up to the standard of the old team headed by Guy Russell. But it was clear we should soon settle down into a first-class ship. It was decided by Vernon that I should stay on my full two years until the autumn, which pleased me much as I had seen enough of the East Indies station to want to see more. About this time the Conservative Association, which had adopted Father as their Parliamentary Candidate for West Gloucestershire, fell out, I think unwisely, with him and he resigned. Briefly, they had promised to pay expenses and the agent’s salary, which they had not fulfilled and father had himself to find the money. Secondly, they disagreed with his strategy. Father energetically canvassed the hard line Socialist areas, as he rightly knew there were many doubters in these Socialist strongholds and would vote for a genuine Forest man like Father, who had an appeal far greater than the average petty Socialist politician and who was universally liked and respected. As his second priority Father said canvas the rural areas, most of which will anyway vote Conservative. As events proved, Father was right and the Constituency Committee’s views wrong, but I rather doubt if Father would have got in at the next election on a straight Conservative ticket! Father took it all very magnanimously, and immediately said he would help to the best of his ability any Conservative candidate put forward. During the year two very great Frenchmen died, Marshal Foch who proved himself an exceptionally good Supreme Western Front Commander, and Monsieur Clemenceau, the great French Prime Minister of war time days. Late February or early March found us again on passage to the East Indies, which started with a good work up at Trincomalee where I took a few days leave and shot a couple of bears and a leopard. Usual August week at Colombo, and a pleasant series of visits up to East Coast of India where we visited the new commercial port of Vizagagapatam [Visakhapatnam, Andhra Pradesh], on which great hopes were pinned, Cuddalore and Cananora, which revived memories of the great days of the ‘John’ Company [East India Company]. Madras, perhaps the quietest of the great Indian ports, nevertheless all the more pleasant for that, was again visited. By this time it must have been September, and the time came to be relieved by Millington, a torpedoman who qualified a few courses after me. I took the train to Bombay, and picked up the P&O mail steamer back to England. A pleasant and uneventful voyage which included a call at Casablanca. In May of 1929 Baldwin had called a General Election on largely the slogan of ‘Safety First’, which did not appeal. The result was the Conservatives were soundly beaten and the Labour 65

Party as the biggest party, under Ramsay Macdonald, formed a Government. 1929 saw the start of the great American slump, which was to engulf the whole of Europe. On arrival in Vernon, I was told I was to take my full foreign service leave and join at the end of the year, relieving Stuart Paton as head of the Experimental High Power Electrical Department under the overall direction of “Dasher” Grace (Com.N.V.Grace), who was the experimental electrical Commander. A wholly admirable man, with perhaps slightly unadventurous views on new equipment for the Navy. Searchlights were our chief concern, and I soon had ideas how to improve radically the performance and above all the control of these sources of illumination. 1930 I soon got absorbed in experimental electrics in Vernon, and in particular the searchlight side. Using my knowledge gathered at Greenwich I started off by experimenting with ‘voltage control’ instead of the existing ‘current control’ for the searchlight lamp. This proved itself and rendered a finer control of the lamp’s performance possible and was indeed adopted later for all searchlight lamps in the Navy. Then I tried a 48" searchlight mirror in place of the 36" we had as standard, as if focused properly the intensity of the beam would be nearly doubled, and the range of illumination of a target increased by perhaps as much as 30%. I found the work most stimulating, and was perhaps a little sad when I was told in the autumn that I had been selected for the staff college and was to do the 1931 staff course starting in January of that year, so would only have a year in Experimental Electrics. But to turn to wider things. The great depression caused an acute crisis, and Macdonald with Baldwin’s support formed a National Government. Though Macdonald has since been criticised, we at the time and for that matter still do think Macdonald’s action was truly patriotic, for he put the country before party which, alas, many of his party were not prepared to do. Then the Naval Conference in Washington was convened, and due in great measure to America’s insistence we reduced from seventy to fifty our cruiser strength, which was at the time quite inadequate.36 Stephen Roskill’s Naval Policy,Vol.1 [1968], between the wars describes these events with limpid clearness. But in 1930 the great depression was on us with a vengeance, and the unemployed rose to two and a half million. Even though one had a job in the Navy, one could not but be aware of the acute psychological distress these great unemployment figures caused among our people. One used to see in every town the unemployed loafing round – poor chaps through no fault of their own and looking very sad. But it was then clear to us what long term damage these unemployment figures would do to our country, and this subject was frequently debated in the Wardroom Mess of Vernon. 36 The Five-Power or Washington Naval Treaty 1922 between the UK, the US, France, Italy and Japan, was intended to prevent a future arms race by limiting the construction of ships. The implications for Britain’s ability to maintain fleets simultaneously in the North Sea, the Mediterranean and the Far East were substantial. The terms were modified by the London Naval Treaty of 1930, and largely abandoned after 1936. 66

The airship R100 did a trip to Canada, and until the R101 disaster in October when on an experimental flight to India, we believed there was a great future in airship transport as opposed to aircraft transport, which due to the slow development of the petrol internal combustion engine had very serious limitations and hazards. Right up to the outbreak of the war, I always felt there was a great future in airship transport, though of course its extreme vulnerability ruled it out of count for war purposes. A very pleasant time in Vernon this year – a carefree bachelor life with lots of games. I found the work on the experimental side most interesting. There were a lot of pleasant and able men in the mess, Rhoddie McGrigor, a future First Sea Lord, Charles Lambe also a future 1st S.L., George Creasy and a number of others who reached high rank in the Service.37 Jock Hughes Hallett, an outstandingly clever and provocative character who always told us he would be Prime Minister one day. After reaching Vice Admiral’s rank he took up politics, and was soon promoted to Minister though he had not reached Cabinet rank when the Conservative Government, of which he was a member, fell.38 I looked forward to the staff course and extended my historical reading, which always much interested me, as what better base for a study of war than a sound foundation of history. I paid fairly frequent visits to Longhope, where my father still found time for lots of interests and work. 1931 1931 was spent mainly at the Naval Staff College at Greenwich, and it proved to be one of the most absorbingly interesting years I have ever spent. In addition to learning the mechanics of staff work, how to prepare papers and memoranda, and where to find information on which to base memoranda, it was in reality a most enlightened general education. We learnt about the world, about economics, about society, about the various systems of Government all over the world, about Foreign Policy, about trends and so on, and, above all, about the British Commonwealth and what particular problems were besetting it. This course was intended among many other things to teach one how to debate, perhaps how to handle politicians in addition, of course, to Service officers of other nationalities and so on. It certainly awakened one’s imagination, and encouraged one to look at problems from a wider aspect than the strictly professional service aspect. The staff at Greenwich were good, Tom Calvert the Director, very much an old-time sea dog who saw a great deal further than one sometimes realised. The Deputy Director – John Godfrey – a man of transcending intelligence with a great capacity for teaching from history. He in World War II became the great Director of Naval Intelligence, whose reputation will last as long as the Admiralty Intelligence Department exists.39 The Commanders on the staff, Bill Tennant, Hookey Holland, John Leach, John Harding and others, were first rate and did well in the Second World War. Then the Commanders and Lieut. Commanders with the course were as about as bright a 37 Admiral Sir Rhoderick McGrigor (1893-1959); Admiral Sir Charles Lambe (1900-1960) ODNB; Admiral Sir George Creasy (1895-1972) ODNB 38 John Hughes Hallett (1901-1972) ODNB 39 John Godfrey (1899-1971), ODNB 67

crowd of officers, some of considerable intellectual stature, as one would find anywhere. To name just a few who became Commanders-in-Chief, members of Board of Admiralty, commanders of the Imperial Defence College, or won V.C. in the Second World War - Brind, Daniel, Packer, Brooking, Warburton Lee, Eccles, self-etc. etc. etc. Two very clever soldiers with us were Le Fanu and Roberts, who both did well in World War II. Of the debaters I think Pat Brooking was the best, though Daniel, the solider Roberts, were not far behind. Middleton, a very able Torpedo Commander, was one of the cleverest. As the youngest member on the course, and one of the least experienced, I watched and listened to start with and learnt a most amazing amount about many things one just did not know existed. I was chosen to give the lecture on “the nature of a future war and Naval Policy to be adopted”. I looked at the lecture the other day (forty-four years later), and whilst I made some quite good guesses and forecasts which came true in World War II, some of it was not very prescient! But above all what the staff course did was to awaken and stir one’s imagination, and I don’t think there can have been anybody on this very friendly course who did not much benefit from it. But 1931 was a bad year for the Navy. There was the so-called ‘mutiny’ at Invergordon in September as a result of pay cuts to the seamen of the Navy. Much has been written about this, but the following points are clear. The Board of Admiralty never should have agreed to these cuts because of the economic situation. When the trouble occurred both First and Second Sea Lords should have resigned. It is true to say some of the officers in seagoing ships were not nearly as closely in touch with the lower deck as they should have been, and they should have been able to contain what was in fact a spontaneous outburst of the lower deck. There were, of course, just a few ‘agitators’ in the lower deck, but they should have been located and isolated before trouble broke out. Altogether not a creditable chapter in the Navy’s history. This came as a profound shock to all of us, as apart from isolated incidents usually due to bad officers, over the last century and a half no serious mutinies had occurred since the mutinies of the Nore in the eighteenth century. In 1931 occurred Baldwin’s famous attack on the press Barons (Beaverbrook and Rothermere) who he likened to harlots who wanted “power without responsibility”. Due to the worsening crisis Ramsay Macdonald formed the National Government on the basis of four Labour, four Conservative and two Liberal members of the Cabinet to combat the acute economic crisis. This was I believe a wise and farsighted action by Ramsay Macdonald. We went off the gold standard in September, having stuck overlong to the monetary policies espoused by Sir Montagu Norman, the Governor of the Bank of England. In November a second National Ministry was formed, as a good proportion of the Labour Party had deserted Ramsay MacDonald. The year ended with an intensification of the world economic crisis, which was having the effect in Germany of encouraging the nationalists in their bid for power. To return to the staff course 1931. The staff course indeed proved itself to be a wonderful stimulant to looking at the problems which could confront one in an absolutely impartial way, and not to rely on the slogans which were nothing less than a substitute for failing to think out a matter! 68

Dart Torpedo carrying Aircraft, We had an interesting week with the R.A.F. Staff College when they visited us at taking off from HMS Courageous. Greenwich, but what perturbed one was that one and all they had been indoctrinated with Trenchard’s fallacies about the use and purpose of air power. For instance, they refused to recognise in war the first call on a nation’s resources must be to ensure the security of the main base – in our case the British Islands. It astounded me, as this principle had been enunciated and indeed proved time and time again from the ancient Persians, Greeks, Romans and through the Middle Ages and down to the present day. I felt at the time that Trenchard was motivated perhaps by political considerations and not by true reasoning. He felt perhaps that the R.A.F. would have no future as an independent service, when he invented a theory for air power that it was completely independent of the Torpedo firing, at Zanzibar other two services. But this theory had dreadful effects on us in the Second World War, and seriously jeopardised our chances of victory. It all comes out crystal clear in Stephen Roskill’s famous Naval Policy up to 1935, which repays study as long as one can foresee. 1932 A happy Christmas in 1931 at Longhope. I had been appointed to Courageous, one of our recently converted aircraft carriers, as Squadron Torpedo Officer to the newly appointed Rear Admiral Aircraft Carriers. This post was held by the R.A. Reggie Henderson, a tremendous if rather eccentric character. Here was a great opportunity, for it was clear to me there was much scope in the job as it was necessary to develop both tactically and technically the use of the aircraft torpedo. It was already clear that the aircraft torpedo weapon would eventually supercede the big gun as the Navy’s main weapon. 69

I joined Courageous in January, and found in the large Wardroom which included many Naval observers a fairish number of congenial souls. The first thing I decided on, and got the Captain’s approval, was to be provided with an aircraft so that I could observe and photo all torpedo attacks carried out by our old Dart torpedo aircraft. Ned Austin, a shrewd and first-rate pilot, was the Squadron Commander, and he gave me much help in developing the tactics of torpedo attack and improving the reliability and technical performance of the torpedoes themselves. I had one or two exciting trips in aircraft, both landing and taking off, and apart from one incident which resulted in a minor prang when I volunteered to try out the new experimental arrester gear for aircraft, I had no serious mishaps, and did not have an involuntary swim! I and my old friend, Charles Thomson of Enterprise days, who had become an observer, perfected an aircraft torpedo attack teacher, which yielded great dividends and improved the marksmanship of Sopwith Camel, Deck Take-off the torpedo pilots. We were I think given an award of £100 by the Admiralty, and this attack teacher was standardised for use in the Fleet Air Arm and later by the R.A.F. Then I also designed a scheme for landing aircraft on deck at night, called a Sector Landing Light. It shone a beam divided into three sections in the direction of aircraft approaching the deck, red sector – too low, green – correct, yellow – too high. This was taken over by the Electrical Department of the Admiralty, and it was eventually I believe patented by somebody, who I hope got something for it. This light had, of course, to be completely stabilised to compensate for movements of the ship. Everybody was very enthusiastic, and I had as good a torpedo party as one would expect anywhere, and one of which was capable of phenomenally long hours of work. But by and large, we made tremendous strides in the use of the aircraft torpedo attack, and it was soon realised in the Admiralty and elsewhere, that this might be the decisive weapon of the future, as it has proved to be in the Second World War, i.e the sinking of Bismarck, the Taranto raids and above all, the decisive effects of American torpedo attacks on the Japanese fleet which did more than anything else to bring about the defeat of the Japanese navy in World War II. The RAF I soon discovered in their staff divisions were so mesmerised by the bomb, and the controversy about bomb versus battleship that they neglected completely the torpedo as an aircraft carried weapon, which was infinitely more effective as an anti-ship weapon than the bomb. In the lower echelons I found, however, some far seeing RAF pilots held my views. But it needed no great intelligence to appreciate [that] to sink a warship it was better to make a hole in it and let the water in than make a hole in it and let the air in. Later there was some controversy about the ‘B’ bomb, which was in fact a free rising mine which if laid in the path of a ship might puncture a hole in the bottom and let the water in. But, alas, interservice jealousies at the staff and Ministry level did much to hamper development. 70

1932 Flycatcher Fighter, taking off from HMS This was a bad year for our economy, in fact the whole world Courageous. was in the grip of a most acute economic crisis. But I sensed the Admiralty were doing well sticking to essentials, and though delayed we were building ships at a modest rate. Admiralty recognised how important was the Fleet Air Arm, so we were exempted from the drastic fuel economy measures which had to be imposed in the rest of the Fleet. We did far more sea-time than any other ship, and during the working up period, which was for us about eight months in the year, we spent four or five days a week at sea. But the feeling we were doing something worthwhile made for an excellent spirit in the ship. Our first Captain in Courageous was Varyl Robinson, a first rate and truly delightful man who had been mixed up with CMBs in the first war, with Heneage Legge, our Commander, a great character with a quite bottomless sense of humour, as indeed was necessary with all commanders of aircraft carriers! Later Frankie Elliott relieved Robinson and though very efficient did not I sensed get on so well with the Admiral, Reggie Henderson, as Varyl Robinson had. One staff officer in Reggie Henderson’s staff was Reg Portal, brother of the man who later became Chief of the Air Staff in the Second World War. Reg Portal was a pioneer in aircraft torpedo work, and much encouraged me to put aircraft torpedo attacks very much on the map. We developed Retrieval! various modes of attack, which were used in the Second World HMS Courageous, 1932 War and in a way copied by the Americans. 71

When in Courageous I also tried to look at all aspects of life in so far as naval personnel were concerned, and got to know my men in the torpedo division very well indeed. I think it may have been true to say that some of the old rules for officer-like conduct had in a few cases been overlooked, such as that the first duty of an officer is to ensure the comfort, well-being and conditions of men under his charge are as good as is humanly possible, and that these considerations must come before the officer’s own comfort and conditions. In the wider sphere the Ottawa Conference was held amid much trumpeting, but not I fear much achieved due perhaps to the inward-looking attitude of some Canadian politicians.40 In the holidays that I had there was much to do. People were most hospitable, and invited me to many house parties. We had quite a number of friends in Shropshire, and what with the Yates at Madeley, the Lynch Blosses at Peplow, and Meyricks at Wellington most weekends were fully and enjoyably taken up. Economy was hitting people hard. Father in his cheerful way got by, but said once he had never been so hard up in his life! Flemings, the family leather business which Uncle Jim had run with great success and good profit for many years, went into liquidation and nothing was left for the shareholders - a bit of a blow for father. My brother was working with Shell in London, and Charles Ackers shut up Huntley Manor and lived in the rest house he had built on the main A40 in Huntley Hill Wood. My sister Jane’s health was not too good, and she spent quite a lot quite a time in various convalescent and nursing homes. David was doing well at his private school near Winchester, and was destined for Eton when he was thirteen. Work in Courageous was most fascinating. We perfected various methods of torpedo attack by aircraft, and had meetings with the Mediterranean Fleet in which all three aircraft carriers worked together and developed methods of providing the Fleet with the all the aircraft services needed. About one third of the flying personnel in Courageous were RAF and I found at our level we could not have all worked better together, and it was only when one got on the staff and Ministry level that suspicion and non-cooperation were so frequently encountered. I trained an RAF men’s whaler’s crew that won all the whaler races! The head RAF man in charge of all flying was a character if ever there was one, Wing Commander Collison, a Canadian by birth who was one of the First War aces and heavily, and I believe deservedly, decorated. The squadron leader, Dusty Durston, an ex RNR Merchant Service Officer, was first-rate and eventually reached the post of C-in-C Coastal Command. Courageous was a very happy ship, and the fact that we had two services on board, RN and RAF, put each of them on their mettle. I met from time to time my old friend Geoffrey Blake, who was now I think Fourth Sea Lord, and I got plenty of encouragement from him. 1932 was a pretty strenuous year, and having the good fortune of having a challenging job there was never a dull or idle moment. The Admiralty in their wisdom excluded the aircraft carriers from their stringent economy measures, so we could make much progress. We had surprisingly few fatal casualties. The aircraft we had, Fairy IIIF, Flycatcher, Dart, Nimrod, were 40 The Imperial Economic Conference, Ottawa, 1932, to discuss the economic depression, resulted in a series of agreements for imperial preference tariffs. 72

pretty robust. The only tricky one was the Ripon torpedo bomber. I had one or two exciting runs, but in each case we managed in getting back to the flight deck without damage to wind or limb! 1933 1933 saw the beginning with some slight signs of recovery in our economy, though there were still over 2 million unemployed. But what we perhaps didn’t realise in the services at that time was the appalling effect this was having on our ability to rearm, especially as the unwise Ten Year Rule in which Winston Churchill had played a big part, was still in force.41 We were just losing the capacity to rearm, and it was no good saying ‘moral is to the physical as three is to one’ and hoping for the best. It is not infrequently forgotten that the ‘moral’ depends on having reasonably up to date arms and methods with which to combat one’s enemy!42 Some fascinating combined fleet exercises with the Mediterranean Fleet when the combined air strike force inflicted much ‘damage’ on the battle fleet. Something like two-thirds of the torpedo hits were obtained. Denny, the FGO of the Mediterranean Fleet brushed this result aside to me, saying “all aircraft will be shot down by our latest close range AA weapons”. But when I showed him the meticulous records taken of this attack, which showed in fact only a quarter of the torpedo bombers were even fired at, he slightly modified his views. Reggie Henderson and Chatfield, the Mediterranean C-in-C, were I believe greatly impressed. I thought at that time the Fleet, which was still very battleship minded, underrated the possible effects of the torpedo bomber and grossly overestimated the effectiveness of the Navy’s close range AA weapons. The Second World War, which nobody guessed could be on us in six years’ time, emphasised this. I remember to a shocked audience once advancing the view that the aircraft carrier was in fact the capital ship of the present Navy. But my view was I found already held by quite a number of thinking officers. This year among the many pleasant weekend parties, I attended was one at Stokesey Court, the home of General and Mrs Rotton, where I met my future wife, what tremendous luck for me! I thought the party was going to be rather dull, but it was far from this! The Rottons were very kind people, who lived in an immense but pretty hideous house built in the middle of the last century at a cost reputed to be £250,000! Good pitch pine panelling, and a lovely garden. Ruffie Allcroft, to whom the property would go, was Mrs Rotton’s son by her first marriage to the Mr Allcroft of the great glovemakers, Dent Allcroft & Co., but who had died quite a long time back. The daughter, Jewel Allcroft, was most hospitable and thoughtful and helped her mother and stepfather, General Rotton, look after the house parties. The summer of 1933 was a good one, and we managed in continuing the great progress made with the torpedo bomber tactics, and I became quite an expert air photographer of these! I soon learned air photographs of all the attacks are essential if the pilots ere to learn to improve their performance. This with the torpedo attack teacher which we 41 The Ten Year Rule, adopted in 1919, stated that armed forces estimates should be drawn up on the assumption that the British Empire would not be involved in any major conflict in the next ten years. It was officially abandoned in 1932, but intense pressure from Government kept spending down. 42 It is not clear here whether WWD means ‘moral’ or ‘morale’, or perhaps something of both! 73

had evolved were greatly liked by the pilots, who felt they now knew what they were doing. A very nice RAF pilot, by name Esmonde, was particularly enthusiastic, and he earned a posthumous VC in the war attacking the German battlecruisers as they steamed up the channel. Courageous was due for a fairly big refit, which would take some months at the end of the year, so it was decided I should leave in the late autumn in order to allow my successor, Jock Hughes Hallett, to get into the saddle before the new Admiral, Ramsay, took over in the new year. I was told I had been earmarked as the next fleet torpedo officer of the China Station in HMS Kent, under the pretty formidable Admiral, Sir Frederick Dreyer. When I went to say goodbye to Reggie Henderson he was complimentary about all that had been achieved, and said ‘you will not get promoted next January!’ I had never dreamt I would, but because I was only technically in the zone for promotion for Commander and it was most unlikely that the Admiralty would in my case make a special case. Anyway, I was promoted 18 months later and then was the youngest commander but one to be promoted in the Navy! Reggie was wise - I needed more experience, and special and exceptional early promotion in peacetime do not by any means always work out for the best. I began to see quite a lot of Elizabeth Phipps in the autumn, and was entertained by her dear old mother, Lady Normanby, at Mulgrave Castle. As I had some time before joining Kent, I thought I would do a foreign language study course with old professor Nohe in Germany in the Black Forest. My brother, who speaks German well, strongly recommended it and said I would like him and not have a dull moment! How right he was. So I went to Marxzell in the Black Forest, about twenty miles I suppose from Stuttgart, and met an amusing crowd there. Terence Rattigan (now Sir Terence) the playwright, Jock Gibb, a most versatile man who has achieved much with public work, and another man whose family had been involved with the Blue Funnel line, and who brought out a racing MG car in which I had a few perilous drives. Marxzell was great fun, and old Professor and Frau Nohe were great characters. Terrence Rattigan in the play ‘French Without Tears’ parodies life there in his inimitable and charming way. 1933/34 The Nazis were just coming to power and the Professor, who had much too keen a sense of humour to stomach Nazi doctrines, ED & WWD- Engagement and Wedding Photo made no bones about his dislike and contempt for them. 74

As students we used to tease the Nazi politicians who seemed absolutely devoid of a sense of humour. On the other hand, it was clear they were bringing back to the Germans a sense of self-respect, which they had lost since the Treaty of Versailles.
