It was difficult not to laugh at figures like Goebbels and Goering, and of course Hitler, they seem so utterly absurd and ridiculous. Though we had a foreboding not entirely shared by the old Professor, that these men might be very dangerous indeed, for the Germans as a nation had not the sense of the ridiculous which in this country would have ensured their being laughed out of court. I managed in mastering German grammar quite quickly, but found speech much more difficult; in fact, I was never very fluent though I could read books and understand them. But maybe my mind was not on my work, for I thought a lot about Elizabeth Phipps! I spent Christmas of 1933 at home. My father kept his end up in spite of a number of economies he was forced to make. But he was always of a very frugal nature, and never minded tightening his belt. He managed in getting a little shooting, and kept himself very fit. I managed seeing quite a lot of Elizabeth, and was always most hospitably entertained at her home, Mulgrave Castle. A bit to my surprise I found she reciprocated the affection I had for her, so in February, or was it early March, we became engaged. I never dreamed I would be half as lucky as this! Father and family seemed delighted, and Elizabeth’s family gave me a very warm and generous welcome. There was not much time, as Kent was due to sail at the end of May or early June for the China Station to become the Fleet Flagship of the Commander-in-Chief, Admiral Sir Frederick Dreyer. But nothing was impossible for Lady Normanby who in a mere five weeks set about arranging the marriage, which was to be in Lythe church where the Phipps had worshipped for some centuries. Everybody was asked! Many of my relations, old Aunt Addie, Uncle David, Charles and Jane Ackers etc., were put up at Mulgrave and by many neighbours within a range of fifty miles or so were put up by friends of the Normanbys. My old friend, Terence Back, consented to be my best man, and right well and joyously he performed this duty! What fun it all was but, oddly enough, as one of the principals, one does not remember and see as much as one might, as life is such a whirl at that time. We had a wonderful pre-wedding dinner at Mulgrave the night before, and I think close on forty were there! Elizabeth looked absolutely charming, and I was congratulated by many men there who said how lucky I was. The bishop of Whitby, (Right Rev. Woolcombe) assisted by the Rev. Faulkner, the father of my first lieutenant in Thanet, who was doing temporary duty at Lythe Parish, married us. Elizabeth was given away by her brother Oswald, and Francis Egerton supported Lady Normanby. A truly inspiring service and what wonderful wedding presents we had. Elizabeth’s bridesmaids were Joan Phipps, Jewel Allcroft, Dorothy Lane Fox, Griselda O’Brien, Mary Egerton, with David Ackers as page. I remember catching sight of my father, and how happy he looked, almost overcome with happiness. I thought for a moment how my mother would have enjoyed it, and how wonderfully she would have got on with Lady Normanby, and with whom she would have had so much in common. I thought fleetingly of my parents’ very hurried marriage in Slough because father had suddenly been recalled to India about thirty-one years back! Jane and Charles were there, the former looking rather better than she had of late and just as beautiful as ever. 75

Terrence Back was in every sense a tower of strength. He took me for a drive in the morning of the wedding, and because of a ‘sea fret’ it was quite foggy. The wedding was wonderful and how splendid Elizabeth looked being led up the aisle by her brother. The reception was magnificent and what better place than Mulgrave Castle with the lovely pictures in each of the main rooms to have a reception. We were most awfully lucky with our wedding presents. A brief description of them is contained in my father’s diary. Lady Normanby gave me a splendid gold watch from Cartier which has been with me ever since, as well as a gold wristwatch which I still wear over 40 years later! We went off in my fast Rover car, which I had purchased about six months previously, and I suppose it must have been well after 5:00 PM before we left. The guns on the quarterdeck fired a salute to mark our wedding.43 The only two people I would have liked to have been at our wedding were Elizabeth’s father, who had died 18 months previously, and my mother who had died about nine years before. Our first stop was Harrogate, and then on to the Lake District for an all too brief but no less enjoyable honeymoon. We walked a lot and did a little modest climbing, and saw some of the Egerton cousins in the Rochdale’s house which was not far from Keswick. Time to return to Kent at Chatham where I got an uproarious welcome from the wardroom as soon as I stepped on board! May 1934 onwards On return from a very brief honeymoon, we went down to Chatham where I rejoined HMS Kent from my leave. We had the usual difficulty getting rooms and your mother had her first experience of the suspicious landlady who opened the door only a crack so that she could inspect the possible ‘lodger’. However, we eventually got rooms not far from the dockyard which were similar to the rooms you hear described in Trollope and Dickens. The chairs in our sitting room all had antimacassars, and there was a splendid aspidistra in the window and the mantelpiece was crowned with a big photograph of our landlady, her late lamented husband and half a dozen children sitting next to their parents in order of height with their hands on their neighbours’ shoulders. This gave an impression of a human staircase. We met the officers and some of their wives and found out who might be coming out to China, where the ship was destined and on which station we would fly the flag of the Commander-in-Chief, Admiral Sir Frederick Dreyer. The ship, recommissioned during this period and having completed a brief refit, was busy preparing herself for sea. Although the last commission had been a splendid one, this promised, from what we could see of the new officers, to be even better. Ion Tower, our new captain, as fine an officer as one could hope to find anywhere, a splendid leader and most knowledgeable, modest and competent officer. Alas, he was killed in an air raid in London during the last War when he was about to go as one of Admiral Cunningham’s Admirals in the Mediterranean. His wife, Sophie Tower soon became a great friend of ours. Ian Tower, who relieved a very able officer, Algy Willis (now Admiral of the Fleet Sir Algernon Willis) soon had the officers and the ship’s company striving to make HMS Kent the finest cruiser in the Navy. Ion Tower had a most attractive personality and behind the modest and unassuming approach he had great strength of 43 The quarterdeck at Mulgrave was the long lawn in front of the Castle looking out towards the sea, with small cannons at the far end which had probably belonged to Captain Constantine John Phipps (1744-1792). 76

character - for nobody could push him about - an ideal quality for a Flag Captain to that dominant and forceful character Admiral Sir Frederick Dreyer! Our Commander, an old Staff College friend of mine, was Bertie Packer, another magnificent officer who knew exactly how to run a ships company. Even tempered and just, he soon reached the stage where the ships company would respond wholeheartedly to him. Bertie Packer was a first-class games player and one of the Navy’s best tennis players. His wife Joy Packer, the authoress, came out to China and we saw quite a bit of both of them. Then there was a fine backbone of Lieutenant Commanders. Tom Pakenham the First Lieutenant and Gunnery Officer, a great character with endless capacity for work - rather keen on MRA44 at that time - who however did not lose his sense of humour and proved himself to be a first rate gunnery officer. We got to know his wife Clara quite well, also a great character who entered into the life of the ship. Next in seniority came Jock Findlay, an ex-observer, who had a very pawky Scots sense of humour, but who pulled his weight fully in the ship in the capacity of ‘mate of the upper deck’. I came next in seniority after him. Then there were a good number of fine messmates and competent officers to make up the wardroom - Jack Scatchard, Stuart Moore, Lombard Hobson among the watchkeepers. Old Waldron, the silent old paymaster who never missed out on any activity. Tony George, Morris Macmillan, Andrew Yates, and many others all helped make life go with a swing. The time came for us to set sail. I liked the look of my Torpedo Party, a really good chief torpedo Gunner’s Mate, a good Gunner and Warrant Electrician, a sprinkling of older hands among the young men. We soon left the basin at Chatham and went down the narrow channel to Sheerness, where we made fast to a buoy and ammunitioned ship. Elizabeth came down and spent the last night before we sailed in rather a quaint little old hotel at Sheerness where many naval officers’ wives, over the centuries, have stayed before their husbands sailed away. As far as I remember, Father came down to wish the ship Godspeed and waved to us as we sailed past Sheerness Point. We set sail for Malta after stopping for a few hours to do some wireless calibration trials at Spithead and passed Gibraltar without stopping. Elizabeth came down to Southsea and I caught a glimpse of her before we sailed. It was a lovely May day as we sailed down the Channel. We were all kept busy on passage, testing ourselves out the various stations, such as fire stations, collision stations, taking in tow, being Aerial Patrol flying over the taken in tow, which a newly commissioned ship always does as soon as she leaves harbour Meditteranean Fleet in harbour at for the first time. This settling down is a wonderful experience for a ships company as it Malta enables one to get to know exactly how good, or not so good, the Officers, Petty Officers, and Leading Ratings are at their particular job. It enables everybody to start getting the feel of their ship. 44 MRA or Moral Re-Armament was a non-denominational, religious revival movement founded by the American pastor Frank Buchman. 77

We entered the Grand harbour in Malta and secured to buoys in Bighi Bay. I noticed that rather formidable figure Admiral Sir William Fisher, the Commander-in-Chief of the Mediterranean Fleet watching our efforts from his offices in the Baracca. However we did not do too badly. Tom Pakenham and I were the fo’c’sle officers [forward part of the ship below deck], so we felt we had made a good start. There is a picture in the loft at Coglan of the Kent entering the Grand Harbour. Admiral Fisher decided to come on board and walked round the ship’s company where he got a variety of answers, some unexpected, from a very tough old Petty Officer who was the Captain of the Quarter Deck. After spending a couple of nights at Malta, where we met a lot of old friends as the Med Fleet was in harbour at that time, we sailed for Port Said and had an uneventful passage to Aden, though we found it mighty hot going down the Red Sea with a following wind. A day at Aden and a comparatively pleasant passage across the Indian Ocean to Colombo and Trincomalee. The monsoon had not quite broken and it was pretty stuffy between decks. Neither Colombo nor Trincomalee seemed to have changed much from my Enterprise days in the 1920s. Just time to see the few old friends at Colombo who I knew well in the 1927-29 period. Next stop was Singapore and as we secured alongside at Keppel Harbour, I saw a remarkable old China man with a bright red face come alongside in his sampan. He apparently knew the ship well and greeted the commander as a long-lost friend. He was our Sampan Man and rejoiced in the nickname Tomato Face. We carried his sampan on board from place to place and one of his duties was to ferry the officers to and from shore at any time of the day or night at every port we visited on the then China Station. He was a splendid chap and conversed fluently in pidgin English on almost any subject under the sun. He complained to me that it cost him four Shanghai dollars (six UK shillings) to transport him and his sampan from his home near Tsingtao to Singapore. I suggested six shillings for a 2000-mile trip was not too expensive, but he would have none of this and persuaded the commander to reimburse him from Wardroom funds. We were now on the China Station and had a quick look at Singapore before sailing for Hong Kong, which at that time was our main base on the station. A look at some of the main problems, as they seemed at the time, might not be out of place. Though not more than 34 years ago, there was then apparently little presage of the not far off disintegration of the British Empire and the collapse of our own military position in the Far East. Let us first see the extent of the station. It covered half the Pacific, the whole coast of China and Japan, the Malaya Peninsula, French Indochina, the Dutch East Indies, and along the top of Australia. Our duties also took us far up the main rivers of China i.e. the Yangtze and the West River [Xi Jiang], where one would reach places well over 1000 miles from the open sea, right into the heart of Asia. The British Naval forces on the China station consisted of five big County Class 8 inch gun cruisers, one aircraft carrier - Hermes, one smaller D Class 6 inch gun cruiser, a flotilla of destroyers (9 ships), usually 5 or 6 sloops, a squadron of submarines and a depot ship and about 8 special flat bottomed river gunboats. Next of course to the Japanese, we were the principal naval force on the China Seas. We saw very little of the Japanese Navy, who kept very much to their own waters, and for security reasons never seemed to show themselves. Oddly enough the American Navy visited the China Coast rather seldom. Their main base of 78

course was in Hawaii, with a good base also at Manila, which was the headquarters of what they called their Asiatic Squadron. They had in 1935 a couple of modern cruisers at Manila, one of which was commanded by Captain Nimitz, later to become famous as American Commander-in-Chief of the Pacific in the Second World War. A truly great sailor, but more about him later. The French had a cruiser and some smaller vessels based at Saigon, which we met occasionally when we were in what one would now call Vietnamese waters. What was the role of the China fleet as we were called? It was to safeguard British interests in these waters, to put down the still rampant piracy on the China coast, to act as a sort of general policeman in the whole area, and to forestall trouble wherever possible and to foster liaison with the Australian and the New Zealand Navies. In other words, by their very presence we gave visible and indeed tangible support to the Ambassadors, Consular officials, British representatives and British nationals who lived and worked within the limits of the China Station. It must be remembered China was still in a state of turmoil - differing warlords were still fighting each other, though Chiang Kai-shek, the followers of Sun Yat Sen, was in the ascendant and it was his government with whom the British government treated. The Japanese also had considerable military forces deployed in China. We were also directed to maintain friendly relations with the Americans, French and Dutch who had considerable possessions in the Far East and whose interests would, in the event of conflict or troubles, almost certainly coincide with ours. Though none of us realised it at the time we were witnessing the sunset of colonial empires. But what about the Japanese, who had a Navy in Japanese waters far, far superior to ours and who were hostile to us for they regarded, or came to regard, the Far East as their sphere of interest, and found it difficult to tolerate the presence of American and European powers in those waters. We were aware of the War Plan, which, from the mid-1920s had been the main British Naval War Plan. It envisaged war against Japan as a result of some overt or hostile action of the Japanese against our vital interests in the Far East, or indeed hostile action against Australia itself. This plan envisaged the transfer of the main British fleet to the Far East to be based first at Singapore and then gradually moving northward so as to exercise control of all seas in the approaches to Japan. It would take time to concentrate the main British fleet in the Singapore area and the forward elements could not be expected for at least a month after the beginning of an emergency or outbreak of war. Our forces on the China Station were essential ‘light’ and ‘fast’. We had no battleships, which at that time were still regarded as the backbone and mainstay of the Fleet. Our role was to dispute where possible the command of the sea by Japanese forces, and to provide what support we could in controlling the approaches to Singapore and Hong Kong. In other words, to avoid if possible, getting cornered by superior forces and to keep the flag flying where possible until the arrival of the main British fleet, when we could, as it were, maritime-wise, go over to the offensive and reestablish our control of the seas in these areas. So we had a varied task before us. Although the Japanese were aggressive and had substantial land forces committed to campaigns in various parts of the mainland of China, it did not 79

then seem as if a maritime war was imminent - yet it came just over four years after I left the station! Various plans, such as those for the destruction of the oil fields in the southern half of the station, were continuously revised, for at that time Japan had no oil of her own under her specific control. So there was plenty of interest and variety to be met on the station. Battle efficiency in ships, both singly and collectively, stood high on our list of priorities, and with a Commander-in- Chief of the calibre of Sir Frederick Dreyer, this meant a mighty high standard. It seemed that the English and Chinese got on well together, for perhaps above everything else, they had much the same sense of humour! Our plans represented a nice balance between battle training, which we did mostly in the north in the Wei Hai Wei area; combined operations training with the army at Hong Kong and Singapore and on the other side of the coin numerous visits to places all over the China Station, mainly I suppose, for heartening the morale of our countrymen occupied in these places, and for showing that the long arm of the British Empire still meant something. But there was no doubt that a few days visit to some out of the way little place once every two years did an immense amount of good and was warmly welcomed by those whom we visited. For it was seldom possible to arrange visits to minor out of the way places more than once in every two years. Singapore fortress was far from completed as a result of much governmental procrastination in the years prior to 1934, but work was going at full stretch when we were there, with the result that the fortress itself and the main naval base was completed prior to the outbreak of the Japanese war in 1941. The main base during the period 1934 and 1935 was however Hong Kong where we had a good, though small dockyard, ammunition storage, stores depot and a store base for the Fleet Air Arm aircraft. Wei Hei Wei which was in fact an island in a bay in the Gulf which approaches Shanghai, was our summer headquarters. We had a naval hospital there and a small stores depot, all of which were under the command of the Senior Naval Officer, who in fact was the Surgeon Commander in charge of the hospital - a man of parts - for when the fleet was not there, he was very much out on a limb. Looking at the Station as a whole as it was in 1934 shows a very different pattern of power and life to what prevails now. In the far North was the Russian port of Vladivostok, on which was based a small Russian fleet, which we never saw. Then there was Japan, very suspicious and secretive, whose people however were very friendly to us when off duty. We were told that even with Korea and parts of Manchuria which they were occupying with their troops, that a population explosion was near and that they MUST be given substantial tropical territory in which to expand. China was in her habitual state of chaos, though the writ of Chiang Kai-shek ran over most of it. The Japanese had occupied Korea, and at times fought an unofficial war with Russia in Manchuria. The Japanese were also supporting sponsored forces near Canton, which just after we left the Station, was allegedly ‘bought’ by the Japanese general from a Chinese general for $2 million in negotiations which were also conducted at the Repulse Bay Hotel, Hong Kong! 80

There were still a number of warlords and rebellious forces, including the Communists in China, and our gunboat forces which reached up to ChungKing on the Yangtze and high up the West River above Canton, not infrequently had to deal with most unexpected situations. Further south French Indochina was quiet, and as far as we could judge, was ruled well by the French from the capital of Saigon. Siam [Thailand] was firmly ruled by a monarchy and again gave the impression of happiness and a measure of prosperity. The Siamese, like the Chinese, are basically peaceable people bound close to the land and prefer, or seemed to prefer, to live and let live, but this was of course before universal education. Then Malaysia with their senior independent Sultans was both prosperous and peaceable, though there was evident friction in Singapore between the Malays and Chinese, who combined to make up the population of this rich island. Relations between Europeans and Malays seemed universally good - but may be some of us were living in an atmosphere of a time when Raffles developed that part of the globe. The Dutch East Indies, Java, Sumatra and the Celebes, were prospering under firm Dutch rule, and though they took much out of these rich islands, they brought order and a reasonable measure of administrative efficiency to these large islands, to the lasting benefit of the inhabitants. Our relations with the Dutch were close and friendly. Sarawak was ruled by Rajah Brooke, and, under the semi primitive conditions which prevailed, seemed happy and reasonably prosperous. Australia was outside our station though we had some liaison with their Navy. Finally, the Philippines, where the Americans were making tentative and perhaps rather more positive progress, towards democratisation than we were, was an interesting and stimulating place to visit. The US had no colonial tradition, and in some respects, were less inhibited than we were at dealing with local and domestic problems. British interests were, I suppose, mainly commercial. Shanghai as an international port, was in some respects, the centre from which all trade in central and northern China radiated. Many big firms had very substantial interests in China, the biggest being Jardine Matheson, and Butterfield and Swire. We met, from time to time, the Keswick brothers who were contemporaries of ours and who largely owned and ran Jardine Matheson. To sum up, when we arrived on the China station in 1934 it was in a political sense much the same as it had been fifty years ago. There was little doubt who was in charge and there was also little doubt that the influence that we, as a nation, brought to bear was just as much for the good of the people of these areas as for British financial interests in London. Even in our most far reaching, and as we thought, forward thinking discussions, nobody suggested or even dreamt of the dramatic and perhaps traumatic change which would take place in the coming 15 years. We thought that gradually over the next 150 years some form of democratic government by peoples of these areas would evolve itself, bearing in mind the widely differing habits, customs and beliefs and ethnological backgrounds of those who lived within the compass of the China Station. May 1934 – September 1940 HMS Kent China Station After a short stay at Singapore we steamed north to Hong Kong, which we found even more beautiful than we had been led to believe. There is some truth in the saying that Hong Kong and Sydney are two of the most beautiful harbours in the world. The island itself, which seemed a veritable hive of activity, was most striking, with lovely bays and wooded hills and mountains running down the centre where some of the more prosperous and well-established families lived. Then across to Kowloon and the leased territory where there was a wonderful expansive country crowned with the mountain of Tai-Mo-Shan, a little short of 3000 feet in height, and intersected by lovely inlets from the sea. Through this ran the railway line to Canton [modern Guangzhou] which crossed the border at the Customs and Control station of Shai-To-Hok. There is any amount of rain at Hong Kong, and at certain times of the year, it is so damp that clothes and boots left hanging grow mildew overnight. In the middle of Hong Kong Harbour was situated Stone Cutters Island, where our wireless station was situated as well as a small naval hospital. What first struck me, even then in 1934, was the large number of skyscrapers. Land on the island which belongs to us in perpetuity and on the leased territory which is to be rendited [returned] to China before the end of the century is immensely valuable and, like New York, skyscrapers were sprouting everywhere. What we 85

saw then has been completely dwarfed into insignificance by what exists now, both on the island and leased territory. The harbour was full of ships, local coastal vessels occupied on the China coast trade, ocean going vessels, both carrying passengers and merchandise to and from the southern parts of China. In many ways Hong Kong could be regarded as the port of Canton. Finally, of course, the whole harbour was crowded with junks, sampans and the like, on which many Chinese families lived permanently and which traded indiscriminately in and around the Hong Kong area. We sensed a feeling of urgency and bustle at Hong Kong which was not noticeable at Singapore. The rickshaw coolies were frequently laughing, betting and running races with each other. They could be no respecter of persons for if you were upset from your rickshaw into a pool of mud, your coolie would laugh his head off! The big firms of Jardines and Butterfields, together with the Hong Kong Shanghai Banking Corporation had their headquarters at Hong Kong. The Hong Kong Club and Sports Club made the officers honorary members and we were soon made very welcome there among the many Europeans whose business took them to these parts. There was a lot to be done at Hong Kong, a certain amount of stores to be taken on board, a few minor repairs to be carried out and so on. Hong Kong dockyard was always out to help and the standard of work was very high there. We also embarked our official Chinese sailors and extra stewards which go to swell the numbers on board every British warship in the China station. The Chinese carried were divided into three categories; the official Chinese allowed to be carried dressed as blue jackets [i.e. regular sailors] by Admiralty regulations; this probably amounted to about 30 or 40. Then came the official, yet unofficial, Chinese sailors; these were allowed on board in addition by regulations drawn up and approved by the Commander-in-Chief of the China station. Finally came the absolutely unofficial Chinese allowed to live on board and work by permission of the Commander of each ship. These were special sampan men for various officers’ messes, stewards and ‘boys’ to help with the chief and petty officers’ messes. Boys were usually ‘makee learn’ to help with Bosuns, in Carpenters and Shipwrights Shops, and in various other skilled and semi-skilled trades. Having spent a few days getting as it were, kitted up, we set sail for our northern exercise base in Wei-Hei-Wei. This is an island situated in a fairly deep bay in the Gulf leading up to the approaches of Peking. Situated in the latitude of southern Japan and on the southern Bay opposite Chinwangtao and the approach to Tientsin, it had a wonderful climate and good weather. On the island was the Naval Hospital which was splendidly situated for people to recuperate. The island was about three miles long and one and half miles wide and had once belonged to us, but under a more recent treaty, we had rendited it [given back] to the government of China on condition we could go on using it as before; a compromise dear to the Chinese hearts, which pleased and suited everybody1. On arrival there we anchored in the bay just opposite the island and met the rest of the Chinese fleet, the cruisers Suffolk, Cumberland, Berwick, Cornwall, the aircraft carrier Eagle, the s/m depot ship Medway, and the 1 Wei Hei Wei on the northeast coast of China had a turbulent history and was the site of the Sino-Japanese naval battle of 1895. The British leased the port from 1898 to 1930, as a strategic point from which to deter Russian expansion and provide a British naval base. Wei Hei Wei was returned to China in 1930 but the island of Liu-kung-tao was leased to the British, until effectively brought to an end by the Japanese invasion 86 in 1940.

Wei Hei Wei: view from the flotilla of destroyers and another one of submarines with a few of the sloops of the China Staisland to the mainland showing the tion which usually called in between their cruises. British fleet at anchor We soon set about ‘working up’ and spent four to five days at sea each week firing our guns and torpedoes and testing our aircraft which we carried on board for spotting and reconnaissance. Just as we were nearing completion of our working up the Commander in Chief of the China Station, Admiral Sir Frederic Dreyer, decided to transfer his flag to us from the Suffolk, and we became the flagship of the China Station. A word perhaps about our Commander in Chief would be appropriate. Frederick Dreyer, a formidable personality, stood a good 6 foot 6 inches, was one of the great characters of the between war years in the Navy.2 He was a very clever man, especially in the technical field, and he invented the ‘Dreyer table’ on which all naval gunnery control was based. He was very early promoted to Commander and then to Captain, and was Admiral Jellicoe’s Flag Captain in the Iron Duke at the Battle of Jutland. One of the greatest, if not the greatest, gunnery expert the Navy has had, he made signal contributions to the improvement of its effectiveness. He had held many of the high appointments, such as Assistant, and later Deputy Chief of the Naval staff at the Admiralty, Admiral commanding the Battle Cruiser squadron and so on, prior to being appointed Commander-in-Chief for the China Station. Had it not been for the Invergordon mutiny he would probably have been appointed Commander-in-Chief of the Home Fleet, with the possibility of First Sea Lord to follow. There was a feeling at the Admiralty among the Sea Lords at that time that he would not have been the right man to 2 Admiral Sir Frederic Dreyer (1878-1956), does not appear in the ODNB, but there are numerous sources available about him, including critical ones. This passage is fairly typical of WWD’s summing up of more difficult characters, taking time to make a balanced assessment, but acknowledging weaknesses and the need to handle ‘with a light touch’. 87

restore the morale and discipline of the Navy. Perhaps a mistaken view, as in fact, Frederic Dreyer had a considerable understanding and sympathy with the sailor of his day. There may have been other reasons. Frederic Dreyer was a very clever man indeed with a clear cut and logical mind, which saw a problem in its entirety - almost a mathematical approach to problems as he saw them. Of all the distinguished Admirals whom I have served as a staff officer, he was I think the cleverest. As mentioned before, he was a most impressive personality, a good speaker in public and private, and an absolutely indefatigable worker, he never let go of a problem until he had really got to the bottom of it. Quite a widely read man, he ordered his life on strict and rigid routines. Though in the middle 50s when I met him, he had a most tremendous zest for life and was quite one of the most indefatigable sightseers and collector of bits and curios I have met. But behind this imposing exterior there were one or two weaknesses. He, I suspect, sometimes guessed that his staff, after a time, also detected them and woe betide them when this happened. He was quite ruthless and at times, not always just, though he never knew this. He liked a measure of flattery and he did not often like to be contradicted, though again, if handled with a light touch, he would take a surprising amount from his juniors. Members of his staff closest to him usually eventually fell foul of him, the Chief of Staff, the Flag Lieutenant, and the occasional Staff officer. He feared, I think, that those of his staff who served him did not always appreciate that he was, in fact, such a splendid and able man as appearances indicated. Perhaps it was an underlining trait of jealousy. His contemporaries were afraid of him and sometimes did not always entirely trust him. He was in their opinion, over Germanic and over ambitious and too ruthless in outlook.Yet he could be charming and he did many a kind act by stealth. A very complex character who was tremendously respected, and indeed in places, feared by officers and sailors alike. Personally, I had a great regard for him and his charming and saintly wife. He encouraged me and except for one occasion when for some reason he turned very nasty, he could not have been kinder and supported me more. To sum up, Frederic Dreyer, was in a sense, a product of his early upbringing in the Navy. He liked to do everything himself and he was not at all a good de-centraliser. In those days, i.e. Fred Dreyer’s young days, proper staff organisation was quite unknown and many of Winston Churchill’s strictures on the lack of it were fully justified. The Captain of a ship was in ‘absolute’ command and ‘absolutely and personally’ responsible for all that went on in their ship. A Chief of Staff and the carefully planned organisation for a staff, either on a functional or technical basis, really didn’t mean a lot to him. Nevertheless, Fred Dreyer did allow us quite wide scope as his staff, but one was not always certain exactly how far one could go without referring back to him! In fact, it was rather exciting at times to see what sort of reception we received after some event in which one had played a modest part! But, at no time was there any doubt who was in charge and on whom the ultimate responsibility fell. With his wide-ranging knowledge and his fertile imagination, allied to a commanding presence, Fred Dreyer served his country well as Commander-in- Chief of the China Station. 88

Other members of the staff one met for the first time did much to provide what was a pretty happy, and I believe, efficient team. Frank Atwood (Commodore) as Chief of Staff did not have an easy row to hoe. A most able staff officer he did a lot in a quiet and unobtrusive way to make the staff machine run smoothly. He relieved G.P. Thompson - an exceptionally able submarine officer, who alas, could not get on with Fred Dreyer. G.P. Thompson later became famous as the Chief Censor in the last war. Then of the Commanders, there was Rowley, the S.O.O, one of the ablest officers of his time who, alas, was lost in the last war when his cruiser was sunk off Crete. A delightful messmate was Desmond Tufnell, the Intelligence officer, an abnormally keen golfer and one time interpreter in Japanese. J.A.S. Eccles who relieved Desmond Tuffnell, already one of the Navy’s great characters - a first-rate interpreter - imposing presence who even Fred Dreyer could not cow, and who after a distinguished career became my predecessor as the Commander in Chief Home Fleet. Toby Everett, who later relieved Rowley, and whom I served happily with later in our careers. Ronald Bayne, the Fleet Gunnery officer, who helped me a lot with advice. A first-rate staff officer, but who did not quite hit it off with Fred Dryer. Andrew Yates, the Fleet Signals Officer, one of the cleverest men of his time in the Navy, but who was in a sense his own worst enemy. He liked to give the impression that he was a dilettante and one hour’s work a day was all that he needed. Behind all this lay a very keen brain, allied to an ability to work accurately with exmap of northern cruise ceptional speed. But unfortunately, old Fred Dreyer thought Andrew Yates’s attitude was a HMS Kent 1935 little too laissez faire. Then there was Horne, the Secretary and Flag Lieutenant who was a little too highly strung for Fred, and who later was relieved by Sandy Gordon Lennox who soon had his C-in-C ‘under control’. There were a number of other staff officers who played their own not always insignificant part in this organisation. Of the senior officers on the station the following come immediately to mind - Rear Admiral Chilton (R.A.Yangtze), an able and delightful officer with the courtliness of an old world diplomat. He acted as C-in-C during Fred Dreyer’s illness in 1935, and who soon gained our respect. Bill Davis (First World War VC) commanded the Cornwall, one of the best ships on the station. Errol Manners. still a considerable athlete, commanded Suffolk. George Fraser known as the ‘Horrible George’, in place of his proper name, Captain The Honourable George Fraser, who commanded the aircraft carrier Hermes, with Ned Pleyell Bouverie as his Commander. The names of the commanding officers of Adventure, Medway, Berwick and Cumberland have temporarily escaped my memory. George Hammick, only recently died, was in charge of the destroyer flotilla. Andy Lovatt, a friend of mine, and whose wife came out to China with Elizabeth, commanded one of the ships of this flotilla. Frankie Elliott was the Commodore at Hong Kong and always gave us a warm welcome at that port. By and large the staff were a happy team, and all the ships on the station, keen, happy and well found. To an extent not perhaps 89

possible in our present day, the influence of the C-in-C Fred Dreyer was felt from the most senior officer to the most newly joined rating on the China Station. Wei-Hei-Wei provided everything wanted for working the ship up into an efficient state and we soon realised a good standard of battle efficiency. In the late autumn we got a little duck shooting in the rice fields and swamps in the neighbourhood. The time came, as Autumn of 1934 set in, for the fleet to disperse and we all went our different ways, and later assembled at Hong Kong about Christmas time. Our first visit was to a port on the west coast of Japan, by name I think, Myazu [Miyazu]. A pleasant place with wonderful views of the Autumn colours of Japan. We were introduced to the custom of drinking green tea - rather a syrupy concoction with lots of sugar and saki, which was, or could be, rather a potent form of rice spirit. One had to beware when drinking. No heel taps with this and rather like vodka, don’t mix it with water. We found time to pay a visit to the northern island of Hokkaido, which was beginning, even then, to get very cold. Though south North Island Japan of the UK in latitude they have a polar air stream which keeps them cool. A lot of the Japafrom HMS Kent nese fishing industry is based on Hokkaido and there were many modern canneries to be seen at Hakodate. This northern island is also the home of the original aborigines of Japan, known as ‘the hairy Ainu’3. They were more European in build and showed no signs of Mongolian and Chinese features, from which race root stock the present Japanese nation sprang. The Japanese countryside is pleasant for walking, and the Autumn tints of the maples and other trees were particularly striking. This was the period of rising tension between Japan and the European nations - they were highly suspicious of us. Throughout the full 18 months on the China Station the only Japanese warship I can remember seeing was an old Japanese destroyer at Shanghai. A thinly disguised Japanese Intelligence officer always made himself evident at Japanese ports of call. The one we had was not very astute and somewhat unburdened himself during a ‘Saki Session’ at one of the Inns at Miyazu. So we christened him ‘The Spy’, to which name he cheerfully answered, and made him an honorary member of the wardroom. We provided him enough inaccurate and highly tendentious information which must have given the Japanese Intelligence department acute indigestion and we insisted that when he entertained us on shore that all bills should go direct to his Intelligence Department. The time came to leave Japan, and our next call was Shanghai, where we would take part in the Armistice Day celebrations on 11th November. The Army had a battalion there and we arranged for quite an effective parade on the Shanghai Racecourse to which great numbers 3 The indigenous group inhabiting Hokkaido were known as the Ainu. The men tended to have long beards and moustaches, hence the rather derogatory term ‘hairy’. They were considered by 19th century travellers to be part of a ‘lost tribe’ of Aryans. They were subjected to forced assimilation after the annexation of Hokkaido in the early 19th century, though have recently been recognised by the Japanese government as an indigenous people. 90

of Chinese flocked. This was still the old Shanghai as the old timers knew it. The Shanghai Club - which was situated in the Bund - had the longest bar in the world. We were secured to the two best buoys just opposite the Cathay Hotel in the Bund. The French Quarter of Shanghai, with the French Club as its focus, was one of the favourite places in which to spend an evening. All forms of cabaret, nightclubs and the sort, abounded, and provided your purse was long enough, you could see as wide a variety of entertainment as anywhere in the world. I met Tony Keswick, who ran Jardine Matheson, and a man by name William Teeling, who later became MP for Brighton. Tony Keswick lived at the lovely Jardine bungalow near the golf course which was reached, as a rule, by way of the Bubbling Well Road. right: HMS Kent illuminated below: Shangai taken from HMS Kent To my great joy Elizabeth had arrived just before us in SS Patroclus and had taken a little room high up in the Cathay Hotel which at that time was the biggest skyscraper in Shanghai. This was November and I had not seen her since I saw her for a few moments at the Queen’s Hotel, Southsea, in June. We had a great time together: 5 months or thereabouts, seems an awfully long time when one is newly married!4 For the first time we illuminated ship - a most spectacular sight - and you may see a photograph in one of the albums of the Kent at night, illuminated by outline circuits as it lay off the Bund at Shanghai. We, as a nation, then mattered quite a lot. Many of the important businesses in Shanghai were in British hands. Most of the Shanghai and Yangtze pilots were British, with that great character, Captain Pote Hunt, who later took us up to Hankow, 4 The Navy did not pay for travel by wives and families. Those who could afford it had to make their own arrangements and find accommodation. This was often a mixture of rented rooms and staying with friends and acquaintances. Elizabeth was far from well off and had only a very modest marriage settlement but found ways to stretch the money as far as possible. 91

as the doyen of the pilots. The range of shops in the Bubbling Well Road and elsewhere was almost unlimited. The shops were small and every owner regarded the sale or purchase of some ‘objet d’art’ as an entertainment and an exercise of wits in itself and not to be hurried. In fact, even in those days, if you went into a shop and slammed a few $5 bills down on a ‘take it or leave it’ basis, the owner would probably decline to serve you! The Whangpao, an estuary leading up to Shanghai, was a fascinating sight. ‘Go Downs’, or storage sheds as we would call them, were everywhere; innumerable junks ferrying goods and people to and fro. British names of many of the older and well established firms helped to remind the visitor of the splendid and effective pioneering work done in the 19th century by our trading fraternity. Shanghai was a wonderful place for entertainment, but soon officers and sailors alike found they could not keep up the pace without acute financial embarrassment, so the time was deemed appropriate for us to leave. We steamed southwards, and in two or three days arrived back in Hong Kong, looking prettier than ever. Hong Kong in winter time has a delightful climate and we found lots to do, both work and play. Bertie Packer and I won the Hong Kong Gulf foursome at a lovely course near Fan Ling just on the Chinese border. Elizabeth and I took a little flat in the Gloucester buildings not far from the centre of Hong Kong. This proved a most convenient centre from which to travel round the town and island. The Thieves Market was always a source of endless entertainment, but one had to be a little careful what purchases were made. An expedition to Canton will always be remembered. The island, on which as a result of last century’s wars, our trading concerns were concentrated, was known as the Shameen. Shopping there and in the city of Canton was an endless source of entertainment. I noticed two Chinamen almost coming to blows during a bargain, and to my surprise, on getting close to them I realised they were arguing in ‘pidgin English’ which was largely the lingua franca for trading in China in those days. My Chinese guide reminded me that one of the Chinese was Cantonese whilst the other came from Fukien Province, so it was natural they would talk in pidgin English! Then one day, a few days before Christmas, your mother and I decided we would scale the highest mountain in the leased territory called Tai Mo Shan. So having motored to its base, we purchased the services of two itinerant Chinamen to carry our picnic hamper for us. What fun it was, I suppose the height cannot have been much over 3000 feet, but the gradient was easy and we reached the summit without undue difficulty. On one side we saw Canton and the delta of the West River and on the other, Hong Kong Island with a mountainous range of the leased territory lying between us and Hong Kong Harbour. In some ways it resembled the west coast of Scotland, though the hills and mountains were perhaps rather steeper than the more gentle slopes usually met with in Scotland. When we reached the summit we had a wonderful lobster lunch, washed down with some excellent Hong Kong beer. Unfortunately, the lobster did not entirely suit your mother who had a rather disturbed Christmas in our flat. Hong Kong was a very gay place at Christmas and we enjoyed together our first combined experience of naval hospitality. Old Fred Dreyer was a most hospitable C-in-C and made all of us feel very welcome. 92

Soon after the new year we started on our southern cruise with a visit to Manila, which was the headquarters of the United States Asiatic Squadron. There Captain Nimitz of the US Cruiser Houston, gave us all the very warm welcome and looked after the Kent wives who had arrived at Manila a few days before the Kent. Manila, and the whole of the Philippines, still had very much of a Spanish atmosphere. The Americans were very hospitable indeed and showed us round the various bases they had. They had a big naval and air force base not far away from the main town, and also a magnificent combined services club where our hosts entertained us royally. The Army general there might almost have been Macarthur himself, and certainly impressed us as being a very energetic and live wire. right: HMS Kent 1935 below: The inhabitants i.e., Filipinos, were welcoming and the women looked most attractive Baie d’Along,Vietnam, visited wearing their Spanish shawls and dresses. The impression one gained was that it might later in the cruise almost have been Andalusia, but without the hardness of the Spanish scenery and character. We were flown up to a hill station just over 100 miles from Manila. The airfields looked rather frightening from the air as the landing place consisted of one single strip in a particularly narrow valley. However, we landed safely after passing uncomfortably close to some rocks. The climate was lovely and cool and we enjoyed a big log fire for the first time in the evening for quite a few months. We entertained our hosts on board and our ships, unlike the Americans, were not dry, these parties were most popular. I went one day with Elizabeth on a very pleasant canoeing trip to a place called Pak San Jan, where we ended up getting very sunburnt, shooting the rapids and paddling along in a fairly swift stream. Of the Americans we met, Captain Nimitz stood out - obviously 93

a highly accomplished professional officer with a wide strategic outlook, which was to prove of such value to his country when he was American C-in-C Pacific in the Second World War. I heard our C-in-C, Admiral Dreyer, had a very healthy respect for his wisdom. Our next cruise took us to the area of the Malacca Straits where we called at Singapore, Penang, Medan in Sumatra, Bangkok, Saigon and Baie d’Along. The southern cruise was crammed with interest. below: Official visits were punctuated by We had many discussions with the Army and the C-in-C used his great authority and weight picnics and visits to places of interest to hasten the completion of the Singapore defences. Even then in discussions with us, he – as in this visit to the Kota Tinggi often said, that Singapore defences or not, it would not hold out long, unless we had an ad- Waterfall, which remains a tourist equate fleet to command the South China Sea. Perhaps this was fairly obvious. But the lack destination today of command of the seas and the air was in some measure responsible for the loss of Singapore and the collapse of the Allies’ whole eastern position in the Second World War. In addition to lots of work, there was plenty of hard play at Singapore. The governor, Sir Shenton Thomas, and his wife very kindly asked us to stay at the large and imposing government house.Very comfortable! The Thomas's could not have been kinder and more thoughtful to a young officer and his newly married wife. The Thomases had a terrible time in Japanese prisoner of war camps during the war, and I’ve heard, they never spared themselves in trying to ameliorate the lot of other prisoners of war. Singapore was at that time, rich and prosperous and the big merchant firms living in conditions, ‘Taipans’ as the Chinese called them, were expected to live.5 The Malays and the Singapore-born Chinese presented a political problem which was quite apparent then. Most of the money, and certainly the majority of skilled and semi-skilled working people, were of Chinese extraction. The dockyard was in the process of being laid out and the only dock was the great floating dock which had been towed there a few years previously from England. We went on later to Penang, which again was quite one of the most beautiful places in the Far East, and your mother took the opportunity of staying with some Biddulph cousins of hers in Kuala Lumpur. The scenery and bathing at Penang, with the background of luxurious vegetation, was exceptional. 5 The word ‘Taipan’ is derived from the Cantonese meaning a powerful businessman or entrepreneur, not to be confused with the Australian venomous snake of the same name. 94

After a few days there, when I inspected the defences, which were still on paper, we went across the Straits to Medan in Sumatra and went off by car to Prastagi [Berastagi] - the hill station situated on a lovely lake at, I suppose, about 3000 feet level. Many pleasant people mostly Dutch, welcomed us both at Medan and Prastagi. As yet, no inkling to hint that the world in which they were living would collapse about their heads within 5 or 6 years, and that those who could not escape to Australia or Ceylon would be hard put to survive the below: Angkor Thom rigours of a Japanese prisoner of war camp. Sumatra was barely scratched, large areas of tropical jungle, which was and still is, awaiting development. The people were similar to Malaysians in appearance, except for a very few primitive natives who lived commonly in long huts near Prastagi. We next called at Bangkok and were struck, as everybody is, by the strange forms of architecture and towers peculiar to the Thais. The ship anchored some way from the port and the Falmouth, the C-in-C’s yacht, went into the harbour. Again, we had literally a very royal reception and attended the performance of the Ramayana by the court players. We saw around the palaces in Bangkok and caught a glimpse of the white elephant they had there, which was very much the colour of a middle white pig! Elizabeth and I stayed with some very nice people, by name Preston, who looked after us wonderfully. He was, I think, in charge of the Siamese branch of the Burma Trading Company. The local consul general, a very distinguished figure, was a match for the C-in-C, and it was great to listen to these two imposing figures debating the many problems of the Far East. Then from there, the Kent went round by sea to Saigon, the capital of French Indochina. We went on a visit to Angkor with the C-in-C and his wife. It was decided that the Flag Lieutenant required a rest, so Elizabeth and I accompanied the Dreyers to Angkor, and what fun it was! We went up by train to Siamreap [Kong Siam Reap] on the border of Siam and French Indochina, and from there motored a few miles to Angkor, where we stayed in a pleasant little simple hotel in the ruins. These fascinating ruins of the Khmer civilization, brought by the more virile and militant Hindus from India, would take a book to describe. above: The vastness of the main temple at Angkor Wat with its endless Corinthian columns and W & E and Admiral Dreyer at its five big domes, shaped and looking like a pineapple, was something quite different from Angkor Wat anything we had ever seen. Then in the evening a troop of pretty little Cambodian ladies gave their traditional dance by the light of torches and the moon. The grace and simplicity of movement of the dancers was wonderful to see. There were other ruins of great attraction. The Angkor Thom was an older and more austere temple surrounded by Garoudas, a sort 95

of mythical dragon, would strike fear into anybody after dark. Then the Nunnery on the edge of a lake and a little temple at Banta Serai with wonderful Hindu carvings, were of exceptional beauty. We had a good guide and with such an indefatigable sightseer as Fred Dreyer we did not miss much. All too soon we had to leave Angkor and went to Phnom Penh, then the capital of Cambodia, and where we were greeted by the French administration. The temperature was quite insufferable and I had every sympathy with our host, dressed impeccably in a frock coat, who said sadly, ‘Ah but this is not Paris’. We were glad to leave Phnom Penh for Saigon which we reached after crossing the great Mekong river, in what appeared to me to be a very unsafe raft. The French showed us Saigon, and were determined to match the Americans in their hospitality. and we had some very pleasant evenings on board the French flagship, where the French naval Commander-in-Chief, Admiral Richard entertained us delightfully. Admiral Richard had a fairly clear idea what might be the weaknesses of the French position in Indochina, and I often wondered what the French government thought of his views, if in fact they ever read them! Saigon had some good shops and it was an airy and spacious town in those days, with the French club, the Circle Sportif, on the outskirts, but has probably changed out of all recognition now. There were no skyscrapers there and life proceeded at an even slower place with a competent and firm French government with little thought of ‘self-determination’. Who could have forecast the traumatic experiences of that country starting with the Japanese occupation during the last war and ending with the Civil War being fought now between North and South, with a bitterness which is hard for a European to appreciate. His dress may seem rather casual, but it is a very well-cut tweed islands off the approach to Hanoi, set sail for Hong Kong, where we arrived to find the suit, to which the flat cap adds a weather though still pleasant was beginning to warm up. A few days there then north again nicely casual countryside air. this time to Japan. where we visited Nagasaki, Kobe, places in the inland sea and finally Yokohama. As ever, the English folk were very hospitable and though the Japanese government were hostile then to the British, they were very correct, as the Germans would say, in their behaviour to us. The embassy was most friendly and I came across a particularly nice secretary at the embassy, by name I think Geoffrey Harrison, who is our Ambassador in Moscow now. Visits to Hakone and other beauty spots were great fun, though we did not in fact climb Fujiyama we frequently saw it from the simple little hotels in which we stayed. Our Japanese friend, ‘the Spy’, greeted us on our on our arrival and was given an uproarious welcome in the wardroom. Andrew Yates and Jas Eccles immediately set about inventing some further unlikely stories for the Japanese Director of Intelligence. 96

A highlight was the Emperor’s ‘Chrysanthemum Party’ which is held in the palace grounds and to which we most fortunately received invitations. In a way a little like a Buckingham Palace garden party, everybody in their best and formal attire and chrysanthemums at every turn, from miniature ones to ones that were the size of a football. It is part of the religion of some Japanese to cultivate chrysanthemums, and there can be no other place in the world where so many remarkable ones are seen at any one time. We took the opportunity on this visit of ordering our red china dinner service, which you know well, from a firm in Kobe or possibly Kyoto, which is a particularly nice town being the old capital of Japan. One thought, I suppose, a bit about the Japanese and their problems in those days and I suppose foresaw a clash. We were always hearing about the population explosion in Japan and that this would lead to war. In fact, this really had nothing to do with it. It was the wish for national aggrandisement and recognition, which in fact is contained in their tradition, and which made war inevitable. One did not find much in common with Japanese men, though their women folk were quite charming and simple little people who added perhaps much to the gaiety of life. Then on the other hand the first rate, and as it were, top Japanese, kept themselves very much to themselves and did not mix much in society with Europeans. What was evident was the stupendous industry of the Japanese and their submissiveness to rule and authority. The military were never in evidence except at the Emperor’s garden party where a good third of the men there were in uniform. In those days most of the houses were of very light construction and a stone building was a great rarity. Good manners, especially where the women were concerned, was most noticeable. There was not among the men the sort of jolly and independent outlook we met with the Chinese. The visit to Japan certainly opened one’s eyes to quite a different form of civilization from what one had previously met, but we never seemed to cut through the armour of Japanese secretiveness, and we left it with the feeling that one really did not know what they thought or felt. A burning and intense patriotism was evident, beyond that it was difficult to see. Jas Eccles who had lived some years ‘native’ in Japan said the same thing, and he still could speak Japanese quite well when he was on our Staff. After leaving Japan we went north to the mouth of the Yangtze, and picked up that old character, the senior Yangtze Pilot, Captain Pote Hunt, and went up the Yangtze, calling first at Nanking [Nanjing], where we spent a couple of days. Apart from the impressive Sun Yat-Sen6 memorial there, and a few contacts with friendly Chinese, we saw nothing of note. Then on up to Hankow [Hankou], a fascinating place over 1000 miles from the sea. Things were fairly quiet on the river at that time though there was some trouble further up through the gorges at Chonking [Chongqing], which for long was Chiang Kai-Shek’s headquarters. We lay in the middle of the river and met various people of importance and otherwise. There were still among the trading fraternity some of the ‘good old days’ folk but they were getting fewer, and most of the younger men realised our tenure in Hankow and the other Treaty Ports was 6 Sun Yat-Sen (1866-1925) was the revolutionary and statesman who founded the Republic of China after the last Qing Emperor was deposed in 1912. Sun Yat-Sen founded the Kuomintang (National People’s Party), the country’s first political party, of which the leadership passed to Chiang Kai-Shek after his death. 97

likely to be of short duration. A large and busy port, there is nothing special in Hankow. Up and down the Yangtze one sees hundreds of families who seem to live permanently afloat in their junks ferrying produce up and down. Elizabeth stayed in a hotel at Hankow, and it was there that we discovered that some little person was on the way! The C-in-C left us to visit the Gorges in one of the gunboats, and we sailed down the Yangtze and after stopping, usually at night, reached the open sea and set course for Wei Hei Wei calling at Tsingtao [Qingdao], the one-time German port on the Shanking peninsula. Meanwhile the Abyssinia crisis had blown up and the Cumberland was detached to join the Mediterranean Fleet. This, alas, put a stop to the hope we had of getting a few days leave in Peking [Beijing]. Instead, we settled down to armament and other practices at Wei Hei Wei. I persuaded the C-in-C to try a method of torpedo attack that I had devised, known as the ‘double broadside’ attack. Quite effective in peace, but I always had some doubts of its wartime practicability. Fred Dreyer seemed to like the ingenuity of the idea! In addition to armament practice we settled down to work up for a regatta. I and Jock Findlay had a hand below: in training and organising the Kent’s regatta crew. We did not do too badly, though Cornwall Wei Hei Wei by night. came out as the handsome winners of the fleet regatta. Wei Hei Wei was a splendid place, and Elizabeth took a little two roomed bungalow with a small garden as our home. A large and amusing old Chinaman with a big Alsatian dog announced that he was to be our gardener and had some lengthy discussions with Elizabeth. Over the weekends we used to organise bathing picnics on the many sandy beaches round the bays. Wei Hei Wei was a comparatively peaceful area and there were few active bandits or pirates around, though it was unwise to get too far away from the ship. There was a splendid canteen for sailors and what with ample games facilities, the sailors came rather to like Wei Hei Wei, after the somewhat dubious flesh pots they met in other ports on the China Station. The C-in-C on one of his trips to visit the tomb of Confucius, contracted dysentery and was seriously ill. In fact, the Rear Admiral Yangtze, Admiral Chilton, came up for a couple of weeks to take over, whilst Fred was completely out of action. No better place than Wei Hei Wei in which to convalesce, and with Lady Dreyer to keep an eye on him, he was soon on the mend. One night, on the 30th of June 1935 at about 2 am, I heard in our bungalow a great knocking at our front door, and thinking it might be a gale warning or some inconvenient message, I went to see what it was all about. Our sampan man ‘Tomato Face’ was there with the broadest of broad grins on his face as he handed me a message from the Duty Commanding Officer, which read as above:Yachting -Commodore Attwood, follows: Sophie Tower and Elizabeth 98

‘Your name is on the promotion list to Commander, dated 30th June, well done’. What a thrill this was, much before I had expected it.Vaguely, I thought I might pick it up in six months but more likely in a year’s time. I was the youngest but one on the list of 33 names, and I think the third or fourth most junior. A great event - promotion to Commander is always the most uncertain hurdle to surmount; only about one in three or four get it and there is always keen competition, so luck plays a mighty big part, and many good fellows are unfortunate, but perhaps best of all, it gives one the actual confidence needed. I had worked, I think, to the best of my ability really, in all my jobs, but one is never certain how things will work out until one is actually promoted. I had put forward a goodish number of novel and maybe revolutionary ideas, and one might so easily have been labelled as ‘unsound and dangerous and not to be promoted’! Tom Pakenham and Jock Findlay who I had jumped for promotion were particularly generous in their congratulations. I am glad to say they were also promoted later. Tom Pakenham eventually reaching the rank of Captain. After retiring from the Navy, he ran a hotel in Kenya, and then took orders, and when last heard, he was the resident British chaplain at Malaga in Spain. To return to Wei Hei Wei, we now had to make plans for the future, my relief, one known as Codger Millington, had been nominated and expected to relieve me in late autumn. As our first born was due to arrive in December, we decided Elizabeth had best travel home in the autumn so as to get settled down in England before the event. We met many nice folk at Wei Hei above: Wei, some of whom worked in Shanghai and used to holiday Canadian train crossing the Rockies there in the summer. A charming Mrs Boothby, whose husband worked in Shanghai and whose clever son became a diplomat, were particular friends of ours. Elizabeth found a nice companion and monthly nurse, Miss Rayden, who wished to return to England; and so they set off early in October 1935 for England, via Japan and Canada. Meanwhile the ship paid another visit to Japan where with JAS Eccles, Andrew Yates and others we had many adventures. The Japanese secret police were particularly suspicious of JAS, but soon found their match in him. To revert to Wei Hei Wei, there can have been few simpler and more idyllic places than that bay and island where people lived. Good weather, temperate, all the local Chinese entered into the spirit of life there. The Chief Tailor who produced a Commander’s hat from nowhere, rejoiced in the name of ‘Sin Jelly Belly’. The Sampan men used to vie with each other and we sometimes organised races, with a prize of five Chinese silver dollars for the winners. A very healthy place and being far away from the flesh pots of Shanghai and such places, everybody lived a healthy and outdoor life. We soon returned to Wei Hei Wei, and my relief came up in one of the Jardine boats from 99

Shanghai. After a brief turnover I caught the next boat down to Shanghai in company with Bunny Rundle (Lt. Commander A. M. Rundle) who was the pilot of our seaplane, and who was returning to England to take over some flying appointment there. Bunny was a character if ever there was one. One of the batch of our first naval pilots to qualify, he soon became a legendary figure with his exploits in some of the very rudimentary and not always reliable aircraft which we had in our aircraft carriers. A happy go lucky figure, a magnificent athlete, and one of the strongest men I ever met. He never bothered about time. He only caught the Empress of Scotland as she sailed from Shanghai for Canada by climbing up a rope as the ship steamed down the Wangpo [Huangpu] river on which Shanghai is built. He was a great companion to have, provided one felt absolutely no responsibility for his activities! After stopping in Yokohama and Hawaii, we soon reached Vancouver after a very pleasant voyage during which time we came to know Bishop Embling, who was returning to England after being Bishop of Korea and North China. A splendid looking man over 6 foot high, lean, with a most attractive way of putting subjects for discussion before his friends. I would hazard a guess he was an outstanding success in his post, he never pulled his punches, enjoyed mixing in every company and must have inspired many a young person during his lifetime. He later became Suffragan Bishop of Hull, but since the war, like so many friends, I have lost below: Snow covered Rockies sight of him. Honolulu was an attractive place to visit and I found paying for a round of big drinks at the Waikiki Beach hotel a little bit of a strain on a young commander’s purse! We did a little surfing before returning to the ship in the evening prior to sailing for Vancouver. As we passed Victoria on our way up to Vancouver, we realised the truth of the claim that the harbour vies with Hong Kong and Sydney as being one of the most beautiful in the world. By now it was getting very cold and with the snow-capped Rockies behind Vancouver, it was clear we should find the weather very different from what we had been accustomed. The problem in our four-day journey by CPR [Canadian Pacific Railway] train across Canada was to take enough exercise to settle the gargantuan sized meals which we were supposed to consume! What a sight it is going through the Rockies in winter, and what a fine engineering feat must have been the building of the railway. The magnificent fir trees draped in snow gave an impression of Fairyland. Bunny Randall who had misjudged the time we stopped at stations, only caught the train by jumping onto the buffers between the two rear carriages and sitting there until the next stop. As the temperature was near zero, most people would have frozen solid but not so Bunny who appeared in our compartment later literally black with cold. The train officials found it difficult to credit this feat as we passed through numerous tunnels - but they did not know Bunny! A short stay at Montreal where I met my sister-in-law Katharine, for the first time, and heard news of Elizabeth who had preceded me by about month.7 A very pleasant meeting. 7 Katharine Phipps (1905-1985), was a delightful, strong-minded person who disliked ‘society’ and spent above: Katharine Phipps much of the 1930s in Canada. She had a wonderful rumbustious laugh. She returned to England to help with the war effort, and later married Roy Harding, but after his death took off again for Australia, where 100 she lived for the rest of her life.

There is rather a sameness about Canada in winter if one excludes the Rockies with their grandeur. It is largely a case of miles and miles of snow punctuated by the very occasional square wooden house of no very great artistic merit. But in later years when I visited Canada in the summer, I realised there was much in the countryside which was very beautiful. An uneventful trip across the Atlantic in one of the intermediate CPR passenger ships. We were I think the last ship to leave Montreal before ice closed the port. The ship arrived in Liverpool and it did not take me long to get down to see Elizabeth who was staying at her mother’s house in 90 Eaton Square, having engaged a small domestic staff to run the house. I soon saw Father who looked in just as good a heart as ever. I had about 5 weeks leave due to me before taking up an appointment in the Tactical Staff Division at the Admiralty. We soon set about looking for a house to take and after quite a search decided on 14 Milner Street, just off Cadogan Square, and within a few minutes’ walk of Sloane Square. After some bargaining, I think we got this pleasant little house with a rental of 4.5 guineas per week. It had three to four bedrooms and the usual dining and drawing rooms and suited us very well. But now the important event of Georgina’s arrival was imminent, and on the night of the 22nd of December 1935, Elizabeth was taken by me to the nursing home in Welbeck St, and Georgina arrived safely the following day to everybody’s enormous joy. We sent a telegram to Lady Normanby, who was touring the Far East with Oswald at that time, and I phoned my father who was especially delighted that she should be called after my mother. To my unsophisticated eye I thought Georgina looked a specially good baby and indeed she was. But perhaps fathers often think like that. Elizabeth was soon back in Eaton Square where we below: Georgina as a baby stayed until March 1936 when we moved into the house we had taken in Milner Street. My job at the Admiralty was an interesting one as it concerned itself with staff advice on the use of torpedoes, mines and all methods of anti-submarine warfare. Our director was Captain Cantlie, a very shrewd Scot with a distinguished record in submarines in the First War. Though perhaps not a brilliant staff officer and liable to be bested in the cut and thrust of debate, he was nevertheless a man of mature and sound judgement, and of the type which long formed the backbone of the Navy. I relieved Gervaise Middleton, one of the best and certainly most orderly brains in the Navy, so was off to a very good start with a splendid turn over. Our job, and perhaps mine in particular, was to advise on and to assess the use and employment of all underwater weapons, to advise on how to combat submarine warfare in the future, and to assess the value of air attack using torpedoes and other underwater weapons. It was particularly interesting having now to assess what was to some in some respects the pioneering work that Ned Anstice, I, Charles Thompson and others had done in Courageous in the early part of this decade. Our forecasts of the precise effectiveness of torpedo attack by aircraft proved uncannily accurate, when Prince of Wales and Repulse were both sunk by Japanese torpedo aircraft in 101

the last war. Why our assessment was not taken to heart is quite another story and may be related another time. Then of course we had to assess for anti-submarine warfare the effectiveness of the Asdic in particular.8 On reflection I believe it is true to say that we were a little bit too sanguine on the effectiveness of the Asdic as a detecting advice. But it was at a time of great interest at the Admiralty. The Government had woken up to the threats of a resurgent Germany and Hitler, and we were told by HM Government to rearm as quickly as possible regardless of the ten year rule. This was not easy as many things had been allowed to decay and we had in a large measure gravely prejudiced our capacity to rearm other than at a slow rate. Our marine engineering industry, armament industry and so on were in very poor shape and it was physically impossible at the start to rearm other than slowly. I was closely in touch with folk in the Plans Division who were responsible under an exceptionally able Director, Tom Phillips, for the overall plans of rearmament. We had a big shipbuilding programme underway - squadrons of battleships, carriers and cruisers were projected and any number of flotillas of destroyers, frigates, etc. The Board of Admiralty were a fine team, with [Sir Ernle] Chatfield, the First Sea Lord; [Sir Dudley] Pound9 the Second Sea Lord; [Sir Reginald] Henderson (my old chief in Courageous) Third Sea Lord; Geoffrey Blake,10 Fourth Sea Lord; [William Milbourne] James,Vice Chief of Naval Staff, as able a team as ever served the Navy, and who in a large measure were responsible for the Navy being able to take the tremendous strain when war broke out in 1939 and carry the whole weight of naval responsibility until the Americans started to be effective towards the end of 1942. There was a spirit running through the Admiralty when I arrived which brooked no delay, and naval officers and civil servants alike, strove without personal consideration to have a Navy on a war footing with the least possible delay. The old days of arriving at 10.00 a.m. with two hours off for lunch and finishing at 6:00 p.m. sharp were gone forever, and officers were in soon after 9.00 a.m., very often with a sandwich lunch, and not infrequently did not get away until after 7.00 p.m. But above all, our professional leadership was of a high order with Pound later as C-in-C Med, [Sir Roger] Backhouse and later [Sir Charles] Forbes, as C-in-C Home Fleet, and Percy Noble in the Far East, there was no lack of confidence in the fleet. 11 The political leadership with Eyres Monsell, Duff Cooper and later [James, Earl] Stanhope was not perhaps of the same order as the professional leadership, but nevertheless sufficed and the Sea Lords could feel they had good backing. It was during my time at the Admiralty 1936 to 1937 that the controversy over the control of the Fleet Air Arm came up and not unnaturally, being one of the Staff Divisions concerned, I got drawn into it. Macwilliam [?], Mountbatten, Langley and I were among the Commanders most concerned with putting the naval case.12 8 Asdic was a system of underwater sonar used to detect submarines invented towards the end of World War I. 9 Sir Dudley Pound was Second Sea Lord from 1932-35 and chief of naval personnel, before becoming C-in-C Mediterranean. He rejoined the Board of Admiralty in June 1939. 10 WWD’s memory is mistaken here. Sir Geoffrey Blake was second in command of the Mediterranean Fleet, and while confidently expected to become First Sea Lord, he suffered a heart attack in 1937 and retired, ODNB. 11 All three appear in the ODNB. 12 See Rodger for an analysis of the controversies over the control and operation of the Fleet Air Arm, 102

The RAF still under the guiding spirit of Lord Trenchard had shown on the staff level little appreciation or knowledge of the needs of air power for maritime purposes. The officers who were seconded to the Fleet Air Arm did their best manfully and tried to cooperate, but on the Staff at Whitehall, what cooperation we got from the Air Ministry was of a grudging nature. Behind it all lay the fear that the Army and Navy would take over the Air Force, and their entity would be submerged in the older services. I found they simply would not recognise that the aircraft torpedo was far and away the most effective weapon, much more so than a bomb against ships, that mines could be laid by aircraft were of immense potential value, and that an anti-submarine weapon superior to the airborne depth charge was an absolute essential. The RAF doctrine that air power was all important and that provided you struck at the enemy hard enough, little attention need to be given to so called defence measures, and this gravely handicapped our country. AJP Taylor the historian,13 has commented on this with much truth. In other words, they in fact did not believe in the fundamental truth that the first call on an island country’s resources must be the security of the Main Base. From the refusal of recognising this, sprang the RAF desire to put the bomber programme before the fighter programme. Had it not been for Sir Warren Fisher, (Head of Treasury), and other Chiefs of Staff under the Minister for Coordination of Defence, it is probable that we should not when the crunch came in 1940 have had sufficient fighters to win the Battle of Britain.
