To get back to the problem of the Fleet Air Arm in 1936/37, an unanswerable case was prepared by the Admiralty for having our own Fleet Air Arm, for procuring the type of aircraft required, and for training and for manning it. This had the support of Sir Winston Churchill who was out of office at the time and many other folk. The RAF hotly opposed it and Lord Weir proved one of their more formidable supporters. It so happened that through David Orr Ewing (Captain D. Orr Ewing RN) I knew Sir Thomas Inskip, the Minister for Coordination of Defence.14 He married David Orr Ewing’s mother who had been widowed early in life. He used to discuss in very general terms his problems with me during various rounds of golf which we played, and at the houses of mutual friends. It was apparent to me he was soon convinced of the force and logic of the naval arguments but could not understand why the Admiralty had not pressed harder to take over Coastal Command. I believe the reason for this was that with war lurking in the offing, the Admiralty thought that the disruption of taking over Coastal Command might initially militate against its efficient functioning. But this is in a measure hearsay, as I never after the war had an opportunity of discussing this with Lord Chatfield.15 Life at the Admiralty for a young Commander in one of the Staff Divisions was both stimulating and challenging. It was a novel experience to be prodded by the Treasury to rearm quicker and to spend more money. I remember having to justify expenditure on building up pp. 374-376, 385-387. 13 A.J.P. Taylor (1906-1990), ODNB, author of many books. WWD was probably thinking of Taylor’s Origins of the Second World War, 1961. 14 William Douglas Weir, 1st Viscount, 1877-1959) ODNB. Sir Thomas Inskip (1876-1947) had a legal background and his appointment was controversial. 15 Admiral of the Fleet Lord Chatfield (1873-1967), ODNB, was Inskip’s replacement. 103

a big mining depot at Milford Haven, and being told in so many words that the work ought to be more quickly done and the money spent quicker! A few of the more far-seeing trawler captains were anxious that their trawlers should be capable of being fitted with Asdics, and suggested they should have a Government Subsidy to allow them to build faster ships, be more effective as anti-submarine vessels, and incidentally in peacetime to get to and from their fishing grounds in shorter time than their rivals! This is the first time one had worked in close contact with the senior civil servants of the Admiralty, and what an able set of men most of them were. There were only a very few of the ‘no change at any price’ men. I met and got to know [Sir Henry Vaughan] Markham (afterwards Secretary of the Admiralty), Le Maitre, James and hosts of others who put their all into the good of the service. Then as I mentioned before the naval leadership was first rate. The Sea Lords were men whose abilities stood out, and my late Chief, Admiral Henderson in Courageous, was as able and unconventional a controller as we have ever had. He was most interested in fast motor torpedo boats of the Hard Chine type, developed and built by a colourful character called Scott Paine, at Southampton.16 They were all powered with Napier Lion aero engines, and were certainly the forerunners of all our fast motor torpedo boats, motor gunboats, fast motor patrol boats etc., etc. He gave us some exciting rides in the Solent. Scott Paine was not without a business sense, and I believed did well with his various ventures which paved the way for the adoption by the Navy of planing boats rather than round bilge types [i.e. hard chine square sections that enabled the hull to skim the surface]. Among the Captains in the Admiralty the ablest undoubtedly was Tom Phillips, Director of Plans, later Vice Chief of Naval Staff, and eventually lost in the Far East with the Prince of Wales, who had a mind like a razor, tremendous administrative ability and any amount of drive, all linked to a clear idea of what the Navy wanted.17 Though I was not in the Plans Division, my work brought me in close touch with him, and he always liked to hear young officers’ ideas and in fact sometimes adopted them! He was a great strategist and was a match for the extreme protagonists, who said that the aeroplane with its bombs would do away with the battleship. In these controversies which arose when the government set up the Bomb versus Battleship Committee, my friend Gerald Langley, quite one of the cleverest and ablest, if slightly eccentric men the Navy has ever had, towered over the opposition and ruthlessly demolished the specious claims made by enthusiastic but woolly-headed aviators. HM Government rightly decided then that the battleship’s day was not yet over. It was I often think a pity they did not then make clear, as even in those days it was clear to some of us that soon the aircraft carrier would take the place of the gun battleship as the core and trunk on which naval power must be built and deployed. Then we used to hear whispers of Watson Watt’s experiments and the initial and halting steps towards the development of radar detection.18 This all sounded most exciting to us as it pointed to a whole new vista of tactical developments. My old friend and best man Terence Back was in the Tactical Division for a short time, and Daddy Brind (Captain Brind), afterwards C-in-C Far East, who had been our senior hand at the staff course in 1931 was Deputy Director of the Tactical Division.19 16 Hard Chine refers to the hull design of an MTB. Hubert Scott Paine (1891-1954), ODNB, designed and built flying boats, seaplanes, MTBs, motor and rescue launches at the British Power Boat Company in Southampton. 17 Admiral Sir Tom Phillips (1888-1941), ODNB 18 104 Sir Robert Alexander Watson-Watt (1892-1973), developer of radar, ODNB

Whilst there was still among some naval officers a deal of conservatism and resistance to change, the more forward-looking people who saw in the Fleet Air Arm an all-important and vital role to play were increasing in influence. Even though the First Sea Lord, Admiral Chatfield, was a great gunnery specialist, he was as alive as anybody to the path naval aviation must play in our Navy. , Admiral James who was Deputy Chief of Naval Staff, as it was then called, played perhaps a lesser part than the man of his attainments might have achieved. I think his colleagues felt he did not know the ‘nuts and bolts’ of the service as he should.20 They were probably right, but then the service was I am sure rather too materially minded, and insufficient people of the potential character of Admiral Richmond had addressed themselves to the strategical problems which face our country.21 This was certainly very true of the Air Force who was were alas still bemused by Lord Trenchard’s doctrines, but not as much as the Army, where one met every now again some young colonels of wide ranging and questing intellect who could see the defence problem as a whole. But let us turn to our life in Milner Street, and before this a word about Georgina’s christening by the Archbishop of Canterbury at Lambeth Palace. It was a wonderful occasion. The Archbishop gave us lunch with our special friends, my father, Lady Yate, old Miss Newton King and others, we attended a most moving service in Lambeth Palace’s private chapel. What a wonderfully impressive man Archbishop Lang was.22 He was of course an old friend of Elizabeth’s family but left us all in no doubt how pleased he was to meet us. Then back to Eaton Square where we gave a little tea party timed for 5:00 p.m to celebrate Georgina’s entry into the Christian faith.23 Canon Wyld was well over 90 and arrived soon after 3:00 p.m, and though he was a splendid and saintly old man, I found entertaining him until 5:00 p.m somewhat taxed my imagination. Our house in Milner Street was a nice little one. We had a good old nanny (Nanny Griffiths) who looked after Georgina and had her own ideas on how children should be looked after! Then we had two servants, a cook and a housemaid which enabled us to entertain a bit, meet our friends and widen our circle of friends. This was the first time we had an opportunity to unpack all our wedding presents, and we soon realised how lucky we were. I joined Wentworth Golf Club near Sunningdale where one could play golf and tennis, and which was a most pleasant place to visit over the weekends. The economic position, thanks in some measure to our rearmament, was gradually improving and though we never had much of a margin (our gross income was about £1800 p.a.) we lived an interesting and stimulating life. I got an old 20 horsepower Vauxhall car which did us well and survived certainly one trip to the continent. We saw quite a bit of our respective families and my father always enjoyed his visits to London. My brother worked in London for Shell, and my sister when she was not ill, had a little flat in London to which she 19 top: ED and Georgina on the lawn Sir (Eric James) Patrick Brind (1892-1963), ODNB 20 at Coglan Admiral Sir William James (1881-1973) 21 middle: WSD with Buddy Admiral Sir Herbert William Richmond (1871-1946),ODNB, retired after a combative career with his bottom:WWD with Georgina superiors in 1931, and devoted himself to naval history. He became Master of Downing College, Cambridge. 22 (William) Cosmo Gordon Lang (1864-1945), ODNB 23 WWD was not ‘religious’ in outlook but felt that good Anglican Christian principles underlay the conduct of an upright life. He was a regular churchgoer and supported the parish and diocese of Gloucester in retirement. 105

would go from time to time from Huntley Manor. Elizabeth’s mother spent some time at Eaton Square, and often asked us to some of the pleasant lunch and dinner parties she gave. We also got to know Elizabeth’s cousins, the O’Briens and saw a certain amount of Donough (Lord Inchquin), and Fion a younger brother. An interesting character we met who lived in Halsey Street was a German attaché to their embassy, Count Pückler. A very nice man who had a charming wife. He wrote quite a good book called ‘How strong is England’ which acted as quite a good counter blast to some of our defeatist politicians and writers who kept saying in so many words, “why rearm, you will never catch up with the Germans. . . . and so on.” Pückler obviously disliked the Nazis, for at heart he was an aristocrat of the old school, though looking forward as far as Europe was concerned. He was an immense and profound admirer of this country and I know that he let his countrymen know if it ever came to war, they would have ‘no pushover’ with Britain. Alas, he was killed in a tank on the Russian front during the war that was to come. Elizabeth and I went to a levee and to a court ball at Buckingham Palace which was great fun. We visited our relations of Bridgewater House and saw the lovely collection of Titians and other famous pictures, some of which are now housed in the Scottish National Art Gallery at Edinburgh. Cousin Violet (Lady Ellesmere), Elizabeth’s cousin, was one of the characters of the time. She always spoke her mind and on one of the occasions ordered some quite well known yet uninvited guests to leave her dance at Bridgewater House. Gate crashers were not welcome! Then during our stay in London, the King died and was succeeded by Edward VIII. who later abdicated. Perhaps in the Navy we had a very special regard for King George V, he was so obviously a naval officer and was never happier than when in the company of his naval friends, preferably on board a ship. Before Edward VIII succeeded there had been a usual crop of rumours about Mrs. Simpson which only proved to be true, and which ended in Edward VIII abdicating after making a rather pathetic broadcast to the nation. Books galore have been written about the abdication and nothing would be gained by going over the course again. What did people feel? Tremendously shocked. Maybe we are a bit prudish, but there is absolutely no doubt that Stanley Baldwin’s actions represented and were endorsed by the great mass of the British people. I think everybody felt he had let the country and his position down. Some felt Edward VII’s friends should have spoken up sooner about the course he was following. But who were his friends, and who knows whether or not they did? I had come to know him slightly during the 5 days he spent in Enterprise during his return on the king’s first illness in 1928. He then seemed a very nice and likeable man, very keen, I supposed to be with it and I remember on one or two occasions I thought he was rather unsure of himself. I think the main feeling among our friends was one of great sadness at the course of events. Oddly enough this event gave one rather more respect for our government than it had merited in the past. Baldwin’s vacillations and somewhat tardy acceptance of the necessity to rearm had caused much uneasiness with many thinking men, not only confined to professional soldiers, sailors and airmen. The opposition in Parliament were not effective, they were to some extent dominated by their left wingers and pacifists, though Attlee and Bevin were 106

respected and Morrison regarded as a clever opportunist. It is of course the privilege of our countrymen to criticise, sometimes quite unreasonably, our political leaders. Some of the conservative leaders, such as Samuel Hoare, John Simon, were regarded as being pretty stuffy. I believe the Labour Party lost much by opposing rearmament and conscription right up to the last moment. The so-called man in the street had no illusions about the Germans, and did not trust the French an inch. Winston Churchill lost some regard by his support of Edward VIII at the abdication time, and was regarded by many people still as a dangerous and reactionary crank, which his opposition to Indian reforms suggested. My father often said Winston dreams of the Indian and North West Frontier province of the 1880s and 1890s. Our life in London was stimulating and we made quite a number of friends such as William Sidney (now Lord de Lisle,VC), and Elizabeth’s Egerton and O’Brien and Foster relations. Occasional visits to Coglan, where my father in spite of his loneliness lived a very full and useful life, and to Mulgrave where Lady Normanby and Oswald all made us very welcome indeed. Life was in a sense on a fairly even social keel. Somewhat of course modified from our pre-war Edwardian days, but there was still a considerable amount of gracious living, good manners, and artistic perception, though perhaps rather less formalised than in the earlier years of the century. HRH arriving on board ship at Dar-es-Salaam (1928) Germany and France were disturbed, the latter was viewed with distrust and with some justification. Russia was still regarded as an ogre and stories of Stalin’s purges did little to make people want to adopt their form of government. America with Roosevelt at the helm was slowly recovering from the disastrous slumps of 1929 and the early 1930s, and had embarked as a start on a major warship expansion programme. Parts of the British Empire were rumbling, but who could have dreamt that in spite of a victorious war, our great Empire would be virtually dissolved inside a couple of generations, with the exception of Africa which was soon to follow. On the whole India was well handled and in spite of troubles when war came, we did not have a full-scale insurrection on our hands. The dissolution of the British Empire in such a short time will prove a worthwhile study for the historians who are to come. Why was it dissolved in little over a generation of time whereas it took some centuries for the great Roman Empire to dissolve and fragment itself into barbarism. Is it really more a question of spirit, had we and indeed have we lost the confidence to lead and rule? What makes us so apologetic and so on! There are many questions on which you and those that follow will speculate. Perhaps you will attribute it partly to the tremendous scientific and technological achievements of recent years which have in a sense caused this world to shrink over a hundredfold. Maybe when more leisure comes my way and if my memory still serves, I will write some essays of the many changes and causes for them in my lifetime. 107

We have perhaps strayed far from life in London in 1936 and 1937. It was a time of challenging thought, and I think in a sense one matured in judgement, and then learnt at firsthand how in fact our country and Empire is run. One met from time to time people like the Halifax’s, Inskips, etc. etc., as well as folk in distinguished positions in other than political spheres, and there was much to be learned from listening to them and testing out one’s own views. We certainly lived in a gracious atmosphere and if conventional in some ways, it still provided any active mind with much substance for thought and action. In the summer of 1937 we became aware that we should be adding to our family in the early spring in the following year, and it was time to think about future plans. Meanwhile my brother and I went for a fascinating fortnight’s motoring holiday in Austria and Hungary. We met many of his friends, Count Weber, Herr Spitzner and others who worked with him in the Shell organisation. They were hospitality itself, and what with trips to Salzburg,Vienna and Budapest, and bathing in the various ‘Sees’ in the Austin Tyrol, we could not have had a more enjoyable holiday. But it was only too evident that the Nazis were strengthening their grip on the country. The older Germans we met could still laugh quietly at Hitler, Goering, and Goebbels, but not so with the younger ones, who said in so many words you will soon see the light and liquidate your “Jewish run Government”. The cultured Austrians simply loathed the Germans, especially the Prussian Nazis. We found some of the entertainments in which we participated turned out to be rather in the nature of gastronomic test matches. Budapest was a lovely place and we spent much time bathing and swimming on the Margareten Island, and later went to Lake Ballaton, about halfway between Budapest and the Austrian border. This was a lovely place for a sailing and swimming holiday. The beautiful places we visited in the Austrian Tyrol (Salzburg, Innsbruck etc.) and in Vienna, made our holiday very worthwhile. I was particularly glad in Vienna to see the Stephansdom, the Schönbrunn Palace, the opera house and many other places. Austria with its mixture of Baroque and occasional Norman architecture must always be high on any visiting list. Meanwhile Elizabeth went up to Mulgrave and started considering plans for our next move. Georgina was growing apace and delighted the heart of her grandmother. During the Autumn of 1937 having done approaching two years in the Admiralty, the appointing people in the Second Sea Lord’s office started thinking out one’s next move. Having been lucky enough to get an early promotion to Commander, the usual plan would be to go to an executive seagoing job such as Commander of a battleship or aircraft carrier, or Captain of a destroyer or frigate, and so qualify for early promotion to Captain, that is, if one is still regarded with favour! I understood that I was provisionally marked down for the Ark Royal, our newest aircraft carrier then being built. But Admiral Backhouse, the C-in-C Home Fleet, and as nobody knew then First Sea Lord designate, wanted to change his Fleet Torpedo Officer so I was to be sent a Fleet Torpedo Officer of the Home Fleet in Nelson which was the Fleet flagship. I soon found there was not enough useful work to do, and set about taking on other jobs such as provisional Staff Officer Plans. I did not relish this change of appointment, but the appointing authority made a bargain with the C-in-C that after a year I would be sent to an “Executive” job, as Staff jobs alone did not qualify one for 108 promotion, and it would be hard luck if I missed the chance of early promotion to Captain.

Our time in Admiralty was soon drawing to a close and we started packing up our possessions. I was due to join HMS Nelson early in January before setting sail for the spring cruise to Gibraltar, Lisbon and elsewhere. Nelson was lying alongside the South Railway Jetty at Portsmouth, and joining her reminded me of joining another and more lovely looking Home Fleet flagship, HMS Queen Elizabeth in January 1922 at the same place as the newly fledged Sub Lieutenant in charge of the Gunroom! It is of interest to think again of the years 1936 and 1937 and try to capture what one thought then, and how one felt about the future. There was among both the informed and the less informed much criticism of the Government. It was felt they were very tardy in recognising the threat first of Mussolini’s Fascism and then of Hitler’s Nazism, and their putting the country into a state of preparedness was reckoned to be too slow. It was felt at times that the Government were not seized with the urgency of the problems facing us in rearming. There was a lot of blame attached to Mr Baldwin, but those who criticised him most vociferously conveniently forgot the pacifism of the opposition, the almost ‘peace at any price’ atmosphere among some of the so-called intellectuals and so on. There was perhaps an attitude of appeasement prevalent in some quarters, all of which would even have tied the hands of a more forceful and virile government. It is probably true to say that the attitudes of Mr Baldwin and his government were in fact a very true reflection of the people of this country, who first of all were recovering from the First World War where many of the best were killed and secondly from a severe depression which lasted from 1929 up to the middle of 1932. Over the period after the formation of Mr Baldwin’s government the country suffered much from the almost virtual demise of the opposition which clung feverishly to pacifist doctrines that have never had much of an appeal to the British people. Life in the Armed Forces over the years 1936 and 1937 was thoroughly exciting as it was evident we should, unless a miracle happened, soon be called upon to defend our country. Life still had a measure of Edwardian graciousness, which with a very few exceptions is absent and unknown to those who have lived after the Second World War. Nevertheless, if it comes to generalising there was, taking all in all, a healthy purposefulness in the country once the threats of continental dictators became apparent. Drug taking and general permissiveness in society was hardly ever encountered, and certainly the ‘tone’ to an outward observer was not bad. Whilst it is a national habit to denigrate our countrymen’s achievements, there was the powerful and underlying confidence that when it came to the crunch, an Englishman was still worth TWO foreigners! Let us return to the South Railway Jetty at Portsmouth, one January evening in 1938, when I boarded HMS Nelson to become the Fleet Torpedo Officer of the Home Fleet. By no stretch of the imagination can Nelson or her sistership be called beautiful. They were built to the Washington Treaty specification of keeping in within the specified displacement tonnage of 35,000 tonnes and consequently had the ships main gun armament of nine 16 inch guns grouped together before the bridge, hence they always in silhouette gave the impression of being cut off short at the stern. I soon found among the Staff and among the Ships Officers many old friends. Makeig-Jones, an old friend of Queen Elizabeth days, was the Captain and 109

HMS Nelson a splendid one too. He alas was lost early in the war as Captain of Courageous. Then on the staff, Brian Schofield, a truly splendid Staff Officer Operations, shortly afterwards followed by Cecil Hughes Hallett; Schofield was our navigator in Enterprise in the 1920s. Then Gerard Tuck, another old friend, was Fleet Gunnery Officer. Keith McNeil Walter, (later Submarine VC), Assistant Operational Staff Officer. Bob Sturgess, the splendid and distinguished Fleet Royal Marine Officer. A very happy and as capable a team as one would expect anywhere. The Captain of the Fleet, Alban T Curtis, a character and old type World War I Destroyer Captain, could be relied on to keep the staff ’s feet on the ground. The Chief of Staff, Rear Admiral Henry Moore, did a remarkable job; he had relieved Bertie Ramsay who had fallen out with the C-in-C and left about a year before I joined. Henry Moore was a quiet and essentially very humble man, as good a brain as one could find anywhere in the Service, a first rate seaman and the most loyal of Chiefs of Staff. His judgement was cool and discerning, and behind an almost diffident manner, he hid substantial reserves of character. He had been Director of Plans before he joined and was therefore well in the picture of what the Fleet might be required to do in the event of war. Henry Moore taught me many things about Staff work and checked the tendency to make too hasty and ad hoc recommendations! Such success as I ever achieved as Chief of Staff for the Home Fleet after the war, was in no small measure to Henry Moore’s training.24 Towering in the physical sense, for he must have been 6 foot 4 inches at least, as well as in some respects the mental sense, was the Commander-in-Chief Admiral Sir Roger Backhouse.25 The most likeable man in every way with a charming and devoted family, he would if he could have done every Staff Officer’s work for him as well as his own! A man with probably as encyclopaedic knowledge of the service as even old Fred Dreyer, he certainly knew most of the answers. He was only happy if he was working anything up to 20 hours a day. He also was greatly liked and respected by everybody, rather soft spoken and it was evident to 24 WWD was always alert to learning how things operated at a high level; he also learned lessons in leadership from several captains, put to good effect when he became Captain of HMS Mauritius in 1943. 25 Admiral Sir Roger Backhouse (1878-1939), ODNB 110

all that his detailed knowledge of the material of the service particularly in the gunnery field was quite unrivalled. He had a shrewd understanding of the sailor’s mind, and though he was never happier than with a full in tray in his after cabin, he got round the Fleet, and was well known and perhaps mildly feared by the officers and men of the fleet. A gunnery specialist of repute he did much with his even more formidable brother, Admiral Oliver Backhouse, to promote the gunnery efficiency of the Navy. He had a fine intellect though it was in no sense a wide ranging and commanding one. He did not appear to have any hobbies, intellectual or otherwise. His whole life was devoted and indeed dedicated to the Service. He never really understood how to use a Staff in the proper sense of the word. He in fact liked to do all the work, draft the reports, signals etc, and we the Staff to check the details and verify facts. But this method of doing business was far far beyond the compass of any one man however able, knowledgeable and dedicated. I remember well once discussing with him in his cabin a fairly complex torpedo subject with considerable technical undertones. He was sitting down writing out the report while I was walking up and down dictating what should be said. After some minutes I said laughingly to him, “Let’s swap hats, you are doing my job and I am doing yours!” He smiled back at me and said in his perfectly charming manner, “You must allow an old man his foibles, now what should our next sentence be?” One would find it hard anywhere to find a more courteous, thoughtful and delightful man. He epitomised in many ways the very best style of old world naval officer. But alas, as we shall hear later, he over centralised, never relaxed, and killed himself from overwork, when First Sea Lord at the Admiralty. One of the Navy’s most besetting sins was the tendency to over-centralise. It stemmed from the fact that the Captain of a ship was in absolute command and responsible for everybody and everything that went on in that ship. This was a responsibility that could in no sense be shared. Admirals, most of whom were powerful characters and eccentric captains of ships in their younger days, in many cases found it impossible to delegate and decentralise properly in so far as their own Staff were concerned. They did not really like having a Chief of Staff and preferred to do all the work themselves using their Staff Officers as technical experts in certain specialist spheres. The two most striking cases of this under whom I served were Freddie Dreyer and Roger Backhouse, both men of great intelligence and commanding ability who threw themselves in to their naval careers with a fixity and singleness of purpose which would have done credit to the adherents of St. Paul and the early Christian Church. This is why both Admirals Dreyer and Backhouse changed their first Chiefs of Staff, both very able men. Whilst after the First World War a proper staff organisation had evolved at the Admiralty, the staff organisation of commands afloat in some cases did leave quite a lot to be desired and there were many gaps. For instance, soon after I joined having been told to include war plans in my responsibilities, I found that our operational plans for offensive operations against Germany were almost non-existent. It was necessary to guard against producing too rigid plans as by doing so one might quite inadvertently sacrifice the priceless tactical and strategic mobility of the fleet and miss some fleeting chance of delivering a heavy blow at the enemy. The wardroom of HMS Nelson comprised a pleasant and varied set of officers though it was 111

at first slightly strange to be in a ship at sea with absolutely no executive responsibility for its conduct. Jeffrey the Commander, an early promotion to Captain was an outstandingly nice man. Sam Woods rose to have a distinguished war record in the submarine Service, relieved me in 1960 as C-in-C Home Fleet and so on. Most of the staff became Admirals and had useful and purposeful careers in the Navy. Let us return to the Fleet we assembled with the rest of the Home Fleet at Portland and set sail for Gibraltar where we met units of the Mediterranean Fleet. There was the usual get together with the Mediterranean Fleet where we met our opposite numbers, Grantham and others on the C-in-C Med’s staff. Admiral Pound, the C-in-C Med, was in some respect similar to Admiral Backhouse, perhaps rather a colder and more distant character but an absolute whale for work (his nickname was ‘The Old Whale’) with a fund of physical energy which put men 20 years younger to shame.26 It was interesting comparing staff; with the exception of Grantham, I think our staff were of higher quality certainly intellectually than the Med staff. At the end of the meeting, Admiral of the Fleet, Lord Chatfield came out to visit the Fleets. I remember noting then how spry and young he still looked much younger and less tired than the two Commanders-in-Chief, one of which was soon to relieve him as First Sea Lord! It was clear even then that neither C-in-C had fully appreciated the tremendous menace of the torpedo carrying aircraft to capital ships. They were perhaps told by their gunnery advisers that the ship’s anti-aircraft fire would inflict such heavy casualties on attacking aircraft that the attacks would fizzle out. Some of us knew well this was unlikely to happen and though I believe in a carefully staged exercise that I convinced Roger Backhouse of this, not sufficient was done to develop appropriate countermeasures and better anti-aircraft weapons. It was always said our carrier aircraft would destroy every aircraft before they became a menace. Fundamentally this was right, but what would happen if our aircraft were not available when required? It was indeed fortunate the Germans never appreciated the lethality of torpedo carrying aircraft as if they had, we might well have found ourselves in a precarious position with the whole command of vital sea areas in jeopardy. After a short visit to Malta, we returned home calling at Lisbon. A most pleasant visit, and as ever the Commander-in-Chief was splendid at all the ceremonials which an official visit of this nature to our oldest ally entails. A little golf and roulette at Estoril livened up our visit, though I was more successful at the former pastime than the latter. Appointments were made soon after our return to England. It was known that Charles Forbes was to be the new Commander-in-Chief and that Admiral Backhouse was to be the First Sea Lord in place of Lord Chatfield. An event of great importance took place at Mulgrave on the 9th April 1938. Johnny was born and I had the good fortune to be on leave at the time. I remember being shown him soon after his arrival and thought he looked a bit aggressive and rather less attractive than Georgina! Elizabeth had a fairly straightforward passage and it was particularly nice that one of our family should be born at her own home. Lady Normanby was there at the time and she wisely sent me out for a walk with Oswald immediately prior to the birth! A very pleasant leave of about 10 days. My father was simply delighted as this was the first grandson 26 Admiral Sir Dudley Pound (1877-1943), ODNB. 112

of his surname. The christening took place in Lythe Church in May. My old friend Guy Russell was godfather with Oswald and my sister Jane the other godparents. As conditions in Europe were getting more and more ominous it was decided to have a change of C-in-C in the middle of the summer, so that Admiral Backhouse could get into the saddle as first Sea Lord by the end of the year 1938. The arrival of Admiral Forbes brought a new air to the command. Admiral Forbes enjoyed a certain measure of recreation and was not such a centralizer as his predecessor. He was a very shrewd if hard bitten Scot. I had known him when he was my Captain for the last year I was in the Queen Elizabeth. A trifle conservative, he was not new to staff work, having been Admiral Jellicoe’s Staff Officer Operations at the Battle of Jutland. He did not, I think, ever have a real understanding of the implications of maritime air power, and he found it difficult to accept the vulnerability of the warship against WWD with Nanny and both children aircraft torpedo attack, though he rightly discounted the wildly extravagant claims of the RAF on the efficiency of bombs against warships. He was a conservative in tactics and did not like the new ideas of having to prepare for small independent actions which we believed would be the rule in any future wars, rather than set piece battles as at Jutland. After much argument he deferred to our views, though he was supported in these discussions by his chief of staff, Rear Admiral King. However, he did give way and he accepted the new ‘Battle Instructions’ which our Staff and the Med staff had drafted during the preceding months. As a strategical brain Admiral Forbes always seemed to be one of the best we have had, though in the tactical field he was not so happy. A strong and determined character he had none of the charm of Admiral Backhouse and did not evince any great understanding of the feelings of folk, officers and men alike. On the other hand, he was hard on himself and even when you put a point of view which may have been anathema to him, he would always be prepared to listen and let you have your say. Not very imaginative, he had however all the qualities of steadfastness of his nation. His Chief of Staff, Rear Admiral King, I had known when a Staff Officer in Queen Elizabeth just after the First War. A clever and able staff officer. He perhaps saw too many sides to a question and experienced much difficulty in making up his mind. He loved drafting papers and orders himself and would spend hours at this pastime, which should have been left to the appropriate Staff Officer. In a sense he was complimentary to his C-in-C who had a clear and incisive mind. King was very thorough and easy to work with. Perhaps rather a shy man he had none of the warmth of his predecessor, Henry Moore. Though in many ways a good Chief of Staff, I and some others of us on the staff thought he saw too much wood for the trees! When at Portland in the late summer, the King accompanied by the Duke of Kent paid us a visit and stayed on board Nelson. I had many friendly talks with the Duke of Kent who I had looked after as Prince George in Queen Elizabeth. He certainly seemed to be enjoying him- 113

self and it was also evident how much the King enjoyed being back in a ship again. This was the first time I had met George VI, and he seemed so much more at ease and less shy than when we had seen him in the distance before.27 Then Winston Churchill spent a night on board at Portland. He certainly was in one of his belligerent moods and made many suggestions for offensive action against the future enemy we should soon have to face. I had a little talk with him, though much impressed with his spirit I could not help feeling some of his ideas did not maybe make sense from a naval point of view. But maybe he was, as I later found out, trailing his coat. August found us back at Portsmouth for our summer leave period. And we had the good fortune to take for a short period a nice house at Curdridge, near Bishops Waltham. It could not have suited us better. And Georgina and Johnny with old Nanny were there, and prepared to take the fullest possible advantages of the visits to the sea. Ion Tower asked me if I would care to go shares with him in a delightful yacht called Corrie, owned and sailed by old Fred Hughes who was one of the great sailing characters on the Solent. Corrie would by present day measurements be known as a 7 metre, Bermuda rigged and quite the nicest boat to handle that I have ever experienced. She was one of a small class built in the early part of the century as being better than the 6 metres. I’ve always heard Corrie was so much the best of her class and that [it is surprising that] more were not built. Fred Hughes was about as expert a boat handler as one would meet anywhere in the Solent and he kept his boat at moorings View from Corrie’s deck in the Hamble River, not far from Warsash. She sailed beautifully and would point closer to the wind than any modern craft. Kept spotlessly clean by Fred and everything was very shipshape He knew the Solent inside out and never needed a chart. But his talk and fund of anecdotes of the past made a day with him all the more exciting. He knew the Solent in the heyday of Edward VII and Tommy Lipton, and of course sailed with George V in Britannia on a number of occasions.28 Fred had I suspect in the past lived in more expensive ways when their family had a nice house not far from Fawley. He had a number of sisters of his own age (60 plus) called ‘Cat’, ‘Bobsey’ and others, who were characters in quite different ways, but were united in their love of sailing. We took Lady Normanby, who was staying with us at Curdridge over to Cowes on a lovely day and how we all enjoyed it. I do not think she quite realised the hazards of going ashore from Corrie in Fred’s little pram dinghy. Our time at Curdridge slipped by only too quickly. We had friends to stay including of course my father who loved to get his feet again on a yacht. Prior to this in July, Nelson paid a visit to Kristiansand in southern Norway. In the same month my brother was married at Longhope to Patsy Macgill with whom he had been friendly for a long time, a description of the marriage will be found in my Father’s Diaries. Our time in Curdridge could hardly have been more pleasant and we will not forget some of 27 The future King George was born Albert Frederick Arthur George, but took the name George when he. became King in 1937. 28 Sir Thomas Lipton (1850-1931), grocer and yachtsman, ODNB. 114

those lovely sailing trips up the Beaulieu to Spithead, up and down the Solent to various places in the Isle of Wight, and of course to Cowes where old Fred Hughes regaled us with stories of Cowes and ‘The Squadron’ during the yachting seasons in the early part of the present century. But throughout all the anxieties the European situation could not be brushed under the carpet. In July and August, the crisis of Czechoslovakia over the Sudeten Germans led by the ubiquitous Konrad Henlein [a Sudeten German politician] reached crisis stage. As we suspected then and know well now this was only part of Hitler’s policy of ‘Grab’, aimed first at European conquest and then at world conquest. Winston Churchill’s Gathering Storm (vol. 1) tells graphically of the sequence of events. What did one think? I doubt if anyone anybody imagined the full catastrophe into which all Europe was plunging. I remember well often discussing the problems facing us and I think in so far as thinking service officers were concerned, we had all passed the stage of thinking WWD with Elizabeth, dressed in whether or not a war was imminent. It was now a problem of when the war will break out. Sunday best with the usual fox tippet There was on the surface in Society here and there a sort of euphoria rather on the lines of around her neck, both clutching pet dogs exclamation of ‘eat, drink. and be merry. for tomorrow we die.’ There was quite a lot of irresponsible talk about the effects of bombing rather as there was when the effects of the atomic bomb came to be known decades later. Perhaps we did not know much about the effects of bombing but there was little doubt the possible effects of it were widely exaggerated. On the other hand, the Government perhaps tardily but albeit at this 11th hour wholeheartedly threw themselves into A.R.P precautions. But with hindsight it is easy enough now but who could have said at the time that the evacuation of children from some main industrial targets was not a sensible precaution! But at heart people were in spite of past pacifist resolutions just as sound as ever, and the feeling one got from the so-called ‘man in the street’ was that the sooner Hitler and his gang were sorted out the better! I think there was even a measure of doubt about the soundness of France. Mussolini was dismissed as a bombastic filibuster, and again people would say ‘Oh, the Italians are no good - remember how they ran at Caporetto’, ‘need not worry about them’ and so on. The general unpreparedness of our military position was suspect, but again the great mass of people would say ‘Oh the Navy is all right and they will just have to hold the fort until we have rearmed ourselves’. Comforting perhaps, but again much of the effects of air warfare introduced a new dimension into our thinking. The Nelson was at Portsmouth so even during my leave I kept very closely in touch with what was happening.Various precautionary measures were set in motion and in early September we moved up north to Rosyth. Our problem, as before World War I, was what was to be the Fleet base? We no longer had a massive German High Seas Fleet to oppose us. On the other hand, there were some fast battle cruisers and pocket battleships which would pose a serious problem. Then of course there were the ubiquitous German submarines which had 115

brought us in the First World War to within sight of defeat. Plans had of course been made beforehand but because of the 10 year and other rules, much remained to be done to implement these plans, in particular where harbour defences were concerned. Our defences with static guns were pretty well non-existent. Ammunition reserves as far as the Fleet concerned were satisfactory with the exception of reserves for anti-aircraft weapons. But the bases which must be used for the Fleet were Scapa Flow and Rosyth, with emphasis on the former. Our C-in-C, who had been on Admiral Jellicoe’s Staff, had no doubts that Scapa was the place for the main fleet. We had some reports on the progress of the defences of Scapa Flow which indicated they probably would not be completed before 1941/1942. A very complete system was envisaged by the Admiralty with causeways over some of the entrances and full yielding booms with nets at the Hoxa, Swither and Stromness entrances. As I was the underwater defence expert on the staff, I asked the C-in-C if I could visit Scapa without delay, do what I could to accelerate the work there, and report back to him. This was readily agreed, and I flew up in a Walrus amphibian aircraft which was well suited to this sort of job. I could visit all the islands and numerous inlets and entrances to Scapa Flow in this manner. My pilot was a charming man by the name of Casson, son of Sir Hugh Casson, the actor.29 We had a slightly hazardous flight up to Scapa as fog and sea fret were down to sea level, but by following the coastline up and taking a careful departure from Dunnet Head at the entrance to the Pentland Firth we landed at Lyness which contained fuel tanks and was also the base of Metal Industries Ltd., who were salvaging the German fleet. Here I met a splendid man who was in charge of the salvaging work and just the man to get a move on the job. Commodore (RNR) Mackenzie was a redoubtable character, about 5 foot three inches tall and about the same width, he was immensely strong and one of the best practical seamen it was my good fortune to meet. We soon went out to the site of the main Hoxa boom at the entrance at the Hoxa entrance and greatly speeded the work of laying the first line of buoys and nets. I remember one very powerful Orkney Islander fell overboard when working from our trawler; Mackenzie just leant over and picked the man, some 14 stone in all, out of the water with one hand and dropped him on the deck of the trawler none the worse for his immersion. We soon had the Hoxa and Switha booms in some shape which would at any rate present an ‘obstacle to an enemy submarine’. The semi fixed defences for the Stromness entrance were soon in some shape and after the best part of a week, I felt for these entrances there was some sort of obstacle, though far from being 100 %, to enemy submarines. However, in flying around, Mckenzie pointed out there was a gap; through which a vessel could enter the Flow from the open sea, near Kirkwall at St Margaret’s Hope. This had been closed in the First War by a sunken merchant ship but had been removed, and it was the Admiralty plan to build a causeway across this entrance which was both narrow and exceedingly hazardous. Many a seamen would have judged the hazards of entering through this gap were far too great to be practical. However there it was, Mackenzie and I reckoned a very skilful, determined and lucky submarine commander might at certain states of the tide squeeze through and get into the Flow. By luck, there was the hull of one of the old concrete barges, 29 WWD has confused the name here with that of the well-known architect Sir Hugh Casson; he meant the actor and theatre director, Lewis Casson (1875-1969), whose son John Casson (1909-1999) was a naval officer in the Fleet Air Arm (both appear in ODNB). 116

some 300 /400 feet long, built in World War I, lying in Lyness, so we went round and purchased it for £50. I told Mackenzie, I would guarantee this this from Fleet funds if necessary. We planned to fill this barge with rubble and scrap and sink it in the middle of the gap at St Margaret’s Hope. This would not by any means prove to be a 100% stopper but might well have added to the hazards of entry by stealth as to prove impractical for any enemy submarine. The Munich crisis was at its height and we reckoned we could get the barge ready and tugs to tow it in place in about a week. I flew back to the C-in-C and reported the state of affairs. I said that with hazard the Fleet could go to Scapa, but that St Margaret’s Hope’s entrance should be blocked forthwith. Meanwhile the barge we bought should be used as a stopgap. The C-in-C reported to the Admiralty. Admiralty experts had some doubts as to the efficiency of the barge that I and Mackenzie had purchased, but recognised it would greatly add to the hazards of entry. Meanwhile all other efforts should be devoted to completing the second and third lines of the booms already started. Chamberlain at this time brought back the paper which was said to indicate ‘Peace in our time’, and our project for sinking the barge in the entrance was cancelled in favour of making a more permanent obstruction. [Gunther] Prien (1908-1941), the German submarine ace, entered through St Margaret’s Hope in the late autumn of 1939 and torpedoed and sank HMS Royal Oak before the permanent obstruction for the entrance had been put in place. I always felt that the Admiralty were inclined to be perfectionists and if the C-in-C had insisted come what may, in an attempt [being made] to obstruct the entrance partially or even temporarily, they would not have objected. Certainly, the transitional solution of our immediate difficulties with Germany by the Munich Crisis agreement gave us a little breathing space. Whilst it is only too easy to criticise selling the Czechs down the road and trying to make an accommodation with Hitler, the grave unpreparedness of this country at the time for war should never be overlooked. How did we feel in the Fleet? I think the attitude of mind was to be thankful for being given more time to prepare ourselves for a war posture. On the other hand, it now seems we overrated the preparedness of Germany for war. In the Fleet we continued at high pressure getting our plans and the means of executing them into shape. Some anti-submarine booms were at our recommendation laid and so on, but what lagged behind everything was the almost total absence of anti-aircraft defences which in the main were the Army’s responsibilities, and who being last in the rearmament queue were sadly behind what was required. Altogether a busy time in the Fleet. Charles Forbes was a better organiser than his predecessor and did not over centralise to the same extent. King, the Chief of Staff whom we liked, covered the ground well, but was curiously indecisive at times. Like some staff officers he saw too many sides of the question, that any decision made caused considerable anguish. Forbes was in some ways the old-fashioned type of naval officer brought up in the blue water school. A very shrewd strategist, he did not however I think understand the full impact of 117

the air and of aircraft on maritime warfare, and gave the impression of resenting the ‘intrusion’ of aircraft, whether Naval or RAF, on naval matters! As the autumn drew on, Tom Halsey, (Appointments Commander) in the Second Sea Lord’s office drew the attention of his Chief that I should be given an executive job; and as by that time my old friend of China days, JAS Eccles, had gone to Ark Royal, I was offered the Hood, the biggest and one of the most powerful warships in the world, as her Executive Officer, and second in command. This was great luck. I had a most distinguished list of predecessors, and it was a challenge to see if one could match up to them. Hood was due back in Portsmouth at the end of the year from the Mediterranean for an eight month’s refit, and then to join the Home Fleet. There was a magic about the Hood - the most beautiful of all our warships and at the same time one of the most formidable. The picture by Claude Muncaster in Coglan, of Hood in Pentland Firth was hung in one of the Academy exhibitions in the 1940s and gives a vivid impression of the strength and beauty of the ship. It was decided that Derek Hall Thompson who did the long Torpedo Specialist course at Vernon after me should be my relief and accordingly he arrived soon after Christmas. As Hood had already arrived at Portsmouth, Elizabeth and I started looking around for rooms there in which to live whilst the ship was refitting. We spent Christmas at Mulgrave as far as I HMS Hood, can remember, and also spent some time with my father at Coglan. He was very active in by Claude Muncaster. Watercolour spite of his 74 years, organising the ARP in the village and taking on numerous other jobs of a similar nature. The thought crossed my mind then if one lasts to his age and is as fit and active mentally and physically, there will be nothing about which to complain! The warmth of the welcome we had at Mulgrave was wonderful and I came to have an increasing and affectionate regard for Elizabeth’s mother who though shy and reserved had a very unselfish and warm heart. Then one January I walked across the Southern Railway jetty at Portsmouth and was met by Hookey Walker the Captain, and David Orr Ewing the Commander. It was a cold January day and as the new Captain of Hood was still overseas (Captain Irvine Glennie) I took on as Captain and Commander. Half the ship’s company were on leave and most of the Officers of the old Commission were still there. A goodish wardroom but not outstanding. David Orr Ewing took me all over the ship and told me exactly how he ran it and the various pitfalls to avoid. Altogether a most helpful turnover which stood me in good stead later. The ship’s company had all the makings of being first rate, but somehow in the Mediterranean never quite reached the heights. I liked the senior ratings very much. There were to be of course quite a number of changes with virtually a completely new wardroom. But anyway, it was soon clear if the ship did not become one, if not 118

the best in the Fleet, there was only one person to blame, namely the author of these discursive notes. I soon felt that the dockyard was not giving the urgency to refitting the Hood which perhaps I thought should be the case! I may well have been wrong as the yard was full of hosts of other ships, but in a visit to the Admiralty and when calling on my old friend Admiral Backhouse, the new First Sea Lord, I hinted at this. The effect was immediate! Within a few days of my return the number of men working in the ship was nearly doubled and there seemed to be no lack of a sense of urgency! Meanwhile Elizabeth and I had rooms in Shirley Road in Selsey. Not very good and not very close to the sea but the best we could obtain. Nanny and the children were installed there and we certainly enjoyed our time at Portsmouth with occasional visits to friends nearby, including Elizabeth’s old cousin, Louise Foster, Lady Normanby at Mulgrave, who lived in a lovely house called Old Buckhurst near Withyam in Sussex. The old C-in-C early 1940 Portsmouth, Admiral of the Fleet the Earl of Cork and his wife were good to us and we visited Admiralty House on occasion. It was fascinating watching the Hood being repaired and refitted. Elizabeth bought some very pleasant furnishings for my cabin which was strategically situated to overlook the quarter deck. Johnny still has some of these furnishings! To make the Hood go faster, I arranged when in dock for the ship to be completely scraped underwater by the ship’s company. A truly formidable task, but the sailors entered into the spirit of it and it put about 1 ½ knots onto our top speed which prior to this had dropped to about 28 knots. Then it was time for our new Captain, one Irvine Glennie, to join. He had commanded a cruiser in the New Zealand station and prior to that had spent all his life in destroyers where he had a most distinguished career, being an early promotion both to Commander and Captain. I had not met him before but he had a reputation of being a firstclass leader in every sense and a seaman to his fingertips. He said he never had any use for paperwork but for all that he could put a case either verbally or in writing as well as anybody I know. He arrived one morning to have a look round before joining and by mistake I gave him a wine glass full of neat whisky instead of sherry! Without a wink he said, ‘You are hot stuff, Commander’, and then started to choke and laugh! Glennie is about as near ideal a Captain of a big ship as any Commander could want. Incisive, clear, but with a quite wonderful way with men. Malefactors would do anything to avoid having a ‘talk to’ from the Captain. He punished lightly and if the rogue with a good hard luck story occasionally got away with it, the ships company knew they had a man, as their captain whom they would follow anywhere. Glennie was not an intellectual, essentially a very humble man, who always assumed again and again the best of everybody. He just loved the sea, was a very good ship handler. An absolutely forthright character, the only type of person who really caused his ire to rise were the occasional prigs and hypocrites. They got short shift from him regardless of their status. A most engaging character with an enormous fund of common sense which could be drawn on whenever required. He was a truly splen- 119

did man to talk over problems with, and I learned a tremendous lot in the handling of Officers and men from him. Our wardroom started to build up. First our Padre, one Harold Beardmore was an old friend and absolutely splendid character. A fine rugger forward who feared neither God nor man, and who had been a midshipman in Coastal Motor Boats in the First War. He had a powerful bulldog with him and the two of them would soon make the way straight for any delinquent!30 I soon realised with the power of his calibre that if we could not run the ship with the powers temporal and spiritual in close alliance, there must be something wrong with the Commander. It worked out magnificently and I shall never forget one old persistent offender’s face when I said to him at the Defaulter’s table, ‘Now I think you had better go along and have a long talk with the Chaplain and see if he can help you’. He replied immediately, ‘Please Sir, not that, I will never come before you again’. Harold was an absolutely invaluable asset to any ship, officers and sailors alike. He became Archdeacon in South Africa, and eventually ended up as Bishop of St Helena, after he retired from the Navy after the war. I kept in touch with him and visited him only a couple of years ago in 1968 a few days before he died of cancer. He knew he was soon to start on a long journey, but was in a sense looking forward to it. Then Bob Currie was the Gunnery Officer, only to be promoted Commander soon afterwards. A very able man indeed who became an Admiral before he retired. He went out of his way to work in with the various ways I ran the ship. After all, every Commander has his foibles and likes to run a ship his way. ‘Tiny’ Gregson relieved him, a fine figure of a man and the best heavyweight boxer the Navy has ever had. Tony Pares, the Torpedo Lieutenant, a charming efficient and quiet man, and quite a good watercolour painter. [Robert] Grogon, the ‘chief ’ who ran the engineering department in his stride, at the same time always kept one or two high grade racing cars. The old Pay a nice old chap with the occasional chip on his shoulder. The overworked mate of the upper deck, Lieutenant Commander Brownrigg, and whom I harried mercilessly I fear. He was sound enough but not very far seeing. Then Alec Mackenzie the PMO and later became Medical Director General, a first-rate athlete and a most conscientious doctor. Le Bailly, a young Lieutenant E, who I see is now an Admiral. Cairncross, the Marine, perhaps a bit formal; and as good a Gunroom of Midshipmen as one would want anywhere - Power, Mackenzie, Nall etc. - one never called on the Gunroom in vain. The ships company soon proved themselves. A fine old Master of Arms, called Green, with whom until recent years I have been in touch. A magnificent Sergeant Major of Marines, Chief Gunner’s mate and so on. The Senior non-commissioned Officers played a big part in the affairs of the ship, as indeed did also the Warrant Officers who kept the traditions of their fine branch up to shining standard. Alas, many of my friends were lost when the Hood was sunk in action with the Bismarck in May 1941 off Iceland. In spite of the time at Portsmouth’s Dockyard, the ships company and the new wardroom soon started to take shape, and it was clear we were in for a good commission. There was 30 Chaplains in the Services generally performed the functions of a welfare officer, which was helpfully distinct from that of the Captain’s responsibility for his crew, both in terms of discipline and welfare, but could work powerfully in support. 120

plenty of work to be done whilst in Portsmouth Dockyard and special attention was paid to the various measures necessary to bring the ship to a complete state of war readiness. In view of the fact that Hood for a ship of her size had rather less reserve buoyancy than was entirely comfortable, special attention was paid to the watertightness of doors, bulkheads etc, a thoroughly unromantic and unexciting task albeit mighty necessary. As we lived more or less permanently in our ship there was a tendency in the British Navy to pay less attention to this problem, in perhaps the interests of living comfort! Even in 1939 the Hood was a very fine fighting unit, though it proved later indeed that she had not been reconstructed to modern standards of armour protection etc., as was being done to HMS Renown, another ship of the battlecruiser squadron. I was fully aware of this and occasionally discussed with others what would be the correct tactics if Hood met a ship like the projected Bismarck or Tirpitz which had a main armament of such heavy calibre guns as would penetrate Hood’s vulnerable parts. The ships company were kept busy chipping off very considerable layers of paint which had accumulated both internally and externally over the years of peace. One soon got to know them well and what a fine set of men they were. Good Chief Petty Officers, Petty Officers, and some very promising leading mates. I liked also the engine room department with a Chief Stoker who had many of the splendid characteristics of past members of this department. A good detachment of Marines, who however rightly spent much of their time at the Royal Marine Barracks at Eastney, doing various parts of their military training which cannot be done in a seagoing ship. As expected, it soon became known we were to be the flagship of the Home Fleet Battle Cruiser Squadron, and that Rear Admiral Jock Whitworth was to be our Admiral. A man with a great reputation of being a fine seaman, he had at one time been Captain of the Home Fleet, and so was not unacquainted with the administrative problems of running a Fleet. Thoroughly likeable and a very straightforward character. It was evident that he and the Captain (Irvine Glennie) would get on well together, as in fact they did. Whitworth was a sound and practical seaman. He was not maybe a very profound thinker and not widely versed in the strategical and tactical problems which might have to be faced. But in all fairness not a great many Flag Officers were. He exhibited many of the best qualities of the old time destroyer Officer, resourceful, adaptable and determined. He knew an efficient ship when he saw one, and though quietly spoken and most courteous in manner, he could if the need arose speak his own mind determinedly and with conviction. From the Commander’s point of view, he was always most reasonable and never as some Admirals do, made the lives of the Commanders of their Flagship a burden. He never tried to get his way by shortcuts and was most punctilious in channelling all his requests through the Captain. As time wore on, I became very fond of Jock Whitworth and his delightful wife. Glennie was quite ideal from the Commander’s point of view. My old friend Stuart Paton had been his Commander in Achilles before and told me how lucky I would be. He was right! With Irvine Glennie most things in life were either black or white, there were in his view not many shades in between, but as I have said before, his understanding of men was quite unsurpassed and he knew well when and where not to turn the blind eye. 121

When Whitworth joined the new Commander (N), Frankie Lloyd, also joined, a first rate officer in every way and as quick and accurate a Navigator as I have ever met. He proved to be a splendid support in the wardroom, and with the ‘Chief ’ Grogan, the PMO, McKenzie, and the Padre Beardmore, there was a strong team which ensured that the Officers led the way. below: HMS Hood conducting battle As our refit was coming to its end, the full power trial was necessary. Unfortunately for him practice on the high seas. Picture the Captain was sick at the time, so I took the ship to sea for a full day’s power trial out in from London Illustrated News, the Channel, south of the Isle of Wight. We passed the Queen Mary at speed in opposite dipasted in a cuttings album rections. The biggest warship afloat meeting the biggest merchant ship! A fairly fine day, belonging to Katharine Phipps. typical of the Channel in summer, visibility on the whole good, but uncertain. It was excitbottom: ing seeing many of the passengers of the Queen Mary waving to us as we passed. ‘The Armament ‘ from pamphlet on Hood written by WWD It was for me a most exciting and encouraging experience. I had never commanded or handled a warship before and to start off with the Navy’s biggest was especial fun. I soon found the Hood handled perfectly. She had quite good brakes with her four large propellers and bigger stern turbines, and apart from a tendency to wash down the quarter deck when turning at speed she was as easy a ship to handle as any. Possibly her deep draught and low silhouette made her less susceptible to windage [air resistance]. I had a feeling when I brought the ship back and berthed safely and without delay that I could return my ‘L’ plates to the Admiralty! Having Frankie Lloyd on the bridge was a splendid help as he by reason of his trade as a Navigator had had much ship handling experience. But to turn back to the wider aspects of our country’s predicament. In March the Germans occupied Czechoslovakia in contravention to their most solemn promises to Chamberlain at Munich, and it was pretty clear war was coming soon. Mr Chamberlain’s reaction was perhaps a bit surprising after the Munich Settlement, but it was clear and unequivocal, as his famous speech in Birmingham at the latter end of March showed. It was clear the Government now felt war to be inevitable and if there was any doubt left in people’s minds our guarantee to Poland made this clear. Though from a purely military point of view our guarantee can really have been little solace to Poland. They had just seen the subjugation of Czechoslovakia and realised only too well their turn would come next. The story of these times is given in many official histories and indeed also by Winston Churchill in his matchless prose in ‘The Gathering Storm’. At a cinema performance held in Ark Royal in Portsmouth in April, the First Lord quite unintentionally made newspaper headlines by 122

telling all concerned in a brief speech of thanks, that the anti-aircraft guns were manned at the very moment he was speaking! Conscription was introduced in April and we moved nearer to war with every week that passed. There was however still a ray of hope. We were in consultation with the Soviet Government and in April Mr Litvinov started preliminary discussions with our Ambassador in Moscow to see if some joint action could be worked out to restrain Germany.31 History has now been written about these discussions. Suffice it to observe that in the initial stages the Russians were probably sincere in their attempts to come to some agreement with us. However, for reasons of their own, possibly conditioned by the very natural suspicions on our side and above all by their appraisals of British and French military effectiveness, nothing solid ever came out of these discussions. Possibly the dismissal of Litvinov by Stalin early in May may have indicated the death knell of any policy rapprochement with the Russians. This is not a history of events leading up to the outbreak of war, beyond recording that the situation deteriorated in a steadily increasing way until in August we were confronted with the German Soviet Pact, which in fact divided up Poland and made the outbreak of war inevitable in a matter of days. To return to our own domestic life, we had enjoyed our stay in Shirley Road punctuated by visits to Coglan and Mulgrave. As war seemed inevitable, we decided it was better to make our home some way from seaports and main industrial centres which we guessed could be subject to bombing attacks. Accordingly, Elizabeth after looking round came on a little house As typically for many service called Rugden, in Howcaple, not far from Ross-on-wye and about 7 miles from Longhope. families, there was no permanent This belonged to a Mrs Weinholt, a widow who lived nearby and wanted to let it. Though family home, and life for WWD built as the agent’s house of what was once a considerable estate nearby, it had a nice garden and ED in these years meant a and tennis court, a bus service of sorts into Hereford. It proved to be a nice little house series of rented rooms, flats and though very cold in winter, but fulfilled what Elizabeth and I reckoned be the essential houses, punctuated by visits to requirements to bring up a family with the least outside disturbances. Our neighbours, old family at Mulgrave and Coglan. General Sir Sidney Clive (Marshal of the Diplomatic Corps) at Perrystone House, and Mr and Mrs Lee at a big house nearby, together with General and Mrs Alfre, our next door neighbours, made us all most welcome. Elizabeth’s cousin, Drusilla Clay, lived a couple of miles away at Brockhampton Court and her other cousin, Bridget Simmonds, was not far off. As weeks went by the imminence of war became apparent. Elizabeth was by now installed at Rugden, and in July I spent 10 days leave there which was especially enjoyable and refreshing after the rush to get the ship ready for sea. My brother and his wife were at a place near Hampton Court and were looking round for some place for them to have their first born, Jennifer, who arrived later in 1939. My sister was busy alternating between Huntley and London with essential visits to Eton where her splendid young son David was working. Charles Ackers had taken on various jobs in addition to his own concerned with the control of timber, and as already mentioned, my father was busy organising Longhope to meet the rigours of an all-out aerial war! 31 Maxim Litvinov (1876-1951), who was Jewish, was at the time the People’s Commissar for Foreign Affairs, until replaced by the less anti-German Molotov, architect of the Nazi-Soviet Pact. 123

We had simply lovely weather and enjoyed many walks near Rugden; the vicar was a particularly nice man, as indeed were many others of our friends in the neighbourhoods. John Maclean (now Lord Lieutenant). Graham Ling (killed in North Africa), the Clives, the Lees, the de Wints, the Aldrich Blake’s etc. I met Kit Steele (Sir Sidney Clive’s son-in-law), and listened to his views, not always sound on what our policy should be and what military steps were desirable! Archie Clive, a very clever and able Guardsman, whom I met later in the War Cabinet offices, occasionally turned up. Old Sir Sidney Clive and Lady Clive were always most welcoming, and Georgina and Johnny paid visits to Perrystone Court not infrequently when out on walks. The more one thought about the impending war, the more one’s thoughts were dominated by the big question mark of what would be the effect of aerial warfare. It is difficult sometimes to imagine now with all the experience we have had behind us, why there were so many question marks. I think we grossly overrated the effect of aerial war on our transport systems and communications. In fact, as we now know, over land the effect was virtually negligible, but we were not to know that then. Horrific figures would be quoted which in the event proved wildly exaggerated. The news in August of the signing of the Ribbentrop/Molotov Pact made it clear that the outbreak of war could not now long be delayed many days. It was clear from the frenzied propaganda that Germany might attack Poland any day, having fixed Russia and our guarantee would become immediately operative. This was in no sense a ‘War out of the blue’ as the 1914/18 war was. This was a deliberately provoked war as revealed at the Nuremberg trials after the war. Looking round one’s family and friends, one wondered who would survive it. We were thankful The family at Rugden, 1940 our children at any rate were too young. I never thought my nephew, David Ackers, would be lost, though in the middle of the war I had a sinking feeling when I heard he had joined the RAF and qualified as a fighter pilot. He lies buried in Normandy where he was shot down at the Battle of the Falaise Gap. My brother-in-law, Oswald would no doubt be called up, and one was anxious as he had no brothers and only distant cousins as next of kin. I soon returned to Hood at Portsmouth and we set sail for Invergordon and started to ‘work up’. We went there westabout, as it was thought the Germans might provoke war by carrying out an attack on a big British warship before war had started. This was the last thing they ever dreamt about, as Hitler in his megalomaniac dreams thought we would not honour any of our undertakings and go to war, when we were so obviously unprepared. We always made much play with our unpreparedness for war and much of this is true, but as we suspected then and now know, Germany thought we were much more unprepared and soft than we were. I doubt if they had taken to heart Count Puckler’s book referred to earlier in this narrative. 124

At Invergordon we spent four to five days a week at sea and soon got the ship into shape, though we had not in fact fired our main armament by the outbreak of war. However, opportunities were soon found after the outbreak for a full-scale battle practice. Many sailors joined us and soon we were up to war complement with the Reserves who had been called up some weeks previously. A bit of overcrowding in some places but on the whole our accommodation plans in Hood to expand to the full war complement were pretty good, and below: everyone soon settled in. Regulations aboard HMS Hood drawn up by WWD. Every aspect of life was The very cramped conditions in a good warship are not always appreciated and reservists regulated as the ship prepared to be who had lived ashore in some cases in comfort for many years found life a bit of a squeeze. battle-ready. However complaints about But the spirit was splendid. I welcomed every man as he joined the ship, and invariably he food were always regarded as something had a smile and often a joke as he came over the side! I have seldom felt so happy as it was needing to be addressed evident we had as fine and determined a set of men behind us as men could want. The rest of the Fleet were either at Invergordon or Scapa Flow - the Reserve fleet had been mobilised, and some of them together with some of the armed Merchant cruisers were destined for the Northern patrol and were assembling at Scapa Flow. It was interesting being at Invergordon again; the first time I visited it was in 1918 in old HMS Neptune as a very young midshipman when we were refitted there in the floating dock. Lovely countryside - we sometimes used to go for walks up towards Ben Wyvis, and when anchored at Nigg opposite the entrance at Cromarty, had many an adventurous game of golf in that rather mountainous little golf course. Then the Officers club and the tennis and football grounds were splendid and had been kept up well between the wars. So officers and men alike were well able to make full use of the ample recreational facilities when exercises and seagoing permitted. I saw a little of my old friends on the staff of the Fleet Flagship Nelson. They were at it like beavers but told me as I guessed the C-in-C’s main anxiety was that he had no base with proper anti-aircraft and anti-submarine defences. Scapa was to be the Fleet base and which, as in the First World War, was best situated to control maritime activities in the North Sea and approaches to the Baltic. On I think September 1, the C-in-C took the Fleet to sea and we carried out in conjunction with the Sunderlands of Coastal Command, various patrols and sweeps between Iceland and Norway. Ships were now fully darkened at night and war routine was adopted, namely a proportion of the ships company always ready at any time for action. I closed down some of the after cabins and very nice ones they were in Hood, and shut it all up to increase buoyancy, were we to be hit by torpedoes and suffer underwater danger. I occasionally spoke to the ship’s company 125

over the Broadcaster, a relatively modern innovation only installed in the last refit. Prior to that orders, messages and information were passed by ‘call boys’. I reckon the more you kept the ship’s company in the picture, above all whenever possible with the reasons for your actions, the better results one got. This certainly paid off 100%, and the response one got was most encouraging. Possibly a fault, some naval officers always in their dealings with men kept a strong silent war attitude - utterly wrong I believe in the 20th or even in any other century. Why many of our greatest Admirals always kept both officers and men informed of their intentions! September the 3rd dawned when we about halfway between the Orkneys and Iceland in quite good weather and a calm sea. I suppose one felt a sense of foreboding in the air. We could pick up the BBC radio, and the news the night before was not encouraging. Then a message came through by wireless, that the Prime Minister would make a broadcast to the nation soon after 11:00. Immediately facilities were made in all ships of the Fleet for this message to be heard by everybody; it would be true I believe that this gave us a sense of foreboding. As the morning wore on one came across the odd group of sailors working on the upper deck who would say ‘Well, I suppose we will hear the news straight soon.’ I think here and there some people may have had the feeling that, like at the Munich crisis, by some conjuring trick a rabbit would be again pulled out of the bag! At about 11:15 we all heard clearly the Prime Minister’s voice with much sadness announced the failure of all his efforts to keep peace and that we were now at war - a very dignified statement said with much feeling, and which I’m sure echoed the sentiments and innermost feelings of our countrymen. Immediately after the announcement I asked the Captain to speak to the ship’s company. This is where he was at his best, speaking impromptu straight from the heart. A very good brief address in which he made it clear where our duty lay and how privileged we all were to be serving in this magnificent ship for the defence of England. I finished up the broadcast by giving out a few notices in changes of routine etc., introduction of censorship and so on, occasioned by the fact that we were now at war. What was the feeling in the Wardroom and among the ship’s company at the announcement? I think first of all it was one of relief that all this uncertainty was over, and our job in the years that lay ahead of us was clear for all to see. There was no feeling, as in World War I, that it will all be over by Christmas, which as a small boy at Summerfields I remember well 25 years before!
