Now we certainly felt it would be a long job but there was I sensed an underlying feeling of satisfaction that at long last we could get to grips with the problems, and that much of the rottenness of the inter war years would be swept away. I think we felt perhaps that here we were face to face with destiny, and what a truly glorious tradition that we in the Royal Navy had succeeded to, and how we were determined to live up to our heritage. The news of the torpedoing of the Athenia, a perfectly innocent passenger ship with heavy loss of life on the afternoon of the first day of the war, brought home to us that the Germans were determined to conduct war by the most ruthless means, regardless of any agreements that had been signed in the years before the outbreak.32 32 SS Athenia was a transatlantic liner working between Glasgow/Liverpool and Canada. She carried 1103 passengers and 315 crew and was sunk by torpedoes in the Western Approaches. 117 were killed. 126

I remember asking our splendid Sergeant Major who always accompanied me on the 9:00 p.m. rounds of the ship what he thought, and he said roundly in words to the effect that the Germans were ‘bloody’ and ‘ambitious’, and that we were long overdue in taking them on and sorting them out. He said also he hoped, and so did the whole marine detachment, that when the war had been won Germany would be occupied for a long, long time. The Master at Arms told me also that these sentiments were very general throughout the ship and hoped it would not long before we tried conclusions with the German battleships Scharnhorst and Gneisenau! Our main concern perhaps at sea was the submarine threat - what a target and what a prize a torpedoing of the Hood would be to a German submarine commander! We judged rightly that the German submarines would be on their war stations, and that unrestricted submarine warfare would be the order of the day. So we relied on our destroyer escorts and constant zigzagging to frustrate attempts to carry out successful submarine attacks. I do not think any U boat actually ever attacked Hood though some may have been frustrated by our escorts. Ark Royal had certainly one narrow squeeze when a defective German torpedo exploded in its wake. But the C-in-C’s main problem was the lack of a secure base, with the result that the Home Fleet was kept almost permanently at sea for the first four months of the war in weather conditions which at times were very severe. We found that the Hood was not always as seaworthy as we would have liked, and that water leaked in where it should not. And the menace of the German magnetic ground mine laid by their aircraft and submarines forced itself with unpleasant effect on our thinking. It was necessary to ‘degauss’ all ships, so that the natural magnetic field of a ship would not operate[trigger] the firing mechanics of a ground mine in shallow water. This we did at Greenwich in between one of our sea trips. The method consisted of wrapping a copper strip round the hull of the ship just above the water line and passing an electric current through it continuously so as to neutralise the natural magnetism of the ship. The first four months of the war which takes us to the end of 1939 are fully described in Volume 1 of the Official History of The War at Sea by Stephen Roskill.33 The anxieties of the command having no secure base - the change of plan in mid-1938, which made Scapa the main Fleet base in place of Rosyth, all seemed to complicate the issue and contributed to the lack of readiness of our main base. We started at Scapa as our base though in fact we were pretty well constantly at sea. Some statistician produced some figures and I believe we were at sea something like 85 out of the first 95 days of the War. In the last week in September the Fleet carried out a sortie towards the Skagerrak [the strait between northern Denmark and Norway], to cover the withdrawal of one of our submarines (Spearfish) from the entrance to the Baltic which had been damaged and was forced to proceed on the surface. The Home Fleet covered this operation which took place in fair weather. There were a few German aircraft about and I watched one do a spectacular dive 33 S. W. Roskill, The War at Sea 1939-1945: The Official History of the Second World War, HMSO, 3 vols., 1954-1961 127

bombing attack on the aircraft carrier Ark Royal. With all the guns firing at full speed Ark Royal took avoiding action and the bombs missed. I was on the bridge at the time and the ships company were at action stations, and I was talking to the Captain when I noticed a lone German aircraft which had not been fired at, passing at some distance up our port side at a height I suspect of about 10,000 feet. As I watched it, I noticed it turned towards us and said to the Captain, ‘I think this chap is coming for us.’ Alarm bells rang as the aircraft put itself into a steep dive towards its, and left us in no doubt of its intentions, and as I watched him, I noticed the bomb released some considerable distance away from the fore and after line of the ship. I said to Glennie ‘It will fall short’, but as I watched the bomb getting larger and larger, appearing to travel almost horizontally instead of vertically downwards, I had doubts of my estimate of where it would fall. As it appeared to be upon us, all of us ducked on the bridge to hear the bomb go off with a loud bang as it struck the side armour of the ship a glancing blow. Our close range anti-aircraft guns were much too slow and only started on the aircraft after bomb release. They may have frightened the pilot but certainly not more than that. I immediately went below to see the extent of the damage and found a little internal damage in the stoker’s bathroom from shock which was the compartment bounded by the side armour plate struck by the bomb. I asked two rather frightened stokers who were washing in a state of nature what happened, but got nothing more than, ‘Orrid bang Sir, everything shook, and the lights broke’ from them. The event which was for me the first time I had been bombed brought home again the ineffectiveness of our own anti-aircraft fire. We returned in due course to Scapa after the damaged submarine had been safely escorted to Rosyth. The C-in-C sent for the Captains of all the ships present, and left them in no doubt about his dissatisfaction at the performance of our anti-aircraft gunfire. The real trouble went much deeper than that. Our equipment and above all its system of control was painfully inadequate, and it was not till we borrowed from the Americans some of their systems that we had systems of anti-aircraft gun control which had a good chance of destroying the enemy aircraft. In the coolness of hindsight, we cannot acquit ourselves of some blame in not recognising this and not ensuring greater efforts and greater research were devoted to anti-aircraft gunnery. Take a look today at the modern AA guided weapons, the bombing aircraft of the last war would not have had the remotest chance of being able to attack ships with its bombs or torpedoes. During our continuous patrols at sea, we had one excitement in the second week of October when the German battlecruiser [Scharnhorst] carried out a very brief sortie which was followed by a more ambitious one in the middle of November, when the [armed merchant cruiser] Rawalpindi was sunk whilst on Greenland / Shetlands patrol. There were one or two attacks which really amounted to a little more than armed reconnaissance on Scapa in October with the result that the Fleet moved temporally to Loch Ewe as their main base. I had been there once before the war in the old Queen Elizabeth in the early 20s and little change was apparent.Very bare, a lovely semi tropical garden at Pool Ewe, and the rest about as bare West Highland scenery as one would meet anywhere in Scotland. 128

I remember well walking on the quarter deck one fine night in the middle of October at Loch Ewe when the Aurora Borealis was exhibiting itself in the most spectacular way in the northern skies. What a sight that can be! As I walked with Irvine Glennie, I remember making some remark to him to the effect that I wonder if Germans could use this light sky for any surprise attack. By coincidence, this happened to be the night of the 10th of October when the German submarine ace entered Scapa Flow through Kirk Sound at St Margaret’s Hope and torpedoed the old battleship Royal Oak with a heavy loss of life. The block ship for that hole in the defences had I later heard arrived only that day at the repair anchorage at Lyness in Scapa Flow to be prepared for sinking in the entrance. We visited the Clyde from time to time on our patrols and though it was a longish distance from our patrol area it was at least a secure anchorage, and ships companies when in harbour could be certain of an undisturbed night’s sleep. These visits presented the Commander with a problem - night leave to the men could not of course be granted, and there was still plenty of drink in the public houses. Some of course fell by the wayside, and indeed who would not after being cooped up for months on board. But I’m glad to say Hood had substantially less numbers of absentees than any other big ships. Our old Master-at-Arms was wonderful at dealing with men as they came aboard ‘having perhaps had drink taken’. I must jot back again. It was I think in October that Winston Churchill paid a flying visit to the Fleet at Scapa or Loch Ewe, stayed on board for lunch and gave a good talk to the ships company. I met and had quite a number of talks with his rather unusual Parliamentary Private Secretary (Brendan Bracken) who was quite determined that his chief should get the uninhibited truth regardless of the normal service channels of procedure! Nevertheless, it was all in a good cause and provided one did not acutely embarrass or hamper progress already under way, it was right [that] folk like BB should have the ‘facts of life’ as the man on the job saw them. Winston seemed to be enjoying himself and again was determined to get to the bottom of things, though even then I thought he underestimated the difficulties of producing quickly a really effective anti-aircraft gunfire system and equipment for the Fleet. At a later date you will hear of some of the redoubtable Professor Lindemann’s schemes which alas were of little use. An event at Greenock which gave us all much to laugh about. Gracie Fields gave a concert to the Fleet and afterwards had a standup supper in Jock Whitworth’s cabin, to which many of us were invited. She was as great fun off stage as on the stage. I noticed Monty Banks, who was I think her husband, emptying a box of the Admiral’s cigarettes into a small handbag, and the Admiral’s very old fashioned and excellent chief steward go up and speak to him in a disapproving way. Monty did not mind in the least and said, ‘Oh cigs are in short supply now in England’.34 Our patrols continued in usually thoroughly bad weather, and ships were beginning to show the strain. A number of defects showed themselves, partly as a result of having been the show piece ship of the British Navy for a generation. The heavy seas which broke the forecastle 34 The Services had more plentiful supplies of tobacco as cigarettes were considered essential for morale and continued to be available duty-free until 1989. WWD smoked at this time but gave it up after the War for reasons of economy. 129

found out some serious leaks round the two forward turrets barbettes, and at times parts of the main deck were awash. Our splendid First Lieutenant, Dick Jessel, was always at hand, and organised drying parties available at all hours with his accustomed efficiency. The ship had to be forced into heavy seas and it was said sometimes by other ships of the fleet that we looked like a ‘half tide’ rock! What a tower of strength Dick Jessel was - always ready to smile at the dirtiest of jobs! In the latter half of November one of our patrols had taken us well out into the Atlantic south of Ireland, and it was decided to send us into Plymouth to give us 48 hours leave to each watch. What an excitement this caused after nearly three months of almost continuous sea going. In any case the ship required a number of things to be done to repair storm damage and our condenser tubes, which were still the original ones, were giving us cause for concern. So, off the first watch went on leave. Just after the second watch went off one of the real panics. which one gets occasionally, started. The Scharnhorst and Gneisenau were making a sally. The Rawalpindi was sunk in the Denmark straits. And it was thought that the German battle cruisers might get into the Atlantic and gravely damage our main seaborne trade in these areas. Winston and the First Sea Lord insisted we should go to sea forthwith. We pointed out this must take us at least 12 to 18 hours. Immediate recall telegrams had been dispatched to everybody on leave but many of the ship’s companies lived in the Midlands. However, the Admiralty would brook no delay and we were told to make up from the barracks at Plymouth those men who did not catch the ship. We left by the next tide some eight hours after the order with about 300 men drafted on the spot in the barracks, to make up the shortage. A remarkable evolution and the splendid way most of our men somehow got back was remarkable. But with a modern warship one cannot just put men on board and say, ‘Fight it efficiently’! They all have to be trained in their particular job, for it is in the sense a team job and every person has an important part to play. However, we set about in the first two days getting our temporary new crew into their job and how wholeheartedly they threw themselves into it. We joined up with the French battle cruiser Dunkerque and another of their later cruisers and patrolled in company. We exchanged many friendly messages. The Dunkerque looked a magnificent ship. She rode the seas much better than we did and did not plunge through every wave as we did. I sometimes wonder what sort of showing we would have put up if we had met the German battle cruisers. Definitely rather chancy; after all it takes a ship at least six weeks to two months to train a ships company fully and we had only two days. On the other hand, all the key ratings caught the ship so I expect we might have not done too badly. After five to six days we returned to Plymouth, collected the members of the ship’s company we had left behind and went up to the Clyde to welcome and escort the first Canadian convoy in. As the year drew to an end it was worthwhile to take stock of how and where we stood. These first four months of the war were known as the ‘Phoney War’. They were certainly not phoney for the Navy. We had worked our ships and their companies to full capacity and the ships both internally and externally were showing signs of hard wear, but individually the 130

ship’s internal organisations soon adapted themselves to war routine and the armament stood up well to the buffeting it got. One of the highlights was the destruction of the German pocket battleship Graf Spee accomplished by Commodore Harwood’s squadron, consisting of the Exeter, Ajax and Achilles. The dispositions to achieve this were worldwide and the story is told vividly in volume 1 of the official Naval History. It was of a special interest to me as in peace at the Staff College we had worked on many examples of this sort of problem with much the same sort of forces available worldwide. The result of this event turned out not far different to some of the Staff College examples worked on 8 years previously! The action itself was splendidly conducted by Commodore Harwood, and even in the light of after knowledge, it would be hard to fault the Admiralty dispositions to catch this raider. Perhaps whilst memory serves, it is worthwhile to recapture the sort of life I led at sea. This is the sort of typical day on patrol, usually in bad weather. All the ships company would go to ‘action stations’ at first light of dawn, as in these pre-radar days this is a time when one might surprise an enemy, or in turn be surprised, or alternatively at 6:00 a.m. whichever was the earlier. Ships in line astern in fairly rough After various tests and exercises, when it was light we would send half the ship’s company weather. Undated. away to breakfast and clean. And for the remainder of the 24 hours, half the ship’s company would be at ‘action stations’, the other half watch keeping the ship clean and generally keeping the ship’s economy ticking etc. If it was possible we might have some anti-aircraft practice, at smoke bursts or any enemy reconnaissance aircraft, which occasionally obliged but we never shot one down! Then during the day, we would probably also do some tactical exercises with other units of the Fleet. And on a few occasions when we thought we were in a ‘quiet area’, we carried out full calibre gun practices ‘thrown off ’ against other units of the Fleet. This ensured the shots always landed in the sea usually about half a mile astern so that the target ship could estimate the accuracy of the ranging by the firing ship. My own routine as Commander was something like this. I found out first if the Captain who lived pretty well permanently on the bridge or in his bridge sea cabin, whether he would like me to take over whilst he relaxed. Normally he asked the Commander N to do this, as he said I had a ‘whole time’ job keeping the ship running smoothly and efficiently. Then say at 6:00 a.m. we went to ‘action stations’ and I satisfied myself that the internal repair and damage control organisation was functioning properly. Then about 8:00 a.m. I slipped off for a quick wash and breakfast and put the sailors not at ‘action stations’ to work on routine repair, maintenance and cleaning work, see any men who had requests, discussed the various problems with Heads of Departments, Gunnery and Torpedo Officers etc. Daylight hours were fully occupied and considerable time was devoted to making the rounds of the ship, in seeing everything was secured and that the ships company’s living quarters were 131

kept ship shape and hygienic. A session in the Commander’s office was always necessary to ensure appropriate tasks were being tackled and routine for the following day mapped out, as well as making a list of work to be done on return to harbour which could not be tackled at sea. For instance, touching up the camouflage painting was one thing that always required attention! I usually went the rounds of the ship a number of times with the Chief Bosun’s Mate who was a first rate seaman and who was of much help in ensuring everything was properly secured. Then again, we usually went to ‘action stations’ soon after 8:00 p.m. to ensure everything was right before sending half away to ‘pipe down’ [dismissed from duty]. The three watches of the night were first watch 8:00 p.m. to midnight, the middle watch midnight to 4:00 a.m., the morning watch 4:00 a.m. to 8:00 a.m. Pipe down was usually at 9:00 p.m. but sometimes a little later when we were in areas which could pick up the 9:00 p.m. BBC news. Then rounds between decks with Master at Arms and Sergeant Major. A good stretch as the ship was over 300 yards long. If the weather was threatening a final round of the upper deck with the Chief Bosun’s Mate during which time one not infrequently bathed one’s skin! A talk to the Captain, and finally to one’s own cabin to rest. Then once during the middle watch, I did rounds between decks and on the upper deck if the weather was bad. This has taken a rather long time to tell but one’s routine was of course subject to endless changes and variations. On going to sea and returning to harbour lots of things had to be done such as streaming and recovering paravanes, getting the ship’s boats ready for use in harbour, providing working parties for stores, mail, food etc.35 And how important was the mail; its prompt arrival did more for a ship’s company’s morale than anything I know, and just the odd senior officer here and there did not always appreciate this. In between one’s day to day jobs it was interesting to speculate on the course of the war maritime wise. We realised the quiet phase or so called ‘phoney war’ would not last long, and we might find ourselves at the receiving end of the much vaunted German Air Force. Anyway, it seemed hard to imagine being worked much harder, but then the Home Fleet bore the brunt of the strain in the opening stages. The submarine menace was ever with us but we felt that with a proper screen of destroyers we had more than a sporting chance of sinking the submarines. The absence of a secure base gave anxiety to the Command, and as we will hear it was not until March 1940 that the defences of Scapa Flow A/A and A/S were completed and ready to receive the Fleet. Ground mines laid by submarines or aircraft proved yet another unpleasant hazard. Nelson, the Fleet flagship was mined going into Loch Ewe in December. The C-in-C was not amused! Christmas Day was by chance spent in harbour and as a reminder of old times, Glennie and I visited all the messes to wish them good cheer and received some amusing and thoroughly forthright replies! Materially the Hood was beginning to show her age and in particular the condensers, whose tubes had not been changed since the ship was built, were beginning to show disquieting weakness here and there. If anybody could keep the engines going it was our Chief Grogan, 35 Paravanes were water kites, first developed in WW1. They were strung out and ‘streamed’ alongside a ship as a devices to 132 cut tethered mines

but as a result of these defects our maximum speed at times was reduced to 25 knots. The newcomers we had in the ship since mobilisation soon showed their worth - men from all walks of life. Soon we had a splendid team of young men as candidates for commission. They had in most cases already just about completed their education. I used to see each candidate and among other things verify they had the necessary fairly rudimentary educational qualifications before going before a Board. One young man, a Wykemist, was hesitant about his educational qualifications, and it took me quite a while to find out that he had got a First in Greats [Classics] at Oxford. In sending him away, I made the laconic remark ‘Just adequate educationally’. He did very well later and I believe commanded a frigate at the end of the war. It was encouraging to see how the officers stood up to war strain. Most increased materially in stature and the fussers ceased usually to fuss, and the quiet and hesitant frequently blossomed forth. The Reserve Officers, many of whom had been in the Navy between wars, fitted into the pat- HM the King delivering his tern of ship’s life almost instantly. Life in the Wardroom was fun. The Padre, and his fierce Christmas message. looking bulldog Bill, was just as welcome between decks as he was in the Wardroom. K. Phipps cuttings album. We had one or two discussions about how the war would end and none of us could guess. We were convinced thanks to our command of the sea that we would win it eventually, but how and when was not disclosed to us. Jock Whitworth and his pleasant Flags, Mike Williams (retired recently from being Governor of Guernsey) were always most welcome in the mess. And when we were in the Harbour, Irvine Glennie seldom missed an opportunity to pay us a visit in the Wardroom. Now for 1940. I had good news of Elizabeth and our family. Oswald had joined the Green Howards and was expected soon to go to France. 1940 The beginning of the year found us based on the Clyde though we spent most of our time at sea, and only called at our base for fuel and stores. It was very cold indeed and it is said this winter was one of the coldest on record. We certainly had as a matter of routine to free the upper deck from ice from time to time whilst at sea. Neither officers nor ships companies were supplied with proper winter clothing as is needed when patrolling off Iceland in winter. Many voluntary organisations filled this gap splendidly by sending us gifts of warm clothing. And it was my good fortune to be able to thank these people when Admiral Whitworth, Glennie, I and the Master at Arms met their principal organiser for ‘Hood’ comforts in 1941. The scenery in the West Coast of Scotland is fine and beautiful, but the continuous snow capped mountains and snow covered approaches to the Clyde became a bit monotonous. Some recreational facilities and a canteen were started ashore at Greenock for the ships 133

companies, and it was during this time that magnificent ship the Queen Elizabeth quietly came down the Clyde, did her trials, and sailed for America to help with the trooping and other transport problems. A magnificent ship and in her day without question the finest merchant liner afloat. What a target for a submarine. The Admiralty decided, as the event proved rightly, to sail her unescorted on the open seas and to rely on her high speed to avoid attack. A ship going at 30 knots and zigzagging presents a tremendously hard problem to a submarine with a submerged speed of 5 to 7 knots. No destroyer can screen adequately at 30 knots, for [that is] not only their top marginal speed but asdics do not work much over 20 knots. Our condenser troubles alas steadily increased, and it was soon clear that the only solution was to retube all the condensers - a job which would normally take four to six months in a modern dockyard. Careful preparations were put in hand by the dockyard of Plymouth, and as you will hear when the time came to be done the work was completed in the unbelievably short time of six weeks. An event in February livened everybody up and that was the Altmark incident in Jossing fjord in Norway, when the German supply ship was boarded by members of the crew of Cossack commanded by Captain Philip Vian. The Altmark had been the parent ship of the Graf Spee and had on board a number of prisoners taken from the crews of merchant ships sunk by her. Nearly 300 prisoners were rescued, and brought back to Rosyth in Cossack. A magnificent performance which needed the fullest support and cooperation of the Admiralty. The story has frequently been told, though perhaps minor in scale compared with the cataclysmic events to follow. It did much to benefit the morale at a rather quiet and frustrating time. A day or so after this incident the German battle cruiser attempted a sortie to interfere with our shipping convoys between Norway and the UK, and we all went to sea to take up covering positions adjacent to the Norwegian coast. The enemy did not venture far up the coast and soon set sail for home owing to the intense cold. Their large warships got stuck in the ice in the approaches to Jade, Weser and Elbe rivers, thus presenting our bomber aircraft with a heaven-sent opportunity which alas due to weather and other causes they could not take. For once in a way the day of 20th February, on which we reached our rendezvous, all the Norwegian coast was uncannily clear and by a mirage effect though over 40 miles distant, the Norwegian coast appeared as clear as anything just a few miles away over a flat calm sea. I remember Glennie turning to me as the sun rose and saying, ‘Surely they are all in there, let us have a look’. The time came for the Fleet to return now to its proper base, Scapa Flow, which is incomparably the best location from the strategical point of view. We arrived there on the 7th March to find among other things two dummy imitation battleships already anchored in the Flow. These were very realistic imitations of the Revenge class battleships and were intended to deceive the Germans, which they did for a little, but not a long time. Scapa with its extra anti-submarine nets and a further row of anti-torpedo nets was a very different place to what we had first seen. Among other things the colonies of seals which lived on Flotta had gone elsewhere. We soon settled down to a routine of practices and within 10 days of our arrival, we had our first serious air raid on the Fleet by bomber aircraft. The raid was met by our fighter defences with shore and ships A.A.[anti-aircraft] gunfire. Some of the attacking air- 134

craft were destroyed and on our side the cruiser Norfolk was hit and damaged by a bomb. This gave us some confidence in meeting attacks though special care had to be taken in marking the positions of where mines were laid by aircraft. We organised a special marking team which helped to locate precise positions of all mines laid. By this time, we had heard all the special gear required for our refit was ready at Plymouth and accordingly we went there in the last half of March. With extra manpower provided, we immediately set about the formidable task of retubing all Hood’s condensers with the latest special cupro-nickel tubes. The Admiral Superintendent and the Engineer Manager of Plymouth Dockyard were men of outstanding ability, and they programmed to do the work in 6 weeks. The opportunity was also taken at Irvine Glennie’s insistence to double up our long range anti-aircraft armament. This would give us eight twin AA 4 inch as opposed to our original four twins. Arrangements were made to give the ship’s company a good fortnight’s leave in various batches during the refit. Elizabeth came down to Plymouth and we found some digs in which to live. Ten days or so after the refit had started, we heard news of what was to prove to be the beginning of the Norwegian campaign. The history of this campaign has been frequently recounted and in no books better than Stephen Roskill’s Vol. 1 of the War at Sea. As it is now known, we had intended in a sense to forestall the German invasion of Norway though we had not the remotest idea that the Germans were planning one. It says much for German security arrangements and for our own lack of intelligence that we did not have any idea this operation was impending. The C-in-C had some doubts about our own security which were confirmed by the mining of his flagship Nelson in the approach to Loch Ewe at the end of 1939. It is only fair to say that the C-in-C might have expected some hints from intelligence sources of the invasion of Norway. The German invasion of Norway started on the 7th April and soon spread to cover the whole country. The boldness and comprehensiveness of the plan took everybody by surprise. Nobody would have guessed that virtually simultaneous attacks would have been launched on Narvik, Trondheim, Bergen and Oslo. Our Admiral was at sea flying his flag in Renown and encountered the two German battle cruisers off Narvik, who were covering the operation in bad weather and mountainous seas. In a brief encounter he got the better of the German battle cruisers who broke off the action and disappeared into the mists and rain squalls of northern latitudes. Our feelings can well be imagined. Here was the chance of showing our worth against the German battle cruisers and we were in Plymouth dockyard with our defective condenser tubes on the jetty! Feelings in the Wardroom were at boiling point. It is perhaps a moot point that if we had been in company with Renown on this occasion, it is just possible we would have crippled the German battle cruisers in their brief encounter, but again on the other hand they were a little superior in speed, and when the encounter took place had the weather gauge.36 36 ‘Had the weather gauge’ meant that ships were positioned upwind and had a tactical advantage, allowing them to choose whether to attack or not. More often used in the days of sail, WWD probably meant here that the enemy had the advantage of wind and following seas. 135

Captain Warburton Lee, who was a great personal friend of mine of long standing, fought one of the most gallant actions of the war against substantially superior forces off Narvik. He was killed in this action but inflicted very severe damage on the German forces which contributed to their virtual destruction by Warspite and other forces of the Home Fleet a little later. We could at best only be spectators and try to guess what was happening. With our command of the sea, I thought we could isolate Narvik and Trondheim areas by cutting off all communications with the south, but we had not I think fully appreciated the impact of the German Air Force in operations of this nature. We had until later virtually no air force of our own, other than that supplied by aircraft carriers, which at that time only carried aircraft suitable for working over the sea, and not for supporting land operations. Soon after this campaign started, we were asked to supply approximately 200 men to act as shore parties at Andalsness and other places where British military forces had landed. We sent these men up to Rosyth where they embarked in warships and were ferried across. Two of the watchkeepers and four midshipmen went with them. They went off in good heart and I am glad to say all returned with I think the exception of three casualties suffered in Norway. It was about this time the Admiralty asked for names of officer volunteers for especially hazardous jobs. I put my name in but never heard any more of it. May well be the volunteers were oversubscribed or in any case the Admiralty might have just liked to have a list of names of officers who would like to try their hand at anything. There was much fighting in the Norway campaign and the German Navy in light craft suffered crippling losses, one of their battle cruisers was severely damaged, their latest cruiser sank and so on. Though we were not to realise it then, this well nigh calamitous losses of the German Navy put any idea of their being able to help an invasion of this country later in the summer under Operation Sealion [German invasion plan] as being completely out of the question. We suffered substantial losses in destroyers, one cruiser sunk, but the most severe was the aircraft carrier Glorious in June, when the attention of the public was devoted to other things. It is still perhaps early days to give any final assessment of the Norwegian campaign. The German planning was very bold, but they suffered such losses as to have a permanent adverse effect on their naval operations. They achieved their object in occupying Norway and having as it were the northern flank of Europe under their control! How did we fare? Firstly, our plans were a good deal too ad hoc. Far too much intervention by the Admiralty who virtually took charge of certain operations instead of leaving it to the C-in-C. Both the First Sea Lord and First Lord must be held accountable here. It is always tempting when as sometimes happens you have, as you think, more up to date intelligence to intervene. As ‘juniors’ later at the Admiralty, I and others have remonstrated against this tendency. Far more often than not Admiral Forbes’s plans were right, but I think it fair to say an almost disproportionate amount of ill luck attended them. There was a lack of appreciation among the Chiefs of Staff of the conditions of modern amphibious warfare. Insufficient regard then was paid to the air element, as in later times too much regard was paid to this and caused us perhaps to be over cautious. 136

There were indeed very few failures at command level of units of the Fleet. The Army was very inexperienced, not only in the sort of mountain warfare required in Norway but also in amphibious operations. We in the Navy thought they were too rigid in outlook and too anxious to preserve their administrative tail, regardless of what might happen to the fighting end. Though the Germans achieved their main aim, it was possible to rescue the King, the gold reserves of the country and a nucleus of Norwegians, who did so much to keep alight the resistance to the invaders, and prepare for the time when the country would again be reoccupied by their own troops. A study of the Norwegian campaign will always repay the reader, for it was not really appreciated perhaps until then, that the exercise of the command of the sea can only be fully achieved if a measure of command of the air over the sea is also achieved. In the Norwegian campaign we seldom had any measure of command of the air, either over the land where our soldiers were fighting or the adjacent seas. We suffered heavy maritime casualties for this lack of cover. To turn back to Plymouth, everything was done to speed up work on the Hood. Elizabeth and I visited Mulgrave for the 7th to 10th of May when further important events were about to start. Oswald was in Germany [France] with his regiment and from what Lady Normanby told us in very good heart.37 The Hood was still at Plymouth nearing completion and we felt a little bit out of it with the Home Fleet fully engaged in the Norwegian campaign. It would, I think, be appropriate to sum up a little later what we felt about this campaign at the time, but what perhaps is now a measure of hindsight - what we now know. There was a feeling that the Norwegian campaign was a little more than a prelude to what was about to happen. I think some of us thought it would be a massive attack on France through Belgium to coincide with an Italian declaration of war and attacks on France, or as it were on two fronts, thus ensuring their rapid collapse. News came through in the early hours of the 10th as we were about to return to Plymouth of the German attack on Holland. It seemed all very confused this blitzkrieg type of war, and one could not but regard the outcome, having knowledge of the strength of opposing forces, with much concern. I think I heard some say ‘Holland won’t last more than a few days’. How right they were for in three days the Dutch resistance was broken, and in five days the Dutch Army surrendered. This change in events caused immediate redisposition of naval forces. The decision to evacuate Norway was taken by the Cabinet and substantial naval forces were stationed in the southern end of the North Sea. The evacuation of Norway was not however completed until June concerning which I will comment on later. It was clear on the 10th and 11th of May 37 WWD is mistaken here, the Green Howards were not in Germany, and some repetition about leave at Mulgrave has been omitted. 137

The original caption to this photo, that the main German offensive had started. The centre of the French army in the Ardennes which was the frontispiece of a appeared to have collapsed. But again I think some of us thought of our reverses in March pamphlet written by WWD after 1917 in France when we retrieved our position, and guessed and hoped it would soon be the sinking of the Hood, read ‘If put right. I do not think any of us had any idea of the speed of advances made possible by anything looks right it is right’ modern tanks and close support aircraft. It began however to dawn on us, as we heard of (Sinbad). The long clean lines of advances of up to 50 and 60 miles a day with tank spearheads going even further. Hood made her one of the most admired of British ships. By the third week of May Hood was completed at Plymouth and we busily prepared ourselves for sea. As at that time no dry dock was available at Plymouth for Hood, it was decided we should be docked in the Gladstone Dock at Liverpool as soon as possible. Our extra AA armament of some 16 x 4 inch guns all looked impressive and gave us confidence that we should render a good account of ourselves. The news continued to be disastrous. By about the 20th May or soon afterwards it was becoming apparent the British Armies in the north and the French Armies in the south had been separated by the German drive. Even to us who only heard reports from the newspapers and other sources the possibility of the destruction of a major part of the British Army in France became a distinct possibility. I remember some of the staff examples on which we had worked on my staff course in 1931. As far as I remember we reckoned that in the most extreme emergency with the greatest of luck and little interference from the air, we could not expect even to evacuate more than about 10,000 a day. I wondered knowing we had well over a quarter of a million men in France whether we should be allowed some three weeks or so for an unimpeded evacuation. Little did one guess that when the crunch came at the end of the month and in early June, this figure for daily evacuation would be multiplied by about six. As the official history records, in the event at Dunkirk it was hoped to evacuate about 45,000 men, and in fact in fact we evacuated 338,000 odd. But another point which I discussed with Glennie and others was how we could get by with the whole coast of France in German hands, with many bases near our trade routes from which their submarines and surface ships could operate. It has been said perhaps in rather 138

different contexts at the Staff College, that as a result of our submarine experiences in 1917 and 1918 it would be beyond our resources to sustain this country’s war effort and food under these circumstances. This was I think the view held in some of the Admiralty staff divisions before the war, and was a contributory cause in stressing the vital importance of keeping France on her feet in any European war. But as the days passed it was clear that France would soon follow the way of Holland and Belgium and would shortly surrender. What were our feelings then? I must confess with a fairly tolerable knowledge of the strategic implications one could not help feeling we were in just as perilous position as when Napoleon was at the height of his power. The lower deck was an encouragingly robust space - when talking to the Master at Arms and the Sergeant Major one day after rounds, I asked him what the feeling of the lower deck was to these catastrophes. They both said in words to the effect ‘the ship’s company reckons we are better off without these ‘continentals’, and can see now who is the better man, ‘Itler or us’. I believe that this was the basic feeling which ran through most of our countrymen. I sometimes wished I had not done so much staff work and did not realise the quite appalling difficulties which now faced our country. It is no purpose of these random notes to describe the course of military events in these never to be forgotten weeks. We were extremely fortunate in the weather for the Dunkirk evacuation as indeed for the other operations at Dutch and Belgian ports. But it was our control of the seas that made it possible to rescue so much of what mattered and to put heart in the brave men and women of the countries overrun by the Germans. That we and in particular the Navy were made of stern stuff, and would in due course return to set them free. But perhaps we should return to the Norwegian campaign which would be wound up by our final evacuation from Narvik in the middle of June. As we all know one of our most serious losses was suffered here in the loss of the aircraft carrier Glorious which with her two escorts was sunk by the battle cruisers, Gniesenau and Scharnhorst, when almost within the Arctic Circle. What of the German side of this campaign? They achieved their end, they safeguarded their iron ore supplies from Narvik, they controlled the whole Norwegian seaboard. They did this but at a tremendous naval price to themselves. The cream of the German light forces had been destroyed or damaged, their heavy ships had been so damaged as to be unable to take any active part in the important campaign in 1940. From our point of view some serious defects became apparent as summarised so ably in Vol 1 of The Naval War by Stephen Roskill. There was too much interference from the Admiralty. Admiral Forbes’ judgement was more often right than not. He had by then fully appreciated the limitations imposed on control of the seas by aircraft. The British ships had proved themselves in fighting spirit and endeavour more than a match for the Germans. Admiral Sir Charles Forbes was not however very fortunate, on more than one occasion he missed by a proverbial hair’s breadth scoring a resounding naval success over the Germans. Among some folk in the Fleet, he had an unfortunate nickname of ‘Wrong Way Charlie’. There is little doubt much of the interference, or better still intervention, in maritime operations was prompted by that powerful personality, Winston Churchill, first as First Lord and then as Prime Minister. This is never a case on which one can dogmatise, but the historian will I 139

believe come to the conclusion that the efficiency and conduct of naval operations in this campaign was on more than one occasion prejudiced by Admiralty intervention. Admiral Pound, the First Sea Lord was inclined to intervene too frequently, but more of this later when I saw a close hand how the central direction of the naval war worked. Though perhaps not appreciated at the time, the mounting toll of our merchant ship losses gave more than a passing cause for concern during the months of March onwards in 1940. Having finished our refit we soon went to sea for exercises and shaking down. There was a feeling that we must get to grips with the enemy with little delay! As already mentioned early in June we went to Liverpool for docking and certain underwater repairs, also the fitting of the latest degaussing equipment. This is the time Italy entered the war and I remember the evident joy of the waiters in the Adelphi Hotel where Elizabeth had come to stay for a few days, and where the excellent head waiter, an Italian, was arrested and taken off to an internment camp! The collapse of the French took place in the middle of June just after the Italians had entered the war. Marshall Petain asked for an Armistice on the 17th of June and five days later what amounted to a virtual surrender was signed. After working up at Scapa we were informed that we were to be the Flagship of a special force, known as Force H, based on Gibraltar and commanded by Admiral Somerville. This force consisted of the carrier Ark Royal, and a number of escort destroyers, and cruiser Sheffield. We were delighted at the thought as we guessed, rightly as it happened, that there would be much naval activity in the Mediterranean. Force H, an independent command, was as it were to act as a stopper to the Mediterranean, and be available to work in the central Atlantic. Everybody knew that with James Somerville as he was affectionately known, we would not have a dull time. The problem of the French surrender had posed fairly formidable ones to the Admiralty. The surrender stated that the French fleet were to be demilitarised under German and Italian control. Admiral Darlan, the French Commander-in-Chief and later Minister of Marine and finally French Prime Minister, had stated that the ships would not be surrendered to the Germans and would not be used against us! This was in flat contradiction to the Armistice terms signed by Marshal Petain. The main part of the French Navy had concentrated at Oran perhaps so as to be out of the reach of the Germans. Many British naval officers knew Admiral Darlan, an officer of great ability who was said alas to be rather an Anglophobe. Admiral Pound was never on very friendly terms with him though with some of the French Admirals we had very cordial relations. We arrived at Gibraltar on the 23rd of June in company with Ark Royal, and much enjoyed being there. Admiral Somerville who joined us at the end of the month was rightly very critical of the defences of Gibraltar which in all spheres needed gingering up. It would be fair to say that up to this stage the war was rather a distant phenomenon and had not perhaps greatly affected the way of thinking of many of the residents. They were soon to be rudely shocked out of their complacency. Force H formed at Gibraltar consisting of ourselves, Ark Royal, Valiant and Resolution, the cruiser Arethusa and some destroyers. 140

But let us meet James Somerville, our new C-in-C. James Somerville came from a family who had served many generations in the Navy. He was a clever and very quick-witted man with an Irishman’s sense of humour, though he was not I think an Irishman by birth. Originally a torpedo specialist he pioneered much of the introduction of what was in his time modern wireless equipment in the Navy. He had a very quick wit indeed and was worshipped by the sailors for he never stood on form and got down to brass tacks on any point with a minimum of delay and maximum of wit. There are many stories still told about him when he was Commander of one of the Iron Duke class battleships in the Mediterranean just after the First War. He kept a tame bear as a pet on board and this bear used at times to swim over to other ships and cause consternation on board! James Somerville was a great personal friend of Andrew Cunningham and it was perhaps appropriate that Andrew commanded the force in the Eastern end whilst James commanded Force H which looked after both the Western end of the Mediterranean, and also the approaches of the Atlantic to the Straits of Gibraltar. James Somerville’s previous command was Commander-in-Chief of the East Indies before the war, from which station he was invalided home with suspected TB. There was a tremendous argument about it as James Somerville disputed that he had TB. Nevertheless, the medical profession is a strong union and James was invalided out of the Navy. However, with the outbreak of war and armed with a Harley Street certificate that he was clear of TB, James came back and was given a number of important jobs before he was allotted the job of being in command of Force H, whose composition we have already given. James Somerville was later to be my Commander-in-Chief in the Eastern Fleet whose headquarters was at Mombasa, was young and youthful in appearance. A great devotee of physical fitness, his first request to me was to provide him with a skiff so that when in harbour he could go for a row before breakfast! A restless and inquiring mind, he was not easily put off what he wished to achieve, and woe betide the officer or man who tried to pull the wool over his eyes. But one of the liveliest intelligences I have met in the Navy. A formidable debater with a sense of the ridiculous, pretty ruthless and those who did not measure up to his own standards got short shrift. James Somerville was one of our great Admirals in the war, with as shrewd and cool a judgement as one could hope for in any circumstances. A very pleasant man to meet who backed his subordinates to the hilt when the need arose. He had some passages of arms with the Prime Minister on later occasions when some of his actions were called into question. The electrical effect of James Somerville’s personality was immediately apparent. Everybody seemed to get on their toes. Maybe they did not wish to experience the effect of his mordant wit! It was clear soon after his arrival that something to do with the French Fleet was afoot. It was thought paramount to our safety and future conduct of the war that the French Fleet, which was superior in numbers to the German fleet, should not pass under German control. With great skill and determination Admiral Cunningham persuaded the French Admiral Godfroi to immobilise his ships at Alexandria. But it was not possible to achieve this with the French Admiral Gensoul with the main fleet at Oran This has been recounted in many 141

books but suffice to say that Admiral Gensoul was given the alternative of bringing his Fleet out and join us, demilitarise his Fleet, or sail to any French West Indian port. Failing all these solutions being acceptable, the French Fleet was to be destroyed. To get back to Force H, we sailed on I think the 2nd July to present these alternatives to the French Admiral. The British Force consisting of four capital ships, cruisers and a flotilla of destroyers sailed for Oran. Glennie discussed with me the heart searching instructions given to Admiral Somerville. We could not somehow believe that we would be called upon to open fire on our late allies and I certainly thought some compromise would be reached. I kept the ships company informed broadly speaking of the course of events. Ships were at action stations. Still somehow everybody believed we should settle matters without opening fire throughout that long day. Events drew to a climax. The British force steamed up and down opposite Oran harbour, cleared for action, and finally after some abortive negotiations which Captain Holland (exnaval attaché, Paris) conducted with Admiral Gensoul, Admiral Somerville warned the French Admiral that he would open fire if the French did not accept the alternatives by 5:30 p.m. I still believed and I think so did many others that some solution would be found. We could not imagine harming the ships in harbour which were in a sense ‘sitting birds’. This went tremendously against the grain. Just before 6:00 p.m. the Captain told me to broadcast from my action station in the lower conning tower that we are about to open fire on the French Fleet, which we did a few minutes later. All French ships were destroyed or heavily damaged with the exception of the battle cruiser Strasbourg, and some French destroyers which escaped in the gathering dusk, so in a sense Admiral Somerville did not fully achieve the Cabinet’s directions. The loss of life on the French side was very heavy for the Bretagne blew up. To say that carrying out these instructions were done with horror and at times some incredulity was understating the case. As we returned to harbour people were silent and just would not talk to anybody. Both Glennie and Somerville looked terribly distressed. They felt that left with a little time they could, as Admiral Cunningham did in Alexandria, have reached some form of arrangement which would not have had to resolve to the extreme measures taken. The bitterness in the French Navy was extreme and a few days later Admiral Somerville received from the French fleet all British decorations which had been bestowed on French officers. Even in the cool knowledge of hindsight it is difficult to say whether or not we were right to take this action which was distasteful in the extreme to every British officer. On the whole I believe it was wrong now, as I did at the time, for I think some accommodation could eventually have been reached with the French. And when the time came for us to land in North Africa 2 ½ years later we would have met with no resistance. Furthermore, I think this action on our part brought out a latent dislike of the French for us and in some sense rallied defeated forces behind Petain. Serving officers have at times most distasteful and distressing things to do. Few actions could have been more distasteful than that carried out by Admiral Somerville.38 38 Rodger, pp.408-09; he notes that Cunningham succeeded by appealing to the ships’ captains and companies over the head of the French admiral. He also notes that the destruction of the French fleet at Oran 142 convinced the Americans that Britain would fight, and Roosevelt therefore provided much needed equipment.

Our time at Gibraltar was very busy. French aircraft from Algeria or Morocco in retaliation for our attack on their Fleet attacked Gibraltar one night. They did little damage and one aircraft was alleged to have been shot down. The anti-aircraft guns of the Fleet seemed to put up the most effective opposition to raiders. The static AA defences of Gibraltar were out of date and pretty ineffective. Then a few French aircraft carrying Frenchmen who wished to join up with the Free French and continue the fight against the Germans flew in to the airfield on the North Front. Some refugee ships who had escaped with British nationals and Frenchmen who wanted to join de Gaulle came from the south of France and we above: Seized French Warships met one or two retired ex British naval officers. News cutting, July 6th 1940. K. Phipps cuttings album. France was making many hostile speeches and though Spain was still in an appalling state after their civil war, it was possible if not probable that that they might come in against us. Sir Samuel Hoare, our ambassador in Madrid, visited Admiral Somerville on board Hood one day. The Admiral who took a robust view of our chances against the Germans found Sir Samuel somewhat depressing. There was at that time a strong German military mission in Spain, busy installing some siege guns capable of firing at Gibraltar and hampering ships in passage through the Straits of Gibraltar. We plotted out the position of these heavy siege batteries and worked out as far as we could methods of firing at them from the big battleships including ourselves in harbour. The trouble was our guns being high velocity flat trajectory guns could not get at gun’s emplacements sited in the folds of the Hills. The Frontier post at La Linea was of course closed to all men in uniform so there was no chance of renewing acquaintance with those many lovely places in the cork woods and near Algeciras. Much work was going on extending the airfield which just over two years later housed all our aircraft destined for the attack on North Africa, with a runway twice the length we had in 1940. About a week or so after Oran, Admiral Somerville took the Fleet to sea, three battleships (Hood, Valiant and Resolution), the aircraft carrier Ark Royal, the cruisers Sheffield and Penelope, and some destroyers of the F class for a sweep in the western Mediterranean to impress upon the Italian Navy, as Admiral Somerville observed, that the Mediterranean was ‘No Mare Nostrum’ of theirs! We had the cruiser Sheffield fitted with the latest air detection radar equipment. Judged by modern day standards this was very much of a bow and arrow equipment, but we got ample warning and the broadcast such as ‘two enemy formations of aircraft about 20 in each formation approaching the Fleet from a direction say 0.90 degrees’ became commonplace. We swept towards Cape Bon [northeast Libya] and found no Italian warships nor for that matter any merchant ships about. The aircraft attacks which seemed to concentrate a bit on Hood perhaps because she was the largest target were carried out in formation from a height of about 15,000 feet. Rather frightening as we heard the bombs whistle down, though we 143

had quite a number of near misses, none hit us. When walking around the upper deck amidships where the anti-aircraft guns were in action, I remember nearly having a fit finding one of the supply hatches to the magazine wide open. When I recovered my breath, I asked the captain of the gun how long he thought he would take to get to the nether regions for which he was destined if a bomb went down the open hatch and exploded in the magazine! Life at sea was never dull. A submarine attack was carried out on us in the approaches to the Straits of Gibraltar, but did not succeed though later one of our destroyers was sunk by a torpedo. Perhaps above all the sunshine and warmth did more than anything else, and again we knew we had one of the finest fighting Admirals in the Navy commanding our force. I saw a little of Peter Reid (the Commander) and Bernard Rawlings (the Captain of Valiant). Both splendid officers. Rawlings was promoted to Admiral a few months later and became one of Andrew Cunningham’s stalwarts in the eastern Mediterranean and after that a most successful Force Commander in the Pacific. He had been our instructor Commander in Vernon when I qualified in 1926. A man with a great sense of humour and a discerning eye for what are the important things and what are the trivia of life in the Navy. Admiral Somerville came and dined in the wardroom one night in the harbour and by the time the evening was finished we thought he could hold his own with the youngest and most athletic member of the mess. I always found him great fun and listening to what he called his light-hearted talk when walking up and down the quarter deck, there were shafts of insight and great wisdom. He was tough and hard and could be quite ruthless with anybody who through idleness or faults of his own making did not measure up to the standards he required. At the same time, as we were busy in the western Mediterranean, a somewhat abortive if gallant attempt was made by the aircraft carrier Hermes and cruisers Dorsetshire and Australia to disable the latest French battleship Richelieu in Dakar. My good friend, Robin Durnford Slater who was Commander of the Hermes took part in this operation. Towards the end of July or beginning of August it was found one of the guns of B turret had become cracked, probably due to a defective driving band or some other cause during the Oran bombardment, and it was decided we should be replaced by Renown and returned to Rosyth to have the gun changed. After stopping at Scapa Flow, we went to Rosyth and rehoisted Admiral Whitworth’s flag. I think everybody in the wardroom was mighty sad to leave Gibraltar with Admiral Somerville’s force, but from a technical and tactical point of view Renown was a better escort for Ark Royal than we were. She was, since modernised, a bit faster but above all had very nearly twice our endurance at sea for her boilers were far more economic in oil fuel than our old-fashioned ones. We went to Rosyth and spent I think five days in the dry dock there where there was the only crane available which could lift one of our 15 inch guns out and replace it with a new one. Elizabeth came up to South Queensferry and stayed I think at the Hawes Inn for a few days. The work was soon finished and we went out into the stream and anchored below the Firth Bridge. During this time, we heard much of the intended invasion of Great Britain and in mid- August the Luftwaffe launched their attacks on us and were met by Fighter Command of 144

the RAF. In view of the fact the conditions were likely to be critical and as yet we were unaware of the effects of wholesale bombing, it was decided to take advantage of the offer by our old Phipps cousins in Toronto, Canada, to provide a temporary home for Georgina and Johnny and old Nanny. Accordingly, the arrangements were made in July and they sailed for Canada where they were splendidly looked after.39 It was a tremendous wrench for Elizabeth to part with the children, and we discussed this many times, but at that time I had some doubts whether the RAF would in the first instance hold the Luftwaffe.40 I foresaw grave food shortages for our shipping losses had gone up at an astronomical rate, and much disruption of life here due to bombing. As it happens, my decision was wrong and we should have kept the children with us! Hindsight is easy but in those days there were many unknowns. Furthermore, the disappearance of Oswald gave Lady Normanby great anxieties. It was known he was wounded in France but not how badly and in the evacuation, he and others had been left behind in a hospital near Dunkirk. This was a time of very great anxiety for Lady Normanby and Elizabeth, and it was not until well on in above: the Autumn when the Battle of Britain was over that we heard Oswald was a prisoner of First page of letter written from HMS war.
