At this time Georgina was nearly 5 and Johnnie just over 2 years old. The letters were in the event never given to the children and after her death, they were found in Elizabeth’s jewellery box. 40 It is hard to imagine what led our parents to the decision to send the children away with Elizabeth remaining behind. Did she feel she could not abandon her mother when her own brother was missing? Did they fear the country was going to be overrun with tremendous loss of life? There is an underlying tone of desperation in the letters. Or did she feel that she simply could not leave her husband? She adored WWD, as she wrote, ‘His bright life will always influence you, and his steadiness. He is like a rock, and his smile is bright and makes one’s heart leap.’ 145

was right and others wrong, for Admiral Forbes foresaw at the end of September that invasion was simply not on, an opinion not shared by others until many months later. Well, the Battle of Britain had started in mid-August, and we were cheered by the first communiques which gave heavy losses to the Germans and light ones to ours. I think some of us had a little suspicion of the proverbial optimism of the RAF. Nevertheless, even halving our claimed ratio of success it was clear to us that the Germans were not succeeding. The skill and excellence of our Hurricane and Spitfire pilots and their aircraft evoked the admiration of every serving officer in the Navy. This battle went on throughout the remainder of August and into September. The story has often been told and in some respects, it was a closer thing than people realised at the time. But the German Air Force took a beating from which they never fully recovered and, above all what with Winston Churchill’s speeches, the admiration of the civilised world was showered upon us. It was perhaps before many of his countrymen that the American President came to realise that we would pull through, and that every help short of war should be given to us. At the beginning of September Glennie sent from me and told that I was required for a special planning job at the Admiralty and was to be relieved soon. My feelings to put it mildly were one of acute disappointment. The thought of leaving one of the finest seagoing fighting ships for an office chair in Whitehall was hard to contemplate. However, there it was. Glennie was kind enough to say he had done everything possible to avoid this. ‘Tubby’ Cross, a commander in Operations Division with a good record in Submarines was to relieve me, and in mid-September he joined Hood at Rosyth to take over. The turnover was soon completed. The Wardroom dined me the night before I left and what perhaps touched me more than most things was to see the old Master at Arms, Sergeant Major and others come onto the upper deck with a goodly proportion of Hood’s ships company after the midday meal, when all might have been sleeping on their half day, to give me a rousing cheer and send off as I left in our picket boat. I had been lucky having spent 20 months in one of the finest and happiest ships afloat, the last 12 months being while we were at war. Fortunately, it is not given to us to have prevision so I did not realise as I waved goodbye that most of the ships company and Wardroom would be lost just over seven months later. After leaving the ship I spent the afternoon in Edinburgh and walked down Princes Street which looked as beautiful as ever and wondered if this city would be subject to bombing attacks. I took the night train down to Kings Cross from Waverley Station. All trains were fully darkened and there was insufficient light to do much reading after sunset. On arrival in London next morning, I took a look around before calling on Captain Daniel, the Director of Plans, to find out what my job was to be, but more of this later. After the bombing and reports one somehow expected to find large areas of London laid flat, but in fact rather the reverse was the case. There were just here and there destroyed and damaged houses but the very great majority of the houses seemed undamaged. London did not at that time look thoroughly scruffy as it did later. People seem to be going about their business as usual. Occasionally one heard the distant ‘crump’ of a bomb possibly being exploded by one of the 146

squads whose job it was to destroy unexploded bombs. The underground stations looked a bit dirty and were rather fusty for many people used to spend the night and sleep down there, and at nights one had to step carefully over the recumbent ‘corpses’. But certainly, from the porters and ticket collectors at the station there was an atmosphere of ‘We can take it chum - one day ’itler is going to be sorry he ever took us on.’ I then had the problem of finding somewhere to live and it was evident that these modern flats made with steel and concrete frameworks withstood bomb blast and shock much better than the older buildings, however massive they were. I remember seeing some figures in an official paper about resistance factors to bomb blast which made me convinced that a good modern building with plenty of stories above me was about as safe as it was possible to achieve. Furthermore, one could sleep well at night knowing one had taken every practical precaution and did not feel it was necessary to go to sleep in the basement, which in fact seldom was any safer than on the ground floor. I found plenty of flats vacant and for a very modest sum took a flat in Nell Gwynne House, a modern block just off Sloane Avenue in Chelsea. My flat was on the ground floor and in a sort of well with seven or eight stories above me. Apart from the fact one seldom got much daylight, it was a pleasant little flat where one could have a camp bed for Elizabeth when she came to stay. I looked in at my Club, the United Services, which was full of people; many old Admirals and Generals were there in uniform offering their services in any capacity. I then went into the Admiralty which at that time had not yet been hit and saw the Director of Plans, Captain Charles Daniel, who I’d last seen as Captain ‘D’ in the Home Fleet in a Destroyer Flotilla. He was one of the Commanders in my Staff Course in 1931 so we knew each other well. A very clever and able officer indeed with as quick a brain as I have ever met. He had been made Director of Plans about six months previously when there had been a bit of a purge in the Plans Division. The Director, Captain Danckwerts, and Deputy Director, Captain Edelsten, had been moved on as the First Lord thought perhaps they were not flexible enough. Winston Churchill did not tolerate what he considered to be obstruction, but nobody could deny these two officers were both first class brains with a great intellectual grasp. However, Danckwerts had been ill and Edelsten had been due for a sea job so they were moved on and replaced by Charles Daniels and [Captain Edward Gerald] Bellars as Deputy. A good team. I suspect Danckwerts who had a very mordant tongue and used it perhaps too freely for his views, however sound, to gain general acceptance. He was our Gunnery Officer in HMS Neptune when I first went to sea, and I still remember being told ‘Young man. you have not come to this ship to think, you are here to do what you are told’. However, even in these days he was always worth listening to, as he had an imaginative and well-ordered brain. To get back to Charles Daniel, a first-rate Director of Plans, with a very fine team of commanders under him. The most able being perhaps Commander Griffiths who was lost in ‘Bermuda’ later in the war.41 Griffiths would I think put a view better than any Commander I know. Everybody, from the First Sea Lord downwards would always listen to him. Charles 41 It is not clear who this refers to, or to what ship 147

Daniel himself had a very well-balanced intellect. was slightly portly with an amusing twinkle in his eye.Very quick in debate, I always thought he was one of the best debaters of our Staff Course in 1931. His views on the correct maritime strategy to be adopted were clear and right. He had enough sea experience already in the war to be able to assess perhaps more clearly than others what was and what was not practical. Tom Phillips, the Vice Chief of Naval Staff had a high opinion of him, and relished meeting somebody who was as quick witted as he was himself. And Gerald Bellars, the Deputy, was a good foil to Charles Daniel. Very able in the technical sphere, he had invented some outstandingly successful bits of gunnery equipment. He had not however the width of view of Charles Daniel, nor was he always very patient in explaining a point of view to people he regarded, probably rightly, as his intellectual inferior. Having expressed some sadness about leaving the active fleet, when we might at any moment called upon to throw back an invasion attempt on this island, I asked what my job was to be. It appeared that the Prime Minister wished to have somebody to examine and above all to propose future operations, offensive operations, etc. etc. to him! In other words, he made it clear he regarded at times the existing planners the champions of Negation and he was determined to circumvent this! However. that splendid wise man, Pug Ismay, Military Secretary to the Chiefs of Staff, saw how an organisation like this might be made to work and to work most usefully. There was already one section in the Joint Planning Staff which worked under the joint Directors of Plans, and which lived and did their business in a basement near the Cabinet offices. Accordingly a Future Operational Planning Section was set up within the framework of the Joint Planning Staff. Winston thought that this was his section to report directly to him, so that he could spur the Chiefs of Staff onto more vigorous action! However, Ismay arranged the reports of this section should be vetted and seen first by the Directors of Plans themselves, and then by the Chief of Staff before the Prime Minister received his copy! Our chairman was Oliver Stanley, late Secretary of State for War. The three service representatives were Charles Lambe (Navy), Brigadier Guetterbock (Army), and Group Captain Yool (RAF); then the working staff were Robertshaw and self (Navy), Bourne and Heyman (Army), Gilmore and another RAF Wing Commander (RAF). Our terms of reference were to prepare plans for operations which would be ordered as and when the occasion demanded. We would be housed somewhere where we could work unimpeded and I think the Prime Minister hoped for a steady stream of plans which he could approve. But it was not just as easy as all that. Every plan had in a sense to fit in with the overall strategical policy. It has to be costed, after all the ways and means must be available to carry it out, and so on. The Section was however a useful adjunct to the war planning machinery, for the three main planning sections wete the Strategical Planning Section (Bill Andrews) as the Naval Head, the Future Operational Planning Section with Charles Lambe as the Naval Head, and the Executive Planning Section whose job it was to provide the wherewithal and find the means with Charles Hughes Hallett as head to carry out the approved plan. In other words, they had to give to the Force Commander, whose job it was to prepare the final plan, something which was a workable 148

proposition. The intelligence side had a similar sort of organisation for intelligence played a vital part in the preparation of all plans. This then was the setup. Obviously very interesting, but who would not rather have been at sea to meet the enemy in person! After spending a night or so in London I went up to Mulgrave where Elizabeth was with her mother. A very pleasant week’s leave. I was given Oswald’s bicycle which was to come in most useful later in London. As far as I remember Lady Normanby had not yet heard that Oswald was safe and a prisoner of war. I got in touch with Captain Tennant who was one of the beach masters for the evacuation at Dunkirk and it was clear from this and other inquiries that he had been left in hospital with other wounded on the outskirts of Dunkirk. We had every reason to hope that he would be all right as the Germans abided by the Geneva Convention, but it was most distressing not having news of him and how badly he was wounded.42 Mulgrave was properly prepared for invasion though it was recognised that if invasion came it would be in the south. However, with stories of possible parachute landings all hands were mustered and with the firearms in the ‘armoury’, or better still the gun room at Mulgrave, a good account would be taken of any intruders who arrived by air. We used to listen eagerly to the reports of the air battles over London and the South Coast and when I was in London, I heard of tremendous damage done in the docks, mostly by fire. It soon became apparent that the fire resulting from bomb damage was far in the way a greater hazard than the bomb damage itself. At this stage of the air battle, September 1940, the bombing attacks which were mostly directed on London were in daylight raids. One diversionary raid was carried out against Newcastle or some northeast coast port which proved a disastrous failure for the Germans. Thanks to good radar warning and prompt action by defending ‘fighter squadrons’ which were resting from service in the south, practically the entire German bomber force was shot down into the sea before they reached their targets. A very pleasant week’s holiday, though with one of the decisive battles of the war being fought over London and the southern countries, one felt hardly justified taking a holiday at all. We had heard good news from old Nanny and the children who were settling down in Toronto under the watchful eye of Elizabeth’s Phipps relatives. He [Albert Phipps] was the much respective respected president of the Imperial Bank of Canada and [of] his two sons, Norman Phipps was serving in the Canadian Army whilst the other, Geoffrey, was running a large ammunition factory outside Toronto. It was a lovely early autumn. Cloudless days most days and we went for many walks in the neighbourhood. Our little car was stored at Mulgrave and we did not use it at all as petrol was severely rationed. We saw old Lionel Foster at Egton and various friends around. Rationing was fairly strict, however we could supplement to a certain extent from the Home Farm. Lady Normanby was in splendid heart and despite occasional fits of depression, as confident of the eventual result of the war and set an example to all the neighbourhood in helping the war effort and keeping our spirits up. 42 At this stage of the war there was no sense that Germany did not abide by the Geneva Convention 149

Then splendid speeches by Winston Churchill did much to keep everybody in fine spirits. We went for some bicycle rides and soon found Lythe Bank, and other pitches were a trifle steep for my liking! The time came for me to go to London and take up the appointment. Though I was sorry to leave Elizabeth at Mulgrave, I was glad to get back in a sense to the frontline where there was evident a feeling of exhilaration. Fortunately for me, Elizabeth soon followed me to London where we shared our little one room flat together. We had a few false alarms about invasions which never came off, but which certainly kept everybody on their toes. Our section immediately got underway with a number of plans, our first job being to get the intelligence organised. This seemed a good deal more complete than I had been led to believe, and apart from failures in the first two years of the war on the operational intelligence side, I do not rate our intelligence as hopelessly inadequate as some sensational writers would lead their readers to believe. Let us look again at the personalities of the Operational Planning Section and see where we stood. Colonel Oliver Stanley, our head was first rate, a very well-balanced mind. Quick to see our arguments and not obsessed by any theories of how war should be conducted. He had a ready turn of wit and might well have succeeded Anthony Eden as Prime Minister, but alas rather suddenly in the early 1950s died from I think heart trouble. He was the ideal head of a section like this, always ready to look at new ideas and concepts ‘de novo’, a correct idea of the roles of the Navy, Army and Air Force, and above all the realisation of the political influence which must influence all military operations. He saw the importance of the correct functioning of the Chiefs of Staff machinery and was a friend of Pug Ismay, whose job it was to see the processes worked smoothly and efficiently. Not always an easy task with such an unorthodox man as our Prime Minister. Oliver Stanley in appearance looked perhaps more like a very smart Colonel in the Household Brigade, rather than a one-time Cabinet Minister. One of the most charming and pleasant people I have ever met. Then the three heads of sections were Charles Lambe (Navy), Brigadier Gueterbrock (Army), Air Commodore Yool (RAF). Charles Lambe, an old friend of mine since I suppose 1926 when we were both in Vernon together qualifying as torpedo men, was quite outstanding. He had just come back from Commanding a ‘D’ class Cruiser. If there is an opportunity later, I will give a fuller assessment of Charles Lambe, but at this stage it was clear he was head and shoulders above anybody else. Gueterbock, perhaps rather an over precise Army staff officer. Nevertheless, a very competent organiser and staff officer in the best Camberley tradition.43 Quick with his work and who never let us forget that the Army moves on its administrative tail, and that if provision is not made for this, it will come to a halt overnight. Intelligent and within a limited sphere imaginative, a highly professional officer of much administrative skill, he was in every way an admirable counterpart and cooperator with Charles Lambe. Before joining he had been in an air crash when he was on his way to be the Army Chief of Staff in the Narvik campaign, and was just passed fit for service again when he joined us. William Yool, the airman was in a sense rather a misfit in this section. Though 43 Canberley was the site of the Army Staff College until 1997. 150

very earnest and extremely painstaking with detail, he was so obsessed with the extreme interpretation of Lord Trenchard’s gospels that he could never see that all the operations must be joint, and that in many cases the air component could only play a very minor part. He so often situated the appreciation by putting the cart before the horse. Starting with the premise that the air component is all important and could do pretty well everything unaided, he tried to make the operation fit his concept. He was a trial at the time to Lambe and Gueterbock. He should not have been appointed to this post as by no stretch of imagination was he up to the original thinking required in a section like this. Then our two army majors were outstanding. Slim Heyman, whose girth was I suspect above General Montgomery’s limit. One of the best draughtsmen I have ever met. Original and unorthodox ideas, a bit of a rebel against the military hierarchy with perhaps a rather too keenly critical tongue. He became a Major General and did well in the war, but died some years ago after holding an important post in the Road Traffic Research Department. Geoff Bourne, one armed having lost an arm in a skiing accident, was a very good practical soldier with a flair for political issues. Not quite such a brilliant draughtsman as Slim Hayman, these two nevertheless somewhat overshadowed their chief Gueterbock in military ability and outlook. Bourne had a distinguished war record after outstanding service in Malaya as Director of Military Operations, and in Berlin as Military Commandant where he proved more than a match for his Russian counterpart. He became the Commandant of the Imperial Defence College and was eventually for this and other services made a Life Peer. On the naval side Robertshaw was my opposite number. A sound perhaps a little pedestrian navigator. He was excellent at analysing and directing the intelligence available. Then of our airmen, Wing Commander Gilmore had a very balanced view of the possibilities and above all limitations of aircraft. He was an excellent collaborator and produced many valuable ideas in our deliberations. In a sense he provided the balanced air view which his Chief Yool could not. Then the other Air Force officer was a Stores Officer who concentrated on the supply aspect ‘aircraft wise’ of our problem. Among the G2s,44 we were I think a good team, I found Slim Heyman and to a lesser extent Geoff Bourne were superlatively good at translating our ideas to paper and serving them up in an attractive way. We first of all rather camped out in some offices in Storeys Gate and moved shortly over to some rather nice ones in that fine old terrace in Whitehall known as Richmond Terrace, since alas demolished. One or two bombs had before our arrival landed on Whitehall which had done neither the plaster nor the windows any good. But we soon set about and made ourselves comfortable. The six G2s worked in one big room with a special chair for the Intelligence man, a retired RN Commander, who provided us all with a lot of our information. The G1s shared the biggest room, and Oliver Stanley had a little office to himself adjacent to the G1’s room. Our job was to look at the whole strategical canvas of the war and after making an examination suggest specific operations which could be carried out now and in the future. 44 ‘G’ refers to one of the staff officer functions in the military HQ; G2 covered Intelligence and Security, G1 all matters relating to personnel. 151

With our depleted resources, with the Army virtually without equipment, with the RAF stretched to the limit in the Battle of Britain, and with the Navy grossly overstretched all over the world keeping our sea communications open, there did not seem much we could advise. However, there were quite a number of minor operations which might move prove practical one day; and furthermore, there were a number of major operations such as our re-entry into Europe which required thought. We started off first with minor operations such as possible Channel Island ones, Norwegian ones, and certain ones in the Mediterranean such as the capture of Pantelleria, and indeed Sicily and Sardinia which again might be on one day. Then one day just after daylight raid when a few bombs had been dropped nearby, Winston Churchill came into our office to see what we were doing. He was smoking a cigar dressed in a sort of battle dress of RAF blue and obviously enjoying himself. After talking to each of us he addressed us in the following terms: ‘Gentleman, I am glad to see you here addressing yourself to matters of immediate and future importance. You have not come here to idle your time away, and I wish you to draw me a plan to win the war!’ With that and a scornful flourish of his cigar as we heard a bomb explosion in the distance he left us. As can be guessed he made a considerable impact even upon us who were perhaps fairly hard boiled in the military sense. I had not seen him since he visited the Hood when I had had quite a long talk with him. We drew a plan described in more detail in the next pages to win the war, and said in so many words we would win the war if we did not make stupid mistakes frittering away our resources, but it would be a long job, perhaps 10 to 12 years! Nevertheless, if the Germans made lots of strategical mistakes it could perhaps be achieved in four to five years from now! I heard Winston approved this appreciation in principle, but how much attention he paid to it is for conjecture. End of Volume 2 152

Loosely attached to the Joint War Planning Staff was the Combined Operations Organisation under Roger Keyes (Admiral of the Fleet Sir Roger Keyes). This organisation, whose terms of reference were rather vague, had the task of developing combined operations material, training men in the execution of combined operations, and making plans for small raids and incursions into enemy held territory.1 Roger Keyes was a powerful personality, a Member of Parliament, and personal friend of the Prime Minister. He was, if ever there was one, a ‘Fighting Admiral’. His leadership in the First World War at Zeebrugge, the part played in the Dardanelles and in other operations showed that he was imbued with the offensive spirit. His motto might have been ‘L’attaque, toujours l’attaque’. The relationship of this organisation with the Joint Planning Staff was not always easy. Roger Keyes, having very much the ear at the Prime Minister above: and not overburdened with a sense of proceeding through normal channels, naturally caused Director of Combined Operations, feeling in the Joint Planning Staff that they were being short circuited and that ill-digested Admiral Sir Roger Keyes with the Prime plans were being sold to the PM. However, whatever can be said for and against this organ- Minister, watching a commando exercise isation, it did encourage the preparation and execution of raids, it did emphasise the need for on the River Clyde, 1940. a far more rapid development of combined operation material, and maybe it kept everybody Image courtesy of Combined Operations, on their toes. It so happened that most of Roger Keyes’ staff were retired officers brought www.combinedops.com back for the war and this may have aroused suspicions in the hearts of the ‘regulars’ in the Joint Planning Organisation, that ideas and suggestions were not as up to date as they might be! We will return later to this Organisation to which I was lent for a short spell at the end of 1940. Getting to grips with the overall strategical position was our first aim, and until this was achieved we were not really in a position to judge the real value of any plans produced. A few of the factors that obtruded themselves on us were as follows, and these were taken into account when preparing our paper ‘to win the war’ as asked for by the Prime Minister soon after the Future Operational Planning Section was formed. Firstly, the material, namely the military resources of the country. Fighter Command were concluding what is always called the Battle of Britain. They had inflicted such heavy losses on the enemy aircraft, that it was out of the question for them [the Germans] even to have sufficient air control over the narrow waters to make the launching of an invasion Fleet a possibility. This was quite clear to us. However the RAF had suffered very heavily, the replacement of planes destroyed and above all of the trained pilots lost, was falling well behind the casualty rate, and what was even more serious, was the grave shortage of machine gun ammunition. For without this Spitfires and Hurricanes would be unable to destroy enemy aircraft. We had been laggardly in building and putting into production an adequate number of small arms factories, and furthermore the Air Staff had been out in their calculations for possible war expenditures. 1 According to Rodger, ‘combined operations’ was a term coined during WWII to denote multi-service activities involving air, land and naval forces acting together and co-ordinated by a Combined Operations headquarters (p.728). In 1940, WWD would have been involved in the early development of this type of approach. 157

The delays in these respects were in some ways due to bureaucratic obstruction in giving the necessary financial approval in the mid and late 1930s to the building of the necessary factories. It would indeed have been tragic if we had failed to win the Battle of Britain because of insufficient small arms ammunition. The Germans were switching to night bombing of London first, and later other cities, with a view to inducing the state of mind where we might come to terms. In those days our counter to night bombing was almost completely ineffective as some of us knew. Night fighters with appropriate equipment were very sparse and much development was required in this equipment if it was to become effective. AA gunfire was noisy but had little effect other than keeping up the morale of the defenders. Balloons were some hazard to enemy aircraft attacking low, and therefore made precise bomb aiming difficult. This did not affect medium or high-level bombing. A gutted John Lewis store from From the armed forces point of view, the Army had lost most of their equipment in France. Illustrated London News, November Our tanks were no match for the German tanks, and being in a sense at the end of the 1940, in K. Phipps cuttings book rearmament queue, the soldiers used to say we would not have a force of over a dozen divisions properly equipped before 1942! But when we [I] arrived in Whitehall the Army’s chief concern was in producing anti-invasion measures with which the Navy was closely associated. We in the Navy thought the best plan was to make the beaches themselves too unpleasant on which to land. The Army in some respects took the other point of view, namely let them land, then round them up and destroy them. Probably the right answer was a combination of both, but this stage was never reached when these rather differing points of view went beyond the realm of abstract discussions. The Air Force were rearming and, as some said, in spite of Lord Beaverbrook, aircraft were coming forward in increasing numbers. The prototype for the three heavy bombers, the Lancaster, Stirling and Halifax were giving satisfactory service. The fighter aircraft were being armed with cannon guns which were more effective than machine guns for air combat. The Navy had suffered heavy losses but these were more than replaced by new construction coming forward and what was perhaps most important of all, the new types of aircraft carrier with armoured decks (Illustrious class) were just beginning to come into service. Alas appropriate aircraft for them lagged behind due to the system of before the war where the RAF had the ultimate responsibility for naval aircraft. Destroyers and frigates were beginning to come into service at a much-needed rate. To sum up from the Armed Forces point of view, the Navy and the RAF could hold the ring whilst the Army re-equipped and built itself up. But even at this stage the most sinister sign of all was heavy merchant shipping losses which far outstripped our capabilities of replace- 158

ment. Unless exceptional replacement measures were taken and the rate of loss curtailed, it was a matter of plain arithmetic how long the island fortress could survive! The minimum import tonnage required to sustain the country’s full war effort was calculated and this meant tightening our belts in no uncertain manner. We were not yet on top of the submarine and the number of commerce raiders needed to be brought to book. Perhaps, to use an old strategical adage, our first aim must be to ‘secure our main base’ i.e. to ensure the integrity and existence of the UK before we could carry the war as it were into the enemy’s lands! Then we must take a look at who we had still as friends and who as probable enemies. In Europe we had no allies left. France under Petain and Laval would be strictly neutral and certainly after Oran would never lean towards us or give us any covert aid. The Army and Air Forces of the combined enemy were far superior numerically to ours though not in quality. On the naval side the advantage was with us. The Balkans were uneasily neutral and it could not be long before the Germans and Italians would overrun the Balkans. Turkey was a great question mark. The Central Powers could overrun Turkey but we doubted whether it would be to their advantage to take on such a tough customer so far from their own main base. Russia of course was an enigma. Nobody could hazard a guess how long the Ribbentrop/ Molotov agreement would last. The attitude of America and Japan remained in doubt. It was even then clear to us that eventually America would come in, but some folk wondered whether it would be in time. In regard to Japan, I don’t think anybody doubted that she would come in as soon as she could, to swallow up the British Far Eastern Empire, Australia included, and without undue hazard to herself. This then was the bird’s eye picture of the situation when we sat down to draw up a ‘Plan to win the War’. It was clear we could only keep to generalities and in the sense our appreciation was really more a political one than a military one. After all, military forces whether Navy, Army or Air are only the means of implementing and giving effect to political decisions. So, we assumed firstly that the enemy would be wise and prudent and not make any mistakes! We concluded that under these circumstances by husbanding our resources, by taking such offensive action as would cause the enemy a disproportionate effort to counter it, and not entering into new military commitments which we could not sustain, we should, by exercising to the full the control of the sea, eventually perhaps in ten or twelve years’ time, we would reach a position where it would be for our enemy to sue for peace. We believed we would hold the Middle East and Egypt, and we believed eventually bit by bit we would capture the whole of the southern shores of the Mediterranean, except Algeria and Tunisia. We assumed America would in a sense contain Japan, and that for this reason our Far Eastern empire would not, as long as this balance remained, be attacked. We visualised the circumstances over the years that conditions might be made to be so intolerable for Italy that she would not wish to continue the war, whilst we realised Central Europe was by and large economically self-sufficient. Italy was the most vulnerable to the severance of seaborne trade. Spain, we hoped to keep in an uneasy neutrality. But it was also clear to us that in a sense at this stage the Central Powers were in a state of unequilibrium. They had to ‘go on’ or ‘go back’, and we thought their obvious and best plan would be to capture the Balkans, 159

Yugoslavia, Greece, Bulgaria, and Romania and the islands approaching the Dardanelles. In fact, we were in no doubt that this would be their next move. We considered ‘invasion’ off, as with the mounting effectiveness of our countermeasures and our victory in the Battle of Britain that it just was not a practical operation of war. In other words, we believed that the next clash would be what we called the Battle of the Suez Canal. About Russia, we felt the Germans would go for them just as soon as they had their other liabilities settled, possibly after the capture of the Balkans, the destruction of British Middle East forces and capture of the Suez Canal. Our air colleagues thought Germany could be brought to her knees by bombing. A view shared by no other service and not by any means by all airmen. We were seeing how London could stand up to bombing, and how in a sense bombing steeled a people’s morale. Most of us even then thought precisely the same effect would take place with the Germans. It was suggested that our effort could seriously hamper Germany’s oil supplies and from numerous papers we saw this did seem a very vulnerable bit of their economy. Nevertheless, for want of proof of the precise effect of bombing and an assessment of the enemy’s adaptability to consider ways of countering these attacks, some of us I think remained sceptical of what were claimed might be decisive results in the German oil economy. The post war bombing strategic survey emphasises again and again how wildly optimistic were some forecasts of the effect of bombing, both against the economy and morale of an organised and high-spirited nation. All this amounted to the fact that if America did not come in, we believed that the war might last ten to twelve years, as indeed it did in Napoleonic times. That we should win it eventually. That much depended on our full and continued control of the seas of the world. That the Balkans would soon be attacked and the next major battle in the years ahead of us would be for the Suez Canal and southern shores of the Mediterranean. We foresaw that if the Americans would come in on our side there would be a relatively quick end of the war within five or six years, as they were economically and potentially militarily, far and away the most powerful nation on earth. But in the main, our concern must at this stage be to avoid major military defeat in other areas where we could not sustain ourselves, but at the same time to impose - by raids, limited expeditions, air attacks etc. - on the enemy a much greater effort than we spent on mounting these operations. However, we added as a rider that if on the other hand an evil genius whispered into Hitler’s ear bad advice and he made some of the following strategical mistakes, the war might end in our favour in four to five years! In outline the mistakes he might make were:- 1. To start on the Balkans i.e. capture Greece and Yugoslavia and not whilst the moment was propitious carry it to its logical conclusion with the capture of Libya, Egypt and Palestine. 2. Attack Russia without any plans to bring the dissident peoples such as Ukrainians, Georgians, Baltic nationals, into their orbits of sympathy. This seemed to us a possibility in view of Hitler’s embroilment with racial theories of the superiority of the Nordic race. 160

3. Divert full military effort on Russia before they had liquidated their military responsibilities in the Middle East, and adopt a military plan against Russia which was unsound i.e. extend their communication lines beyond the limit before the main military forces had been destroyed. A fault Napoleon made. 4. To antagonise the Americans to a state that they would give us so much aid military and economic that this would be tantamount to a declaration of war. 5. Have no political or military coordination with Japan, about entry into war etc. Coordination between naval forces might have yielded great dividends. Sitting on the various official reports which have been being produced since the war makes judgement of past events easy. But it is clear Hitler made all these five errors which we forecast as possibilities in 1940, and quite a number of other ones such as treatment of subject races, Jews, etc. which made their defeat inevitable. Hunches and inspirations in strategic matters are no substitute for cool and careful analysis with every conceivable fact available, including the most important of all, the morale and spirit of the people concerned. About ten years after the war, I met General Heusinger who was in a sense Pug Ismay’s opposite number in the OKW (Ober Kommando Wehrmacht) during the war. I took a liking to him and met him subsequently on a number of occasions in Paris at NATO meetings and in London on similar business. He was I think a Bavarian and typical of the best type of German military staff officer, not arrogant, not overbearing as some Germans are, but always prepared with his well-ordered mind to listen carefully to all that is said.2 I taxed him with what was in many major respects the stupidity and shortsightedness of German strategy, and asked him why in the autumn of 1940 with so many cards in their military hand, they made so many blunders. I asked him for instance when they had the military resources, they did not once and for all liquidate the Balkans and the Middle East finally and capture the Suez Canal; and why for instance they did they not carry out heavier air attacks on Malta, and how it was that Hitler bungled his affairs so much with Franco? Again, why did they attack Russia on an initially sound military plan before their other military obligations in the Middle East had been liquidated and so on. I reminded him that Hitler had made many of the strategical mistakes we hoped he would when we made our appreciation in October 1940. It was most interesting, he said, Hitler had so dominated Generals Keitel, Halder, etc. that he never listened to their considered advice, nor for that matter to any staff advice if it went contrary to his instincts. He preferred to rely not infrequently on some of the cranks and adventurers in his entourage. I pointed out that to launch an attack on Russia, which must absorb three quarters of the German military resources, with the Balkans and the Middle East unsettled and in a sense under British control, was folly of the first order. I suggested the German aims should surely have been to link up as it were with Japan so that Russia and in a sense the eastern part of the British Empire would be encircled. He fully agreed and said some of the arguments I had put to him had at the time occurred forcibly to him. But he said Hitler was pathologically and fanatically opposed to Russia and the Communist system. 2 Adolf Bruno Heinrich Ernst Heusinger (1897-1982) was born in Brunswick, Saxony. 161

He regarded Russia as the source of much of the world’s evil, and it was little short of an obsession with him, that it should be destroyed with no delay and finally and thoroughly so that the Third Reich could last for 1000 years. He said Hitler regarded the Middle East as being very much of a sideshow, and nothing to be compared with the importance of liquidating Russia. He therefore swept aside any suggestions for other courses of action. Heusinger said the German military leaders in his judgement were not in the same street for strategical judgement and determination as the British. He pointed out the German military leaders, and there were some able men among them, who thought otherwise to Hitler were either sacked, put in some backwater, or in some cases liquidated. This goes back a long way, and the sordid rise to power of Hitler over the complaisant backs of some leading German military figures is now past history. Then from the military point of view I asked him why, once this attack on Russia was launched, did they do so much to alienate Ukrainians and all other separate peoples whom they overran on their first headlong advance! He again countered this by saying that if people were not ‘Nordic’, they must be reduced to the status of slaves. What he told me confirmed all our worst fears that Hitler was insane and fundamentally a very evil man. I still pressed him why did the self-respecting German generals stay with him. To which he replied that defection would in war be almost treachery and that they hoped sooner or later to unseat Hitler, as in fact they very nearly did towards the end of the war, when the assassination plot only failed by a narrow margin. I certainly had the impression that the ‘machine’ for higher direction of war in Germany was a very poor one, and not within hundreds of miles of the British machine which owes so much to Lord Hankey (Sir Maurice Hankey) as he was then.3 To get back to 1940 we did not at that time realise how incompetent the German machine for higher direction of war was. We saw the efficiency of the military machine in the field and respected it. We thought perhaps its direction was up to its ‘field performance’ - which in fact it was not! We felt from the Naval and Air point of view that we could match the Germans and better them on a qualitative basis. We reserved our judgement about the Army as until the Army’s equipment was on a par with the Germans, especially in so far as tank and anti-tank equipment was concerned, we could not form any reasoned judgement. Our purpose was to examine what sort of operations could be carried out and cost them in furtherance of what we believed should be our grand strategy. In other words, to impose on the enemy far far greater expenditure of effort for any specific object than we need expend ourselves. Command of the sea made this possible. After all there was a hostile seaboard from North Cape almost continuously to the northern shores of the Mediterranean. We first looked at Norway, which in fact had only been evacuated quite recently. From an examination of the rather slender information we still had, it was clear raids and temporary occupations of strategic points such as the Lofoten Islands could be mounted without much difficulty, provided we could provide the necessary air cover to achieve and maintain our 3 Maurice Hankey, 1st Baron Hankey (1877-1963) ODNB 162

position. The Lofotens particularly attracted us and in fact an operation on these lines was later carried out. Innumerable raids could be carried out on the Norwegian coast but there were not a great many worthwhile targets, and one always had to remember that the local population would suffer much from the Germans for allegedly helping us, when the raiding forces withdrew. In Europe there were quite a number of plans, and in particular a plan was examined which was in fact too large and out of all proportion for capturing and sealing off the Cherbourg peninsula. Then what to do if the Spaniards contemplated mounting an attack on Gibraltar was examined. Assuming they had German assistance and support, it would be a major operation to capture the surrounding heights from Tarifa above Algeciras and La Linea (on the Ronda Road) and probably as far as Marbella would be necessary to allow the full use of Gibraltar and the straits between Spain and Africa. This was reckoned to require about four divisions of troops at least, with full support. It was also far beyond our capacity in 1940. For apart from our forces in the Middle East under General Wavell, we had barely the equipment for one division and it was just not on at that time, with invasion scares still in the offing, to denude ourselves still further in the UK. Then perhaps one of the most important jobs was to examine how, when, and where we should re-enter the Continent with a view to encompassing the final defeat of the Germans. A fascinating task. We first of all favoured a direct assault over the Pas de Calais area, a place much favoured by the RAF for they could, they hoped, give continual and full air control over the areas of passage and assault. The RAF for good technical reasons (the short range of fighter planes) held steadfastly to this for a long time. However, there were many disadvantages of this area not the least being the very formidable resistance by fixed and other defences, as the Dieppe raid showed later, that could be brought to oppose invading army forces. We looked at other areas and after a most exhaustive examination came down in favour of the Cherbourg peninsula, as the beaches between Oustreham [Ouistreham] and Grandcamp were suitable; there was sufficient area and communications inland to deploy major military forces, and once Caen had been captured the way to Paris and the flat northern plains of France were open. Furthermore, with the development of fighter aircraft of increasing range, we felt by this time we could build up our forces to launch an invasion [and] that air cover and the necessary air superiority could be maintained over the area of assault. The areas north of Le Havre might be suitable but here the enemy could reinforce more quickly than further south. On the other hand, the Brittany Peninsula was a possibility but the difficulties of providing air cover might prove insuperable. So, after a pretty thorough examination we recommended that when the time came for assault we should go for the Cherbourg Peninsula. But this was in an atmosphere of unreality for we had virtually none of the craft yet to be designed and built for major assaults, and for carrying troops and tanks ashore. We had no craft as yet to neutralise beach defences and surmount beach obstacles. We had nowhere near the fighter aircraft required, nor for that matter the Army’s support aircraft required to follow up a 163

landing once it had been established! So, we regarded it perhaps as an exercise in crystal gazing. Looking at later history when the full examination of various alternatives were being looked at two to three years later, it is of some interest to see that after many changes and alternative plans, the eventual plan adopted in June 1944 was very similar to the one that the Future Operational Planning Section recommended in October and November 1940! Still less did I dream that I should be the Captain of the Cruiser that led the invading force into the invasion of Normandy. A little short of four years later. Then other operations in the Mediterranean were looked at in outline, the captures of Sardinia and Sicily, the capture of the small island of Pantelleria some 80 miles from Malta. But more about that later! Then, as is now known, we had to consider methods of ‘friendly’ occupation of the Azores and also the capture of the Canaries should Spain come into the war against us, as a safeguard for our mid and south Atlantic shipping routes. These examinations had in many ways to be rather cursory as a detailed beach reconnaissance is necessary if an opposed landing is considered likely. But again much of the planning had to be on the basis of ‘when’ and ‘if ’ the necessary landing craft became available, many of which were not even at the drawing board stage, such as LCM (landing craft men) and LCA (landing craft assault), LCT (landing craft tank) and hosts of others, the enumeration of which would fill at least two foolscap pages. The training aspect of these specialised craft was also not one to be disregarded. All we had at that moment were two converted assault ships Glengyle and Glenearn, each of which carried some 20 assault craft similar to what became known as the LCM. The rest of the support had to be provided by naval gunfire until such time as a port could be captured and cargo ships with tanks, artillery etc., unloaded onto the jetties! I think however these examinations did prove a real stepping stone for many of our assaults which were undertaken when the tide had turned, and we were attacking. The Combined Operations Section under Roger Keyes did a certain amount of planning but these were only very much of the sort of hit and miss [hit and run] raids. They had however considered the possibility of the capture of Pantelleria but had drawn up no specific plans for this purpose. Then one day in the first half of November I was told by Charles Lambe that Sir Roger Keyes had persuaded the Prime Minister, rather against the First Sea Lord’s views, that the capture of Pantelleria was, both on practical and political grounds, most desirable and that I was to be lent to Roger Keyes’ staff to plan the operation! Rather a surprise, I did not know at that time that Roger Keyes had extracted a promise from the Prime Minister that he was to command the operation and that I was to be his Chief of Staff and Planner! I got hold of all the information I could and went along to the Combined Operations Office to see Roger Keyes. I had not known him well before though he had been kind to me when he was the C-in-C Portsmouth in the late 1920s and I had been one of the young officers who used sometimes to take out one or other of his nice daughters! A short description of this remarkable man might be appropriate. He was at this time just past 70 but seemed to have lost little of his fire and was a Member of Parliament. Roger Keyes was in every sense a thruster and no respecter of persons. A great fighting record during the First War, he took his 164

cruiser through the narrows of the Dardanelles during that campaign. Later he earned great fame by organising and leading the attack on Zeebrugge for the purpose of blocking up the German submarine base. Like his close friend, Winston Churchill, he always liked to be within sound of the guns! Between the wars he held most of the important posts an Admiral could hold, except the First Sea Lord, i.e. Admiral commanding Battle Cruisers, Deputy Chief of Naval Staff, Commander-in-Chief Mediterranean, and Commander-in-Chief Portsmouth. There are some who said he should have become First Sea Lord instead of Admiral Field.4 Had it not been for his great fondness for polo, and his entirely unfounded alleged favouritism to officers who played polo in the Mediterranean when he was C-in-C Mediterranean, he would have probably achieved this post. As it was, a much cleverer man but far less forceful in the shape of Admiral Field became First Sea Lord. Roger Keyes was in no sense a paper man, he disliked paper and administrative work of all sorts, but usually took care to have a good staff on whom he placed implicit trust to do this work. He was not a good speaker or for that matter debater, but he had boundless courage both physical and moral. He once said to me ‘it is agony in the House of Commons being floored time and time again by agile debaters just because one’s tongue is not quick enough to say what one knows, thinks and feels.’ A lesson I think many lesser men might take to heart. Roger Keyes was a very keen horseman and with his spare and agile figure not one to be trifled with on the polo field, and also a keen shot with an enormous zest for life. Extremely ambitious all his life, he did not pay over much attention to what are regarded as strict procedural channels. He knew many of the politicians of his day and had been a lifelong friend of Winston Churchill since the days when they were both thrusting young men. My father knew Roger Keyes who was in his own service (Indian Political), and whom he also described as a thruster and keen sportsman. Roger Keyes took a prominent part in the debate in the House of Commons when Neville Chamberlain was ousted. Here then stands a man young for his years, still full of burning ambition to take an active part in the war. He never I really think understood the Chiefs of Staff machinery for the conduct of war, and whenever he had what he thought was a good idea, went straight away to the Prime Minister and urged it to him without processing it through the Chiefs of Staff. He was not loved by the Chiefs of Staff. The First Sea Lord (then Dudley Pound) had been his Chief of Staff when Commander-in-Chief, Mediterranean, and maybe he never realised their roles now were in a sense reversed. His department lived in some rickety buildings since demolished near the RUSI [Royal United Services Institute] in Whitehall. I went up to see him straight away and got a very warm welcome from him. He said he had been discussing the desirability of capturing Pantelleria with the Prime Minister who had agreed that the operation should be planned, and if carried out he would command it, and he hoped I was to be his Chief of Staff. This operation was given the code name of ‘Operation Workshop’ and is referred to both in Vol. II of Winston’s History of the Second World War and Vol. I of The Official History of the War at Sea. From what information I had been able to obtain beforehand, I sensed this was a pretty hot issue and that I should have to tread with a with a deal of caution if tempers were not to be 4 Admiral Sir Frederick Field was First Sea Lord from 1930-1933, ODNB 165

lost, and worse still wrong decisions made. I immediately got down to planning it, and found in fact there was no plan at all, nothing more than some disjointed intelligence material about its apparently formidable defences. Anyway, to the planner nothing should be impossible and providing one does not overrate the difficulties and brings off complete surprise, it is miraculous what can be achieved. We had two Glen ships with the heavy duty derricks, known as Glengyle and Glenearn, commanded by two retired officers, Captains Petrie and Paget, both fine and resolute officers. These ships each carried about 24 landing craft, about 16 at davits (eight each side) and eight inboard on deck. Then in a very rough and ready state we had two Commandos which had been recruited from the Household Brigade and other sources. They were in training in the Firth of Clyde where the germ of a combined operation training base was in the process of gestation. So much anyway for the present on what assault forces we were likely to have. The staff we had at Roger Keyes Combined Operations HQ were, through no fault of their own, a bit out of touch as many of them had retired a goodish number of years before the war. However with the aid of one or two first rate soldiers and a Wing Commander lent to us, I drew up a plan for carrying out an assault and landing on the islands about 2.00 a.m., with a view to completing its capture in 12 to 24 hours. There were one or two isolated places where our landing craft could beach with apparently little opposition. We should expect a measure of air cover from Malta though this would have been decidedly thin. We intended to capture the HQ near the little town and main battery at the east end by landing on the south and east of the island, whilst the diversionary bombardment would be carried out by cruisers on the town. Against determined opposition, as might be expected from the Germans, an operation of this type would inevitably end in failure, for it was in fact much more difficult than the later operation against Dieppe. On the other hand, we guessed - I think rightly - that we should get neither determined nor skilful opposition from the Italian garrison. Among the Commandos there were some of the most resourceful and determined characters I have ever met. Moreover, some had already proved themselves in operations of a most unorthodox character. Anyway, I drew up a plan with Roger Keyes as the ‘Commodore’ in Command, an organisation which much appealed to him and which would not cross wires in any way with the Naval Command arrangements and responsibilities of the Mediterranean Station under Admiral Cunningham. The plan drawn up relied on good weather or at least, fair weather, and this factor would have played a large part in the success or failure of such an operation. We had a good signalman, Lt. Butler on the staff and I immediately had him transferred to the operational staff for this operation. Keyes’s secretary (Woolley), who had been with him during the First World War - also a retired officer, was a great help. The Army Commander Brigadier Haydon was in charge of the Commandos. An Irish Guardsman of great charm and ability. Anyway within 72 hours of one’s arrival an outline plan had been drawn up and agreed. Roger Keyes, rather to my surprise I thought at the time, only looked at it rather superficially. Nevertheless, he much liked the essential which made for ‘surprise’ at every turn, and without delay he gave it his formal blessing. It now came to training those who were to execute it, ensure proper provision of force, Navy, Army and Air and so on. As yet no combined operation other than hasty evacuations had been carried out against what amounted to 166

a Fortress Island. To say the least of it, the plan was a hazardous if bold one, and there were quite a number of reasons why it might founder hopelessly, such as bad weather, a security leak etc. In other words the success depended on tolerable weather and complete surprise. The plan catered for the permanent occupation of Pantelleria as an adjunct to Malta. The Joint Planners and Chiefs of Staff were far from enthusiastic about it, not I think of the plan itself but because they did not believe we had the resources, naval, air, and land, and perhaps particularly Air, to maintain it as a stepping stone to Malta once it had been captured. The opinion of the Commander-in-Chief, Mediterranean was asked, and he came down emphatically against it on the grounds that there were other more important things such as the Dodecanese which should be taken first, and he believed the cost of maintaining and supplying Pantelleria within close range of enemy air bases in Sicily would strain our resources beyond the limit. Nevertheless, we only heard bits and pieces of the argument and disagreement going on above us. However, at this stage I think about mid-November, we had a plan agreed by the Force Commander designate (Roger Keyes) and not cavilled at as an operational plan by any of the fighting services. But a complete difference of opinion existed as to the timing and appropriateness of the operation between the Prime Minister and Roger Keyes on the one hand, the Chiefs of Staff and the Commander-in-Chief Mediterranean on the other hand! Even at that time I must confess to admitting I thought the correctness of strategical judgement lay with the Chiefs of Staff. However, I soon dismissed these thoughts from my mind as my task was to do my level best to ensure the success of the operation when it was ordered. I remember discussing the operation one day with Roger Keyes, and I told him that an operation of this nature against the Germans would be little short of suicide and I reminded him of the difficulties of the Suvla landings in the First World War. 5 He said he intended himself to land in the first wave of assault boats. I tried in vain to discourage this but not with much success. I pointed out that very likely he would be killed and he immediately replied, ‘What better way to die!’, to which I replied that I was still young and wanted to see a lot more of the war before having to cross the ‘Styx’! We had a good laugh. On physical and indeed moral courage there can be few to touch Roger Keyes, even though he did not always follow ‘old school tie’ precepts in getting his way. Now before we move up the Isle of Arran to train the force, it is worth a pause to a look at other aspects on going to the Admiralty in the latter part of September. Elizabeth was most anxious to come too. However. we agreed after much persuasion on my part that she should stay initially at Mulgrave until I saw how the land lay in London and what the bombing was like. The day bombing gradually died away in October and instead there was what the Germans called ‘nightly terror raids’ on London to break the spirit of the people. These took place every night. As we now know, the weight of these attacks was very light, compared with what we delivered on Germany later, though we didn’t know it at the time, but every night was made a bit hideous by the anti-aircraft gunfire which was noisy but ineffective. These raids made folk more determined to defeat the Germans. 5 The Suvla Bay landing was part of the Gallipoli campaign in Turkey in 1915. 167

However, towards the end of October, Elizabeth decided to join me in London and this made a tremendous difference. She slept on a rather uncomfortable little camp bed in our flat and did work during the day with the POW [Prisoner of War] parcel organisation in Carlton House Terrace. However, it was great for me and, as by reason of our flat’s location we had taken all practical safety precautions, we decided that the risks of being in London during the bombing was worth it. A view not shared by all our relations! It certainly seemed as if Operation Workshop would take place and accordingly the force to execute it assembled at Lamlash in the Isle of Arran for training under the direction of Roger Keyes at the beginning of December. The Glengyle and Glenearn were there with full complement of Assault Landing Craft, with some above:POW Parcels Appeal miscellaneous craft and the two Commandos under the direction of Brigadier Haydon, as previously mentioned, an exceptionally able Irish Guardsman.6 We used the Brodick Hotel as our headquarters and at that time the Duke of Montrose was in residence at Brodick Castle. I met his sons who were near contemporaries of mine and once before the war had met their delightful father who had a very soft spot for the Navy. Roger Keyes knew them well. The Brodick Bay Hotel did not turn out at all badly as the Headquarters and there was no nonsense about rationing. Officers were in one of the Duke’s houses in the Bay, which was I think a onetime Dower House. It was definitely a case of starting from scratch, there were no ‘pro formas’ on which to base one’s plan or training programmes. The above: POW parcels appeal; when two Commandos with their officers were a pretty wild lot at first, until some good old parcels did arrive at Prisoner of War fashioned Guards RSMs [Regimental Sergeant Majors] put some discipline into them. The camps, they often proved lifesavers. officers were a pretty adventurous crowd - Laycock, Lovat, Randolph Churchill, Nicholson, From Katharine Phipps cuttings book. quite a number of MPs who wanted unorthodox adventures, and quite a sprinkling of men who had already made some mark or another in an adventurous life. The day we arrived Roger Keyes told me he had got hold of a couple of ‘Commanders’ to help with the training of the Commandos for getting in and out of landing craft. These two reported for duty to me at my office next morning at 8:00 a.m. One dressed in a Commander’s uniform turned out to be Admiral Sir Walter Cowan, who had a most distinguished fighting record in the First War and had the reputation of being a martinet of the first order. The other, a charming old chap was Admiral Hallett, who had also a distinguished record in the Navy in the years gone by. I must admit to a little surprise. Admiral Cowan had nearly started a mutiny in one ship in which he served just after the First World War because of his severity, but Admiral Hallett was known to be a man of great charm who could lead anybody 6 When WWD refers to a Commando, he means a Commando unit which normally comprised 450 men. 168

anywhere! One could not but respect Walter Cowan who like so many people of his kind could not be bettered if you stood up to him, knew your duty and refused to be browbeaten. I sent them off one to each Commando to start the training and familiarise themselves with the two assault ships which would carry the force to the scene of operation. One of the Commandos contained not a few Glasgow-Irish from the Gorbals district of Glasgow. They were tough to say the least of it and maybe resented Army discipline, so I sent Walter Cowan one morning to teach them how to disembark from and embark in the landing craft with the maximum efficiency, and in absolute silence and in the minimum of time. Later that morning I walked down to the jetty at Lamlash, which is the harbour for Arran, to see how they were getting on. I approached unseen and silently to see the Commandos sitting round with cowed expressions on their faces, listening to a colourful flow of invective which would have done credit to a mid-nineteenth century sailing master rounding the Horn. I heard one of the Commando’s NCOs say to his neighbour in broad Scotch ‘Praise be to the Lord, they will follow ‘im anywhere and to the gates of ‘ell if need arises.’7 Then Haydon had a full-time job getting his troops fit and disciplined with a knowledge of how to use their rather specialised weapons and to impress on these individualists, for many officers were individualists in the extreme, that they must conform to the general plan of action. We used to have many arguments in the mess in the evening, Usually I had a full night’s work on my plate tying the many loose ends together, preparing rehearsals which would simulate reality and so on. One evening, Randolph Churchill was laying down the law in a more than usually aggressive way, and this means a lot, so Haydon decided next day to give him the task of capturing a strong point namely Goat Fell, the highest and most inaccessible peak on Arran Island the next day. Randolph, who carried a lot of weight, was quite subdued for some days afterwards. Lovat was also a most independent character and usually preferred some task, entirely on his own. But there was little time to listen to and take part in the spirited discussions in the mess. Roger Keyes’ son, a young Lieutenant in the Navy had got himself attached to the expedition and had somehow obtained two old I think coastal motor boats. We somehow rigged them up with some armament, but like his father young Keyes was no respecter of ‘service channels’ and I was frequently hauled over the coals by the Admiralty for his activities! Nevertheless, we got usually what we wanted. I had to pay London many visits getting essential equipment, amending our plan and finding out how our activities were being supported or frustrated by the Admiralty, War Office and Air Ministry. I remember a particularly sharp interview with the Second Sea Lord (Admiral Little) when trying to obtain the services of some officers Keyes wanted. However, Little, though very angry at the time never bore me any ill will. 7 Sir Walter Cowan (1871-1956), ODNB. Cowan’s career was extraordinary and he could never be accused of not leading from the front. Retired as an Admiral in 1931, he persuaded Keyes to let him join the Commandos with the rank of Commander. He fought in North Africa, was captured in May 1942 while single-handedly fighting an Italian tank crew armed only with a revolver, was repatriated in 1943, rejoined the Commandos and fought again in Italy. By 1945 he was feeling his age and reverted to the retired list. 169

It soon became apparent that the launching of the expedition was in doubt. Keyes sent me to see the Prime Minister whom I told [that] as an operation of war it had I believed a sporting chance of success against the Italians. I refused to be drawn into any discussions as to whether it was the right thing to do in the strategical picture. I was of course aware of the intense opposition by the C-in-C Med against it (Admiral Cunningham). Nobody could ever accuse Andrew Cunningham of a lack of offensive spirit, but he felt it was low down on the priorities to be dealt with in the Mediterranean, and the capture of Pantelleria would result in far far too great a drain on our Mediterranean resources particularly ‘air’. He agreed it would assist marginally in the control of the narrow central Mediterranean waters, but unless we had adequate air and surface crafts available this should not be undertaken. Furthermore, the First Sea Lord and Naval Staff were solidly of the opinion that the time was not right for this operation. Churchill, on the other hand with his burning desire for offensive operation at almost any cost, coupled with a half promise to Keyes that he should command the operation, was adamant it should be undertaken. In discussions with the Prime Minister, I always refused to be drawn but stuck to my point as a professional officer that this very hazardous operation had a chance of success. Hindsight tends to confirm that it would have succeeded as an operation to capture Pantelleria, but with the advent of the German Air Force in strength in Sicily, it would have proved an intolerable strain to maintain the island. It will be remembered we were hard put to maintain Malta in the years that lay ahead of 1940. COHQ in London kept us well informed of what was in the wind and Keyes himself paid a number of visits to Whitehall. Planning proceeded and we hoped to be ready to sail with supporting craft, i.e. destroyers and the cruiser flagship, by the end of December or beginning of January. But delays kept putting us back and I managed to snatch a few days leave at Mulgrave at the end of the year where Elizabeth had returned from London when I had more or less left for Arran Island. However, I was back again at Arran in the New Year having as far as possible avoided becoming the meat in the sandwich between the Prime Minister and Roger Keyes on one hand and the Admiralty and Chiefs of Staff on the other. Not always an easy task. I was myself doubtful whether this was the strategical moment to launch this operation which might well have suffered very heavy casualties. On the other hand, I believed the plan drawn up was one of great boldness in conception, and by the very nature of its boldness would contrary to the views of the ‘Jeremiahs’ have succeeded. I think even though I was a young commander my views carried a little weight. On January 1st when I was looking through the Admiralty General Signals in the evening, I came across a list of promotions and idly glanced through it to see who were lucky. To my intense surprise, at about the most junior place but two, I found my name and realised that with Atkinson (later killed at Singapore), we were two of the youngest Captains in the Navy. In the all absorbing and ever exhausting problems which had been facing me, I had never thought about it and assumed with luck I should get promoted in due course perhaps one or two years later. Keyes was delighted and said ‘If you had not been promoted now, I should have seen you got it next time’. I imagine that I was promoted on my record in the Hood. 170

As the New Year came in with successive postponements, it became increasingly unlikely that Operation ‘Workshop’ would be launched. It was later shelved indefinitely. Perhaps if it had been attempted the writer might not be writing this in comfort nearly 30 years later! Immediately ‘Operation Workshop’ went into suspended animation, I returned to Future Operational Planning Section, and we looked at many other things - plans for major raids on Sicily and Sardinia with the possibility of their capture as a logical follow-up. With the forces we had then at our disposal this was far beyond our resources, but it was always useful to have it as it were plans on the shelf which could be taken down and re-examined, and if necessary put into effect as soon as the proper moment arrived. I evolved what I thought at the time was rather an ingenious plan to attack Sardinia. The essence of the scheme was to have two assault convoys - the first one would precede the second one by about two days and would sail as if it was a normal Malta convoy - it would be heavily protected and would I hope have gathered all the enemy opposition - surface and air. In the second day in the Mediterranean at Cape Bon on the African coast after dark, this convoy would alter course about 130° to port and steer northwest towards the Bay of Cagliari in Sardinia. It was hoped this alteration would not be detected by the enemy. The second assault convoy would have passed through the states of Gibraltar in darkness two days behind the first one, and it was hoped this passage would not be known to the enemy. Both assault convoys would simultaneously converge on the Bay of Cagliari and arriving there at the same time would it is hoped effect complete surprise at dawn on the ‘D’ day selected. It was all of course rather a nice matter of timing but it had an element of novelty, and if Cagliari was to be attacked it seemed to be an original and quite likely successful way of doing this. Winston Churchill got to hear of this idea and to my surprise I got a message from him - Would I please go and see him that night in his office at 10:00 p.m. I had a talk with Charles Lambe, my immediate boss, and we went along and had a talk with ‘Pug’ Ismay. to find out what was in the Prime Minister’s mind. It was clear Roger Keyes had heard vaguely of this scheme and told the PM that I had a wonderful scheme for capturing Sardinia! This was a rather unusual way of conducting business which in a sense amounted to bypassing the Chiefs of Staff! However, we agreed beforehand that I would stick to the purely technical and operational aspects of the operation and not the strategical aspects or wider aspects of it. Dudley Pound, the First Sea Lord, was told of course about my invitation to see the Prime Minister and seemed quite happy that I should not commit the Chiefs of Staff. I arrived punctually at the PM’s office in the basement of Storey’s Gate not far from our own offices and spent an interesting hour with him and ‘Pug’ Ismay. The PM cross examined me very closely on how my scheme would be translated into an operation, and I think I convinced him that a novel operation of this nature would with luck and determination succeed, but I had to observe that as far as I could see at that time we had neither the forces (mostly Army and Air) nor the rather specialised equipment in sufficient quantity to do it. The PM did not like this at all and asked me why I said this. I pointed out as he knew that the success of an operation of this nature depended much on the degree of training of the personnel concerned, and this had to be full and thorough,.and the provision of adequate 171

numbers of landing craft and close support craft, not the least being the provision of adequate air cover which in those days could only be done by the very early capture of an airfield nearby. I suspect the PM felt I was rather more cautious than he had been led to believe, but I again stressed it was a perfectly feasible operation with good chances and success provided we had not only the forces to carry it out, but also more important the forces to follow it up and carry it through to its proper conclusion. I could see Pug Ismay agreed with me, and at times suggested points for discussion which would bring out various points and aspects of importance. Eventually the Prime Minister decided that this was a matter he would discuss further with the Chiefs of Staff, before directing that detailed plans should be drawn up. He was just as charming as ever and thanked me for showing him a most ingenious plan for what might be an operation of massive importance which might soon be ordered for the discomfiture of Signor Mussolini! It was fascinating watching his face during these discussions. I soon found that if I wanted to deflect his powerful mind from one train of thought, and this was mighty difficult, one’s best chance was by quoting historical analogy. Technical arguments and specifically staff supply ones which we adduced were always highly suspect. He said once in the course of our discussions ‘My dear Captain, difficulties are there to be resolved not enlarged upon’ but it was his questing spirit for ACTION, and again ACTION which so inspired all those who worked with him, even if at times it drove them sometimes to distraction, when our available resources immediately to hand were sometimes not even 10% of what was required. ‘Action this day’, a series of essays by six men who worked very closely in contact with him and of impeccable integrity, gives as good an insight into Winston Churchill’s mind as any I know. But perhaps the gun is being jumped, so I will later include a short essay on this unusual man drawn from my own experience which was rather more on the fringe than in the centre and in daily close association with him. We concentrated then on various plans for capturing the Dodecanese and in particular Rhodes. The idea was to capture the Dodecanese and so bring pressure on the Turks to come in on our side. However, it was again clear to us even then that by no stretch of imagination had we sufficient forces or equipment to launch a major operation like the capture of Rhodes which would certainly require two Divisions of troops. However, various operations were examined and the results of our work sent to the C-in-C Med, whose staff did not always welcome them, as they had better things in their opinion to do! By the end of February work had eased down in the Operational Planning Section as it was clear, apart from our raids, our resources were quite inadequate for anything more ambitious. There had been some criticism, I think rather unjustified, of the Foreign Operations Division of the Admiralty as a result of the escape through the Straits of Gibraltar in the previous autumn of the French cruisers bound for Dakar.8 It was decided to make a change so my friend and one time colleague as Commander of Renown was made Director of Operations (Foreign), and I was made Deputy Director.
