So I gave up my desk in the War Cabinet Joint 8 Three French cruisers and accompanying destroyers escaped from Toulon and reached Dakar. In September 1940 a force under de Gaulle attempted to persuade the Vichy authorities in Dakar to change sides. This 172 was unsuccessful and British and Australian ships bombarded the port of Dakar and ships. The engagement was largely unsuccessful, and Dakar remained in Vichy hands.

Planning Office in Storey Gate, and went to work in the Admiralty. David Luce, an ex-submarine Captain, came in to relieve me. Life in London was as busy as ever. There were many night raids on the capital, in fact almost nightly. The Admiralty was hit one night when I was working in our underground offices. We worked by day in the usual above ground offices, and by night in the underground one. It took place only an hour or so after our splendid Hall Porter had told Ralph Edwards, the Director of Operations (Home), whose office was hit, to get below. We owe a lot to him as he was quite insistent that after dark we should all transfer to the basement offices of the Admiralty. I found Oswald’s bicycle invaluable, as I used it regularly to go to and from the Admiralty from our flat. I remember one night in 1941, cycling back across St James’s Park, I suppose about midnight, when an air raid, not a very heavy one, was taking place. As I rode down Birdcage Walk, I heard the usual whistle of some bombs followed by a perfectly gigantic flash and an explosion which did not however throw me off my bicycle. The explosion was followed by I suppose a couple of seconds of complete silence, and then immediately by the tinkle of falling broken glass from houses on both sides of the park, and the quacking of almost every duck in the park. The roads were nice and empty and though the lighting was very poor in the darkened streets, one could not come to any great harm on a bicycle. Life was rather different in the Operations Division (Foreign). John Terry or I were always in the Admiralty, day and night, or at a moment’s call. We took it in turns to sleep there and go and bath in our Club in the mornings. There was a lot on, and our job was to see that ships and routeing authorities had all the information available. We also had to ensure that dispositions were arranged to meet operations, such as Malta convoys and raider hunting operations. We had to look ahead and forecast when certain operations would be necessary and ensure we had all the forces available. We had also to try to fit in repair and refit programmes with operational needs. John Terry was excellent to work with, a clever and sharp intelligence, he knew his own mind and proved a good judge of what to do. He never minced matters with his superiors such as Assistant Chief of Naval Staff Foreign (ACNS(F) [Admiral Sir Henry] Harwood), the Vice Chief of Naval Staff (Tom Phillips), or the First Sea Lord. A quick and orderly mind he proved to be an excellent D.O.D(F) and a good colleague of the Director of Operations Division (Home), Ralph Edwards, who was in this post outstanding. We had a mixture of Reserve Officers and Commanders on our staff, divided up in both geographical and functional responsibilities. An excellent team, the reserve officers such as Bailey and many others were absolutely first rate, and the staff officers were in many cases better than the regular officers, some of whom had been sent in rather part-worn from sea service to recuperate. A very, very lively team. Harwood of River Plate fame was our boss.9 A good strategical brain he saw most of the problems on a large canvas. He was not however quite as incisive or clear on the day-to-day problems which required detached and meticulous attention. For all that, a generous hearted and impressive man who suffered a bit from not being as quick in debate as some of his colleagues. Obviously, he was a better man at sea than in a high pressure executive Admiralty Department. 9 Battle of the River Plate, December 1939, when the German battleship Graf Spee was pursued and scuttled 173 in the River Plate. A notable film of the action was made in 1956.

Elizabeth found herself very busy working with the prisoner of war people in Carlton House Terrace [British Red Cross], and we managed to see just a very little of my father who was doing a grand job keeping people cheerful and happy at Longhope. The spring and late winter of 1941 was a time of exceptional naval activity. The Army were concentrating on building themselves up at home and giving all the support possible through our forces in the Middle East which later included Greece. The Air Force were in much the same boat, they had to make good the losses of the Battle of Britain and were building up the project dear to many Air Marshals’ hearts, namely that of Bomber Command. This Command was at that time the only means where we could strike at the Germans themselves, and for this reason and also perhaps because of Professor Lindemann’s power of persuasion on the Prime Minister, received very favoured treatment. The Photos of WWD around this time are development of Coastal Command and Army Close Support airforces lagged a bit behind rare, but typically show him in uni- and even at that time without the advantages of hindsight, we on the naval side thought our form, looking rather thin, probably on great effort, industrial and otherwise, on building up Bomber Command was a misdirection leave at Mulgrave (above) or Coglan of our strictly limited resources and industrial potential. When one arrived at the Admiralty War Room and looked at the chart of the oceans of the world, the first impression 1 had was how few ships and maritime aircraft we had to safeguard our shipping, which by this time had been put into convoy in the North Atlantic and Mediterranean and to some extent in the South Atlantic and Indian Ocean. The War Room, or better still the Map Room, was in the big conference room on the first floor of the Admiralty, and was where we had our daily 9:30 a.m. staff conference with the VCNS, or occasionally the First Sea Lord presiding. The Oceans of the world were shown in map form and the location of our ships and forces shown on each map in the anticipated 9:00 a.m. position of the day in question. Enemy positions and enemy reports together with locations of important neutral warships were also shown on the map. One could and indeed did spend much time in here reflecting on possible courses of action. But if one did not know and feel the conditions of the sea and realise what the fog of war, doubtful visibility and extreme exhaustion might mean, one might well form quite a wrong impression that it was all much easier than it was. It was salutary to remember the area of visibility of a ship lookout was probably not much larger than a pin’s head and even an aircraft’s observable area was probably not broader than a thick pencil line across the map following its track. These were the days before airborne and ship borne radar, which have now utterly altered the scope of distance reconnaissance. Terry and I had adjacent offices in the north block of the Admiralty, and next door we had two large rooms where all the commanders lived and worked. Either Terry or I always slept at the Admiralty so that in the event of any incident requiring action an authoritative source was there to advise on the best course to be followed. Our responsibility was to keep check on all British warships and merchant ships all over the world except the Home Station, i.e. 174

the eastern half of the North Atlantic down to the latitude of Gibraltar. Terry was a very good staff officer with as clear a mind as one could would meet anywhere. Quite tireless and not given to fussing, I believe we were a pretty good combination running ‘Operations, Foreign’. But a look at the map gave one cause for hard thinking. Just after taking over at the Admiralty in early March, our old friends in the Commandos under the command of Brigadier Haydon carried out a most successful raid on the Lofoten Islands and showed their work most effectively. But on the ocean warfare side we had many commerce raiders to combat. In spite of the destruction of the Graf Spee, there were at times, the Scheer, the Thor, the Pinguin, the Kormoran, the Atlantis, the Orion, the Komer, and also the German battle cruisers Scharnhorst and Gneisenau, as well as cruisers Hipper, Prince Eugen, and others at sea. The story of these raiders with their successes and failures is told very well by Stephen Roskill in vol. 1 of his War at Sea. They stretched our resources to breaking point. Had some of them been more adventurous especially the German battlecruisers and Hipper, our losses would have been far heavier. The plan was if possible, to keep one battleship, usually one of the old ‘R’ class with each convoy of importance and lesser convoys had cruisers. Then in addition groups were made up which whenever possible contained an aircraft carrier to search for the raiders who in most cases attacked independently routed ships. However, the battle cruisers did sink over 100,000 tonnes of our shipping in February and March before returning to Brest. Then there was the question of the Canaries - if the Germans moved into Spain, or Spain came in against us, Gibraltar would again be a fortress under siege, and it would be necessary to forestall the Germans by occupying the Canaries and, whilst in F.O.P.S, we had drawn up plans to achieve this. This was a big operation and plans were approved in April to do this, though thanks in admirable measure to the First Sea Lord’s restraining hand, no precipitate action was taken which would certainly have brought Spain into the war against us! At times we thought the Prime Minister would have ordered the operation which might, if carried out, have resulted in the eventual fall of Gibraltar and the loss of many of our Mediterranean interests. It was clear events in the Balkans were moving to a crescendo and we wondered how the Yugoslavs, Greeks and others would stand up to German pressure. The Army of the Middle East under General Wavell had a great success early in the year driving the Italians out of Libya to beyond Benghazi and successes were being achieved which would deprive the Italians of their naval bases in the Red Sea. These successes made our naval task easier especially, as even then it was becoming apparent that without carriers to give air protection, working in confined waters on enemy held coasts was hazardous. As March wore on, the pressure brought to bear on Yugoslavia became intolerable and before long Belgrade was blitzed by German aircraft and on the 6th of April the German army attacked Greece. One of the most difficult problems facing us was whether or not to send troops to help defend Greece. In the various appreciations which I helped prepare we were 175

in no doubt that the military support we would give Greece would not prevent her being overrun by the Germans. On the other hand, there was the political side which I suppose was, ‘could we afford not to go to the help of our ally Greece?’ We, as military planners in the naval sphere, foresaw yet another Dunkirk under what might well be far worse conditions. We knew from experience evacuations are very expensive operations and many warships will be lost. To make matters worse General Rommel had arrived in North Africa and inflicted a smashing defeat on our Army which was forced to evacuate the whole of Libya and in particular Benghazi, which we had hoped to build up as a minor naval and air base. This had a most adverse effect on our naval position in the eastern Mediterranean. We were by now committed to supporting our Army in Greece and our position was uncomfortably flanked by enemy held territory. From the reports coming through from Greece, we felt it would not be long before the Germans took over from the Italians and soon recovered the unexpected and splendid successes the Greeks had achieved against the Italians. Attention became more and more focused on the Mediterranean. At the end of March, we achieved a considerable naval success in what is known as the Battle of Matapan.10 We tried insofar as is possible to keep track of all warships taking part in the operation from the Operation Room of our main office. Winston came in more than once with the First Sea Lord, and as ever evinced great interest in what was going on. This certainly gave us a bit of a fillip which was needed in view of the succession of disasters which lay ahead of us in the Mediterranean. By the third week of April, it was clear we should have to evacuate our Army and Air forces from Greece. This was carried out with great skill and not very heavy losses during four days following the 24th of April. The problem of Crete now remained. Early I think in April, the Prime Minister impressed with the importance of severing the sea communications between Italy and Tripoli suggested that we might take the battleship HMS Barham, run her ashore in the approaches to Tripoli and bombard the town and harbour with her main and secondary armament! This struck horror into our minds as being a crazy operation in the extreme which would result in the loss and possibly the eventual capture of one of our battleships without any commensurate gain. Bombard Tripoli by all means with ships underway, but to turn a battleship into an indifferent fort which could soon be rendered useless by air attack seemed to us the height of folly. However, what the First Sea Lord thought about it we don’t know. Admiral Cunningham was asked to carry out the operation. He dissented most emphatically and strongly with the whole idea and said he would take the Fleet to the central Mediterranean and bombard Tripoli which he did later, but the sacrifice of a valuable battleship with all their crew was no operation of war. This was one of the Prime Minister’s worst naval ideas and perhaps unfairly some of us felt it should have been killed at its inception, without having to worry the C-in-C Med with an idea of this sort. Modern ease of communication puts enormous temptations in the way of people in a position of power who are given to backseat driving. 10 The battle of Matapan, off the southern coast of Greece, took place on 28 March 1941. A British force 176 decisively defeated the Italian Navy, securing British naval dominance in the eastern Mediterranean.

One morning Tom Phillips (VCNS) sent for me and asked me what my views were as to the strategical position in the Mediterranean. We had just evacuated our forces from Greece and were waiting uneasily and wondering where the next blow would fall. I remember stressing the need for air power cum [with] sea power as a prerequisite to maintaining the command of the Mediterranean seas. I said to have unimpeded command, we should have Gibraltar, Malta, Sicily, Crete, and Cyprus. We should then not only have control of the sea routes, but could prevent the Axis overspilling as it were into Asia Minor, and so secure the Suez Canal and Red Sea for our use. I said if we achieved this, we could also so isolate hostile land forces in North Africa that they would drop off like overripe plums into our hands. But if this could not be achieved, the barest essentials for a measure of control over the central Mediterranean were Malta, Crete, and Cyprus to safeguard the approaches to Asia Minor and the Levant. He agreed, I think as did the First Sea Lord later with this proposition. The point was could we hold Crete sufficiently long to build up our air power from it, and so exercise control of the Mediterranean and deny and hamper the use of the Aegean to the enemy. The importance of Crete was recognised but alas in the short time available since Greece came into the war, little had been done by us, or them, to put the island into a proper state of defence. Furthermore, it was clear from many intelligence reports that the Germans would soon launch an air and sea invasion of Crete. We did not think the Italian Fleet would after their Matapan experience intervene with our Fleet. On the other hand, the Germans had complete control of the air, our aircraft were virtually non-existent. and their dive bombers and air transports and paratroops would be able to land in Crete. It was known that the Germans had their special Paratroop Division specially trained for this operation, and were far in advance of us at this type of warfare in 1941. It was at this juncture that the Prime Minister thought he would like a plan prepared and sent to General Wavell to hoax the Germans into landing in Crete and then inflict a complete defeat on all their troops landed. Accordingly, ‘Bomber’ Bert Harris who then was ACNS (Air), Dykes (Deputy Director Army Plans), and self were asked to prepare a plan. We did this with some misgiving as we were far from certain that our land forces, most of which had been hastily evacuated from Greece and had lost all their equipment, would be able to contain a determined parachute cum glider and air transport landing. We believed, as did the C-in-C Med, that with considerable loss we could prevent any landing by sea. I rather doubt if the hypothetical plan we drew up was much good. We had only rather out of date into intelligence information, and I expect General Wavell had other things to do than to study plans for an operation drawn up by folk, who were not completely in touch with the situation, as in fact was inevitable! The story of the air attack on Crete has been told well on more than one occasion. The Navy succeeded in their task in destroying such sea borne landings as were attempted but at very heavy cost to themselves, for there was virtually no air cover and German dive bombers had it to themselves and were faced only by the anti-aircraft fire of ships which, as already learned, was far far less effective than had been supposed. We had expanded charts laid out in Operations (F) Room so that everybody could see the course of operations. 177

I got the impression that some of our seniors and indeed the Prime Minister himself had absolutely no idea what it was like to operate under continuous air attack, and were unduly critical of Admiral Cunningham and his Fleet who in fact surpassed themselves in determination and bravery. In fact, in addition to the losses of 3 cruisers and 6 destroyers, every other warship almost without exception was damaged. It looked just at first as if we might hold Crete as the fighting for the airfields at Maleme and at other places was fluctuating to say the least of it. Very heavy losses had been inflicted on the airborne troops which were just about the pick of Germany. As we now know, the Germans were in two minds about abandoning it and the heavy casualties which they suffered made them decide never to carry out an operation like this again. It decided them against later in the war in carrying out an airborne attempt for the invasion of Malta. But the losses were very heavy on both sides, the army had lost all their equipment, not only were naval warship losses very heavy, but we lost 250,000 tons of shipping in the Greece and Cretan campaigns in the shape of supply ships, auxiliaries, transports and so on. One felt helpless as a spectator just plotting out on the charts in the Operations Room from intercepting signals just what was happening. Though Whitehall interfered during the course of the battles in the Mediterranean far too much, the C-in-C Med never lost his balance, and never, as General Wavell once did, make a sharp reply to the effect that the length of the butcher’s bill was no criterion for measuring the success of an operation. Whitehall did however make it clear at a later stage that should Admiral Cunningham call off the evacuation of the Army from Crete because of exceptional casualties, he would have the Government’s support. But Admiral Cunningham was made of the stuff of which great war leaders are made, and to our eternal relief made the signal, ‘We must not let the Army down, the evacuation will continue’. I think those of us who already had fighting experience realised the men on the spot were not far off breaking point. A thought often crossed my mind that as soon as possible those in control at Whitehall should only be people with present war fighting experience. Even among the Captains, it was clear how different judgments would be between those who had, and those who had not had naval fighting experience. Now some of our Sea Lords, First Sea Lord,VCNS, the Controller, and in fact at that time most of the Board had not yet had fighting experience. Again, hindsight is easy, but I believe that if the Army and the RAF had made preparation in the six months before, for airfield and shore defence in Crete, and if the RAF had been less rigid in their doctrine in regard to a number of advanced bases, we would have held Crete and so much facilitated at a later time our control of the central Mediterranean seas. Speculation will go on for years as to whether our decision to go to Greece’s aid was justified or not. I had much doubt at the time as we forecast, alas only too accurately, the very heavy losses to the Army, Navy and Airforce which would be the result. On the other hand, even at this time the political reasons for going to Greece’s aid were very powerful. We now know that this action we took not only virtually destroyed the crack German 11th Flieger Korps, never to be replaced, but also delayed Hitler’s timetable for the attack on Russia, so that as we shall hear later, ‘General Winter’ in Russia came to the aid of the Russians just in time. The facts are, as referred to in an earlier part of this narrative, Hitler’s correct strategical course of action should have been to finish off the Middle East before attacking Russia. This 178

would certainly have meant postponing the attack on Russia until 1942, and might indeed have influenced the Japanese to postpone their attacks on America and ourselves, which took place towards the end of the year. It is perhaps of more than passing interest to see how Russia would have stood up to a simultaneous attack on her in the spring of 1942. After the United States Fleet had been immobilised and we had perhaps lost Egypt, there can now be little doubt that Russia under these circumstances would have suffered a complete defeat and it would have been left to the USA and ourselves to fight a long-haul maritime war. Though I believe we should together have eventually won it, it would have taken longer than it did and whether or not we in this country should have been so exhausted to take any part in the final settling up is more than likely. These wider speculations are worth the study of those that follow us. May 1941 Meanwhile let us turn back to the war at sea and how we were tackling the problems in Operations (Foreign). The Scharnhorst and Gneisenau were in Brest receiving the attention of the Royal Air Force, and it was expected that soon the Bismarck would come out from her working up in the Baltic. Though it was not known, it was suspected she was well over the 35,000 tonne treaty limitations kept to scrupulously by us with the ‘King George V’ class of battleship. We now know she was about 51,000 tonnes, an immensely heavily protected and well designed Battleship, capable of 30 knots and carrying eight 15 inch guns. It became clear to us on about the 19th of May that the Bismarck and a Cruiser probably Prinz Eugen were about to break out. The story of the steps taken to intercept Bismarck and her consort before she could get into our main Atlantic trade routes are told most lucidly by Stephen Roskill in the official history. So, I will not repeat the fascinating pattern and sequence of events. On the evening of the 23rd of May just as I was leaving the Admiralty about 9:00 p.m. the first sighting report of Bismarck and Prince Eugen by Suffolk was intercepted. I had a look at the chart in the War Room, and it did not seem to me that the enemy would be intercepted by our forces until early next day. So, as it was Terry’s ‘night on’, I went back to our flat for a little sleep. One of the last images of HMS Hood, I came in soon after 8:00 a.m. to be told by Terry as he hurried along the passage to the War in pursuit of the Bismarck, taken by Room, ‘I am sorry, your old ship has gone’. It was just like being hit in the lower part of the an aircraft from Coastal Command stomach and gave one an empty incredulous feeling. I knew of course Hood’s deck armour was insufficient protection to prevent the penetration of modern 15 inch shells into the magazines, But I hoped and believed if she came into contact with Bismarck, the ships would be so manoeuvred that the range of fighting the action would be below 16,000 yards which would afford the magazines adequate protection with Hood’s heavy side armour. As it was Hood was sunk at a range probably over 20,000 yards. It was never finally decided how Hood sank. I gave a good deal of evidence at the Admiralty inquiry which disposed of rumours that 179

the torpedo heads had exploded. There is little doubt the German 15 inch shells penetrated one of the two aft main 15 inch magazines of the Hood, and blew her up. I went along immediately and got in touch with what was happening. The action and chase were within the area controlled by Operations (Home), so all we had to do was to be ready to bring in reinforcements when and where necessary. Force H consisting of Renown and carrier Ark Royal had already sailed from Gibraltar to be in a position as it were to intercept the enemy if they broke south. The Rodney, another battleship and four destroyers were ordered to rendezvous with the C-in-C, who was in King George V. The aircraft carrier Victorious with a completely scratch crew of Swordfish and Fulmars were ordered on the evening of the next day, the 24th, to carry out an attack on Bismarck. In dreadful weather they scored one hit which however did not seriously affect Bismarck. We had been called upon to appreciate the enemy’s probable course of action during the day. And as soon as it became evident, they were not returning home via Iceland, we reckoned that clearly they would make for Brest. Bismarck had a bad oil leak which left a telltale trail. We made this appreciation before in fact the German Admiral in Bismarck decided to abandon his foray into the Atlantic and make for Brest. Then our shadowing cruisers Suffolk lost contact, and it was not until about 30 hours later that she was located by a Catalina flying boat of Coastal Command. This was the most anxious time and Winston paid one or two visits to the Map Room and brought the American Admiral Ghormley, the US Naval Liaison Officer along with him. Eden also looked in from time to time. Ghormley, a nice old chap said he thought we were ‘crazy’ not to stop all Atlantic convoys, but admitted that we had the situation in hand. In bad weather, the Ark Royal aircraft carried out a successful attack on Bismarck on the evening of the 26th and scored two hits, one of which wrecked her steering gear. This sealed the fate of Bismarck. Four destroyers later that night carried out a torpedo attack on Bismarck but scored no hits. The King George V and Rodney came up in on the morning of the 27th and finally dispatched her. It was our job to see that Admiral Tovey, the C-in-C, had all the information available and the maximum number of forces were brought in together. It is one of the best examples of correct Admiralty control. This time the action was left to the men on the spot, though I seem to remember a somewhat peremptory signal being sent to Admiral Somerville to tell him not to allow himself to be engaged by Bismarck - an unnecessary injunction. I enclose a note I sent to Ludovic Kennedy, the author of Pursuit about what happened in the Admiralty War Room.11 I’ve made no attempt to tell in detail all the moves which led to the destruction of Bismarck, for not only did it compensate for the loss of my old ship Hood, but proved to the world above:A picture of the Bismarck and to our enemies in particular that attempting to break out into the Atlantic to attack our receiving a direct hit. From Katharine shipping was fraught with the gravest of hazards. The loss of very many close friends in Hood Phipps cuttings album was indeed grievous. Fortunately, some of them including the Padre (Beardmore) had left the ship before the action, but nevertheless the loss of this splendid ship left a big gap in one’s 11 WWD sent a six-page letter dated 14 January 1975 to Ludovic Kennedy, author of Pursuit: The Chase and sinking of the Bismarck, Viking, 1974, and copied it to Stephen Roskill. 180

circle of friends. Looking back on it, the Hood should have been modernised as was done to Renown. For too long in peace, she was held as number one prestige ship, and attempts to modernise her, through that reason and for lack of money, were frustrated until too late. I wrote a tribute to my late shipmates which was published in The Times. From the naval point of view the stage had been reached when it can be said that the Germans had suffered a decisive defeat and their attacks by surface warships had failed. Their two battle cruisers were damaged and immobilised in Brest with the Prince Eugen which had slipped in there after parting company with the Bismarck. The Bismarck had been sunk and the Hipper was back in Germany repairing defects which had occurred on her last cruise. However, the Battle of the Atlantic was far from won, and in fact we had to deal with the serious attacks of aircraft on Atlantic shipping and submarine attacks which were to prove increasingly threatening. We had in the previous year when the Germans attacked Norway and Denmark taken the very wise precaution of occupying Iceland, for if this island fell into German hands, our position would be lethal in the extreme. The passing of the Lease Lend Bill in March eased our position, as not only could the American naval forces give overt help, but our ships could be refitted in America thereby easing the strain on our hard-pressed dockyards. Much discussion ensued between Admiralty and Air Ministry. We wished the U Boat shelters at Brest and elsewhere and all U Boat building yards to be attacked by RAF Bomber Command. But alas they had their pattern of attack on the industrial targets and neither of these targets were particularly high on their list of priorities. The RAF regarded Bomber Command to be a weapon to strike at the hit him harder than anything before, as enemy’s economic life and planned their operations on this basis. They stuck to their guns revealingly shown by the amount of with great determination and would not be deflected, as they deemed it, onto military attention he gave to it, both at the time objects such as U boats, U boat building yards, their naval bases, and later army objectives and some twenty years later. 181

such as bridges, communications etc. We now know that our view was right and the RAF view wrong, for the report of the Strategic Bombing Survey after the war showed what very limited success Bomber Command achieved on the economic life of our enemies, and by inference how much more might have been achieved by concentrating to a far greater extent on ‘military’ targets. But this is a digression, and will I hope be considered again in the proper perspective when certain lessons are suggested from our war experiences in World War Two. Air attacks on our main discharge ports such as Liverpool further added to our difficulties, and the paramount importance of providing sufficient escorts, both surface and air in the face of the mounting scale of U Boat attacks was ever more on our minds. The monthly shipping losses rose from about 200,000 tonnes in the early part of the year to over 300,000 tonnes in June. This could not be borne for long, for our building rate of replacement ships was not a great deal more than one million tonnes a year, and as yet the huge American shipbuilding programme had not got into its stride. It was clear to us at the Admiralty that it was going to prove a race against time whether we could bring our shipping losses into manageable proportions before our war effort started to falter. We used to look anxiously at the charts in the Admiralty map room showing losses and replacements together with the volume of essential imports which must be maintained if we were not to starve. A look around the Admiralty at that time is worth a few minutes pause! Thomas Phillips, the VCNS, was very much the driving part of the staff. Quite tireless with a first-rate brain as quick aa a flash. Strategical judgement good, though a little blind to the vulnerability of warships to air attack at that time, he had as clear a picture as anybody of the naval problems which faced us. He was prepared to discuss with anybody naval problems and was no respecter of seniority or for that matter juniority. It once struck me as odd that I, as the most junior Captain in the Admiralty, often argued with him! Then Harry Moore, my late Chief of Staff in 1938 was Assistant Chief of Naval Staff (Trade), and he was quite magnificent at it. With Bob Mansergh (Captain M.J. Mansergh) as the Director of Trade, whose responsibility was to make up the convoys, do the routeing, pass to the command authorities concerned all information regarding submarines and so on. Then A.J. Phillips, ex-captain of Norfolk in the Bismarck chase, was a very competent Director of Local Defence. Ralph Edwards at that time the most outstanding Captain in the Admiralty, was Director of Operations (Home), and played no little part in coordinating the forces employed in the Bismarck chase. Charles Daniel, Director of Plans, was in the best tradition as Director of this important Staff Division. Charles Lambe was to relieve him in the middle of the year. Then of course we had as Assistant Chief of Naval staff, A.J. Power, a fine sea leader but not really quick enough at the cut and thrust of debate. Harwood our boss in ACNS (F). Bruce Fraser, an excellent Controller who did wonders to produce the new ships and repair the old ones. The First Lord was A.V. Alexander who took little part in the operational side, though, I think, was a good First Lord. The real First Lord was Winston who never lost his interest or indeed his grip on the Admiralty. Even now one would not infrequently meet him in the corridors or poring over the OIC plot (Operational Intelligence Centre) in his siren suit, 182

which contained every single form of intelligence. Much of it was of great value, as by that time the boot was on the other leg. We were able to decipher most of the German codes, whereas they could no longer decipher ours. The fact that they could decipher ours for much of 1940 was in no small measure the reason for the lack of success in the naval operations associated with the Norwegian campaign. One of the most acute brains in the country presided over this centre, Commander, and later Captain Wynn, now Lord Justice Wynn. It would be difficult on the intelligence side to estimate fully the value of this priceless information and above all the interpretation put on it by Wynn and his staff. Then we had the press side which was handled by Captains Brooking and Baxter, both retired officers of considerable ability. My old friend, John Dillon Robinson served throughout the war in the Press division. The Training and Duties Staff Division was run by Rivett Carnac, and the Signals Division which looked after all communications was headed by Llewelyn Morgan. In the Operational Research side, there were first class scientists such as Blackett, Fowler and many others whom I got to know well, when we were wrestling with problems which required acute analysis if correct solutions were to be reached.12 There were of course many others, but due to the pressure of work one only came into contact with those whom one worked with for there was little time for ‘coffee’ housing. By this time, we had a new Combined Operations Division under Mountbatten which had been set up to train, and to get built the multifarious types of landing craft required for our eventual return to Europe. Meanwhile throughout May it became increasingly clear to us that Germany was preparing to attack Russia. We eventually had the most specific intelligence of German intentions, but in spite of this fact and the Prime Minister personally warning Stalin, the latter would not give it full credence and made the most inept preparations to meet a possible German attack. June-July 1941 As the inevitable assault on Russia became more a matter of days than months, we thought a lot of how the involvement of Russia would affect us in general, in particular and more especially how it would affect our maritime problems. How did the situation then seem to us? Our Army friends in the Cabinet office and War Office were very pessimistic about the battle efficiency of the Russian army. They pointed out that Stalin had liquidated most of their best officers in the big purges which he carried out a few years previously. Our intelligence on the Russian army was exceedingly scanty. They had taken some exceedingly hard knocks from the Finns, whom they had attacked in the previous year. It was not known how the Russians had fared against the Japanese in their unofficial war of the previous years in Mongolia and Manchuria. On the other hand, the Germans had an almost unbroken sequence of rapid successes in the military field and had pretty much everything their own way. On the air side we did not have such a high opinion of the Germans, though apart from 12 Patrick Blackett, 1st Baron Blackett 1897-1974), physicist and developer of operational research, ODNB. Sir Ralph Fowler (1889-1944), mathematical physicist and weapons researcher, ODNB. 183

the scanty intelligence we had even less of Russian aircraft and their military methods of employment. Some of the more pessimistic military figures expressed the view that with luck the Germans could capture Moscow within six weeks of the outbreak of war, if they had worked out their logistical problems correctly. But some were even then, and this is before the attack, doubtful because of the almost complete lack of communications in Russia and absence of commercial petrol supplies, of Germany achieving a rapid success. They pointed out how easy a good communications system made the German task of moving quickly. Then those from the Political Intelligence Division which was headed by Sir Robert Bruce Lockhart, said there was a possibility of Ukrainians and others rising against the Russians and collaborating with the Germans. Then there was also the enormous question mark. Would the Russian people rally behind their Soviet leaders, or would they reckon this was the time to strike them down, and introduce a more humane system of government than they had suffered under for the previous generation? Many of these questions in the light of after-knowledge perhaps seem plain silly! But nevertheless, some of the questions I have posed were debated with much thought and no unanimous opinion emerged from these discussions. Then we had a look at the matter from a naval point of view. We had no opinion of the competence, efficiency and indeed zeal of the Russian Navy. We thought they were indoctrinated by [the] political tenets of communism to the exclusion of all else. We had heard what happened to the officers who visited England before the war and had allowed themselves to appear friendly. Our forecasts of the Russian Navy proved only too true, and we had little help and a great deal of obstruction from them during the war. We saw that the entry of Russia would in fact still further stretch our naval responsibilities. It was even then clear to us that the Russians in spite of their boasting were far from self-sufficient, and they would want to draw copiously on the USA and ourselves both for new materials and finished articles to fight the war. They had no aircraft at that time to compare with the Hurricane and Spitfire, and would certainly want these. Then from an overall military point of view, if the Russians could hold the Germans and many were doubtful how long they could - the balance of advantage would be with us, for we foresaw a Russian campaign as being a tremendous drain on German military resources, and would allow greater opportunities for raids on the coast of Europe and finally full scale re-entry into Europe. But these were speculations. We wondered also whether Japan would take the opportunity to attack Russia and wrest most of Manchuria and her Pacific provinces from her. Things were ominously silent from Japan. They were obviously hostile to us. They had occupied in fact French Indochina and were evidently biding their time to strike at us. We thought perhaps that there was a close tie up between the Germans and the Japanese. As we now know, it was almost non-existent and there was no attempt even to consider concerted military actions. The Japanese were probably as suspicious of the Germans as they were us of us, though it was clear they had a most healthy respect for German military efficiency. These then were some of the thoughts which passed through our minds immediately prior to the German attack on Russia. I think we felt on balance and in the very long run it was to 184

our advantage for the Germans to attack Russia, because even if they were successful, they would find as many other conquerors have done, that Russia was a completely indigestible morsel to assimilate! The attack on Russia confirmed our worst fears about Russian military efficiency. They appear to have made many mistakes about which they had been warned and which every prudent military man should avoid. Intelligence was still scarce and the news we got was of the scantiest, for the Russians did not believe in having military correspondents, and only through their Political Commissars gave out what they thought was required. However, within a few days it became apparent the Russians would want almost every article of war they could get from the Allies. Winston Churchill made it clear that despite profound differences in political ideology the Russians’ cause was ours and vice versa. We soon had underway plans to run convoys to Murmansk and Archangel, and though the Germans made the most strenuous efforts to capture these ports they never did, and with many vicissitudes these ports remained the principal supply ports of the Allies to Russia. It was about this time that Lord Beaverbrook, with a Staff of supply experts, visited Moscow to find out and to draw up a list of what the Russians wanted. It was clear that one of the main tasks of the Home Fleet would be in to ensure ‘safe and timely arrival’ of convoys at Northern Russian ports. It must have been about this time that Charles Lambe became Director of Plans and asked if I could go as his Deputy Director. John Terry readily agreed and said he would find another Deputy Director of the Operations Division (Foreign) and accordingly I transferred offices. Charles Lambe decided wisely to divide up the Plans Division’s responsibilities. I was to be in fact what the old prewar Director of Plans was. I was to be responsible for the staff side of all naval planning for the provision of types of warships, and for pretty well everything which had a planning aspect to it. I was to be regarded within the Admiralty virtually as Director of Plans and should attend the numerous meetings with the Sea Lords and others as such. He would concentrate his outstanding abilities on Combined Planning and Combined Strategy. He would work in close touch with the two other Directors of Plans, i.e. Director of Plans (Army) and Director of Plans (Air) and report direct to the Chiefs of Staff Committee. This was an eminently sound division of responsibilities. Charles rightly saw that most of the major strategical decisions had yet to be made, that in the nature of things we should move over to the offensive, and that it seemed probable sooner or later that the Americans would enter the war, and so on. Try to capture the situation in August 1941, Russia in almost headlong retreat before the Germans. We had had a number of successes in the Mediterranean, but the whole part of the northern shore, and a good part of the southern shore, were under Axis control. Our losses had been very heavy. Malta was under heavy attack because the Germans had suffered very serious losses from our ships using Malta to attack their convoys to North Africa. Our position in the Far East was very weak. There were rumbles of trouble in India, and it appeared the Japanese were establishing their position in the Far East preparatory to another 185

jump forward.The combined system worked admirably. Charles Lambe and I met every day, usually at about 9:00 and we had our staff conference. We discussed all things and everything! He kept us all, and me in particular, in the closest possible touch with all Joint Planning activities. We had to know each other’s minds absolutely and completely, for when one was absent, as indeed we were at various conferences and the like, we had to stand in effectively for each other. There’s been a book about Charles Lambe by Oliver Warner (Admiral of the Fleet), not I think a very good book. It gives to my mind an unbalanced and very disjointed picture of one of the outstanding officers of our time. Charles Lambe’s great contribution was his guidance and influence on the Joint Planning Committee and Chiefs of Staff, and indeed also the Prime Minister. Charles held this position from early 1941 to 1944, and he had a decisive influence in the reaching of many of our strategical decisions. He showed himself to be an outstanding negotiator with the Americans and was deeply respected by them. Eisenhower had an immense regard both professionally and personally for Charles Lambe. Charles Lambe It might not be out of place to give a short appreciation of this remarkable officer whose record I wrote in the Dictionary of National Biography published in 1965.13 Without any form of intellectual or social arrogance, he did many things superlatively well. The fact that he was born with a silver spoon in his mouth was I think a slight disadvantage for him, for he had probably less of the rough and tumble and knocks which less gifted and less well-heeled officers experience. An absolutely first-rate brain, widely read, with a coolness of judgement unusual for one with so many talents. He had moral courage of a high order and never suffered from what Admiral Godfrey once described as some officers’ besetting sin, i.e. O.V.V.S.O - ‘over veneration for very senior officers’. He could argue persuasively and attractively and never seemed to have any prejudices, except perhaps if someone was trying to humbug him – a trace of annoyance would then pass over his face. Widely read on many political theories. He had what I think now was an over-sympathy with views of the political left. Nevertheless, this did not affect his strategical judgement. He took a pragmatic approach to the problems which faced us and was quite well read historically. A splendid leader, he would support his subordinates and even when they erred, he would support and take all responsibility for errors on his shoulder. But above all he was an ‘easy’ man, one could always discuss any point with him without prejudice and with coolness, which was like a douche of cold water. He had the most lively sense of humour, and could retail incidents with the Prime Minister and others in a most entertaining way. His clear-cut mind saw always to the root of the problem. He was a magnificent decentralizer and never fussed over people who were working with him, and provided you kept in touch, always gave you all the support and encouragement needed. Perhaps best of all, was his balance and his strategical judgement allied to an acute political judgement. Behind all this lay a most attractive personality which however never baulked at unpleasant issues should they need to be tackled. I will not dwell on his considerable artistic talents which seemed to preserve his balance and perhaps also 13 Sir Charles Edward Lambe (1900-1960), WWD article revised appears in ODNB. Oliver Warner, Admiral of the Fleet: The Life of Sir Charles Lambe, London, 1969. Oliver Warner (1903-1976) was the author of numerous books on naval topics. 186

enabled him to give his absolute trust as I believe he did to me. Working with a friend who in fact was only one year my senior in age made for efficient and smooth working in the Plans Division. Charles Lambe eventually became First Sea Lord and died after only a very short period in this post. Though he held many important posts with much distinction he never gave better or more valuable service than when he was Director of Plans for the three war years when all the strategical decisions were made. Shortly after I left the Future Operational Section in the Cabinet Office, the Prime Minister brought about a change in the Combined Operations Organisation. Keyes was removed and Mountbatten put in his place with vastly increased responsibilities and with a seat on the Chiefs of Staff Committee. This was a move in the right direction as an immense amount of planning and design work was required and orders for craft, ships and boats placed before we could be in a position to land large military forces anywhere against determined opposition. The Americans were developing this slowly in America. I was sorry for Keyes, but he was not the man to build up a large and complex organisation to provide all the material necessary to launch an invasion. Mountbatten had all the drive and panache with a very distinct flair for material development which was so necessary in this new field. Mountbatten, I heard later, tried to persuade Lambe to let me join his organisation, but I am very glad Lambe held out and I stayed as Deputy Director of Plans. I gathered also it was suggested that I might relieve the Marine Joe Hollis who worked with Ian Jacob, to be one of the two Deputy Secretaries of the Chiefs of Staff and War Cabinet. Much as I liked Pug Ismay, I let it be known I felt I was doing an adequate job where I was in the Admiralty and still had great ambitions to return to the sea and to finish the war in a fighting capacity! To return to the War, it is difficult to single out what impressed me most at that time. The Americans had occupied Iceland in August and so relieved us of this vital responsibility. The Scharnhorst and Gneisenau had been bombed pretty frequently at Brest, but alas in mid-July the sorties of Bomber Command were cut down. Much progress had been made in protecting convoys at sea. The first of the escort carriers, Audacity, had proved her worth and with new techniques we were finding ways of dealing with the latest U Boat tactics. There was a special battle in one of the Gibraltar convoys, where we gave the U boats and German longrange aircraft a severe lesson, which forced them to change their tactics. George Creasy, as Director of Anti-submarine Warfare proved again his outstanding worth, and with others had many an argument in the special Battle of Atlantic Committee set up by the Prime Minister. It was one’s job in ‘Plans’ to sit back as it were from time to time, survey the whole picture, try to peer into the future and see what lay ahead of us and make preparations accordingly. These perhaps were some of my thoughts on becoming Deputy Director of Plans in the late summer of 1941. The exercise of a proper maritime strategy had been gravely hampered by the inadequacy of air power in the areas we wanted to operate. Time and time again both in the Norway campaign, in the Mediterranean, and off the coast of France we had suffered crippling losses through this lack. This was in part measure due to our own lack of foresight. 187

We had placed far far too much reliance on the effectiveness of ships anti-aircraft fire. There is no real excuse for this, as in 1936 and 1937 we had produced casualty tables in my own division, the Tactical Division, on the likely effect of our own AA fire, and these cannot have given any cause for satisfaction to those who mistakenly believed that ships without air cover could withstand heavy air attacks. So, the first thing to be done was to expand vastly our seaborne air potential and this meant increasing the Fleet Air Arm, building more carriers, and so on. Due to the shortage of our marine engineering capacity, the light fleet carrier capable of rapid production with a speed of 25 knots and unarmoured, was designed and production started. Then escort carriers, which were nothing more than converted merchant ships, were put in hand and accelerated. It was already clear to us that in fact the aircraft carrier was the core and basis on which naval strength must be gauged and that the battleship must now take second place, and be regarded as the escort and protection for the carrier. These views were not wholly held by the Sea Lords, but I like to think they were fervently held by many of the enlightened Captains who already had a measure of fighting experience. The old adage of ‘finding’, ‘fixing’ and ‘finishing’ came to mind, and it was clear that maritime aircraft could certainly achieve the first two and possibly the third as well. It was also clear that even greater efforts would be required to combat U boats, though in this respect the danger had not been underestimated, and an enormous programme of escort shipbuilding was underway. But a lot was needed to bring RAF Coastal Command more into the picture. Individually, they had done splendidly but even then Coastal Command was in a sense ‘the poor sister’ as regards the Air Ministry was concerned, and far too little effort had been devoted towards their material development. For instance, no A/S [anti-submarine] ‘bomb’ had yet been produced and reliance was placed upon the depth charge, modified for carriage by aircraft! However, in September a new directive was issued to Coastal Command which put them under operational control of the Admiralty. Their three duties were firstly, reconnaissance, secondly offensive action against enemy ships and submarines, minelaying and` the escort of convoys, and thirdly, the air protection of our own shipping when outside the range of our own Fighter Command’s short range aircraft. But then the broader canvas of the unfolding picture must be considered, and one often looked at those huge maps of the world in the war room and wondered what next? Two great countries were as yet not involved in the war - USA and Japan. How long would they stay out and what would be their means of entry? These were questions which posed themselves time and time again to us. September 1941 By that time the Americans were in fact already taking a considerable part in the Battle of the Atlantic. This was made possible because of the President’s especial power as Commander-in-Chief of all United States Armed Forces. US naval forces were cooperating with ours and the Canadians, both on sea and in the air, and were escorting convoys, flying patrols etc., etc. When and how would the Americans come in, for by that time we all had no doubt they would come in, and it was clear that their President realised, quite apart from anything else, that this was in the best interest of the United States. 188

Then the future of Japan was causing much speculation. Some of us thought with the successful German attack on Russia she would waste little time and endeavour to capture the Russian eastern provinces, but they may have realised that this would be no pushover for them. But then surely the ‘ripe plums’ of the British Empire, i.e. Australia, New Zealand, Malaysia, Burma and India, surely might be theirs for the asking. They must have known we were stretched strategically to the limit. Some folk in [the] Admiralty thought in view of our dangerous and overextended position that we should transfer our main effort from the Mediterranean and Middle East to the Far East. This could be argued with a deal of logic for we were in no doubt of our inability to hold to the extent required in the event of invasion threats to these members of the British Commonwealth. It could be argued that as we could not use the Mediterranean regularly for our merchantmen we might as well abandon it. However, we examined all these points and were left in no doubt that we must at all costs hold the Suez Canal and keep the eastern basin of the Mediterranean in ours or friendly hands. For if we did not, the whole backbone of our strategy would be broken. So, despite most urgent pleas for reinforcements of modern equipment and ships, we stuck to our recommendation that the Middle East must in defence matters take priority over the Far East. But this brought up the problem of the Australian and New Zealand Divisions in the Middle East. Trying to penetrate the Japanese mind is something we often tried. Nevertheless I, possibly from my many discussions with JAS Eccles, my old friend, who knew them well and spoke their language, formed the opinion they were not half as clever as they were believed to be. We had between us had some experience of the stupidity of the Japanese official mind in 1934 and 1935 when we were there. We believed they would go their own way without regard and without consulting their possible European allies i.e. the Axis powers. This, I think, has been shown to have been the case. My own feeling then was that when they had digested Indochina, they would carry out a lightning attack on Malaysia and Burma and establish themselves in Singapore, and in fact swallow also the remains of the Dutch Empire in Java and Sumatra. I thought they would go step by step. I never dreamt how wrong one would be in in this event! But there was a clear warning of this when the Americans froze the export of scrap iron and oil to Japan in either August or September. We examined the matter economically, and it was clear to us [that] action like this was a blow at their most vulnerable part of the economy and might well bring them to a halt unless action was taken. After most careful examination of all the implications of this action of the Americans by the Joint Planning Staff and others, we recommended our findings as follows: ‘ The action taken by US Government made war with Japan inevitable and we had passed the state of whether Japan would come in. We had no doubt she would come in, and in our estimate the question was when. This was estimated to be probably about 8 to 10 weeks from the beginning of October 1941’. In the event, the Japanese attacked the US fleet in Pearl Harbour without any declaration of war on the 7th of December, 1941. Strangely enough the Prime Minister at this time is 189

reported to have dissented from our findings, and said he thought ways could be found to keep the Japanese out of the war for a bit longer. Then a look at northern latitudes. The Russians had at last slowed the German advance, but whether this was because of logistical difficulties of the advancing Germans, or skilful resistance by the Russians we were not to know. But one thing was clear, we were faced with a problem of great naval difficulties escorting convoys round the North Coast of Norway to Murmansk and Arkangel. Again, here we could well have done with aircraft carriers fitted to work in Arctic waters to provide these convoys with that protection and reconnaissance which is so necessary for the long and hazardous sea voyage. We should require more escorts to do this, and we should require sufficient strength for the covering force to discourage attacks by the German battlecruisers or Tirpitz. Then back again to Mediterranean. This was a landlocked sea and many of us stressed that air power was absolutely paramount there if any form of control was to be exercised in the sea lanes. Aircraft carriers would have to be there in considerable quantities if they were to be effective in providing the necessary air cover. We certainly had not got them at that time. Provided we could hold Libya, we could maintain the Eastern Mediterranean, and provided air reinforcements in sufficient strength could be flown into Malta, we should be in a position to hold the central part of the Mediterranean in dispute, and so hamstring the flow of supplies to the German and Italian armies in North Africa. So looking at the worldwide situation in the autumn of 1941, it was clear to us we were poised for the final step which would involve the Americans and Japanese in the war. We had no doubt that the combined strength of America, Russia and ourselves would overcome the Axis powers and Japan, but it would be quite a long job. We were, I think, even then just becoming aware of the stupendous industrial potential of America which was greater than the rest of the combatants put together. We had a certain number of ‘unofficial’ talks with the Americans through their liaison teams, and found them most eager to learn. We did not find a great deal of understanding at first - this was before they came in - from their Naval Headquarters in Washington and elsewhere, though the extensive employment of exchange officers helped. The Prime Minister's visit to Argentia [Placentia Bay, Newfoundland] in the summer of 1941 to meet the American President did much to help understanding and paved the way through a lasting friendship between these two great men, which did much towards sensible and smooth working in the war.14 But it was perhaps the Far East, which gave us maritime-wise the greatest concern. The Defence Committee in a sense wished like all political figures to have it both ways; in other words, they wished to supply the Russians, to establish control of the Mediterranean and use the Suez Canal, i.e. stabilise the Mediterranean in our favour, and still be strong enough to repulse Japanese attacks on Malaysia and the Far East, even though French Indochina was 14 Rodger, pp.421-422 190

now under Japanese control. It was pointed out that Singapore was supposed to be an impregnable fortress etc., but few of our political leaders realised the shore defences of Singapore with which I had been concerned in 1934/35 were only intended to prevent invasion or assault from the sea, and were not designed to prevent backdoor attack from the mainland of Johore. We felt that it would be most imprudent to establish a fleet in the Far East which was not a balanced fleet, i.e. carrying its air component with it. We knew the strength of the RAF in those waters was very tenuous and none had much experience in working with the sea. Stephen Roskill relentlessly in Vol. 1 describes the sequence of events which led to the Prince of Wales, our latest battleship, and Repulse, being sent to Singapore. There was little doubt the First Sea Lord was strongly against the despatch of the Prince of Wales. We produced endless appreciations, pointing out such action as desired by the Prime Minister was purely making her a hostage to fortune. Unfortunately, the Foreign Office agreed with the Prime Minister that the publicised dispatch of the Prince of Wales to the Far East might act as a deterrent to the Japanese in entering the war. At our level we thought this was utterly unrealistic and were in no doubt that something far far beyond our capacity to provide would be needed to deter the Japanese from hostile action. I remember to this day vividly the foreboding I felt when we heard of the decision to sail the Prince of Wales to the Far East. It was hoped that the Indomitable, our latest aircraft carrier then working up in the waters off Jamaica would be able to join the Far East Fleet, and provide an element of air cover. Unfortunately, the Indomitable grounded in the approaches to Kingston harbour and was delayed and consequently never sent east. It is sometimes difficult to picture now the tremendous pressure under which the First Sea Lord was put by the Prime Minister. However, it is on record that the First Sea Lord was against this move, and only as a sop agreed to the matter being reviewed when the ships got to Cape Town, and Admiral Phillips had the opportunity of discussing matters with General Smuts, the Prime Minister of South Africa, and a great World War I figure. We were in plans horrified at what we regarded as a major strategical blunder fraught with the gravest of risks. We shall hear later what happened and I never realised then, that I should be one of the two officers put on to carry out a departmental inquiry into the disaster which later befell Prince of Wales and Repulse. In September, Harry Moore left ACNS (Trade) and became the the VCNS in place of Tom Phillips, who was appointed Commander-in-Chief Far East designate in the place of Admiral Leighton. Harry Moore was a good choice as VCNS though not perhaps quite so dynamic or with as much fire as Tom Phillips, but he had an immense capacity for work, even tempered, with a wide knowledge of strategical matters, well liked and trusted by everybody. Tom Phillips left UK in Prince of Wales at the end of October. 191

The damage caused by German surface raiders was considerable and up to the end of 1941 amounted to nearly one million tonnes. Now that our intelligence was good and we had at times the means of breaking the German cyphers, most of the raiders were brought to book or returned to Germany. I met Captain Rogge in 1959 at Hamburg as he had then been captain of the Atlantis. He described to me vividly his sinking by the Dorsetshire at the end of 1941.15 But the price paid by the Germans was large, and out of proportion to the results achieved. Even at that time it was thought that with the onset of long-range aircraft, the day below:This page of ED’s album was of the surface raiders was over. labelled ‘Last photos before Dunkirk’. Dogs appear in many of the photos We continued to live in our little flat in Nell Gwynne House, and on the whole nights were and were no doubt a comfort in more peaceful. There were occasional raids, but by this time much of the enemy’s bombing uncertain times.WWD was always was concentrated on our industrial towns and apart from nuisance value did not worry us or very fond of dogs. spoil our night’s sleep. The good news of Oswald’s safety had come through before the end of 1940 and both Lady Normanby and Elizabeth had heard from him. He had a foot wound which was liable to be troublesome but as far as we could gather was in good spirits. There were great hopes in due course that he would be exchanged with badly wounded or ‘grands blessés’, but there were disappointments in store for everybody. Mulgrave housed a big contingent of WAFs, and a few WRNS who worked the early warning radar sets in that part of Yorkshire. A very effective dugout had been built near the kitchen garden to which people could repair in the event of raids. Katharine, my sister-in-law, had a job in the Midlands working in a war factory. My brother had moved to Molesey, where he worked with the Department of Shell which arranged fuel supplies for the Americans. He had tried to join up but they bowled out his thyroid defects and he was not allowed to join the Army. My sister, Jane, immediately joined up with the Free French and worked for a time at their headquarters in Carlton House Terrace. She on occasion took ‘the General’ [de Gaulle] round London, and said she only once saw him smile. She was in the Nuffield Officers Club off Grosvenor Place having dinner one night when it was hit by a bomb. Apart from severe shock and bruising she was not much the worse for wear. After a spell in the hospital in Fulham Road, she went up to Mulgrave to recuperate. My father extended his ARP duties and also worked on various war agricultural activities. Charles Ackers, my brother-in-law, became timber controller in his area, and generally seemed to be pretty busy arranging for home grown timber to take the place of timber imports, which were much restricted. My nephew, David Ackers was at Eton and seemed to be enjoying himself. He wanted to go into the Air Force when old enough as he felt he would become a good pilot. 15 Atlantis was an auxiliary cruiser designed to prey on merchant shipping, captained by Bernhard Rogge. She captured or sank 22 Allied ships before being sunk by HMS Dorsetshire. 192

My job in Plans Division brought me into close contact with other departments and organisations, such as the Ministry of Economic Warfare which had the redoubtable and argumentative Mr. Dalton as its head.16 We had one or two differences with him, not because he was not efficient and competent, but because he thought we were capable of doing more than we could. He found it difficult to appreciate that there is no such thing as absolute and 100% control of the seas. It is a matter of degree, but it is beyond the limit of man to devise a system which prevents everything from finding the odd loophole here and there. Then the Ministry of Supply, and various other government departments all came our way. Not least being the Treasury, who at usually very awkward moments wanted some tonnes of gold shipped from Cape Town to Fort Knox in America, where the Americans held their immense stockpile of gold. I was Chairman of the Naval side of the Staff Operations Executive [better known as the SOE] and had to arrange a number of clandestine operations, usually with the aid of Combined Operations organisation under Mountbatten. We had to be very careful as there were a number of other organisations, such as SIS (Special Intelligence Services) who also had work to do. SOE were more concerned with acts of sabotage and such whereas SIS were concerned with special intelligence. But some more of SOE later, and various operations successful and otherwise which were hatched in the Admiralty by some pretty unusual and unorthodox folk. Then I sat on the main Political Intelligence Department Committee as the Naval representative and came closely in touch with Sir Robert Bruce Lockhart, who became a great friend, and Dallas Brooks, their Chief Military Advisor.17 Dallas and I were shipmates in Courageous in 1932-33. An outstanding officer in every way, won his DSO at Zeebrugge for great bravery. A most gifted athlete, international in at least two sports, he [Brooks] became later head of the Marines and was, after he retired, one of the most successful Governors they have ever had in South Australia. This Department dealt with Propaganda and it was very important and became increasingly so as we went over to the offensive, to link our operational propaganda with our intentions. Bruce Lockhart was quite outstanding. He had Kirkbride to help him and a number of very clever men, either career diplomats or in other walks of life. Richard Crossman was one of these and not a very satisfactory performer for he thought he knew all the answers to propaganda, and at times caused much anxiety by acting irresponsibly in his propaganda to Germany.18 My task was to keep them as it were in the strategical picture, though with some of the brighter and more irresponsible members of this organisation one had to be very discreet. On the other hand with Bruce Lockhart and Brooks one had no secrets and they were privy to all our plans and intentions. 16 Hugh Dalton (1888-1962), Labour politician, ODNB. The Ministry of Economic Warfare’s remit (WWD mistakenly calls it ‘Economic Affairs’) was to deprive the enemy of supplies. Dalton was also in charge of the SOE. 17 Sir Robert Bruce Lockhart (1887-1970), diplomat and writer, ODNB. For Sir Reginald Dallas Brooks (1896-1966), see Australian Dictionary of Biography. 18 Richard Crossman (1907-1974), Labour politician and diarist, ODNB. Bruce Lockhart wrote of Crossman in 1945 that 'I have no hesitation in saying that his virtues greatly outweigh his faults. In other words, if he doesn't win a prize for good conduct, he certainly deserves a commendation for distinguished service'. 193

Then we had a certain amount of loose contact with the operational research people which contained Professors Blackett, Fowler and many other men of outstanding intellectual calibre. Their work on analysing methods of dealing with U boats was of immense value, and jogged people out of the more humdrum methods and ideas which had been in force up to date in regard to anti-submarine warfare. Later I worked closely with the Operational Researchers. As November drew to a close there was, we all felt an impending feeling that something was going to happen. The great German offensive against the Russians had not succeeded though they were in occupation of nearly half of European Russia. Both Moscow and Leningrad were still in Russian hands and our convoys of valuable stores were getting through to Murmansk and Arkangel. In the Mediterranean we had very heavy losses as well as some successes. The aircraft carrier Ark Royal was torpedoed and eventually sank in the latter half of November. She should not have been lost, and I believe if greater attention had been paid to damage control procedure and watertight door drill, she might have been saved. Then in November the battleship Barham was torpedoed and sunk at sea by a U boat which carried out an attack with great skill. Successes were also obtained in the central Mediterranean by forces based in Malta, and our submarines and naval aircraft were inflicting very heavy losses on the Italians who were hard put to it to keep intact their communications with Tripolitania. The rate of loss on either side of the Mediterranean was very heavy and it was apparent that before long the Med fleet would be reduced to the strength it had immediately after the evacuation of Crete. Many appreciations were prepared by us on what should be our redispositions if Japan came in, for it was clear anyway to us that her entry was now probably more a matter of weeks than months. We were inclined to think Japan would attack the eastern part of our Empire as well as the Dutch East Indies, and to accept the fact that the Americans would come in. One or two of us thought the Japanese would adopt a ‘bolt out of the blue’ policy - attack first and declare war afterwards; but we thought this would be more likely to be directed as us, and not at the Americans. In other words, we thought the Japanese maritime strategy would be cautious and step by step. We were perhaps a bit orthodox and did not think the Japanese would challenge the US Fleet for command of the Pacific until they had tempted it over to Asiatic waters and substantially reduced its strength. We believed the Philippines would hold and the Japanese would be forced to attempt to reduce it piecemeal. There were ideas of reducing our strength in the Mediterranean and attempting to build up a sizeable balanced force at Singapore, but as ever the very grave shortage of fleet carriers made this impossible. If the Army could hold the Cyrenaica bulge and we could use Benghazi, our position in the Mediterranean would be strengthened, and it might as a gamble be worth reducing our strength of capital ships and aircraft carriers. The position in Singapore gave us no very great confidence. The aircraft there were inadequate in numbers. And maybe there was a feeling in Whitehall that those in the Far East did not realise the urgency of the situation and that before long they would be fighting for their lives. The air defences of Singapore were pitifully inadequate to meet a sustained assault by Japanese forces based in 194

French Indochina. There is an old adage of which we were reminded and that was, ‘If you cannot be strong in every vital theatre of war, you must decide which has priority and regardless of other effects, give that adequate forces’. It was one of the hardest things I have known, trying to look in the future and decide what was best. The Prime Minister was in a sense all for results now - very understandable, but in war one cannot let the ‘morrow’ look after itself. The terrible nemesis of our lack of preparations in those lean interwar years was about to descend on us. After all it was not till 1934 or 1935 that the ten-year rule was suspended by the Government of the day, and we were considering a period only six years after this suspension. My own views at this time, somewhat contrary to some others, but with which quite a number agreed, was that the Middle East must take priority over the Far East. For provided we held the Middle East, we could prevent the physical junction of the European Axis forces and Japan and would be in a position to dispute control of the all-important Indian Ocean. If the Middle East went and the Suez Canal fell to the Axis powers, the time would come when we would be squeezed out of the Far East by the Japanese from the East and by the Axis forces coming down from the West. Our vital oil supplies, on which so much of our war effort depended, from the Persian Gulf would be denied to us. One could perhaps argue well the other way that with a powerful Far Eastern array of forces we could maintain our position and eventually reconquer the West from the East. But the cold hard facts of life made it clear to us that it was immeasurably beyond our capacity to build up sufficient Far East forces at this stage to stop the Japanese. As the event turned out early disasters to our own forces and the virtual destruction of a large part of the main American fleet at the outbreak of war forced our hand. Perhaps in the long run fortunately, and by eliminating our chances in the Far East [it] forced us to hold on to the Middle East position, which, thanks to the steadfastness of Admiral Cunningham perhaps more than anyone else, we did. Then looking at the oceans of the world, we had been very successful in the latter part of 1941 in destroying nearly all German surface raiders and supply ships. Our intelligence was excellent and plans made centrally by the Admiralty proved singularly successful. The Battle of the Atlantic was see-sawing. We still were suffering heavy losses but our anti-U boat measures were beginning to become increasingly effective. We had fairly close contact with the Americans, and though the President had given the all clear after the Argentia Conference in the summer to close cooperation, this had not got as far as Joint Planning, and in fact we knew very little and could only guess what the American ideas were. Admiral Stark USN had been relieved by Admiral Ernest King USN as Chief of Naval Operations. Admiral Stark was a great friend of this country and saw alike in naval matters to ourselves on a wide range of subjects. Ernie King was in many ways a great man but he was a hard-bitten Yankee and at times a pronounced Anglophobe. It may well have stemmed from the fact that he took no part in World War One with Admiral Rodman’s Forces who joined the Grand Fleet, and had for many years the superiority of the ‘Britishers’ thrust down his throat by his more fortunate compatriots who had served with us. 195

We made many appreciations of what we would ‘like’ the Americans to do when they entered the war for by now it was no longer a question of whether, but when. Our plans not unnaturally called for military action to defeat Germany first, and deal with Japan later. There were overwhelming reasons for this. It was by no means certain how much longer Russia could hold out and Germany’s military defeat could be encompassed more quickly if her main army forces were engaged in Russia.
