We, in this country, were then at the zenith of our war effort or very close to it, and after that we must look to, alas, a declining war effort. The sooner Europe could be freed from Nazi rule, the sooner could the long haul be started in rebuilding her and setting free the people of Europe. Furthermore, we were in no doubt, as so clearly expressed by Winston Churchill, that Europe should be freed by Western democratic peoples, and not by a communist dictatorship from Russia. Japan on the other hand could be isolated and dealt with piece meal by classical maritime methods laid down by Captain Mahan and many other naval writers. There was NO hurry about Japan, but there was a hurry, in fact the future of Western and Christian civilisations were held to depend on a relatively early victory in Europe. Can one capture one’s thoughts at the time? We saw the glimmer of victory ahead. We had yet suffered no military disaster of such magnitude that the whole prospect of our ever winning the war had disappeared. The very serious losses from U boats were we thought at the time within sight of being contained. So in a sense, hardened to recurring losses, we looked to the future. It turned out very differently from what we thought. On Sunday, 7th December, the main Japanese carrier force attacked the main US Fleet, under Admiral Kimmel, in Pearl Harbour, and very nearly annihilated it. The only fortunate part was that the two US aircraft carriers of their Pacific Fleet were at sea at the time and avoided being attacked. At one stroke this extinguished the US command of the Pacific, and any hope they would have had in conjunction with us of disputing the control of the South China Sea. The news began to trickle through into the Admiralty, as far as I remember from about noon onwards. There had been no declaration of war and everything was very muddled. We knew a surprise attack had been made - the extent of the damage suffered was unknown. At the same time almost, and without any declaration of war the Japanese commenced attacks on the Philippines, Hong Kong, Malaysia and Singapore. One of the feelings most often expressed on hearing that the Japanese attack on the Americans was one I think of immense relief. We were in no doubt now that with the enormous industrial resources of America combined with President’s (President Roosevelt) leadership that victory would be ours in the next three or four years. The news of the extent of US losses at Pearl Harbour was kept a strict secret and even in Plans Division we could only deduce what it was. But as the days passed, it became clear it was far far more serious than when we had first heard the news. The Joint Planners immediately brought up to date and somewhat revised their appreciation of what was the best military thing to do now. I was fairly closely concerned with the preparation of these papers. 196

It was clear the Americans had suffered a massive defeat and that our ideas of linking up with them and controlling the sea communications of the Pacific was little more than a pipe dream. Of course, looking back at it now, the correct military base of the British Fleet in the Pacific should have been Singapore or Manila! But democratic nations in peace simply cannot execute plans of this nature. They just do not have the initiative. No democratic nation could ever approve for itself, a ‘bolt from the blue’ strategy, which is what both the Japanese and Germans could and did, and which confers massive initial advantages on the attackers. There are however disadvantages, which I think transcend all else, of dictatorships in war and this is a subject on which I will reflect perhaps rather later! It was becoming easier to piece together the likely Japanese strategy. We had now lost for the time being the control of Pacific Sea communications except in the vicinity of North and South America. It appeared clear the Japanese wanted to establish themselves in the Philippines, Malaysia, Java and Sumatra and in the numerous islands in the approaches to Australia and New Zealand. The great question mark to me at that time was - well and good, but has the Japanese Empire the military resources, naval, air and army to hold this vast area in the face of what will become the vastly superior military resources of the United States of America? I felt at that time that they had bitten off far far more than they could possibly digest and consolidate. After all the country’s war capacity can almost be judged in the material sense from her steel production, and Japan’s was very small compared with the US, or even ours and Germany’s. It struck us that they were taking on a gamble in which the eventual chances of success seemed remote. After all it is to be remembered the classical military teaching reminds one not only of the importance of obtaining the control of sea communications, but having the means to consolidate the use of them. Look at the map of the Pacific and not one of us thought the Japanese even if they captured every base in the Pacific would be able to hold them. Maybe some of the foregoing is hindsight, but one thing was clear that already the position of Prince of Wales and Repulse and allied naval forces in the Far East was one of extreme hazard. Perhaps the reader will wonder why ‘Planners’ seem to be able to forecast with some degree of accuracy when attacks and warlike actions will take place? There are a lot of hard facts provided by intelligence, and knowledge of timetables imposed on military communications which make for sensible forecasts. For instance, we know precisely how long it takes to mount an expedition of say ‘X’ Divisions. We know the economic effects on our enemies’ economy of the reduction or deprivation of certain essential imports. We are concerned with the weather - only certain operations can be carried in good weather, the moon has an effect because of lightness at night, tidal conditions are often vital, namely only at certain states or certain tides can certain operations be carried out. The probable availability of forces and a hundred and one other factors. All these added up, usually end up by pointing clearly when certain attacks can be launched, and where certain attacks can be expected. 197

As previously mentioned in our various ‘appreciations’ we were led by both political and military factors to the conclusion that Japan would strike in the early part of December 1941. In wartime good intelligence backed by a good political sense enabled ‘appreciations’ to be prepared which were not far off the mark when it came to crystal gazing. ‘Hunches’, such as Hitler had from time to time, are no substitute for careful examination and planning, and as we know led to irretrievable disaster. Let us look at what was going on in the South China Seas. Our prognostications had occurred and the main prop for our military position i.e. the US Pacific Fleet was no more. Tom Phillips had had some consultations in Manila with the US naval commanders, but beyond loosely coordinating their actions there was at this stage little more that could be done. It was clear to us that Prince of Wales and Repulse stationed at Singapore were in a highly vulnerable position and that it was only a matter of time before they would be destroyed by superior forces. But we were now past the stage where backseat driving could help anybody. The Prime Minister expressed the view that the time would surely come when these ships with others should ‘lose themselves’ in the South China Seas. Meanwhile, Admiral Phillips’ concern must have been with the integrity of the Malay Peninsula and wished to use his forces to disrupt the invasion of the peninsula which had commenced in the night at the outbreak of war (7th & 8th December). Such intelligence as was available to Admiral Phillips made it possible that success might attend a sortie by his two powerful ships into waters where the invasion was taking place. He accordingly set sail leaving his Chief of Staff behind at Singapore. With the expectation that firstly, he would have fighter protection off Singora [Songkhla] near where the landings were taking place, and secondly, his approach would be undetected. As it happened neither of these conditions were fulfilled, and in due course he decided to return to Singapore. Alas, a false report that enemy were landing at Kuantan deflected Admiral Phillips off his course and it was here that both below: ships were heavily attacked by Japanese torpedo planes and eventually sunk. Much has been The Prince of Wales and Repulse hit written about the causes of the loss of these two capital ships which was the biggest single by torpedoes, with a destroyer disaster the Navy suffered in World War Two.19 I have often talked about it to Admiral Philmanoeuvring in the foreground. lips’s Staff Officer Operations (Commander Michael Goodenough), who was my Assistant Picture by a Japanese pilot when Vice Chief of Naval Staff. The bare bones of this story are told admirably in Vol. One of the War at Sea. To say that the loss of these ships came a surprise to us in Plans Division would not be true, but the speed and completeness of their destruction did come as a surprise. It was a very black morning when the news came through. Admiral Pound immediately rang up the Prime Minister who made the announcement in the House of Commons that morning. I’ve often wondered whether if in Admiral Phillips’s place I would have done anything different. I and the Director of Operations (Division F) were immediately put on to conduct an Inquiry 19 Rodger, pp.455-456. Admiral Tom Phillips died with his flagship; 2081 of the 2921 of the crews were rescued by the accompanying destroyers. 198

within the Department i.e. Admiralty, into the loss of these two ships. I do not know what happened to our report as it was never quoted later, but speaking from memory, I have included some of the conclusions we reached in the following paragraphs, which endeavour to pinpoint some of the causes of this major disaster. Firstly, these ships without proper air protection should never have been sent to Singapore and thus placed Admiral Phillips in an impossible position. War entails taking risks, but these must be sensible risks, and those of us with experience of the effect of skilled air attacks on ships were in no doubt ships should not be exposed without some form of airborne protection. Though Admiral Phillips was aware of this, it is possible his lack of actual experience combined with the great gallantry of spirit made him under-rate the efficacy of Japanese air attacks. Secondly, in this event his moves on the 8th, 9th and 10th December cannot be faulted. Any of us with any spirit would have gone to Kuantan on being told of the landings at this vital area, but on reflection, he should have broken wireless silence and requested air cover. Whether this would have made much difference is a moot point. The Japanese torpedo bomber pilots were skilled and determined. A few would no doubt have been shot down, but we just had insufficient fighters and no proper air direction system for them to cope with an air attack as was launched by the Japanese torpedo pilots. I think probably both ships would have been sunk, or very severely damaged even if the sporadic air cover we could provide had been there on the spot. Thirdly, the serious damage quite early which put the Prince of Wales out of control from a single torpedo hit was to say the least of it unfortunate as it left her a sitting target, as in the case of Bismarck, for subsequent attacks. Fourthly, our air forces as with our military forces were no real match for what at that time were the cream of the Japanese armed forces. Fifthly, the results of the Japanese torpedo bomber attacks were almost precisely what had been forecast in the casualty tables compiled by us in the years before the war. So, we had no right to be surprised at what had happened. Unfortunately, the Japanese had like the Admiralty, realised the immense value of the aircraft torpedo as a weapon, and spent much time in developing it and the aircraft which carried it. December 1941 It was time to look again at the strategical position. We had perhaps over-confidently thought that with the with the entry of the Americans into the war the result was a foregone conclusion and it would be over in a matter of a very few years. These disasters, firstly the destruction of the US Pacific Fleet, and secondly, the destruction of the nucleus of our Far East Fleet, left a wide open void stretching from the entrance to the Red Sea to the West coast of North and South America. The fall of Hong Kong would be inevitable. How long could Singapore hold out without the advantage of controlled sea communications? 199

The Dutch East Indies would go, how long would Burma hold out and so on. And behind all this, could we and the Americans build up sufficient forces quickly enough to counter the eventual threat to Australia and New Zealand? These were some of the thoughts that came crowding in our minds. Could the Japanese build up as it were an outer ring of islands, so as to isolate that part of the Pacific and China seas? All these thoughts made us wonder very hard whether we should have ourselves sufficient stamina and endurance to see this aspect of the war through to the end. But we gained comfort from the thought of the perfectly staggering logistic problems with which the Japanese would be faced, and we wondered whether ab initio in our prime we could have ever taken on such a task of consolidating ourselves, as had the Japanese in the Pacific, with the remotest chance of success. At that time, we, I think, underrated the basic efficiency of the Americans and the speed and effectiveness with which they could act. It was not a happy time for anyone. We could see the eventual destruction piecemeal of our naval, air, and land forces in the Far East. They would no doubt fight effectively and gallantly, but all they could do would be delay further Japanese advances and further stretch them. We felt we had a good chance of holding our position in Burma, because of the staggering difficulties of maintaining effective supply lines for the Japanese from Japan to Burma. Rangoon [Yangon] of course was a key here, and if this could be held the Japanese invasion into Burma would never get very far. There was I think at this stage a tendency to overrate the efficiency of the Japanese and underrate the efficiency of the Americans. One did not perhaps appreciate that they (the Japanese) had made one of the biggest military strategical blunders in history by embarking on an action which called for material resources to maintain their position far far beyond their capability then, or in the foreseeable future. The more one examines the Pacific theatre, the more it becomes apparent the whole structure of a nation’s position depends on its ability to control and sustain the sea communications of these areas. The Japanese might have controlled their position in the South China Seas if they had stuck to that after the capture of the Philippines, and not, as they did, sally forthwith into the wider areas of the Pacific Ocean. The war then by the end of 1941 was all embracing and it was clear that at the rate the weapons of war were being produced and men and women mobilised, it would not last into decades as some wars in bygone centuries had. It could be decided in a very few years. Nevertheless, there were many hard years ahead. The tide was still ebbing as far as we were concerned, and by this time we were absolutely at full stretch. Joint Planning concentrated on preparing papers to show our interests with the Americans were one, and that the key issue was to finish off Germany first. We pointed out that the defeat of Germany would spell the defeat of Japan absolutely and inevitably, but that the defeat of Japan would not necessarily spell the defeat of Germany. At the end of the year the Prime Minister went in the Duke of York to see the President, and for joint discussions with the Chiefs of Staff. Lambe went in the party and kept me in touch with what was happening. If we got the Americans to agree the priority number one was the defeat of Germany, we must have as it were a cut and dried plan to show them how this 200 could be done.

It was evident re-entry into Europe was essential at the same time, but our problem was to judge the time. Meanwhile, already the Russians were calling for a second front. Winston Churchill gives us his thoughts in Volume 3 of his book ‘The Grand Alliance’ as he travelled over to America in the Duke of York. It was already clear to us now that the Americans were in, they would [be] the eventual dominant party and like to have their own way! Our problem was to get agreement in broad principles as to what our strategic priorities should be. There was already rather wild talk about the second front landing in Europe in 1942! We realised this was utterly unrealistic - much training would require to be done and a great big building programme of suitable landing craft. Quite early on we had favoured the capture of the southern shores of the Mediterranean and the restoration of this through sea route - the Mediterranean as our first priority. The arguments for occupying Algeria or Morocco to us were overwhelming for with this, the Axis forces in Tripolitania would fall into our hands like override plums. The impression we had was that the Prime Minister did not in the first case like this very much. He favoured possibly landing in the Balkans, or in Europe, or even going up through Spain. These ideas may only have been put out to stimulate us to further thought. But the more we looked at it, the more we favoured landing in North Africa in Algeria where at any rate we should not get very determined resistance. The President was always in favour of an early landing in North Africa, though it was some time before he carried his Chiefs of Staff with him. The Prime Minister’s memo quoted in his book (vol 3) giving the proposed plan and sequence of the war, sets forth clearly his ideas and indeed those of the Staff. We had quite a number of looks at this, in the drafting stage and played some small part in its drafting. This is the first occasion we had met our opposite numbers in America. Lambe had a tough row to hoe with the American Director of Plans - Rear Admiral Kelly Turner. We found that the President’s views strangely enough often were closer to our Staff ’s view than those expressed by his own professional and military men. The political importance of landing in Europe must never be forgotten, but it was for us to be able to advise when this could be done without the prospect or indeed the certainty of a bloody nose! At the end of the year, I went up and spent a short and pleasant weekend at Mulgrave. We had good news of the children and old nanny in Canada. One of Charles Lambe’s wisest moves was to make a rule that he always take the same day off each week regardless of meetings. If he had not made this rule, he would in all probability have worked a seven-day week for months on end to no good effect on his judgement. I always took his place at meetings when he was away and consequently had a few nearly all-night sessions at Chequers when the Prime Minister wished to consider strategical plans, either with the Chiefs of Staff or occasionally only with the First Sea Lord. Ministers had little say in the strategic direction of the war. The Prime Minister was in fact, I think correctly so, the PM and Minister of Defence. It is true that there was a Defence Committee which was called from time to time to consider major issues of policy, and in this they did wonderful service. But it would be true to say the Prime Minister ran the war in a military 201

sense on the advice of the Chiefs of Staff Committee, or perhaps one might suggest occasionally with the grudging acquiescence of the Chiefs of Staff! But it was never to be forgotten that in the final analysis, the Prime Minister never ordered any action against the unequivocal advice of the Chiefs of Staff. His experiences, perhaps in the First War had warned him of the dangers of flying right in the face of considered military advice. We were absolutely at full stretch at the Admiralty. The problems were coming in thick and fast. We started as a rule at 9:00 a.m. and went on pretty well every night till 11:00 p.m. and often till 2 or 3:00 a.m. One of our problems was to produce carefully balanced ‘appreciations’ in answer to the Prime Minister’s ‘Prayers’ for consideration the next morning. As these requests sometimes did not reach us till midnight one had sometimes to do a sustained bout of work to get them into shape in time. The Prime Minister’s request usually came in the form of ‘Prayers’. We not infrequently got them either typed or in longhand in red ink, at literally any time, missives like this – ‘Pray let me have the naval view on etc’, and ‘Why cannot action be started within 24 hours?’, with a tab on it ‘ACTION THIS DAY’. Sometimes we used to dub the more impractical of these missives as ‘MIDNIGHT MADNESSES’. However, there were many indeed very much to the point and our aim always, however difficult and however intractable they may have been, was to take an imaginative and realistic view of them. above: In Plans Division we had some first-rate Commanders and above all skilful and accurate Photos of Georgina and Johnny, taken draftsmen. Saumarez and Oliver were the two who did much for me, both alert, clear in the Shrine Peace Memorial park, thinkers and admirable draftsmen, though Saumarez sometimes liked to insert a little acid Toronto into his observations and minutes! We were tremendously lucky with the girls in the office who cheerfully would take dictation at any time of the day or night and gave of their very best. A facility for clear and rapid dictation is an absolute must for a responsible Staff Officer in war. Let us get back to the New Year and try to recapture our feelings. We realised perhaps the next six months would be absolutely critical, for not only must the Allies make and execute the right plans, but we in this country would have to prop up and assist our newfound allies who had suffered grievous setbacks, and were in no sense yet pulling their weight. In fact, almost the entire weight of the war maritime-wise was on our shoulders and ours alone, and we had anxious thoughts how far and how long could we shoulder this almost insuperable burden without partially collapsing. We remembered the enormous strain to which the Mediterranean fleet had been subjected to during the evacuation of Greece and Crete and how near some had been to breaking point. This strain was to be now worldwide in so far as maritime affairs were concerned, for every hour of the day we had a ‘battle’ on our hands. It was indeed a period where one could say the issue was in the balance.Vol. 2 of The War at Sea tells in majestic tones without the least trace of prejudice the story of grave happenings, how they were met, and how we braced ourselves as never before in our long history for the future. There was a feeling, I think, even more so than at the time of the Battle of Britain, that we were living and taking part in one of the great historical periods of our country. 202

The news of the Prime Minister’s and Chiefs of Staff ’s Conferences in Washington was encouraging, and it was perhaps only then we realised the staggering results of which the Americans were capable in war material. Some of the figures reported by the Prime Minister, and given in some detail in Vol. 3 of his Grand Alliance, tell of what might be expected. We had heard the Prime Minister had got rather overtired in America but we had little anxiety that his robust constitution would soon put him back into his usual form. I now had some further thoughts on our shipbuilding programme and became convinced we wanted more and more aircraft carriers, knowing that aircraft can be built quicker than ships and with the prospects of tremendous naval aircraft supplies from America, I was sure that we should go ahead imaginatively with a large building programme. This took a bit of pushing through but with the help of Admiral [Sir Arthur] Lyster, the then 5th Sea Lord, we got an impressive programme underway. But the ‘lotus years’ between the wars hampered us at every turn. Having only just got control of our Fleet Air Arm, we had as yet nothing like enough of the right type of aircraft for naval use. All we could get, with a few honourable exceptions, were land based aircraft such as the ‘Spitfire’ converted for sea use. But the advent of the robust and stronger type of American naval aircraft held out great hopes for us. Then I thought we might use the hull of the battleship Vanguard, then building and convert her to a carrier. It was clear Vanguard would not be required in the war with the enormous preponderance of this type of warship and that we could not have enough aircraft carriers. I found among my contemporaries enthusiastic support for this idea and started an investigation into how this could be done. It was clear from these investigations that she could be converted into a very fine redesigned type of armoured aircraft carrier, and completed probably quicker than she would have been as a battleship. January 1942 It was difficult with so many events crowding in on each other to keep a balance. Perhaps not much has been said of the Battle of the Atlantic for in those days this was always on our minds - we looked at the weekly losses and weekly import figures which at times came perilously near to the minimum figure required to maintain our war effort and feed our people. Towards the end of 1941 we were it seems going some way to getting the measure of the U boat in the areas where they were operating. The changes of areas of operation combined in later years with different tactics made possible by the introduction of the ‘Schnorkel’ and ‘homing torpedo’ brought a new dimension to the submarine threat which always threatened our capability of continuing the war. With the advent of firstly Russian and then American participation our naval responsibilities had vastly increased. To keep Russia in the war a tremendous volume of supplies had to be shipped around the North Cape of Norway to Russia - it may well one day be judged that the impact of these supplies on Russian morale and their capability to fight on, made the ultimate difference in Russia between total defeat in 1942 and total victory in late 1944. It is from this background that the value of these operations to keep Russia supplied may in the end be judged. Two large convoys were escorted to Russia in January and another two in February. But we had little naval support from the Russians and no thanks! Similarly, one 203

might have imagined that the addition of the American naval effort to our problems would have eased the strain. In fact, in the opening months and in fact until almost towards the end of 1942, the reverse was the case. The Atlantic was for responsibility divided down the middle into two halves. We looked after the eastern half and the Americans, assisted very materially by the Canadians, the western half. The German U Boat Command was quick to see where they could achieve most of their U boat effort and transferred in January their main U Boat effort to the western half of the Atlantic which was now an American responsibility. They soon reaped a rich harvest and the gravely mounting losses followed. Something like three million tonnes of shipping were lost in the first six months of 1942, and a substantial proportion of this was British. But what surprised us was that the Americans had absolutely no organisation whatever for protecting shipping off their coasts. No convoy organisation, no control of shipping organisation, in fact there was nothing at that time in the United States Navy Department which remotely corresponded to Trade Division and Ministry of War Transport, which tightly controlled every ship’s movements and what went in her. The First Sea Lord went over to America mid-December 1941 and was there for nearly a month discussing with the Americans the two great maritime nations’ respective needs. Lambe was with him for part of the time, and we were kept closely in touch with whatever was happening. Frankly in moments of irritation we felt that the American Navy Department were slow to learn and obstinate putting into effect sensible seamanlike measures. We turned over to them 24 first rate anti-submarine trawlers which we could ill afford. We offered 10 of our corvettes and also a squadron of Coastal Command maritime aircraft which operated from Rhode Island. But more of this later. We had ever since the summer of 1940 given all our war experience and this was impressive in size and value to the Americans. The year started in the Mediterranean with our land forces in occupation of the Cyrenaica bulge [eastern Libya] and once again we could start using Benghazi which would greatly help us ensure regular supplies of essentials to Malta. Malta was always a key to our position in the Mediterranean for with it being used as an active air, submarine and a possible surface ship base, we could and did threaten and impede Axis supplies to their forces in North Africa. One could not but help regarding our position in North Africa and the Mediterranean very much as a matter of communications. Could we supply our forces round the Cape with a journey of say 8000 miles more surely and more regularly than the Germans could across the 100-mile gap in the central Mediterranean between Sicily and Tripoli? Events in the Mediterranean finally showed that because of our superior ability to supply over 8000 miles, we defeated the Axis forces who relied on little more than the 100-mile sea passage. Alas, General Rommel started a counter offensive early in January just as a raid, and it proved so successful that we were soon pushed back almost completely out of Libya. I have often wondered if the military command on our side had been more skilful and may be more resolute at El Agheila in January 1942, when Rommel attacked, whether the whole story of the subsequent Mediterranean campaign would not have been vastly altered in our favour. This setback was a sad blow to us as it was so clear that the sea control of the Mediterranean rests in no small measure on control of the air above these narrow seas, and this must in the main 204 be provided by aircraft based on nearby airfields.

However, it was clear as a result of our successes in interrupting the sea communications between Italy and Tripoli, that a major effort was about to be launched by German aircraft against Malta. Convoy operations were planned from both Egypt and Gibraltar to reinforce Malta. But the Far East was where we appreciated that an unrelieved succession of disasters would below: befall us. We thought much about it and produced a number of a military appreciations, all German Tank and crew, North Africa of which indicated we should lose Malaysia, and Singapore would not be capable of holding from K Phipps cuttings album. out for a great length of time, and that the Philippines would fall, and in due course the whole of Java and Sumatra would go. And finally, we could see nothing to prevent the Japanese establishing themselves in New Guinea as the first stage of a threat to Australia. However, unless the Americans failed to rebuild and repair their fleet and, which we thought most unlikely, proved themselves without the will to fight, we guessed contrary to some opinions expressed in Australia that at this stage it was unlikely any attempt would be launched to capture Australia and possibly New Zealand later. In spite of the speed of the Japanese successes and their great toughness and ability to travel light, we just could not see with their industrial and logistic resources how they could go further afield to Australia and New Zealand. But this though perhaps long-term consolation did not blind us to what was happening in the Far East. Malaya was being overrun at a speed far greater than the Army thought likely. Our military effort in spite of a few isolated cases was utterly disappointing, the Air Force with their inadequate numbers and types of aircraft were soon wiped out of the sky, and as we have already heard, our main naval forces had collapsed with the loss of Repulse and Prince of Wales. One felt at that time the Japanese had very much their first eleven out, brim-full with confidence and fanatical bravery, and our forces in the Far East were rather of the second or third eleven. One cannot be strong everywhere, and even General Wavell’s great personal courage and inspiring leadership as the overall Supreme Commander could not stem the rot. In slight contrast, or was it better publicity, the Americans appeared to be putting up a better fight in the Philippines, though in the early part of the new year Manila fell and not long afterwards their island fortress of Corregidor. General MacArthur on leaving said ‘we will be back soon’ and in fact his robust spirit epitomised the very gallant effort put up by the US forces in the Philippines. But the Japanese were not wasting time. The Netherlands East Indies were overrun in February and on the 15th of February, one of the most sombre days in our history, Singapore surrendered. This was to have far reaching effects politically. It was the first time that a large British army had surrendered to an Eastern power. We kept on pumping in reinforcements right up to the last moment. How wise this was is hard to justify. Perhaps in the cool light of after-knowledge we should have called a halt early on and written off Singapore, but was this really possible? After all, Singapore had the reputation with the public of being the most 205

powerfully defended fortress in the world. In the first five weeks of the year no less than 45,000 men and immense quantities of war material were landed at Singapore and it was only a week before its capture that further reinforcements were stopped. On the other hand, if we had been able to slow down drastically the advance of the Japanese down the Malay peninsula, it could be contended that we might have stopped them short of Singapore. Nevertheless, I still think this is doubtful and the Chiefs of Staff and Government were faced with that dreadful decision of when to write off a military commitment with the tremendous emotional connotations which such a decision would entail. With the fall of Singapore, it became clear the whole position in the Java Seas, in Sumatra, Java, Celebes and New Guinea would have to be abandoned. Consequently, the special command known as the ABDA [American-British-Dutch-Australian] command was dissolved. Nobody could have taken a more courageous and robust view than General Wavell, but one man alone cannot retrieve a situation precipitated by years of laggardly preparations. Finally, we had some hope the considerable Dutch, American, British and Australian naval forces would give a good account of themselves. This they did but were almost all annihilated in attempting to prevent the invasions of Bali, Java and Sumatra. The Battle of the Java Sea [February 1942] shows the great determination and courage of all units, and not least by the Dutch Admiral [Karel] Doorman. But the odds were against him too heavily, not only did he have inadequate air reconnaissance but also a mixed force of ships of different nationalities who had never worked together before. One of the sorrier parts of this story is to relate that rather more than half the prisoners taken in these naval actions died in captivity in Japan because of the appalling conditions under which they lived. However, one thing was clear, namely at well planned naval operations like this, the Japanese were not amateurs and the fighting efficiency of their ships was high. February 1942 Whilst these events in the Far East were perhaps engrossing much of our attentions, especially as there was little sign of the momentum of their widespread attack subsiding, there were also major problems at home. The German Battlecruisers, Scharnhorst and Gniesenau were at Brest and we appreciated they would make a determined attempt to escape up channel to their home ports. Careful reconnaissance over the channel was kept by Coastal Command aircraft, and in the first few days of February we distributed an appreciation of enemy intentions, and as recorded in Vol 2 of the Naval History, the Admiralty forecast with remarkable accuracy the sortie of the German Battlecruisers with their attendant destroyers up channel. We had worked out with Coastal Command details of what action to take in the event of a break[out] up channel. In the event on the 11th February, the Germans put into execution a very well laid plan to break up channel. Due to radar failures in two of our vital reconnaissance air sorties we did not get wind of the Germans’ move until the late morning of the day following their departure from Brest, and attacks were delivered piecemeal by Coastal Command torpedo planes, and the very gallant No. 825 Fleet Air Arm Squadron equipped with Swordfish and commanded by Lieutenant Commander Esmonde whom I had trained as a torpedo pilot in Courageous in 1932. The attacks by aircraft were not well coordinated and as expected 206

Bomber Command confirmed that however gallant their air crews were, they were unlike the Germans quite incapable of attacking moving ships with the remotest chance of success. Esmond and all his squadron were lost in the attacks and I was glad that this fine officer, who had already attacked the Bismarck, was awarded a posthumous VC. Destroyers from Harwich pressed home an attack in poor visibility but failed to get any torpedo hits. However, neither the Scharnhorst nor Gneisenau got off scot free for both were mined heavily by mines laid by Coastal Command and Bomber Command aircraft. We did not know this at the time. The fact that these ships could apparently escape unscathed up channel caused a wide outcry and much criticism, and as a result Mr. Justice Bucknill was asked to conduct an inquiry into the matter. It was felt this was a major defeat for us. But the German staff with more prescience echoed what some of us in the staff thought at the time, namely, a clear-cut tactical victory for the Germans but a strategical victory for us in that these powerful ships were no longer situated in a position where they could gravely threaten our central Atlantic sea communications.20 The inquiry concluded that Coastal Command’s organisation for and efficiency in reconnaissance was inadequate and that as we knew, Bomber Command were of little use in attacking moving targets at sea. Furthermore, the inquiry confirmed what many of us felt at the time, namely that the command organisation between Admiralty and the almost independent three RAF Commands i.e. Coastal, Fighter and Bomber, was not nearly close enough. Again and again war experience continued to emphasise that the torpedo carried by aircraft was far, far and away the best and most effective weapon to use against ships. I remember so well the arguments we used in the mid-1930s with Air Staff officers, namely that a torpedo makes a hole in the ship which lets water in and sinks it, whereas a bomb makes a hole and usually lets little more than air in and it remains afloat! But this is a digression! So as to complete as it were the denial of French Biscay ports to heavy German ships, it was decided to work out a plan to destroy the lock gates and the dock at St Nazaire which was the only place in the coast of France where the Tirpitz could be docked. Preparations went ahead in this very gallant and successful operation of landing commandos at St Nazaire and blocking up the entrances took place on the 28th March. We suffered heavy casualties, especially in ships, but the inspiring and unflinching leaderships of Commander Ryder, Colonel Newman and Lieutenant Commander Beattie in face of the hottest opposition resulted in our triumph. There was hardly a sea left in the world where we were not operating. But perhaps what caused us almost more anxiety than anything else were the heavy and what we believed largely unnecessary shipping losses off the American coast and Caribbean, but more of this later. In northern waters the Russians had frustrated the German attempts to capture Petsamo, the Russian nickel port. But it was clear to us the German Naval Command regarded the disruption of our supplies to Russia as their number one aim. 20 See Rodger, p.463. Rodger also argues that the ‘Channel dash’ of the Scharnhorst and Gneisenau was a tactical victory but a strategic setback for Germany. 207

The fighting in Russia was very much of a seesaw nature and at times the Germans almost came within sight of final victory. The Tirpitz set out to attack one of our convoys to Russia PQ12 in March. This was covered by the Home Fleet and Admiral Tovey eventually had a sighting of Tirpitz from one of his reconnaissance aircrafts. It was attacked by some Albacores from Victorious, our aircraft carrier, but alas had no success. This was due to lack of training which is so essential with torpedo aircraft. The Tirpitz missed both convoys and as a result of these operations we gave much thought to what was best and where the future lay. It became increasingly obvious to us that the passing of these convoys to Russia, which meant a sea journey about equal to crossing the Atlantic, was a major fleet operation. In other words, each convoy would have to be covered by the Home Fleet. This naturally in its turn slowed down the cycle of convoys which it was possible to pass round North Cape, and was the cause of many ‘Prayers’ from the Prime Minister. Why could we not have a more frequent convoy cycle? No doubt the Prime Minister was being needled by Stalin, who always kept in the background the vague threat that he would do another ‘double cross’ on us and make a separate peace with Germany. I don’t think for one moment the Prime Minister was taken in by these ‘hints’ but unfortunately they were given a measure of credence by the Americans. There were the usual arguments between Admiral Tovey, the Commander-in-Chief, about too much interference from Whitehall. There was a measure of truth and justification in these protests. Many of the interventions were of vital use to the C-in-C but every now and again some should not have been sent. We thought at the time that the First Sea Lord [Admiral Sir Dudley Pound] was inclined to intervene too much, though with the rule of wireless silence at sea, this has at times full justification. At the First Sea Lord’s evening sessions which often Ralph Edwards, D.O.D (H) and I used to attend, we protested against too much intervention. The First Sea Lord took our protests in very good heart but did not often follow our alternative suggestions! I suppose having special decrypted information available there is almost an unbearable tendency to intervene and forget it is the man on the spot under conditions vastly different from the War Room at the Admiralty who has to decide what to do. Then a redoubtable character, Sir George Binney who was at Summerfields with me, and who was mixed up with the Ministry of Economic Warfare, kept bothering us to prepare a scheme to rescue some Norwegian merchant ships with their valuable cargoes, mostly ball bearings, from Gothenburg. This was done. We had the gravest doubts whether it would succeed if the Germans were reasonably alert, which in the event proved to be so. Of the ten Norwegian ships which sailed, only two reached Britain, the rest being sunk either by German surface craft in the Skagerrak or by German aircraft. February 194221 This must have been the occasion when I travelled from York to London in the same train as Archbishop Temple, who was then Archbishop of York. We had a long and stimulating conversation and his attitude and outlook was delightfully robust. He picked out the great 21 WWD changed the position of the first paragraph following the heading and inserted it here but seemed uncertain precisely when the meeting with Temple took place. 208

moral issues of the war and said that we must not only prevail, as assuredly we would, but continue with the high spirit of endeavour and unselfishness which the war had brought out. He looked forward to an awakening of the Christian spirit. Though he did not mention it, he was I think going down to see the Prime Minister to be offered the See of Canterbury and Primate of all England.22 A conversation and meeting with Archbishop Temple always left one feeling better both inside and outside! His robust and cheerful appearance made one take courage and his inward humble but stupendous intellect encouraged one to look outward and forward to the greatness of a Christian life, if anyone had the sense to see and grasp it. But more later of Archbishop Temple, one, if not the greatest of the archbishops who have sat in St Augustine’s seat in the last century. Much was happening in the Mediterranean in March. It was evident that the enemy were building up their Air Force in Sicily with a view to neutralising Malta and allow their forces in North Africa to be supplied at sea without hindrance. The problem of Malta was getting critical. We had worked out precisely what was the minimum tonnage of imports which was required to keep the population from starvation and to maintain the war effort. Convoys were run from both ends of the Mediterranean; one had to be abandoned but the second under Admiral Vian who fought a very skilful battle of Sirte with units of the Italian battlefleet.23 It was becoming clearer and clearer that who[ever] was in a position to use Malta, would result in the ultimate fate of the Mediterranean seas. The Germans were building up day by day with their Air Force in Sicily. We were reinforcing with major carrier operations the fighter strengths of Malta, in all nearly 150 fighters were flown in by carriers to Malta in April and May. But the situation in the Far East steadily went from worse to worse. Though this was expected, somehow one always thinks that one’s worst fears will not be realised however logically they have been based! After the fall of Singapore, the Japanese wasted little time in forcing their way across the Kra Isthmus.24 It had been hoped we might hold them in that area of very difficult communications, but almost before we knew what had happened Rangoon fell, and our forces in Burma were committed to a fighting retreat up the centre of Burma [Myanmar]. The Japanese wasted little time and soon occupied the Andaman Islands which are strategically placed to control the Bay of Bengal. In fact, we did not see them making any strategical mistakes in the conduct of their campaign. Almost simultaneously with the fall of Rangoon, Java surrendered and shortly afterwards a heavy air raid took place on Port Darwin on the northwest coast of Australia. We anticipated Ceylon [Sri Lanka] would be the next place to be attacked, though because of their other commitments we doubted whether at this stage they would attempt to occupy it. In fact, early in April the main Japanese naval air forces attacked Colombo and Trincomalee, causing us heavy casualties, and at sea. Dorsetshire and Cornwall were on their way to meet Admiral Somerville, who was by that time in command of our seagoing forces, were sunk by Japanese carrier born aircraft. The Japanese were by then in 22 William Temple (1881-1944), ODNB. control of the Bay of Bengal. Their powerful carrier forces were as it were at large in the Indian Ocean and the Admiralty, albeit reluctantly, decided the Fleet must be withdrawn from Ceylon to the east coast of Africa. Nobody could possibly cavil at this time, and we felt certain at the Admiralty that we must extend the enemy’s communications until we were in a position to build up and return to the areas which had previously come under our control. It happened as we now know that the Japanese main carrier forces withdrew to the East to prepare themselves for further operations in the Pacific, and so there was almost a vacuum between the east coast of Africa and the Malacca Straits where there were no major naval forces. But at this stage our naval forces in the Far East were mostly of the second eleven, the old R class battleship and no modern aircraft carriers. It was not very apparent where the Japanese would strike next and what their strategy would be. They were clearly in a state of unstable equilibrium and would either have to go on or go back and consolidate. Their wisest move would have been to go back but none of us thought for one moment they would do that. April 1942 It was I think toward the end of March or early April that as a result of the profound concern felt at the apparent complete lack of any sensible organisation for the protection of shipping in the Caribbean and off the Atlantic coasts of America by the US Navy, the First Sea Lord [Admiral Sir Dudley Pound] was sent over to America to urge them to put their house in order. I was chosen to go with him and briefed myself fully up to date on what was approaching a disastrous situation. The major losses were taking place off the American coast, [and] some outstanding successes had been achieved by the U boats in the Caribbean which boded ill for the vital oil traffic from the Gulf ports. To us it was incomprehensible that further and more active steps were not being taken and it was agreed that the First Sea Lord should urge on Admiral Ernest King, Chief of Naval Operations, and that I should do the same to their Director of Plans, Admiral Kelly Turner. I took passage from Prestwick to Dorval (Montreal) in a Liberator bomber in conditions of pretty acute discomfort. Passengers were accommodated in the bomb compartment in which there was no heating. As we flew at 25,000 feet, and this compartment was pretty draughty, it was to say the least of it cold. We had arctic clothing and were supplied with oxygen masks as the aircraft was not pressurised. We changed masks every 30 minutes throughout the trip as the one which was being worn froze up in half an hour. So what one did was to change masks every 30 minutes and sit on the frozen one to unfreeze it! We were thankful to arrive at Dorval and though there was some snow about it was sunny and there was some warmth in the air. I was met by Air Chief Marshal Sir Frederick Bowhill, C-in-C late of Coastal Command, and given a very warm welcome. A splendid seaman at heart, whose forthright views did not always appeal to the Air Ministry when he was Commanderin-Chief, Coastal Command. He fixed up an aircraft to fly me to Washington straight away which I reached later that morning. I was met by one of our missions and went on to see the First Sea Lord who had arrived the previous night at the Wardman Park Hotel on the outskirts of Washington, where we were accommodated. 210

I had the next room to the First Sea Lord and was a little surprised to find his room guarded by G men who when I first knocked at his door stuck a gun in my ribs and asked me my business in no uncertain tones. We were given offices in the National Public Health Building not far from the Navy Department and soon settled in. I worked with our Joint Staff there, and we found at our level they could not have worked closer and with more understanding than they did with us. I asked what had happened to Public Health Department of the United States and was told that the President had given them 48 hours to clear out of their Washington offices as he guessed Public Health would have to function from the country during the war! I was deeply impressed with the clean lines and brightness of everything in Washington and above all one’s eyes goggled the shops in the main streets which were overflowing with things we had forgotten about. London seemed dirty and drab compared with Washington. Our American hosts could not have been kinder or more generous but accustomed as one was to wartime London diet - I was about 9 ½ stone - it was hard to do justice to the meals which were placed before one!25 We soon had our papers ready which I passed to their Director of Plans for consideration the next day. This picture of WWD was taken some years earlier coming off a sortie from I have been warned Kelly Turner was a very hard bitten ‘Yankee’ with no particular love for an aircraft carrier. He was no stranger the British and that he was very much Admiral King’s (their Chief Naval Officer) man. to the rigours of travelling in whatever However next day I started my discussions with him whilst the First Sea Lord was doing the aircraft was available. same with Admiral King. I soon found Kelly Turner was no great believer in convoys, as a means of protecting shipping against U Boat attack. He said in certain cases they were all right but only IF you had sufficient escorts to protect them. I immediately questioned him on what he meant by sufficient escorts, and when he gave a figure, it was clear that this would never be reached in the foreseeable future. He was echoing Admiral King’s views expressed to the President and Mr Churchill in March that ‘inadequately escorted convoys were worse than none’, which was absolutely contrary to all our experiences. Admiral Kelly Turner evidently was arguing to a brief given him by his Chief and seemed absolutely impervious to any form of argument. At the end of the forenoon, I was somewhat depressed as nothing I had said had apparently shifted his views, though I could see they had fully shifted the views of other members of his Department who joined in the discussions. I pointed out, on the US side of the Atlantic the appalling total of shipping losses were approaching 1½ million tonnes for the first three months of the year! What surprised me was that the enormous amount of information which we had given to the US Naval missions on this subject ever since the war [began] had not filtered through or been assimilated by the Navy Department. 25 WWD was also not accustomed to the level of central heating in US hotels. He told a story that when he and another officer could not sleep at night because of the central heating, and of course the windows did not open, they found their way down to the basement and managed to switch off the boiler! 211

So I went out and had lunch in Massachusetts Ave and after lunch went into a bookshop where I espied Captain Mahan’s classical work on the employment of sea power.26 I quickly turned up the parts which deal with the protection of commerce where the precepts for convoys were clearly and unequivocally laid down. I noted the parts and appropriate references and returned to the US Navy Department Planning Division after lunch. I tried another tack and said something to the effect to Admiral Kelly Turner – ‘I expect you have read that famous American Captain Mahan’s book on the Influence of Sea Power, etc. etc.’ He replied that he had and he guessed Captain Mahan was a wise guy. I immediately said there can be no further disagreement between us, for he lays down clearly and unequivocally the requirements to adopt convoy whether escorted or not, if commerce is to be protected! He looked up at me and said ‘Sure, Captain you are right, but you see Admiral King thinks they must be fully protected if the system is to work’. I said words to the effect – ‘Surely you have impressed your views on Admiral King - after all you are the Director of Plans and here is the lesson plain and clear for all to see’. He said, ‘Well you see, Captain, we Americans have to learn most things the hard way’. To which I replied, ‘Well and good, but you are learning this mostly at our expense, and surely is not a loss of one and a half million tonnes of shipping enough of a lesson?’ Anyway he did admit to the correctness of my views but it was alas clear to me he was partially dominated by a very intractable character, in the shape of his C.N.O, and I then learnt it was just not done in the US Navy for Staff Officers to argue the toss with vehemence and conviction with their Commanders-in-Chief etc. etc. I saw in a glimpse the advantage of our system for whatever could be said of Admiral Pound or the other Sea Lords, they never prevented one arguing with them. But it was clear Kelly Turner was not of the high calibre required to be Director of Plans to the Navy Department which had the biggest Navy potential of any country on earth. However, I think a certain amount of good was done. Captain Creasy and our experts came over and helped them set up a proper convoy organisation. Maybe, the Prime Minister’s urging on the President and his special envoy, Mr Harry Hopkins, may have accelerated matters. The American official historian, Captain Morison, was scathing on this part of the US Navy’s war effort. He said: The writer cannot avoid the conclusion that the US Navy was woefully unprepared materially and mentally for the U boat blitz on the Atlantic coast. He further believes that this unpreparedness was the Navy’s own fault. They had no plans ready for a reasonable protection of shipping and were unable to improvise them for several months.27 One cannot but help feeling there was a slight similarity between this and Admiral Jellicoe’s reluctance in World War One to introduce Convoy. It was not until the end of July that the submarine menace was fully met by a properly organised convoy system. It is quite possible 26 Alfred Thayer Mahan, The Influence of Sea Power upon History 1660-1873, 1890. His text had a lasting impact on naval thought in many countries. 27 Samuel Eliot Morison, History of the United States Naval Operations in World War II, vol.1, pp.200-01. Morison was a Harvard professor of history, appointed official historian in April 1942 and allowed first hand access to sea-going operations; his history comprised 15 vols, published 1947-62. Rodger discusses US attitudes to convoys, pp. 487-491. 212

that the unnecessary and grievous shipping losses in the first six months of 1942 caused the prolongation of the war by quite a considerable extent. Historians and analysts in the decades which lie ahead may be able to express an opinion on this. I had a number of further meetings for the Navy Department people and found in some respects they could move very quickly and were less inhibited than we were, certainly in regard to material developments. But they were at times exceedingly loathe to change ideas. I often used to tell them when they were being more than usually obstinate, that the proposals under discussion were not intended to change the American Constitution! Washington was great fun. I saw my cousin Bertie Pott, who was our successful Naval attaché and his charming wife. They had a nice house in the suburbs and I went out and spent an evening at the Chevy Chase Club and danced well on into the night. To my surprise, I saw Dudley Pound there thoroughly enjoying himself and dancing away like a man half his age. We did perhaps achieve something, if only a certain speeding up in their trade protection measures. I asked the First Sea Lord if I could spend three days leave in Canada before returning to UK. He gladly consented to this and I went up to Toronto and stayed with Albert Phipps, Elizabeth’s cousin and then President of the Imperial Bank of Canada and saw Georgina and Johnnie who were being looked after in quite a nice little apartment not far from their house. The Phipps’ were very kind and financed the expenses of Nanny, Johnny and Georgina whilst they were in Canada. We fortunately were allowed after the War to reimburse them for the expenses involved, but it was nice to feel we had good friends and relations in Toronto who would keep an eye on them through fair winds and foul.28 I met Geoffrey Phipps, their son who was running a big ammunition factory outside Toronto and heard of their other son, Norman Phipps, who was serving in England with the Canadian Army. Toronto was bright and pleasant and Phipps had a nice house in one of the fashionable suburbs. Not a large one, I would say five or six bedrooms, a small garden and nice sized living room. As with all houses in the neighbourhood it did not have more than two stories. Old Nanny, though obviously keen to get back was in good heart and Georgina and Johnny went to a little day school in Toronto. They looked well and plump and seemed to think life was fun but rather missed having pets. My visit to Albert Phipps in Toronto was a very pleasant interlude and I saw some of the tremendous minesweeping shipbuilding programmes being undertaken by Canada. These Albert Phipps appeared on the C$10 ships were built almost anywhere in Canada in sections and shipped down to the Great Lakes Canadian Banknote. to be joined together. I went on to Ottawa after leaving Toronto and had some talks with the Canadian Naval authorities, and in particular my old friend of Vernon days, Commodore Lay, who was just as outspoken as ever and was particularly critical of the abysmal ignorance as 28 Both sides of the family believed in paying one’s debts to the full, but it took until 1959 before WWD was able to discharge this debt. This was due to exchange control forbidding the export of more than £100 per annum from a postwar bankrupted Britain, plus doubtless the rigours of bringing up a growing family on naval pay. 213

he called it of the US Navy in anti-submarine warfare. The Canadian Navy were putting up a positively tremendous effort and they were not too proud to learn from us, in fact very much the opposite as all their senior officers had been trained in the British Navy. I cannot remember that there was ever a subject of major importance in dispute between the British and Canadian Navies. I soon arrived in Dorval, the airport for Montreal and was introduced by the Air Chief Marshal, Sir Frederick Bowhill, to a co-passenger who was one of the wartime high-ups in the Ministry of Supply. Sir Kenneth Lee, of Tootals, the big Lancashire textile people. This was a most fortunate encounter, as Kenneth and I became close friends and we saw a lot of each other until he died only a few years ago at his nice house Lukyns, near Ewhurst. We were to fly back to England in a Liberator converted bomber which at that time was running almost a ferry service across the Atlantic. It looked pretty rough, and in a sense unkempt, as indeed it was. After take-off there was some defect in the oil system which necessitated the pilot turning back. But it corrected itself after a fashion and we went on to Gander, the big air staging post In Newfoundland where we landed. Quite a number of defects revealed themselves and it took over 24 hours to correct these. Meanwhile we took walks around the snow-covered airfield for there was no sign of spring yet in these latitudes. However eventually we donned our flying suits with oxygen masks and climbed into the bomb department. Halfway across, one of the air crew said there was no oil pressure and we would have to ‘force land’ in the middle of the Atlantic. We were then feeling so cold we really did not mind very much. However the aircraft kept airborne and I was thankful to see the outline of the coast of Northern Ireland under us as we steered for Prestwick. As we approached Prestwick on a lovely spring morning, I have never seen Scotland look better. Then we started to circle the airfield, the pilot announced that the oil had leaked out of the recuperator system and he could not get the landing wheels down, so we resigned ourselves to a crash landing. I remember talking to a senior Dutch official who had escaped from Batavia [Jakarta], who said this was not his first air crash and he hoped it would not be his last! As it was evident we would have some sort of a crash, it was interesting to note the reactions of passengers of different nationalities. The French talked rapidly and gesticulated, the Dutch kept up a continuous stream of guttural invectives, and the English just looked glum and depressed. I saw the ambulance and fire engine driving round the airfield in anticipation, and when the crew member came round for the last time to tell us about crash drill and what to do if the aircraft caught fire, I asked him if, as the pilots had got his side wheels down, whether the brakes would work. He replied, ‘alas no’, and with the knowledge that a Liberator would run for about four miles before stopping without brakes, I looked hopefully for a soft ploughed field at the end of the runway, only to see a stone quarry in full working order. However, with commendable skill the pilot brought the aircraft in right at the end of the runway along which we ran at frightening speed for about half the distance and then tipped up on our nose amid the splintering of the front fuselage, and came to a stop fortunately without catching fire, as the aircraft’s front wheel had failed to come down. The Emergency Organisation of Prestwick did not take long to get us out and we were thankful to be on dry land without a scratch. 214

I was behind my schedule and got into a small internal transport aircraft piloted by a Czech. We lost our way as it was foggy and his instruments were not working and force landed on an airstrip near Birmingham, but soon got our bearings, filled up with petrol and got back to London. A journey from America not without incident. I went straight back and as I had preceded the First Sea Lord who had still some more business to do in America, I went into a conference with Charles Lambe and the Sea Lords concerned. I told them fully the form, and expressed the view that this aspect of maritime warfare had never seriously entered into the US Navy’s main plans. After all they were entirely self-sufficient and they regarded the methods of specific protection of open seaborne and coastwise shipping [as being] of little importance. I made it clear they were far, far more deferential to senior officers’ views however mistaken they may have been than we were. That whilst I now believed Admiral Kelly Turner, the American Director of Plans, realised what should be done with the least possible delay to stop the near catastrophic scale of shipping losses, he did not have a great influence on Admiral King, their Chief of Naval Operations, to bring this about. Admiral King had his eyes set on the Pacific and the reestablishment of US naval control in that area. They simply failed to realise then the effect of the unnecessary shipping losses being incurred by us and the Allies in the Atlantic. I said I thought the man to put pressure on was President Roosevelt who knew quite a lot of naval affairs and naval history. The US President is in fact the US Supreme Commander of all ‘military forces’ and can therefore give directions which must be obeyed. Captain Roskill in Vol 2 of The War at Sea gives a very clear and indeed charitable description of all the actions taken by us to get the Americans to put their maritime house in order. I have sometimes wondered whether our visit did much good, perhaps it did. More and more United States officers were realising their defects in this aspect of naval war. I said at great risk that it was it was in a sense more serious than the results of Pearl Harbour which already were well on the way to being remedied. But one of the reasons why ideas which may be alien to official views are never adopted, is because of the monolithic structure of the US Navy. It was just not done to disagree and argue with your seniors, and maybe this reminded one of the Victorian Navy before Admiral Fisher started people thinking in a revolutionary way. I reminded our folk at the Admiralty that to get the US Navy Department to agree with us, a two-way approach was needed and this had to be carried out simultaneously at the very top level and at the same time at the working staff level. Soon after I got back, I took Elizabeth up to Mulgrave as an addition to the family was expected in June. Regular letters were coming through from Oswald and hopes were expressed that there would be an exchange of the badly wounded. This very nearly came off in 1942 but was cancelled at the last moment on a whim of Hitler’s, and partly because I believe Duncan Sandys, an MP and son-in-law of Winston Churchill, made some very silly observations in the House of Commons. I often talked over the possibility of getting Georgina and Johnny back to England as it was clear there was no question of the country being overrun and it was a time when families should be together if possible. We decided that we should make the attempt when the submarine danger was at a low ebb and it was believed this would be the case soon when the Americans got their side of the Atlantic in order. 215

Furthermore, we felt there was a limit to which we could ask the splendid Phipps family in Canada to look after our young! We were only allowed to remit about half the cost of what their maintenance came to and with currency restrictions in force and the Canadian dollar linked to the US dollar it would be a long time before there would be free interchange of currencies. Then back to the overall naval picture again! Malta was under terrific pressure and one of our main concerns was the flying in of our fighters off our aircraft carriers to Malta. A difficult operation to plan but one which was outstandingly successful and caused the German Air Force based in Sicily to suffer prohibitively heavy losses in their attacks on Malta. The losses and difficulties in running convoys to Russia in the long summer days when there was virtually no darkness increased and the saga of PQ16 journey to Kola Inlet in May has not been told often enough.29 But it was perhaps the Indian Ocean which concerned us most. We did not know whether or not after the April sortie of the main part of the Japanese fleet against Colombo, Trincomalee and elsewhere, they would stay in the Indian Ocean and establish themselves there. We pulled out one of the appreciations we had made against this eventuality, and with all eloquence we could we pressed for the capture of Madagascar. Alas, the French would not play, and we were convinced after our Dakar experiences that to capture it in an expedition commanded by General de Gaulle would only stiffen French resistance. If we held Madagascar and indeed Aden in the North with Durban in the South, there would be no question of the Japanese being able to exercise effective control of the Indian Ocean. Accordingly, the expedition to capture Madagascar was assembled in Durban in April and set sail for Madagascar in the first few days of May. Admiral Syfret commanded the naval side and my old marine friend General Sturgis the army side. The operation went like clockwork and as it proved just in time for later in the month the Japanese landed a few people and with a midget submarine torpedoed and damaged HMS Ramillies. After Diego Suarez was captured and largely on the insistence of General Smuts, the rest of the island was captured. But at no time did the French without a considerable show of resistance lay down their arms. Whilst all this was going on the Americans were busy in the Central and South Pacific and we were trying to pierce the intentions of the Japanese whether they intended, if they did at all, to stabilise their position in the Pacific. Some of the diagrams shown in vol. 4 The Hinge of Fate by Winston Churchill are instructive. They show the limit of the Japanese conquest up to April 1942 and a possible planned extension. It seemed to us clear that the Japanese must capture New Guinea and establish themselves in the Admiralty, Solomon and New Hebrides Islands before they could regard themselves to be in a position to isolate Australia or New Zealand from Hawaii and America. It would seem also that Midway Island was a key point to prevent US forces from Hawaii driving into the Central Pacific. At least this was how the situation seemed to us. We had no forces of our own to halt the Japanese maritime forces other than those naval ones in Australia under Admiral Grace. Nearer home the Japanese had reached the frontiers of India after conquering Burma [Myanmar], but it was clear the onset of the monsoon and extended lines of communication would delay Japanese advances for many months. 29 216 Seven ships out of a total of 36 were sunk during six days of fairly continuous attack.

It was clear that the Japanese would need to capture Port Moresby [capital city of Papua New Guinea] and the chain of islands to the east of Australia. The Americans were determined to stop this and moved two aircraft carriers to the south under Admiral Fletcher. After a number of airstrikes between opposing forces the Japanese aircraft carrier Sholto was sunk and Shakako heavily damaged. Both US aircraft carriers were badly damaged and Lexington sunk. As a result of the heavy losses experienced by the Japanese, they withdrew from their attempt to capture Port Moresby and control the Coral Sea. It was the first of the new type of naval battles where in fact the surface forces never came within sight of each other. Though there was not a great deal of difference in the losses on either side, this was a decisive victory for the Americans for it called a halt to Japanese ambitions in the islands adjacent to Australia, and whilst the US could quickly replace their losses it was beyond the capacity of the Japanese to do so. Sitting as we were at the other side of the world, it was clear even then to us that with luck the Coral Sea battle represented the turn of the tide. Winston Churchill, in vol. 4, sets out admirably the courses Japan might have taken and in fact did take. He points out as we felt at the time that they were trying to extend their area of control far beyond their capability of holding. Nevertheless, things were far from clear to us. We could not be sure that the Germans would not defeat the Russians, occupy Persia, cut off our oil supplies and as it were jeopardise our whole Middle East position by taking us in the rear. Maybe eventually squeeze India from the west and from the east. We may have felt that the efficiency and capability of Japanese were greater than they were, but the Battle of the Coral Sea made it clear that the Japanese were not invincible. In the Admiralty we were not clear, nor for the matter were the Navy Department, where the American forces were and what was their plan. It was however clear to the American Commander-in-Chief with headquarters of Hawaii, and from all we had heard even at that early stage nobody doubted Admiral Nimitz’ shrewd strategical judgement. Admiral Nimitz very properly had his HQ ashore at Hawaii and never tried to control events from seagoing ships. I have often thought that had Admiral Forbes as the British C-in-C had a proper HQ ashore at Scapa Flow and worked from there, we should have had less interference in ship movements from the Admiralty and that we should have had more successes and less failures than we did in the opening years of the war. I once suggested this to Admiral Forbes who was ‘not amused’ and suggested that a stray Commander, as I was then, had better think of other things! The beginning of June saw us thinking very hard of many aspects of the war. Our shipping losses in the Caribbean were still very severe though at last it seemed that within a matter of weeks a proper naval control of shipping system together with convoy would be adopted. Convoys bringing absolutely essential supplies to Malta were fought through but with heavy losses. But alas in North Africa it was clear the Eighth Army had been defeated decisively by General Rommel and that Tobruk would be invested again. It seemed to us that the generalship in the field of battle was at fault as there were high hopes, and with good reason too, that we should defeat General Rommel. On the other hand, General Rommel was an exceedingly skilful commander who with an inferior force defeated the Eighth Army 217

decisively. Tobruk fell towards the end of June and tremendous quantities of stores including much petrol fell into the hands of the Germans, thus relieving the acute anxieties the enemy had of being able to continue fighting in the desert. But more important still the situation was set for the battle of Midway, of all the battles of the war this was I think the most decisive and most far-reaching and will rank as one of the decisive battles of the world. The story has been told many times and I will not attempt to describe it here. We only got fragmentary reports of it at the Admiralty, and in fact the Navy Department was quite in the dark about it while it was proceeding. Suffice it to say that the Japanese, with a blind attack on [the] Aleutian Islands, intended to capture Midway Island, isolate Hawaii and so extend their control over half of the Pacific.30 Their main aircraft carriers and battleships were deployed to carry out this attack. As a result of strikes by large numbers of American aircraft based at Midway, and from their aircraft carriers, Enterprise, Hornet and Yorktown, all four main fleet carriers of the Japanese fleet were sunk, and the Japanese Commander had no alternative but to withdraw his invasion fleet and to call off the whole operation. Only bits and pieces filtered through to us, but it was clear the main part of the Japanese Navy had suffered a decisive defeat from which it could not recover. But in Plans many projects were being considered. There was a call for a ‘Second Front NOW’ from the Russians and from the Americans, who had not by a very long way appreciated the enormous difficulties and the amount of technical and tactical training required. It was absolutely ridiculous to think in 1942 that we should be in a position to launch with a measure of success any invasion against the continent of Europe. Our own view often expressed in meetings was [that] we should not even be ready for this in 1943 and that early in 1944 was a more practical date. From the day almost of the American entry into the war we had favoured a landing in North Africa taking as it were the Axis forces in the back and so clearing our sea communications through the Mediterranean. In The Hinge of Fate the Prime Minister describes how the original projected Operation Sledgehammer for 1942 was buried. The Americans were itching to employ their gathering land forces as soon as possible but we felt they must be ‘bloodied’ as it were in some other sphere of lesser importance before they would be up to taking on the formidable might of the highly professional German army. It was evident that a long time must elapse before substantial forces of the American Army could be employed in the Pacific area. For this would be essentially a maritime war until the mainland of Japan had to be broached. There was the alternative of landing in Norway, but again almost insuperable army problems presented themselves here due to the almost complete lack of communications. I am afraid one used to smile when the ‘Prayer’ for a reexamination of the invasion of Norway was sent to us. I used to turn to my Army opposite number and say ‘yes, we will land you anywhere north of Bergen, just say where!’ The soldier’s imagination boggled at the thought of supplying much more than a Brigade Group 30 The attack on the spread-out chain of the Aleutian Islands, Alaska, was a diversion intended to draw the US fleet away from the battle for Midway.
