In June 1942 the Japanese attacked and occupied several islands for a year until they withdrew in May 1943. 218

along a single railway or single road. Actually more might have been achieved with a host of small supply craft working in the numerous fjords. But the Army were right - it was no area where decisive attacking military forces could be deployed. Lambe had done some excellent work on the Americans, their Navy Department, and they were at least in strong support of the landing in North Africa, though we felt they were over anxious about landing inside the Mediterranean. But it would be true to say the President was always a keen supporter of this provided we made plans to land on the continent of Europe in 1943. For there was much political pressure, hard to appreciate at this day, to land on the continent and take the weight off the Russians who were, they claimed, carrying 90% of the war load! We were in mid-1942 stretched almost to breaking point maritime-wise. I attended many conferences both with the Americans and with others to recommend what next to do! Then in June a splendid event occurred. Elizabeth had gone up to Mulgrave in May and I had a telephone call from Lady Normanby on the evening of the 14th of June to the effect that we had added a daughter to our family. The arrival of Anne Sophia gave us great pleasure. All seemed to have gone well and I managed to get up to Mulgrave for a couple of days a week later and saw Anne Sophia for the first time. A pleasant surprise! Much jubilation at Mulgrave as this was the second birth to our family at Mulgrave. Johnny had been born there in 1938. To return to events which if possible were moving at a greater speed than ever. We had established very close relations with the Americans over here and to a certain extent with Georgina welcoming her younger sister our opposite numbers in Washington. In some ways the overall American Naval organisation for the conduct of war was better than ours though their head was called Chief of Naval Operations (CNO), neither he nor the Navy Department ever concerned themselves about precise dispositions for naval operations. This was left to the Commander on the spot, who did or did not - usually the latter - inform the Navy Department of their intentions. This enabled Admiral Nimitz to have untrammelled control of all operations and dispositions of the Pacific. Furthermore, the Americans had achieved before the war the supreme success of ‘cracking’ with a lot of aid from us the Japanese cyphers. This greatly helped Admiral Nimitz and the US Commanders. We had also for periods broken the German cyphers which helped us, whilst we believed ours were now ‘secure’ with things like ‘one time pads’, i.e. only once used cyphers. On the other hand, for quite a time the US cyphers were far from secure. In July there was a great meeting in London to settle the future strategy. It had been clear to us all along that General Marshall and Admiral King had totally opposed views. General Marshall was convinced we should land in Europe forthwith and drive on to Berlin, whereas Admiral King was chiefly interested in the Pacific and sought to drive us across the Pacific to Tokyo. Our views were that neither could be achieved in 1942 or even in 1943, but probably in 1944! The President fortunately set out his views in a splendid document, quoted by Winston Churchill in The Hinge of Fate, which categorically says that we must aim to defeat Germany first. 219

The American leaders still thought we could land in Europe in 1942. The interchange of meetings between our Chiefs of Staff, the American Chiefs of Staff and many others are described in detail in The Hinge of Fate. It was a case of very hard bargaining, but it was probably due to General Marshall as much as anybody else that he gave way about landing in Europe this year. He was always prepared to listen to arguments and to reason, whereas we sometimes got the opinion that Admiral King’s ideas were set before he arrived. One evening when I was in Washington in May, my friend John Grindle, took me up to have supper with a friend of his who was something akin to the Director of Military Operations at the War Office.31 His name was Brigadier Eisenhower. A more forthright and charming person one could not meet anywhere. Our talk ranged over all aspects of the war. He was an unknown Brigadier in the US War Department and he wanted to learn everything and listen to everybody. I have always heard General Marshall set great store by his judgement which was thoroughly sound and down to earth. But there was something extra about him of which one became aware as our talks ranged far into the night. He was a very humble man and had absolutely no national prejudices at all. He had an immensely high opinion of the British fighting man and held in high regard both our sailors and soldiers. He seemed at first acquaintance a superlatively good ‘ordinary man’ which is perhaps what he would like to consider himself to be. I shall long remember that evening with Eisenhower at his official house in the Army camp, just above Washington, where most of the military quarters were situated. A most attractive character, very down to earth with absolutely no prejudices whatever. Quite a quick brain, he worked, I would think, more on personality contacts than anything else. We discussed war history in which as far as American history was concerned, he seemed well acquainted. He had served quite a lot in the Philippines and had a considerable admiration for that colourful character, General MacArthur, but the man he worshipped before all else was General Marshall, whom I also met on more than one occasion. He also reckoned Field Marshall Dill, our representative out there, was a very ‘wise guy’. I suppose one would not say General Eisenhower was a very profound thinker nor perhaps a very great strategist. On the other hand, he had the humility to listen to other people and perhaps his great claim to fame was in his judgement of men and situations and how to get the best out of them. None of us had any idea, in April 1942, that this was the man to be chosen to command the Allied armies, first in North Africa and finally in France, and would eventually be the First Citizen of the United States. He had a store of natural personal magnetism which was evident for all to see. We were entertained that evening by his charming wife who in character seemed to be very similar to her fine husband. There will no doubt be many books written about General Eisenhower, but I doubt if any of them will bring out adequately his outstanding and essential probity of character and intellectual integrity. I met him on many occasions later and he was always just the same and just as friendly as when we first met in his quarters above Washington. I went up again to Mulgrave in the latter half of July for a very pleasant christening of Anne Sophia, which took place in Lythe church where we were married. We had a little party 31 Captain John Grindle (1900-1991), part of the British Admiralty delegation to Washington. 220

afterwards which Lady Normanby gave for us. But events were moving fast. We had held the air attacks on Malta and it was possible anyway to reoccupy the Malta submarine base. Our Army had been decisively defeated by General Rommel in North Africa and Tobruk had been captured. The Axis advances had taken them to El Alamein where this advance was decisively checked, but was little more than a stone’s throw from Alexandria and the Nile Delta. A brighter side. We saw with some relief the large reduction of shipping losses due to the full-scale adoption of convoy in the western Atlantic adopted by the Americans. July 1942 It seemed about this time that we sensed that the main Japanese maritime effort would be in the Pacific and that the Indian Ocean would be an area where command was disputed. The advent of Japanese submarines off the east coast of Africa suggested that the control of the seas of the Indian Ocean had very much taken second place in the Japanese plans and their chief Indian Ocean object would be to disrupt our use of this ocean by submarine attack. But as already referred to, July was a memorable month in the strategical sphere for the Allies. The American Chiefs of Staff had given way to our urgings and their own President’s ideas and had agreed not only was the defeat of Germany to be the first objective, but that as a start the occupation of North Africa was to be our starting point. It was agreed that this should be a combined British /American operation with the object of clearing the northern shores of the African continent of Axis forces. The Prime Minister, who took an exceptional interest in code words, decided on the name ‘TORCH’ for this operation. All of us in Plans Division and indeed also in the Joint Planning Section were simply delighted, as ever since the end of 1941 we had been urging this operation, as not only being the most desirable strategically, [it] was far and away the most practical. We realised above all how much we, and even more so the Americans, had to learn before they could match up to the highly efficient and determined German army. This operation we believe would prove absolutely invaluable training for the more formidable task of landing on the Continent of Europe. Looking back, it was interesting also to recollect in the old F.O.P.S. days in autumn of 1940, this had been suggested as one of the ways of going over the offensive and eventually returning to Europe. Some of us started looking ahead still further. We realised the Americans were intent and absolutely set on invading Europe through the front door, i.e. the coasts of France and possibly Belgium. Nevertheless, some of us hoped we might invade Europe through the back door as it were, and in a sense forestall the Russians who made no bones about their intentions of turning Europe, when they won, into a Moscow dominated Communist Paradise. We suggested conquering the Balkans and Italy first and then striking up the centre of Europe through Austria, Hungary and possibly Czechoslovakia. However, we realise that having achieved one success getting Americans to our way of strategical thinking, i.e. TORCH, we would not be likely to do this again and even the tremendous eloquence and imagination of the Prime Minister could not achieve this. The Prime Minister we had reason to believe rather favoured this as he, unlike the Americans, was never under any illusion as to the ultimate Russian aims and he foresaw more clearly than most the dangers of Europe becoming communist dominated. 221

We started working very closely with the Americans for Operation TORCH, and though the Prime Minister wanted I think to put the CIGS (General Brooke) in command, it was agreed an American should command it.32 We hoped it would be General Marshall, the United States CIGS, but I believe the President felt he could not spare him. It was clear now the American mobilisation plans were revealed that the time would come when the US forces, certainly in so far as land forces were concerned, would predominate and therefore as the US said, being the principal shareholders, would have the right to choose the Chairman. There was also materially a feeling among the Americans that they did not want to be put under a ‘Britisher’, and they would with their technical knowhow prefer to learn their own way which was sometimes the hard way! However, the choice fell on General Eisenhower and it would have been impossible to choose a better man than him. He earned absolutely golden opinions from us all, and he had what few Americans had, an understanding and a certain instinctive knowledge of how we looked at things. He was pretty tough on his own people and I have seen him absolutely rend American officers who were in his judgement being tactless and stupid. The US, or rather the combined HQ, was at Norfolk House in St James’s Square where all the planning was done. Another thing that struck me, as indeed it did when I was in America, and that was the separateness then of the US army and the US Navy. A West Point man just did not know an Annapolis man!33 They had no joint organisation at all. Each at times were regarded by the other as blockheads! In a sense, we were the jointing substance between the US army and US Navy! When in Washington this was very apparent and a certain measure of cunning had to be exercised in reaching agreement on joint schemes. When talking to the Navy it was no good saying ‘This is what your Army thinks etc., and it seems a good idea’. If you did that, it would be turned down. I soon learned the approach was ‘Though I am not an Army man myself, I had in mind an idea, on the following lines etc. I have not a clue what your Army folks think, but what is more important what do you think?’ Then almost immediately one would get - if the idea was good - instant agreement. In the same way the US Air Force were rather a law unto themselves, but they worked closely with their own Army. The US Navy pretty well had an Air Force of their own within the US Navy, which included their matchless MARINE CORPS and so problems of cooperation did not so often arise. As Andrew Cunningham once said to me when talking of inter service cooperation – ‘It is best to make the RAF work with the US army or perhaps the US Navy. Whilst the US Air Force works splendidly and willingly without restraint with our Army and our Navy!’ That is what he called the best international interservice cooperation, and he was right! Mountbatten’s organisation at Combined Operations HQ was making gigantic strides. Many new types of craft were being produced in vast quantities, the training HQ at Inveraray was a hive of energy and projects. It was desirable as soon as possible to get some actual experience with an opposed landing and consequently an attack on Dieppe was planned. It had been approved in April and the plan was to carry it out in June or July. For a variety of reasons, it was postponed. Whilst the planning of the operation was entirely the responsibility of the 32 The CIGS (Chief of Imperial General Staff) from December 1941 was General Sir Alan Brooke, later Viscount Alanbrooke (1883-1963), ODNB. 33 West Point, New York, was and still is the site of the US military training academy, and Annapolis, Maryland, the site of the equivalent naval academy. 222

Force Commanders and Combined Operations HQ, we were invited to comment. Frankly some of us never liked the plan very much, for any real chance of success it relied on an absolute and untrammelled surprise which in in the event they did not achieve. The decision we questioned [was] not to use the RAF for bombing beforehand, which we believed to be mistaken, and we had doubts as to the adequacy of naval supporting gunfire, though this was guessing as we had not then the knowledge we had two years later of the well nigh decisive effect of supporting naval gunfire. The Naval Force Commander, my old friend John Hughes Hallett, had much the same misgivings as we had. We knew the helplessness of landing parties against fixed defences and the lessons of our disastrous failures in the First World War at Gallipoli had not been lost on us. However as is often said one cannot make an omelette without breaking eggs. Indeed, General Montgomery who was, I think, GOC Southern Command, had grave misgivings about it. The operation was cancelled in July, then revised and carried out in the middle of August. From the word go it was clear from intercepted signals that this operation was not going well. The Germans were alert and they decisively repulsed our attempts to capture their headquarters after landing. Our casualties especially among the Canadian troops were very heavy. We lost rather over two thirds of the men committed to the assault, over 100 aircraft and over 30 landing craft, not to mention a destroyer. Anyway, judged in the context of world events this was not a decisive reverse, but it did convince us [that] not only training is necessary on a wider scale than previously thought for assault, but much greater attention must be given to provision of close support ships and bombardment. We certainly learned lots of lessons from this failure which proved invaluable beyond all computation in the many invasions which we and the Americans were to undertake in the years that lay ahead. Convoys to Russia presented an unending and perhaps most difficult problem. Reference has been made to the sortie the Tirpitz made against two of our convoys and the steps taken to deal with it. But the most disastrous of all was PQ 17. The story of this is told in vol. 2 of Roskill’s History as coolly and dispassionately as it is possible to tell. There has recently been much publicity in an action bought by Captain Broome against a sensationalist author, Mr Irving and his publishers, which I’m glad to say Captain Broome won and was awarded very heavy damages.34 The disaster was due to the signal Admiral Pound, the First Sea Lord made to tell the convoy to scatter. We had decrypted by special intelligence German signals to the Tirpitz and her escorting forces which ordered her to attack the convoy before the Home Fleet could intervene. This decision was made at a meeting held in the First Sea Lord’s room in the early part of the evening, but a grave error in drafting of the signal was made by the First Sea Lord. The convoy was told to ‘scatter’ which meant ‘sauve qui peut’ [save whoever can] whereas it should have been told to disperse, which would have allowed the escort commander time to organise the ships into groups and provide each group with such protection as is possible. I was not at the meeting that night as it was finally an operational matter. The DOD (H), Captain Eccles, felt it was a wrong decision, as did the Assistant Chief of Naval Staff (Admiral 34 Captain Jack Broome (1901-1985) commanded the convoy’s escort group. He was accused of cowardice by David Irving in his book The destruction of Convoy PQ 17, Cassell, 1969. Broome sued for libel and in 1970 was awarded exemplary damages and costs of £40,000. Irving has since continued to make a career as a historian of World War II, Nazi Germany and as a Holocaust denier. He has been involved in numerous libel lawsuits. 223

Power). Nobody seems to have pounced on the errors of wording of a ‘most immediate’ signal which led to this disaster. Most of us on the staff were absolutely horrified when we knew what had happened next morning, as we had no illusions that the great majority of the scattered convoy would in the days ahead be sunk easily and effectively by German submarines and aircraft. Alas this proved only too true, some 23 ships out of the 36 in the convoy were sunk. It was clear to us this was a great error of judgement. All the information we had should have been passed to Admiral Hamilton and Captain Broome, but it was wrong and utterly wrong to order him to scatter the convoy. That would and should only have been done if Tirpitz had come in sight and was in fact done by Captain Fegan in Jervis Bay when a German Battlecruiser attacked his convoy.35 In that case, I think, only two merchant ships were lost in addition to Jervis Bay. I think Admiral Hamilton was slightly to blame for not sending the escort back to the convoy and disobeying Admiralty signals. In fact it is easy to say now the Admiralty signals should have been disregarded, but in ice cold and bad weather, great weariness and mountainous seas, it is easy to say this should have been done, but what would one have done oneself? It is appallingly difficult. I think if I had been in Broome’s place, I would have stayed with the convoy and kept asking for clarifications and repeat back of the signals, but who knows I was not there, and it is easy enough to say this twenty years later in the light of after knowledge. Broome’s orders were clear and concise. But it can never be gainsaid that this was a major disaster for the British Navy, and it is surely a lesson that in the ultimate and final situation the decision must be left unequivocally to the man on the spot. August 1942 We had decided the time was appropriate to get Old Nanny, Georgina and Johnny home. So, with rather less difficulty than I had imagined I fixed for them to come home in one of the intermediate cargo / passenger ships belonging, I think, to the Canadian Pacific Shipping Company. They had quite a good and uneventful passage and I went over to Northern Ireland and met them off Bangor where the ship anchored before proceeding to her final port of destination.36 I borrowed the senior officer’s boat and got on board soon after anchoring to be greeted by two little people who had evidently enjoyed themselves and done full justice to the menu. Old Nanny was looking tired but obviously rather glad to be back ‘in it’ again! She, I think, felt that the Canadians, kind and welcoming as they always were, just had no idea what wartime restrictions were and conditions of life in Europe. We boarded the ferry steamer at Belfast, which was nearby having got all the luggage and set off for 35 Jervis Bay was a converted armed merchant cruiser, with Captain E.S.F. Fegan, as sole escort for convoy HX84 sailing November 1940 from Halifax to Liverpool. When the German battleship Admiral Scheer attacked, the convoy scattered as the Jervis Bay drove straight at the German battleship. Hopelessly outgunned, she was sunk but the convoy largely escaped. In the event five out of 38 merchant vessels were sunk by the Admiral Scheer, and one later, not two as WWD thought, but in general this could be seen as minimal losses in the circumstances. 36 WWD would have been privy to the latest information on the Battle of the Atlantic. The children’s return took place in the gap between setting up proper cover on the western side the Atlantic, and the resumption of German ‘wolf pack’ attacks in the Autumn of 1942. It must still have been an anxious time, as shown in WWD’s eagerness to get the children off as soon as possible. 224

Heysham. My memory is a little hazy here but I think we spent a night or the best part of it at Bangor before coming over in the steamer. An easy passage across the Irish Sea to Heysham, where Elizabeth was waiting for us and how pleased all the family were to be reunited again. We got onto a leisurely train which took us to York and then after the usual change at Malton arrived at Whitby. What a welcome we all got from Lady Normanby and everybody started off on their best behaviour.37 This was before Johnny had declared open war on all the Governesses. After a couple of nights or so at Mulgrave, I left the family there to get to know each other again and returned to London. Old Nanny very obviously wanted to go on holiday which she was persuaded to take and our three children settled down to enjoy themselves and at the same time to keep their mother reasonably occupied. We had decided, so as to see more of each other, to bring the older children down and live at a country hotel not far from Hartley Witney, some miles beyond Farnham. I could as a rule get away for a night or two most weekends to come down and live in the country, which was certainly a relaxation after London where occasional air raids still made the night hideous. Let us see how plans were shaping up in Whitehall. We were busy drawing up and getting agreement on a combined plan for British and American forces to land and capture North Africa. The US planners were at this stage very, very cautious, and thought we were crazy to attempt a landing inside the Mediterranean. We pointed out that this was child’s play compared to their favourite project of a frontal assault on the continent of Europe. I think in many ways at that stage the US planners, relying as they did on unmeasurable material superiority, preferred to blast their way in through every front door, whereas we, who at every turn had to count the material cost because we often did not have it, preferred to go in by the side or back door, and to use every stratagem or bluff that we could think about to reduce frontal losses. However, the Americans stuck to their guns and it was decided our main assault should be in the neighbourhood of Algiers and that the Americans should land at Casablanca and also at Oran to clear that vast land area from possible German control through the Vichy French. I was fairly closely concerned with the planning of these operations and still think it was a pity we could not get agreement on our more adventurous plan which, in so many words, entailed our main landing as far east in Algeria as possible in the neighbourhood of Bone, with the Americans at Algiers and Oran. However, agreement was reached on the outline plan already described. General Eisenhower was to be the Supreme Allied Commander. Admiral Cunningham, the Naval Commander in the Mediterranean; General Anderson, the British Army Commander The family together again in Algiers; General George Patton (US Army) to be in command of the assault at Casablanca, Mulgrave, 1942 with Air Chief Marshal Tedder in command of all the Air Forces. General Alexander would, when our military forces in the eastern end of the Mediterranean joined up, command all Army units US and British alike when they had joined [united]. Similarly, the same applied to naval forces. 37 Georgina and Johnny seem to have accepted without question the presence of an additional child in the family, and never showed any signs of jealousy. 225

I met the colourful character General Patton more than once at Norfolk House where much of the Planning was done. He had, on the first occasion we met, two magnificent pistols with mother of pearl on their butts stuck into his belt. He took them out and said he could hit a tennis ball if I threw it into the air. I did not encourage him to try as he was as good as his word. But behind all this theatrical and colourful exterior a more determined and resolute leader of men would be hard to find anywhere. He was worshipped by his staff. We found the US naval staff a bit weak and I suspect their best operational planners were all in the Pacific. But Georgie Patton was an individualist and I suspect at times gave more headaches to his Supreme Commander than all the British Generals put together. However, a plan was settled and agreed with little delay for TORCH and whilst the Americans first quite unrealistically thought we could do it in September, we felt late October was the earliest it could be launched. In the event it took place early November. The enormous number of preparations, Army, Navy and Air, many of which have to be interlocking is quite extraordinary. Then the very important business side of political preparations and where possible subversion has to be arranged. The numerous fake plans and counter-intelligence lines have to be developed carefully and sometimes slowly. After all if one’s assault arrives totally unexpected, the chances of success are certainly increased tenfold. We had a pretty good team of counter-intelligence experts. The story of ‘The Man who Never was’ played a part in foxing the Germans. The corpse floated ashore with genuinely bogus papers certainly added confusion to the enemy’s ideas. 38 But why they did not penetrate all these ruses is a mystery to me. Perhaps we should leave it for the moment and it was clear the Planners and Commanders were going ahead at full speed. Admiral Cunningham was head of our mission in USA at the time, having been relieved a few months previously in the Med by Admiral Harwood. However, he soon came back and with his old Mediterranean staff he took part in the planning of Operation TORCH. But it was necessary to look again, not that we ever ceased looking at it, at the U boat threat. Certainly, losses had been reduced in July and August. But as forecast the U Boats attacked off Trinidad and sank a number of Brazilian ships in a manner that brought Brazil into the war against the Axis. This had not been expected and though we did not expect much materially from Brazil, it was a great advantage to have a coast line to help control the Central and South Atlantic. New U Boat tactics were frequently being employed. They were developing the ‘wolf pack’ tactics and in fact were developing a system whereby an attack on a convoy would be a carefully controlled and coordinated affair. U Boats were being built faster than we could sink them and it was only towards the latter end of the year that the gigantic US ship building programme held out hopes that our replacements could more than catch up with our losses. Our imports at times month by month fell to the lowest figure known and below what we considered the danger line. Whilst we realised U boat war had its ups and downs, it was clear that the decisive point had not been reached and in the months which lay ahead would be decided whether or not we could maintain our war effort and feed our own people at an adequate level. 38 226 WWD means rather the ‘genuine’ corpse with ‘bogus’ papers! Made into a popular film released in 1956.

One of the interesting jobs that came my way was to be a member of the Air Travel Priorities Board. As can be imagined, everybody from almost every Ministry wanted to travel by air to the most inaccessible spots. Air travel had really caught on and in any case few people could afford the time which travel by sea meant, unless they were going in a warship on a special mission. The Government, realising the complexity of the problem and the fact that our effort must be concentrated in the provision of combat planes rather than transport planes, appointed a small committee consisting of Air Commodore Coryton (Director of Air Operations), self (Deputy Director of Plans), and Brigadier Mallaby (Deputy Director of Military Operations) to have absolute power as to who and who should not be allocated air passage! We were a closely knit team which stuck together against all criticisms, especially the Foreign Office who had little idea of the very restricted facilities we had for providing air travel. We usually met once a week to decide on applications and during my time as member of this team we gave absolute priority to submarine officers destined for Malta and Spitfire pilots also for Malta. In other words, we related our resources to what was immediately needed in the operational sphere. For it was often a question of days or even hours whether the aircraft or submarines could be kept operational or not for want of personnel. There were of course also many important diplomatic passengers and special undercover agents had to be transported near to their scene of operations and so on. A fascinating job, as it brought one into contact perhaps with some activities of which one would not otherwise have become aware. Alec Coryton was first rate, as quick a brain as one would want anywhere and enormous success as the Director of Operations in the Air Ministry. He and I and also Mallaby were absolutely as one on what were the strategic priorities. I met Alec later, firstly when he commanded the Bomber Command groups in Lincolnshire and later in Cairo, when he was deputy C-in-C of all the Air Forces in the Eastern end of the Mediterranean under Sholto Douglas. Mallaby became I think, one of the War Cabinet secretariats later and has since retired. We were often shot at by various Ministers, one of whom said ‘who are these transpo dictators?’ That was, I think, when we had excluded an ambassador’s valet from an aircraft going I suspect to Madrid. Then the PID committee to which I have already referred was of much interest.39 Donald Maclachlan (NID Naval Intelligence Division) and I were the Admiralty representatives. With the knowledge we, or perhaps especially I, had of impending and possible future operations and future strategy, our function was both negative and positive. For by that time our BBC propaganda to Germany and countries overrun by them was pretty effective. Bruce Lockhart, their head, and since then until his death a few months ago, told me he could get Goebbels on the air within twelve hours, if a particularly damaging accusation was made about him or his Department! Our negative job was to see that our propaganda did not inadvertently betray, as it might well, our future intentions and operations. Our positive job was by inference and by subtle methods of propaganda to suggest our strategy and future course of operations was likely to be quite different from what was intended. And later to see that ‘Deception Plans’, of which I shall talk later, were disseminated at the precise 39 Political Intelligence Department, generally called the Political Warfare Department, for home and overseas propaganda. 227

psychological moment. Maclachlan being a clever journalist and above all a very responsible one was first-rate, as indeed were many in the NID’s department which did not suffer from a lack of brains. A lot of the work was done over the telephone, but we tried to meet about once a month just to make certain nothing was missed and no cards were dropped! Then again as mentioned before, I was a naval member of the Special Operations Executive and Clandestine Warfare Committee. We used to interview some pretty strange characters, professional incendiarists who specialised in arson, burglars who could burgle pretty well any safe in existence, professional tricksters and financial adventurers. As might be expected, some of our customers had been ‘inside’ and jokes about being an involuntary guest of His Majesty were not always received well. Then we had a number of foreigners whose countries had been overrun and who for one reason or another were anxious to serve their own country and do the Germans some major harm. We planned a number of operations from burning down some of the warehouses at Casablanca which contained valuable war material for the Germans, to demolishing the Axis agent’s house and wireless set in Tangier, which gave our enemies warning and information of the forces and supplies which we were passing into the Mediterranean. But the number of operations planned were legion and would form the subject of a whole book. In fact, many books have been written about it which have come preciously close to infringing the Official Secrets Act. Much of the basic information was provided by the Ministry of Economic Warfare who knew well in what respects the shoe pinched. On the committee we had to be careful not to let the Foreign Office know in too much detail what was intended. The wiser men preferred not to know so that they could express with a show of genuineness ‘pained surprise’ at what might appear to be a particularly outrageous act of sabotage in a neutral country! There were however still in that admirable department, peopled probably by the best intellects in any Government department, a number of ‘Better Notters’ who in wartime must be held rather in reserve! Originally in so far as SOE was concerned, we held our meetings in the Foreign Office but after a time this came to the notice of the Foreign Secretary (Anthony Eden) and thereafter we held them in the Admiralty or the War Office which were perhaps less respectable than the Foreign Office. I remember once we had a meeting to plan some sabotage to be carried out by a ferocious looking dissident Frenchman (Capitaine de Frégate L’Anglais), probably an assumed name.40 He had removed a ship which was renamed Fidelity from Marseille, probably by bribery and threats, which looked thoroughly like a merchant vessel, was sturdily built and could carry a considerable armament. L’Anglais, with his trim beard and roving eye looked the part of the pirate Frenchman. His opening remark at the meeting, after looking carefully at some of the more respectably dressed and respectable looking members of the Committee, said in broken English ‘You see English are Gentlemen, but I (a pause) Captain L’ Anglais am NO gentleman, (a further pause) I will do anything’. 40 Definitely not a real name; ‘Capitaine de Frégate’ or Frigate Captain simply indicates a rank equivalent to a Royal Navy Commander. L’Anglais was a name adopted by several people and may or may not have been an official codename. 228

He wanted to be given a roving commission in the Western Mediterranean for little short of piracy off the Spanish, French and Italian coasts. We fitted his ship out at considerable effort and he had with him a pretty determined looking young French lady who I guess was nearly as hard a case as he was! Well, we could not do all he required as, whilst keen to incommode the enemy, a ship operating like this without any form of control was a liability. However, he did a certain amount of work but alas his ship and crew were all lost when in [a] convoy which was attacked by a U Boat pack and suffered heavy casualties. L’Anglais reminded one of the old privateering days where adventure and independence were the only watchwords of the day that mattered. He refused to join up with the Free French, so we got round it by giving him some sort of British Commission. He did not approve of General de Gaulle any more than the Vichy French. August 1942 August also saw much sea fighting in the Pacific. The landing of US forces at Guadalcanal and numerous battles which continuously took place in Solomons [Islands] areas, went on until nearly the end of the year. They were probably some of the bloodiest and most hotly contested of the whole war. The American Navy took tremendous losses as indeed did the Japanese. The former were with their vastly superior resources able to replace their losses whereas the Japanese were not. We knew little of what was going on except that the US asked for a Carrier to help and eventually Victorious was sent. The air losses and carrier losses suffered by the Americans were stupendous. The battles of Savo Islands, Eastern Solomons, Cape Esperance, Santa Cruz, Guadalcanal and Tassafaronga will long be studied as examples of some of the most determined and relentless fighting in the whole of the Pacific. We were asked from time to time to take the pressure off the Americans by diversions in the Indian Ocean, but there was little we could do for our Forces were fully occupied preparing for Torch and resuming Russian convoys as soon as possible. In other books are related the results of the Prime Minister’s visit to Cairo in August when major changes in command were made. General Auchinleck was relieved by General Alexander. Many of us had much sympathy for the ‘Auk’ as he was affectionately called. There is no doubt he was a fine military commander, but he was not a good chooser and much of the blame for the repeated defeats we suffered can be laid at the doors of some of the junior generals commanding formations. Nevertheless there can be little doubt that the Army changes which the Prime Minister made in consultation with the CIGS and General Smuts were right. We had suffered too many reverses and we wanted new leadership at the top. The combination of General Alexander and General Montgomery brought that much needed confidence to our Army which were rather puzzled at their last set of reverses. Admiral Harwood was in the Eastern Mediterranean but was reported to be not too well. He was later to be relieved by Admiral John Cunningham who took over the Eastern Mediterranean and was in fact the Commander-in-Chief, Eastern Mediterranean, when I joined in the early summer of 1943 in Mauritius. But to get back to the future strategy of the war. The first great decisions had been taken i.e. to clear the Mediterranean by capturing North Africa and as the Prime Minister was fond of repeating of ‘attacking the soft underbelly of Europe’. 229

There does not seem to have been any serious anticipation of this on our enemy’s side. I asked General Heusinger after the war, and he said so much attention was riveted on the Russian campaign and the importance of finishing it before the US would have mounted to sufficient strength to invade Europe. The Prime Minister's description of his visit to Moscow in Vol. IV and his encounter with Marshal Stalin make fascinating reading. The subheadings in chapter 27 of his book tell the story ‘A bleak opening’ – ‘no second front 1942’ – ‘hard words’ – ‘a dark background created’ – ‘I unfold the Torch plan’ – ‘I draw my crocodile’ – ‘May God prosper this undertaking’. There can be little doubt Winston Churchill’s handling of the Russians was absolutely masterful. It proves again and again that however unpleasant a task one has, provided one is not browbeaten and refuses to give way on any essentials, respect will be engendered mutually and maybe later trust. Whilst the Heads got on well together there was not much cooperation on the military level. Generations of distrust cannot be swept away with a wave of the wand. When we heard the result of the Prime Minister’s visit to Moscow, we were universally thankful, the only fly in the ointment being that we had promised by implication that we would land in Europe in 1943 and few of us believed that we should be ready then for a head-on collision with the German Army. However, we did land in Italy in 1943 as we shall hear later. Meanwhile we prepared various appreciations of where to go after clearing the Germans out of North Africa - Sicily, Sardinia or the Balkans. Eventually after much discussion we came to the conclusion Sicily was slightly the better alternative as it was a more convenient place for jumping off against Italy which would be necessary if she was still fighting by then. However, schemes for landing in the south of France as well as in the Adriatic were considered. But as often happens in war, the purely military pros and cons get overruled by political considerations, so we had, as it were, every alternative ready. September 1942. A short weekend at the end of September at Mulgrave as ever refreshed one a lot, and it was fine to see our family united again. Georgina and Johnny appeared to approve of their younger sister and spent a not inconsiderable part of their time roaming round the woods and playing pranks on the various nurses and governesses who had the questionable pleasure of looking after them. I very occasionally, rather too occasionally for my liking, saw my father who was setting a fine example of what a 77-year-old, fit in wind and limb, can do. The gardener, Reggie Little, had been sent down the mines and the cook had gone off to work in some war canteen, but he still had the faithful Bertha Wilkins who looked after him. and eked out the pretty inadequate rations as far as was possible. I thought he looked a bit thin when I saw him, but there was no lack of spirit and woe betide the air raid wardens of Longhope who were not up to scratch. We decided to move the family south so that we could be all together and Elizabeth started to look round for some residential hotel in the country not far from London where I could come on my days off at the Admiralty. 230

It must have been about this time when I spent the evening and best part of the night at Chequers when the Prime Minister was having one of his meetings with the Chiefs of Staff and Defence Committee to decide on future plans for the war. A lovely atmosphere and one that was certainly conducive to clear thinking. I don’t think Chequers was ever bombed. The greatest hazards were driving down there and back at night with the very dimmed headlamps which had to be used. Another meeting, this time in the War Cabinet Office in Storey Gate, I shall long remember - it was about re-entering Europe via Norway, a very favourite subject of the Prime Minister’s. In vol. 4 of his book there are plenty of references to this project which was one of the Prime Minister’s longest and most closely kept favourites. From the Naval and up to a point from the Air point of view, this presented no special difficulties though to use a modern terminology, the cost effectiveness of this type of operation was not very high because of the considerable distance by sea from the main base, i.e. UK. But from the Army’s point of view this was a non-starter, because the means of supplying troops with the almost nonexistent road and rail communications would reduce the operation to little more than a light raid. However, the Prime Minister decided one day the Chiefs of Staff and Directors of Plans should meet that evening at 10:30 p.m. It was clear the Prime Minister was determined if it was humanly or indeed inhumanly possible, he was going to get the Chiefs of Staff acquiescence to this. However, we had found out what the subject for discussion was and decided the best man to ride off the Prime Minister was Alanbrooke, the CIGS, who to prepare himself for the fray spent the afternoon resting. The meeting took place with the Prime Minister in his best form, for there was nobody who would be more entertaining than him and he was a wonderful talker. At about midnight when he assumed the Chiefs of Staffs’ resistance had been lowered, he started on this favourite subject i.e. to ‘roll up Herr Hitler’ from the North. I sometimes wonder if it was from Jackie Fisher’s idea before World War One of putting our Army on the WWD’s father, still a very upright Pomeranian coast some 90 miles north from Berlin that the germ of this idea was derived. figure, a couple of years later with the However, this time the CIGS with his dry inimitable humour kept interjecting with a series family at Merstham of wonderful stories mostly about Ireland which deflected the Prime Minister. The CIGS was himself no mean raconteur and he kept up story after story with the usual charming introduction, ‘Prime Minister, you have not I know heard this one’, and so on. This went on with few breaks until about 2:00 a.m. by which time the Prime Minister was getting grumpy and said, ‘Well gentlemen, we don’t seem to have decided much tonight, so we had better turn in’. Those of us who were there to record the decisions which we devoutly hoped would not be taken, were truly thankful to hear this remark. But when it came to trying to get his own way, there were in the Prime Minister’s case ‘NO HOLDS BARRED’! But what a dynamo of energy was the Prime Minister, not infrequently when one was studying the overall situation on the Admiralty Map or War Room, one would find this 231

rather strange figure clad usually in RAF battledress, looking at much the same problem has happened to be engaging one’s own attention. One had perforce to be a bit careful about expressing views too forcefully to him as he might well confront the Chiefs of Staff at one of their meetings with a remark like this: ‘a very shrewd naval member of the staff said so and so. What pray are the objections of the Chiefs of Staff to following this advice?’ But one must never forget the Prime Minister was determined to get at the truth and nobody knew better than him that the best and most brilliant of concepts get stifled or emasculated in the paths known as the ‘usual service channels’. Let us take a look again at the general situation in Plans. I had a modest hand in sponsoring a vastly increased size of the aircraft carrier programme and consequently of the Fleet Air Arm were well under way, and our warship building programme thanks in no small measure to the Controller, [Vice-Admiral Sir] Bruce Fraser, and his successor [Vice-Admiral Sir William] Wake Walker, were keeping pace with our requirements. We placed some shipbuilding orders in America and got most of our Fleet aircraft from that source. They seem to have almost limitless industrial resources, probably about twelve to fifteen times as great as ours. The submarine campaign was still giving us much anxiety. Successful attacks were being made by U Boats, sometimes packs of them in the North Atlantic and off Freetown. We were losing oil tankers at a greater rate than they were being replaced. Many attacks were launched by U Boats off the Venezuelan coast from where much of our fuel supplies came. Nevertheless, we felt that with our mounting anti-U Boat measures and the outstanding successes of the escort support groups commanded by such redoubtable characters as Captain [John] Walker and Peter Gretton, we should not anyway lose the war from this cause! Planning for Operation Torch got well underway and it was scheduled to take place at the end of October, a perfectly stupendous bit of organisation. A somewhat amusing incident occurred at the beginning of September. A meeting was held to decide on the make-up of the convoys, and who was to go in them, which ships should go in which convoys, and so on. All bearing in mind the assault convoys had to be tactically loaded. At the meeting which was presided over by a Lieutenant General, the War Office had provided two Major- Generals, eleven Brigadiers, four Colonels and four Majors. The Admiralty - one Captain, (Cecil Hughes Hallett) Head of Executive Planning Section, and one Commander. The Air Ministry - one Group Captain and one Wing Commander. Cecil Hughes Hallett, who had a very lively sense of humour, opened the meeting by saying, ‘On behalf of the Admiralty I object to the number of Brigadiers present!’ And without the least glimpse of a smile the Chairman sent away six of the Brigadiers! It shows the difference between the services. At the Admiralty perhaps because of the shortage of staff we always tried to send for Interservice meetings, one or at best not more than two to represent ALL Admiralty interests, whereas the War Office who never seemed to be short of staff, had every conceivable Staff Division or Department represented! I doubt if they do business any quicker by this method. However, planning went on at full speed and the various threads were pulled together in a cohesive pattern. Also, deception planning was put into the foremost part of our activities, as 232

much if not all depended on our being in a position to achieve surprise, and at first sight what chance was there? Surely, we felt common sense observation would allow the enemy a good chance of deducing what was about to happen. Admiral Cunningham was put in charge of the whole of the naval side of the Operation and it was clear there was to be no backseat driving from the Admiralty. Admiral Harwood was to confine himself to the Levant and Eastern Mediterranean and support the Eighth Army advance when that did happen. In mid-September 1942, an attack was carried out on Tobruk from the sea which proved to be a disastrous failure. It was at best a pretty rash conception and was intended to take the pressure off the Army in the Middle East who were reported to be in more need of help. We knew there had been some leakage of information and as the Operation proceeded it was clear from intercepted signals that the Germans had a very clear idea what was up. Nevertheless, the many attacks we were making in the Mediterranean on General Rommel’s supply lines were causing him the gravest anxieties. By air, submarine and mine attack the Axis shipping losses in the last two months of 1942 were over 300,000 tonnes. The new Command in the Middle East, Alexander and Montgomery, wasted no time and preparations were speeded up for a major assault on General Rommel’s position. However General Montgomery had his own ideas as to when an attack could be launched and he was absolutely adamant he would not launch it before ready. With Malta crying out for aid time was not by any means on our side. The Prime Minister did not waste time and prodded all concerned in the Middle East to get a move on! I saw some of the interchange of telegrams between the Prime Minister and Generals Montgomery and Alexander, but Monty stuck to his guns and would not agree to advancing the date of his offensive in the Middle East which he forecast as mid-October. This allowed him just inside two months to retrain his forces and get a well considered plan prepared and worked up. Monty was in a strong position for, as he observed to one of his staff, he was at this stage ‘unsackable’ and no amount of prodding either from the front or behind would make him alter his plans. In August we had carried out the exceedingly expensive operation of supplying Malta which we all guessed would last them about two months but not a lot more, so the time factor of getting into a position where Malta could be supplied was most important. In October it was evident that the U Boats were going to attack valuable shipping which passed round the Cape. Warnings were sent to the authorities at the Cape. Perhaps we at the Admiralty thought they were rather slow at taking sufficient A/S precautions, but the fact remains three big liners which were quite irreplaceable were sunk by U Boats in October. It is true the forces they had were at that time pitifully inadequate, but even so it is probably better to sail ships in convoy even if one has no escort at all than to sail singly. Meanwhile, in September we had thanks to the determination of the escort commanders and masters of merchant ships got through another convoy to Russia (PQ18), but we had little difficulty in convincing the Prime Minister, who had to break the news to Stalin, that we had insufficient forces to run both the landing in North Africa and continue with Russian convoys. The Home Fleet could not be in two places at the same time! News of the 233

tremendous actions in the Pacific and the desperate fights for Guadalcanal Canal gave us much cheer, for it was clear that the Americans were getting the measure of the Japanese in spite of the latter’s absolute fanatical bravery. October, I suppose was a month when it could be seen that the tide had definitely turned. On the 23rd October, General Montgomery launched his attack on the enemy forces at El Alamein and after some ten days very hard fighting, broke through the enemy’s defences, and inflicted a decisive defeat on General Rommel’s forces who had not the resources to recover from this defeat. We had been so long inured to defeat that the Eighth Army were just a bit slow in following up this victory with the result that we missed an opportunity of capturing at this stage most of General Rommel’s army. The days were pretty tense at the Admiralty and I am certain our Army colleagues were more than fed up answering the inevitable question of ‘how goes the battle?’ News was better from Australia as the Australians inflicted some serious defeats on the Japanese in New Guinea and drove them back from the approaches to Port Moresby. This again helped to dispel the myth of the invulnerability of the Japanese soldier or sailor. By the beginning of November, it was clear that the 8th Army were about to achieve a great victory in Libya and that General Rommel would soon be put to flight. Large numbers of Italian prisoners were taken and the German defences cracked. So now I remember saying to our military liaison officer in the War Room (old Colonel Miller) that Rommel’s next stop was Tripoli! He said they might stand halfway in the Gulf of Sirte at El Ageila, but did not think so. End of Volume 3 234
