Autumn 1942 above: Meetings were held frequently by the Prime Minister not only to decide on issues con- Main Armament, HMS Mauritius cerned with the North African landings but the strategy to be followed after that had been completed. We had as the background Winston Churchill’s visit to Moscow in August and his effect on Stalin. The story of Winston Churchill after a particularly tough and uncompromising interview has often been told. How when he got back to his bedroom and suspecting that the walls had listening devices, he went round and in no uncertain terms said exactly what he thought about the Russians, their behaviour, their lack of cooperativeness and their gross inefficiency. These impromptu speeches may well have had the effect desired for at the meeting next day the Russian policy of lack of cooperation and rudeness had completely changed. General Smuts paid many visits to the UK and nobody could have welcomed his visits more than Plans Division! For in the many arguments, debates and discussions which went on at Defence Committee and Chiefs of Staff level, General Smuts’ views and opinions were often sought and almost without fail he supported the views which we military planners put forward, and not always the ones favoured by the Prime Minister or other Ministers! We reckoned he was our best support and when things were at deadlock, we used to suggest to the Chiefs of Staff that the Prime Minister should seek General Smuts’ views. The Prime Minister had a most profound respect for his ‘military views’, probably more than anyone else’s. He liked to hear Mr. Menzies’ views and occasionally Mr Casey’s, both Australians and men of outstanding vision.1 But in his own cabinet there was nobody who was in a sense in the same street as Churchill and he seldom asked their views. He was at times particularly scornful of Stafford Cripp’s views which he said were argued with ruthless logic from false premises. For Attlee, he had considerable respect, with his practical and down-toearth way of doing things.2 1 Sir Robert Menzies (1894-1978), constitutional lawyer and Prime Minister of Australia 1939-1941 and 1949-1966; Richard Gardiner Casey (1890-1976), Australian parliamentarian and diplomat, keenly interested in science and engineering. 2 Sir (Richard) Stafford Cripps (1889-1952), politician and lawyer; Clement Attlee, 1st Earl Attlee (1883-1967), both ODNB. 239

In Plans, and on the War Planning level we found business could be conducted far more expeditiously with Attlee than with Churchill. Attlee was a first-rate chairman, a very clear head, completely devoid of personal prejudices as far as we could see and a whale for work. I can think of no better combination than Winston and Attlee as the two principal political figures for the conduct of war. Eden conducted foreign affairs with his accustomed skill, and there were few rows between the Foreign Office and the military men, which is surprising as after all the Foreign Office’s raison d’être is to do things if possible by peaceful means. In fact, it was often the case of the Foreign Office suggesting we do things by military means which perhaps were rather beyond our capabilities. We occasionally saw Mr Bevin, who as the Minister of Labour was doing a tremendous amount of all important and effective work. To keep up morale I visited one or two factories and told them at various meetings how the war was going, and above all what an important impact their particular work and products were having! Naval Captains in uniform seemed to have been much in demand - perhaps a breezy touch of the sea enlivens what must have been some pretty dreary work. But I never saw solemn or sulky faces, or if I did there were very few. There was no doubt everybody was in it to the hilt and there was a feeling of togetherness which one got as one walked around the workbenches that is not noticeable now. Production figures tell their story, and by the end of 1942 we must have been near our peak and what a peak that was. No combatant country in the world could touch the UK for economic effort per capita of the population. We were far far more efficiently organised than Germany, and when one considers our limited resources and the fact that most of our food and tremendous quantities of raw material had to be brought in by sea, one wonders at the majestic results we produced. Much credit for our war organisation must go to Lord Hankey whom I met often at the Club, or for a short walk after dinner before returning to one’s office. I’m glad Stephen Roskill is now publishing what sounds to be a great book on him.3 I think it a pity Hankey’s services were not used more in the war. It is true that he, as did many of us in Plans Division, differed from the Prime Minister in certain aspects of strategy. Hankey was doubtful of the efficacy of the bombing of Germany and the claim made by the extremist air strategists for it, and he disagreed in putting our major industrial effort into this. Professor Lindemann had alas a greater influence than Professor Tizard, and Winston Churchill put top priority in the building up of Bomber Command.4 In the light of the knowledge we now have, there is little doubt Hankey was right. It was a most illuminating experience talking to him and listening to him reminiscing on the differences between Lloyd George, Lord Haig and his Ministers in the First World War. Hankey knew the Navy well in those days, and he played no small part in getting Commander Henderson, a Commander in the Trade Protection Division of the Admiralty in World War I, to see him in 1917 and explain to Lloyd George that in [the adoption of] Convoy rested our only hope of defeating the U Boat threat of those days. Hankey knew the French well and he liked Foch, the Supreme Commander, for whom he had a great admiration. But it was a corrective just to talk for half an hour of what 3 Maurice Hankey, 1st Baron Hankey (1877-1963), civil servant, ODNB. Stephen Roskill wrote a three volume biography, Hankey: Man of Secrets, Collins (970-74). 4 Frederik Lindemann,Viscount Cherwell (1886-1957), scientist and politician, ODNB; Sir Henry Tizard (1885-1959), physical chemist and science administrator, ODNB. The two men were at loggerheads, both over strategic goals and the best means of taking them forward. 240

happened in the First War, and to ask oneself if we were falling into the same pitfalls again. But in this war the politicians were far more ‘military minded’ than in the First War, and similarly the ‘military’ commanders (i.e. Admirals, Generals and Air Marshals) were much more aware of the political implications of their actions. So there was not the acute friction and absolutely different standpoints which had to be reconciled in the First War before a policy could be carried through. Hankey had, I sensed, as acute a strategical instinct as anybody I have ever met. There are few people, if any, other than Hankey whose strategical judgement one would accept blind as it were. He had as profound a knowledge of the effectiveness of war in the air as anybody living, but he also had a most realistic appreciation of its limitations. He saw what he thought before the War to be wild exaggerations being verified. In fact, he once in so many words said to me, ‘We have and are still distorting our policies because of unsound claims of the effects of bombing’. He reminded me that every new mode or device of war generates its own antidote and called to mind Mr Baldwin’s statement that ‘the bomber will always get through’. With the development of radar and fighter control, this decisively put paid to the claim that the bomber will always get through. I knew Hankey’s elder son and his daughter who have inherited not a little of their father’s transcending intellect. I often thought the ideal war combination would have been for Hankey to decide on strategical priorities and for Churchill to inspire and direct our countrymen towards those ends. But I think Churchill with his lifelong urge for ‘ACTION’ and again ‘ACTION THIS DAY’ paid too much heed to Professor Lindemann and his theories of destroying Germany from the air. The fact that Lindemann was a German by birth and perhaps of Jewish extraction may have been at the root of his pathological hatred of the Germans. In many ways Lindemann was a sinister character though nobody could doubt his inventiveness and his dedication to Churchill. Once later after Lindemann had been ennobled I heard Churchill say to one of his staff, ‘if the Prof ’s blood is not too blue, ask him to come and see me here!’ My work brought me into contact with Professors Blackett and Fowler, both men of great intellect. Our work was on operational research matters and we considered methods of protecting convoys and worked on such problems, firstly from the theoretical aspect of the optimum size of convoys, optimum numbers of escorts per convoy, and what is most efficient, fewer large convoys heavily protected, or more small convoys less heavily protected. The thousand and one factors such as port loading and unloading capacities came into it. Then we worked much on the theoretical aspects of the Bay [of Biscay] antisubmarine offensive, for most of the German submarines now operated from French Bay ports. With Leigh searchlights we tried to catch the submarines at night on the surface and attack them before they dived. This was at first partially successful. But then the best methods of using flying hours available for anti-submarine work was susceptible to mathematical analysis and so on. Blackett had been a naval officer and left Dartmouth about four years before me. He left after the First War and studied physics at Cambridge. He became with Rutherford one of the men who split the atom. He is now President of the Royal Society, a Nobel Prize winner and one of the great scientists of our generation. A wild Irishman and still quite a rebel at heart, he used to have political leanings far to the left, but these have I suspect been modified since he is now a member of the Upper House. 241

Fowler, who I admired particularly, was primarily a mathematician and looked at all our problems with the most discerning eye. He had written a number of works and in addition to being a man of outstanding intellect he was as nice a man as one would meet anywhere with an amusing and whimsical sense of humour. I sometimes used to lunch with him at his club, the Athenaeum, as we both thought a change of atmosphere from my own club, the Senior, would be beneficial to our peace of mind. With Blackett and Fowler, it was always a stimulating experience discussing problems with them for they took nothing for granted and with great ease demolished quite a number of pet shibboleths which Naval Officers perhaps cherish overmuch! On the other hand, they were both eminently practical men and would realise soon enough what was and what was not practical. For instance, it was possible to devise certain air and sea search patrols which would be ideal from a mathematical point of view but which would need a senior wrangler of unlimited endurance to conduct. Talking to Fowler gave one an insight of the tremendous intellectual satisfaction one experiences in resolving and investigating mathematical problems. The widespread introduction of mathematicians and scientists into the Services and especially Staff divisions was absolutely invaluable for not only were preconceived notions often ruthlessly demolished, but whole new avenues for investigations opened up. A Service is bound to be conservative in thought and perhaps in approach, but probably the Navy least of all the three fighting services because of its day-to-day physical contact with the realities of life. Winston was very alive to the stimulus scientists could give, though many of us thought it sad that he preferred Linderman to Tizard. Tizard was a tremendously able and practical scientist. He saw clearer than anybody I suppose the possibilities of radar. His intellectual integrity was of the highest which I don’t think could always be said of Lindemann’s. He had few prejudices and I think no illusions. It was a pity there was a feud if that is the word, between Lindemann and Tizard, though the feud was on the former’s side. Much has been written about these two men in various books. We had a deep and profound respect for Sir Henry Tizard’s intellect and judgement. He had the gift of clear exposition and was of an even and charming disposition. Unlike Lindemann he was not a complicated character. I think the judgement of science will go in favour of Tizard in all that he advised and recommended, and not to the same extent with regard to Lindemann. One of Winston Churchill’s characteristics was his love of history of which he was no mean student. In drafting minutes for the Chiefs of Staff to send to the Prime Minister which suggested that he should alter his line and think again, it was always best, if possible, to use historical analogy. Fortunately, I had recently read all his historical books on his great ancestor, Marlborough, and could sometimes quote his [Churchill’s] arguments against his present ideas.5 For instance, a minute could sometimes start ‘It will be within the Prime Minister’s recollection that on the eve of the battle of say ‘Malplaquet’, the Great Duke observed to Prince Eugen etc. etc.’ Then the argument could be used to cast doubts on the Prime Minister’s propositions. He had a profound respect for historical analogy but absolutely none for present day technical arguments and seldom accepted them. I remember well spending hours pointing out the impossibility of executing the Prime Minister’s ideas on boiler cleaning of destroyers in order that they could be used more frequently and the 5 Winston S. Churchill, Marlborough: His Life and Times, London, 1933, 4 vols. 242

cycle of Russian convoys accelerated! No amount of hard facts seemed to sway the Prime Minister. I think perhaps he suspected most ‘technical experts’ were obstinate and pigheaded, and he was prepared to show he could at least match them in these qualities. I occasionally met the Prime Minister in the ‘dungeons’ at Storeys Gate which was the main cabinet underground offices. He was practically always cheerful and often had some apposite remark to make such as ‘Why did we not let you go and capture Pantelleria’! In the early part of the autumn my friend, Air Commodore Coryton, was promoted to Air Vice Marshal and given a group in Bomber Command under Bert Harris, the formidable Cin-C Bomber Command. I paid him a visit at his station a little bit later, an experience I will not easily forget! November 1942 The introduction of pack submarine tactics by the Germans from the summer of 1942 onwards brought many problems in convoy defence. The passage of a convoy across the Atlantic or from Gibraltar to UK was in fact a continual battle. Protecting aircraft in a sense kept the submarines heads down and attacked them when they could. Whilst escorting destroyers, frigates and corvettes dealt with the submarines as they disclosed their presence in the vicinity of the convoy. There were many stirring battles and one of the main problems was to provide continuous air cover. There was at that time that gap in the middle of the Atlantic which could not be covered continuously from either side of the Atlantic by aircraft. However, with merchant ship aircraft carriers, CAM ships (i.e. ships which could catapult aircraft but had no facilities for them to return with the result the aircraft and pilot had to ‘ditch’) and other devices we managed by one or other method to get the convoys through. After some heavy attacks which brought serious losses in the summer and autumn of 1942, the attacks were defeated with heavy losses to the enemy until the end of the year, when a convoy was heavily attacked and lost no less than thirteen ships.6 The C-in-C (Western Approaches), Admiral Sir Percy Noble had done splendid work at Liverpool where his headquarters were situated, and had produced a morale in the Navy and in the Merchant Navy which was second to none. He had got the Navy and Coastal Command of the Air Force to pull together as never before. He was relieved at the end of the year by Admiral Max Horton, one of our submarine aces, and one of the most successful and ruthless naval commanders we have had during the past century. As Roskill points out, he was the right man to put against Admiral Doenitz, the German Admiral, who was conducting the submarine campaign. Max Horton was a character, quite ruthless and in some respects like Jackie Fisher. Woe betide the officer who tried to pull the wool over Max Horton’s eyes, he caught the next train out of Liverpool! Max Horton was feared by many but there can have been nobody who did not admire his efficiency and overmastering drive. A good organiser, he delegated well and even at the busiest times as C-in-C he usually found time for a round of golf. Rather inscrutable a character, there can have been few who could better him at poker. A bachelor, but one who liked company and could be as gregarious as anybody. Kept himself fit and believed in the motto of ‘mens sana in corpore sano’. He had done outstanding work as Flag Officer Submarines prior to this and had done much to bring 6 WWD is probably referring to PQ18 convoy to Russia which sailed in September 1942 and lost 13 vessels. The disastrous losses on the PQ17 convoy was discussed earlier in his memoir. 243

our submarine service to the highest pitch of efficiency. When Dudley Pound was obviously tiring, some of us hoped he would become First Sea Lord but perhaps fortunately did not. He was wonderful at dealing with his own service, but at various meetings I attended with him at the quasi-political level, he clearly showed he was rather out of his depth dealing with the somewhat intangible problems which arise in discussions with politicians. To my surprise I found him of all people rather indecisive when talking on strictly professional matters with politicians. He gave the impression with them at times of not knowing his mind, whereas in fact few people can have been more incisive and clear [about] what to do than Max Horton. Very surprising because in the rapid give and take of debate there was few who could out score Max Horton. His predecessor Percy Noble was quite a different character. Nothing like as forceful or knowledgeable as Max Horton, yet in every sense and in the best sense of the word ‘a great gentleman’, with the power to make all people work together in harmony and with the greatest effort of which they were capable. All people liked Percy Noble whilst most people feared Max Horton, though he was a good friend to officers who gave of their best and would support them through thick and thin. In a way these two diverse characters were the antithesis of each other. Percy Noble, almost an Edwardian figure of great charm and courtesy, spotlessly dressed, almost obscuring what was a very well-balanced intelligence and great power of leadership. Max Horton, a buccaneering character who looked the part and would not have been out of place in Elizabethan days. I have perhaps over-lightly touched on the submarine threat to our existence but it was ever in the back of our minds and every 9:00 a.m. report we used to scan the shipping losses column anxiously. By the end of the year 1942 our imports were running below 34 million tons a year, which we estimated was the minimum required to feed the country and sustain the war effort, and all our oil reserves had fallen to a dangerously low level. We had together with the Allies lost nearly 8 million tons of shipping and had only replaced with new building something like 7 million tons. This was a staggering figure when it was remembered the total shipping in existence in the world at that time (enemy, neutral and allied) cannot have exceeded 50 million tons. The enemy submarine losses had indeed been heavy, but not so heavy as to prevent a substantial increase of German submarines available for operations by the end of the year. The time for the landings in North Africa drew on. It was originally intended to carry them out at the end of October but as we foresaw the Americans were not ready and the date was fixed for the 8th of November. The plan consisted of simultaneous landings at Casablanca, Oran and Algiers, to be followed by a rapid advance along the coast to Tunisia. The HQ for the operation until established ashore would be at Gibraltar, and as such a tremendous amount of preparation was necessary. All the aircraft for instance had to be parked on the relatively small Gibraltar Airport before they could be flown in to captured airfields in North Africa.Vice Admiral Edward Collins, who was irreverently nicknamed as ‘Fat Fred’, was the Flag Officer at Gibraltar. Poor chap, he made dreadfully heavy weather of his responsibilities, so heavy that we thought and indeed hoped some more dynamic and adaptable personality would be sent in his stead. I have seldom attended such a depressing conference as when the plans for Torch were unfolded to him. His face fell and fell as each new item of responsibility 244

was explained! Reluctantly, as he was an old friend of his, the First Sea Lord had decided to replace him. But on return to Gibraltar, Edward Collins had explained to the Government what was in the wind, and the Governor had telegraphed to the Prime Minister that this was no time to swap horses at Gibraltar. So Fred remained at Gibraltar and in the event did not do too badly. Probably the most able officer of his time, Commodore Oliver, was sent out as his assistant. Meanwhile Gibraltar continued to look more and more like a furniture removal van carrying or attempting to carry far too much stuff! I forget how many hundreds of aircraft were parked on the airfield and I remember saying to somebody at the Admiralty, ‘I hope no disgruntled Spaniard tosses a Molotov Cocktail over the boundary fence, for if he does the air side of the operation is OFF’. But strange to relate, Spaniards seemed to have been completely oblivious to what was going on in spite of the fact that their workmen came to and from La Linea to work in the dockyard. One of the main features of the plan was to hope for support from the dissident French ashore in Algeria. General Giraud had been smuggled out of France after escaping from prison and had been taken by one of our submarines and landed with various other agents, including ‘Jerry Wright’ a Captain in USN, to help organise the revolt in Algeria. The story of this trip makes a truly ‘James Bond’ type of story. But perhaps one of the greatest anxieties we had was when at the end of September, a Catalina crashed off Cadiz, and the officer who was carrying top secret dispatches for the Governor of Gibraltar was drowned with all the secret documents which contained the whole plan and date of the operation on his person. We wondered and hoped his body would never be recovered for if it was the whole operation would be prejudiced. And at this stage it was just not possible to carry out another operation without substantial delays. We just waited and waited and hoped the plan had not been compromised. We knew a body had been washed ashore at or near Cadiz and it seemed this might have been the body the officer concerned. An odd report suggested some intelligence had reached Germany, but nothing to confirm that it was about this impending operation. However, it was rightly decided not to alter our plans and to take a chance that they had not been compromised. The Germans showed absolutely no sign that they suspected something was up. Though one of the assault convoys were sighted by a U Boat and we knew this, there was no indication from German agents either in Tangier or Spain that something suspicious was underway. They must have been very incompetent as anybody seeing the vast assembly of aircraft in Gibraltar airfield should surely have had his suspicions aroused! We were taking a chance on the weather especially for the assault on Casablanca, for the Atlantic swells might well make landing through the surf impossible. The story of this assault is the first since the turn of the tide, has often been told and in no better place than Vol. 2 of Stephen Roskill’s Naval History.7 It makes absolutely fascinating reading, and to reread chapter 13 of this book cannot but bring back vividly what happened. So I will not redescribe it beyond picking out here and there a few instances. We had three 7 S.W. Roskill, The War at Sea, HMSO Official History of World War II, 4 vols. 1954-61. 245

of our best Flag Officers, Syfret, Burrough, and Troubridge, in charge of the assault in the Mediterranean, and Admiral Hewitt USN in charge at Casablanca. In spite of our attempt to subvert the French Armed Forces and the over optimistic forecasts made by Mr Murphy, the US Consul General at Algiers, we were met by pretty fierce French resistance, especially the French Navy. At Casablanca and Oran, the French Navy came out and was destroyed almost to a man by British and American warships. We tried to ram the booms of the harbour but the ships in most cases were sunk by the French i.e. Broke,Walnut and Heartland. The most determined resistance was put up at Oran which had not forgotten our assault in 1940 on them, and all batteries had to be systematically silenced before the ships could be berthed in the harbour and unloaded. We had some idea from our knowledge of the plan what was happening. Intercepted signals gave an idea and not infrequently we had messages from the Prime Minister to report on progress. Broadly speaking the attack on Algiers had seemed to have gone well, but that difficulties were being experienced at Oran and Casablanca. Nevertheless, by the evening of the first day Algiers was in our hands and the other two ports were about to fall. Bougie and Bone were soon captured by assault from the sea. And two days after the assault Admiral Darlan, who happened to be in Algiers and who had assumed command, ordered all hostilities to cease. Admiral Cunningham, who had always been regarded with favour by the French, saw Admiral Darlan who tried I think in all good faith to get the French Fleet at Toulon to come and join us. However unfortunately the French C-in-C, Admiral Laborde, was known by us to be a violent Anglophobe with the result that the French Fleet scuttled itself when the Germans entered unoccupied France, as they did later in the month. It was clear the operations were being successful and that all that was now required was to keep the momentum of the Army up to the desired level. On the eastern side of the Mediterranean the Eighth Army was advancing steadily towards Tripoli. There can be little doubt if we had as Admiral Cunningham wanted, changed our aim and landed further east we should have forestalled the buildup of the German troops in Tunisia, and probably saved ourselves a good two months of hard fighting. The political problems in Algeria were immense. Giraud did not really have much following, De Gaulle probably less, and in fact until he was murdered later in the month, Admiral Darlan had far in a way the most powerful following. We thought perhaps that the French would flock to our side to a man. While some did, a great many did not and preferred to sit on the fence. It is sometimes forgotten the French are great legalists, and a rule or constitution that they reckon is not quite legal is to them quite unacceptable. After a slow reaction the Germans were attacking our ships and land forces with submarines and aircraft and we lost some very valuable liners which were returning empty after landing their troops in Algiers. It must have been a few days after the landing that the Prime Minister returned to one of his old loves, that is to bring Turkey into the war. We simply could not see what would bring Turkey in anyway at this stage. They were hopelessly unprepared with modern weapons and would merely provide German aircraft with bombing practice at the expense of the towns 246

and villages of Turkey. As we saw it, Turkey’s best plan was in her own self-interest to wait until the last moment and then hitch herself to the winning bandwagon. The War Cabinet I think shared this view and Winston said he thought they were wrong and he was right! Eden was I believe sound in this. We could see at this stage little military advantage of bringing the Turks in on our side. The first thing would be a string of requests to rearm them at the greatest possible expense. Stalin did however I believe support Winston as I think he might have wanted additional help to control the Black Sea if the German advances continued much past the Crimea. December 1942 As the month drew on the Eighth Army continued their advances in Libya. Benghazi was reopened and it was evident the next largest target would be Tripoli but the logistics of that could not be solved overnight. The advance of our 1st Army in Algeria and the Americans was not as fast as it had been hoped in the bad weather, which was after all predictable [and] played a considerable part in this, and also the rawness of American troops which was inevitable but made for slowness. However, it is worth turning back to what was happening in the far North. Convoys had been resumed, and as ever the appalling weather conditions took their toll in almost complete darkness throughout the 24 hours. Very cold, almost always rough, the ships were often covered in ice. The German sent out Lutzow, Hipper, and six destroyers to attack the inward and outward convoys which usually crossed near the north Cape. A most confused series of actions took place between what were superior forces on the German side and inferior on ours. Due to the determination and gallantry of our escorting destroyers, the Germans were driven off and the convoys both escaped unscathed. It was in this action the Captain Sherbrooke of HMS Onslow was awarded the Victoria Cross for a most skilful and determined defence of a convoy against much superior forces.8 In many ways this can be regarded as a classic of how actions should be conducted against such superior forces. It must have been either toward the end of 1942 or beginning of 1943 that Alec Coryton asked me to spend the night with his group of Bomber Command to watch the operations. Alec now commanded a very fine bomber group in Lincolnshire composed entirely of our new heavy Lancaster bomber aircraft. There were I think altogether five bomber groups which came under the overall command of C-in-C Bomber Command, the aggressive Bert Harris, with headquarters at High Wycombe. I went down by train to Grantham one late afternoon and then went out straight to the HQ to arrive just in time for the briefing of the bomber crews for their night’s operations. A most thorough and careful proceeding. The attacks were to be on the Ruhr industrial plants and I think Dusseldorf was the principal target for our group. The targets were shown from intelligence PR photos and advice was given as to approach and return courses to minimise the effect of ‘Flak’ and avoidance of night fighters. I watched all their faces carefully as the crews took note of the points in the 8 Robert St.Vincent Sherbrooke (1901-1972),VC, DSO, was the officer in command of the destroyers. During the action Sherbrooke was seriously wounded in the face and temporarily blinded but continued to direct the ships under his command. 247

briefing. Some were anxious and rather tightly drawn, some cheerful and others with just a ‘business as usual’ look on their faces. But all obviously determined and convinced that the job they had to do was of vital importance. I could not but help wondering as I watched them, for how many would this be the last briefing they would ever attend. For it was known that the Ruhr defences were being built up with considerable speed and effect. Alec Coryton at the end of the briefing made some quite admirable remarks, summing up in his own inimitable way and sent them all off with a good laugh. A very brave set of men for the odds were not always good. As a rule, air crews were restricted to a maximum of 30 sorties over enemy territory. A most wise and far-seeing rule, for the problem of keeping morale and efficiency up with bomber crews, was one that needed sympathy, knowledge and imagination to a high degree. Then from soon after 7:00 p.m. onwards the aircraft were dispatched. It was amazing in this completely darkened airfield how aircraft seemed to have no difficulty keeping to the runway with their heavy bomb loads, to become airborne well before the end of the airfield runway was reached. Alec and I then went off and had something to eat and listen to the news. Aircraft were not expected to start arriving until soon after midnight, so we dozed after discussing every single subject under the sun, with his staff, some of whom were professors in private life and folk who followed the most diverse professions. I believe one of his best intelligence officers was by profession a butterfly expert and birdwatcher. Then just before midnight we went up to the control tower and down again to the Operations Room to hear how things had gone. The weather had apparently been reasonably clear and aircraft did not report difficulties in identifying their targets. ‘Flak’ reported to be heavy and some aircraft hit. A number of night fighters also were met. Aircraft started to land, a damaged aircraft was diverted to a nearby airfield and we started to count the numbers. Would all the Group return? In all I think nearly 100 aircraft from the Group took part in this raid and we wondered how they had fared. There were I think five or six airfields to each group. So, we had at our particular one about 20 aircraft to expect to return. It is always rather a tense time sitting round the Ops Room hearing the reports of returning aircraft as their numbers were checked by the control tower. I remember a little WAAF officer with a drawn and anxious face, reporting aircraft identification as they came in. I wondered whether she had particular anxiety for one of the air crews who took part in this raid. They were a brave set of women who took part in this operational organisation for whatever happened to air crews, and the casualties were sometimes heavy, they just had to carry on. We went along to listen to the debriefing. I cannot remember how many from the Group failed to return. I know from the particular airfield where we were, two were shot down over the Ruhr and one came back badly damaged but managed to get down in a nearby airfield. The briefing was most thorough and from the air of relief on the pilots and observers faces which could not be hidden, it was clear in the main most of the targets had been reached. But how difficult it is looking down on a blazing inferno to know whether or not one’s bombs were ‘On Target.’ It was clear to me leadership of a very high order was required at Squadron, Wing and Group levels. Some of the characters I met, including Gibson the man who got the VC for the Mohne Dam raid, were men of the highest metal 248

and calibre. We were fortunate to have pilots and air crews of such high calibre whose nerve never faltered, in spite of increasingly heavy casualties. It was at once clear how everybody worshipped Alec Coryton, who would fight to the last ditch for any of his officers who merited support. I am sorry that Alec, who was never afraid of speaking his mind which was much more often right than wrong, fell foul later of Bert Harris, the C-in-C. But later I met Alec in Cairo as Deputy C-in-C Air Force, and he later became C-in-C British Air Forces in the Far East during the Burma campaign where he acquitted himself to fine effect. It would not be out of place to refer to the veritable revolution that the wholesale introduction and development of Radar had on Naval Warfare. One could as it were ‘see’ in the dark up to the limit of the horizon, and the outstanding success of 10 cm. radar which was made possible by the invention of the magnetron, put us a long way ahead of the Germans and indeed of all our allies including the Americans, who took our ideas up avidly in some technological fields. Our aircraft could detect German submarines on the surface, as could our ships. So no longer would submarines keep up with convoys and shadow them on the surface at night or in poor visibility. Then with radar we could have ample warning of the approach of aircraft and if practical and available direct defending fighters on to them. Then some fighters for use at night were being fitted with radar which enabled them to detect and eventually attack approaching bombers. The side that had to put it in a nutshell ‘the technical edge’ on the other had the scales heavily weighted in its favour, as I was to find later in the War, when I commanded one of our newest cruisers. Then magnetic mines had concerned us much, as the waters around the British Isles are shallow and are suitable for the laying of magnetic ground mines. But our mining and torpedo branch had done wonders to counter them, but more of this later. A point where progress had not been made as quickly as was desirable was in our anti-aircraft armament. Neither long range nor short range AA armament were effective, and they did not prove a deterrent to enemy aircraft who pressed home their attacks. We had suffered very heavy losses from this cause. The US long and short-range anti-aircraft systems were ahead of ours. We just had not put anything like the development effort into AA matters required before and during the early stages of the war. We had not faced the problems fairly and squarely, for the lessons and the exercises which took place showed us that we were woefully ineffective in AA fire. A measure of blame must go to the Gunnery Department of the Royal Navy before the War, for not gripping this problem imaginatively and quickly enough. My friend Gerald Langley, an aviator by profession and outstanding technical brain and debater, was put in charge of the Gunnery Division, in I think 1941 or early 1942, and did an enormous amount to lift our gunnery ideas up to the level required, when air targets which do not go just ten times as fast as warships, but sometimes twenty or even thirty times as fast. As the year drew to a close, we were I suppose as hard at it as ever in Plans in preparing plans, policies of the future, but by this time it was clear to us that this was not going to be a 249

long war, and we had every reason to hope that within two years the complete defeat of the Axis could be encompassed. Our immediate future was charted. But it was necessary to see where and better still how, to achieve our aims with the minimum of delay. The Russian armies had staged a tremendous revival and had surrounded the German Army of the South at Stalingrad. It was clear to us that this army would not be able to last through the winter, and that the Germans were faced with the biggest military disaster of the war. Plans were put in hand for a meeting with the Americans which took place in January 1943 at Casablanca. Meanwhile we had produced two papers for the Chiefs of Staff to put to the War Cabinet. As Winston remarked in his book, our papers differed sharply from the Americans but more in priority and emphasis than in principle. In so many words, we favoured knocking Italy out of the war and following up Operation Torch, whereas the Americans were in favour of holding [our] hand in North Africa and invading Europe i.e. France straight away in the autumn of 1943. The taking over of unoccupied France by the Germans in November added emphasis to our arguments. It was as much as anything a logistic argument. Once one is in an area it is best, if at all possible, to continue and avoid the endless delays of packing up, re-sorting and starting out again. We also, I must admit, saw the desirability or indeed the possibility of making the Mediterranean into an Allied lake again! The immeasurable advantage of this state of affairs needed no emphasis from any sailor. I have not referred to the almost incessant coastal battles at sea and in the air which took place round our coasts. The targets were of course our absolutely vital coastwise traffic which was essential for our war effort. We developed motor torpedo boats and fighter aircraft to protect our convoys whilst we took the war into enemy waters off the German, Dutch, Belgian and French coasts by launching attacks on all their shipping by torpedo carrying aircraft, by motor torpedo boats, and by constant mining. For by this time, we had far outstripped the Germans in the development of magnetic and acoustic mines. I managed to get up to Mulgrave for a few days at the end of the year and had a splendid time with the family. Lady Normanby was in good heart and in spite of the fact that a lot of WAAFs and a few WRNS were accommodated there, she was right on top of the world. Occasional letters from Oswald who was I think at that time in a prisoners hospital. January 1943 The Casablanca Conference was the main item to concern us in January. Lambe went with his Army and Air Force colleagues. It was a happy idea to have the conference there, for climatically it would make for relaxed discussions and it was sufficiently far from the war zone to distract people who might want to go and see how the fighting was going on! There was the problem of Generals Giraud and De Gaulle. The fluctuations of De Gaulle’s temperament, his arrogance and touchiness are described vividly in chapter 38 of the Hinge of Fate, but eventually Giraud, who was a much less difficult man than De Gaulle, agreed to meet him and shake hands. Winston in this book speaks with great fairness and indeed generosity of De Gaulle, but as he said, one of the biggest crosses he ever had to bear was ‘La 250 Croix de Lorraine’ - the Free French emblem.

above: The Casablanca conference, January Lambe kept me in close touch. His tact was needed for the US Navy headed by Ernie King 1943, with General Giraud (left) and and their new D of P was just as difficult as Kelly Turner. King was determined in spite of General de Gaulle (second right) with his President’s ruling, that the Pacific should have priority in so far as the US Navy was President Roosevelt and Churchill. concerned. However, we got the US Navy to recognise that the defeat of the U boat was to Image International Churchill society remain the first charge on the resources of the Allies. There was a good deal of argument between the Joint Planners and Chiefs of Staff as to which should be attacked first - Sardinia or Sicily. We favoured the former but the Chiefs of Staff and the US Chiefs of Staff favoured the latter so they won the day. There was not much in it. The main point was Sardinia was a lesser nut to crack and could have been captured at least two months before the attack on Sicily was launched. However, on the military side the decisions of Casablanca were unquestionably sound. The only slip was the bringing out of the phrase ‘Unconditional Surrender’ by President Roosevelt here somewhat unexpectedly and indeed without much premeditation. Many books have been written questioning the wisdom of this. On the whole I believed at the time it was unwise, as I knew it would cut a good deal of ground from our feet in respect to our underground warfare and propaganda activities. The Prime Minister also thought it wrong though he was in no position to say so at the time. The President, Lambe told me, seemed in good health and was very much in charge of his team. Generals Marshall and Eisenhower as ever [were] first rate. The Airmen a bit over keen on the daylight bombing concept with their Flying Fortresses. The good news of the Eighth Army advance towards Tripodi helped matters and there is no doubt General Alexander made a tremendous impression on the Americans, as indeed did Admiral Cunningham. Eisenhower had evidently developed a great regard for Admiral 251

Cunningham. Lambe found the US naval planners had swung to being overcautious now, and it was evident that though King paid a measure of lip service and maybe a bit more to the concept that the defeat of Germany must take priority over all else, he was determined that the main weight of the US Naval effort should be devoted to the Pacific. He had evidently so instructed his Planners, which meant the main weight in European waters must still be shouldered by the British. Lambe was very amusing about De Gaulle and Giraud; he remarked as history so often shows, no two people can be more venomous to each other than two Frenchmen! Churchill summing up of De Gaulle in chapter 37 of his book is as true now as it was when written then. I think it will be judged that the Casablanca Conference was a great success - politically we and the Americans got on well together and indeed so did we in the military sphere using the term in its broadest sense. Perhaps from the strategical sense the greatest triumph was to get the Americans to agree that the first charge on the Allied sources must be the defeat of the mounting German U boat campaign. We had worked mighty hard in the Admiralty to get universal acceptance of this cardinal aim. Churchill had kept Stalin informed and though some of Stalin’s telegrams were rude, it was clear that Churchill and Stalin had a measure of mutual respect for each other which led to understanding. It was a tragedy to the Allied clause that Roosevelt thought he knew better and could do ‘a deal’ with Stalin when they all met later in the year, in Teheran and later at the Yalta. It was clear after the Casablanca Conference that there would soon have to be a conference to include the Russian, for it was absolutely vital that the Allies should not only have an agreed and coordinated strategy, but they should have some idea what the other parties intended to do! Aircraft accidents were taking their toll of valuable officers. It was I think at this time the Brigadier Dykes, the splendid Army Director of Plans was killed when the aircraft in which he was returning from Casablanca with many of the Plans made crashed. By good luck Lambe was travelling in another plane. The tide was beginning to flood for the Allies, it was no longer a question of whether we would win the war it was a case of when. The outline plans had been drawn and the first direct steps taken. The Russians had inflicted early in February a decisive reverse on the Germans by capturing General Paulus’ army at Stalingrad and the Americans had forced the Japanese to withdraw finally from Guadalcanal. Lambe and I discussed our futures a bit together for we had both been in the Admiralty and War Cabinet offices since September 1940. We came to the conclusion that we certainly could not possibly leave together as I suppose we had a lot more knowledge than most of the naval planning and policy problems, which were not only pressing at the moment, but likely to come up in the future. The whole future strategy would have to be resolved when Churchill, Roosevelt and Stalin met, though the guidelines were clear. Our voice, i.e. the British view, was codominant with the Americans at the moment, but with the vast increase of their military and economic power taking place week by week, it was clear that the 252

Americans would have a greater say and we should have a lesser say, for we had already reached the optimum point of our war effort. We came to the conclusion Lambe must stay on for eight months to a year yet, for his position in the Joint Planning Staff was almost unique and his judgement and views were profoundly respected, so it was time for me to go now and get a Deputy well in the saddle before Lambe could go. Lambe asked me who should relieve him and without hesitation I said Grantham in a year’s time for his judgement, knowledge and insight where I think second only to Charles Lambe. Grantham had recently lost a cruiser which he commanded in the Mediterranean but was now in the Indomitable, one of our latest aircraft carriers.9 We had a look around for my relief with the aid of the Naval Secretary, and we came to the conclusion that R.D. Dickson, a most successful Captain of the fast minelayer Manxman, who had much recent service in the Mediterranean would fit the bill, as indeed he did. Meeting the Naval Secretary, Freddie Hamilton, a friend of mine of long standing, in the corridor one day, he said what about going to Mauritius next month? I fairly jumped at it as she was one of our latest cruisers, and this sort of post was usually given to a senior captain and not one of only two years seniority! I found Mauritius had after refit recently joined the Far Eastern fleet with base at Mombasa. Even though there was no great naval activity going on there at this moment it was likely there would some soon in the Far East. So, Bertie Dickson relieved me as Deputy Director of Plans in February and I went straight away and did it an excellent week Ships’ Damage Control course at a house not far from Barons Court underground station and then went up to Mulgrave for a bit of leave. I would have to fly out to Mombasa and put myself in the hands of the organisation of which I had once decided on priority of air travel. Being appointed Captain to one of our fighting cruisers, I got priority and it was early in March that I went down with Elizabeth to London to collect one’s things, get all one’s documents, which included a false passport to be used if one was force landed in enemy territory. I was described as a ‘textile agent’. Alas, I had to return this passport as I don’t think the Foreign Office really liked being party to forging passports! Then in London I met my father, well and cheerful as ever, who seem pleased and though he was obviously anxious that I was going back to sea again, for he remembered that my last ship the Hood was lost, a little time after I left her. Then my dear sister Janie who was now doing an absolutely splendid job organising the GTC, the Girls Training Corps. She worked permanently in London and wore a smart khaki sort of uniform - she looked very nice and it was clear how much she was liked and admired. A glimpse of my brother Howell who was living at Molesey and working in Bushey Park on some fuel problems on behalf of Shell. Elizabeth was with us and we all went out to supper on my last day together, before catching the evening train down to Plymouth where we were to embark in some Catalina aircraft and fly to Gibraltar as a first stage. Admiral Willis was there and he was to be the seagoing Commander of the Mediterranean Fleet for operations that lay ahead i.e. the attack on Sicily etc., after we had cleared the Germans out of North Africa. 9 Guy Grantham (1900-1992), later Admiral Sir Guy, ODNB 253

I remember so well how well Janie looked and never dreamt for one moment she would be dead within the year. She was happy in the knowledge that she was doing a great job and was loved and liked by the girls. David her son had been accepted into the Royal Air Force and was doing some training at Oxford before being sent to Canada to do his flying training. The Plymouth train soon set off from Paddington after saying goodbye to Elizabeth and my father, brother and sister who looked perhaps a little sad as they walked away talking, I think, to Mrs Willis, the wife of Admiral Willis. On arrival at Plymouth, we went straight down to Mount Batten to embark on the Catalina aircraft [sea-plane]. The conditions for take-off were described as marginal - quite a short choppy and steep little sea. On the other hand, with the strength of the wind we should not want a long run to become airborne. Willis and I and some other passengers soon made ourselves comfortable. We had the all-clear and after a few bumps ending with a big one we were very soon airborne. The plan was to cross the Bay of Biscay in darkness, when interception by enemy aircraft would be unlikely, then do the latter part of the journey by daylight. This all worked out according to our plans. We of course flew over the sea as we could not afford a forced landing even in a neutral country like Spain or Portugal. Catalina flying boats were quite comfortable and the crew soon produced some hot coffee and filling sandwiches. They were Canadians just recently qualified as aircrew and this was their very first operational flight. As we approached the Straits of Gibraltar fog shut down and the pilot with whom I was talking wondered whether it be best to go down to sea level or go up. At present he was flying at I think about 1000 feet. I said immediately go higher, fly out into the Mediterranean where it is usually clear and don’t drop below 4000 feet as there are some high mountains not far from the Straits of Gibraltar and anyway Gibraltar itself is pretty solid and is 1400 foot high! He immediately did this and sure enough we soon found ourselves just east of the Straits, when it was clear with bright sun shining which enabled us to make a good landing in Gibraltar Bay. A warm welcome from everybody at Gibraltar, old Edward Collins, the Admiral was almost benevolent. We went down and had a look at the Ops room in the Rock which had been used to conduct the invasion of North Africa the previous November. The aircraft had a small defect which required a remedy, so it was not Janie Ackers with her son David who until the next morning we set out with another Catalina on our next leg which was to Port had just joined the RAF. Bathurst [Banjul] in Gambia. There were a few passengers this time but nobody of especial Photo taken in 1943. Janie looked interest. In due course we arrived at Port Bathurst but where was the other Catalina? It impossibly glamorous in uniform. turned up 11 hours later, they had a fault in their compass and this was not discovered until they sighted the coastline of Brazil which made them retrace their steps. Fortunately, Catalinas carry about 20 hours fuel supply. A night in a very pleasant government Rest House which had been the home of one of the administrators in peacetime. Port Bathhurst, a pleasant sleepy little tropical place which relies entirely on its river for the livelihood of the inhabitants. Bright topical flowers with any number of Red Flame Forest Trees and poinsettias. Then on to Takoradi [Ghana] where I spent the day with the resident Naval Officer by name 254

Sandford, who showed me the tremendous development which had been done there. Quick look at Accra [capital of Ghana], and on to Freetown [Sierra Leone] where I stayed two nights in the mess, for the aircraft required some repairs. Freetown was at that time a main convoy assembly anchorage and there was a lot going on. As I had a day to spare, I went with the local padre there, by name Gamon, who was in my term at Osborne and later took orders, for a walk over the hills to a nice bathing beach where we bathed to our heart’s content, but kept in shallow water as there were a few sharks on the lookout for the over adventurous. Hot steamy and topical Freetown was not a comfortable place to live in in pre airconditioning days. Then from Freetown, where I noticed a convoy was being assembled, to Leopoldville in the Belgian Congo [Democratic Republic of the Congo] where I spent the night in a rather second-class little hotel. We parted company with the nice young Canadian aircrew who had enjoyed the experience and who then set course in a leisurely way back to European waters. Leopoldville [Kinshasa] which was in the Congo, is a fine town with broad avenues and appeared to be effectively administered by fairly numerous Belgians. The next stage of the air travel was run by the Americans across Africa and we were invited to take a seat in a completely stripped DC-3 used for transport of heavy stores. It did not even have cushions for the seats. However, it was not long before we reached Elizabethville [Lumumbashi], a very fine city and capital of Katanga province. Lovely avenues and fine bungalows for the employees of the Union Minière, which is the giant copper concern, providing much copper for the allies. Still very hot, quite good food at the hotel but like many hotels the sanitary arrangements were not all that could be desired. We got in late in the evening so stayed the night and took off about noon next day. There was only one other passenger beside myself, an American GI from Texas with whom I played numerous games of chess. The pilot had never seen African wild game before and was determined to remedy this defect on this flight. His plan was to go down to about 50 feet and see if he could scare any rhinoceros out of their habitual immobility. I noticed one who gazed at us as we approached him [and] just tossed his head as we passed, as if to say, ‘That’s for you’. We saw a lot of game, zebra and deer by the pack, a lot of giraffe, but I don’t remember seeing any lions or elephants. Quite a lot of hippos were to be seen in the Congo. Altogether a most fascinating if rather frightening trip across Central Africa where I suppose human habitations must have been hundreds of miles apart. Rather dry and arid as much of Central Africa is. We saw and flew around the base of Kilimanjaro with its snow-capped peak, a stupendous sight. However, it was soon over and late that afternoon we arrived in Nairobi airport [Kenya]. The US pilot was anxious after ‘a night checking over the high spots in Nairobi’ to fly me down to Mombasa, but I said ‘no’ firmly and I caught the night train from Nairobi to Mombasa which I remembered from old Enterprise days 15 years before. Nairobi was quite unrecognisable, fine houses, buildings and avenues. Obviously, any amount of prosperity, the US had done good business there and were running the airport most efficiently. I looked in at the new Stanley Hotel for a drink before going along to the station. A very comfortable journey down to Mombasa through the Serengeti Game Reserve. Again, I did not see any lions but any amount of other game. A comfortable night and before 255

long we had reached the terminus at Mombasa where we breakfasted. I changed into a passably clean uniform and went down to report to the C-in-C office. There I met Ralph Edwards who was Chief of Staff to James Somerville. The whole fleet was evidently mighty well organised and on its toes. I saw also Danckwerts, who was Deputy C-in-C to James Somerville and held the fort while James Somerville was away. A warm welcome from this very clever and perhaps at times slightly arrogant man. Then in a few moments James Somerville came in looking younger and better than ever. A long talk with putting him in the latest picture in in regard to government thinking etc. etc. After meeting most of James Somerville’s staff, and they were as one would expect a pretty able crowd, I was told by Ralph Edwards, the Chief of Staff, that the C-in-C planned to go to Durban the next day in Mauritius and that the idea was I should relieve Derek Stephens, the present Captain, on arrival in Durban. This idea commended itself much to me as it gave one a chance of getting to know the ship and the officers before one took over, and because as a Captain must in a sense be ‘isolated’. Bill Tennant was the Admiral in command of our squadron, the 4th Cruiser squadron with his flag either in Gambia, a sister ship of Mauritius, or Glasgow, one of the big town class of cruisers. I knew Bill well, not only was he a distant neighbour of ours at Longhope, but he had been one of the instructional commanders at the Staff College which I had attended in 1931. Derek Stephens, my predecessor, had been a submarine specialist. He had the reputation of being an efficient captain but a very difficult one! The Commander, Patrick Brock, a first rate ‘honest to God’ torpedoman who qualified as a T specialist three to four years after me. The Mauritius, I was told, had a high reputation for battle efficiency. All to the good and later in the morning I went on board to be met by Derek Stephens who introduced me to the Heads of Departments who gave one a very warm welcome. The Mauritius was lying at fore and aft buoys just opposite the main jetty in Kilindini, as the port of Mombasa is now called [which] had changed out of all recognition since I was last there in 1928. A veritable Fleet, two battleships or it may have been three, one aircraft carrier, a squadron of four or five cruisers, and a flotilla of destroyers were all in harbour, and made an imposing sight. Derek Stephens took me round the ship meticulously and it was not long before I felt I knew it. He was a good ship handler and I looked forward to seeing him handle the ship when we left next morning for Durban. The officers seemed a nice bunch of people. Sarell the Gunnery Officer, a very very clever and able officer; Moseley, the navigator;Vickery, the Chief and a host of others mostly RNVR. But for all that as fine a crowd as one could meet anywhere. Nice set of young men in the Gunroom. My first impression was that while the ship in most respects was an efficient one, it was not an altogether happy one, and it was not difficult to see why. Derek Stephens had an uncertain temperament and folk were never quite sure of themselves with him. All smiles one day, all frowns the next! He was, nevertheless I think, respected by the ship’s company who much liked to listen to his speeches, which were seldom without a ready turn of wit. Patrick Brock, the Commander was the cornerstone and lynchpin of the ship. The soul of loyalty, very efficient and in spite of perhaps rather a shy and forbidding manner, the most sensible and sympathetic character. The Ships Company were a veritable cross section of the Commonwealth, some Canadians, quite a number of South Africans, a few Australians and a very 256

HMS Mauritius in camouflage good bunch of New Zealanders. The Britishers were from all parts of the UK though shades of grey/blue paint the ship was designated as a Chatham (Home Port) ship. It would be invidious to choose, but as a crowd the New Zealanders were the best of all, and the South Africans individually were in a number of cases outstanding. A few days later our new Padre Jock Henderson joined. Quite outstanding in every way and old Padre Beardmore was as good as his word, when he said to me before I left England from his HQ at Portsmouth, that he had sent us the best RNVR padre in the service! Jock was an enormous success from the word go, and the Bishop of Glasgow had been most reluctant to relieve him from his incumbency at Ayr. Jock is now the Bishop of Bath and Wells, and WWD shortly after joining HMS continues with the high promise he showed when he joined in Mauritius as a newly joined Mauritius, his relaxed smile shows his Padre. pleasure at being afloat once more.
