Somehow a ship, especially when at sea, feels alive, and this stimulates all Brock on the left. After 3 ½ years of who serve on board. It was hot and at times very hot, and the glare had to be watched. rationing, the men look thin and spare. Dark glasses were the order of the day on the bridge, but I was delighted to see that regula- Image courtesy of Mary Rawstorne. tion tropical helmets which were a nuisance when last in the East Indies Station had more or less died out, and instead people wore light uniform caps. I visited all the boiler rooms and engine rooms during this visit which at 22 knots did not take us long. We were soon alongside at Durban and after the C-in-C had left to talk with the C-in-C (S Atlantic) Admiral Tait, on improving methods of dealing with U boat attacks which had taken place near the Cape, we gave Derek Stephens a rousing send-off as he stepped ashore to take passage in the next ship bound for the UK. The opportunity was taken to dock and scrape the ship’s bottom so that we could do our top speed of 30 knots without undue difficulty. What a splendid place was Durban. Everybody seemed to welcome us and it was wonderful not to have to bother about blackouts, ration cards or any of the numerous restrictions to which we had 257

got used in England. I went and played a round of golf with some borrowed clubs at a nice golf course nearby and made quite a number of friends. After about five days it was time for us to return to Mombasa, and this time I was in command. I practised handling the ship and found her very responsive without any unexpected tricks. The trip up through the Madagascar channel was uneventful. We had to zigzag just in case the odd Japanese submarine reported in these waters was lying in wait for us, and back in Kilindini where we underwent a concentrated period of battle training for the next three weeks. As a result of the various tests, Admiral Tennant left me without doubt we were the most efficient fighting unit in the Eastern Fleet. Much credit for this must go to the Commander and Ivan Sarrell, the Gunnery officer. We certainly had a phenomenal gunnery record. I introduced a number of new features which I had tried in the Hood and I think everyone felt proud of their ship. We carried a Walrus amphibian aircraft on board in which I used to fly as often as possible. I used to fly it quite a lot, but the pilot wisely would not let me land it opposite the ship in case we capsized, a thing not difficult with the Walrus! We flew over Pemba, the island of cloves, which gave a very distinct aroma. In fact, at 5000 feet one could smell it. I soon got the feel of flying this aircraft which presented no terrors. After leaving Durban I spoke to the ships company, for I think the sooner they knew their Captain the better. I dwelt on the wonderful privilege we all had of taking part in this epoch-making period of the history of mankind, of the many problems we all individually as well as collectively had to face. I mentioned without breaching the Official Secrets Act the strategical problems we had to face, and perhaps what part Mauritius might play in the actions which lie ahead. I suppose it was all pretty plain and humdrum stuff but I felt perhaps a bit uplifted and to my surprise the ship’s company, the great majority of whom were not regular sailors, seemed to like what I said and listened intently. For I am still sure if you appeal to men’s highest feelings and instincts one is seldom disappointed. I think if you are to trust people, they must first of all trust you. And how important it is to ensure that trust is merited. Our training in the Navy gives us, as probably nothing else does that little bit extra, which makes command real and incisive. One of the sailors was heard to say, which pleased me much, ‘I hope ‘ee takes us into action’!10 Extract from WWD’s papers: WWD took enormous trouble drafting out what he said to the ships company.This is the opening from seven handwritten foolscap pages on the Durban address, which would then have been committed to memory for delivery: 10 Drafts of a number of WWD’s weekly talks to the ships company survive among his naval papers in Churchill College, Cambridge. 258

'As this is the first time since our arrival at Durban that we are all together I am going to take the opportunity of speaking to you. When a new captain joins a ship it is important that he should see the ships company as soon as possible and that the ships company should see him. [A man of war is a single indivisible/(erased)] The reason is this - a man of war is a single indivisible unit and we shall never reach the highest pitch of battle efficiency if I do not know of what you are capable and you do not know what is in the back of my mind. I have already seen a few familiar faces who were members of a very fine ships company on the China station before the war but the great majority of you are so far unknown to me as I am to you.' He continued with news from home in a tone of restrained optimism, news of the war’s progress, and reemphasized the need for ‘battle efficiency’ and the responsibility of every single member of the crew to bend himself to the task. He ended by quoting Drake’s words that he had used with regard to the company of HMS Hood, ‘I must have the Gentlemen to haul and draw with the Mariners and the Mariners with the Gentlemen. . . Let us show ourselves all to be of a Company'. Let this always be the motto of the Mauritius and let us go forward in good heart as one company.’ WWD Papers, Churchill College, Cambridge April 1943 I don’t think we can have been back more than two or three weeks when I was sent for by the C-in-C and told Mauritius was to be detached from the Fourth Cruiser Squadron, and was to join the Mediterranean Fleet to take part in the massive assaults planned for that area. I was sorry to leave the squadron and the efficient fleet, but perhaps glad that immediate active service lay ahead. So off we sailed I think in the last few days of April to Aden at high speed where I was entertained by that remarkable character, Charles Larcombe, who was the Commodore Aden. He gave us a small sack of mocha coffee which was greatly appreciated in the months which lay ahead. Then off up the Red Sea early May where it can be mighty hot. I offered a challenge to the stokers to steam up the Red Sea on one boiler room, whilst those off watch cleaned the other boiler. In this way we could arrive with the Mediterranean Fleet with the maximum time available before the ship could claim her four days off ‘boiler cleaning time’. The stokers, many of whom were pretty tough Durham miners, accepted this challenge in the great heat and comfort and did this remarkable job so that within 72 hours we were waiting our turn at Suez to go through the Suez Canal ready for prolonged service in the Mediterranean. Suez was crowded with ships for up to that time all the Eighth Army supplies came to Suez after their long journey around the Cape. 259

It is interesting to reflect on the switch from my previous job in which one had a measure of responsibility for planning and advising on all matters, from the largest strategical concept to the smallest operation, and to be able to advise whether or not the plan proposed is a viable and sensible one with reasonable chance of success. The present one was a definite active responsibility to carry out one’s part in any particular operation ordered, some of which I had a hand in planning at the Admiralty and Cabinet offices before I joined Mauritius. There can be few more interesting experiences than planning operations and then going and carrying them out in person. The importance especially with wartime ships companies of keeping everybody in the picture can never be overestimated. I used to have when possible a weekly talk to the ship’s company on the war, as with one’s background knowledge one could fill in Passing through the Suez Canal with a good deal of information and forecasts with some certitude what next! I got some pretty acute questions which was much to be encouraged, for the eternal truth is that you can lead men anywhere when they know what the idea is and above all why. I told the ships company to look at the map of the Mediterranean and guess where we were going next. It was not difficult to strike a winner! And again, I explained the whys and wherefores of some training, which I had introduced and what a resulting change this made. The idea of a Captain going about with tightly sealed lips leads straight to disaster. You must share your problems with as many people as possible. The Ships Company had an idea fostered a bit by Derek Stephens that they were going home soon to [be] given leave. I cannot think why because in fact the ship had only been overseas about six months when I joined her. Even in peace time an overseas commission was usually 2 to 2 ½ years! However, it was an illusion which they cherished until we reached Chatham over a year later to prepare for the invasion of France. There were any number of Army establishments on the Canal and at Suez, and before long a pilot came on board to take us through the Canal. We skirted past a couple of sunken ships in the Canal which had been the victim of German mines dropped by aircraft. Then one stop at Port Said to fuel alongside the oiling jetty. I went up to see the resident Naval Officer, a retired captain called Wace, who I used to play cricket with before the war. May 1943 We had now entered the Mediterranean and looked forward intensely to what lay ahead of us. The Suez Canal was a very busy place with convoys of supply ships going up and down with military and air force camps on both banks; but still with the ubiquitous camel and his Egyptian master travelling along the canal’s edge, and by the sweet water canal from Ismailia to Port Said. There was plenty of work for Egyptians, either they were local contractors, lorry drivers, storekeepers or employed on any duty in connection with the Army. Though much political play was to be made later with armies of occupation denying political freedom to 260

the inhabitants etc., I doubt if the Egyptian labourer ever ‘had it so good’ as when we were in fact in virtual occupation of the Suez Canal area. He seemed contented and was always prepared to crack a joke with the soldiers for whom he worked. May 1943 was a good month for the Allies. The Eighth Army was advancing rapidly and Tunis and Bizerta [Tunisia] were captured early in the month. The final stage of the North African campaign had been reached, and on the 13th of May all Axis forces in North Africa surrendered. There had been no evacuation or attempted evacuation. It was a good day for the Navy, for we saw the end of these forced evacuations, Dunkirk, Greece, Crete, and many other lesser ones which had cost the Navy so dearly in ships, and it was now that ‘the boot was on the other foot’, for the tide had turned and from then onwards we were fighting on a rising tide and no more [longer], as we had for three and a half years, been fighting on an ebbing tide. Having left the Admiralty in March when one was closely in touch with what was happening and above all why it was happening, one ceased to be as it were at the centre of things and only observed events from the periphery. The various Admirals I had met since leaving the Admiralty, naturally wanted to know about the thinking at Headquarters, and I believe I did help a bit and at the same time learned how events struck people on the spot. Before leaving the Far Eastern Fleet I had some very stimulating talks with James Somerville, Bill Tennant, Ralph Edwards and Bob Mansergh, who was then Captain of Gambia. I think it would be fair to say that May also saw the turn of the tide in the Atlantic battle against U Boats. No less than 37 U Boats were destroyed and the shipping losses greatly reduced. Our special Bay Offensive patrols with the new 10 cm radar was having a marked effect on the U Boats. But let us get back to Port Said. After fuelling and collecting a few stores, we set off after dark and set course for Alexandria. I took the opportunity of giving the ship’s company and particularly the anti-aircraft crews plenty of practice and alerts. For I reminded all concerned that in the Mediterranean there were two types of people and ships – ‘the Quick and the Dead’ and that Mauritius was going to belong to the former category. I noticed from records that if a ship survived its first four months in the Mediterranean it usually lasted quite a long time, the simple fact was that Commanding Officers and their ships were not always attuned to the speed of modern warfare, especially in so far as aircraft were concerned and they were caught napping. For the Mediterranean, a degree of alertness and awareness of what might happen was an absolute must. Many of my colleagues had lost their ships in the Mediterranean within a few months of taking over, and I was determined I would not lose mine through lack of alertness. Above all the anti-aircraft armament had to achieve a degree of alertness never dreamt before. They had if they saw fit to open fire without asking for anybody’s orders. More often I reprimanded people for not opening fire than for opening fire too soon or at wrong targets! The Mauritius was with her many practices in 261

good fighting trim and I had so reorganised the damage control organisation that even if t orpedoed we should not lose the ship as had happened with some other cruisers. From the fighting and battle efficiency point of view I soon found we were streets ahead of most of the other cruisers in the Mediterranean which had not perforce had the chances of perfecting their battle efficiency as we had in the practice areas of Kilindini. We left Port Said after dark and arrived off Alexandria early the next morning. We entered harbour down the rather tricky swept channel and secured to the buoys inside the harbour which was crowded with ships of all sorts. I called on Admiral John Cunningham who was Flag Officer of Forces in the Levant and saw some friends on the staff there. Robertshaw who had been my colleague in FOPS, Heneage Legge, my commander in Courageous in the early 30s, and others were there. I was told I was to sail for Malta as soon as some stores and personnel were put on board. Unfortunately, these did not arrive until late with the result we were confronted with getting out of Alexandria harbour after dark with no lights. My pilot, Moseley, was a great optimist and said we would have no difficulty. In the event he was over optimistic as after clearing the harbour and turning into the swept channel he did not check our track with the shore transit beacons which were lit at the time. Neither he nor I had noticed there was a small sand shoal known as the ‘Hydrographics Shoal’ near the channel. In the event we turned a bit wide and touched this shoal and remained stuck for some time. When I realised we could not free ourselves immediately, I reported our mishap to Alexandria Naval Headquarters. After a time with some rather ingenious schemes we had worked out at our damage control exercises in the Eastern Fleet, we so readjusted the trim of the ship that with a good heave we slid off the shoal after about 6 hours. It was necessary to return to harbour to see if any damage was done to the ship’s bottom as we had grounded near the Asdic dome. We docked and immediately next day the contractors carried out a very full examination. The opportunity was also taken to treble up the close-range anti-aircraft Oerlikon armament of the ship. A mishap like this is always a serious affair. In this case, arrival at Malta was in fact delayed by about a week. A court martial is invariably held in the case of grounding to establish where the fault lay. 11 In my case I was rightly so held to blame and was mildly reprimanded, and at the same time the court drew attention of the convening authority to the skill shown in getting the ship off the shoal undamaged. Moseley our navigator was severely reprimanded and there was some talk of relieving him, but I insisted that he had learnt his lesson and would be most unlikely to be careless again and anyway it was my ultimate responsibility, and if they wanted to relieve him, they would have to relieve me also! I still had confidence in him. Looking back to this incident, I would probably not have allowed this mistake to be made if I had been a professional navigator myself, but I think many Captains more experienced than me would have made a mistake of this nature. Moseley was a very good shiphandler but inclined to take chances on navigational matters. This alas was a case where a chance should not have been taken. After a week at Alexandria where we polished up our anti-aircraft armament and landed our Walrus aircraft with the aviation spirit they carried, we set sail for Malta and were welcomed 11 The fact that WWD was to be court-martialled caused consternation in the family at home, not realising 262 that this was standard practice. In the event all was well.

by Admiral A.J. Power who was temporary temporarily Flag Officer (Malta) at the time. We immediately set about having rehearsals with the Army. We were to lead the attack on the Avola beaches of Sicily, not far from Augusta and our main job was to provide artillery support for the army ashore. Accordingly, we embarked our bombardment liaison officer and went to the Suez Canal where the Army under General Dempsey was stationed to practise with them. This all sounded a most exciting job. Before I left the Admiralty it had been decided Sicily was to be our next target. It was tremendous luck to find oneself assigned the job of leading the assaults for this venture. Our cruiser squadron was known as the 15th Cruiser Squadron under Admiral Harcourt, whose flag was in Newfoundland, and was assigned to bombardment and close support duties of the various assaults. I called on Admiral Harcourt who was very much on the ball and a very good seaman. I had not known him well before but he had got the reputation of being a first-rate fighting admiral and very good seaman to boot. The other ships of the Squadron were Newfoundland - Captain Slater a very great friend of mine with an endless sense of humour, and one with whom I had much in common; Uganda - Captain Andrews, an ex T [torpedo] specialist, a most original character perhaps at that stage a little inexperienced but he had a good ship! The fourth ship of the squadron was Orion which was a different class to the others, which were straight forward colony class cruisers, pretty similar to each other in all respects. Orion had eight 6 inch guns, whereas we all had 12 mounted in four turrets. Menzies, a rather wild and slightly eccentric ex-submarine specialist was her Captain. He could be relied on to do the unexpected and the remainder of the squadron always remembered he loved to do quite unpredictable manoeuvres without any warning at all, to the hazard of other ships of the squadron! We spent the best part of a week practising bombardment firings just below the Gulf of Suez with the Army and reached a good state of efficiency. I spent an afternoon with General Dempsey watching him take part in a local cricket match with the Green Howards on the banks of the Canal. His side had some Yorkshire and English professionals,Verity,Yardley and one or two others, so we saw some quite good cricket. He was obviously a military commander who had the complete confidence of his army. Then I got to know some of the other Divisional and Brigade commanders and made it clear to them that they must not be afraid to ask for anything, if we just could not do what they wanted I would tell them. This week the Suez Canal practice over, did us all an immense amount of good. I got the impression that Mauritius and Newfoundland were the two most outstanding ships for accuracy and promptitude. After returning to Malta, we attended a conference where the plan for the assault was unfolded. We would be under Admiral Troubridge, a splendid man in every way who would be in charge of the assault on the Avola beaches. The plan was to put the best part of two divisions ashore there, for the purpose of advancing north to capture Messina after occupying Augusta, Lentini, Syracuse etc. Though nominally under our Admiral, Rear Admiral Cecil Harcourt, the bombarding ships or close support ships as they were called, worked independently in such a way that they were always available to meet calls for supporting fire. This gave one any amount of independence, and in a sense bombardment ships had a roving commission so that they were always available for support when required. This in turn meant we 263

had to keep very closely in touch with one’s forward observation officer, i.e. a Gunner Officer, together with a naval telegraphist who was specially trained for these duties. But above all one had to know the Army plan for the advance and be up to date in their movements, for one had to be prepared to engage troops and tanks which came into the open, and great care was necessary in the heat of battle that you did not in error fire at one’s own troops! Then there was always the possibility of a lurking submarine waiting to have a shot at one and of course the ubiquitous enemy aircraft, the JU88, a good general-purpose bomber which the Germans used extensively. As we shall hear later, the Germans soon came to realise artillery bombardment ships were a great deal more than just nuisance value for on a number of occasions naval gunfire support for land operations proved of a decisive influence. We soon found that bombardment ships were often the special target for air attacks. It was splendid working again under Tom Troubridge for I kept closely in touch with him ever since we were in Queen Elizabeth just after the First World War. He radiated confidence and efficiency and having already taken a prominent part in the North African landings knew the form well. But throughout the Mediterranean command there was boundless confidence. Andrew Cunningham personified this and I could not ever imagine anybody doing anything which was not of his best with Andrew about. I hardly knew him then but knew his staff well. Then at Malta there was also stationed the covering force of battleships and aircraft carriers whose job it would be to see that there was no interference with the landings. Admiral Willis, whom I had flown out to Gibraltar with in the previous March, was in command of this force. Grantham was Captain of the Indomitable, which got torpedoed but not very badly damaged later. Packer in Warspite, Halsey in, I think, King George V, and a host of other ships were with us. Approaching the Grand Harbour, Malta, Malta Harbour was crowded as in the old pre-war days when the Mediterranean Fleet was at with the damaged aircraft carrier HMS full strength. Every billet was filled and overfilled. Malta looked pretty battered. Many of the Indomitable in the foreground. houses and famous old Auberges in Valetta were destroyed. The Maltese still looked hungry and there were few stout monks and priests to be seen in the streets. Every second person one met in the streets was in uniform. General Eisenhower had his headquarters in Malta, as of course did the other Commanders, Andrew Cunningham, Tedder the airman for a short stint, Generals Alexander and Montgomery. The last named, true to form, remained in ‘purdah’ to all but his own army subordinates in his caravan which was parked somewhere on the island. Then the dockyard looked a pretty sorry sight for it had suffered probably the most intense bombing ever experienced anywhere over the previous two years. Few stores or sheds were not open to the sky, but totally undamaged was the giant ‘eye’ carved on the rock wall of the dockyard which the priests reminded us was God’s eye set to watch over us all. The dry dock was in service and the harbour as well as Sliema, Halfar and others were 264

crowded to the limits with landing craft. The Governor General Gort was in good heart and it was said during the worst time of the siege, he lived entirely and solely on the Malta rations, which I don’t think represented much more than 1500 calories a day. Fortunately, our food and rations were adequate and nobody went short. About the only food one could buy Captain Rodionov, the Russia observer, in the open market at Malta were oranges which were then in plentiful supply. I called on smoking, ‘quite a pleasant fellow. . . Mabel Strickland, an old friend from Villa Bologna, who gave me an enormous basket of very much on his dignity’, perhaps in them. part on account of the odd bits of uniform he is wearing. But the dockyard had a tremendous job servicing all the ships and the hundred and one assault crafts of all types which had to be ready for the assault. To get back life into the Maltese workmen of the dockyard and to make them work as they had never worked before was a problem not easily susceptible to solution. The Commodore of the dockyard, a great character, Piers Kekewich, hit upon a most ingenious idea. He asked the Roman Catholic Archbishop of Malta if he would in full robes walk around the dockyard with him and encourage the workmen to greater efforts. This he readily assented to do and the effect was electrical. The Maltese workman is a simple man and in most cases extremely devout and ruled by his priests, was overcome when he saw the spiritual head of his church and the temporal head walking in company and in great friendliness together round the dockyard. The combination of the spiritual and temporal powers overcame them all and from the time of this inspection of the dockyard I was assured by Piers Kekewich that the output of work at the yard was at least doubled! There was much to be done in the ships, and with our new addition of Oerlikon gun armament we felt we could give a good account of ourselves whatever came our way. I was sent for by Admiral Harcourt a day or so before we sailed and told I was to have the Russian observer, a Russian naval officer Captain Rodionov, for this operation. He’d been a young Warrant Officer in the old Tsarist Navy and had risen to the rank of full captain in the Russian Navy. He came on board and we kitted him out with steel helmets and antiflash HMS Mauritius leading the destroyers gear, a most important item if one was liable to be subject to bomb flash. He seemed quite a pleasant fellow but obviously had to be very much on his dignity. We managed somehow to shed his shadow, i.e. the secret policeman who had to follow him round and report back all he said. Before leaving Alexandria, we [had] disembarked our aircraft and there was no special use for Walrus amphibians and carrying some hundreds of gallons of petrol on the upper deck was an additional fire hazard. We were known as the Inshore Bombarding Force and to our four cruisers were added four destroyers – Laforey, Loyal, Lookout and two tribal class.12 Their Captains were Tubby Hutton, (Laforey) a first rate destroyer officer, Tweedy (Loyal) an efficient but rather argumentative fellow, and Derek Holland Martin and Tyrwhitt, both of whom reached the top in the years after the war. These destroyers were very experienced in the assault work as they had taken part in the North African campaign. I was very pleased the way the ship was reacting, everybody was intensely alert and knew what was required of them. Lee said he could get a job with him after the war in the USA, broadcasting at $50,000 a year! As the first night drew on, I thought it wise to be in the main anchorage where one could be of most assistance to the merchant ships and landing craft. Furthermore, we also at night laid a smoke screen from specially equipped craft to cover the anchorage in which there were so many ships – ‘sitting birds’, to an enterprising motor torpedo boat! The hospital ship Talamba arrived after dark and anchored fully illuminated in accordance with the terms of the Hague Convention to seaward of the main anchorage. She was soon bombed and set on fire and sank with heavy loss of life. Uganda and Mauritius helped in the rescue work. This certainly gave us a taste of the regard the Germans were likely to have for the Geneva Convention. We never took a hospital ship again to an assault area. It was heartrending to watch her sink engulfed in flames from end to end. Next day I took a cast up the coast and saw Admiral Troubridge enter Syracuse which had been captured on the previous evening. I went as far as Augusta and met a certain amount of opposition from shore defence batteries, but knowing Augusta had powerful 268

For instance, the attacks were more in passing numbers than in big formations. It was I think on the second day that I saw a very determined aircraft lining up to us. So I put my usual procedure into action and after missing us with one bomb, he lined up and had a go at the destroyer, Eskimo, with my old friend Jack Eaton in command with Admiral Troubridge on board. Unfortunately, Jack had not noticed him early enough and his ship was hit in the stern and put temporarily out of action. The problem of getting enough sleep every 24 hours was one which was always present, for I noticed when one had spells of up to 48 hours on end without sleep, one’s reactions were very slow. I made all the key officers in the ship work out a routine on these lines, for time and again mishaps happen to ships, or opportunities Admiral Troubridge watching a bombardment are missed due to lack of alertness of the bridge personnel. I always felt our AA control staff was not sufficiently alert or perhaps reacted quickly enough, and I was never really happy until we had a splendid Marine Captain Cole who joined us in 1944 and proved that the AA armament could react instantaneously. On the 12th July an attempt was made to enter Augusta which was the main Italian base from the sea. The ships that entered got a fairly hot reception from shore batteries and decided rightly to withdraw until the batteries could be sorted out! It was difficult to piece together what was happening. After rather a sticky start our warships much helped the Americans in their landing at Gela. It was clear General Patton was going full steam ahead. We had in front of the Eighth Army three fully equipped and highly efficient German divisions. So broadly speaking it was going according to plan. The main Army battles were to come and it seemed probable that the Germans would stand and fight in front of Catania. Meanwhile we decided we would anchor for the night in Augusta and see what happened. We had the full attentions of the German Air force and as it took some time to establish the port’s AA defences, most of the AA harbour defence resting on the warships in the harbour. I remember an attack one night when an ammunition ship was hit ahead of us and after a fizzling like a Bombarding enemy positions cracker for a bit, she blew up with the biggest explosion I have north of Augusta ever heard. A large bit of her engines appeared to pass over the bridge. A few survivors were rescued. Another favourite weapon used by the Germans were circling torpedoes dropped by aircraft. A few attacks were made on Augusta with these weapons but most, if not all, exploded either on the harbour’s breakwaters or on some quays. Though some ships in Augusta were hit by bombs, none I think were touched by torpedoes. We rigged up nets around various berths which were designed to collect the torpedoes before they hit the ships! The nets had to be so designed that we could easily enter or leave harbour. From the time Augusta was captured we worked closely with our Forward Observation Officers in attacking the ever-increasing German resistance short of Catania. The usual plan was to be at sea during daylight hours and return to Augusta at night where we usually had a number of night air attacks. We had not seen anything of the Italian fleet though their submarines, as well as a Ammunition ship blowing up after few German submarines, were always a possible hazard so it was unwise to remain stopped in being bombed in Augusta harbour the open seas for over long. The weather was gorgeous, and one could not have been fighting a war under more pleasant climatic conditions. Captain Cowley Thomas, a resolute ex-submarine specialist was the Naval Officer in charge at Augusta and soon with our aid got the AA defences into some sort of shape, and soon after Admiral Macgregor came up and made his headquarters at Augusta. He was in charge of all the bases and supply arrangements for the Eighth Army. He had some brushes with the redoubtable Monty who at that time had not fully appreciated the tremendous tactical advantage control of the sea gives. But more of this later when we look at the course of the Sicily campaign. 270

25th July 1943 Most days were spent at sea. And by now our anti-aircraft armament was getting a bit low, so it was decided the 16th Cruiser Squadron, as we were known, should return to Malta for replenishment of ammunition as well as fuel and stores. We collected the whole squadron together and with our escorting destroyers led off to Malta at a speed of 20 to 22 knots. Just after passing Syracuse, I noticed one of our escorting destroyers with the submarine contact flag at the clip which means ‘suspect possible enemy submarine’. We were second in line, Newfoundland leading. I increased speed slightly, and put the ship into a slow swing towards the contact so as to reduce our torpedo target to a possible enemy. As I was doing this, I saw an explosion in the stern of Newfoundland and at the same time our Asdic listening watchkeeper reported torpedoes approaching. Increasing immediately to full speed, I put the wheel hard over and we swung towards the suspected direction of the torpedoes. The Newfoundland went out of control temporarily as her rudder had been blown off and she had to steer by propellers which providentially were not damaged. The destroyers were soon after the Italian submarine and sank her about an hour later. Meanwhile we escorted Newfoundland towards Malta. Bill Slater with a ready turn of wit made from Newfoundland the signal to me ‘Bad luck, for you will now have a lodger’. Referring in a somewhat insubordinate way to the fact that our Admiral, Cecil Harcourt, would transfer his flag to us. However, nobody could have been nicer than Cecil Harcourt who came on board and hoisted his flag in Mauritius that evening. Newfoundland was not badly damaged but had to be sent to America to have a new rudder fitted. Cecil Harcourt’s valet, Francis, was sleeping in the Admiral’s pantry right after near the Admiral’s quarters when the torpedo hit and had a very close shave indeed. Francis is now chief valet of the ‘Senior’, my club, and we often reminisce over those days. He became a great favourite in Mauritius. So our squadron of cruisers was down to three. Cecil Harcourt, for whom I developed a great regard, was an unusual type of Naval Officer, small and spare he had as a young man been invalided out of the Navy with polio and became a diplomat.15 He became an ardent Christian Scientist, and got reinstated into the Navy after being about four years out of it. A salt horse specialist, a teetotaller, but as cheerful and happy a man as one could find anywhere.16 A very experienced seaman and small ship handler, I learnt a lot from him. Very alert, knowledgeable and right on the ball. Not perhaps a very great intellect but for all that shrewd, and he never let his religion and ethical beliefs be thrust down anyone's throat. A most equable temperament, always alert and quite prepared to delegate full responsibility. He kept himself very fit and never missed the opportunity to take exercise. Fundamentally a very unselfish, generous and humble man, he had an abiding respect for our C-in-C Andrew Cunningham, who in his turn held Cecil Harcourt in high regard. Cecil married late in life, a widow with two daughters both of whom married famous musicians, Louis Kerstner and Yehudi Menuhin. After the war Elizabeth and I went occasionally to musical parties held at their flat in the West End of London. Cecil was not perhaps a very original mind, but on the other hand he had an essentially practical down-to-earth approach and was a fine sea going officer who commanded much respect. He ended his service career as Second Sea Lord 15 Cecil Halliday Jepson Harcourt (1892-1959), ODNB 16 ‘Salt horse’ refers to those officers who did not specialise in one particular technical branch (gunnery, torpedoes, navigation) but remained generalists. 271

We were bombed once or twice when General Stewart was on board which I think emphasised it was just not just a cakewalk being a close support ship. Cruisers of Mauritius class were particularly well suited for support as they carried a numerous and very heavy artillery armament, and could at times bring it to bear far far quicker or more effectively than shore-based artillery. We saw quite a lot of Admiral McGrigor, stationed at Augusta and who [was] anxious, as were most of us, that opportunity should be taken to land raiding parties behind the lines and cut the coast retreat road from Catania to Messina. But every time these ideas were turned down by Monty who preferred to go by road. 272

Looking back on it, I think opportunities were lost and the fact we did not do so astounded the Germans. I often used to cruise up the coast past Catania and occasionally engage enemy batteries. But apart from the railway gun in the tunnel below Taormina we were not seriously hazarded though often fired at. I suggested to Admiral McGrigor we might get the Terror with her 15 inch guns to knock in the face of the tunnel as the railway gun retreated through the tunnel onto the causeway behind, [and] I should torpedo the Causeway! However perhaps this rather light hearted plan was not as practical as it seemed to me and was not carried out. Both McGrigor and Andrew Cunningham felt that many good opportunities for harassing the enemy by a fuller use of the sea were missed, because of a certain obstinacy on the Eighth Army Commander’s part. Maybe he remembered our failure at Tobruk in the previous year. It was pleasant at Augusta and I stretched my legs ashore once or twice. We let the sailors have a look round and they did not find much, and were much incensed when the Town Mayor prior to their landing closed all the wine shops. They serenaded him and called him with some justification, ‘a cherry nosed old so and so!’ Unfortunately, this was reported back to General Alexander and I had to send in some sort of apology some weeks later for my ships company’s unparliamentary language. But the best way of exercising was bathing. As usual whenever one went for a swim there was an air raid and we occasionally felt a slight shock when bombs fell in the water. Cecil Harcourt was a keen swimmer and never missed an opportunity. 5th August 1943 However, after much hard fighting and close support from us, Catania fell on the 5th of August and the Americans just beat us in the race for Messina which was captured on the 17th of August. I sometimes think if we had better systems of observation and communications, we could have harassed the Germans more on the coast road than we did. Though again it is true they did most of their movements by night. Thanks to great skill on the German and Italian parts, the bulk of the German and Italian Army escaped across the straits of Messina, and whether we liked it or not, and unlike in North Africa, the Axis forces were not destroyed. Stephen Roskill gives some very wise thoughts on this in chapter 6, Part 1 of vol. 3 of his War at Sea. I think the fault lay basically in the planning, nobody seemed to have prepared HMS Mauritius at Augusta, and worked out a ‘cut and dried’ plan before the whole operation started to prevent the August 1943. enemy escaping from Sicily once the operation was seen to be doing well. This often happens as detailed plans are also often required to exploit a success. We had none this time, and the fact remains that over 100,000 combatant Axis troops escaped with much of their equipment to fight again in Italy. So perhaps the historian will say the capture of Sicily was a tactical success of substantial proportions, but it failed in that the best part of six divisions of enemy troops were allowed to escape and fight another day. 273

Plans were immediately put in hand to cross the Straits of Messina and shortly after [to] carry out a landing with the purpose of capturing Naples. We wondered why the not unsubstantial Italian naval forces based in Taranto had not intervened. There were cruisers and destroyers there which resolutely handled might well have caused us much embarrassment. August / September 1943 It should be mentioned that there were outward signs of the imminent collapse of Italy. The resistance they put up was patchy and news came through on I think 25th July, that Mussolini had been dismissed and that Marshall Badoglio had taken his place. Though Marshal Badoglio had said he would continue the war with Germany, we had no doubt that at the first opportunity he would make peace with us. It must have been either at the end of July or early August that intelligence came through [that] two fast modern Italian cruisers and some destroyers were likely to make a sortie from Taranto at night and attack our shipping which was supplying our forces from Augusta and further up the coast of Sicily. Accordingly, Mauritius and another cruiser and two destroyers were detailed to go up the Bay of Taranto and intercept and destroy this force. I was the senior officer and in consequence in command of the force. Having in Mauritius this excellent modern surface detection radar which was kept in admirable fettle by a young special service radar officer, by name Patterson, I felt the odds were loaded on our side. I decided first to locate the enemy and then make an approach to them from just abaft the beam and to hold any fire until we were at very close range, for if we made the approach from the opposite direction of the moon it would be unlikely that we should be detected before we opened fire. So off we sailed at sunset and shaped course for the Gulf of Taranto. At, I suppose, a little before midnight our radar operator reported two large objects and 2 small objects bearing about NE from us at extreme range. This was precisely where I guessed the Italian warships might be. I warned the force of suspicious contact made and increased speed to 25 knots to close the enemy as quickly as possible. Our ‘plot’ was started and the ‘schoolie’, who was the plotting officer, reported that the contacts which were at extreme range appeared to be moving rather slowly. I spoke to the ships company over the broadcaster and tell them that we had something suspicious on the plot and they might expect soon to be in action with the enemy. But after about 10 minutes of plotting, the enemy seemed to be no nearer though the two large contacts or two small fitted in exactly what one might expect i.e. 2 cruisers and 2 destroyers. We continued endeavouring to close for another 10 minutes without apparently getting any nearer when the radar officer came up to me and said there was something funny about these contacts - they did not he felt seem to be absolutely real - I asked him if there were any rain clouds about or flocks or birds low in the water which might produce this result. Then suddenly he said - are there any high peaks on the other side of the Adriatic which might be playing tricks with us? As like a motor car speedometer, our distance scale might as 274

it were be one whole turn out, which in this case meant about 120 miles had to be added onto the range shown on the scale! A careful look at the chart showed that in all probability these contacts were in fact two high peaks and two lesser peaks from the mountains in Cephalonia on the other side of the Adriatic! These contacts were held for another half an hour when for some reason or another they faded from the plot to confirm the diagnosis given by our radar officer. This was all rather an anticlimax as I had planned what I had thought would be a tidy little operation which would encompass the destruction of the entire enemy force without serious hurt to ourselves. After cruising around for some hours, we set sail back for Augusta just before dawn broke. In the event the Italian force did not leave Taranto and did not then or later attempt to attack our shipping. Our participation in future operations was a subject for much conjecture. The arguments and discussions which led to the decisions taken are given in full in chapter 7 of the official Naval History and it is of little value to go over them again now. We felt the obvious answer was to capture Rome as quickly as possible and go by sea rather than slowly up the dusty roads of Southern Italy. However, it was decided the Eighth Army was to cross the streets of Messina in pursuit of the retreating Germans who had by now nearly a week’s start. Heavy bombardments were carried out by ourselves and other ships but it was evident the bird had flown, and the only thing to be seen were the enormous white sheets hung out of the upstairs windows at many of the houses on the toe of Italy. Cruising up and down the Straits of Messina on the 3rd September, we felt in the sense that we were wasting our time. But by then the surrender of the Italians was to be expected at any moment. In a ship one naturally gets rather an insular point of view, but in discussions in the wardroom we often felt the Army Command did not make the fullest use they might have of the Navy’s ability to land them far up the coast behind the enemy’s lines. But then we probably underestimated the logistical difficulties of keeping an army supplied over the beaches. Operation Baytown, as the crossing of the Straits of Messina was known, took little time and we wondered what next was in store for us. As is now known by that time we had decided that the main part of Naples was to be captured as soon as possible, and that landings were to be made on Salerno Bay, a little way to the south of Naples Bay. Due to certain disagreements at Chiefs of Staff level i.e. between the US Commanders and our own and having regard to the long-term overall plan, the organisation and detailed plans for this operation were only completed at the last moment. It is remarkable that such a good plan was in fact evolved with the means to implement it. For the US commanders thought we could switch without delay by mounting an attack across the Channel. 275

September 1943 Operation Baytown has already been discussed. The wardroom in one of their more ribald moments suggested that the bill for this expenditure of naval ammunition should be sent to Monty, for the enemy had departed some four or five days previously, and we fired a lot of stuff into thin air! We were informed that an operation just south of the Bay of Naples was being planned and that we were to take part in it, but as yet no operation orders had arrived. We understood the General in command of the whole operation was to be General Clark, US Army, and that Admiral Hewitt (USNavy) would be the overall Naval Commander. It was I think late on the afternoon of the 7th September that Admiral Hewitt’s flagship arrived in Augusta and delivered to me my orders for operation ‘Avalanche’ as the attack on Salerno was to be known. It took two men two journeys up and down the gangway to carry the orders for the operation. We were, as soon as I opened them, due to sail at dawn the next day. There was clearly no time to read and absorb all the orders. So I told the pilot (Moseley) to lay them out on my cabin table and I went over to see Admiral Hewitt before he sailed. The conversation I had with him was something like this – Self: ‘Admiral, your orders have been received, it took two men to carry them on board. Must I read them?’ Admiral: ‘No Captain, you know what supporting ships have to do, just read a couple of pages of chapter so and so, and you do the rest as you think fit!’ What a splendid reply, and an injunction we carried out with strictness and which served us in mighty good stead in the adventurous days which lay ahead. Americans always pack their orders out with quite an enormous amount of intelligence information, and it is mighty hard to dissect what one has and what one must not do! So apart from the relevant few pages, Admiral Hewitt’s orders remain sealed in my after cabin. It appeared we were to support the American section of the landing. The air support was to be provided by our own escort carriers under Admiral Vian, which with their Seafires would cover the landing until the airfield at Montecorvino was captured when they could be operated from there.17 We sailed from Augusta shortly after dawn on the 8th September in company with Uganda and Orion, and had an uneventful passage through the Straits of Messina. A hot and lovely day. Shortly after sailing we heard over the wireless that the Italians had requested an Armistice and had ordered all their forces to cease hostilities. We immediately wondered what effect this would have on our assault, which in a sense was planned rather on the light side. There was clear evidence however that the Germans had plenty of land forces and, as our experience in Sicily showed, were full of fight. Furthermore, the German air force and their light naval craft such as E boats [fast attack boats] were not to be underrated. Admiral Harcourt, wisely I think, made a signal to all our forces that stiff resistance must be expected and that the Italian defection to the Axis would not be likely to affect materially the scale of the resistance to be met. 17 The Seafire was a Spitfire adapted for operation from an aircraft carrier. 276

It was a hot day indeed as we rounded Sicily and killed time along the North Coast. We had alas no more our very pleasant US newspaper man, Paul K Lee, who left us, nor the Russian Naval Observer who presented us with some very fine reproductions of pictures in the Her- Landing craft are making smoke to con- mitage and other art galleries in Russia. fuse enemy gunfire as they closed on the beaches on the morning of the assault. As the day wore on, we altered course to the north where we should pick up the remainder While effective, the smoke must have of the assault force. Since time was still available, I stopped the ship just after 2:00 a.m. oppoadded to the difficulties of identifying site Capri and waited there for the remainder. However, at 3:00 s.m. or thereabouts we targets accurately. started off again and the assault started. Salerno Bay is a wide open bay nearly 20 miles across from Salerno Port in the north and Paestum in the south. A rough landing field for aircraft was situated and the key town of Battipaglia was about a further four miles inland. We wondered how well it was going to be defended having had little serious and heavy resistance on the beaches in Sicily. We wondered if our luck would still hold good. In the event it did not entirely do so. The assault went ahead and there was evidently heavy resistance being encountered on or near the beaches. The destroyers closed in and provided invaluable close support and demolished a number of German field batteries. On page 177 of volume 3 of Naval History, there are some good photographs of Mauritius supporting the landings and in my own photograph album there are a number of photographs taken on the assault day. The destroyer Laforey did particularly good work engaging a German battery at point blank range and putting it out of action. She was hit a number of times and we sent our doctor over to attend to the wounded. The fighting is vividly described in chapter 7 of the Official History. Enemy troops and tanks as well as field batteries were located close to the beaches and were engaged by warships at close range. It was a little time before our Forward Observation Officer who had been landed with the first wave got communication with us. It was soon after midday that the British assault had succeeded and at any rate established a bridgehead, but the airfield had not been captured. On the other Transferring the doctor to HMS Laforey hand, the Americans were having much difficulty overcoming the stiff resistance on their to tend the wounded after being hit five beaches to the south of the British. However, thanks again to close supporting naval fire times. the obstacles were overcome. Ships, and in particular landing craft, were fairly frequently attacked by German aircraft and a number of E boats came out to attack us at night. We soon got contact with our Forward Observation Officer and from the afternoon of the day of the assault onwards we were constantly called upon to give fire support. I think he and his telegraphist must have been good mountaineers as they established themselves well 277

behind the lines in the high ground leading to Salerno so we could get a good bird’s eye view of what was happening. As it covered the main supply road from Italy, his observations were quite invaluable. We hit a number of reinforcing tanks coming up this road and on one memorable occasion hit an ammunition supply convoy which made one of the biggest explosions seen for many many miles in southern Italy since the war started. From the 10th September onwards we were seldom idle by day answering calls for support fire, and seeing how effective well controlled support could be, there was great competition for our services. I had to adopt a careful rationing system to avoid having spent all our ammunition too quickly. For I knew our reserves were small and we should have to return to Malta to replenish. The value of this supporting fire by Mauritius is referred to on page 177 of the official history. However it was on the 11th September that the Germans sprang a nasty surprise on us by the use of wireless controlled bombs known as FX 1400 dropped from a great height. As soon as I knew this type of attack was on the cards, I never let the ship be stopped for a single minute for I knew there is nothing harder to hit and keep in the bomber aircrew’s sights than a weaving ship acting irregularly. On the first day of the attack the Uganda was hit near to us. I had seen an aircraft moving around a great height above us, and I suppose something told me to keep moving! Anyway the Uganda was hit and badly damaged and had to be towed away, as was the US cruiser Savannah which was also hit. Meanwhile the German counterattack had been launched and was not far from succeeding. Tanks had come down the valley of the river Sele and we certainly engaged them at long range. Soon after our F.O.O. located the German HQ situated in a nice villa high up in the hills above Port Salerno. We soon engaged this target and landed a salvo on the lawn in front of the villa just as the German officers were going in for their ‘Mittag Essen’. There was talk of evacuating the US forces if the German attack succeeded and much naval support including the battleships Warspite and Valiant were sent up, for at this time the American beachhead was under fire from the tank thrust. However the arrival of the heavy ships and of General Alexander restored the situation, the attack was contained and German forces were relentlessly pounded from the sea and from the air. September 1943 It was apparent all was not going well and that the German counterattack intended to divide the British and American forces was making some considerable progress. Later some of the American landing beaches came under heavy fire and all the unloading in the American sector had been stopped. We were constantly being called on to give fire support against the Germans and from the remarks of our various Forward Observation Officers showed our shooting was most effective. A direct hit with a high velocity 6 inch shell will knock out a tank. We heard, this must have been about the 13th September, that the Americans were contemplating evacuating their beachhead. An operation which we on board certainly believed to 278

be totally impractical. However, the prompt dispatch of naval reinforcements in the shape of cruisers Aurora and Penelope, followed by battleships Warspite and Valiant, helped to steady perhaps some rather shaken nerves. General Alexander arrived a day or so later and the critical day, which was the 14th September, passed without disastrous results to the allies. The story of the Salerno landing is very well told in the official history and it is clear that the naval bombardment before the arrival of the battleships on the 15th September played what may now be considered a decisive part in halting the German counterattack. Uganda was out of action and until the arrival of Aurora and Penelope, the main weight of bombardment fell firstly on the cruisers Mauritius and Orion and secondly on the destroyers the Laforey, Loyal, Lookout and others, not forgetting the Dutch gunboats Flores and Zoembe. Commodore Oliver with his headquarters in Hilary was a tower of strength and steadiness in these hectic times. The wireless controlled bomb attacks continued, and Warspite was hit and badly damaged on the 15th September. By this time, we were beginning to get low on ammunition ourselves. However, we had enough for a couple more days and left the area on 17th September for Malta to replenish. During the night enemy E boats attacks as well as submarine attacks took place, so we and our destroyers patrolled the anchorage to seaward for the purpose of discouraging anybody from attempting to hinder the unloading. One night we picked up some German radio telephone conversations between E boats. Fortunately, I had not forgotten all my German and I listened in to what they were saying. It was obvious at once they were near to us. The conversations went something on these lines. From the Senior Officer to other E boat Commanding Officers – ‘Do you see heavy ships with big cruiser leading?’ Reply, ‘Yes, who shall I attack, I must get closer they are still far away.’ Senior Officer, ‘We will close them, you will attack leading heavy cruiser.’ As we were the cruiser in question it was an interesting conversation to eavesdrop! Whilst this conversation was going on we had detected enemy objects some way away and ahead of us on our radar. I increased speed to 28 knots and put down a 12 inch gun salvo after a few minutes in their direction. They turned away and disappeared towards their base near Naples at high speed. It was no part of our job to try conclusions with highly manoeuvrable E boats who might well end up by torpedoing us, and hence we were correct in taking action which was effective in scaring them away. I could almost hear the E commander saying as our salvos fell about them ‘Gott sei dank - they have already seen us!’ It must have been 17th as I’ve already said when we set sail after dark and shaped course for the Messina Straits. We passed the Warspite in tow just after clearing the Straits and I gave Bertie Packer, her Captain, a cheerful signal and told him I looked forward to another game of tennis in Malta, where we had already played during a visit there a few weeks beforehand. Just after dark on the return passage we met a convoy of American LSTs and LCTa and all types of landing craft. They appeared to be executing an alteration of course when we found ourselves among them. One, not noticing us, charged towards us. I immediately stopped the ship to lessen the effect of impact and sure enough the large LCT hit us amidship and smashed our sea boat. Just prior to the impact the bow lookout in the LCT came to life with 279

anguished cries to his Captain, ‘Back her Skip, back her’. No damage of a serious nature was done to the ship though the bow of the LCT looked a bit dented. However with mutual expressions of regret we passed on our way. A few days rest at Malta whilst we replenished ourselves with ammunition, got a new sea boat and repaired the damage done in our collision and back to Salerno. By this time the Army were making considerable progress and the 15th Cruiser Squadron was augmented by the cruisers Sheffield and Aurora. We carried out a number of bombardments but at nothing like the pressure and urgency of our previous ones. October 1943 It must be about this time that we heard that the First Sea Lord Barrage against enemy aircraft was very ill and reported to be dying, and it was, I think, on the attacking at night 6th October we heard of the appointment of Admiral Cunningham as First Sea Lord. Admiral Hewitt’s command was also dissolved about this time, as by 1st October Naples had been captured by the Army and its need was no longer apparent. Just before we left Salerno an unexpected autumnal gale swept the Bay and seriously delayed the unloading, but it was not at a time when its effects had any adverse results on military operations. But the beach looked a sorry sight with landing craft strewn in all attitudes along it! Our next port of call was Taranto where we went to find our old friend Admiral McGrigor, installed as Senior Officer there. He (McGrigor) had just had a visit from the Russian delegation headed by Vischinsky, who had made him very angry by asking for a list of prominent Italians who had been or would be l iquidated. I doubt if the Russians got much change out of McGrigor. It must have been there that General Aosta, the Visiting generals at Malta, probably Italian C-in-C visited Admiral Harcourt to discuss certain items on the terms of surrender General Alexander. Such visits laid down in the Armistice conditions. A fine man, one felt sorry for him, as he evidently felt helped to maintain morale as well his position very deeply. as cementing inter-service cooperation. We heard fragments of what was going on in the Eastern Mediterranean and [the] Aegean in particular. We had all along intended to capture Rhodes but the news we had was only fragmentary. I had hoped with the surrender of Italy that the garrison of Rhodes would not have allowed themselves, as in fact happened, to be overpowered by the much smaller German garrison. In this event we occupied the smaller islands such as Leros and Kos whilst the Germans established themselves in Rhodes. As described in various books we attempted again what we should not have done and forgot the lessons learnt earlier in the war, namely to attempt to hold the islands and supply them without the necessary command of the air as well as the sea, spells disaster. In this event after quite heavy losses in ships we had to evacuate the 280

islands we had occupied. It was in this fighting in Leros that Lieutenant Alan Phipps, a cousin of Elizabeth’s, who had been landed to help with the communications was killed in action with the German forces. His father, Sir Eric Phipps (our Ambassador in Berlin) was the distinguished diplomat who foretold the war with uncanny accuracy. Various changes in command took place. John Cunningham became C-in-C Med in place of his namesake Andrew, and Willis went to the Levant to try and sort out some of the difficulties there. He was partially successful and persuaded the Chiefs of Staff that little was to be gained by holding on to the various Dodecanese islands until Rhodes had been captured. Things now quietened down a bit in the Mediterranean. After a visit to Naples which was still in a very considerable mess, we went to Taranto where we immediately had an impromptu regatta. Occasional visits to Malta where we took the opportunity of catching up with our ship maintenance routines. There was in fact a lull in activities. There was some talk of us being sent to the Levant to help out there but in retrospect I am glad we did not go as however lucky we would have been, it is more than likely a cruiser of our size would have been bombed and damaged. Mails were a bit irregular, but in December I had a letter from Janie saying she was in hospital and just had a blood transfusion but ending with some good jokes and written as courageously as ever. Knowing how she had survived other crises, I was not more than passingly anxious about her. Cecil Harcourt told me one day he had a letter from the First Lord asking him to be Naval secretary, the last possible job he wanted to do! However, there was nothing for it and he was told he would have to go. We spent the week before Christmas at Malta and saw a few friends who were there, including Dippy Evans, one time captain of Kenya until he got invalided out and was now on the Administrative Staff at Malta. I thought quite a bit about the family and once or twice very especially of my sister Janie to whom I was deeply attached. I wondered what sort of Christmas the family would have at Mulgrave and how they were all getting on. Admiral Harcourt was still with us when we were ordered to Algiers which I had not visited before. A harbour full of British and US ships, but by now the French were running everything except the Port which we still controlled. The Germans were trying hard this time, making use of the long hours of darkness, to get some very valuable cargoes into their Biscay ports. We hastened to Gibraltar and reached there shortly afterwards to prepare for a patrol which would cover the approaches to north Spanish ports. Unfortunately, in the many emergency stops and starts we had developed a rather serious boiler defect which had to be remedied forthwith at Gibraltar. Admiral Harcourt transferred his flag forthwith to another cruiser and carried out an Atlantic patrol in her. Meanwhile just after he had sailed on the 27th of December there was an action in the northern part of Biscay between the cruisers Glasgow and Enterprise and two groups of 281

German destroyers. Three German destroyers with sunk and the rest escaped. We stayed on at Gibraltar, spent Christmas there, to get our repairs done. We were sorry to miss the opportunity for an action though in this event we should not have been well placed to intercept the German destroyers. This was the last we were to see of Admiral Harcourt in the 15th Cruiser Squadron, for he was relieved by Admiral Mansfield, another old friend of mine and one time Commander of Courageous. Cecil Harcourt was as fine a seaman as one could find anywhere, a charming character of even temperament. Though small, and perhaps unimpressive at first sight, the more one knew him the more one liked and respected his judgement. Singularly free of prejudices and though a devout Christian Scientist, teetotaller and non-smoker, he was never a ‘wet blanket’ - in fact rather the reverse at any gathering. He did not like people to try to pull the wool over his eyes but who does! An acute intelligence, he soon saw through anybody who was regarded as a ‘front man’. He was as good a mixer as I’ve ever met and had a wide range of knowledge of men and affairs outside the strict confines of the service. He was a good deal wider in outlook than most of his contemporaries. As soon as our repairs at Gibraltar were completed, we were sent on a Bay patrol for the purpose of intercepting any further blockade runners. My chief anxiety was to avoid being torpedoed by one of the many German submarines who were in the Biscay ports and who were constantly crossing the Bay of Biscay. When we had been four days on patrol and when at the northern end of our patrol, we were ordered to finish our patrol, and as we were a good nearer Plymouth than Gibraltar, I decided to go to the former to refuel, of which we were getting short, rather than the latter. The Admiralty were surprised but we were given 48 hours leave to each watch which pleased everybody and allowing 24 hours for travelling this meant 72 hours away. But on opening our mail of Plymouth, I had I think the saddest shock I had yet had. It was a letter from old John Dillon Robinson, sympathising with me on the death of my sister Jane. She had died on the 22nd December nearly a fortnight before. My father’s and Elizabeth’s letters telling me of her death were lost by enemy action. She had a number of internal operations and died eventually from internal haemorrhages. Fortunately, my father and brother were able to see her, as indeed did her husband Charles Ackers, before she died.18 A very very gallant and dear character whose energy and charm invoked the best in people. That picture of her by Luke Fildes in my drawing room tells much. We had much in common and looked at many of the problems through similar spectacles. She was not entirely happy with her husband who though devoted to her, could just not comprehend her likes and tastes were not necessarily the same as his. She was clever, lively and artistic with a great zest for life. Her spirit was stronger than her body. She was wholly devoted to her only son David Ackers, who was killed in action eight months later. My father was deeply grieved and said often he wished he had been taken first. 18 At this point WWD inserted the aerogram letter from Buddy describing the funeral at Huntley. Jane or Janie, was vivacious and talented, and wrote short comedies for radio, some of which were broadcast. She was considered by all to be very beautiful and always dressed exceedingly well. 282

I went up to Mulgrave for a couple of nights and arranged my father to meet me at Plymouth where we had a short time together. Looking rather older and lined he still retained his indomitable spirit. To my joy there were very very few leave breakers, but alas somebody got a rumour going among the Stokers’ messdecks that we were now going to the Far East or some such cock and bull story and all sat down in their messdecks. However, I spoke to them, as indeed did the Padre and Commander and they soon realised wartime is no place for ‘sit down strikes’ but it is amazing how catching rumours can be, and brought home that even the best ship’s company can be unbalanced by ill-founded rumours.19 Our new First Lieutenant, Patrick Bayley, joined us at Plymouth in place of the excellent half Norwegian Andersen, who was I think the longest inhabitant on the ship. Both good officers. Bayley became a Vice Admiral in 1969, and having just been working with the Commandos, soon found himself at home on board. We were soon on our way back to Gibraltar and the Mediterranean, after a short stay at Gibraltar where I got Admiral Burrough, the Flag Officer there, to give the ship’s company a good pep talk, which he did with good effect. Janie Ackers painted in 1925 by January 1944 Luke Fildes. She retained her beauty We sailed for Malta where we took the opportunity to make some adjustments to the ships and vivacity and always looked company and check over our armament. While this was going on, we had heard of the atwonderfully dressed in the latest fashion. tack on Anzio on the 22nd January 1944, for the purpose of landing a substantial force behind the German lines in Italy, and making straight for Rome. This was a splendid concept and with dash should have succeeded. The opposition was negligible. Nevertheless, the US General in command was of an over cautious nature and was determined to consolidate fully his beachhead before advancing on Rome! This he laboriously commenced to do. Meanwhile the German reaction had been rapid, and having nearly thrown our land forces back into the sea at Salerno, they were determined to do so without fail at Anzio. Their main counterattack commenced on the 3rd February, some fortnight after we had landed. We meanwhile had joined Admiral Mansfield’s force soon after the assault; of the original four cruisers of 15th Cruiser squadron only Mauritius and Orion were still serviceable, and a week or so later Orion had to leave us with major engine defects. So we were the sole survivor serviceable but by now we were joined by Phoebe and Penelope and the USS Brooklyn, whilst the splendid French cruiser Gloire soon joined us. 19 This was the cause of some discontent, as the writer of WWD’s entry in the ODNB says, the ship was ‘in a very sensitive state of discipline which was aggravated in January 1944 when she arrived in Plymouth Sound with her ship's company expecting to pay off. It was a discouraging start, but Davis, with his gift for making people work together, turned the commission into a triumph.’ WWD’s leadership from the start of his tour helped to cope with these problems. 283

The cruiser Spartan was sunk by one of the new wireless-controlled glider bombs. They were launched by low flying aircraft usually at dusk or dawn, and controlled by the parent aircraft onto the target. My first job on arrival at Naples was to conduct an exhaustive inquiry into the loss of the Spartan. Her captain, Pat Mclaughlin, was a contemporary of mine and could be expected to have a good ship. It was tremendously hard work finding out from the survivors actually what did and what did not happen. After about three days of intensive interrogation, I knew what had happened. I do not think any blame can be attributed for being hit, though it was true Pat Mclaughlin was new to the Mediterranean, and may not have developed that seventh sense that most of us developed of when and where danger threatens. On the other hand, I was not entirely satisfied with the internal organisation and damage control arrangements of the ship. I believe they might have saved her, but in a brand new ship as Spartan was, it is always difficult to strike a proper balance in working up, and by this time personnel in ships were getting pretty diluted. I was sorry for Pat Mclaughlin, a jovial character, if rather a rascal, at losing his brand new ship. I still felt that one of the weaknesses in our organisation in the Navy is in damage control. A number of ships including Ark Royal should never have been lost if ships had been trained and better organised to meet this threat. February 1944 It was not long before we were at Anzio bombarding and having occasional cracks at a heavy battery on the coast which fired at times with accuracy and alertness. Early in February the enemy launched their counter-attack and a considerable anxiety was expressed by the Army. All ships came up for bombarding duties and it is now clear from the official history that they were most effective. The Gloire with true Gallic panache had I suspect fired her whole outfit of ammunition off in a day! The Americans were also very liberal with their ammunition. I adopted a very strict rationing system, depending on the type of supporting fire required. For ordinary counter battery work I was particularly careful not to fire too much. We had already fired an enormous quantity of ammunition and if the ammunition stocks were to last and our guns not to wear out, great care was needed. At first it almost seemed if the German counterattack might succeed. But our naval bombardment support fire evidently played a major part in halting the enemy’s drive. Quite a good picture appeared in the Illustrated London News, a copy of which is in Coglan, of Mauritius engaging the enemy at this critical time. Each cruiser was usually allotted two destroyers, and one time I had two American destroyers, both having the name with something Jones in it! So before leaving Naples I sent for the commanding officers and told them my plans and what we hoped to do. They were bright young officers and I saw their eyes goggling until one could not contain himself any longer and said ‘Captain, are there not going to be any dispatches?’ meaning what about the written orders? So I immediately said, ‘There is not time for any for that and anyway the typewriter had broken down’! A smile you could see across the equator spread over both their faces, ‘You mean we have to work on our own initiative without orders?’ I said ‘Yes’ in no uncertain terms and ‘If you don’t, you will hear from me!’ They were both first rate and one could not have wanted more intelligent and thrustful support for which they got all the encouragement I could offer. 284

The tremendous support we gave the Army is described graphically in Admiral Mansfield’s report. right: After the barrage: empty shell cases There was no time for relaxation and as soon as one had embarked all one’s ammunition and litter the deck fuel at Naples, off again to the fighting area. Apart from the possibility of glider bomb attacks there was not much ordinary bombing though one saw quite a lot of air combats including an attack by German fighters on a squadron of US [Flying] Fortress bombers, not by any means a one-sided affair, there were substantial casualties on both sides. What a majestic sight were the Fortresses, in tight formation as they sailed on towards their targets. Occasional Spitfires were seen but most of their work was further inland. I remember seeing one shot down over the sea. And I sent the Dutch Gunboat Flores to rescue the pilot if still alive, as he had been seen to bail out on his parachute. Shortly afterwards I received the following signal from Flores ‘Have recovered body of pilot. . . regret dead. His identity disc shows C of E. Is it in order to bury him in accordance with the rights of the Dutch Reformed Church?’ To which I made an appropriate affirmative reply. The Dutch were great fellows and never forgot correct procedures! The artist Claude Muncaster, now a Lieutenant RNVR, was at Naples and asked to come out for an operation. He came and drew the picture you see overleaf of Mauritius supporting the Army off the coast of Italy. It was one of the few really cold days and there was snow on the high hills above Monte Cassino, most unusual for Italy. He later completed the picture and it hangs in the blue bedroom at home. It showed us engaging what was a thoroughly troublesome battery situated near the coast. Anzio was always a ‘might have been’, the conception was good and if the Army Commander had been a thruster of the order of George Patton, I have little doubt Rome would have been taken and the German front at Monte Cassino collapse. There is the story of the 285

HMS Mauritius in action at Anzio, American GI at the landing jetty and one of our naval officers had been up to see the US 1943. Painting by Claude Muncaster Army Commander’s staff about bombardment support. The young GI said to the naval officer ‘Say, Britisher, have you any good generals?’ To which the naval officer replied, ‘Yes we have got a lot of qiite good ones now who have had a deal of fighting experience’. The GI said, ‘Well let’s have one, the fellow up there’, pointing in the direction of the HQ, ‘is a bum’. The main German counterattack developed at the beginning of February and rather like Salerno produced a critical situation, though in this case there was no talk of evacuating the Army. So it was a case of giving the maximum support possible regardless of the risks involved. We were engaged fairly frequently by shore batteries though fortunately never hit. When practical I always made the destroyers lay smoke screens to shield us. There are some photographs in my album showing this. Then there was a possibility of attack by glider bombs which had sunk the Spartan at dusk. Some glider bomb aircraft appeared but they had no success. Sarell had previously devised a special form of barrage which would probably have destroyed the glider bomb in flight. We had four cruisers, Orion, Mauritius, Phoebe and Penelope as well as the US cruiser Brooklyn.
