After a time, Orion and Phoebe developed engine defects and Penelope with her Captain Tiny Belben, was torpedoed and lost on passage between the bombardment area and Naples. So our forces were rather reduced. But by this time the attacks by the German armoured groups had failed and it is clear from the official history that the effects of ships’ gunfire was largely responsible for this. We started doing bombardments at night and there is rather a good photograph of Mauritius in the official war history doing this. I did not particularly fancy this form of support, as firstly it was not easy for our Forward Observation Officers to see the effect of gunfire, and our accuracy of fire because of navigational uncertainties at night was likely to be less precise than in daytime. It also advertised to the lurking enemy submarine U boat our presence! However, every device had to be tried. Perhaps the most successful was in broad daylight engaging the German heavy battery at Cape Circe. This battery had been quite effective in 286

harassing our convoys, so I was told to silence it! As we were in a sense a sitting target, I decided to carry out some bombardments going stern first. This meant setting the ship’s course 180° out on the bombardment plotting table. This evidently for a long time utterly confused the enemy spotting officers. Then I arranged for an occasional mock firework explosion on board to simulate a hit when in fact the enemy’s shell landed many thousands of yards away. We silenced it for a time. The railway along the coast also carried a certain amount of traffic. One day I closed the coast and engaged the train scoring a hit on one of the centre carriages and breaking the coupling. The rear part of the train which came to a halt immediately disgorged a number of troops whilst the front part with its few carriages beat the top speed record for Italian engines in racing for some less dangerous part of the track. I reported by signal ‘Have Bisected Troop Train’, which caused some amusement at Staff HQ. One evening with two destroyers I received information that German torpedo boats and destroyers would after dark attack the landing area. I immediately went to the north of the landing area with my very little force so as to be in a good position to intercept. Sure enough, about midnight the radar operator reported some small contacts close inshore steaming south. I closed, but the contacts were uncertain and confusing, and might have been our own motor gunboats operating in this area. So, I thought it would be best, if possible, to identify them before engaging them. I fired a salvo of ‘star shell’ in their direction; again, we did not see much but the contact faded in the northward direction. I closed but could not regain contact and as the waters were mined where I would have to steam I eventually withdrew. Disappointing as in fact subsequent investigations showed that these contacts were two or three German torpedo boats who evidently did not like their assignment. Being wise after the event is always easy but I should have had greater chances if regardless of other things, I had closed to a very close range before disclosing my presence. But I might have been torpedoed for my pains as the light was not entirely favourable to me for carrying out an unseen attack. In actions I Anti-aircraft guns with a member of fought later I always made it a rule at night to take a chance and close to almost point-blank the guncrew on watch. range before disclosing my presence. But that is all a different story of another day. March 1944 March was a busy month off Anzio. A new American General had taken over and whilst the German attacks were held, the big offensive round Monte Cassino was well underway. Various hideous devices such as one-man torpedoes were tried by the Germans on the ships in the anchorage at Anzio. We always patrolled at night to seaward as one was less likely to be surprised if at sea and moving. Enormous amounts of stores were landed at Anzio. So much so that John Cunningham was heard to remark that there was no room for any more stores until the Army advanced and 287

captured new territory. We heard that we would soon be required in home waters to take our part in the invasion of France, and it was a case of ‘pull devil, pull baker’ [tug-of-war] between the Med and the Home waters. Our reputation as a bombardment support ship had evidently spread to Whitehall, as Admiral Andrew Cunningham, who was then First Sea Lord, said we would only require a few days practice before playing a part in the bombardments off the coast of France. In April it was decided we must return home and prepare ourselves for the invasion of France which was to be known as Operation Overlord. I wondered what pattern the operation would take, having in 1940 and 1941 been concerned in drawing up what were then very ethereal plans to re-enter France! Perhaps a few thoughts about old Sir Dudley Pound, the late First Sea Lord, who died from a tumour on the brain in the previous autumn, would not be out of place. Though I had never served at sea with him, we all of course knew him well by reputation, and during over two years at the Admiralty often closely in contact with him, one got to know him well. Donald Maclachlan is writing a life of Dudley Pound and I have been able to help him from time to time. Dudley Pound was a very reserved character with a quite prodigious knowledge of the material of the service. He was fully aware of the enormous advantages scientific advance would and did play in maritime warfare. He was one of the most even-tempered men I have ever met. He was quite prepared to listen to opinions being expressed by junior officers even if he profoundly disagreed with them. He was in a sense much too much a centralizer. With his lovely handwriting he wrote himself many of the signals sent out by the Admiralty. He had been a phenomenally successful Staff Officer, and maybe when he reached the supreme position, he did not realise this was not right! I think in his heart of hearts he would agree his first love was tactics and second perhaps strategy and the wider aspects of war. As a tactician and ship handler he can have had few equals. But sometimes he did not give the impression of having a very sure touch on strategical matters, though he had a great respect for his two VCNS, Tom Phillips and Harry Moore, and would always listen to what Charles Lambe had to say. But perhaps his crowning virtue was his intense loyalty to Winston Churchill whom he regarded in a sense as his own Commander-in-Chief. We thought at times he was not forthright enough at dismissing some of the Prime Minister’s more fantastic and impractical ideas, but Winston was not an easy character - what geniuses are! He preferred just to play out time without giving an abrupt professional ‘No’! But when it came to procrastinating, there can have been few to match him in what he did in effectually turning down schemes. Dudley Pound had enormous vitality in spite of an arthritic hip which caused him continual pain. He loved a day’s shooting, and would be quite prepared, perhaps rather like Jackie Fisher, to dance up to all hours. But there can have been few men living with a higher sense of duty. Perhaps outwardly a bit cold, but this was really innate shyness. He did not have favourites, and was quite impersonal in his relations with most people. I have seldom seen him really angry. He had infinite patience, but his brain was not quick though for all that 288 pretty shrewd as his nickname ‘The Old Whale’ suggested.

Was he a leader in the full sense of the word? I think ‘no’ must be the answer. His gigantic knowledge, his high conduct, his dedication to the Royal Navy and all it stood for was never questioned. But he did not have that magnetic quality which attracts people, and which commands intellectual as well as emotional respect. Oddly, he and Charles Forbes ought to have changed places. For Forbes was the better strategist and Pound the better tactician. He will not go down in history as one of the great First Sea Lords. But in the measure of time, he will perhaps be judged more for the many unwise ideas emanating from Winston Churchill and many other people associated with him in the Government and which he effectively scotched, than for the original strategical concepts initiated under his regime as Chief of the Naval Staff. But there was at the time no effective alternative to him who would have commanded the respect of the sea-going service and at the same time [be] capable of giving an adequate account of himself in political debate. He literally worked himself to death. Only a man of such superabundant energy and I think also spiritual humility could have lasted as long as he did. With the passage of time, I hope a mellow view will be taken of Dudley Pound, who stood after all like a rock when repeated and totally unexpected disasters flowed in and on the Royal Navy and this country, during some of its darkest hours. April 1944 To turn back to our future moves which have already been referred to, we left the Anzio beachhead towards the end of March and by then, though an apparent temporary stalemate was in existence, it was clear then that we should soon break through to Rome. I had been in command of Mauritius just a year and was tempted to look back on what an exciting time we had had. Luck had been with us. We were the only ship to do the three invasions without a break. Others had been torpedoed, bombed or had broken down, and now we were going to have a chance of taking part in the principal maritime invasion which far exceeded in size and importance any other recorded invasion in history. We hoped our luck would hold! One had learned an immense amount and developed, I think, a sort of sixth sense which told one where opportunity and where danger lay. This of course reflects itself right through the ship and I was told [that] the ships company, referring to their Captain, reckoned ‘He knows, watch him - and jump to his order’. It is also immensely encouraging knowing one’s whole ships company to a man has implicit confidence in one. We had been through hazardous times together and there is nothing like a common danger to weld a body of men together. I had very few cases of broken or cracking nerves, and of these hardly any really genuine cases. But it is sometimes worth remembering when one encounters a man who is near uncontrollable panic, it is often efficacious to show such temper and determination as will make the individual concerned far far more frightened of oneself, than of the potential enemy. Andrew Cunningham was not wrong when in the critical days of the Crete evacuation and some ships were near breaking point, going on board and telling the Captains that they have full authority for dealing with cowardice in war, as the Naval Discipline Act prescribes. In Mauritius we were stretched at times but nothing like the tenseness to which some ships were stretched earlier in the war. We had a very good solid set of officers ably led by Patrick 289

Brock. In wartime much more depends on the Captain, and it is not long before the wartime Captains stand out head and shoulders above others. Oddly and sometimes surprisingly I found some of my contemporaries just did not stand out as Captains of war. They were up to a point adequate, but they did not have that seaman like sense and instinct which is all important. A few very clever specialist officers who had a great love and ability for tactical matters fell into this category. They should not have been sent to sea but who knows until they prove in practice to be inadequate. Then some others do not have a seaman’s eye and are congenitally bad ship handlers. Well with those you have just to regard them as one would a clumsy car driver who bumps into everything and cannot be relied on for good tactical handling of a force. John Terry, my contemporary in Dido, was quite a good fighting Captain but a very bad and at times thoroughly dangerous ship handler. One way or another, I very soon fell into the knack of ship-handling. It is easy enough provided one has a good eye and good nerve. The over anxious ship-handler is a menace to his ship and to others. Andrew Cunningham once asked me if I had been handling ships all my life, and was surprised when I told him I was really very much a novice at it. But what enormous fun it is. One soon gets the feel of the ship, of the wind and the tide, and with the ship with no vices like the Colony class cruisers, there are few things one cannot do.20 There is of course the nervy and jumpy Captain, but he seldom lasts long, as in a trice a ships company realises if their Skipper is on edge. After a brief call at Malta, we went on to Algiers to collect mails and give passage to men due to return home. As ever a few friends joined up. After calling at Gibraltar to top off the fuel, we set sail making a wide detour across the Bay of Biscay and entered the Irish Sea. We steamed up it in thick fog and called in at Scapa for a few hours before starting on what was sometimes regarded as a slightly hazardous, mostly from mines, journey down the east coast of England. Our charts were not up to date and many changes in the channel south of Flamborough Head were not known to us. So we embarked, rather I fear to Moseley’s disgust, a pilot to take us down the last part of the journey to Chatham where we were destined. We passed Whitby by day and I caught a distant sight of Mulgrave and wondered what the family were doing. It all looked very peaceful and Whitby much the same landmark as it had been for centuries past. Our plan was to have a brief refit at Chatham, change some of the ships company, and give everyone a good bit of leave, for they had been over 18 months away from home. I thought some of the ships company were getting pretty stale and some were obviously pretty tired, so after consultation with Brock, we decided to change everybody who had been in the ship for more than two years. This meant a bit of an upheaval but was I am sure wise in the long run, for I hoped directly after the invasion of Europe to take the ship out to the Far East to try conclusions with the Japanese! 20 WWD loved motorbikes, cars and mechanical objects. His intuitive response to engines, large or small, and how they behaved no doubt contributed to his ability to handle a ship well. 290

Jack Tovey, late C-in-C Home Fleet was the C-in-C Nore and could not have been more helpful. A most impressive character he gave a splendid talk to the ships company. Then by great good fortune, Angus Cunningham Grahame, a very old friend of ours, was Commodore at the Barracks, and lived in a nice little Commodore’s house adjacent to the Barracks. He and Patricia were kind enough to put Elizabeth and I up there, which could not have been more pleasant for us, and it gave Elizabeth a chance to meet some of the Officers’ wives. Elizabeth had been able to do a bit of helping to solve some of the domestic problems of the sailors’ wives.21 I was rather surprised there were not more, as I suppose over Admiral John Tovey, addressing the 70 per cent of our ship’s company and officers were ‘hostilities only’ and knew little of life in ships company at Chatham the Royal Navy in war. We were for the best part of three weeks at Chatham settling the new members of the ships company in and storing up, changing some of our guns which were now very well worn, and doing a deal of overdue maintenance work. But taking it all in all the ship had been well built at Swan Hunter’s yard, and it stood up to the pretty continuous racketing I had given it since taking over command. But a bit of leave was what many people wanted more than anything else, so the maximum possible was taken and I spent the last 10 days of April with the family at Mulgrave. Great fun, Lady Normanby in splendid heart, and the children keen to take on all and sundry. I saw my father who was as ever in robust health and carried his 79 years pretty lightly. My brother’s marriage had alas fallen apart in the early part of the year and he was left with the children, Jennifer and Rosemary. Elizabeth and Lady Normanby stepped in and gave them a home at Mulgrave until such time as my brother could make some other arrangements for them, not an easy task in the fifth year of the war. We had a few changes in the wardroom. Moseley, the pilot, left and was replaced by a particularly nice and efficient fellow, Ian Hogg, who only recently retired as a Vice Admiral having had a career of much success. The ‘Chief ’Vickery, left and was replaced by Caruana who at one time was in the term above me at Osborne, and one of the few full blooded Maltese officers in the Royal Navy. A new Marine Captain, Cole, joined also a bit before we left the Mediterranean. A first-rate officer who controlled our main armament fire with much effect. There were also a number of other changes. The gunroom changed with startling rapidity. We had young Robert Cunningham Graham who unfortunately had a breakdown which necessitated electrical shock treatment. A nice young man when he was in one of his good Jennifer and Rosemary, the two days but at times could be impossible. He was later invalided out and lives near his parents at daughters of WWD’s brother, Buddy, Dumbarton. so the house was busy with children of similar ages. 21 Elizabeth wrote personally to all the sailors’ wives emphasizing how important their contribution to the war effort was and inviting them to contact her about any difficulty. 291

I liked the look of the partially changed wardroom and ships company and in the first week of May we sailed for Scapa Flow to do a short work up. We followed the same channel up the east coast and passed Mulgrave where the cannon was fired in our honour. I expect I should not have told them when we were passing. Unfortunately, it was a steamy misty day and one could not see a great deal of the country. No sign of any E boats which sometimes attacked ships on passage up the east coast route. Arrived at Scapa to find Harry Moore there as C-in-C and my old friend, Bill Slayter, ex-Newfoundland, as the Chief of Staff. A good team. We immediately set about working up and practising bombardments. I think some folk thought because we had probably more experience than any other ship of the Navy, we did not need this practice, but I quickly disillusioned them. There was a very good ‘working up team’ at Scapa and they soon put us through our paces and corrected a number of faults which had crept in. Then after about three weeks at Scapa we went down to Greenock on the Clyde and opened our orders for Operation Overlord, the invasion of Europe! The naval part of this was known as Operation Neptune which I shall always remember as HMS Neptune was my first ship! May 1944 I read the orders of Operation Neptune with quite exceptional interest to see among other things if our suggestions and forecasts made in the autumn of 1940 bore any relation to the real plan! Perhaps here it should be borne in mind that there were and had been many differences of opinion between the American and our own Chiefs of Staff on the planning, timing and sequence of the various offensive operations, which were taking place or about to take place in the European waters, in the Mediterranean, and in the Far East, i.e. Burmese waters. These are all related in the various official histories of the war. What was perhaps not fully realised was that the decision (a correct one) to invade Sicily and follow up through Italy effectually postponed the feasibility of any attempt to re-enter France from 1943 to 1944. Furthermore, the lack of assault craft and landing craft which were wanted in their thousands for the invasion of Europe was also a deciding factor. We had not built sufficient ourselves and it is probable the decision to build up Bomber Command caused insufficient priority being given to the equally and possibly more important requirement of having sufficient specialised craft to assault the shores of France, and to carry our forces over to the mainland. The Americans were in a sense still obsessed with the Pacific, and furthermore due to political pressure from Chiang Kai Shek and the Americans, we had promised, as it now seems unwisely, to reopen the Burma front before we were established in France. The original plan was to carry out the invasion in May, but the late delivery of landing assault craft, as well as the trained crews to man them, had fallen behind; and it was accordingly decided the assault was to take place on the 5th June 1944. First of all, the place of the landing. This was the stretch of coast between the southern entrance of the river Seine along the coast westward to Barfleur, a distance of something like 292

60 miles. Oddly this was the area suggested by us in 1940. Various other alternatives up the coast from Le Havre to Calais had been suggested and considered most carefully. The RAF naturally favoured as close to the shores of England as possible so as to allow time to provide the maximum possible fighter cover. At one time the Pas de Calais area i.e. Boulogne, Le Touquet and Abbeville was much favoured, and it is not surprising that in the Germans appreciation that this is where they thought the invasion would come. But in fact, the advantages of the area chosen were overwhelming, not the least being certain difficulties the Germans would experience reinforcing in that area. It seemed to be inconceivable that the Germans with their good staff work would not appreciate where we would assault. After all, there was no doubt we would assault. We had advertised to the world we should and once ashore and after defeating the German Army, we would make for Berlin! The difficulties to be expected landing on the Belgian or Dutch coast were considerable, not the least being the ability of the enemy by reason of his good communications to reinforce the threatened area quickly. There were certain attractions of assaulting further westward on the Brittany peninsula, but the navigational and tidal hazards were considerable. The beaches were not particularly extensive, and the provision of adequate fighter cover by reason of its greater distance from UK airfields would be very considerable. So the more one looked at it, the clearer it was the area selected far outweighed in advantages other areas, having regard to the practicability of getting ashore and establishing ourselves and subsequently reinforcing at a greater rate than the enemy could. To this day, I am puzzled that the Germans did not spot this as far in a way the most obvious area. I asked General Heusinger after the war and from his remarks I deduced that the Germans were not very good at assessing the practicability of seaborne assaults. The plan and conduct of assaults is admirably described in chapters 14 and 15 of volume 3, part II of the Official Naval History, so I will not give more than the briefest outline. First of all, the original plan to which for over a year an immense amount of attention had been given by General Sir Frederick Morgan’s staff, envisaged the landing in this area of three divisions in the assault. This was in fact all he was told by Chiefs of Staff that we had and this implied all the landing craft likely to be available. It was not until December 1943 that the Supreme Commander General Eisenhower was chosen. Both Generals Eisenhower and Montgomery, who was to be in command of the British part of the assault, thought the assault should be carried out by five divisions, and the frontage of the assault increased so as to make likely the early capture of the port of Cherbourg, from which army stores could be unloaded. This meant a rather hurried recasting of the plan and scraping round for the additional landing assault craft and shipping, to make up the assault to five divisions with a rather greater reinforcement rate. But it says much for the original plan, C.O.S.S.A.C as it was known by the authors, that these alterations were embodied in it without in any way spoiling the general cohesion of the plan. Briefly the plan was that the British forces should land at the three eastern ends of the assault areas, known as Gold, Juno and Sword, and the Americans at the two western ends of the area known as Utah and Omaha beaches. There were two task forces to cover these landings, 293

the Eastern Task Force British under Admiral Vian, and the Western Task Force American under Admiral Kirk USN. The whole naval force was under the command of Admiral Ramsay who was the Naval Deputy to General Eisenhower who was the Supreme Commander. General Montgomery was the British Army commander, and General Bradley was the US Army Commander. Bombarding ships, which we were, were allocated to each of the assault areas and in most cases had pre-set targets so that the twenty-three odd German batteries, including the heavy fixed defences of Le Havre, could be engaged whilst the transports were unloading their cargo. I remember some days before the operation looking in at the Admiralty, and noting that Mauritius was the most western position of bombarding ships in the assault plan, and we were supposed to be anchored. I pointed out we were well within range of the German heavy batteries, 8 inch, 11 inch, 12 inch, at Le Havre and I thought we should be in rather a hot spot if we spent the day there! So, I asked one of the operational research people what they thought of it! He replied ‘Oh, that’s all right we have worked it out, and you would in that position get hit not more than 2.73 times a day, with shells of 11 inch calibre’. I said ‘Do you think a cruiser is a sort of Aunt Sally, capable of absorbing punishment from all sizes of guns?’ However, I had a laugh with Professor Blackett (now Lord Blackett, OM, President of the Royal Society), who was in charge of Operational Research, and who had in his early years been a naval officer. But as soon as I saw the plan I decided not to put my anchor down, but to keep on the move, as previous experience in former bombardments had indicated this was the wisest course to adopt. Now for the plan, the first waves of the assault forces were all carried in assault craft and came from areas round Portsmouth and Portland, the other convoys came from all over the South Coast, and as far afield as Greenock where we were stationed. Map 25 on page 35 of volume 3, Part 2 illustrates very clearly the sequence of events in an assault. First, the swimming tanks, then the smoke layer, then the support landing craft, then tank landing craft, then assault landing craft, followed by rocket landing craft, followed by further tank landing craft, then the main follow up bodies of infantry landing craft with the bulk of the assault forces. These all follow, as it were, in sequence, spaced out with a total distance apart of some six miles between the leading swimming tanks and the last wave of the infantry in landing craft. Then of course the track into the beaches had to be swept by minesweepers and special marks set up for the landing craft to use as navigational landing marks. The plan was to land that is the first wave of the assault craft about half an hour after the first twilight and some four hours before high water so that the landing craft would not get stranded on a falling tide. These conditions were likely to occur on the 5th, 6th and 7th June. Furthermore, a moonlight night would help in the approaches. These conditions only occurred for three or four days in each month and it is again surprising that the Germans didn’t appear to appreciate how narrowly we were restricted as to choice of days for the assault. Then as we could not guarantee capturing a port it was necessary to construct artificial harbours off the beaches. These were known as Mulberries and were constructed by sinking 294

a number of old ships to act as breakwaters. and then constructing floating pontoons which went up and down with the tide, and which were joined to the beaches by a floating roadway, and so were suitable for unloading heavy stores which were required to be removed by lorry or tank transporter vehicle. They did wonderful service and allowed the army to build up their stores, ammunition and artillery at the rate necessary for rapid advances. Pipelines were to be laid across the channel known as ‘Pluto’ to supply tanks, aircraft, and other forces with fuel. Then air bombardment had to be coordinated with the assault to incommode defending forces and to prevent them building up their defences. There were the usual mine hazards which perhaps in these shallow waters were liable to be more real than in the Mediterranean. Let us see what happened. The bombarding and support force for the Sword assault area consisting of two battleships (Warspite and Ramillies), one monitor, (Roberts), 5 cruisers (Mauritius, Arethusa, Frobisher, Dragon and Danae), and thirteen destroyers, assembled at Greenock. We were to sail on the evening of the 3rd June so as to be in position to start our part in the assault at about 5:00 a.m. on the 5th June. Admiral Patterson who was holding the post of Assistant Chief of Naval Staff Weapons, hoisted his flag in us a couple of days before we sailed, and was to be the senior officer of the bombarding force. Kelsey was in Warspite. Middleton in Ramillies, Dalrymple Smith a term mate of mine in Arethusa, and the names of the other captains escape me at the moment. I had an opportunity of seeing a few other friends, Freddie Dalrymple Hamilton with his flag in Belfast, which was commanded by Parham. They asked me to go over and talk to them on bombardment experience which I did one evening. It was pleasant weather at Greenock but not settled. However, there was little time to worry about this, but concentrate on what lay ahead of us. The day we were due to sail I had a signal from the Admiral to say we were to take Marshal Stalin’s two special observers. I really hoped I had done with the Russians, but this seemed to be our fate. They were a Russian General who had been a corps commander on the Eastern Front and presumably a successful one, and Admiral Kharlarnov, who was Russian Head of the Naval Mission to Great Britain. The signal said they would bring their ‘servants’ with them. I knew these were the NKVD (Secret Police) folk whose job it was to keep an eye and report back every word they said to the Politbureau. I was determined not to have these fellows on board my ship. So I arranged with Brock, the Commander who looked most imposing with his long grey beard, that they were to be sent ashore. This is what happened. We were due to sail at, I think. 6.30 p.m. on the 2nd June, so I sent our boat to collect the party at 6.00 p.m. When the boat came alongside the gangway, the two senior members i.e. the Russian Admiral and the Russian General stepped out first followed at a distance by the ‘servants’. As our main guests reached the top of the gangway, I stepped forward to greet them. At the same time, the formidable figure of the Commander stepped forward just behind them, and said in no uncertain terms to the ‘servants’ who were following that there was no room on board, and bustled them back into the boat and sent them ashore. It was all done so quickly the ‘servants’ did not realise what had happened until 295

they were landed at Greenock Pier without ceremony. The effect on the Russian General and Admiral was instantaneous. The Russian General said to a liaison officer and interpreter smiling from ear to ear ‘Our servants are not to come, this is splendid, now we can talk’. As soon as we got down to my cabin, I immediately placed half a tumbler of neat whisky in his hand which he consumed without delay saying it was the best drink in the world. He certainly talked most expansively and up to a certain point so did the Russian Admiral, who I suspect however feared he would get into trouble for allowing his ‘servants’ to be sent back. I told Patterson about it afterwards and he laughed immensely. I went up to the bridge and we were soon getting underway and led a long procession of warships down the Clyde. One’s memory went out to those tough days in the first winter of the war in the old Hood, and how long it had taken for the wheel to complete the full circle. Then what a tremendous project in which we were now taking part. The vast amount of planning, the great and singularly successful efforts of ‘deception planning’, which made the Germans think even after we had landed that the main assault would take place in the Pas de Calais area. As we steamed down towards the Irish Sea passing Arran on our starboard hand and the impressive Ailsa Craig an hour or so later, one thought much of what lay ahead. Some of our working up practices before sailing had taken place near Arran, which I first got to know well with Roger Keyes in 1940. Though there was much optimism on all sides, I knew well the dangers ahead. The near shave we had at Salerno and the critical times at Anzio. The Germans were not to be underrated and I could not but feel that they must have appreciated our intentions and the timing of them. I thought at any rate we should have a nice lot of submarines waiting to do their worst and torpedo as many of our ships as possible. Then we should have E Boat attacks, and surely the approaches to the intended invasion beaches would be well mined. Then what about the weather, the open beaches on either side of the Channel even in June can be hazardous and difficult to land on when the weather is unkind. We had always been led to believe that an opposed landing against an alert enemy is just not on until the beach defences had been properly flattened. We did not have to go back to our experiences at Gallipoli to remind us of that. Whilst in the three previous invasion assaults I had taken part, the beach opposition had been less than expected, it seemed in this case where tactical surprise was unlikely, that this would not again be the case. It was altogether a great adventure, the biggest invasion in history with a lot of unknowns ahead. On the other hand, the Germans were showing signs of grave strain. Their strategic direction completely centralised in Hitler’s hands was bad and continued to make mistake after mistake. They had not got control of the air. Their Navy was small and their submarines must have realised that the balance of the Battle of the Atlantic had tilted decisively against them. All these thoughts passed through one’s mind as we steamed south. Our Naval Commander-in-Chief Admiral Ramsay who was to visit us later, issued the following stirring message which was read to everybody in every ship on sailing. 296

‘It is our privilege to take part in the greatest amphibious operation in history and a necessary preliminary to the opening of the Western Front in Europe which in conjunction with the Great Russian Advance will crush the fighting power of Germany. This is the opportunity which we have long awaited and which must be seized and pursued with relentless determination. The hopes and prayers of the free world and of the enslaved peoples of Europe will be with us and we cannot fail them. Our task in conjunction with the Merchant Navies of the United Nations and supported by the Allied Air forces is to carry the Allied Expeditionary Force to the Continent to establish them there in a secure bridgehead, and to build it up, maintain it at a rate which will allow us to match that of the enemy. Let no one underestimate the magnitude of this task. The Germans are desperate and will resist fiercely until we outmanoeuvre and outfight them, which we can and will do. To every one of you who will be given the opportunity to show by his determination and resource that dauntless spirit of resolution which individually strengthens and inspires, and which collectively is irresistible. I count on every man to do his utmost to ensure the success of this great enterprise which is the climax of the European War. ‘GOOD LUCK TO YOU ALL AND GODSPEED’ As we steamed down the Irish Sea on the 3rd June the weather steadily worsened. and I wondered what conditions were like in the Channel, and how we would fare at dawn on the 5th of June which was to be the day of the assault. We had fortunately in the overall orders made provision for the possibility of a 24-hour delay if the weather was hopeless. There was a special prearranged coded signal which allowed for this. I suppose soon after 6:00 a.m. on the 4th when we were about halfway across West Bay, we got this signal. I immediately told Wilf Patterson, our Admiral, who reversed the course of the bombardment squadron for 12 hours, so that in 24 hours’ time we should be where we were on receipt of this signal. I hoped everybody got the signal and heard only later that one of the main American assault convoys did not, and had to be turned round by messages from destroyers specially sent to them for this purpose. The importance of signals getting through can never be overestimated. History shows time and time again the dire results which arise when important signals are not received. In this case if special additional steps had not been taken to turn the American assault convoy, the invasion assault would have ended in disaster. During the time when we had some 24 hours to kill, I had some long conversations with our Russian guests and particularly the Russian General. A British Brigadier was with the party and acted as a very efficient interpreter though it was clear enough from his expression what the General meant. It was evident both our Russian guests were tremendously impressed with the whole organisation and apparatus for an invasion of this magnitude. The Russians were in fact little interested in amphibious operations for as is often quoted, they were certainly at that time a land animal with little or no knowledge of maritime warfare in its broad context. The Russian General kept impressing on me the hope that we had not underrated the Germans, for as he said that they, the German Army, were the finest 297

fighting machine in the world. He said, knowing there was nobody to report back what he said, that one German division was equal to two Russian divisions, and he could not be sure of holding a German attack unless he was in superiority of a ratio of three to one, and when it came to attacking, he said it was imperative to have a superiority of five to one, if one was to be successful. He ended by saying in so many words ‘I know, for I have had to fight some very stubborn defensive battles and recently in the south of our front, I have won some battles and beaten the German army opposite me’. It was most interesting, the Russian Admiral who was a much more suspicious character did not take much part in the conversation. I tried perhaps with some success to reassure the General. I told him of our experiences in Sicily and particularly at Salerno and Anzio, where we had met very stiff German Army opposition. I don’t think in reality either the Admiral or the General had much conception of what a major amphibious assault was like. Neither I think really appreciated the vital importance of the air, and how it is essential to have almost complete command of the air, during the approach and over the beaches while the assault forces are landing. We steamed away westward and hoped the weather would get better. It was still rather unsettled and cold for June. I felt at the time we really had not been very lucky with the weather. A rough patch in the Mediterranean, in July of all months, made the Sicily invasion in the previous year difficult. Salerno had been ideal, but a later totally unexpected gale had slowed down the Army’s advance because of lack of supplies. Oddly enough, Anzio had been good in spite of the fact that the assault took place in winter when bad weather could be expected. The English Channel is notoriously uncertain. Nevertheless, by all averages we had reason to hope for good weather in the first week in June. But this seemed doubtful as mentioned before, the tide, moon and other conditions made assaults practicable only for about three to four days in each month. June 5th had been cancelled and postponed to the following day. Would this be all right for we only had one more day i.e. 7th June, on which assaults could be carried out in June. Our doubts were set at rest for during the night of the 4th/5th of June, we got the signal from Admiral Ramsay, confirming that the assault would take place on the 6th June with ‘H’ hour for our beach known as Sword Beach at 07.25 a.m. This at any rate set our minds at rest, and we just hoped the weather would continue to improve, which it did but only perceptibly. An astonishing feature of our perambulations up and down the English Channel was the complete absence of any German aircraft. There were any amount of our Coastal Command on anti-submarine and reconnaissance duties, fighter aircraft on air protection duties and various other aircraft striking at enemy installations, particularly their radar installations in occupied France. The plan was for all forces to pass on the carefully prepared time schedule through an area known as Area Z, just south of the Isle of Wight, steam south through a broad channel known as the Spout, which had been meticulously swept clear of many German mines by our minesweeping forces. 298

5th June 1944 As we retraced our steps there was a sense of uncanny calm, convoy after convoy were passed making for their various rendezvous, yet no sign of enemy activity, no submarine scares, no torpedoed ships to succour, no bombing attacks. As the evening wore on, we steamed down the Spout channel, a little in advance of the main assault convoys. We led the way, and what a privilege it was, to do this in the biggest recorded seaborne invasion in history. The weather had certainly improved a bit though it was still nasty for small open assault craft, and I reckoned a goodish number might fail to make the enemy coast because of the weather. But still as the evening wore on there was no sign that the enemy had appreciated anything was up. Even the paratroop landings just after midnight opposite our Sword beach seemed to have stimulated rather a slow reaction. I decided to have my supper on the bridge. Thanks to some quite excellent caviar and vodka brought as a present by our Russian guests, it was a more than usually good one. I reflected that those of you who read this may be amused that your father led the invasion forces to the coast of France eating caviar sandwiches and sipping vodka. 5th/6th June From midnight onwards streams of aircraft - our bombers passed overhead, and we heard the distant crump of their bombs as they were released at the coastal batteries and other communication targets in the area about to be assaulted. We steadily steamed on expecting at least E boat attacks, but nothing materialised. Whilst we had in previous invasions met only very moderate resistance to ourselves - in fact much less than expected, I felt it unlikely our luck would hold and that we should be subjected to every form of attack, bomb, submarine, E boat, mine, torpedo attack from destroyers, enemy heavy shore gun shore batteries and so on. I thought at any rate this time we should at least find ourselves having to cope with the whole catalogue of defensive measures available to a modern military power. But as yet nothing. No ships torpedoed by submarines, and as yet nobody mined. It all seemed uncanny as we approached the area where the enemy should have anticipated we were bound to assault. As we now know, it was only after 3:00 AM when our assault and bombarding ships were becoming visible from the shore to the naked eye, that the Germans came to a full alert. As soon as it began to become light shortly after 4:00 a.m., the daylight bombers (US) over 1000 of them went into the attack. It was still rather cloudy and overcast overhead and it seemed as if they would have difficulty identifying their targets. Meanwhile we continued to edge forward slowly towards our bombardment position which was at the extreme eastern end of the assault line just opposite the heavy German battery at Houlgate, which was to be our first target. Then a few minutes after 5:00 a.m. we heard reports and some people saw the green flashing light or Sword Beach which was being flashed by a special midget submarine X-20 to indicate the ‘all clear’ for the assault. 299

6th June 1944 We were delighted as we knew that this situation was all set for the assault in the right place and about the right time. By this time, we were just about in our allotted position so that we could engage the enemy battery at Houlgate at 05.50. It must have been just before this that our Asdic operator sung out up his voicepipe ‘torpedoes approaching’ and at the same time there was a report of enemy destroyers off Le Havre, about 8 miles distant. Fortunately, I had exercised my discretion in not anchoring the ship as the orders prescribed so was readily manoeuvrable. I immediately turned the ship bow on towards Le Havre and heard the torpedoes pass us by. Unfortunately, the Norwegian destroyer Svenner was hit and sank almost immediately. In one of the photos in my album she is seen on fire just prior to sinking. Wilf Patterson was keen to go after these German torpedo boats which we immediately started to do. But I was rather doubtful of the wisdom of this course as our main purpose was to support the landing and silence the big German battery at Houlgate, and in any case pursuit of the German destroyers who had the legs of us across mined waters was a pretty chancy business. After about five minutes when it was clear there was no hope of catching the German torpedo boats, we returned to our billet. Meanwhile tremendous bombing attacks mostly by Fortresses and our own tactical bombers had been going on unceasingly on the German batteries. We heard also that the parachute landing just after midnight had been successful but that they were meeting very stiff resistance in attempting to achieve their aim of capturing certain bridgeheads over the River Orne. At 5:30 the bombing attack ceased and pretty well the entire line of warships opened fire on their allotted targets, a very impressive sight, the heavy thuds of the 15 inch guns of Ramillies and Warspite must have encouraged our troops and maybe dismayed the Germans. There was a certain amount of sporadic battery fire against the ships. And there are in my photo album, photographs of enemy shells falling in our vicinity. One heard a certain amount of the whistle of shells passing overhead but nothing of any serious consequence. I noticed our Russian Admiral guest usually ducked as he heard the whistle of enemy shells over us. This must be a subconscious reflex action, as firstly, the thin plating of the bridge is no protection against enemy shells and secondly, the shells travel faster than the velocity of sound and therefore the shell that is going to hit you hits you first before its accompanying whistle is heard. But I have often noticed this among personnel not accustomed to being under fire, that there is always a tendency to duck behind something however flimsy. The Russian General was on the other hand quite impervious. He said to me in so many words ‘but what are the Germans doing - have you already destroyed their defences?’ We got down to Houlgate; but though I think we silenced them, I could not be sure we had destroyed their fully equipped shore defence battery. We were ably supported by the monitor Roberts just behind us with their 15 inch guns. So, we shifted our fire to other pre-set beach defences. For this invasion most of the spotting and control of ship’s gunfire was done by spotters in aircraft and in some cases by the pilot himself, for some Spitfires were specially fitted for the control of ships’ gunfire. 300

Meanwhile, the assault convoys had reached their lowering positions and as far as we could see in the rather uncertain light everything on the Sword Beach was going to plan. The fire from enemy defences seemed fitful, rather sporadic and uncoordinated. It seemed that the tremendous bombing followed instantly by the ships’ gunfire had virtually swamped, if not stunned the defences. Some of the close support craft closed the beaches and opened fire on the suspected enemy batteries. But what surprised me was the almost complete absence of enemy gunfire opposition to the assault craft. I had thought that in spite of our bombing and ships gunfire, the ships in the assault anchorage would come under heavy fire as they lowered their assault craft. The sea was still a bit unpleasant with the remains of the previous day’s blow to incommode landing. The first assault craft and tanks having cleared the beach obstacles touched down soon after 7.30 a.m. and from intercepted signals it seemed the following waves were coming along well on time. By 10.00 a.m. the whole of the First Assault Brigade on Sword Beach was ashore and though the beaches were still under fire mostly from German mortars, the Army were advancing inland and unless a heavy counter-attack could be mounted quickly it was evident we were ‘come to stay’. The beach obstacles were reported to be pretty formidable and we suffered heavy casualties among the landing craft but relatively light ones among the personnel who landed in them.22 The whole story of the assault is told admirably in the official History of the War, so I will only give my impressions supporting the assault on Sword Beach just opposite Ouistreham and Caen. It was some 878 years ago that William the Conqueror set off from Caen to invade England, so perhaps it was appropriate we should return the compliment against the ‘German’ Franks! The day was still overcast and not very warm for June - not a single German aircraft as yet but what still astounded me was the lack of reply from their batteries. Bombing seldom puts batteries in armoured casements out of action, so why had not the heavy batteries got down to making life unpleasant for us. About this time or in fact rather earlier, we laid smoke between La Havre and the assault area, and this may well have hampered the visual observations of the German battery commanders. We soon got in touch with our Forward Observation Officer who called for fire support to help our forces advancing towards Caen. As the day wore on it seemed from intercepting signals that the assaults on the three British beaches, Sword, Juno, and Gold were succeeding. Not much was heard how the Americans were getting on. But it seemed the assault on Omaha Beach, the western next but one of the assault, was running into difficulties. However, by the late afternoon it was clear that with the possible exception of the assault on Omaha Beach the assault had been a success. Our casualties in ships and personnel had been far far less than expected. The history of this campaign gives us British casualties on D Day in the assault as a little over 4000, and the Americans about 6000. Exceptionally small when compared with those terrible casualty lists from the Western Front assaults in the First War. 22 WWD’s assessment of the success of the assault seems in retrospect over-optimistic, no doubt because he was not able to see the problems of the advance beyond the beach. The story is told in great detail in Stephen Fisher, Sword Beach:The Untold Story of D Day’s forgotten Victory, Penguin, 2025. 301

As the evening came it was clear, taking it all in all, the Army had achieved the objectives it had set itself for the first day, but where was the German Air Force, for which we had long had a healthy respect? I thought anyway on the first night we should have some pretty determined air attacks and that if handled with skill and courage, German E boats and submarines could do great damage in the anchorage offshore. We formed up in a circle with the other warships as it were round the Sword anchorage, and later Admiral Vian came and anchored near us. Just before dusk a most impressive sight passed overhead. A long column of troop carriers and towed gliders passed overhead with reinforcements for paratroopers previously landed. There seemed countless numbers of them. and I watched them land near Caen which was still in German occupation. A few got shot down in the air and burst into flames but the great majority seemed to fetch up near Caen. The gallantry of these men evoked tremendous enthusiasm among the ships company, some of whom were heard to remark that life at sea was the safest and most comfortable form of occupation imaginable! As dusk began to close down, the anchorage was covered in smoke, and it was time to reflect on what the night had in store for us. Our planned defences I thought were first rate, for they embodied all the experiences I and other various folk had gained in the three previous seaborne assaults. To seaward there were patrols to prevent E boats and submarines getting into the anchorage; round the anchorage there was contained a fairly dense smoke screen which however the freshening wind blew away. Overhead flew night-fighter cover of a number of Beaufighter Squadrons. Apart from one air raid in the late afternoon, I do not remember any really concentrated air raids during the night, though the occasional nuisance bomber or reconnaissance aircraft came over to receive a mighty hot reception as the photos in my photograph album show. One or two LSTs were hit, probably by enemy battery fire and caught fire, and there were also a few fires on the assault beaches which were however quickly extinguished. I decided to put the anchor on the bottom at short stay to keep the ship stationary, as otherwise with the strong tidal stream one would have got mixed up with ships unloading in the anchorage. If I remember right, Wilf Patterson went over to see Admiral Vian in Scylla who had anchored nearby. Apart from sporadic anti-aircraft fire at low enemy aircraft, the night passed off without any undue alarm and excursions. Unfortunately, the last wave of the airborne gliders with troops to support the parachute landing near Caen did not pass over until after dark at about 11.00 p.m. and got fired on at by our own forces, with alas, some casualties. The difficulties and problems of identification at night are exceedingly hard to resolve. And as the Commander-in-Chief Admiral Ramsay had warned all concerned during the planning, this might well happen under conditions where visual identification would not be possible. Another problem had obtruded itself and that was the use of Oyster mines by the Germans. These mines were at that time quite unsweepable and were laid in the anchorage by aircraft and E boats. They were operated by the difference in water pressure caused by the passage of the hull of a ship and were only effective as ground mines in relatively shallow water. 302

As the historian relates, by nightfall on D Day about 133,000 soldiers had been landed on the coast of France, together with their supporting vehicles - over 900 tanks, some 240 field guns and approaching 5,000 tons of stores and ammunition - a truly memorable performance. The casualties for men, ships and aircraft had been far less than expected. The Germans were in fact stunned by what had happened. To illustrate how out of touch the German High Command was with those in the field is the fact that until about D Day plus three days, the Germans still thought the main attack would come in the Pas de Calais area, and so did not release their reinforcing troops to oppose the invasion as soon as they might have, though the almost total destruction of all the Seine bridges was a contributory cause for this. The first night apart from being rather noisy was without serious incident in so far as the British assault area was concerned. As dawn broke on the 7th June, we could feel that the invasion now launched was well on the way to success. Nevertheless, the weather was still unkind and after what appeared a calm night it was still blowing quite hard at daybreak, and some small craft were not going to have at all an easy time. General Montgomery landed in the morning and set up his headquarters in France. Meanwhile Apollo carrying General Eisenhower and Admiral Ramsay paid us all a visit, and from the signals they made, it was clear they were well pleased with the progress. The chief problem after confronting the enemy forces on land was to ensure the buildup of our stores, ammunition and the like was adequate to the needs of the ever-mounting numbers of soldiers landed. This was not easy the beaches were still heavily obstructed, the little ports such as Ouistreham and Port-en-Bassin had a very limited capacity and it was taking time to construct the Mulberry artificial harbour both in the British and American assault areas. Also, the oil pipeline, known as Pluto [Pipe Line Under the Ocean] had yet to be laid though the plans were far advanced. The weather gradually improved and much useful work was done salvaging the various numerous numbers of landing craft which had come to grief on the day of the assault. It was not long before we received calls for supporting fire from our troops opposite Sword Beach There are many calls on Warspite, Ramillies and Roberts for heavy support fire and later Nelson and Rodney joined and gave most impressive support, for these ships could hit enemy targets as far as 17 miles inland to the acute discomfiture of the Germans. The skill with which air spotting arrangements had been concerted and arranged proved of inestimable value. The Naval historian has much of interest to say on the effect of naval gunfire in Vol. 3 part II, and there can now be of little doubt that the effect was decisive. For Rommel reported to Hitler a few days after the assault forces had landed, ‘the effects of heavy naval bombardment are so powerful that an operation either with infantry or armoured formations is IMPOSSIBLE in an area commanded by the rapid firing artillery’. Whilst our 6 inch guns in Mauritius could reach 10 or 11 miles in land, the guns of Rodney and Nelson could reach 17 miles. This had a decisive effect in breaking up enemy concentrations preparing for counter-attack and furthermore, though in this campaign not much used, bombardments could also take place at night. 303

With steady improvement in the weather our spirits rose and we reflected on the special instructions issued to cope with Oyster mines which were now being laid by German aircraft and E boats. A nasty proposition with so much shallow water about. It was not long, I think the 10th June, before the Prime Minister was with us. I gathered later no less a person than the King himself had to be brought in to prevent the Prime Minister landing with the first assault wave on D Day! There had been a few bombing attacks on the unloading beaches and there was one big oil fire which seemed to burn for a number of days. Sure enough, the Prime Minister who was I think in the Destroyer Kelvin passed us at the eastern end of the assault area and steamed towards the Houlgate and Benerville area. When about halfway between us and the beach, the destroyer opened fire in the direction of the German forces. Suspecting the Prime Minister was urging the Captain of the destroyer on and knowing that quite a number of Oyster and magnetic mines have been dropped there, I made the peremptory signal to Kelvin ‘Do not close the beach any further - recent mine danger’. I did not know that in fact Admiral Vian was on board at the time. However, I gather he supported my order and told the Prime Minister he had chanced his arm sufficiently and then returned the main anchorage. The Prime Minister laughed some months later, when I told him what an anxious few minutes he had given me! Bombardments were a fairly regular occurrence, and in a sense unlike other assaults one had not the freedom to go where one liked because of the mine danger of recently laid mines and a large number of existing minefields. Fortunately in the Mediterranean the water was often too deep for effective mining. Again and again, the heavy bombardments from battleships were frequently called for with decisive results. About this time our Russian guests left us. I think they must have been much impressed, in sending their signals back to Russia. For this was about the only time related by Winston Churchill in Volume Six of ‘Triumph and Tragedy’ that he got really appreciative signals from Stalin. One evening I had a signal from a destroyer from Andrew Yates (Captain A.S.V.Yates), who was in the radar and radio experimental establishment, saying he was bringing some friends over and could they stay the night. I said of course yes, and to my surprise with Andrew Yates arrived Professor Blackett, Professor Bernal and another eminent scientist whose name escapes me. They all had been much concerned with the operational research and radar aspects of invasion and were a tremendous asset. I told Blackett so far we had not been hit as many times as his operational researcher thought we might! I said I thought one of the reasons was because all the German Gun Crews in open mountings had gone to their shelters nearby whilst the bombing was on and were caught in the open manning their guns immediately the bombing stopped, which coincided with the start of the naval bombardment. They first thought this was another dose of bombing, and those who did become casualties returned to their shelters for a time. The arrival of these very clever men was most refreshing and their views on any or all subjects were well worth listening to. As things were a bit quiet, I asked them to give a Brains Trust on any subject, in the hangar of the ship.23 Every man who could get away came, and we had a mighty stimulating hour when our guests gave 23 The Brains Trust was a BBC Radio programme started in 1941, where a panel of four experts debated questions sent in by the public. The original team included the biologist, Julian Huxley, and philosopher and psychologist, Cyril Joad, with other well-known experts invited as appropriate. It was an outstanding and very popular programme 304

the ships company, many of whom were men of great ability and intelligence, plenty to think about. We managed in keeping off politics though it was obvious some of their views, especially Bernal’s, were a long way left of centre. All continued to go well, and by the middle of the month the British troops had eight Divisions ashore and the Americans eleven Divisions. A formidable striking force indeed with more to follow and with complete control of the air. The King, accompanied by the Chiefs of Staff and Admiral Ramsay, arrived in Arethusa and after looking around landed in one of the DUKWs which had proved such effective amphibious craft. All seemed well for the weather had taken a turn for the better and it seemed as if at long last we might expect proper June weather for the Channel. Then some days after the King’s visit, it suddenly blew up hard one morning and before long a full gale from the North East was blowing, which meant all the ships in the anchorage were on a dangerous lee shore. This was dangerous and might prove disastrous for not only was our average daily unloading rate of something like 23,000 tonnes reduced to a small trickle, but the weather very seriously curtailed air attacks on German concentrations, and so they were in a position to reinforce a great deal quicker than we were. This gale almost unprecedented in the Channel in June lasted for four days and did extensive harm. The US Mulberry Harbour was destroyed beyond all hope of repair. Ours was very badly damaged - a most depressing sight and the best part of 800 ferry and landing craft had been driven ashore, some damaged beyond repair. In fact, this gale cost the Army in supplies some 100,000 tons of stores and 20,000 vehicles and it took over a month to catch up with this deficiency. Meanwhile the Americans under the redoubtable General Patton had broken out of their positions and sealed off the Cherbourg peninsula. It was not until the end of June that the situation was again comfortably in hand, with stores and vehicles being landed at a rate sufficient to keep the Army going. But it took a further month before all the leeway was caught up. If this gale had happened a week earlier, we might well have suffered one of the biggest military defeats in our history. For it is not always remembered even in this technological age that the weather can play a decisive part in affairs and remind us all that we are but puny mortals! I kept the ship anchored at short stay throughout the gale but fortunately our splendid steel anchor cable held in spite of never having had more than two shackles out, we never dragged an inch, though the cable was often singing like a violin. Our Admiral and his staff which included our old gunnery officer, Ivan Sarell, left us and returned to their office chairs at the Admiralty albeit somewhat reluctantly. Immediately after the gale we returned to Spithead to replenish with ammunition and stores and have perhaps a little rest, though I did not feel particularly tired. Some of the ships company were looking pretty teased out, but what a wonderful tonic an impending victory can be! Whilst anchored at Spithead, I thought I would give a little dinner party for a retired fire eater known as Captain Hugh T England, who was in charge of one of the depot ships and had been to almost every landing since the war started. Though I suppose 20 years or so 305

older than us, he still retained his old fire. A man of most violent and tempestuous temper who would really have been more at home in Elizabethan days than in the 20th century. I asked some of my old friends who had suffered under him in his halcyon days, and had been his First Lieutenant and Commander in the days long before the war and during the First World War, to join us. Humphrey Scott, in my term, Charles Norris, a contemporary of mine, and his one-time navigator in a cruiser in the Mediterranean, McCoy, one of the World War II real destroyer characters and hard cases. My Steward, Carter, had got ashore at I think Ouistreham and bought a fat goose. A rare luxury for us in these war rationed days. Hugh [England] was a character. He usually had some of his officers under arrest and not infrequently his officers would hit him back when in his transports of rage. But for all that quite fearless and a wonderful ship handler, and a man who would back his officers through thick and thin, but with a raging fire in his belly at all times. What an evening we had - all my other guests took him to task but he gave as good as he got. I told him he ought to have been the Lieutenant of the boarding party in Elizabethan days - no Spaniard would have withstood him nor his language, which did not stop at incinerating the Pope. At the end of the evening as he had no boat, I said I would send him back in our skimming dinghy which at best of times had a temperamental engine. However, all departed and I saw England down into the dinghy and they set off in the darkness in the direction of his ship at an alarming speed. About 7.00 a.m. next morning Brock came and said, ‘I think Sir, I ought to tell you the dinghy has not returned!’ I said, ‘there is not much we can do about it, wait and see if it is reported.’ About 9.00 a.m. a boat was seen approaching towing our dinghy with a very dejected looking young stoker sitting in it. I asked him what happened and he said after leaving the ship last night, the engine stopped and he couldn’t start it again, so Captain England said ‘Let me try’. He gave a tremendous hoist to the starting handle, the engine backfired with a terrific explosion, and the starting handle flew off into the sea. I then said, ‘What did Captain England say?’ He was rather a shy young stoker and said, ‘I don’t think I could tell you Sir’. So I said, ’What happened then?’ He said, ‘I told him we had no spare starting handle in the boat. Then he went on terribly for nearly 40 minutes and I thought the end of the world would come. Until after I suppose about four hours we were picked up by a passing patrol boat. All this time Captain England was swearing in many different languages and I thought the devil would come and swallow us up Sir, when he called on the Chinese spirits. I never want to take him in my boat again Sir!’ Altogether a good evening, Hugh T [England] is still alive. I saw him only a few months ago still looking pretty spry. Well then back to the bombardment area where we got a certain number of calls for our support especially as the assault on Caen had started. A very tough place as the Germans had concentrated much of their defences around Caen. As June wore on very heavy fighting was taking place in front of Caen and it was here that the Germans were evidently determined to make their main effort. The Americans had reached the coast on the other side of Cherbourg and were mounting an attack with much naval support on this vital port. It was captured on the 26th June but the port itself was blocked to an almost unimaginable degree. My pre-war friend of Scapa days, Commodore 306

Mackenzie, RNR, with his American counterpart, Commodore Sullivan, did a stupendous job and got the port going for the clearance of large cargo ships by the middle of July. By the end of June our naval forces had been reorganised. Admiral Vian having finished his job together with his American opposite number returned home, and Admiral Rivett Carnac set up his headquarters as Flag Officer (British Assault Area) at Courcelles. By this time over one million soldiers had been landed. A stupendous feat inside four weeks with a major gale to interrupt matters thrown in for good measure. There was still much work to be done supporting the Army. They were determined to capture Caen as indeed were the Germans determined to prevent this happening. Eventually after some of the hardest fighting of the war, Caen was captured in the middle of July and the German position commenced to deteriorate rapidly. For by this time the American thrust under the redoubtable General Patton had cut deep into the Cherbourg Peninsula and threatened Caen from the rear. It must have been just after this that Admiral Ramsay came on board to see us all and I got him to talk to the ships company. He gave a fascinating talk and said the Germans were on the brink of collapse, and that he believed there was more than a good chance of defeating the Germans by the end of 1944. This got a tremendous cheer from the ships company. Admiral Ramsay looked youthful and alert, and it was evident that the quite stupendous job he had performed as the Naval Commander had not aged him one bit. Talking to him afterwards he said, ‘If Monty is allowed his way we can finish the Germans this year’. But as you know he did not have his way, and that may have been partly instrumental in causing the war to last till May 1945. Alas, Admiral Ramsay was killed not many months later in an aero plane crash. A very great loss, for if anybody played a major part in winning the war from the naval side, he did. We continued with bombardment support until the third week of July, by which time I had secret hopes we would be switched to the south of France to support the landings planned to take place there in August. But it was not to be, for there was plenty of work to be done off the Biscay ports. I think it must have been either at the end of July or early August we left the Normandy beaches for the last time and after a short spell at Spithead went down to Plymouth to work under the Commander-in-Chief there (Admiral Leatham) in offensive operations against the Biscay ports from Brest to the Spanish border which were still in the hands of the Germans. We were now definitely part of Freddie Dalrymple Hamilton’s Cruiser Squadron, the 10th Cruiser Squadron. and various Forces known as Force 26, 27 and 28, consisting each of one cruiser and two destroyers, were formed from it for patrols in the Bay and elsewhere. This was liable to be exciting work as though we did not know it at the time, the Germans were in fact transferring their U boats from the Biscay ports to Norwegian ports, so we might with reason expect an encounter with one of them. Charles Norris in Bellona in I think Force 26 started off with sinking or damaging a small force of coaster and repair ships off Saint Nazaire, in the middle of August. 307

WWD’s photos do not contain any I had an opportunity to talk with Charles about the little actions which in fact had not been identifiable pictures relating to the carried out exactly as he intended, though the end results were satisfactory. Normandy landing or the Bay of Biscay actions. However, as his account Plymouth was a pleasant place from which to operate, and in between operations I took the here is very much the story of HMS opportunity of doing a little gunnery and torpedo practice in the Bay to the West of Mauritius, it is relevant to include Plymouth. I did not think German submarines would interfere with us. It is strange that pictures of the crew both in moments however much one is in action it is doubly important to keep going at practices for gun of relaxation and in action, where control, and gun crews get into bad drill habits if one is not in a position to analyse results every man had to fulfil a particular carefully to see if any errors in drill are causing unsatisfactory results. In action one does not role and act as part of a close-knit have to produce a fall of shot diagram [i.e. showing where the shot lands relative to its aim] team. These photos were taken by and allowing for inevitable optimism, one sometimes thinks one is shooting better than is in Rev. Jock Henderson who played a fact the case. Sarell had been relieved by Thomas some months before. Thomas, a promoted vital role in helping to create a happy, gunner, was a good Gunnery Officer, but not of course in the outstanding class of Sarrell, well-disciplined and battle-ready ship. who by then had been promoted to Commander, and was I think serving in the Gunnery Images courtesy of Mary Rawstorne. Division of the Admiralty. 308

There were signs by the middle and end of August that the whole German position was beginning to collapse and I wondered if what Admiral Ramsay had told us was likely to come true. After the Seine there did not seem to be any positions where the Germans could build up a defensive position until the Ruhr. However, that is jumping ahead rather much. There was tremendously heavy fighting round La Falaise, and it was here that a few days later a decisive defeat was inflicted on the German Army. My little Force known as Force 28 consisted of Mauritius, Iroquois, a Canadian tribal class destroyer and Ursa, a British destroyer. I had studied pretty carefully most small ships actions and was determined to profit to the full by them. So I sent for the Commanding Officers of these two ships and told them exactly how I intended to conduct actions, which in all probability would take place at night. My rules were as follows: - Never open fire at medium or long range - Close the enemy to decisive gun range where pretty well all shots of the first salvo should hit. In other words, close to at least 5,000 yards, before opening fire. Using our radar which was much superior to anything the Germans had, approach the enemy, if possible down moon, and from abaft the beam, for on the bridge lookouts always concentrate on the objects ahead and before the beam, and seldom, I think, of ships coming up on them from astern. Always manoeuvre in line ahead and never on a line of bearing as Mountbatten once did, and got himself torpedoed for his pains. Don’t worry about station keeping, probably four cables is about the best distance for mutual support, and never wait for orders, but keep the command informed of your thoughts and actions. Ursa’s Commander, Commander Wyburd, was an experienced and resolute CO and could not put a foot wrong. The Canadian in Iroquois, not so experienced but very enthusiastic and keen to learn, and as he had the most modern radar gear and equipment, much would depend on the information supplied from this source. I said normally I would lead the Force into action but if we were fighting in very shallow water, I would make the destroyers lead in, and follow up on behind covering them with our heavy gunfire. As to speed, I told them only to use high speed after their presence had been detected. I told them, rather to their surprise, I intended to conduct actions at about 15 knots. Finally, I informed them not to be too alarmed at German shore battery fire, from my own experience which by then was probably as extensive as anybody’s in the Navy, shore battery fire always looked more dangerous than it was. Then I informed them our job was to bring enemy coastwise traffic to a complete standstill by sinking anybody who put to sea from their ports, such as Brest, Lorient, St. Nazaire, La Pallice, and La Rochelle, Bordeaux etc. There were some German destroyers, big mine destruction ships called Speerbrechers, minesweepers, armed trawlers and miscellaneous types of patrol vessels. Furthermore, due in some measure to the French resistance movements inland, the German liked when possible to move their stores, supplies and personnel by sea. I will now describe from memory what happened in two interesting little actions on the 15th August and the 23rd August, and if I can locate copies of my dispatches of these actions I will be able to describe in more detail and with greater accuracy what happened. We were 309

given complete latitude by the C-in-C to organise our patrols as we thought best and he confined himself to providing us with as much intelligence as possible, and some of this was very good. We also had the task of landing agents at night and collecting such information as we could of what was happening in the Biscay Ports of France. I came to the conclusion it was best to show ourselves usually in the forenoon off the coasts of France and then disappear certainly not later than noon to seaward and remain out of sight of land - then after dark close the shore at slow speed and patrol likely routes close inshore which the enemy might use. All this seemed to work out well for it lulled the German command into a sense of false security, that we were either not there or very occasional visitors to their close inshore routes. The German air reconnaissance seemed to have been rather sketchy and apart from an occasional JU88 we saw little sign of the German Air Force. We left Plymouth at dusk on the 15th August and giving Ushant a fairly clear berth for the Germans still occupied the Channel Islands and their batteries were capable of firing at extreme long range with a measure of accuracy. Though there were plenty of U Boats still about in August, we did not come across any of them. Maybe a cruiser with an escort of two destroyers was not too inviting a subject to attack, for by that time the U boats were suffering very heavy casualties from our escorts and from Coastal Command aircraft, I thought the best plan would be a daylight sweep fairly close inshore in the early morning between the approaches to St Nazaire and the mouth of the Gironde leading to Bordeaux. This would give us an opportunity of testing the shore defences and noting the approximate positions of enemy batteries.
