A certain measure of discretion would be required as there is no point in getting hit unnecessarily. I always felt a certain measure of finesse was necessary when reconnoitring possible positions and the effectiveness of enemy shore defences. Shortly after making the coastline opposite the Ile de Noirmoutier, we were fired at but not very effectively by medium sized guns. As the water was fairly shoal [shallow] between Ile d’Yeu and the mainland I thought we would pass to seaward of the Ile d’Yeu. This did not prevent us getting really quite a hot reception from one or two batteries stationed on the Ile d’Yeu. As we passed further south, various batteries off Les Sables-d’Olonne fired at us until near the Ile de Ré. We came under fire by heavy fixed defences of gun calibre of 8 or 11 inch, and again another reception at the Ile d’Oleron opposite Rochefort, but less accurate than the Ile de Ré batteries. Finally, the usual gun batteries on either side of the entrance to the Gironde opened fire but far from effectively. I hauled out well to seaward with the intention of approaching to the south of the Ile d’Yeu after dark which we reckoned would be the most likely place to meet the enemy traffic. Sure enough, I suppose soon after 11:00 p.m. our radar detected a number of contacts steaming just north of Les Sables-d’Olonne. We closed them immediately and Mauritius led in. By this time the enemy appeared to suspect our approach, so, as he seemed to have two or three destroyers with him, I opened fire on the largest object which was a specially constructed Speerbrecher of about 7,000 tons. She was immediately hit and drove herself ashore on fire 310

where she subsequently sank. Meanwhile the escorts of what seemed to be two German destroyers, a number of smaller craft had made off at high speed towards La Rochelle. We followed them and by this time the lighter batteries on the north side of the entrance to La Rochelle as well as the heavy batteries on the Ile de Ré fired at us. As somebody remarked, it was like hell let loose. We were being heavily engaged from both sides of the entrance of La Rochelle, the German force was retreating at high speed and firing on us while we were concentrating on the German ships. The destroyer fired torpedoes at us and just after I had rung down for full speed the ship seemed to lurch and lose speed as if she was aground. The thought crossed my mind [that] to run ashore within easy range of enemy shore batteries hundreds of miles as it were behind the enemy lines was not exactly an enviable position in which to find oneself. I jumped for the chart and confirmed we were still right in the middle of the entrance channel just as the best part of a tonne of water fell on the bridge from the splashes of heavy calibre shells falling near us. Then I saw on the chart a little 6 fathom patch in the middle of the bay. The effect of going over a sudden shallow patch like this at high speed, we must have been doing over 30 knots, has the effect of giving the impression one has come up all standing. The shell flashes from the heavy batteries off the Ile de Ré were impressive just over the height of our top mast and each one threw up probably well over a ton of water. They were quite accurate for range but not good for line. We pressed on as I saw one of our salvos hit the stern of the German destroyer and start a fire, another of the ships was driven ashore and another disappeared. I thought the destroyer had been driven ashore and whether we liked it or not the time had arrived to turn back amid a veritable tornado of shell splashes. It was just as well we did as we ran over the buoy marking the entrance to La Rochelle as we turned. Fortunately our propellers were turning so fast that the moorings of the buoy were cut outright and didn’t get smashed up with the propeller shaft. We withdrew and took another look at the ship on fire off the Les Sables-d’Olonne and counted ourselves perhaps fortunate that we had not been hit by any of the shore batteries. I have always held [that] shore batteries take a long time to hit moving ships and provided one varies one’s speed and course the chances of not being hit are fairly reasonable. Like many other things enemy shore battery fire seemed more accurate and more frightening than it actually was. It was a relief to have Hogg, our navigator, as I had implicit trust in him and felt at the time of the lurch in mid-channel we just could not be ashore. But in complete darkness one is apt to lose one’s sense of orientation and may do unwise things! By now it was showing signs of becoming light so after inspecting the damage caused by our night’s work, we passed Ile d’Yeu where we got our customary salute from the German battery and went to seaward. In making my report I could not be sure that the German destroyer was sunk so classified it as heavily damaged. In the event she was badly damaged but made harbour only to be sunk by Coastal Command strike wing when at anchor off the entrance to the Gironde about ten days later. 311

Whilst one always hopes to make 100 percent success by destroying all enemy ships this is not always achieved. On the whole the action was a success, we found and intercepted the enemy where we had guessed, and I doubt if any other dispositions would have done better. We chanced our arm on some pretty formidable shore batteries and were unscathed, and we pressed our pursuit home to the limit, maybe beyond the limit of prudence. We carried out further patrols right down to the Spanish border for a further two days before returning to Plymouth. August 1944 The Commander-in-Chief Plymouth was delighted with the results and fully endorsed the various actions I had taken. He laughingly characterised the actions to me as a young man’s actions! There was nevertheless a lot to be learned from even such a minor little brush as this. Looking at the waters off the French coasts, much was very shallow and there were innumerable shoals to catch the unwary! Iroquois, the Canadian destroyer, had the latest radar display equipment in the Navy, and not only was it possible to navigate from these displays in the operations room immediately below the bridge, but enemy objects showed up clearly on the display, so in fact one could conduct an action from the confines of the operations room without ever going on to the bridge! This was to a certain extent a revolutionary concept. After all the bridge is always the place where the ‘eye’ of the ship is concentrated and from where action and all force movements are conducted and co-ordinated. The closer I looked at the charts off the Brittany Peninsula, the more I realised it was desirable that light draught ships should always lead in. So I decided if we encountered the enemy we should reverse the procedure for normal action. Namely the destroyers would lead in, and I in Mauritius would follow close behind. Furthermore, in view of the great technical advantage conferred on us by Iroquois’ new radar equipment, her Captain was to conduct affairs from the operations room, keeping me closely in touch by radio telephone with what was happening. This all sounds very ordinary now but was quite revolutionary in concept at that time. The idea of a Captain taking a ship into action not on the bridge was unheard of and considered a most unseamanlike idea. Having decided this, I again emphasised to the Commanding Officers of Ursa and Iroquois how important was a stealthy approach and slow speed most essential for the wash of a cruiser or destroyer even on a dark night can be seen from quite a distance. We sailed again I think on about the 22nd August and after landing some agents and picking up others off Pointe de Penmarch in Audierne Bay, we proceeded on our patrols. Some difficulty was experienced contacting our agents at night with a shaded flashing morse code, as they spoke Breton and our agents mostly French. However, after a measure of mutual suspicion, contact was verified and all went well. A day or so later, we received intelligence information that the enemy intended to pass a force of patrol vessels with personnel on board from Brest to Lorient at night. After looking at tidal conditions, state of the moon and probable hours of most intense darkness, we guessed they would leave Brest probably about 10.00 p.m. for the Pointe du Raz across Audierne Bay and after rounding Pointe de Penmarch make straight for Lorient. The waters were less hazardous in Audierne Bay than 312

further south and so I decided I would if I could catch the force there and attack them from astern so that they would not be able to retreat to Brest. Accordingly, I held off to seaward well out of sight of land and only closed the land again about 20 miles west of Pointe du Raz by about 10.00 p.m. I reckoned the Force could have left Brest by then and sure enough the radar showed up a number of smallish ships approaching Pointe du Raz on a southerly course keeping close inshore. All seemed to be going according to plan, so I slowly closed the Force from astern and from seaward, my plan being to attack when the Force was about halfway across the Bay of Audierne. All went well and we got into our especial attacking formation and silently closed the enemy. In order that none should escape I told them [that] after action was joined the leading destroyer Iroquois must head off those trying to escape eastwards, whilst Ursa must do the same to those who are trying to get away westwards, whilst Mauritius would look after the main body in the centre. It was a still night and when the range was just about 4,000 yards, I opened fire which was the signal for the commencement of the action. Complete surprise had been effected. The Captain of Iroquois stayed in his operations room and gave me all the information I wanted which was well supplemented by our starshell. Hogg watched the chart like a hawk and prevented us running on any of the fairly numerous sandbanks there. I suppose action was joined just after midnight and it was not long before the enemy force was in flames. A few stray shells came our way, the German shore batteries attempted to intervene, but their fire was quite ineffective. We kept a careful track of all seven enemy vessels. I first thought there were six, then eight, but finally came down in favour of seven. This was far from easy as in the fog of battle, it is not always easy to distinguish friend from foe amid the noise of gunfire, the illumination of star shells and the occasional fall of shot from enemy batteries. But perhaps in the heat of battle close inshore like this, one of the biggest hazards is the navigational one, it is only too easy to put one’s ship ashore. I remembered the many skilful actions fought the best part of two centuries ago by Hawke in Quiberon Bay, by Saumarez and by Boscawen and others in the waters which where we were now fighting.24 It was humbling to remember how much easier was one’s task with a steam vessel and modern equipment, than for our forebears whose consummate seamanship brought success in these hazardous waters. I was most anxious we should get 100% success and this I am glad to say we achieved for all seven patrol vessels were sunk in Audierne Bay. Soon after dawn broke, I told Ursa to finish off one ship by torpedo and told Iroquois to send a boarding party on one which had run ashore and was burning. They obtained some secret signal books which were of value. As dawn broke fully one could survey the scene with sunken ships all about us mostly with their masts sticking out, for the water was shallow and I was able to report to C-in-C Plymouth that all enemy vessels had been sunk. 24 The battle of Quiberon Bay, 1759, was a decisive victory in the Seven Years War against France (1756-1763). Admiral Hawke aggressively pursued the French under the Comte de Conflans into the Bay despite not having a pilot for these difficult waters. Thomas Saumarez, from a family which produced several important naval figures, was Captain of the Belliqueux, a 64-gun ship of the line which had been captured by the British the preceding year. 313

The opposition was not stiff, in fact very much the reverse, as I had foreseen the main difficulty was to lay a good plan and catch them and prevent any escaping. The ships company was overjoyed for this was our second success in a week and somewhat different to bombardment support which after a time could be very dull. In due course we returned to Plymouth and got an even warmer welcome from the C-in-C than ever before. He was kind enough to describe the two actions as thoroughly professional jobs of work. He commented on the novel factors of making the destroyer with the modern radar equipment lead in, and said in any event my instruction to authorise the Captain to be off the bridge and in the Operation Room was a wise one, but he doubted whether it would commend itself to some of the more old fashioned and orthodox commanding officers. There was something particularly thrilling fighting actions and patrolling waters where the British Navy certainly for the best part of 600 years have fought innumerable battles with the French. The siege of La Rochelle, Quiberon Bay, to mention only a few of the better known, but what a coast to blockade as we not infrequently did in sailing ships and often on a lee shore. Alas soon after we returned, I got a telegram from Elizabeth to say my nephew David Ackers was reported missing in flying operations over France. I had only seen him the previous May when we had a mild celebration for his 21st birthday. He was as nice and splendid a looking young man as one could find anywhere, and was then a Flying Officer in the RAF, learning to fly the formidable Typhoon aircraft which did such effective work against the German tanks and other armoured formations at Caen and La Falaise. He was shot down by ground fire about the 23rd August somewhere near La Falaise, and is buried at Haras du Buff, Damigny (Orne) France. I enclose a copy of a rather charming note sent by some of the French people of this little village to say his grave is being well cared for. A very great blow to us all. David had the world at his feet. He was in every sense as sound a young Englishman as one could find anywhere. Loved outdoor things, had a great zest for life, good at all games and sports and quite good at work, and above all had a most attractive personality which made him liked by everybody. I felt much for Charles Ackers, who only eight months previously had lost his wife, my sister, and my father was very fond of David. This is the way of war. [typed copy of letter] Haras du Buff Damigny, (Orne) France Feb 21st 1948 War Graves Department, War Ministry, London Sir, We have the satisfaction and great honour to have the grave of a British soldier in the cemetery of our little village of Cui-Ocagne (Orne). Here is what is written on his cross 152.010 - F/O R.D. Ackers R.A.F.(VR) -18.8.1944 Would you be so kind and get me in touch with some of his relatives with whom I could communicate. I suppose his parents, or wife or children would be pleased to know that his grave is well looked after and not abandoned. We go there regularly to bring some flowers, and we made something decent with tiles around his grave. Everybody in the village hopes that this brave soldier will always remain in our village. As he gave his life to defend France as well as England, and he helped for our liberation from the Germans. I would be very grateful if you could give me the address required. I would send a photograph of the grave to Flying Officer Ackers’ relatives, and I would help them my best if ever they came hereover. Your sincerely M.G. d’Ocagne, Haras du Buff, Damigny (Orne), France. I sometimes kick myself I did not encourage him more to do his war service in the Navy to which at one time he had a leaning. But one never knows what would have happened. We as well as the RAF had heavy casualties especially among the young. Charles Ackers took the shock of David’s death most courageously, but he suddenly seemed to have become an old man. And there is never a lot one can do to help and comfort a person in such distress. There is a very nice picture of David Ackers painted from photos at Torill Freeman’s home at Huntley Manor, which gives a striking likeness of him. My father was very sad and said this reminded him of the First World War when he sometimes dreaded to read the casualty list which contained the names of many young men whose fathers were 315

contemporaries of his. These Spheres in the loft with their photos of many of our casualties in this war will always remind one of the sacrifices made then, and again in the last war.25 We were soon off on another patrol with our faithful two destroyers and this time went right down to Santander. But beyond having an occasional shell fired at one by shore batteries there was little sign of movement. The entrance to the Gironde was still well protected and one got the proverbial salute if one ventured too close. In fact, some of these batteries could fire with some accuracy, which was more than could be said of some of the other light batteries one encountered. I noticed a very young and new midshipman of the watch on the bridge was not particularly enjoying the experience of being under fire, but who does for the first time? So I called to him and said ‘prove to me by Euclid that the square of the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle is equal to the sum of the squares of the other two sides’. It took him the best part of half an hour to prove this, by which time he had forgotten all about the anxieties of being under fire and never looked back! I thought we would go and have a look at Ile d’Yeu again and find out if the alert German battery was still on its toes. But when we arrived there, no firing and many flags flying on the island and soon a sailing boat with a stout Frenchman in the stern was seen approaching the ship waving French and British flags. He announced that he was the mayor of Ile d’Yeu and that they had overpowered the German garrison and had put them all in the local jail. He presented us with a bottle of champagne and said he would like a garrison and a military officer to help him. I was a little nonplussed, but we had a French Canadian Sub-Lieutenant in their Volunteer Reserve on board. So I immediately sent him ashore with the Mayor, with a flamboyant screed installing him as the Military Governor of the Ile d’Yeu. Just to give the Admiralty food for thought I sent a signal on the following lines: ‘Be pleased to inform their Lordships that the German Garrison of the Ile d’Yeu has been captured and I have this day installed Sub Lieutenant - - , Royal Canadian Volunteer Reserve as Military Governor of Ile d’Yeu’. I could just see the anxieties of the legal branch of the Admiralty and Foreign Office on receipt of this signal. Maybe they said ‘Shall we inform Ottawa, and on whose authority has the Captain of Mauritius installed this officer as a Military Governor.’ It was much too difficult for the Admiralty and I was not surprised to receive no reply. Maybe the docket discussing the legal aspects of my action is still circulating around the Admiralty or is buried in the legal department archives of the present Ministry of Defence. One of our anxieties was the mining problem for we did not know where the Germans had laid their minefields and so on. We had rather sketchy information and the best one could do was to put oneself in the Germans’ shoes and ask oneself where one would lay mines and then avoid that area. But by early September it became clear there was not more much more to be done in the Biscay area. Accordingly, after filling up with ammunition and fuel, we were directed to proceed to Scapa Flow to join the 10th Cruiser Squadron for further service in Northern waters which probably meant Russian convoys. So we embarked Arctic clothing which was an enormous improvement on what we had at the beginning of the war. 25 The Sphere was an illustrated paper, similar to the Illustrated London News, published 1900-1964. 316

Alas just before leaving Plymouth, I had a letter from Cecil Harcourt saying that I was to be the next Director of Torpedoes and to relieve Tony De Salis. He was sorry for such short notice but the next one nominated, my old friend and best man, Terence Back, had had a severe stroke when Captain of Bermuda and could not take up this job. I protested to the best of my ability. I pointed out that I had not yet been twenty months in command and I reckoned by now I was beginning to get thoroughly to know the cruiser captain’s job, and that above all I was a ‘lucky’ Captain, which to my mind is the first essential for a good sea officer. However it was all to no avail, the new controller, Admiral Wake Walker wanted even more ginger put into the development of anti-submarine equipment and methods, and as the present first rate incumbent in the job Tony de Salis had been promised the battleship Valiant in the Far East, it was time to have a new Director of Torpedo and Mines Whether this appointment was wise or not I do not know. My own metier was perhaps more on the staff side and I believe if Grantham had not been Director of Plans, this would have been where I could serve most effectively. I still had an almost unrivalled knowledge of past strategical policy. But anyway, in war one must just go where one is sent and do one’s best. It was made clear I was expected to accelerate the development of all sorts of anti-submarine, mining, minesweeping equipment and the like. So towards the end of September, I had to be prepared to leave Mauritius. Charles Stanfield, who had spent much time in combined operations and had done a tremendous job largely in training combined operations personnel in assault, was nominated as my relief. By this time our Commander Patrick Brock, shortly to be promoted, had left. A great standby was Patrick and few Captains could want for a better [man as] Commander. Webb relieved him. We got up to Scapa and did some exercises and I took the opportunity of going and seeing Roddy McGrigor, now in command of the First Cruiser Squadron, and we discussed many means of engaging the enemy. He was a first-rate tactician and picked my brains and experience to the limit. He had had some experience himself, but at that time not as much as I had. As quick as a flash, he was a first-rate seaman and it was clear his cruiser squadron would follow him anywhere. Well, the day soon arrived for me to leave. Captain Stanfield came the night before. I was dined in the wardroom and wished all the officers’ good luck. I spoke to the ships company next day and told them we could look back on their service in Mauritius with pride and now had to put in the final burst to finish the war. I went over before I left and had a very friendly talk with the Commander-in-Chief, Harry Moore, and his Chief of Staff my old friend Bill Slayter. They did not envy my going to Admiralty and said even in the Home Command there was a lot of quite a lot of tidying up to be done. They also said the Battle of the Atlantic may yet have some headaches in store for us, what with the ‘snorkel’ fitted submarines, which to a large measure had greatly nullified the value of aircraft in anti-submarine work, the homing torpedoes, the pressure mines and many other striking technical advances, not the least being the German hydrogen peroxide torpedo of greatly increased performance and indeed the projected HP submarine. 317

HMS Mauritius had a wartime It was interesting looking round Scapa Flow again. I thought of the many times I had been complement of 920 men.When there, and that day in September 1917 when as quite a little fellow I joined my first ship WWD left, the cheer the crew gave him must have been heard from a HMS Neptune as a very junior and insignificant midshipman. There were now nets everygood distance! where, and in a sense the berths were almost penned off so that torpedo carrying aircraft would not be able to torpedo ships in the anchorage, as we had so successfully done earlier It is not known when this picture was in the war to the Italian fleet at Taranto. The scenery was much the same as ever. No trees taken, but probably back in the UK. anywhere except perhaps a few at Lyness. The water as clear as ever, one could see the Image courtesy of M. Rawstorne. bottom at three or four fathoms depth and sometimes more. Leaving the ship especially one which has had so much and varied adventure is always a wrench. When I rung off the main engines from the bridge for the last time after exercises two days before I left, I wondered when and where I should go again to sea. There is a certain serenity and timelessness about Scapa Flow. A place that delights the ornithologists for one meets almost every form of sea bird and the formidable skua gulls were always in evidence. The tremendous stretch of water which must be nearly 15 miles across reflecting the sky and that quaint little town of Stromness in the northwest corner has not I suspect altered much in the last 500 years. But the time soon came to leave. 318

My great friend Jock Henderson, the Padre, left with me, for the Bishop of Glasgow had at last prevailed upon the Naval authorities to release him to return to his care at Ayr, where he was a great strength and support to all and everybody in the neighbourhood. We stepped over the side into our motor boat which took us to Lyness from where we went south. The whole ships company turned out and gave us a tremendous send off, as warm a one as I had heard for a long time. One had I suppose built up a sort of rapport with everybody, that the final parting came as a bit of a wrench. My relief Charles Stanfield was a very efficient fellow and an administrator of outstanding ability. But bless his soul just a bit humourless, and I wondered whether he would remember that a good Captain must also have a ‘blind eye’ as well as an ‘all seeing eye’. Perhaps before we returned to the Admiralty it might be worth looking at the maritime side of the War. One as far as possible kept fairly closely in touch with the side which might affect one, and also from some rather good Admiralty circulars, we had some idea of what was happening. In addition, the News Summaries sent out by the Admiralty gave one a fairly general picture of events. Beginning at home, the German U boats had to a certain extent withdrawn, and were being fitted with ‘schnorkel’, the device which allowed a U boat to proceed on the surface as it were. but totally submerged except for a little breathing pipe or schnorkel. This meant they could not, or only with the greatest of difficulty be detected by radar, and could proceed at greater speed through dangerous waters instead of having to be completely submerged and using up their battery power. In August the Home Fleet aircraft carriers had carried out an attack on the German battleship Tirpitz in north Norway, but had not seriously damaged her. Arctic convoys had been resumed. In September, the U boats started an inshore U boat campaign around the British Islands without achieving any very great success. The Army broke out of the Normandy area in August and were racing towards Belgium and Paris which was captured at the end of the month. We had carried out the invasion of the south of France and after brushing aside initial resistance the Allies were racing northwards. It was clear then that the next place the Germans could stop would be in Germany, in what became known as the Siegfried Line. Brussels and Antwerp were captured early in September and in the middle of September the airborne assault on Arnhem was launched. If this had succeeded, it is possible General Montgomery’s prediction that the war could be over by the end of the year would have been realised. But as is told elsewhere, the Supreme Allied Commander preferred to advance on a broad front which inevitably meant a slower and more gradual advance. The advance up Italy was proceeding. Leghorn [Livorno] had been taken in July and the Germans stood to fight in northern Italy in what was known as the Gothic line. The line was assaulted and eventually broken in August when the Allies started to advance towards Austria. In Southeast Asia, the Japanese army had been routed at Imphal, and were being pursued down Burma. The British Pacific Fleet was being built up and Admiral Somerville, after two very frustrating years building it up, was relieved by Admiral Fraser, the late C-in-C of the Home Fleet, and [Somerville] went as head of our mission to Washington where as ever he 319

made a striking impact. Nobody could have been better than James Somerville to deal with the Americans and the harder bitten the Yankee he met, the better he was! Then soon after the invasion of Normandy in June the American Fleet had what I regard as a decisive victory over the Japanese naval forces in the Philippine Sea, for they so crippled the Japanese Fleet Air Arm, that as a fighting force the Japanese Navy was tremendously reduced in strength. The US Navy, carrying out in conjunction with General Macarthur a classic maritime strategy now with vastly superior forces, captured Guam, the Marianas, Saipan and started heavy raids on the Philippines in preparation for landings there to capture the Philippines which were scheduled for October. Meanwhile the Russian summer offensive was launched to coincide with the invasion of Normandy and it was clear by September that the Russians were approaching the Baltic, Hungary and the border of Yugoslavia. To sum up, it was clear victory was in sight and in spite of the V-1s and V-2s, which were of considerable nuisance value, little seemed likely to prevent us achieving an early victory. The Americans were achieving wonderful results in the Pacific and in spite of the enormous distances involved it did not seem as if the Japanese could last for more than a year. For they had not the capacity, as the Americans had, to replace the heavy material and personnel casualties sustained by both sides. We all hoped our strategy would be followed in France and Belgium, but the setback at Arnhem made one guess the war would in fact last into 1945. The Germans made many mistakes in the strategical field, and Hitler’s insistence that every point however unimportant should be defended to the last spelled early disaster for the Germans. One wonders if the Germans had withdrawn from North Africa, Sicily, Italy, the Aegean, Greece, Stalingrad etc. when their military leaders wanted, what would have happened. Would not there have been a real Fortress Germany, and might not the war have lasted many more years with the possibility of a negotiated peace. I asked General Heusinger of the German OKW why Hitler did not allow withdrawals, he merely shrugged his shoulders and said he was pathological against it, and thought most German generals were soft! We heard a little of the attempt on Hitler’s life in July which alas failed. But it was clear as I travelled south to find accommodation and take up my next appointment at the Admiralty that the war was drawing to a close, and that it was clear that a decisive and complete victory was awaiting us, probably within the next six to ten months. Already maritime wise we were looking to the Far East, and against a certain measure of discouragement from Ernie King, the American Chief of Naval Operations, were building up the British Far East Fleet better known as the BPF (British Pacific Fleet). The momentous flow of events about the late summer and early autumn are described vividly in Triumph and Tragedy from Ch. 8 onwards, and apart from extreme emotional feelings engendered by the Russians’ behaviour in refusing to relieve Warsaw, there is little to add in this little diary of events as they struck me at the time.26 26 The Warsaw uprising, August-October 1944, was the attempt by the Poles to liberate Warsaw and control the city before the advancing Soviet Army arrived. The Polish underground ‘Home Army’ seized much of the city but Germany forces counterattacked, while the Soviet Army stood idle in a suburb across the Vistula. The Germans razed the city and deported the remaining inhabitants. By allowing the Germans to 320

The Second Quebec Conference in the early part of September was one of especial importance. It is only fair to record that Winston even then had his doubts about defeating Germany by the end of 1944. But it took a long time on return to Whitehall to pick up the threads, and the modern thinking of the problems which lay ahead of us. It was not so much a question of deciding strategy for that had already been settled before I joined Mauritius, but the problems were really those of priority, and those of how best and with the least expenditure of effort the broad strategy decided on could be implemented. As a digression I don’t think the Planners at that time had fully appreciated the enormous strategical blunders of which Hitler was capable. For instance, they did not always see that Hitler would hold on to everything however extended regardless of the cost until defeated in detail. This he never saw ensured that his final defeat would take place quicker than thought, for he had frittered away what were still the immense military resources of the Reich. On arrival in London there were still the V-1s and V-2s which were quite a flying nuisance, and I think, as by then people’s nerves were a bit more frayed than when I had been there nearly two years ago, these bombs had in fact a more disturbing effect than they needed to have. When one heard the peculiar noise of the V-1 people started looking anxiously at each other. Then if the engine cut out which meant it would soon hit the ground, everybody dived to the floor to avoid broken glass which in its turn inevitably followed the explosion. The worst instance I remember in Whitehall was when the Guards Chapel in Wellington barracks, filled alas to capacity during divine service, was hit and caused a large number of casualties. The V-2s which were the forerunners of the present-day ballistic rocket, were less alarming for one never heard them coming, though in fact their capacity for damage was greater than the V-1s. I looked around for some digs and after finding my old haunts at Nell Gwynne House full up, got some digs in Warwick Square behind Victoria Station where an admirable Irish woman did for one. We had a double room as Elizabeth wanted to join me and as soon as possible, which was shortly after I took over as DTM, I had now to get a grip of an enormous problem, the details and techniques of which I was quite ignorant. I first saw Admiral Wake Walker, who was the Controller, a man of outstanding ability with a fairly quick temper. A cleverer man, and that is saying a lot, than his predecessor Bruce Fraser, he saw the guts and essentials of almost any problem in rapid quick time and used to get impatient with the long winded. He left me in no doubt, admirable and quite first rate as the work of my department had been, he wished the tempo still further accelerated particularly in the development of anti-submarine weapons and detecting devices. The war record of the DTM Department was impressive. They had rapidly discovered the counter to the magnetic mine by degaussing ships. They had developed our own magnetic mine with astounding speed and many methods of sweeping the magnetic as well as the acoustic mine. The aircraft depth charge had been developed, as still the RAF had failed to produce one A/S bomb! Then various anti-submarine weapons such as the forward suppres the uprising, the Soviets allowed them to eliminate any organised resistance to the establishment of Soviet political domination over the country. 321

throwing explosive charges, the ‘squid’ and ‘hedgehog’ were developed. The aircraft torpedo had advanced a little since my days in Courageous in 1932 and 1933, when much of the groundwork had been laid. Simulators for aircraft attack had been developed on the lines of one Charles Thompson and I produced in Courageous for which we were then given an award of £50! It was an enormous Department and though I was the Director, I was the youngest Captain in it. But what a tremendously dedicated team they were, ‘Tin Eye’ Jackson, Maitland Dougall, and many others. Then many clever RNVR officers, many ex-scientists and electrical engineers. Then another section which did the job of rendering mines safe, a well-known barrister, Ashe Lincoln, who is now a QC took a prominent and indeed courageous part in this work. Half the Department was at Bath where much of the material work was done and was under the Deputy Director, who later was my old friend Robin Durnford Slater. Then we had mine research establishments outside Portsmouth, in Cumberland and of course the main torpedo factories at Greenock, Alexandria (Dumbarton), Weymouth and elsewhere. Though the torpedo and A/S branches were not officially amalgamated at that time, we worked together as a team in DTM. We were responsible also [for ensuring] that the Navy’s material for all underwater weapons was sufficient in quantity and adequate in performance, and [for] safety for handling. A very close touch was kept with the Director of Armament Supply whose job it was to see the contracts were placed. I looked at the whole spectrum of problems facing us. I felt in Mines, with the organisation team of brilliant scientists and engineers under Captain Vaughan, as well as the mine sweeping side of it, was right on top of the world, as indeed it was, for we were usually a jump ahead of the Germans. Then on technical intelligence under Maitland Dougal, we were in the van for with his intuitive mind and retentive memory, we sometimes forestalled the Germans’ technical surprises. For instance, the homing acoustic torpedo developed by the Germans and from which much was expected had been guessed by Maitland’s team, with the result [that] the counter, which had taken many months to develop, was issued in quantity to the Navy within a fortnight of the first use by the Germans of their acoustic homing torpedo. The torpedo itself had not made many strides as one had hoped. The Germans had a longer-range torpedo than us with a more powerful explosive head. Furthermore, they had magnetic firing devices on their torpedoes which allowed them to explode under a ship where it was far more vulnerable than against its sides. Depth charges were really a development of the First World War weapons and though these had been developed to the full, it was obviously necessary to have larger charges and weapons which would throw the charge at the submarines, rather than have to manoeuvre the anti-submarine vessel so as to pass over the submarine, and drop its charge on top of its target. The first advance on this was the hedgehog, an ahead-throwing weapon. Then the whole electrical side also came under D.T.M. This was from the days when the torpedo men had to look after and maintain the ship’s electrical equipment. This came under Captain Wickham, another outstandingly able retired officer who worked in close 322 touch with the Director of Electrical Engineering (Hamish Mclaren). All technical training

and the entry of electrical officers came under our ambit. Among many other activities, Jackson dealt with this, and recruited all electrical officers for the Navy. The scope of the responsibilities was great. We were the largest department in the Admiralty and handled more material than any other. Though staffed by many retired officers as well as acting service officers, there was nothing backward looking about them. My predecessors, Tony De Salis, Henry Phillips and others had done much. In technical matters there is always a tendency to jump in too quickly. Development can be oversimplified and so often it is the case of more haste less speed. On the other hand, a classic case is the Squid, our present and most effective anti-submarine weapon. From the time somebody had an idea and started putting it down on paper to the time a German submarine was sunk by the weapon fully developed, tried and tested, was a matter of only 13 months. A remarkable rate of development for a major weapon of war. The number of establishments for which one was responsible were legion. The Royal Naval Torpedo factories at Greenock and Dunbarton, the Royal Naval Torpedo Experimental Establishment at Greenock, [with the testing station] in Loch Long, the A/S experimental establishment at Fairlie, Portland and other places. Then various mining and minesweeping establishments, at Vernon, Brighton, Eastbourne, Devonport, in Cumberland and in the Forth at Port Edgar. Training establishments in Northern Ireland and elsewhere. Then of course the numerous Admiralty scientific research establishments at Teddington, at Malvern, at Cheltenham and many other places, which did work for us and whose progress affected us vitally. A lot of travelling was essential if one was to know what was going on and be in a position to direct progress. Highly qualified scientists and engineers can be ‘prima donnas’ and indeed some were, so it was very much a case of a velvet hand and unlimited persuasion and infinite patience, as a major requirement in leading a team like this. For to the true scientist or perhaps the dedicated researcher, perfection is the only thing worth attaining, so time is of less importance to them, than perhaps to the down-to-earth naval tactical man who has to provide as ever the practical solution the day before yesterday! In the case of Mining and Minesweeping where we had some pretty difficult characters, I solved the problem by putting an eminent mathematician, by name Collingwood, and a direct descendant of the famous Lord Collingwood of Nelson’s era, in charge. He worked wonders, for not only did he invoke the abiding respect of the scientists, he had the pragmatic seaman’s approach of a first-class naval officer to our problems. I was fortunate in having as my immediate boss, the Controller of the Navy, Admiral Wake Walker. Quick as a flash, he never wasted your time nor did he expect to have his time wasted. A very good brain who died in office from a stroke within a year of my taking over. A great loss to the Navy. He was probably the best Controller of the Navy we have had this half century. Wake Walker, despite my lack of experience in technical matters, gave me the widest possible rein and freedom in all matters. I took care always to keep in tune with the general overall policy, for we were stretched to the limit industrially and, unlike the Americans, could not produce everything we wanted until we were wholly satisfied the priorities were right. 323

Though it was sad not to be associated with the strategical running of the war any more, covering the vast scope of technical development and procurement problems kept me at full stretch. I think we got our priorities right in developing new weapons for use underwater. We developed an electrical torpedo, mines and anti-submarine weapons such as the Squid [which] were most successful. Minesweeping equipment with the counters to homing torpedoes were a top priority, for as we advanced we would be using enemy inshore waters more and more. The original torpedo had not been developed as fast as one would have hoped and I got an exceedingly ingenious scientific engineer, by name Burns, to come and join the Torpedo Experimental Establishment at Greenock. He was so full of brilliant ideas that he could never stick to one long enough to get it even to the drawing board stage. Old Captain Richard, a very brilliant if ever modest torpedoman of the Torpedo Experimental Establishment was often driven to exasperation by this. On the whole this was not a success, though I suppose it is true that some of the concepts Burns suggested are now thirty years later gradually being turned into hardware. But it is easy enough to have ideas, what is the difficult job is with known techniques to translate them into practical working propositions, which can be worked at sea under normal conditions by men of average intelligence. I made arrangements to attend the Staff Meetings or be represented there, so that we on the hardware side of the bench could know and be in touch with what the staff and operators were thinking. This in practice saved quite a lot of time as one sensed pretty soon if certain devices were not likely to be of much use, and so could economise valuable development effort on them. Similarly, one could help a lot in defining for the staff what they really wanted. This sounds like putting the cart before the horse, that is not really so! If one knows pretty well what can be produced quickly and in war, speed is the essence, one can then help the staff to frame their requirements having strict regard to practical limitations. It must have been soon after my arrival that I, with a very very few others, were brought into the picture of the development of the atomic bomb. I knew of course from my early studies of physics in Greenwich in the 1920s discussing with our brilliant Professor D. Haig, the implications of Rutherford’s discoveries. But had no idea such gigantic strides had been made so as to make it likely an atomic bomb could be made. One’s mind boggled at the possibilities and our first thought, with what might happen to London, was had the Germans got it? We were assured from our secret intelligence they were a long way behind us. Not the smallest reason being Hitler’s purges of many of the best scientists who were described as ‘non-Aryan’. Dr Niels Bohr, a famous Danish scientist, fortunately escaped and helped in the development of this weapon, which owes much - more probably than to anything else, to the initial work of British scientists.27 It would I think be true to say none of us fully appreciated the tremendous impact atomic bombs would have on warfare. We had to win the war as quickly as possible with conventional weapons before V-2 rockets with atomic warheads would be fired 27 Niels Bohr (1885-1962), Danish theoretical physicist. After the Quebec Agreement of September 1943, most of the British scientists involved in atomic development led by James Chadwick, were moved to Los Alamos where development under Robert Oppenheimer could proceed more rapidly. 324

onto London. This information about atomic development merely emphasised yet again the absolute need of an early victory in the war. Back into the hurly-burly of Whitehall one soon got a general glimpse of what was happening. In October the Americans by their decisive naval victory in the Leyte Gulf [Philippines] when they sank virtually the backbone of the Japanese Fleet, i.e. three giant battleships, four carriers and ten cruisers for the loss of only one carrier and two small carriers and a few other vessels, all hopes of the Japanese surviving total and early defeat disappeared. In October the Allies’ advance up Italy was held at Bologna, whilst the Russians reached the Baltic and advanced into Hungary and Yugoslavia. Early in November after many attempts the battleship Tirpitz was sunk near Tromso, by a number of Lancaster bombers carrying 12,000-pound special bombs. This cleared our northern flank from surface ship threats. But soon after our failure at Arnhem, it became clear we should not be able to thrust deep into Germany for the Germans had fortified themselves on the Rhine, and it would not be till the following spring that victory could be expected on land. About this time there was a lull in U boat activities though the laying of Oyster mines was causing us trouble for even now a wholly satisfactory counter to this mine has yet to be discovered. After spending a little time in our room at Warwick Square we started looking round, or to be more accurate, Elizabeth started looking and we found a nice little modern house in Merstham called ‘Greenacre’, which was situated at the end of the Rockshaw Road, belonging to Colonel O’Donnell, who was among other things one of the chief Army Censors at the War Office. I think alas his marriage had come apart, as he now lived in London and his wife elsewhere. Greenacre was a very nice modern red brick house which we got at, I think, the modest furnished rental of 8 guineas a week. A pleasant garden with a hard tennis court and right in the country just under the Chaldon Ridge along which passed the Old Pilgrim’s Way. The house stood back from the road and had what they call all the ‘mod cons’. It The family at Merstham had been built by the O’Donnells in the 1930s with a pleasing coloured brick, and about one and a quarter acres of garden. The station nearby, about 1 ¼ miles distant was Merstham, which was on the main Brighton, Croydon, London Line, so we had a good service up and down to London. My trains as a rule went to Charing Cross which was a few minutes from the Admiralty. There was a day school in Merstham which Georgina and Johnny attended and we were clear of all ‘military targets’, so in spite of very occasional bombing raids on London we were never disturbed, though one of the governesses-cum-mother’s help we had, sometimes used to tell me she was kept awake at night by German bombers prowling around. We got my old Vauxhall car down from Mulgrave where it had been stored for the war, and though there was still very strict petrol rationing, I think two to four gallons a month, we 325

could use it very occasionally. I brought down Oswald’s bicycle which had done such yeoman service earlier in the war in London, and used to get to and from the station on it. We soon made friends with a lot of pleasant neighbours, the Caves, Watneys, Mrs Kohn Speyer, and many others who made us very welcome in what was to us a new neighbourhood. Rationing of all sorts was very strict and it was not easy to get even clothes in sufficient quantity or quality. I wore uniform the whole time, and that not only wore well, but was not rationed, so with one’s store of pre-war plain clothes, I was adequately placed. But I think clothes rationing hit the women more than men, for their clothes were not intended or designed to last for decades like ours are! But to look again at the naval situation in the autumn of 1944. It was very much one’s duty to put as it were blinkers on and to concentrate on producing the material required to deal with the latest type of U boat threat. This required tremendous imagination and drive for the Battle of the Atlantic was in a sense a battle for technical superiority. We had made great advances with the ahead-throwing weapons known as Hedgehog and Squid. We introduced things called ‘Sonobuoys’ whose purpose was to listen underwater for submarine noises and signal them to ships and aircraft patrolling for submarines. Then special mines were designed and laid to trap enemy submarines and the not insubstantial list of German submarine losses from this cause testifies to their effectiveness. Ships were fitted with many acoustic listening devices. A homing acoustic torpedo which homed onto a submarine was developed and used with some success. For instance, this could be carried by aircraft who would drop it in the vicinity of a submarine and would hope it would then seek out and home on to the submarine until it hit and destroyed it. But the Germans had not been idle. They had recalled their boats to Norway, and German ports were fitting them with ‘schnorkel’ previously described, which to a large extent nullified the effectiveness of aircraft against them. Then Dr. Walther had not only produced the hydrogen peroxide torpedo but also the hydrogen peroxide submarine.28 This was in every sense a revolutionary advance for it would turn the submarine from being a submersible like a whale which must come up to breathe and charge its batteries, into a true submarine which could operate and remain submerged more or less indefinitely, for it carried as it were its own oxygen with it in the HP fuel. Then great advances had been made in the streamlined design of U boats known as Types 21 and 23. These were prefabricated and with their new enormously powerful batteries were capable of speeds of up to 17 knots submerged, which, when compared to the five or six knots submerged of the traditional submarine, clearly revolutionised the problem in favour of the submarine. Fortunately, due to delays and poor organisation on the Germans’ part, and increasing effect of our bomber raids, a fully sophisticated hydrogen peroxide U boat never took part in this war. The Germans altered their tactics and sent their U boats close inshore round the British Isles where they received a tremendous hammering from our escort vessels. 28 Hellmuth Walther (1900-1980), German engineer and entrepreneur. After WWII he worked with the Royal Navy until emigrating to the USA in 1950. 326

Their new U boats could also submerge to greater depths than before and so be immune to orthodox depth charges. The Admiralty took a grave view of the turn of events and warned the Defence Committee that we might be in for a very very difficult time in the early part of 1945 with the new type U boats and new tactics. Our intelligence of German developments and thoughts was good, possibly so good that whilst knowing what the Germans intended, we did not fully appreciate the enormous difficulties they were experiencing in bringing their wishes and intentions to fruition. However, our job in DTM was to press ahead with all possible material means of anti-submarine war. The Asdic (underwater echo detection) device had done as well at the outset of the war as could be expected, but to continue to be effective far far greater range of detection was now required. I remember attending many conferences with eminent scientists on this subject, most of whom poured cold water on the prospects of effecting much improvement. I remember at one meeting counting over a dozen Fellows of the Royal Society round Wake Walker’s conference table. Actually, I believe what they wanted and needed was a clearer definition of the problem, and this is the job of the Sea Officer whose definitions have to be frequently revised and checked. Eventually by greatly increasing the power input to the Asdic oscillator and lowering the frequency of oscillation, quite staggering improvements were effected. But this is leaping ahead too fast, for these developments did not reach a practical stage until well after the end of the war. However, the researches were put in hand and will continue to help us keep abreast in the modern technical stages of anti-submarine warfare. In wartime it is always well to remember whilst the rate of scientific development is vastly increased, it takes time to translate them into practical and tested hardware. So often one has to back short-term advantages, perhaps slowing down more long-term development. This is where the Sea Officer and especially the Torpedo and Anti-Submarine trained specialist is of such value. For he can probably guess as well as anybody how long a gleam in the scientist’s eye will take to produce a new and effective anti-submarine system which will soon be destroying submarines! I met quite a number of US Naval officers interested and concerned with these problems. At that stage they were technically quite a way behind us, but were coming on fast, though even when I retired some ten years ago I doubt whether in A/S warfare they had fully caught up with our developments. The esprit de corps of the Department of Torpedoes and Mining was tremendous and we had as able and imaginative set of officers as anybody could want anywhere. Some of the retired Commanders such as Jackson, Maitland Dougal, Wickham, and a host of others who came back as Captains and were my Assistant Directors, proved to be exceptional. And one wonders how much the Service missed by not promoting these officers when they were on the active list. 327

The Navy has always suffered a very heavy wastage in officers, in passed over Lieutenant Commanders and Commanders. It is only in war one realises what one has missed. I had close relationships with people like the Director of Armament Supplies, the Director of Mining, the Director of Ordnance, the Director of Electrical engineering, and so on. Wake Walker who once said to me, ‘It is only in war that great organisational changes can be made.’ He added, ‘because people are so busy winning the war that they have not time to obstruct just for obstruction’s sake!’ So he suggested we should set about combining the torpedo and anti-submarine branches of the Navy and setting up a separate electrical branch in the Navy which heretofore had come under the Torpedo branch. This was an idea very close to my heart. In the days before the War, one had always thought this should be done. But then perhaps the entrenched interests with strictly departmental outlooks were too strong to allow change to be brought about. We welcomed this idea and set up was what was known as the ‘Middleton Committee’, presided over by Admiral Middleton, a past director of Torpedoes and Mining with my old friend Terence Back, who was recovering from his stroke, to help him. They produced a masterly report which rapidly was given approval, so steps could be put in hand to implement the recommendation before peace set in. This was a revolutionary organisational change which has brought lasting benefit to the Service. Terrence Back told me one day this had nearly killed him, but instead saved him and made him realise his severe stroke had not deprived him of being some use to his service and to his country. But he said the willpower required to make his brain work again was tremendous. But he succeeded and lived until 1969 in as splendid heart as ever doing useful work for the whole of his life. I met again up again with old Sir Kenneth Lee who had some important job in the Ministry of Supply. He was most welcoming, and Elizabeth and I called on our bicycles one weekend and paid a visit at his lovely home Lukyns, near Ewhurst. It was when spending a day with him we heard of the German thrust in the Ardennes designed to separate the British and American Armies. It looked pretty serious at one time, but Montgomery’s confident dispatches certainly restored confidence and this, allied to the determination and toughness of the American units isolated in the German thrust, brought the situation under complete control within ten days of the attack which was well planned and well-conceived. I often wondered why instead of putting his all as it were in this thrust Hitler did not detach greater forces to halt the Russians who were advancing remorselessly towards Berlin. The winter of 1944/45 was the cold one and with an allowance of I think one, or it may have been two cwt. of coal, we kept the windows tightly closed. My father paid us a few visits and came up to London once or twice. Though still in good heart, he was looking a lot older and thinner. Wartime rationing for single people was pretty hard. However, he kept away at his diary and it is worthwhile some day for you to read through this to catch his thoughts. He was a good 79, and walked a lot with his big black Labrador, Ranter. I was glad that he no longer was the main air raid warden as with slightly increasing deafness he did not always hear the telephone call to warn him of an air raid alert. 328

Oswald was back, and at Mulgrave.29 His time in Germany in various prison camps and hospitals had taken a lot more out of him mentally and physically than one perhaps realised at the time. He no longer was the happy carefree young man, always ready for a joke or prank who we knew before the war. Lady Normanby was in as good spirits as ever, but it was clear she was ageing quickly. After all, 74 to 75 is a good age, and she had her full share of anxieties in the war years. My sister-in-law, Katharine was still working in a factory in the Midlands which made some sort of munitions, but I never discovered what! Travelling was not as comfortable as it might have been but I usually got a sleeper for my numerous journeys up to Scotland and the North Country, and there was usually a service car available to fetch one from the station to one’s destination. A journey to Scotland usually enabled me to bring back some herrings and eggs which seemed to be in much more plentiful supply up there than in England. December saw the Germans Ardenne offensive halted which alas produced a certain amount of bickering between the American Generals and the British Generals engaged in this sector. Monty was not always wise in what he said at his press conferences, however true it was! Oswald Normanby returning to The German U boat campaign round our coastal waters was stepped up in December. My Britain. From Katharine Phipps old ship Mauritius was in action against German destroyers in the North Sea but could not cuttings album. catch them though they inflicted a certain amount of damage before breaking off the action. The destroyers took refuge in one of the numerous fiords of Norway. I had thought this problem out beforehand as a contingency and I think under certain circumstances I should have chanced my arm, brushed aside the German shore batteries which were never very effective, and pursued the destroyers right into the fjord and overwhelmed them with our superior gunfire. But then if I had done this and was not in an Admiralty office, I might not be here sitting in our loft at Coglan writing my memoirs. But I think in naval warfare, as in most other, the boldest course usually pays! It was in the autumn I think of this year that I saw in the Gazette I had been awarded the Distinguished Service Order, for service in the Salerno campaign and a Bar to this for the two actions in August off the French coast. Very pleasing indeed and gave one quite a fillip, especially as the Honours and Awards Committee had been very selective in recommending awards and there was no cheapening of these awards as in World War One, rather than reverse. In addition to this there were other awards made as a result of my recommendations. 29 Oswald Normanby had been repatriated in October 1943 after over three years in captivity, during which he devoted himself to helping blinded prisoners-of-war, including teaching them Braille. He accompanied the repatriated soldiers to St. Dunstan’s School for Blind Servicemen before returning to Mulgrave. 329

As far as I remember, they were as follows: - Captain Coke RM - DSC (Captain of Marines) Lt. Com. Hogg - bar to DSC Reverend Henderson - DSC Bandmaster in charge of gunnery transmitting station – DSC CPO Dawson - BEM and mentions in dispatches:- self - three times30 Commander Brock Lieutenant Commander Saville Lieutenant Commander Mosley Lieutenant Commander Thomas Commander (E) Vickery Lieutenant Commander Bayley and some senior ratings. These were awarded as a result of our active service in the Mediterranean, on the Normandy Coast, and in action with the enemy off the Brittany Coast. I went to an investiture at Buckingham Palace early in the new year with Elizabeth and my father. They were both simply delighted and I had quite a good talk with the King about my experiences in the Mediterranean and off the coast of France. He thoroughly enjoyed it when I told him I was sometimes mighty scared but only consoled myself that the Germans were even more scared than I was! I had met him once before the war, then again when he visited the Home Fleet in the early part of the War, and quite a number of times later when I was Chief of Staff, Home Fleet, and later Naval Secretary, right up to his death. We then went off after the investiture and had a pleasant lunch together at my club. Awards for gallantry, for outstanding service and medals for service are great morale raisers, and from time immemorial have played a valuable part in keeping up a nation’s fighting spirit. On the whole I think we struck a happy mean, though maybe we should have awarded a few more to ratings. Of all the awards, the Victoria Cross and the George Cross stand out in a class by themselves for these are only awarded in most exceptional cases for supreme gallantry, and it is fair to say that the standard required in World War Two for these awards was higher than ever before. It was a considerable part of our duty in DTM to make recommendations for George Crosses and George Medals, for some very very gallant acts were done in diffusing mines, bombs and similar other weapons, which had every type of booby trap designed to destroy the person who was endeavouring to render the weapon safe and find out how it worked! Alas, we suffered quite a number of casualties from this cause. It is much more cold-blooded than in battle, settling down quietly with a new weapon and trying to figure out how it works, where there are booby traps and how to make it safe. 30 See following page. WWD received 4 mentions in dispatches in total. 330

We had a mine and bomb safety section in DTM who were permanently on call and who were always available for ‘rendering safe’ work. The Distinguished Service Order took quite a bit of earning and I know of no case where this award was lightly earned. Subsequent Bars to it were equivalent to the award of another DSO. I was very lucky to have joined that small band of a few dozen naval officers who had earned more than one DSO. Similarly, the Distinguished Service Cross, an order usually given to officers having Commander rank and below was much prized, and though easier perhaps to earn than the DSO was never awarded lightly or easily. Then the various Orders of the British Empire, BEM, MBE, OBE, CBE and KBE were awarded for signal service, not necessarily with the enemy, though a number were awarded when the recipient might have received the DSC or DSO. The CB was occasion occasionally awarded for very fine work commanding a force in action, as also were KCB and KBE which was usually reserved for Commanders of considerable forces engaged in action with the enemy. In the Navy so much perforce depends on the Captain that it is he who is usually decorated in the event of especially successful actions. The Central Service and Honours Committee did a very good job reducing where necessary, sorting out and ensuring that the standard of award was kept high, and that those facing the greatest dangers had priority of consideration. I was very lucky in the war and was recommended for decorations on the following occasions: 1 - for Service in HMS Hood 2 - for attack and invasion of Sicily 3 - for attack and invasion of Italy at Salerno 4 - for attack at Anzio on the West coast of Italy 5 - for 2 actions against German naval forces off the coast of France in August 1944 6 - for service as Deputy Director of Plans and a mention in dispatches for invasion of Normandy. In practice I was awarded DSO for Salerno attacks and a Bar for two naval actions off the French coast, and four mentions in despatches for service in Hood, for invasion of Sicily, for service off Anzio, and for invasion of Normandy. The fine work of Plans Division in the war was rightly recognised by the award of CB to the Director, Charles Lambe, when he was relieved by Grantham in 1944. Few people can have earned the CB more fully than Charles Lambe. December 1944 We spent Christmas up at Mulgrave and what a happy one it was. Johnny and Georgina were giving their various governesses a pretty severe testing out. Johnny was the worst, while Anne Sophia was coming along lustily and was not to be left out! As I think I’ve already mentioned, there were at Mulgrave quite a lot of WAAFS and a few odd WRNS who were employed on watchkeeping duties at the early raid warning stations in the neighbourhood. 331

By the end of the year, I had grasped the extent of one’s responsibilities in DTM and pressed on with certain changes and developments and I hope done a little to keep everybody’s morale up.Visits to outlying stations and giving a talk to the wardroom, and on occasion the ships company was not only great fun, but also I think did quite a measure of good, as it made folk feel they were very much in the picture. One wondered sometimes and hoped this wonderful spirit one met at all sides, whether on the factory floor or among sailors, would carry on when peace came again, and the quite staggering job of reconstructing the nation’s life had to be undertaken. During this part of the war, we were largely financed on Lend Lease, perhaps the most statesmanlike and indeed generous measure ever undertaken by the United States Government. For this we had much to thank President Roosevelt. It could be said it was only common sense for if we had not had it, we should have had to curtail vastly our war effort in order to balance our budget! Nevertheless, Lease Lend and later after the war, the Marshall Plan were measures of great statesmanship which have done an immense amount to preserve western civilization. As one walked around in DTM the closer one was brought into touch with the scientists and the more it came clear to me what we really required above all were practical scientific engineers, who could translate the discoveries of science into practical hardware. We had many basic research scientists, probably as fine and clever a team of men as one could expect to find anywhere, and we had altogether some of the cleverest analytical scientific minds as to be found anywhere. But we were short in the brilliant practical scientific engineer who could make an idea work. In this respect I found the Americans were ahead of us, for in their training at places like the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, they produced some of the most brilliant scientific pieces of practical engineering to be found. For instance, the US anti-aircraft control system for gunfire was infinitely better than ours. There were many issues on which one was called to exercise one’s technical judgement. This is not easy for one had only a pretty sketchy background of engineering knowledge. On the other hand, without being clouded by the engineering desiderata of every problem, one had quite sufficient knowledge to see the background of the problem. But I felt on surer ground on strategic problems - perhaps it was because one had spent so much time in the last ten years on strategical and practical problems, and perhaps little on technical problems. One had to rely in technical matters on experts more so than in other spheres. The thing really was to choose one’s expert. On the other hand, bad technical judgement can have long and lasting repercussions of an unfortunate kind. In anti-submarine warfare, in detecting devices and weapons we led the world. In torpedoes we had not put sufficient research and development effort into torpedoes and their explosives with the result that our weapons, good as they were, should have been a good deal more lethal than they were. In mines and minesweeping equipment we were neck and neck with the Germans, and we owed much to our technical intelligence staff who at times put us ahead of all others. Departmentally I suppose the morale of the Torpedo Department had never been higher for the weapons and devices we had produced in the days of peace and their methods of use were vindicated and correct with startling regularity. The same could not be said of gunnery anti-aircraft 332

equipment which fell far far short in performance of the estimates of the pre-war gunnery enthusiast. On the other hand, low angle armament had fully justified the high opinion prewar gunnery enthusiasts have placed upon it. Nobody could doubt that much of the success that Torpedo Department had in technical spheres was in no small measure due to the work and faith of those who served in responsible technical posts between the wars. There was hardly an instance one could say, ‘if only we had taken another technical course in say the 1920s, we should not be in the mess we are now in’. The same could not be said of gunnery anti-aircraft equipment between the wars, where an inability to face up to the technical magnitude of the problem resulted in far larger losses of HM ships from aircraft attacks that need have been the case. January 1945 The New Year dawned without war being ended. The Germans had been driven from the Ardennes salient, the Americans had landed on the Philippines, Akyab [Sittwe, Myanmar] was captured, and the advance down Burma started. The civil war in Greece ended in no small measure due to Winston Churchill’s intervention for if we had not taken firm action then the main Russian base in the Mediterranean would now be Athens! Our advance in Italy had definitely been blocked. The Russians captured Budapest. As we now know it was clear to all thinking Germans that the war had been lost irretrievably, but with Hitler becoming more and more of a megalomaniac there was no chance of a swing for peace before Berlin was captured. Recollection of how the Germans said after the First War, that they had been stabbed in the back by the communists and the German Army was never defeated still lingered on in people’s minds, and it was clear the absolute and final defeat of the German Army in the field was necessary. It was a cold winter and by now London was getting very dirty. Rationing was strict and one had little chance to put on any weight. I weighed a bit under 10 stone at the time, and did not really start to pick up until a few years after the war. Our little house at Greenacre was enormous fun. We had two Khaki Campbell ducks which regularly laid eggs for the benefit of all of us. I usually spent a couple of days each week travelling and got to know the sleepers up to Glasgow and Edinburgh pretty well. They still were kept in pretty good trim. Then one day a week at Bath with an occasional night spent there with Robin Durford Slater to discuss the many problems which we had. I must confess having one’s department split in two is a disadvantage, but in spite of suggestions it was absolutely essential to keep the main executive side in London, and for the Director to be able to walk down the corridor anytime he liked to see the Controller. The famous Yalta Conference took place in February of the year. It is vividly described in Winston Churchills ‘Triumph and Tragedy’ for then it was clear to us that the Russians were not to be trusted, and had not the least intention of peaceful coexistence with the present Allies after the war. This became increasingly clearer as time passed. The Russians went back on their agreement about Poland, and finally, as the story of the Potsdam Conference after the war is told, it became abundantly clear that there can be little hope of honest cooperation with the Russians. 333

But can an authoritarian regime dominated by Marxist and Leninist principles and rigid to a degree ever understand and trust a highly civilised and democratic system of government as ours or the Americans? Were we not expecting too much? There was no sentiment whatever about the Russians, no sense of gratitude, no chivalry. I think at the time many of us fell into the trap as did President Roosevelt in thinking that basically they, the Russians, were the same as us, and provided we talked openly and frankly all difficulties would be resolved, and the East and West would move forward together in harmony. We launched our offensive in Europe in March and after stiff fighting were soon across the Rhine. Towards the end of March, the Russians continuing their advance captured Danzig [Gdansk], whilst in the Far East Mandalay was captured, and the British Pacific Fleet, as an integral part now of the US Pacific Fleet, started operations against the Ryuku Islands, where our fleet first experienced the suicide bombers then being employed by the Japanese. These bombers were light single-seater aircraft whose pilot deliberately committed suicide by crashing into the deck of an aircraft carrier or warship with his bomb load, which exploded on impact and did quite a lot of damage. It was clear by the beginning of April the end could not be many weeks away. The German Army as a cohesive fighting force had virtually collapsed. We captured Bremen, the Russians captured Vienna and during the month Russian and American forces met on the Elbe. President Roosevelt died suddenly but not unexpectedly on the 12th April. We had heard many rumours of his failing health and it was indeed sad that he should have died within a few weeks of the end of the German war. Quite an unknown man, Mr Truman, took his place and proved a stalwart of the first order. If Roosevelt had lived on, I don’t think he would have shaped events much different to what occurred. I think he realised he had in a sense been hoodwinked by Stalin, and if his health had kept up, it is possible he would have taken a stronger or perhaps more effective line with the Russians. But this is pure speculation. Truman with great humility shouldered the leadership of the most powerful nation on earth with right good effect. But at the time we did not know Truman, and with a slight feeling of misgiving and remembering the stories of President Wilson after World War One, I just hoped it would turn out for the best. By this time both V-1s and V-2s had ceased being a nuisance, and in fact with the capture of the rocket and launching sites in Holland this threat ceased altogether. I took the opportunity of flying over to Holland to see some of the torpedo equipment captured from the Germans. I immediately noticed that many of the children and grown-up people were suffering from starvation, distended stomachs and listless expressions on their faces.31 Though one only saw events from the staff side, as an onlooker one hoped greatly that we should be allowed to go and capture Berlin, but this was not to be, for it had been agreed beforehand, when there was some doubt of the ability of Eisenhower’s forces to get there in time, for this plum to fall to the Russians. It was clear the Germans were collapsing. No success attended the U Boat inshore campaign round the UK, in fact they were suffering very heavy losses with no commensurate prizes. The German command in Italy surrendered at the end of the month, and the news of 31 The Germans had stripped Holland of everything as they retreated, leaving the population in dire need. 334

Hitler’s death, probably suicide, came through early in May. Actually, it was the 30th April that Hitler and Goebbels committed suicide in the Bunker which was their headquarters in Berlin. The Russians captured it within a day or two, so it cannot be said either of these two evil men were hasty in taking their own lives. Then on the 7th May, the German Army signed the terms of unconditional surrender and 8th May was VE [Victory Europe] day. It is hard sometimes to recapture one’s feelings. One felt first that we must finish the other war, the one with Japan, which we thought then might take nine months or so; perhaps being far from being some scene of fighting, we in London had not fully appreciated the staggering blows delivered on the Japanese by American forces and indeed also by our own forces in Burma. One thought immediately, I think, ‘Can we this time fashion an instrument better and more effective than the old League of Nations which can preserve a reasonably fair peace, and allow our children to grow up and live reasonably peaceful and fruitful lives?’ Then another thought crossed one’s mind, ‘Can our own country which had borne the brunt of the war, ever recover itself economically to be of some substance in the post war world’.
