The figures of our indebtedness internal and external made frightening reading. I suppose we were, after over five years of war caught up in the war psychosis, everything had to be done straight away, there was no time for long term planning and cool thought and so on. One cannot suddenly slow down and put as it were quite a different thinking cap on. We had misgivings about the Russians but the main run of public thought they would be our friends forever, and though it is true to say the wiser Labour statesman like Attlee and Bevin had little illusion about Russian policy. I suppose one of our principal thoughts was when would rationing and many war time restrictions be relaxed. Again, with the knowledge one had at Whitehall, one had to realise the answer to this was ‘not for a very long time yet’. We had spent all our capital and we were in sense fighting the war on an overdraft guaranteed by America! I suppose at the bottom of it all was relief. We knew anyway our families would not become war casualties. Though the lighting went up in London on the 8th May and there was quite a lot of celebrations, I don’t remember any spontaneous celebrations such as are described on Armistice Day 1918. I don’t even remember where I spent VE evening. I rather think at home at Merstham, though Elizabeth and I did see some of the crowds gather round Buckingham Palace during the day. I got all the Departmental staff together in the Admiralty and thanked them and drank their health in some concoctions produced from I know not where! What a good crowd they were, the girls in the office, the grossly overloaded ‘clerical officers’ of the Admiralty who went about their duty with a devotion which was the envy of all. My father was truly delighted and felt he had in his 80th year done his job and pulled his full weight in this last war. There was an immense amount of work to be done in DTM, for we had the war against Japan to prosecute and then had to consider running down ourselves. We had the Middleton report on setting up the new Electrical Department of the Navy, and new Torpedo Anti- 335

Submarine branch which had absorbed the old Torpedo branch and the newer Anti-Submarine branch. It would soon be necessary to start counting the cost and it was clear some of the scientists could soon be released to return to their professions. And then the staggering problem of starting up industry again would have to be faced. Much planning and much thought had been given to this and the plan for demobilisation. Whilst much of the Navy would be required for the Japanese war, the same was not true with the Army and Air Force. On the other hand, substantial peacekeeping forces would be required in Europe for a long time yet. The plans drawn up by the Cabinet Secretariat for the transition to peace would now have to be taken out of their folders and used as a basis for action. My first reaction was to get over to Eckenförde, the German torpedo experimental station not far from Kiel, and capture as much as we could about the new Walther H.P. torpedoes and submarines. We had already flown in an occupying party to Kiel under Admiral Baillie Grenham with my old friend Brock as his Flag Captain. So I got into my Dakota which I had with ground staff on permanent loan from the Americans, and flew over to Kiel with a Jeep in the back of the Dakota as no land transport was available. Kiel had been laid flat by American fortress bombers a few days previously before the Germans surrendered, and there were still quite a number of dead who had not been removed lying about which made walking distasteful. The Naval Headquarters were in a ship captured from the Germans which had been their HQ, so was very comfortably fitted out. I went straight with my staff to the experimental station at Eckenförde, and we captured a lot of exceptionally useful equipment. I then commandeered a German trawler and told an RNVR Sub Lieutenant to steam it back to HMS Vernon at Portsmouth with all our specimens on board. He said he had never commanded a ship before, but I told him this was his chance and if he blew himself up it would probably be his fault. He laughed and took on the job and after some adventures the trawler arrived safely at Vernon in Portsmouth. The big slide ruler I have at home is part of the ‘loot’ in I picked up at Eckenförde. I think the original owner had been using it right up to the time he thought he should run for it, as his calculations were all written out alongside the slide rule which he had evidently been using up to the last minute. Kiel was in a dreadful mess as was also some of the surrounding countryside, but I was surprised to see silk stockings, nylon stockings and the like could easily be obtained on the black market which came into being without delay! Food was not in short supply, and it was clear the Germans were feeding much better than our people. It is true rationing of food and goods in Germany during the war was far less severe than in England, an odd state of affairs when we had command of the sea. On the other hand, we were far far more efficiently organised for war and every possible thing was devoted to the war effort and none to luxuries and the like. In other words, [in terms of] per head war output, no nation in the world, either enemy or allied, approached our standard. It was clear a conference should be held as soon as possible to start sorting out what to do with Germany and the future of Europe. This became known as the Potsdam Conference which was convened in Berlin and started its deliberations in July. Meanwhile the war in the 336

Far East was going well - the Japanese forces at Sittang [Myanmar] were destroyed, the Americans were about to capture Okinawa and the heavy carrier raids on the mainland of Japan were also starting. Meanwhile at home the question was, should we or should we not have a general election? I’m sure all of us hoped that the Coalition would continue, and that we should not be plunged into party politics until after the Japanese war was over. But it was not to be. Chapter 35 of Winston Churchill’s Triumph and Tragedy tells the story fairly and clearly. Though some of the Labour statesmen wished to continue the Coalition, it was clear the majority wanted an election. The Prime Minister tendered his resignation on the 23rd May. Polling was to be on the 5 July but votes could not be counted until the 26th July when all the votes of the fighting forces had been collected. Winston Churchill formed a caretaker government on the 25 May, with that rather strange character Brendan Bracken, his one-time Parliamentary Private Secretary, as First Lord of the Admiralty. The start of the Potsdam Conference took place in Berlin on the 17th July with Attlee present in addition to Winston Churchill, as who was to know who would be the Prime Minister after the votes had been counted. Electioneering at this junction seemed distasteful and one of Winston Churchill’s own speeches where he likened the authoritarian regime of doctrinaire socialism to the Gestapo, did not go down at all well and must have lost him many votes. I remember hearing this when staying for a few days with old Kenneth Lee at Lukyns and we both looked at each other and said, ‘what an unfortunate thing to say’. As July drew on it became clear the next step was the invasion proper Japan for which gigantic steps had already been put in hand. However, on the 6th August an atomic bomb was dropped on Hiroshima. Nobody knew about this beforehand though I had heard that the test in the Nevada desert of atomic bombs about six months previously had been successful. The effect I think on the public was one of mystification. People had heard of the ‘splitting of the atom’ but nobody had a clue, so well was the secret kept that this had been developed into an atomic bomb. The Russians declared war on Japan two days later and made rapid advances in Manchuria and in parts of China occupied by the Japanese. Then a day later another atomic bomb was dropped on Nagasaki and virtually wiped out a large part of the town. The newspapers were full of horrific stories, many of which were true of the effect of atomic bombs, and it was not surprising to hear on the 14th August Japan had surrendered, and 15th August was VJ Day, which I think was rather a gayer day in London than VE day for people had just begun to learn to relax. Looking at the Japanese war, it was clear they were completely beaten before the first atomic bomb was dropped. It can and will be argued for generations whether or not it was right to drop this terrible weapon on the Japanese when it did. It is clear that the invasion of Japan might well have cost over a million lives, and that Japan would be so destroyed that the Japanese people would and might well be driven to mass suicide. It is a pity we 337

made any bargain with the Russians [for them] to enter the war against Japan. But this is plain hindsight as when we did we were not 100 percent certain that the atomic bomb would work. But before this happened the ballot boxes were counted on the 26th July and to most people’s surprise and certainly mine, the Labour Party were swept to power and the Conservatives utterly defeated. I thought as did most people the Conservatives would get in with a considerably reduced but comfortable majority. I was in Greenock at the time sorting out some political problems at the Royal Naval Torpedo Factory. I was certainly shocked, as the results started to come through. But I wonder looking back on it all was this such a bad thing. There is little doubt political views had moved to the left a lot during the war. In a sense Monty’s democratic generalship hadbeen very successful. But people wondered by and large if Winston was the man to win the peace and with his pre-war record behind him there was good reason for doubt. But what a shock and set-back for the greatest Englishman of this century. Winston describes vividly his feelings in the last chapter of Triumph and Tragedy, and he quotes in full his last dignified message to the nation on laying down his office. It was however an opportunity which Stalin did not miss, for with a new man in the shape of Truman at Potsdam and no formidable assailants like Churchill to oppose him, he had his way and laid the foundation for many injustices in Europe which one day will have to be rectified. On VJ [Victory Japan] Day, Elizabeth and I went to a celebration at Admiralty House, but somehow it left a sour taste in our mouths because Winston was not there, and the many little men just come to power were busy congratulating themselves. It was indeed sad on VJ Day that the main architect of victory, as he undoubtedly was, could not be present to celebrate the nation’s success. From now on what seemed to us petty political considerations would carry greater weight than in the greater days which were just behind us. One had the feeling of having been uplifted and now cast down. August 1945 My father’s 80th birthday was on the 23rd August, so we decided to have a little family celebration to mark it. My brother was there, as indeed were all father’s surviving brothers and sisters. Aunt Addie, an excellent 82 or 83 with a tremendous wide black hat, with her hair as always flowing and a bit untidy. Her daughter Angela came to look after her. Then old Uncle Jim, still in good heart and had made a living with leather businesses during the war. Still good looking and with his great charm of manner. Then old Uncle George, a gigantic figure whose girth did not decrease with the passage of years. His son Stringer Davis, with his wife Margaret Rutherford, the famous actress whom he had recently married. We mustered as it were at Greenacre in the morning and how they all talked and how delighted they were to see Walter, my father, whom I suspect was their favourite brother. It was a real family reunion and I remember now hearing them talk of the times and fun they all had at Wellclose [Brockworth, Glos.] in the latter part of the last century. The only two not there were my uncles, Cecil and Somerville, who had died many years ago. They talked of 338

many of the pranks they played on people and about their lives, and how life had treated them. In spite of the setbacks and sorrows, financial and otherwise which most of them had suffered, they talked much of the joys and happinesses of their lives. Elizabeth had got together somehow a wonderful lunch and I found some champagne so we toasted my father in good heart, and our two children Georgina and Johnny joined us, and wondered what it was all about, and soon became great favourites with the uncles who all loved children. A fine team they were, apart from my father and Aunt Addie who were just a under 6 foot, all were over. Margaret Rutherford, absolutely charming as ever, thoroughly enjoyed the party and said this is really the old England. After lunch Uncle George thought he would give a song which he started, but was not encouraged by his son Stringer! Lots of laughter from everybody, then after lots more talk and laughter, they all lay down for a little sleep, some on beds upstairs and some on deck chairs on the verandah, for it was a lovely hot summer’s day. It was a great day organised at Elizabeth’s suggestion and one that I know well gave enormous pleasure to my father and to his brothers and sisters. Old father was quite overcome with emotion at the end of the party when we saw them off at Merstham station, or went away in a car which somehow Stringer had hired for the occasion. This was the this was the last time I saw my Aunt Addie and Uncle George for they died fairly soon afterwards. I saw Uncle Jim once or twice later and also just a few days before he died in a hospital at Stroud. The family never lacked courage. They were all alike in this respect and looked at life with an unflinching eye. They had many traits in common, hot tempers perhaps, a bit excitable, very warm hearted, never bore grudges and above all were devoted to children and animals. What good uncles and aunts they always were to us children, many times the nice golden sovereigns or ten-shilling pieces, and many treats and presents, were we the happy recipients. Lady Normanby paid us a visit at Merstham which gave very great pleasure. She enjoyed the quiet life there and talking over with Elizabeth the many problems she had at Mulgrave and elsewhere to meet and find solutions. Well, the war was over and we had to meet the staggeringly gigantic problems of turning over from a war economy which of all the participants was, in this country, the most highly efficient and organised of all, to a peace economy. The German war effort though enormous does not bear comparison with ours for efficiency and getting the maximum out of the people and their country. We owed much to Lord Hankey and his Cabinet and CID Secretariat who did all the spade work and provided the organisation for a nation totally committed to war. One felt I think perhaps above all a feeling of relief, I suppose, that one had survived it. Many of one’s friends had been killed or died. My sister Jane and her fine son David had gone, but we were still a complete family. Oswald was recovering and wondering how to run the affairs at Mulgrave which Lady Normandy had turned over to him. Income tax was still 10 shillings [50p.] in the pound and nobody had anything to spare. In fact, I think everybody one met was considering how they could reduce their pre-war mode and standard of living to fit into post-war conditions. 339

There was a very strong egalitarian mood in England, but it did not go quite as far as saying ‘Jack is as good or better than his master’. Probably the reason for this was that the leadership, both in military fields in the broadest sense, and in the political field, was demonstrably first rate. Who could have had a better and more competent food minister than Lord Woolton and his ‘radio Doctor’ (Dr Hill). The figure of Ernie Bevin towered above many of his colleagues because he inspired folk to put their best foot forward. There was none yet of that spirit portrayed in the film ‘I’m all right Jack’ which was to bedevil the underlying spirit in this country in postwar years. Rationing and the hundred and one war restrictions suddenly became very irksome. Everything was controlled, petrol for one’s car very hard to come by, food, clothes, fuel etc. very strictly rationed. It was becoming clear that these would not evaporate overnight, and in fact were likely to last many years. Our economic position was pretty desperate, we had spent all our capital in the war effort and were importing vastly greater substance in value than we were exporting. We were in large measure being financed by America. We had a Government in power many of whom had responsibility in the war and knew the facts of life, but there was also a vocal section of woolly-headed Fabians who were saying Utopia was round the corner, if we had the courage to grasp it and so on. Georgina and Anne Sophia at To a service like ours which is in some ways steeped in tradition, the proposals of our new Merstham. rulers left a wry taste in our mouths. Discipline and leadership were perhaps the prime internal problems of the service and there were very many things which required changing if true and wholehearted leadership was to prevail. One must always remember that the King’s Regulations and Admiralty Instructions are little more than the framework within which true leadership must be exercised. But much was required to be done to improve the conditions on board ship in which seamen lived. But the autumn of 1945 passed quickly and we started to get the garden into shape at Greenacre and commissioned the hard tennis court. Our two Khaki Campbell ducks were a boon and an asset, and then we brought some dogs into our family, two little dachshunds Dachsie and Dainty who were both great characters. They used to accompany the pram on its walks. We had a variety of governesses-cum-mother’s helps who lived with us. Perhaps the most efficient was a Swiss girl who had been stranded here in the war, and maybe one of the nicest, Sheila O’Brien, who later became a nun. My father continued in good spirits and more than once told us how thankful he was to have preserved Coglan House and property for me. He was very very hard up with the present high rate of taxation but by strict frugality he kept going with the minimum expenditure of capital. 340
End of volume 4 341

Postscript: This copy of WWD’s memoir ends here, in an almost elegiac tone reflecting the somewhat mixed feelings that emerged at the end of hostilities and the need to deal with the huge problems facing the country in a very different geopolitical environment. Interested readers will have to read the original photocopied script to follow WWD’s memoir further. The family acquired its first permanent home after the death of WWD’s father in 1946. We arrived at Coglan House in Longhope, Glos., in the winter of 1946-47 during the harshest weather of many years. ED slipped and broke her wrist, adding to the difficulties. But a large vegetable garden, chickens, and an annually replaced pig (always called Appleblossom), kept the family going. After 1945 WWD continued to have a very successful naval career, and the succeeding volumes recount his time at the Admiralty, in Malta and the Mediterranean, at the Admiralty again and finally as C-in-C of the Home Fleet and C-in-C of Eastern Atlantic Fleet, working at the centre of the NATO Alliance, together with the many shifts and turns of strategy which followed on the Second World War. The very top post of First Sea Lord of the Navy eluded him, and Admiral Sir Caspar John was chosen instead. Retirement in 1960 was extremely busy with numerous local and public commitments in Gloucestershire. He continued to pursue his love and interest in science through the Royal Institution in London, including serving as Treasurer 1960-1971, where his friends included Sir Lawrence Bragg, crystallographer, and Sir George Porter, chemist and nano-scientist. HMS Mauritius was decommissioned in 1952 and placed in reserve until sold for scrap and broken up in 1965. The ships crew association had at least one reunion in the 1970s attended by WWD. Quite a number of former crew members came to his funeral in October 1987. Looking back in March 1980 in some brief ’Random Recollections’, he mused as to whether he had made mistakes or pursued hares down blind alleys. On the whole he thought ‘not many’ and ended by writing that he ‘had a tremendous run of good luck in an exceptionally enjoyable career, for which I owe the Navy everything’. SF and JD May 2026 Farewell to the Navy, 1960. 343
